First things first...For those that say this is similar to Gabriel Knight......get your fu**ing head examined. There is absolutely no comparison.
I love adventure games. My father got me hooked on them when I was little....I remember as a kid I would help him (or try to) solve the old sierra games. I feel like a veteran in this genre...with that being said..........
Kathy Rain does not live up to my personal standards of what I believe an adventure game should be. Its not terrible......but its not good either. Those that have different standards than me will obviously disagree.
One of the main problems is the story and lets be honest, thats what makes or breaks an adventure game. The story feels forced.....like the writers♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the story into this game. As the story progressed I found myself becoming more disappointed than excited. It is supposed to be set in the 90's and other than the story telling me it was 1995. I didn't feel any connection to that decade whatsoever. The protagonist, Kathy Rain, is a cardboard cut out of the classic 90's rebellious edgy teen with a bleeding heart. Kathy didn't feel like a real character but more of a stereotype of what some idiot writer had in mind for the story.
The story starts off with Kathy coming into her dorm drunk and wanting to sleep it off.  Then Emily, her little stereotypical Christian roommate, tells her she has been doing research on Kathy's hometown because..the writers needed the story to advance and tells her she found out that a man, Joseph Rain had died recently. This is her grandfather and despite being gone for 15 years she decides to attend the funeral and start doing investigations......because the writers needed the story to advance. The games handles story progression this way.... ALL......THE..... ♥♥♥♥**G..... TIME.....
The puzzles are even worse than the story.....If you are looking for challenging puzzles....Try grabbing a brick and smashing it to your head about 5 times before you play this game. The swelling of your brain might make them more difficult to solve.
All of the characters in this game are cardboard cutouts of stereotypes. This is why you don't get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ writers to make your game.
I won't reveal any spoilers but....the ending didnt answer any questions......fortunatly the story sucked so badly that I didnt care.
Note: I fell asleep playing this game...so the hours spent on this game can be misleading. The game can be completed in 6-7 hours. (no walkthroughs)

This game is pretty short. I'm generally a slow player, and I was able to complete this game in one runthrough over the course of 5 hours. Like a good book, I just couldn't put it down! The fantastic pixel art drew me in, and the plot kept me playing. Kathy suffers a little bit from "edgy grrrrrl" syndrome, but she's still a compelling, likeable character (at least to me). While a few of the plot twists were predictable, others took me completely by surprise.
If you're looking for a game with extremely challenging puzzles, this probably isn't the game for you. With the exception of one of the puzzles in the finale, I found most of the puzzles easy, and I am NOT good at puzzle games. Solving the puzzles still felt very rewarding, though, and most of them weren't tedious or annoying. The only exception is the "computer" portion of the game, which annoyed me solely because of how often I had to switch the computer off, do something else, then turn it on again, rinse and repeat.
If you're looking for a short game with a good mystery and satisfying puzzles, I highly recommend Kathy Rain.

Kathy Rain plays out splendidly as an investigation into the death of a family member uncovers far more than one could have ever bargained for. Coming out at about 7-10 hours of gameplay providing you take the time to enjoy the game and your surroundings, there's much joy to be had in this title. Some of the visuals are captivating and the sordid and mysterious plot is beautifully embellished by an apposite soundtrack, leading to some real thrills and shivers as you plunge deeper into the depths of what is a dark and harrowing tale (recommend playing alone and during the night for the full impact of the final third of the game, which had me feeling uneasy).
The difficulty of the game is moderate and some of the puzzles will definitely keep you occupied for a while, but the main meat of the game is in the dialogue and examination of objects in order to find new leads and destinations in your quest to find out more about the death of Kathy Rain's grandfather. In that sense, you must be observant and vigilant, though Kathy does a good job of reminding you of what reminds her of what (which might annoy some of the more hardcore adventure nuts).
The game does lack a little richness visually and is a bit light on locations, suggesting that the team couldn't produce a whole lot of art for the game. The locations that do exist are used efficiently and thoroughly, though there are no animations present in the backdrops. Looking at a completely still body of water as though I'm just looking at a painting made one location seem lifeless. However, there are a few locations in this game that are truly beautiful, with one in particular having multiple weather/sky backdrops -- a nice touch. On the whole though, the game feels still and that works far less well for outdoor locations than indoor locations.
7.5 out of 10. Recommended.

I've been a follower of the UBERMOSH series for a while and when I heard that Vol.3 was out, I immediately had to get it.
And it's still just as intense as ever, but now it's moved to the open world, meaning that you're no longer confined to a small area. There isn't any cover so you do have to play this one different tactically. And I like that.
The brainclap introduced in UBERMOSH:BLACK makes a comeback along with several more achievements (I like the addition of the survivor-like achievements as well as the score addition), and the game is still as fast-paced and frantic as ever. And still good fun.
A couple of criticisms though. As much as I absolutely love the soundtrack and how fitting it is, I would love some new tracks so there's more cyberpunk moshing to be had. There is some slowdown when there's a lot going on but neither of these detract from the fun this is.
Yes, some might argue it's more of the same but the open-world arena and the extra challenge presented by a new enemy (they remind me a little of the swarm in SWARMRIDERS in their movements) definitely set it apart from the other entries in the series.
I'm sure there's more to be added to the game but as for some suggestions: perhaps an infinite respawn mode, still within 90 seconds, where you try and gun down as many enemies as possible but perahps there's deductions for using respawns? And maybe some new guns or even more blade moves.
All in all, a highly recommended experience and good for short bursts of fast-paced action. This isn't a game to be played for hours on end but it's good for quick bursts of gameplay.

You’ll unlock all the parts of the map by accomplishing a series of tasks. You have to manage your resources either by picking it up on the map or by making it yourself. Food can be picked from bushes and trees or grown in your fields by your farmers. Trees can be cut for wood, stones and iron can be excavated by your workers. You’ll be making special building like forges to make building tools and whatnot, the usual drill..
The graphics are very cute and detailed but it’s too bad that we can’t zoom back as the camera is really too close. You can use the arrow keys on your keyboard to quickly move around your map. You’ll trade merchandises using a boat, I got attacked by pirates and had to fight them in an Angry Birds mini game! It’s rather well done and fun. You'll unlock more levels of that mini game by building a fort.
The game is very slow compared to other similar ones. Money required is pretty high and your way of making it pretty low so it will be a looooong grind. Expect to keep the game running on itself for hours. The popup messages about the trading prices will constantly pause the game, it’s annoying as they’re pretty common. I don’t understand why they haven’t chosen to let the game run when quit considering the low speed of production.
The game also lacks personality: i.e. In The Happy Hereafter there’s a lot of humor, in Virtual Villagers there’s mysteries and surprises to discover. Those games craft charm and you do eventually get attached to your village. Here there’s nothing beyond the trading messages and the very empty texts of build this or that, point.
TL:DR the game is nice but gets dull, only buy the game in a sale so you won’t regret it. Or buy another one!
Similar games: The Happy Hereafter on Steam, All My Gods and Hero of the Kingdom games.. Outside Steam:  the Virtual Villagers games, Wild Tribe, The Island Castaway games, Gemini Lost, Farm Tribe, Wandering Willows.

I want to recommend the game for anyone who likes Age of Empires, Empire Earth, KKND, Starcraft, other oldschool/cult RTS games.
What makes Cossacks unique?
* Almost unlimited number of units with no lags (very high number that will not be achieved if you want to enjoy this game).
* Many nations, so you wouldn't get tired of this game easily.
* Tactics. Depends on your mastery, you can win a battle with less forces with perfect tactics, e.g. use cavalry against unprotected gunners, use cannons, avoid your army being destroyed by cannons, etc. Also tactics are realistic, so you do what generals did in 17th/18th centuries, it is not some sort of exploit of the game and its bugs.
* Very large maps. That is important for realism, because the war few centuries ago was about moving forces just in a right time and place.
* Different levels of difficulty. It is not easy to beat 7 highest level AI. It is not even easy to beat 1 highest level AI. Also there is multiplayer (but it can be too difficult for newbies).
* Role playing campains. But the role isn't as a unit as in Warcraft for example. It is as a ruler and warlord. I didn't play campains a lot, but my father did.
* Suitable for adults. Suitable for kids.
* Intuition works ok. So you can start the game and enjoy, you don't have to read tricks about this game (e.g. placing storehouse below the resources slightly reduce time to bring resourses to it - there are some maniacs in mutiplayer who know all this stuff).
* I have an old PC and almost every game crashes, but Cossacks don't.

This is really hard for me.  This game has charm, fun references to famous classics, beautiful art, interesting gameplay ideas and it belongs to one of my favorite genres (Metroidvania).  But for the life of me, I just can't recommend it.  See the gameplay time I have on record?  I can assure you, without any shadow of a doubt, that more than half of it has been spent losing and retrying.  This game starts great, but at some point it becomes brutally difficult.
Now, being fair here, the basic portion of the game is easy enough.  The game only becomes harder when you try to find extras and complete challenges.  You might say I shouldn't complain then, but see... this is a Metroidvania.  Its entire premise as a genre is to make exploration fun.  And this game turns exploration into an exercise in maddening frustration.  This should be the best part of the game, and instead it's so bad in comparison to the rest that you'd swear this game started as two different ones that at some point were mashed together for whatever unexplained reason.
See, the more you advance the more abilities you unlock.  That's par for the course for the genre, and it's one of the most fun parts of these games.  The problem is that, unlike for all the other games in the genre, all your abilities are available at the same time.  That might seem like a good thing at first, except that now you're forced to remember an alarmingly large amount of special moves, because the game will force you to juggle many abilities at the same time to advance through many areas, which becomes even worse when you have to deal with Super Meat Boy -like scenery.
I mean, a game like Super Meat Boy is fun because while it offers a challenge it relies on the simplicity of the controls.  Here you have to deal with the challenge while mastering an increasingly complex set of moves.  This becomes frustrating really fast and it's exacerbated by the fact that the controls are not particularly responsive.  Push Up and the game will do Left instead.  That's not a problem in the middle of walking, but it's definitely a problem when you're trying to do a special move and the game does a different one instead, which will happen half of the time.
I can't help but think that most of the positive reviews come from people who don't try to explore in the game, or that never actually bothered to try and finish it.  Or people that have lots of free time so they don't care how much they lose.  Looking at the game's stats, I think it's quite telling that barely over 15% of the people have defeated the last boss.  Clearly most people are giving up way earlier.
I have to be as fair as I can here.  Yes, I had a lot of fun with the game, but the frustration has severely trumped it.  That's why I can't recommend it, unless you're either unemployed with lots and lots of time to waste and nothing else to play.

So I was playing Salt and Sancruary and then decided to take a break with something a little more colourful and light-hearted. This is the story about me desperately trying to love Guacamelee but in the end ragequitting and uninstalling the game altogether just before the last two bosses.
I rate it positive because I hope you, whoever you are, are just better than me in platformers of this sort. Probably, I was just not up to the challenge or whatever.
I have both the original and Turbo Championship but decided to start from the original to be able to appreciate the improvements of Turbo Championship. If I ever want to play this again, that is.
I love the game's artstyle, although the colour-flashing when acquiring a new ability makes me slightly uncomfortable despite having no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. Music doesn't get too repetitive and adds to the overall character of the game. The story is simple but fun, I don't have any particular complaints about any of that stuff.
To the juicy parts now. Mechanics. I am fairly experienced with platformers and metroidvanias of different sorts and I'm not even that bad at them. Certainly, not a pro, but not that bad either. But the platforming elemets of Guacamelee made me ragequit more times than with any other game in my whole life. I think, it's because precision of the platforming is not high enough, Even after some time you cannot really estimate whether you'd be able to reach that platform with the double jump or you'd have to use the uppercut. Sometimes you reach a platform and sometimes you don't - even if it is one and the same spot and you perform exactly one and the same jump. I have to admit, I am spoilt by Ori and the Blind Forest that for me has what can be called ideal platforming where you just jump and you know for certain what the outcome will be.
The inconsistency of Guacamelee was killing me more than anything else. You can jump and reach the platform just slightly - and the game just pulls you up and you're fine. Another time you most certainly reach it but the game is like NOPE and you go all the way down the Tule Tree. Between-the-worlds mechanic is actually very cool as an idea but combine it with inconsistency and lack of precision - and it's just hell. You have to press every button in a very certain fracture of a second or start again from the bottom. By the way, the hitbox of spikes is ridiculous. I would prefer them to have been drawn bigger to see the danger for sure than to be impaled by their invisible extensions.
For the amount of actions that have to be performed in a tight sequence, the game is not very responsive and can ignore your button pushing fairly often. When you have to go like jump-jump again-charge-uppercut to, let's say, reach another platform, be prepared that your uppercut, although pushed correctly, can be just ignored by the game or performed too late. So you have to start again.
The sheer amount of my frustration was unfathomable. The first game ever I ragequitted every single time after a short session. I struggled for like 5 hours and decided that since it does not make me happy and it's not fun anymore but a tedious frustrating ordeal where you have to try certain sections over and over again because the game is like 'whatever, this time you didn't reach', I uninstalled it dispite being so close to the end. Then I went on YouTube and watched a playthrough to discover that you can reach the True Ending only if you found every piece of a certain item. Also sacrificed your mental health, your soul and 3 controllers, apparently. Nope, thanks.
I wanted to love this game so much but I just couldn't. At the same time I don't want to rate it negative because I think the game has a lot of work put into it and for some people it certainly works the way it's supposed to. Since Steam does not have 'neutral', I'll rate it positive.

I bought the game on sale for cheap, but even then, I'm having trouble justifying the amount of time I'm spending for what I'm experiencing. The game consists of many, impressive pieces of artwork, which someone appears to have rather hastily thrown into a 2-D game creation suite and tried to make puzzles around. Animations are jagged and robotic, navigation is akward, and the only true physics objects are horrible beige lines that have no detail at all, and look like someone drew on the artwork with MS Paint. The puzzles often mean either pixel-hunting or memory games, with a little actual problem solving thrown in later on in the game. As a result, if you're someone not particularly good at picking out little details like I am, you'll find yourself often opening up the journal to find hints as to what to do next. Unfortunately, apart from having to solve what turns into an extremely dull puzzle to get to the journal in the first place, it tends to point out only the most obvious aspects of what you're supposed to do, without going into any detail or even a written explanation. By this point, it might seem obvious to open up a walkthrough, and keep switching tabs to that every so often. By that point, however, I might as well have not bought the game at all, and have just watched a youtube walkthrough. In fact, that's how I'd reccomend playing this game. Look up a full, silent-player walkthrough on youtube, and enjoy the art and music without any of the actual, awful game. Disclaimer: did not finish game. Decided to watch walkthrough instead when getting hopelessly stuck for the fourth time on the wooden log level.

Like all games from Amanita, Samorost 3 relies on its stunning presentation and non-verbal communication. The hand-drawn alien landscapes look gorgeous and the point ‘n’ click puzzles lack all kinds of written or spoken text, letting the players immerse themselves in this world of great imagination.
Amanita Design is famous for their fantasy-rich adventure games, where the imagination is always a more important aspect in creating entire alien worlds than any kind of plausibility. Therefore, Samorost 3 may be a sequel, but it is still a unique world anyone can enjoy.
Unlike most Amanita games, Samorost 3 has a defined storyline, one that revolves around the concept of musical harmony. It starts with the gnome we met in the previous Samorost titles finding a mysterious flute fallen from the sky, and throughout his journey, we learn how important harmony can be, as we travel form planet to planet, mending the wounds left on these strange ecosystems by a rogue musician monk.
The lack of text, as usual, can be a big obstacle for those who are not used to Anamita games, but luckily, most of the plot-related puzzles are straightforward or require basic trial and error. (Finding the secrets… well, that is a different story.) The rudimentary physics engine’s role in some puzzles may hold a few surprises though.
Still, in the end, the gameplay is just a means to an end: an end to take in the stunning scenery and to enjoy the simple, yet somehow deep story until we finally guide the little gnome home for some well-earned rest—both for him and for us—after a job well done.

Kathy Rain plays out splendidly as an investigation into the death of a family member uncovers far more than one could have ever bargained for. Coming out at about 7-10 hours of gameplay providing you take the time to enjoy the game and your surroundings, there's much joy to be had in this title. Some of the visuals are captivating and the sordid and mysterious plot is beautifully embellished by an apposite soundtrack, leading to some real thrills and shivers as you plunge deeper into the depths of what is a dark and harrowing tale (recommend playing alone and during the night for the full impact of the final third of the game, which had me feeling uneasy).
The difficulty of the game is moderate and some of the puzzles will definitely keep you occupied for a while, but the main meat of the game is in the dialogue and examination of objects in order to find new leads and destinations in your quest to find out more about the death of Kathy Rain's grandfather. In that sense, you must be observant and vigilant, though Kathy does a good job of reminding you of what reminds her of what (which might annoy some of the more hardcore adventure nuts).
The game does lack a little richness visually and is a bit light on locations, suggesting that the team couldn't produce a whole lot of art for the game. The locations that do exist are used efficiently and thoroughly, though there are no animations present in the backdrops. Looking at a completely still body of water as though I'm just looking at a painting made one location seem lifeless. However, there are a few locations in this game that are truly beautiful, with one in particular having multiple weather/sky backdrops -- a nice touch. On the whole though, the game feels still and that works far less well for outdoor locations than indoor locations.

Ugh Kathy Rain.  A game that is supposed to be following in the footsteps of Laura Bow, at least I’m pretty sure I read that somewhere.  Like Laura Bow you start out in College as a journalism major, unlike Laura Bow you seem to be a punk biker who is a sociopath.  At the end of the day though I quite liked the character of Kathy Rain and the other major character Eileen.  Their voice acting, what little there is, is good.  Whoever voices Kathy does a good job and the same goes for Eileen.  Since you do hear their voices the most, it’s pretty important for them to be pleasing.  That was one of the big problems with games like Gabriel Knight, Knight’s voice drove me nuts.  It was just awful.  The same goes for Laura Bow.  However, I can’t recommend this game too much is simply bad in it.
Like that’s probably all the good stuff.  If a lot of stuff was good, I’d recommend the game, but most of it is quite bad.  So lets go with puzzles.  The game basically has very very very easy puzzles.  Which I guess would be fine, except I think they are also bad.  One puzzle required me to pick up a thermometer, which I attempted already pick up earlier in the game and couldn’t.  No dialogue or really anything lead me to think that later in the game I could now pick it up.  It’s the one puzzle I had to look online for a solution to.  Adventure games need to stop this, either let me pick up every single item I need when I see it, or I guess maybe MAYBE if you heavily stress the fact by the character saying something like, “oh I really need to get a thermometer, I think I saw one earlier I need to go back and get it.”  Then that MIGHT be acceptable.  Otherwise, never do this ever!  Almost every puzzle in this game can be solved in the area you are in, normally I would say this is fine, the problem here is that the areas are so small that it takes seconds to figure out puzzles.  That being said I guess I should give props to the game for having all the puzzles basically be logic puzzles as opposed to random math puzzles like a lot of adventure games do and which I hate.
Before getting into the story, I have to just add that one major problem with the game is the length.  It’s a big problem.  There are so few areas to explore.  Each area, might only have one or two screens to it.  You don’t really feel like you are exploring at all, which imo is critical in an adventure game.  The game also simply ends way too fast.  I suppose it’s possible to tell a short story, this game however fails at it.  There wasn’t any real time to get to know characters or have any feel for the town or even really to ponder what is going on in the game.  I’d say it feels more like watching a movie then playing a game, which I know a lot of games do these days, but I don’t like that.
However, the biggest problem is the story and I’m just going to count everything after this as spoilers.
Sigh, I was really hoping for a new Laura Bow style murder mystery, instead I got a mediocre horror story.  If you want to make a 10-12 hour Kathy Rain murder mystery with Eileen as her partner/girlfriend I would be up for that.  Otherwise…no…just no.

Pleasantly surprised by this title.  You play a young, spunky lady by the name of Kathy Rain.  Kathy was probably my favorite part about the game.  Her voice actress did a great job, and her personality is fun. The game is a point-and-click which I haven't played in quite a while.  It did a great job at feeling retro/nostalgic yet keeping it modern in ways.  I could see others saying that this game is nothing new or not innovative.  But, it doesn't need to, in my opinion.  The story is great.  Almost a Twin Peaks-esque vibe that things are just mysterious enough to keep you engaged.  There are just enough unanswered questions to keep you playing.  The game is somewhat on the short side, but I feel it was a reasonable length.  It didn't overstay its welcome and kept things concise. Definitely recommend for anyone looking for a fun point-and-click game!

This is a great little game, and very reminiscent of Virutal Villagers series from 10(?) years ago.  The Promised Land adds some new features like trading, and a pirates Angry Birds mini-game.  The one big change is that The Promised Land isn't a "virtual" game where things run even when the game isn't being played.  This aspect of Virtual Villagers caused me some major headaches and caused me to have to restart more than once.
In short, it's nice to play after work if you have some time to burn.  The great thing about it is that it is truly a casual game.  Got 15 minutes?  You can play for 15 minutes and quit.  Want to play a marathon session?  Great!  Do it.  Everything will be right as it was when you turned the game off.
I've played now for about 7 hours (EDIT:  I won the game at around 11 hours of playtime) and think I'm about 40% of the way through the game (judging by the buildings, upgrades, and research I've got compared to what I could have).  The one ding I have against it is that I'm starting to get to the middle of the game where you don't have a lot to do except set it to autopilot as you wait for the research points needed for a new tech, or the materials needed for the next building.
But definitely worth a full price purchase of $7.  Even better if you get it on sale!

I bought this game during a sale AND in a bundle, so extremely cheap. Then other games got in the way and forgot about it for a while. When I eventually installed it without re-reading its description, I was expecting a typical time/resource management like the rest in the bundle.
What a pleasant surprise it was to find that it was a city builder, as I love those! Granted, it's not a city but a colony, but the game has more depth than what I expected. Every inhabitant has a preferred task and a task she/he hates, and it's quite fun to concile "personal" preferences with the resources you need to progress. The first moments spent working in a task "locks" the inhabitant into that role (up until you build the school, that is) so you might want to keep that little one away from an undesired profession until he/she gains his/her first star (after that, she/he will just be bad at doing things not from her/his profession). Personally I think one Builder and 2 Scientists are enough for the entire game.
There are a few timed quests, but they're extremely easy to do without re-allocating too many people. The rest you can take as much time as you need to complete. And there's the pirates mini-game (basically Angry Birds with pirates), which I didn't enjoy as much as the main game.
But the main game, well... I enjoyed it so much, that as soon as I beat it I started a new game. And I'll most likely play it again in a few months.
It's relaxing and fun, and for less than half a buck it was most likely the best purchase I've made in years.

username: Thief 2 is the best stealth game
text:
Man do I love the Hitman series. Although the Thief series is my favorite stealth games, this series comes close 2nd(For me it ties with Splinter Cell). Let me get this out of the way, Hitman Blood Money is one of THE best stealth games out there. It's the Chaos Theory of Hitman, where everything has improved to the point of almost perfection. Each mission gives you a TON of options on how to assassinate your targets. You can go through a contract without anyone knowing you where there! You can do a contract without using a disguise! You can go through a contract only using your bare fists! It's up to YOU!
Speaking of missions, each mission is highly unique; a cocaine lab built as a mansion, a opera house, a neighborhood street, and more! The soundtrack for each mission is excellent and perfectly sets the mood. The graphics are quite nice too!
My only gripes are; the first and last levels. The first level is obviously a tutorial. But it's not a good one. It's linear as balls (cough Absolution cough) and unless you spam distractions, it wants you to kill quite a few guards. It almosts gives a false impression on the Hitman series, instead of giving numeral stealthly options to snuff out your target, it wants you to blast your way through without so much as an alternate route. The last level kinda has the same problem, but not as bad.
Besides those levels, any fan of stealth and bald people will HIGHLY enjoy this masterpiece of stealth assassinating gameplay!
10 out of ten

Cossacks 3 is an interesting game with awesome points and poor points and problems I never EVER thought would've been a problem. Let's start.
Cossacks 3 is the third installment in the cossacks series, and is essentially an updated version of the first cossacks game, with updated graphics, a new engine and fancy animations. It has a variety of civilisations with semi different playstyles depending on which one you pick.
There isn't really a 'campaign' of sorts, but more.. short insights. 5 chapter campaigns for certain factions, and one chapter scenarios are thrown in there too. These can vary in mechanics and civs, in addition to adding interesting limitations such as a time limit before enemy reinforcements, or trading to obtain coal via caravans. It works as well as you'd expect, but I feel it could've been made smoother.
Multiplayer I haven't touched, and unless new content forces me to play it or my friends buy the game, It'll stay that way.
The ingame editor is poor by normal standards. It's fun, since you actually have real time editing. You can change unit positions, create formations and even manually build all your faction buildings with peasants. There are downsides though. The map is small, and there's no way to change it. You can't put down any resources, or edit the terrain in any fashion. You're stuck with a plain green which in comparison to large cityscapes, can get annoying quickly. There's no trigger editing or creation for that matter either. You're essentially in a sandbox with free reigns on spawning absurd quantities of units and hurling them at eachother like a kid with action figures, until you get bored.
Here are a couple annoying bugs and problems I've found!
- Saving lags to a frankly insulting degree, and I have to wait on each letter I type before I can add another, so even typing something like "bored" as a savename can take up to 5 seconds to even finish typing, let alone actually saving.
- In missions where you have formations of units that are less than a normal formation, they will quite happily crash your entire game. And good luck saving beforehand, for above reasons. The only way I found of fixing it is by dissolving the formation
- In the editor/sandbox mode upon placing down any unit of any kind, the game will lag, as if suddenly surprised that you did anything besides stare at a chunk of grass. If you put down peasants and try building with them, 9/10 you will crash, because it can barely handle a unit being put down, and now you're trying to actually build. You'd think it was an editor or sandbox with which to build forts and nuke said forts with hundreds of cannons.
All in all, it is a good game. It's by absolutely no stretch of the imagination a great game, and the fact I can't speed the damn game up beyond a slightly fast nomal speed is annoying since I can do that in cossacks 1. However, it's still fun, and even with these gripes I keep coming back to the game, so it must have something going for it, or else I'm just a masochist that loves annihilating bowmen with squadrons of cannon, mortar and maybe a few thousand howitzers.
5/10, will go up to 7/10 and above if the ingame sandbox/editor actually becomes an editor, since the actual editor is confusing, difficult to use and couldn't be more bland if they tried. Also the bugs and problems could be fixed too.. one at a time.

Guacamelee is a fun 2D adventure platforming game with different fighting moves and a variety of enemies and bosses. The game is very heavily based on Mexican culture. You play as Juan, a luchador fighter. He is trying to rescue the president’s daughter who he also is in love with. Across your travels you’ll unlock different fighting moves that also double as a different way to get around the levels. This also allows you to get to certain chests to increase your health and stamina meters.
Gameplay is fairly straightforward. Advance through the levels and locations while fighting off enemies and the occasional boss. It will take some time to get used to using all of your attacks but the more fluid you get, the quicker you can kill the enemies. You are also searching for life and stamina chests that are scattered around the levels. Getting 3 of each will grant you a boost in health of stamina.
The characters and NPC’s are all well done. Even though there is no voice acting in the game, each character had their own voice in my head. They are fleshed out well enough for this type of game. The NPC’s may also contain side quests. The dialog is well done and is pretty tongue in cheek.
Graphics and music are unique. The art style of the game is very minimalistic and extremely colorful. They nailed the Mexican feel they were going for.
. You’ll be fumbling around on the keyboard very quickly.
Controls are generally ok, but probably is one of my few gripes with the game. They seem floaty and unpredictable at times. Platforming with narrow areas to jump on really shows this. I feel they could have been tighter.
Two other gripes deal with fighting. First is the recovery time after getting hit. It’s too short and can lead to some combo attacks from the enemies that feels cheap. Second, certain enemies seem to deal way too much damage. (The enemy with multiple swords comes to mind)

+Imprecise controls
+Recovery time from getting hit

The last Metroidvania game I played (not saying which, as it doesn't matter in this review) left an egregiously terrible first impression of the genre for me. Afterwards, my friend's like "Check out this game" and I'm like "oh, great. Another Metroidvania game." So I picked it up on sale, deciding to give it a try to see whether I'd enjoy it or just quickly get a refund.
In short, I don't think I'm ever gonna ask for a refund for Guacamelee.
When playing this game, I noticed many things that the developers did right about this game that makes it a fair and enjoyable experience to play. For example, when you get a new move to use, the tutorial goat (it makes sense in context) briefly explains the buttons and how it works, then the immediate surroundings provide a safe environment to practice the application of said move before applying it - as well as other moves you've learned prior - to traverse whatever map/dungeon/etc you're going through, as well as using the move in combat. The game does everything in its power to adequately prepare you for the upcoming trials it will throw at you while refusing to hold your hand. That, to me, is excellent game design.
The combat is based around comboing enemies, and you can even throw enemies into enemies to continue your combo; not once do I ever feel like I'm button mashing, and after seeing what sort of ludicrous combo I've done (shown in the top right) as well as the game rewarding you for such things, it just feels like I'm kicking♥♥♥♥♥all the time.
Another thing that makes Guacamelee stand out is the reference to other games (as well as memes) scattered about in the background, and even in the NPC dialogue. Inclusion of such passive easter eggs definitely add to the game's overall enjoyability. The soundtrack is dynamic (and fantastic), the map's puzzles are very clever and well-thought out, and there's many a bilingual bonus for those (like me) who have studied and/or speak Spanish, although I'd like to stress that you can completely enjoy this game without knowing any Spanish at all.
In conclusion, Guacamelee is very well designed, immersive and entertaining to play. I would like to point out that a controller is recommended (I use an Xbox 360 Afterglow USB controller and it works just fine), but keyboard controls can be remapped to whatever you desire.

I really wanted to like this game, I tried very hard to see what the developers were going for, but there are just way too many baffling design decisions.  The positive for me, the humor was very good, it clearly had overlap with the borderlands development.  The mission were fun, if repetitive, and I don't mean in how many times you repeat each mission.  The characters were unique in many cases, and I liked the progression style.
The negative for me, first, and I can't stress this enough, the Operations are 3 player only, the rest of the coop portion is 4 player at least.  To say that makes no sense is an enormous understatement, and I feel robbed for my $29 or whatever I spent.  I could probably have read carefully and noticed this, I accept my responsibility, but me and my 3 friends expected to be able to play this content, but for no logical reason they decided just 3 for these.
I hope you like doing the same things, over and over and over, because you will.  Every mission reuses the same ideas, with no variety.  Horde mode, Horde mode, Horde mode, they use this to death.   Only one presents a challenge, and then only on the hardest difficulty, the rest are trivial if you have 2 or more players.  Some missions start off extremely hard, just to become boringly easy.
By the time you play this game a few weeks you will be sick to death of the movie that plays before every mission.. just one, one movie, not 3 they cycle through, and no way to turn it off.
Voice chat is one of the laziest implimentations I have ever seen.  It functions most of the time, sometimes it goes crazy for no reason.  But every time a cut scene plays while you are loading or exiting the missions, all the voice chat stops, for no reason, again.
A ton of information is made far to difficult to access and the menu's are extremely clunky.
Lastly and far more important, this is a Free to Play Game, that's what it is, they decided to charge full price for it, and then some kind of half F2P model, but it was clearly designed with a F2P game model.  This is really unacceptable.
Gearbox, you have a lot of things I like about you, but you have lost me as a fan with this one and your recent other releases.  You were close with Battleborn, I really wanted to like it, it has a lot to like, but some of the sins are unforgivable.

I really want to recommend this game 100% but unfortunately it has some issues in my opinion. First off, the graphic is really good. The pixel art is nice and full of detail. The protaganist is charming even if she suffers from I'm-a-woman-hear me-roar and I-don't-need-no-man attitude from time to time. The voice acting is excellent, and so is the music. The music together with the 90s setting sets the atmosphere - Twin Peaks anyone?
The gameplay is also fun. It has the traditional point & click gameplay in which you combine different objects to eventually pass a puzzle and advance the story. It also has this intriguing detective mechanic to the game that is really fun. You have to find clues in any way possible, then you use these clues that you have collected to ask other characters about the case. It works really well, and most of the time the people you talk to will have something interesting to say about the things you ask about. At times it really feels like you are doing true detective work. Though, the game isn't too hard. Most of the puzzles has a logical solution, but it requires you to pay attention to the details.
But... adventure games lives and dies on its story. The story in Kathy Rain is really good, well, at least 75% of the game. I don't want to go into spoilers here, but right from the start you get that whatever went down in this small town is not totally natural. I have no problem with that, it actually enhances the story since I love that out-of-this-world stuff. The problem comes at the end, or near to it. The game and story has an actual finish, but it feels really unsatisfying. Like I said, I don't want to spoil anything, but there is way too many lose ends, and nothing about the story is really explained. Sure, stuff can be left up to the consumer to draw his own conclusions, but there is nothing to draw from here. Stuff just seem to happen at random and then it ends. Really disappointing since the road up to that point was great. Maybe, I'm just stupid though and didn't get it :)
Anyway. I still recommend the game because it's a nice experience, it's just that the story suffers, to me at least. You might not see any faults in it though!

Kathy Rain is a traditional point-n-click adventure/puzzle game. The game is set in the 90's and it has a genuine nostalgic 90's feel. The puzzles in the game are excellent: not only inventory puzzles, but also logic puzzles, words and some number puzzles, lots of variety. Most importantly though the solutions can be found with logic and the balancing is perfect; I never felt lost or needed to hunt down a walkthrough. This is a real quality release, the art, voice acting, music, environments, it's all very well done and detailed. The game has a length of around 6-8 hours, depending on if you get stuck and how much exploration you do.
This is one of the best games I've played in the genre, and I give it extra points for all the 90's and Twin Peaks references. I hope they make a sequel, I'm keen to see more adventures from Kathy Rain. :)

The graphics are clean and the gameplay is simple, but effective. Each level consists of 3 additional goals in a variety of categories (collect certain items, don't kill anyone, kill everyone, etc) which provides some small level of replayability - in some cases, not all three can be achieved in a single playthrough.
The game is fun. Kind of easy, but fun. The only REAL problem I ran into is there were multiple instances where the game did not save progress properly - I beat many levels (in some cases 4 complete "worlds") and the save did not get uploaded to Steam Cloud properly (and it did not keep track of it locally), so I ended up having to redo all that progress. It was quite frustrating. However, for the game itself, it was a good time.
It only takes about 5 hours to complete everything there is to do in the game. Consider that when choosing the price you want to purchase at.

While I admit it has got nice graphics, sound and an interesting gameplay idea, the gameplay itself isn't well enough executed. First of all, those dark creatures are just plain and simple annoying. Then, the game heavily relies on trial&error, expect to die a lot. Annoying, just annoying.
And finally, the bomb mechanic makes the game stupidly easy and takes away any stealth elements. Just a place a bomb, detonate, place a bomb right in the same place, run away and as soon as guards come there: Detonate and they're gone. And that's all. Unfortunately some missions even rely on that, else you won't be able to finish it.
I liked the idea of mechanical-spiders not being destroyed by bombs, but unfortunately, only the very last 2-3 maps rely on them.
It is a really great concept, but just not thought out, how about making guards invincible to bombs? Why don't guards disarm bombs if they run over them?

Dynamite Jack is a stealth game with 'explosive' elements, pun aside this game is really addictive, the first couple of levels might not get you hooked straight away though, but it gets more and more challenging as the game progresses, Overall I highly recommend this game to others, but maybe wait until it gets a discounted price :)

Semi-open world stealth/assassination. The Hitman franchise has made contributions to video games in three ways: the series' signature protagonist (Agent 47), Jespyr Kid's sweeping, epic musical scores and the gameplay. That gameplay in turn consists of two factors: discretion and variety. Variety is simple, but interesting: how to complete the contract? WIth finesse, brute force or some combination of the two? Choose your tools (some of which are upgradable), choose your approach (many of which can be unique to each mission) and do the job however you see fit. The choice is up to the player and the agency offered therein is wonderfully empowering.
The discretion component is perhaps the most intriguing, however. The core of the stealth element in Hitman is not about going unseen, but unnoticed. That subtle but important distinction makes all the difference. Darting from shadow to shadow, timing movement to occur in the blind spots of NPCs can be tense and exciting. There's a very different breeed of anxiety that comes from having to follow the mark into an empty room, execute, hide the body and then leave the scene by calmly walking away like nothing happened. No running around, no lurking near anyone in particular, no being out of place (mechanic in a kitchen, for example), always keeping weapons hidden. In effect, the player is encouraged to take no action that draws ANY kind of unwanted attention. It takes some time to get used to, but it offers an unparalleled thrill. This descretion measure couples with specific methodology and skill to determine ranking title, bonus and a new feature: notoriety. The less discretion used, the more evidence left behind, the more attention Agent 47 draws to himself, the more likely he is to be noticed, which in turn makes it more difficult to complete the contract. This cycle is compelling: your actions (and therefore your decisions) have consequences.
The game is not without flaws, however. AI is terrible: entirely too forgiving at low difficulties, brutally unforgiving at high difficulties and at times logically inconsistent. The in-game menu is unreliable: in two missions, it was entirely inaccessbile. There are stability issues, as well: the game crashed 4 times during a complete playthrough. Firearms are hideously inaccurate: 47 either needs to invest in a better arms dealer or spend some time zeroing his weapons.
On the plot side of the house, "Blood Money" is somewhat wanting. Yes, there is a plot, but it's largely window dressing. The story is not told clearly or well. Unknown clones killing other targets -> vague intrigue involving the CIA -> ICA basically hunted to extinction (which happens exclusively through dialogue in the last two missions with absolutely no foreshadowing). Sometimes, the story is relayed as a tale between characters on the way to a funeral and occurs as cutscenes between missions. But not every mission has a cutscene that involves this overarching story. The developments are muddled and exist to justify level design or mission parameters rather than the other way around. No one plays Hitman for story, but it was disappointing to see such a promising plot derail due to narrative failure. Voice acting is extremely hit or miss, the dialogue is wooden and character development is virtually non-existent.
7/10, one thumb up. For fans of the franchise (or stealth games in general), "Blood Money" is a no-brainer. Also, the soundtrack is g*dd*mned AMAZING.

I installed the game at 10pm, just to try it out as I was in the mood for a casual city (colony) builder.
I finished the game at 9am the next morning! I just couldn't stop playing. That's the best recommendation I can give it.
Pros.
Graphics are cute and well detailed.
The music ranges from good to beautiful.
The sound effects suit the style.
Extremely casual and relaxing game, no stress or pressure here!
Over 10 hours of gameplay for a relatively cheap price.
It scratched the "city builder" itch.
Mini-games keep things fresh.
Solid mobile port with no bugs.
Simple to learn and understand.
Cons.
If you like big strategy city building games, you might be disappointed, everything is very basic, but done well.
The are no screen resolutions in the options. Windowed or full screen.
There's practically no way you can lose. No challenge?
I was disappointed when I completed it (I wanted more! ... or is that a pro?)
Very little replayability.
Overall, there's a research tree, an economy, city building, and resource management but all very simple without a lot of depth and there are mini-games. The game, however, is addictive, keeps you interested and entertained, is extremely well presented, and is value for money. As a casual city builder, it hit all the right buttons. Good job Boolat Games!

//Intro
Beginning with the "Heroes Rise: The Prodigy," you’re immediately integrated into the expansive Heroes Rise universe. With nothing short of imaginative effort, Zachary's narration does quite an impressive job at introducing a few key characters whilst allowing you to establish your own unique role in the Millennia City society.
The actions and choices you make throughout your adventure follow you through each sequel, as you continue on.
Upon finally reaching "Heroes Rise: The Hero Project," your hero glimpses at the immense buildup of suspense to which inevitably reaches a much earned climatic conclusion in "Heroes Rise: HeroFall."
//Opinion
The Heroes Rise trilogy written by Zachary Sergi was undoubtedly an enjoyable experience. I highly recommend giving this a try.
With its truly engaging storyline, it helps establish a connection the player has with their own character; a connection inevitably strengthened by one's ability to choose to respond to every event in ways they see fit, whether one wishes to play into the narrative-identity of one's character or decides to be radically different at every step. With these two elements, it proves to be quite a noteworthy “choose-your-own-adventure” game. 8/10
//Pros
Comic book-esque
Action-packed
Myriad of alternate choice pathways
Optional romances
Underlying philosophical themes -- Identity, Freedom, Security, Morality, to name a few.
Genuinly Surprising plot twists
//Cons
No option to choose/create a unique power set
Somewhat limited in regard to fighting options -- you might not like that your hero's creativity is limited to the authors.
Often extremely unpredictable and unwanted consequences based on answer choices -- usually you understand the implications of an action, but some choices are unpredictable
A few typos
Hetero-normative -- if you're looking for a progressive read, you might not find yourself fully satisfied
(This game shows potential for more products like this to be released for the PC market. I'm excited to find out what's in store.)

Cossacks 3 could have been a great game. Let's quickly look at the pros
-Large maps with NO population limit whatsoever, massive armies and battles are possible!
-Large selection of factions, each with unique units and architectural styles
-Naval combat
-Complex economy, much better and complex than AoE's economics and encourages good economic management (not just combat)
The scale and economic complexity of the game is excellent. But remember, I said this game COULD HAVE been a great game, but IT IS NOT. Why?
-Devs too poor to afford servers, so you'll have to rely on peer-to-peer hosting like it's still fukken 2003
-Because devs are too poor to afford server, enjoy lagging and frame-rate drops every time one of those massive battles happen, which they won't because everything will just freeze and quite possibly crash
-Multiplayer maps are only randomly generated, no set maps making multiplayer maps feel bland
-Units tend to bunch up into one another
Seriously, the lack of dedicated servers is the worst part about this game. They've balanced many units and fixed many of the bugs but the fundemental lack of servers wastes the possibility of massive battles, which the engine could readily handle if the game had a damn server.
Don't buy this game. Multiplayer will just dissapoint you.

Dynamite Jack is a nice, albeit rather short, Bomberman-style game.
Personally, I really enjoyed playing through the campaign: most maps are indeed quite easy, but if you want the experience to be more challenging you can just decide to try and get all the secondary objectives on you first try, instead of coming back to collect them one at a time.
This, opposed to just going for the exit, does make the game more rewarding but doesn't really increase its longevity: you will probably get to 100% completion in about 7-8 hours tops.
Still, for me this wasn't really an issue, better an "honest" short title than a game that drags on and on with pointless objectives and impossible achievements.
Also there are many community maps, so if you really like the game you can keep playing it even after finishing the campaign.
As far as the price is concerned, if you like this kind of game I'd say it's worth it; with a coupon you can even get it for 1€, and that's a steal in my opinion.

- pleasant design.

I could go on, but there is no point.

Campaign Clicker is a clicker game that has you run for President by picking a side and clicking the screen to gather votes. You can use the points you get from clicking to purchase upgrades such as merchandise (which will earn you more votes per second) or fingers (more votes per click). There are also special booster chests that fly which can grant you special time limit bonus like 1,000 votes per click and so on. I actually sort of enjoyed the game at first, but all of that changed roughly 5 minutes into it.
Once you use 5 boosts, you are unable to use anymore until the next campaign which starts every 24 real world hours. Without these special boosts, it is nearly impossible to win any campaign, even with a ton of upgrades purchased/leaving the game idle. The only way you can use more boosts in a campaign is to purchase them with real world money. That's right: if you want to win a single campaign, you'll have to fork over some cash. Since paying is just about the only way you'll ever win a campaign, the game is pretty much pointless to play through since you'll lose anyway. Even the coins you get after each campaign don't really help that much.
Even without the P2W factor, the game has a lot of other faults. The UI is really bad/confusing to use; for example. sometimes when I tried to click on a balloon, I would click on one of the option buttons since the balloon was blocked by it. There's a leaderboard ranking in the game, but its completely pointless since your score relies on how much you've paid.
Honestly if they made the game actually winnable and fixed the UI a bit, I could actually see myself having a blast with it. Unfortunately in its current state, it fails to capture my vote.

Campaign Clicker is one of the clicker styled games in the over-saturated market that spawned since the monumental success of AdVenture Capitalist. This particular title centers around the fad of the popular and controversial 2016 United States election. It's a battle of Democrats versus Republicans, and you get to choose the side that you want to be on. There are even unlockable candidates that can be purchased with in-game coins, that are obtained through campaign victories.
The general idea is that the more clicks you make, the more votes you get. You can make your clicks count for more votes by spending votes on fingers, which you can have up to 100 of; effectively making each click worth 100 votes by the time it's fully upgraded. You can also spend votes on upgrading your campaign, such as buying more billboards, newspaper ads, social media experts, etc.; these go towards upgrading the amount of votes you get per second. Each campaign lasts for a full 24 hours, in which time you will need to earn a staggering 323,214,999 votes to win. Upon winning you get 10 coins that will unlock new campaign characters.
Campaign Clicker is by far one of, if not the worst, entry into the newly founded clicker genre. The content is boring, the gameplay abysmal at best, and the pay to win model unforgivable. In fact when the game first announced that I could buy boosts and multipliers, it popped up right in the middle of the screen and I nearly accidentally purchased a $4.00 USD boost. Without these boosts, winning the campaign is nearly impossible, even with the aid of an autoclicker; the amount of clicking needed is just unfathomable. You do start each campaign with some free boosts, but you can only use five in the course of 24 hours.
If you don't care so much about that, take into account that the game CONSTANTLY freezes, becomes unresponsive, and crashes; even when just idling and not clicking. It is best to think of these as novels rather than games. More specifically they are in the vein of the Chose your own Adventure books I adored so much as a kid. And like them the first in this series(Heroes Rise: Prodigy) has a bit of railroading going on. You might just want to scream at the main character.
That said I enjoyed this third installment much better than the first one in the series. Since it is the end of the main character's story the choices have been opened up a great deal and you really get to feel as if you are shaping the world you are in. In addition at first glance it appears there are many carryovers from your choices in the first two of the series, thus lending more weight to those decisions that may have felt pointless at the time. I am not sure how much that actually effects though since I only went through all three games once.
That said while I am divided on whether I would recomend the first installment, and while I am kinda meh on the Hero Project, this third installment I can say is truely an epic end. It is nice to see something end strongly for a change. All to often the last installment, or chapter of a story feels like a let down. It is rather hard to end something well. And for all the faults some find with Heroes Rise's start, it ends in HeroFall on a very solid note.

Out of the trilogy I would say that this is the most satisfying to play as it ties up many loose ends and allows for greater exploration of how a characters powers could be used. My only complaint would be that some of the storytelling feels a bit weaker than the other two installments. I would still encourage anyone to play this game as it has been great fun tracing the career of a hero that I created from scratch.

I was devastated when I relised this is the end of the Hero Rise series but it was an epic ending. There is still so much you can do with the main character I realy hope the creater Zachary Sergi comes back to add on or potentially some one new. I just hope we will see another HR with you being the same main character not some one new.

HeroFall was a great end to the trilogy! It was well written and interesting all the way through. I could have gotten a lot more glory in this game but I make stupid mistakes. STILL this game is great and well worth the money and I absolutely will play it again.

If you're a fan of Choice of Games, have played any of the previous games in the trilogy, or are just looking for a good eBook type game, definitely pick this up.

Puzzles vary from the hard to the trivial [with no risk of getting truly stuck because of the help system], but the whole experience was enchanting, pretty much the whole way through.  Simple enough that a five year old can explore ideas, and succeed with some if not all of the puzzles, but can still enjoy the ones that are too hard to complete.  If I'm going to be at all negative it's that it was too short, as we'd really like to have carried on going.

An enjoyable adventure with a badass heroine and a story that gets gradually weirder and more intriguing... this game had me hooked from the moment I started playing it. It's not a very long game and the puzzles aren't particularly difficult, but I found them enjoyable nonetheless. Not every puzzle was solved by "use object with object", there were some mini riddles that I personally enjoyed solving, and they felt varied too.
Kathy is a great character and I'd love to see more of her in future. She's ballsy, sarcastic, independent, but as you come to learn more about her you see some of whats underneath that too.
The atmosphere of the game was excellent - the art, voice acting and soundtrack really helped convey the feeling of the game. Some of the background music in particular really unnerved me.
There were some interesting features that I've not seen in point and click adventures much that I think worked well - the "think about" option, to provide some more insight on Kathy's thoughts on things, and the closeup of characters speaking with a few different facial expressions. The method of travelling between locations on Kathy's motorcycle was enjoyable too.
My only complaint about this game was that towards the end I felt like I was just going back and forth between a lot of locations figuring out how to trigger the next event I needed to. With some of the animations it felt a bit slow. Also I felt like it ended a little more abruptly than I'd like, and I would have liked the story to last longer.
All in all I'd love to see a sequel or more from this developer, Kathy Rain was an excellent experience and I enjoyed pretty much every moment.

I love Borderlands 1 and 2 (the Pre-Sequel not so much). I wanted to love Battleborn, and on first blush there's a bunch to like. There's loot! There's funny voice lines! There are interesting characters!
The downfall of Battleborn is the gameplay is super lackluster. Brain-dead AI and linear area design make the gameplay boring and monotonous. Where in Borderlands you could approach creeps from multiple directions (and yes, cheese them by sniping outside their range) in this your combat encounters are formulaic.
I can't comment on the multiplayer, as I'm not a multiplayer guy. That invalidates this review, to a certain extent, because this is a MP game, in reality. The single-player is a series of missions string together into a story of sorts, but each mission is way too long, with no checkpointing if you quit. To progress your characters, you end up replaying the same missions over and over. It's lame.
Other details are flawed as well; having in-world pickups in finicky "chests" that the frenetic gameplay doesn't allow time to pause to pick things up, plus gear loadouts that require pickups to activate.
This game had potential, but after returning to it after a long time away just reminds me of how much I want Borderlands 3, and how sad I was to get bored of Battleborn after just a few hours.

This is not a point-and-click adventure game. Like Botanicula, it's a hidden object game in disguise. What made Machinarium so great was that it adhered a defined ruleset, where objects could only be manipulated if they were within arm's reach of Josef. In that sense, it was a true point-and-click - you guided a little character around with clicks, and used his body to manipulate the environment.
Not so in Botanicula and Samorost 3. In these games, YOU are the one in control of the environment, very often without any need for your character to be anywhere near whatever it is you are trying to control. You just tell your little buddy to run to a new area, then click all over the place until you find the little hidden context-sensitive regions of the screen that you can interact with to solve the puzzle. I'd say over 50% of the puzzles in Samorost 3 do not require Gnome to actually touch anything himself.
Thumbs down. Not a true point-and-click. And that's a shame, because Machinarium is one of the best ever made. Amanita, stop making hidden object games. They aren't fun.

Awful in every sense of the word, ESPECIALLY when you compare it to its predecessors.
But, before I begin, there's something you must know - The first two FlatOut games were made by Bugbear Entertainment, and they were phenominal racing games, especially FlatOut 2. This game? Totally different company that completely misunderstood everything Bugbear had done right.
First things first, the AI is pitiful. I know the name of the game is destruction, literally, but it's a RACING game, and I'd rather have people using force to win the race than veering off the track in the first lap to wrestle in the grass like kittens.
On this note, *everyone* targets you. I went into one demolition derby round, and it was hilariously stupid the way it worked. As soon as the countdown hit zero, the twenty-or-so other non-player racers veered to the opposite side like the Persian army and all ganged up on me at once, with the exception of, what, like, two motorists smashing each other's bumpers in. I mean, I played FlatOut 2's derby mode religiously, and it sometimes feels like the AI prioritizes you over their brethren, but even in it worst state it was nothing compared to this insanity.
Now, it's time to compare it to its predecessors - Yes, Flatout 3 was made by a different company than the first two, but being a sequel by its title, I have to rate it in comparison to its past successes in the franchise.
The other NPC's -- The way this development team tried to recreate Bugbear's non-player character gimmick is awful. If you haven't played FlatOut 2, lemme give you the jist of things - There were seven NPC's that were the only opponents in the game. They all had distinct driving styles, color schemes, and skills in different racing areas. They were so memorable thanks to this that you had those names ingrained into your brain after your first couple of races and figured out very quickly whose names to curse every time you launched out of your windshield.
Well, 3 messes this all up. There are something near 15 characters, and some of them are so similar that you have no hope of remembering them. The character models are all very idealized, if you catch my drift, and there's one fully anonymous man wearing a motorcross helmet with practically full-balanced stats that you'll choose every time if you're sane. That's another thing, too - Unlike the original, where you were your own identity, you have to choose one of these punks.
Anyway, 2.5/10, because it technically functions, I guess. Go buy Next Car Game instead, it's made by the same company that made the other FlatOut games. Speaking of which, go buy the other FlatOut games, too, they're super cheap and also on Steam. It's a shame those two don't have online multiplayer anymore, because if they did, I'd force you to buy them at gunpoint.

Getting close to 100% completion, so let's review this mofo.
It's a grindfest with a lot of bad design choices.
For starters, there are two kinds of racing. The first is included in the base game. You send your horse out, and it comes back a minute later with prize money. Minimal involvement on your end. The PLAYABLE horse racing requires you to shell out $4 for the DLC.
Each horse can only mate once, which makes no goddamn sense. Have a cooldown on breeding? Some kind of inbreeding penalty mechanic? Nope. Once your horses have a baby, neither horse can mate ever again.
Then there's the sale mechanic. The sale price is based on level, and there's no way to adjust it. When you sell your horse, all the items you bought for its stall are taken along with it. You get the same amount of money for horse + default items as you do for horse + fancy items. You get the same amout of money for a maxed out first-class race horse as you do for a horse that isn't.
For horse selection on most screens, you have to click the little arrow buttons to cycle through your roster. You can't click them until the walk-on/off animation is finished. Not too bad if you have 1-2 horses, but when you have 4+, it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ There's no way to skip this animation. The only screen where the animation is missing is the stable, but you still have to cycle through ALL the stalls(including empty ones) to get to the horse you want.
The graphics are pretty meh. Except for the $3 dress-up items, which are just atrocious. The english is passable, but it's clear that english is not the devs' first language.
All the achievements are pretty easy to get, if rather tedious. Get it in a bundle, or 90% off.

Cossacks along with Stronghold Crusader, Command & Conquer: Generals & Zero Hour, Age of Empires 1 & 2 and American Conquest is one of few really epic RTS games.
I used to play the original on LAN with friends and the sheer scale of battles was just epic. Its really a lot of fun. I never did campaigns; and skirmishes vs the AI tends to get monotonous as you can easily beat even a 'Very Hard' AI with some basic artillery positionning and unit spam.
Where this game really shines is in the multiplayer. Thats where its fun.
For those new to the game its well worth its price on sale if you can play online or with friends. Maybe even worth full price, its a real RTS gem.
For those who have played before there have been some changes. The 18th century ship of the line has been removed, which used to make for even more overkill battles, but it was a bit too overkill if you got several of them first it could completely tip the game in your favour so its fair I guess.
The game mechanics are the same and its basically just a retexture of the old game. The firing animations and explosions look cooler now. Formations can take up to 400 men which is pretty neat (maybe more I havent tried). There no longer is a 'Patrol Area' command for troops which I find to be a HUGE pity as it was really crucial to keeping my peasants from getting captured. Also cavalry no longer seem to be able to enter a tirangle formation.
Finally the mills no longer auto sow crops which is a shame since you now have to micro manage this to keep your economy steady, take a bit away from the fun of managing your tactics in battle.
Personally mechanics wise I prefer the first game and its expansions because of these small omissions in Cossacks 3. The graphics arent as nice, but then again in Cossacks 3 they didnt do any work on building to unit proportions or implement any new mechanics. So Id still recommend Cossacks: Back to War aagaisnt this one despite the lesser texture quality and  firing/explosion animations.
TLDR though, great game despite the small things mentionned above. Worth a buy, especially if you can play with friends or vs. randoms online.

And under no circumstance may you take off your pants.  Apparently the developer isn't a fan of No Pants Fridays.  They must work in one very boring office...

There is a lot to like about this text-based adventure.  The story is well written.  The music gives you that "lonely" feeling.  These are really the main driving points of this game experience.
The game mechanic is interesting insofar as it forces the player to think.  In principle this works out really well.  The only problem is, in an immersive story setting I found myself often wanting to "do" something that was not allowed in a particular place.  Of course, this is necessary given the somewhat linear story.  Nevertheless, I found myself wanting to look at things or use things that were not a written in.  (Given that this is a free game, this is completely understandable.)
At times, it can be frustrating to figure out you can possibly do.  In a number of places, there really is only one right way to do what you are supposed to do to advance the story.  Perhaps it would have been good for several of the interactive paths to provide further hints or secondary avenues for advancing the story.
All in all, about an hour or so in, I've found that it is pretty fun and a good change of pace from other fast paced games.

This game is worth picking up for 5 to 10 bucks. It has a lot going for it: the style is very appealing, the voice acting is (overall) rather good, the story is decent, the tone of the game is well struck, and the puzzles are fun to solve.
However, this is not a big production. That shows: the game is rather short. I've finished it in 5 hours.
Also, the game lacks a certain complexity. The puzzles are fairly easy, especially since the game hits you over the head with clues, often in the form of thoughts that the main protagonist has. Furthermore, the amount of inventory items you at any given point in the game have, does not exceed 10, which makes the inventory puzzles even more simple.
This lack of complexity also shows in other areas. There are a fair amount of things you can interact with on each screen, but, as I said, don't expect "Simon the Sorceror" amounts of objects to pick up and use. There are also limited areas you can travel to; they seldom exceed more than two screens. There are almost no outside areas you can visit, that could serve as a "backdrop" to the relevant areas. There are little people to interact with, outside of the characters that are fundamental to progressing the story, This makes the setting of the game feel less "alive".
However, it's very difficult to fault the game for this. As I said, it's a small production and for a 5-10 bucks it's definitely worth the experience. I hope to see more from Kathy Rain, in hopefully a longer and more complex game!

This game is un-f-word-ing-beleivably bad. I had played two other games by House of Tales, Overclocked and 15 Days, and they were really good, so I thought I'd try this one, and what a mistake that was...
The game was mostly mechanically bad. It's very difficult to figure out where to make the character walk to transition screens, some of them have click locations, but others you have to walk to a certain part of the screen to get the transition to happen, and to make it all the worse the character just moves where he wants to anyway.
Most of the puzzles aren't overly complicated, though there are a few that are unforgiveable... The real issue is that many of the puzzles involve "go here, then there, then to that other place, then back to there", and the character movement is so bad and slow and you have to go through so many screen transitions to get anywhere that in the end it's just an annoyance. The game is padded with a bunch of walking around. If you end up walking to a location then finding that what you need isn't there, you're going to be angry real fast.
About a quarter of the way through  I gave up and used a walkthrough for every step of the way, because going to one wrong location meant like five minutes of walking around for nothing. I don't want to waste my time walking around when all I was interested in was the story. Near the end of the game I thought maybe I'd try to figure it out on my own again... Big mistake.
The last puzzle in the game was the worst. There are 5 important screens in it that you need to go back and forth between, but you have to walk through 6 screens to get from one to the other, that means there are 36 annoying screens to walk through when all you cared about was 5. To go through them in the most efficient way possible (using a guide) you would walk through 48 annoying screens to solve it. And that's using a guide. Without a guide I'd imagine you'd be doing a lot more than that because there is some trial and error involved.
Don't waste your time with this game. There are a lot of better adventure games than this, and for a story driven game it's just not worth it.
