The Moment of Silence is a game that has some solid ideas but is held back by sloppy game design.
The plot is a decent but run-on-the-mill conspiracy story loosely inspired by Orwille. Whatever plot twists it has are textbook. There is nothing special or groundbreaking about it except the world-building, used as commentary on the fear of surveillance of private communication. This aspect is actually kind of culturally relevant and even somewhat thought-provoking due to the information age we currently live in. The pacing is good, first letting you to know the area Peter Wright, the protagonist, lives in, and getting more tense and action-packed later on.
Puzzles are mostly solid, but some of them rely on typical cartoony adventure game logic (you put a live bird inside your pockets on two occasions) which clashes with the tone of the game. Furthermore, I felt that some of the puzzles were insufficiently hinted/signposted, leaving me confused about what my goals were. As the gameplay makes the game tedious to play (I'll get to that soon), I resorted to using hints a couple of times.
The dialogue trees. Oh the dialogue trees. Each time you meet a new character, you are faced with a laundry list of topics to click through. The dialogue is at times moderately witty but is also extremely long-winded. Once you've exhausted a topic and must backtrack in the dialogue tree, you have to select some variation of "There is something else I want to ask about", which will quickly become a phrase you will never again want to hear in your life. As a result, the conversations become utterly unbelievable and repetitive. The saving grace is that conversation options that have not been selected yet are highlighted, but on the other hand this is also a constant reminder of the checklist-of-questions nature of the discussions. Some of the NPCs are colourful enough, but fail to have any great chemistry with the protagonist due to his nature.
The main character has no personality. He's a very generic Anybody who randomly decides to embark on an adventure because the plot requires him to. You know, in my teens I drew a parody comic that poked fun at thriller/mystery plots, and one of the side characters I came up with was a guy who acted like a stereotypical point and click adventure game hero. He'd unnecessarily voice his thoughts aloud in a deadpan way that told nothing about himself, and engage in conversations in an awkward start-stop fashion as if he was navigating a dialogue tree. Peter Wright is exactly like that. Any traits he possesses are the bare minimum required: a sort-of-negative-opinion of the villainous forces or other obvious but shallow ones (e.g. basic sarcasm). He doesn't go through any meaningful change. And this is not helped by the monotonous performance of his voice actor. At one point you get to briefly control Mrs. Oswald, whose husband is kidnapped in the intro, and I thought she would have been a much better main character with a stronger motivation.
Then there's the backtracking. The game features large, beautifully rendered backgrounds, yes, but traversing through the long corridors and wide plazas quickly becomes tedious. Near the end of the game you have to go back and forth through a series of tunnels just to fetch a single item. Exits of screens are often unobvious and the camera angles sometimes change confusingly. Have the developers ever heard of the 180 degree rule? Combine these with the fact that the path-finding of this game is notoriously terrible - Wright will from time to time run several meters in the opposite direction before going where he was supposed to - and you will soon long for any other control scheme. Luckily, pressing and holding H reveals hotspots and exits, which reduces the pixelhunting.
None of these are absolutely game-breaking, but these do severely bring down a game that isn't really outstanding in the first place.

On the first day God created the dog. God said, "Sit all day by the door of your house and bark at anyone who comes in or walks past. I will give you a life span of twenty years." The dog said, "That's too long to be barking. Give me ten years and I'll give you back the other ten."
So God agreed.
On the second day God created the monkey. God said, "Entertain people, do monkey tricks and make them laugh. I'll give you a twenty-year life span." The monkey said, "Monkey tricks for twenty years? I don't think so. Dog gave you back ten, so that's what I'll do too, okay?"
And God agreed.
On the third day God created the cow. "You must go to the field with the farmer all day long and suffer under the sun, have calves, and give milk to support the farmer. I will give you a life span of sixty years."
The cow said, "That's kind of a tough life you want me to live for sixty years. Let me have twenty and I'll give back the other forty."
And God agreed again.
On the fourth day God created man. God said, "Eat, sleep, play, marry and enjoy your life. I'll give you twenty years."
Man said, "What? Only twenty years? Tell you what, I'll take my twenty, and the forty the cow gave back, and the ten the monkey gave back, and the ten the dog gave back, that makes eighty, okay?"
Okay," said God, "You've got a deal."
So that is why the first twenty years we eat, sleep, play, and enjoy ourselves; the next forty years we slave in the sun to support our family; the next ten years we do monkey tricks to entertain the grandchildren; and the last ten years we sit on the front porch and bark at everyone.
Life has now been explained to you.
-Paul Bird, the creator of the masterpiece known as Alien Insanity

One word review: 8/10 - Lovely! ^_^
You are in charge of an adorable little colony: Grow its population, expand its economy, research new technologies to succeed in your search for a legendary treasure.
You Drag and Drop villagers to assign them to tasks which allows them to specialize in areas like Farming. Starting out simple by gathering basic resources and and trade, you soon unlock many more different resources and buildings. Various special offers and challenges require you to adapt your strategy. In addition, a few minigames offer variation.
If you are familiar with strategy games and simulations, you won't have any difficulties with to this one. The strongest differences to other games of this genre are its strong linearity and complete lack of frustrating elements. There is no death or failure here; the worst you can do is to make nonideal choices which will cost you time and bonuses, but still allow you to progress. If that happens, it is a little annoying that the trading information bubbles pause the game, but if you play somewhat decently, you won't have to endure any long waiting periods anyway.
All in all "The Promised Land" is quite casual, but nonetheless rewarding: You bond with the settlers, you enjoy the cute animations, you strategize without creating spreadsheets and simply relax in a pretty environment. Although I initially wanted to write that it doesn't have any replay value, I actually catch myself revisiting this game once or twice a year. While it is too difficult to be played by children on their own, with a helpful parent at their side they can certainly enjoy this game a lot.
Oh, and one piece of advice that I haven't found in the otherwise great ingame hints: The colorcoded circles around the number of people working on a task indicate which class specializes on it. For example, a blue circle on the Sugar Canes states that this a job best suited for Workers, while a green circle for the Fluffer Farm suggests that Farmers are best at Shearing.
- Little Replay Value
- ~ 10 hours of gameplay
- Only Fullscreen, no window mode
- No Zoom, though a helpful minimap
- Info bubble pauses the game
+ Pretty graphics and cute animations
+ Pleasant music
+ Villagers have basic personalities
+ Nice minigames (Angry Birds style, Housing Puzzle, End Puzzle)
+ Efficiency is rewarded, but progress is granted either way
+ Absolutely no frustration
Get the game, especially on Sale, and you'll happily enjoy ten hours of a mini-vacation :)

This is a beautiful, brilliant game. Tight controls and gameplay that blends skill and puzzle challenges. Engaging visuals, responsive and rewarding combat, exciting original music, and cute references to Mexican culture. Be aware though, this is not a game with an emphasis on narrative. The story is a bit cliche, but for me it didn't get in the way of the experience as a whole. The weakness of the narrative is more than compensated for by the beautiful artwork and hilariously engaging characters. Be prepared to be frustrated, puzzled, and delighted by the joy that is Guacamelee.
------------
-Very original art style and setting
-If you are the completionist type, you will enjoy finding the many hidden treasure chests and side quests, and the metroidvania style play.
-Challenging, skill-based action
-Both new and classic puzzle mechanisms, used artfully in puzzles that will make you think
-Replay value: Gameplay doesn't get old. There is a second ending, hard mode, and a lot of secrets to discover as well!
-If strong narrative is a must for you, then this might not be your cup of tea
------------

Kathy Rain is detective adventure game that deeply homages David Lynch’s work. If it homaged any more you could call it Twin Peaks the game. Inspiration aside, Kathy Rain marries the detective genre and point and click adventure game beautifully with a decent story and 8-bit graphics.
The art is done well, albeit in low resolution graphics. The game has some modern mechanics, but overall the look is quite dated (comparable to Broken Sword). Meanwhile, the voice acting varies between passable and good. Overall, the production quality gets passing marks for an indie development.  Nothing egregious nor outstanding.
The gameplay solid, it is a point and click adventure, but unlike most, there is no inane puzzle logic. Everything was either quite logically or Kathy hints at what she should do next. With that kind of gameplay the detective work shines through nicely. You end up doing interviews, looking for clues and following up on leads.  Puzzles are strewn in, but nothing feels out of place, and themed around unlocking via riddles or codes.  Gameplay is quite excellent for a point and click adventure.
Finally, the story. You will get déjà vu playing this game if you have seen Twin Peaks. Many major elements from Lynch’s work are mirrored here. From the Red Room to the dead girl in the lake, plot points really could not come much closer. To be fair, that’s not a bad thing. Enough is different to call it original, but that does not mean it is not trope ridden. The main character, Kathy, comes off as a bit of a strawman.  Basically, she is the perfect example of a cynical girl from a broken home having made all the wrong choices but having the strength to endure it all anyway. I feel like she’s the best friend from a poorly written RomCom and her temperamental attitude takes a while to get use to as she comes off as rude for very little reason for most of the start of the game. But as it progresses, she chills out and becomes more likeable as her sardonic quips become more sarcastic. Aside from the rough characterization, the story depicts a rural mystery with surreal elements with quite a lot of care.  I won’t get into the details, but this isn’t really a whodunit so much as a “what the heck is going on?”
If you’re a fan of mysteries, point and click adventures or David Lynch this game might be up your alley. There’s very little to criticize beyond the dated graphics and a lot to like.

This is reasonably constructed point and click adventure with some good points but it has some serious flaws that make the price of £14 way too expensive. If you find it on a half price sale it is worth considering.
The premise of this game is that you are a man in New York who, soon after moving into a new apartment, observes a police squad forcefully arresting and abducting his neighbour while his terrified wife amd son look on. In your attempt to support the man's family you discover all sorts of strange facts that suggest dark and conspiratorial motives for his arrest.
The gameplay is that of a traditional point and click adventure. Most of the plot advancement is through conversation and exploring. There are some inventory based puzzles too, but not enough in my opinion.
The good:
Despite the occasional weak translations (to English) the characters are believable and the voice acting is pretty good.
The plot is engaging and sensible and doesn't leave any unanswered questions.
Object based puzzles are sensible.
The bad:
-The pathing is terrible. It is downright  difficult to transition between some screens and the main character will sometimes run around in a circle before going where you want him to.
-The scenery involves huge areas that take ages to get across and redundant screens. This makes moving between locations tedious and annoying. This actively ruins one of the better puzzles because it takes a couple of minutes to go from the place where you push a button to the place where you get feedback.
- Advancing the plot relies heavily on triggers. Sometimes those are sensible (like interrogating a character to reveal a new location) but some triggers are completely irrelevant to the plot (for example you know what to do and where to go but you can't do it until you've talked to your friend in the office, who has nothing whatsoever to do with the story).

As of this writing we enter 2017 with games becoming more and more like movies, seamlessly transitioning from scripted elements back into user controlled scenarios. Graphics continue to push through the realms of photorealism and the ubiquity of smartphones (a pocket computer), and the rise of AR and VR provide some exciting possibilities for us when a company decides to try bundling all of these technologies into one unified experience. This is the context NotGTAV arrives within and comments on.

I don't want to rationalize this game into sounding like some renegade work of genius, it absolutely is not that kind of a game. It is puerile, and lazily ironic, and yes it is mechanically simple. The controls have a bit of lag to them and of course the graphics are hand drawn. Yet, this is what I like about it.

The context of technology in 2017 presents a lot of potential but that potential is frequently met with less and less imagination. Photorealism and immersion are the rule not the exception, and it is a rule that seems to get more strict with time. NotGTAV swims purposefully against this current and in doing so, despite all of its drawbacks, reminds me of what games, of what interactive media, can be.

While Fallout 4 was lauded for bringing a more colorful pallete to the wasteland, Fallout 3 dazzled players and critics alike with a section of the game that deliberately removes color. While Skyrim and others are busy getting remastered, there are little exceptions like Lucius which was released in a "Demade" version with intentionally worse graphics.

I recommend you play this game to help remind yourself of just how broad the world of gaming, and interactive media as a whole, can be. It won't change your life, you won't cry from its story (there is none), and it won't win any awards, but in the context of other deliberately unique games (Mason Lindroth's "Hylics" comes to mind), it will serve to show you what can happen when companies stop choosing games as safe vehicles for profit and focus on simply making good art that challenges not only us as individuals, but the industry as well.

Guacamelee! Gold Edition is gorgeous. It's interesting. It's full of pop culture references. It's polished. It's rewarding. It's
. But most of all, it's
, in both good and bad ways.
I'm not usually interested in
brawling games where hit combos are the focus and often the key to victory. I gave up on Arkham Asylum for those reasons. But Guacamelee!'s combat system is relatively easy to learn, remember, and execute (with a gamepad), even as more and more depth is added. The game made me work to, ahem, "get good," and my fingers definitely imprinted some muscle memories onto my brain, but it was worth the mental and digital effort. Beating the marrow out of skeletons is fun! Dying a dozen times at the hands of the same boss can be frustrating, but figuring out the attack patterns and necessary reactions and finally
is so...
. And scoring large combos, while not absolutely necessary for victory, provided me with more upgrade money and therefore incentive to play thoughtfully. I felt less like I was mashing buttons and more like I had a plan, even if I didn't always carry it out perfectly.
The game does a great job of acclamating the player to the additional combat and platforming mechanics that are introduced as the story is told. I was happy to fail in the face of
the new challenges. But by the end of the game I had hit my own personal skill ceiling. If you're more skilled than me, well, carry on, my wayward agave farmer, but I had had enough.
The combat and platforming involved in the main story is of moderate difficulty, but some of the optional platforming puzzles and combat challenges are tedious and frustrating, if not almost impossible, especially near the end of the game. While I had failed earlier platforming challenges 30+ times but kept plugging away until I succeeded, I simply gave up on many of the later challenges, particularly in the tree tops and the hallways of hell.
I'm typically a completionist when it comes to achievements, secrets, unlocks, etc., in video games. Like collectable pocket monsters, I want to get them all if I can, even if it takes a large amount of time and effort. But not this time. Sure, revisiting areas to explore previously inaccessible nooks was worth my time. It was enjoyable to do what I couldn't do before. The short of it: Guacamelee delivers a satisfyingly solid metroidvania experience while maintaining an aesthetic and an identity all its own.
Mechanically, It's a relatively simplistic game that never bothers to introduce much in the way of equipment or character upgrades.  Beyond the obligatory health and energy boosts, there are scant few abilities to be found as you scale impossibly tall trees and chicken your way through ruins saturated with lava, but the game draws out its platforming sections to such a frankly absurd scale that what abilities it does give you never start to feel tired.  In that vein, the level design is demanding, but also quite forgiving.  Falling off platforms never puts you back more than a few seconds, and the intuitive map makes backtracking for hidden items surprisingly painless.  Combat is frantic but solid, the soundtrack full of energy.  The references to nerd culture populate the latin-styled environments like elderly people at a nude beach, but unlike Old Man Wallace, they remain happily in the background, never forcing you to appreciate them, and the game's off-beat humor holds up all the way through the end credits.
Buy it full price or on sale, whatever fits your budget.  You'll be glad you did.

While The Promised Land is a cute little game and has some fun elements, it becomes quite stale after awhile. I was able to get 2 days of gameplay out of it and I feel like that was worth a couple bucks on sale. But the full price of 6.99 might be a little steep for this title. The only reason I put 2 days into this game is because I was hoping it would get better.
Micromanaging your community seems a little tedious, but there are some fun minigames that mix things up a bit.
- You play a minigame where you fire cannons at stationary pirates on crates and wooden planks (much like the typical slingshot/cannon games: Angry Birds, World of Goo, Crush the Castle...).
- Adding rooms to a house to increase your population is a little bit of a puzzle as you determine which of the limited room pieces fit together to complete the layout of the house (but barely a minigame).
I wish this game had enemies that attack the town, forcing me to make repairs and add defences. But the only enemies are the stationary pirates in the minigame that you fire cannons at (only accessible by clicking the cannon defence structure at the top of the map). There is no way to take any damage or suffer any consequences by losing the minigames and you have unlimited retry's to complete them.
One thing that gets old pretty fast is the character noises. Everytime you grab characters to move them around town, they make a childish whimper - sometimes happy, sometimes sad.
I have not completed the first map, but I am pretty sure it is the only map... I would like to see a snow level, water level, an evil level? Even some additional levels as DLC? (<-- can't believe I said that)
Everything in the game is backed by a tutorial, meaning that the entire game is predetermined as it tells you exactly what to do next. I am not sure if it is actually possible to lose.
This is where I thought it could get better. Maybe you get a new settlement in a different region where you make descisions yourself without the tutorial? Nope.
The music is fair and doesn't get too old until about 6-7 hours in. But I would not buy the soundtrack if one existed.
Overall, I would only recommend this game if it were at least 50% off, but only if you want something with a low challenge and you are in the mood for something cute.
But for the average gamer, and with so many better choices on Steam, I can't recommend this title at full price.

This was an interesting worker management game. Unlike many of the others that involve simply assigning people, collecting resources, and then building, this one has some additional unique features. Most notably, the workers have job likes and dislikes, and they can become skilled in a particular type of trade, such as farmer or miner. They will level up, and become more productive, the longer they do a certain type of task. They can also be sent to school to skill up.
To gain money, resources and products can be traded with the mainland via the ship. New workers are also hired from the mainland this way. Specialty items have to be purchased from the mainland. Every now and then, a certain type of item will become more in demand and be worth more. This is when you assign as many workers as possible to collect and/or manufacture to fill the demand. As the game progresses, workers, specialty items, upgrades, etc, will get more expensive, so taking advantage of the demand spike helps raise money faster.
As part of the story, there are pirates to be dealt with. This is done by firing a cannonball at their "boat" structures. There are a limited number of balls, so they have to be aimed just right in order to cause an optimal toppling to take out multiple pirates. There are a few of these to deal with during the quest, and the final ones can get a little annoying. But, you can retry as much as needed.
There isn't any way to die and resources are infinite, so it really is a casual game. As with most Alawar games, it is very aesthetically pleasing with appropriate music and sound effects. I don't think it's worth $6.99 due to the relatively short play time and no real replayability, but it's worth picking up on sale if you just want to relax and not stress about losing.

I thought this was generally a fun game.  Using just a flashlight and bombs that you have to find in the levels, you've got to make your way past guards and other obstacles to reach the exit. Naturally, later levels get harder, but it's not terribly difficult to finish the game; I did in a few hours, but far from perfectly.  There is some reply value though in that it's possible to unlock extra levels if you don't the first time through, and each level normally has three goals/achievements, like beat a certain time or don't use the flashlight at all, so you can try to "three star" each level if you want.  It's pretty easy to pick up and put down at will since there's no real story to it, and it's not very long, so if you like puzzles (which I think this basically is), I think it's worth a try.

I love coaster games. Got RCT1-3, Theme Park, Parkitect and Planet Coaster. For some reason I never really played RCT3 back in the days, but last year started again and it's still nice!

I still like playing with it, but Planet Coaster is just so much better... And therefore I can't really recommend it...

And wanted to get it released BEFORE Planet Coaster. If it was released in a time without competition, I'm sure the reviews would not be as negative. I for one would just be happy to have a RCT game again :)
But now with Planet Coaster as a direct competitor it's just outshined in almost all areas.

This is exactly the kind of gem that flourishes from indie companies. Never before have I played a game that fuses platforming, metroidvania, and combat together so well. There's secret passages and hidden collectibles to encourage you to explore and revisit areas, and even a whole secret ending if you explore enough. The combat is quick and simple, but has a lot of depth and flexibility, which is basically perfect for a fighting game. Hard mode is a legitimate combat challenge at times, too, which makes it feel like you really had to fight through the game.
What sets this game apart from other metroidvania games is...its humor. I've really not found a game that actually made me laugh more than this. The writers really knew what they were doing with the characters, and all the jokes are sort of off-hand remarks that you don't expect. Plus there's tons of video game and pop culture references, but almost entirely in the background on signs. Seeing strong bad as an actual mexican wrestler is nice to see, and you have to laugh/cringe at the Rage Comic Era Memes™ set up to fight each other in a wrestling match.
And it has co-op, too!
This entire game is a real breath of fresh air from standard stuff, and I wish there was more of it.

The first reason this game caught my attention was the nostalgic look. And it was worth it.
Kathy Rain is a good "old" point & click game with a low-res nostalgic look that could make you think this game came straight from the 90s.
And as a matter of fact the story takes place in the 90s: Kathy is studying journalism at college and lives at the dorm with her roommate Eileen and gets a phone call to be informed about her Grandfather's death. After the funeral, a chat with her Grandmother reveals some strange events that don't seem to add up, and that's where the real investigation begins.
As usual mouse is your friend, but for some odd reason the interface won't use your right click, as everything is set to work with the left click only. Besides that the interface is quite intuitive, so hovering with the cursor over usable items will make appear their names so you know you can use them, while items collected in your inventory can be examined, used or combined. Nothing new, but that's the point of reviving a classic, right? For some odd reason there are two different options for examining an item, and even though you don't get much more information then usual from them, I kind of liked the idea as classic P&C just have the same line for every item.
The soundtrack during the game is pleasant and appropirate, even though the title track and the travel track really are the only ones that really stand out.
Riddles are well built, nothing extremely complicated nor easy as a click (except for
), the best part of the game surely lies in the story that will take you around the town and let you talk with characters... Long and interesting talks. And the story (no spoilers) will really go deep to end up in an unexpected direction.
Definitely a really appreciated work, made with heart and mind, and with this I'm definitely keeping an eye on Clifftop Games. (no, I'm not paid by the publisher nor the developer. I just grew up with games like Monkey Island and Sam & Max)

Ok, so you know what? This game looks beautiful. But the gameplay is terrible.
Upgrading your farm and buying more horses sounds like a ton of fun. But earning money is just sending your horse of on quests and waiting for it to come back. Oh, and if the weather turns bad while it is away, there is a chance of your horse getting sick. Which means you have to spend even more money to cure it. What a pain.
You can increase your horses stats by either training it, mixing potions, or making horseshoes. To do this you must tap arrow keys as they lazily cross the screen. It's like DDR for snails.
If you decided to buy the DLC, you can also earn money in a Mario Kart-esque racing game. It's pretty bad too, but at least more fun than sitting doing nothing. The Dress Up is cool too, it gave me a few laughs, but you have to repurchase costumes for new horses. Which means you must go back to the painful process of earning cash. I wouldn't recommend the Soundtrack / Coloring Book, as the book only has 10 pages and you'll be tired of the soundtrack after an hour of gameplay.
So that about covers it. This is probably a game better suited for young kids than a 19 year old.

This is the first time I have felt compelled to write a review for a game on steam.
I have spent a lot of time in Team Fortress 2, in Paladins 220 hours, in Overwatch 350 hours. I have not spent a lot of time with Battleborn. I have been waiting for it to go Free to Play for months. This game addresses many of the issues that I have with the aforementioned games.
The game just did not appeal to when it released. I have since gotten on board with this new kind of First Person Shooter. I can say that whilst all these games offer something unique, this is my favourite.
This game has all of the aspects I enjoy about the games above; the humour, music, art style, accessibility, and team focused gameplay. It reminds me of so many games that I have enjoyed. It is a great combination of different influences.
The main reason I like this game more than the others, aside from being better in all categories in my opinion, is that each character feels like a playstyle as opposed to a role. In the other games, you need a balanced team, and everyone needs to play the position well or you lose. Here what is cool is that you can just play the way you want to with a character that suits you. You do not have to play a role that you don't enjoy. This is a massive selling point and should be highlighted as the key differentiating point.
I am not an expert on the business of games, but my guess is that the game was not and still is not marketed well. But going Free to Play is a step in the right direction. Give it a go.

Of the five first Hitman episodes (Haven't got the specs to play the 2016 one), I played Blood Money last. And if I loved each episode of the series (I actually kinda enjoyed Absolution, though I could see its flaws), Blood Money is definitely my favorite of all.
Gameplay wise, there are quite some improvements compared to the previous episodes - but I won't detail. Everything is basically better, yet not everything is on point. This is the most sandbox-based episode of the five first, and every level has more ways to assassinate your targets than you may think. Whether you want to find a convenient sniper spot, or provoke a creative accidental kill, or just buy an M4/shotgun and destroy anyone standing against you, the choice is yours.
Graphically, the game is quite somptuous for a 2006 game. When you come from Codename 47, Silent Assassin or Contracts, the game feels way more refined.
The soundtrack is a pleasure. Jesper Kyd outdid himself on this episode, and every music fits perfectly with its situation. In my opinion, it has the best tracks of the series.
And last point: The story. The development of the scenario is just outstanding, and the ending is... genius, I don't even know how to put it without spoiling.
If you are a Hitman fan, just go for Blood Money. You won't regret it.

Kathy Rain is a brief, lighthearted adventure title about a girl embracing her past in response to the death of her grandfather.
The game first struck me as irritating, rather than engrossing, but once you get past the unrelentingly quip-focused facade, there's a sweet experience waiting for anyone who'd like to see Buffy: The Vampire Slayer venture into Monkey Island territory. If you don't like Joss Whedon, or if you like your adventure game puzzles more asinine, out there and demandingly focused around "rubbing everything in your inventory against everything else," then Kathy Rain might not be your cup of tea. There's relatively few puzzles in the game - most of the gameplay is about just following the narrative to the next dialogue point. That said, I enjoyed what thought the game provoked, excepting a single puzzle in the middle of the game that just didn't gel with me.~ The atmosphere is reliably sold through the music and artstyle, though some of the ambient-spooky pieces do repeat themselves with undue haste.
I'm happy to have played this impressive title from a singular Swedish hobbyist, and I am looking forward to their future projects.

Guacamelee! is advertised as a member of the "Metroidvania" genre, which is largely what drove me to it. It draws on some of the key features of its heritage (accumulation of abilities which open paths and expose secrets) while departing from others (extended exploration, moody atmosphere, isolation). The story, while basic, is overbearing (compared to ancestors of the genre); there are a lot of monologues and cutscenes that probably aren't necessary––they're largely used for jokes. Icons like Super Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the Night give broad goals (reach Evil Guy X at the end) and let you work out everything inbetween. Guacamelee! repeatedly says "go here on the map" with small rewards for deviating. But this is a hallmark of modern games, largely.
Like other reviewers have said, this is more of a brawler-platformer. It will appeal to fans of that type of game. The platforming becomes grueling at times, especially if you're using a keyboard. Don't believe other reviews that say it's unplayable with a keyboard; you'll just have to take a break every 45 minutes when your tendons start to hurt.
This is a weak Metroidvania title but a decent brawler-platformer. If you, like me, are/were expecting the former, you're liable to be disappointed.

Ever been stuck home with a hangover and you want to play a game, but just can't bring yourself to do it?  This is your game!  Ever try to force your way through a few dumb episodes in series you're watching and need something to do on the other half of your monitor?  Look no further!  Does grandma call you and tell you about her virtual farm?  At least change the topic with this game.
This is a basic resource management game, with no way to fail or die.  You might beat this game in 7 or 8 hours if you really played with optimum efficiency.  On the other hand, were I to train my dog to touch a mouse, he'd probably beat it in his lifetime, too.  The only way to fail is in your own mind, when you realize how inefficient you've been.  It's a casual game, but I nonetheless found it strangely compelling, and even rewarding.
You start the game by managing a handful of settlers on an island.  You click a villager and drag him or her on top of a food source.  Poof!  That villager now gathers food.  You do this to other villagers to gather wood and stone.  You slowly gather resources and build (a pre-located) farm.  You manage the farm the same way.  Slowly, you build up a small town.
As you grow over this small island, things get a little more complex.  Each settler has a job like and dislike, as well as three basic stats - hunger, social, and injury.  But their stats don't harm them, just make them limp slowly towards a refill station.  If you can match a settler to a job s/he likes, then her/his stats will decrease at a much lower rate than someone who hate's their job.
This becomes important in the later game when you might have a bunch of jobs all lined up to create an industry.  For example: one guy cuts sugar cane, the next makes sugar, and a the next drops it off at a kitchen.   Meanwhile, someone grows corn, carries it to a mill and makes flour.  Those two ingredients make a special food.  That's probably the most complex industrial structure in the game - and there is a long lead into learning it.
What makes the game compelling?
First and foremost, it is cheap; often less than 2 bucks during any Steam sale.
Secondly, it is a simple game, but rewards the player with little upgrades often enough to keep the momentum.
Thridly, it is bright and colorful, and the settlers have cute little graphics, like an exaggerated 'thumbs up' they use when you help them out (via click and drag) or are placed in a happy job, among others.  And I often get connected to individual settlers unlike other games.  Ex:  I'm likely to remember that Marie likes mining and feel bad when I force her to do something she hates just to keep the colony moving.
Fourthly, you can play the game windowed (on Win 10), at a low resolution.  Of course, the game is stuck in widescreen, but you should be able to play the game while having a small video screen up and running on a small part of your screen.
Summary:  This is a cute, colorful, but simplistic casual game that involves (pre-planned) city-building with human and resource management.  It's very casual, with no way of death.  It's not hard at all, but it is rewarding.  It can eat away hours for a splt-screener, a grandparent, or someone like me, unemployed.

A pretty and pleasant game. It doesn't force you to brutalize and wage war against the native population.  Resources are infinite and you won't have to face plundering a land and laying waste to what drew you to it in the first place.   None of the unpleasantness of real life intrudes but this is very much what I like about it.   It is a casual game in this regard, yet it still has enough depth to keep you interested over the entirety of building the community.   I wish life could be more like this and I have been satisfied by the time I have spent with it.   If getting away from games that try to force a lot of ugliness upon you,  in the name of realism,  appeals then this game is well worth the modest price.

Its a kind of casual villiage-building endeavor in a colonial atmosphere, with very little pressure outside the push for that little extra to get some jobs done a bit faster for quicker rewards. There is literally no outside threat that could ruin the settlement, at worst it just means you grow slow if you somehow mismanage things - taking longer to progress overall.
The enviroment operates very much like the old villager gathering/building akin to Age of Empires in the simulation and village-building from a single town center to a larger near-city size. But not quite, your population will remain modest, at most keeping under 50 total at its largest if I guess the buildings right. The enviroment is small, and the overal scope isn't grand, but its a good timewaster.
There is a minigame sidequest that is very much akin to Angry Birds for both distractions and a first-time big resource boost and repeatable minor rewards.
The game has a remarkable feel to it. Not quite stellar, but nearly nothing negative on how it works. It is polished, simple, and very focused on its little quest play you go through. I admit its tone is more geared for younger players, but all ages can still find it enjoyable to go through at whatver pace they feel comfortable with.
Its something worth looking at, and nearly a must get on a good sale for the price - especially with what you could get out of it.

Well, I bought this game in a bundle, so I'm pretty sure I'm not the targeted audience but I nevertheless want to share my opinion, especially after seeing those 100% positive reviews.
First the Graphics which are praised by many really didnt do it for me. I can see the individuality in the art style but i genuinly got disgusted by it. All those freaky, hairy and lumpy things just didnt appeal to me. I couldnt find the charm in clicking on insects and watching some creepy shimpanses bath.
Furthermore i found it difficult to actually distinguish relevant from irrelevant spots, to the point where i missed an entire screen because i didnt anticipate that i can walk through a wall of space mushrooms.
The music is relaxing and since there is no voice acting you need to concentrate on, the sound design creates a feeling of smoothness. But the gibberish they talk got somrwhat annoying and some sound effects like the "barking" dog sounded cheap to me.
I have no idea what to say about the story. Firstly because i havent played far, secondly because most of the time you just travel from one seemingly unrelated surreal background to another while clicking on everything hoping it starts an interaction or at best an animation bubble. At least that's what i did.
I guess there has been a planet eating squid you chase on your do it yourself space craft built out of a bathtub but who am i to know. Definitely nothing that kept me on the edge of my seat, let alone wanted me to find out more.
Finally the puzzles. Well most of the time you simply follow the instructions often given through an unskipable animation you have to watch multiple times to really get.
There are those trial and error moments, but nothing unfair. The integrated help, kind of hidden in the simplistic menu interface approach which at first was quite confusing, is lovingly designed and keeps you from wasting to much time, when all you missed is an item from a totally different place.
So they were okay, while one particular card/animation puzzle was really entertaining and positively stood out.
But i missed some real logical challenges.
All in all this is not a bad game, but nothing i would recommend and definitely not a game that should have only positive reviews. It lacks the wit of grim fandango, monkey island or sam and max and doesnt provide a challenge like myst.
Then again i dont think it wants to play in that league.

This game's story is dumb, you guys.
Really dumb.
Look, I grew up on 90s point and click adventure games just like you (
) And if you're looking for something that just captures the spirit of the era - look no further! It checks all the boxes, from the font choice to the art style. You'd swear up and down it was made in the same Scumm engine as Full Throttle and Day of The Tentacle. Hell, it even has the same issues with questionable voice acting quality - Kathy herself is generally well played, but the NPCs around her range from serviceable to downright atrocious.
But here's the thing - the story in this game... its
It starts out fine - a young journalist comes back home to attend her grandfather's funeral, then gets caught up in the mystery of his sudden illness. Cool! But... about halfway through... something terrible happens.
The writers give up.
See, they set up a lot of loose threads to handle. And, frankly, loose threads are fun - they make for interesting stories. Forcing characters to deal with the implications of their decisions is at the heart of any good narrative. Buuuut... rather than commit to that, they start hand-waving in a VERY big way. Investigation starts giving way to "it's magic, yo". And, ultimately, every single major plotline is resolved through magical means. And not interesting, well fleshed out magic, either (looking your way, The Longest Journey.) No... just boring, half-thought-out dream visions and spirit quests.
It's deus ex machina on steroids. And what’s worse is it undercuts the core premise: its not Kathy’s investigation skills that solve the day, but instead these mystical forces directly spelling it out for her.
Look, you’re not a ~bad person~ if you like this game. Playing Kathy Rain won’t give you cancer or kill your dog or whatever.
But frankly, other than the obvious nostalgia hooks, this game is actually a lot weaker than many of the 90s games it mimics. The UX is bad. The game is short. The puzzles are generally so brainless that they’ll take you literally seconds to figure out. So all that leaves is the story it tells.

So growing up, my grandpa had an old Windows 98 PC, and I got stuck playing the few games we had... This game being one of them!

The only downside is that Steam can't track time (cause it's DosBox) but that's an extremely minor complaint... Though I had to spend a lot of time opening and closing the game to reach the 5 min mark so I could actually post this on Steam... Sorry friends for being spammed with my playing MegaRace 1 for about half in hour...
The objective is simple, take out ALL of the other racers before the race is over, by shooting your lazer weapons at them, or smashing into them until they explode. After beating them you get their vehicle to select. Each vehicle has it's own stats and are good/bad depending on those stats. If you don't win, your game is over and your final score is taken and put on the charts. Nothing else to really say. The default controls are odd (and the game doesn't tell you) but you can rebind them.
To be truthful, this game is more FMV's than racing, but you can skip them all... But you won't want to skip any of them as that is where the true heart of the game is, Lance Boyle! The classy and amazing TV show host that brings the humor to the game. Lance Boyle (Christian Erickson) is probably the main reason why people love this game. I know I do!

I bought this game with low expectations, but it was cheap, so I took a gamble.  I was most put off by the poor English in store page and such, considering it seems to be a quasi-fantasy game roughly about the English settlement of North America.
I was pleasantly surprised.  I started playing it, and I did not stop for 7 hours.  Even now, I only stopped playing because I started falling asleep in my chair.
It's a slow-paced, easy-going town-builder in which you grow your "colony" from a single building and a few colonists into a bustling village, complete with trade, jobs, building upgrades, and scientific research.  I really appreciated that it never makes you feel anxious about staying on top of things, like the Anno series can sometimes do.  You totally set the pace in this game, so if you're looking for a relaxing play, this could be for you.
I was surprised by the quality of the game.  While a few things are a bit off--like the way the colonists perform the exact same animation at the exact same time when they talk to one another--the game shows a lot of polish, overall.  I never felt like my enjoyment of the game was being damaged in any way by a lack of effort or expertise on the part of the game's designers and/or developers.
It's a bit like a slimmed down and streamlined Sims meets Farmville meets Anno, without any stressful situations, pushy monetization, or excessive micromanagement.  Overall, I would recommend this game to fans of its genre, though I would not really know what to call it.

One of the best indi games I've played in a looooong time. The art, sound, and overall concept, are unique and original, instead of the plethora of copy\paste trash that plagues the industry. From the second you start playing you know that the devs put all their heart and effort into perfecting the game. I came into this never playing the first two Samorost games, but it didn't matter.
Instantly the art\animations jumped right out at me, and appreciated how detailed thier hand drawn, 2D world looked. Textures are crisp, models are intracately shaped, and every location is unique and detailed to the very last pixel. There is NO copy\paste in any of these scenes, which is pretty amazing. The "2.5D" art style adds a ton of depth to the scenes. Every time I'd switch to a new zone, I would move closer to my screen, trying to pick out every little detail.
The sound design instantly stood out as well, it is truely unique. While it's typical to build the sound around the setting; in Samorost, the setting is built around the sound as well. Most (if not all) puzzles are designed around audio and visual cues to help you solve them. Once you do, random sounds will combine to form musical "riffs" to form a flowing track.
Aside from the ambient music track, all of the sounds are voiced. They are made with a series of mumbles, coos, and grunts that create every sound. The ambient music was soothing yet haunting, calm but upbeat. Very hard to describe, but it helped set the mood even further.
The only con I had was some of the transitions between locations takes a little long, but it gives you more time to appreciate the hard work that must have went into this game for such a small team.
The game gave me ~8 hrs of play to complete the story and collect all of the achievements (I did use a guide to collect a few). There isn't really any replay value, but the game delivered 100% of it's value (for me) in the time I got out of it.
If you have ANY interest in the genre, then you need to play this game. I bought it on sale, but I would have easily paid full price.

Stunning visuals, mesmerising sounds, and a fantastic and unique soundtrack by one of my favourite musicians:
And his music isn't just limited to the background - many elements of the game affect it and vice-versa.
It also features great level design, splitting the game into multiple worlds so that any backtracking between puzzles is shorter distances within the same world. Gameplay is well suited for people of all ages, and may even lend itself better to younger audiences, because it rewards imagination a little more than it does intelligence.

I'd recommend this game to anyone looking for a relaxing game that still makes use of your brain cells. It's great to play alone or with company (as I plan to with my girlfriend). Combine your intellect and observation power!
And if you're unsure about Point and Click games, then this might be the one to win you over. Just wait for a sale and give it a go. I promise that it won't disappoint.

This game's story is dumb, you guys.
Really dumb.
Look, I grew up on 90s point and click adventure games just like you (
) And if you're looking for something that just captures the spirit of the era - look no further! It checks all the boxes, from the font choice to the art style. You'd swear up and down it was made in the same Scumm engine as Full Throttle and Day of The Tentacle. Hell, it even has the same issues with questionable voice acting quality - Kathy herself is generally well played, but the NPCs around her range from serviceable to downright atrocious.
But here's the thing - the story in this game... its
It starts out fine - a young journalist comes back home to attend her grandfather's funeral, then gets caught up in the mystery of his sudden illness. Cool! But... about halfway through... something terrible happens.
The writers give up.
See, they set up a lot of loose threads to handle. And, frankly, loose threads are fun - they make for interesting stories. Forcing characters to deal with the implications of their decisions is at the heart of any good narrative. Buuuut... rather than commit to that, they start hand-waving in a VERY big way. Investigation starts giving way to "it's magic, yo". And, ultimately, every single major plotline is resolved through magical means. And not interesting, well fleshed out magic, either (looking your way, The Longest Journey.) No... just boring, half-thought-out dream visions and spirit quests.
It's deus ex machina on steroids. And what’s worse is it undercuts the core premise: its not Kathy’s investigation skills that solve the day, but instead these mystical forces directly spelling it out for her.
Look, you’re not a ~bad person~ if you like this game. Playing Kathy Rain won’t give you cancer or kill your dog or whatever.
But frankly, other than the obvious nostalgia hooks, this game is actually a lot weaker than many of the 90s games it mimics. The UX is bad. The game is short. The puzzles are generally so brainless that they’ll take you literally seconds to figure out. So all that leaves is the story it tells.

My opinion is a bit divided on this game.  There were features about it that I did enjoy, but ultimately I'd have to say that the negative aspects outweigh the positive.  For me at least.  I'm in the minority opinion here.  I'll start off with the positive.  I liked that all of the dialogue for the game had voice acting, including Kathy's inner thoughts.  You don't get that in most of these kinds of games, so I'll give the game credit for that.  There will be mixed opinions on the quality of the voice acting, but it was serviceable to me.
Within the story, I do like that it tackles some very heavy emotional issues.  This includes mental illness, death and loss, and very imperfect family situations.  It's gritty and dark, but very humane.  I just wish the story didn't trail off and get weaker the further it went.  Along with this, I did like some of the characters quite a bit.  Kathy is a bit inconsistent, but she's mostly likeable.  I thought Goober was funny, though kind of tragic the more you learn about him.  The grandmother also isn't purely the sweet, loveable figure (towards Kathy she is, unquestionably).  She shows some anger and distrust, which gave her more range than most games show towards those kinds of characters.  I thought Eileen was kind of weak though - so over the top in her chipperness and having absolutely no sense of privacy or personal boundaries.  That was hard to swallow.
Something else done well is the art and graphics.  I liked the contrast of the pixel art for the majority of the scene, and the use of more detailed art to show facial expressions.  There were only a few varieties in the sprites though, so it didn't have as much nuance as it could have, but it added much more than only the pixel art would have shown on its own.  One thing I thought was odd about the pixel art is that everyone's eyes are set against a black dot instead of white, which makes them all look creepy.  Not sure why that choice was made.
Starting off in the negative, I would say the story could have been better (and there will be spoilers throughout, fair warning).  Starting off I think it's pretty strong.  It builds Kathy's character pretty well (though she's very contradictory in nature - spiteful and angry, a smart♥♥♥♥♥who's harsh with her words and even actions, like when she won't give a homeless man $10, yet also very soft-hearted in other ways), and develops her family history.  It becomes apparent quite quickly she grew up in a troubled family situation, with her being so estranged from her paternal grandparents, and not so much by choice.
The first couple of days where you try to figure out the basic details of what happened to your grandfather, who might know essential information, and starting to dig through the surface level events to the darker, hidden truth is quite good.  I'd say the second day especially makes you feel like a detective, as you play different people in order to get the tech. set up you need to further explore the clues you've found so far.  The hints are subtle but straightforward enough (very delicate but important balance), with Kathy giving you enough pointers that you're able to get where you need to go (I'm thinking especially with the voice recording manipulation - that was well laid out).
However, it also becomes clear soon enough that the mystery she's trying to untangle about the possible foul play surrounding her grandfather was supernatural in nature.  Nothing in the trailer or game description suggests this, which I feel is very misleading.  The title especially hints at a strong female character unraveling a bigger plot or conspiracy, not trying to work out a paranormal activity that overshadows events in her life and the town she was raised in.  Plotwise the story comes off less like CSI and more like the X-Files, which isn't what I was expecting or really wanting to be honest.  Those sorts of stories are prevelant enough, especially in hidden object games (the closely related cousin to point and click games).
I don't want to beat a dead horse, but the more I think about the overall story of this game, the less it all makes sense.  I would summarize it in these few questions.  Who paid for her grandfather's storage unit the last 14 years that he's been in a vegatative state (those things aren't free and your grandmother knows nothing about it at all)?  Is the Red Man a force for evil or not (key characters flat out say so, but if that's the case his actions with other characters don't make sense)?  Is the Old God legitimate, a real thing, and how does that work stacked up against the Christian God (what's the reality of the supernatural for the game - is this a dimensional rift or what)?  Why is it that Kathy Rain was the only character that had the inner strength to handle the descent into the Abyss, especially when earlier interactions show she was probably more troubled than other people likely would be (dozens if not hundreds of people go missing or crazy because they can't handle it, yet she did)?  I also have to wonder a lot about the church and its members, since the pastor is clearly unhinged and sacrifices people regularly, yet plenty of people go there without reservation (the sheriff being one of them).  It's not that the game doesn't answer these questions that bothers me so much as that the game's story isn't internally consistent.
A few other simple details in the game design bothered me as well.  I didn't like how, later in the game, certain areas you've been to before became grayed out, with you unable to go there anymore.  I feel like the point of these types of games is to allow the player to explore everywhere, even if it's the wrong place, until they figure out the next step to take.  However here those options are taken away, without explanation, which was disappointing to me.  It felt restrictive and didn't give a chance for me to wrap up what felt like unfinished business in those areas either.  It also raises the question of why not just gray out the wrong places for me to go all throughout the game if that's going to be done later on anyways?
Another one is how the game telegraphs that you'll do things later on in the game without any need to do so.  One that comes up very early is the mausoleum - it says you can enter it, long before you have any reason to think to do so, which tells the player you will eventually do that.  Another example of that is after you encounter the Red Man you don't ever see Sue again and don't talk to Nathan until far later in the game.  I wanted to talk with him very shortly after the experience, and while pursuing that goal the option to break into their cabin comes up.  There's no reason to do so since they aren't there (and the event where you need to do it isn't triggered until much later), but despite Kathy saying she won't do things needlessly, especially something that drastic, you're able to break in, even though it's entirely pointless.  That seemed out of character and weird for her.
There are other nitpicks I have, but they aren't worth mentioning at this point.  I would say overall that I'm disappointed by the direction the story took in this game, especially since there are some pretty glaring plot holes and inconsistencies, along with plain unanswered or unexplained aspects to it.  Especially since it started off so strongly, with the game showing real promise in the first few days.  So for me, I can't say that I would recommend this game.  However, if a mystery game delving into the supernatural isn't a turn-off or a negative for you, then like many who have played this game, I'd say there's a very good chance you'd enjoy this.  I would have myself, but it just fell flat for me by the end.

Before I start. I bought this game for three main reasons.
1. I'm waiting for a huge back catalog of Porn to download from a server before I cancel my server.
2. I like bus games. I like Tycoon games. And, the developer notes look like they were made in Google Translate. I'm excited.
3. Looks to have quite easy to gain achievements and isn't going to make me want to end myself trying to gain them.
Now for the review.
If you are running BullGuard, this game is going to flag up as a Suspicous File. You're going to have to whitelist the application for it to run at all. The reason for the false flag is BullGuard loves to think anything that has an Uninstall file is bad.
This game has no graphic settings or an actual menu system. Once you open it, your screen will go black and then just throw you into the game tutorial. It would be  nice for the game to have some basic Graphic Settings, such as decrease the UI size. The UI is extremely blurry FullScreen on a 1920x1080 23" monitor.  It did, however look fine on my 18" DELL piece of crap monitor.
You have to build the roads between the towns, place bus stops as well as place traffic lights and such. One thing I would suggest is definitely going through the tutorial at the start of the game.
I didn't even realise there was one, so if you need to start it again (it does not restart your game, it's more just hints if anything else) just press the Settings Cog on the left hand side of the screen and it'll restart the hint tutorials for you. You're going to accidently place a lot of stuff as well. Why? You place roads with right click... but you also navigate around the map with right click. Werid.
The game runs nice, and it's quite a peaceful wee game, it does not have any background music (by default) however, so a lot of the time you're literally just watching some buses move without any music or anything, which can get a little dull. There's a guide though that shows you how to enable music.
You start off with two buses, both gasoline, and as you progress through the game you unlock more buses (diesel etc). One problem is though, is that the game doesn't actually tell you how you  progess to unlock more buses. Something I did eventually figure out though, was that if you purchase that type of Gas, IE. Diesel and have it in your Gas Station, you can then buy that type of bus. So from the looks of it, you have to purchase the gas type, to then purchase the bus. Which makes sense, it just doesn't tell you.
Once you have a few buses going, the game does start to go a lot faster and you do gain money quite a bit faster. The money that you gain *only* goes towards buying new buses though. You can place roads, bus stops and whatever else you like without having to pay. Which I thought was quite odd but I'm not going to complain since Buses cost between $750,000 and $2,000,000. Ouch.
A small, yet very annoying bug, is that when you want to right click on the Service Station to purchase a new bus, you have  to be on the Settings Menu to do so, or it won't pick it up, as it thinks  you're wanting to place an item like a road or something. This also applies when you want to Right Click on a bus to change it's path, sell it or send it to the Garage. It seems like they need to add a specific button on the side of the screen that let's you click on these things. It wouldn't be an issue doing it with the Setting sbutton, but it flings a small menu out across your screen at the same time, which is a bit annoying. It does seem that at some points however, that you can click on buses & service station without having to be in the settings menu, again an odd bug, it seems like it doesn't always pick up the click.
Something the game doesn't tell you during the tutorial, or really anywhere, is that your buses run out of fuel and need to be serviced. On the top right of the screen there are some small icons, with numbers under them. (Some have locks when you start the game), these are how many barrels of that specific gas type the Gas Station has left. If it runs to 0, you have to buy more gas - by right clicking on the gas station, something the game does not tell you.
Once you hit 10 days of service, you get a reward of $750,000. Enough to purchase a new, cheapest, bus. This applies to each type you hit a new milestone, 20, 30, 40 & 50 days.
For just under 2GBP, it's a good game that I am enjoying. I'll probably only play it a few times, and then it'll end up gathering dust in m Library, but a good game none the less. It does definitely seem like it should be on Mobile, and not a PC game, which may explain why it has no Graphic Settings what-so-ever, however.
If you're looking for a cheap game to kill some time, I'd definitely recommend it - but don't expect this amazing huge game, because it's far from it.

Like a good sequel should, Secret of the Magic Crystals: Secret of the Magic Crystals doesn’t ignore the formula of fast, fluid gameplay that has made the series famous, but introduces a unique new premise, unprecedented player personalization, and sweeping changes that breathe new life into the multiplayer experience. It’s over-the-top and at times unnecessarily complex, but serves both current and next-generation consoles with ambitious new ideas and tremendous replay value
Much like its predecessors, Secret of the Magic Crystals appeals to a wide audience, from veteran fans to timid newcomers by challenging them to become knowledgeable trainers or fill the up the encyclopedic Pokedex. Thanks to an impressive amount of depth from elemental-based combat, it manages to pull off this difficult task right from the start.
You're a courier in these troubled times with no defined background. Just a seemingly regular guy or gal, you're tasked with delivering a package to the New Vegas strip, but let's just say complications arise. Though the story provides pops of color and a few necessary minor twists to keep things interesting, it's predictable just the same. There are three possible endings to the main quest, and similar to Fallout 3 at launch, once you complete it you won't be able to continue your journey through the wastelands unless you re-load an old save. This is a bummer, especially since that was a major complaint with Fallout 3 and Bethesda later fixed it with downloadable content.
Finally, one subtle, but important improvement that has been made in Secret of the Magic Crystals is its brilliant considerations for two- and three-player games. You can now turn off the computer-controlled opponents entirely, and the mini-games all adjust to your group size in clever ways. Secret of the Magic Crystals veterans will no doubt recall the monotony of waiting for a computer-controlled player to take a turn, and the pathetic artificial intelligence on display in mini-games.
The Verdict
Secret of the Magic Crystals isn't a good video game. It's arguably not even a fun one. But its no-frills approach and exacting, relentlessly repetitious gameplay make it an addictive short-term distraction for the skill and score-obsessed. It's an unicorn that sings only one note, and though it sings it well, it does so while flying needlessly low to the ground.

I bought this game on a sale and I cannot believe how much value I have extracted from the several dollars I paid for it.
I absolutely love trains. I love riding them, I love reading books about them, I visit museums full of olf locomotives and railrodiana, anything under the sun that is related to them I try to include in whatever I do. So it is a mere formality when I found this little gem on Steam. It went straight to my cart and on to check out.
The learning curve was a bit steep since this was only my second train game. I did learn eventually through trial and error. I will say that about 30-40 hours of my playing time was devoted to learning. Despite having to restart, I loved every minute of it. While it says that I have 155.3 hours on record, this should be higher as oftentimes I would play offline. (not sure if Steam track this or not, or when they started tracking if they did).
I cannot recommend this game enough. I think anyone who adores trains and is hooked by them will have a good time with the game. Gamers who enjoy management and economy games will elso enjoy this, provided that they learn the basics of track, terminals, and such.
The campaign is a big challenge. I have not completed the campaigns yet as some of them are quite difficult. The game has tons of replay value. If you are tired of the maps in the base game, there are online communities that offer user-generated maps that you can try. The campaigns alone have a ton of replay value as there are bronze, silver, and gold win conditions. I have been aiming to win gold on campaigns that I have already finished.
If you have any questions about the game, especially if you want to know what to expect, feel free to contact me and I will be happy to respond.

- management is challenging. Staff wages and upkeep costs of rides are so high that You actually have to work to make some money and plan ahead.
- Building coasters is extremeley fun. You can do pretty much anything. Last night I built a looping coaster and suddenly my nephew demands, that the loop is inverted, so that the people are actually not riding inside the loop but on top. Two clicks and it was done. Quite genious.
- Decorating and building structures piece by piece is - in my opinion - much easier than in RCT3. The whole system seems more intelligent.
- Fulfilling different more or less challenging goals each mission gives You points which You can invest to buy new scenery or types of rides or blueprints for rides and buildings. I like that system. Gives You something to work for.
I also experience that the game freezes once per start. But that freeze takes about ten seconds and then the game runs perfectly smoothly. Definitely not a reason for a thumbs down.
TL;DR
The game is very good. Not at all as broken as the reviews make it seem to be.

Battleborn is not Overwatch. They are barely similar. One is a first person MOBA, the other is a hero based arena shooter. That being said, I'm not here to argue which is better. You shouldn't play Battleborn though, unless you want a tedious 8-ish hour single player campaign. The multiplayer is nonexistant, so I literally could not play it other than with bots. It has some interesting concepts and it seems to translate pretty well from your DOTA/League to a first person format.
The rest of this will just be about the single player. You level your character between two options, and you redo this every mission. Some characters have upgrades that funtamentally change how they play, like the DLC lizard assassin man, who you can turn into a glass vampire instead of being a DOT dealer. However, others have basic stat buffs and such, and are pretty boring as a result. The robot sniper is just that, buffs and casting ranges. You go up to level 10, and that seems like not much, but the levels drag out to DOTA lengths.
Each level is what you would think. Go to A, defend B for three waves, move to C, defend D for three waves. It's super boring a lot of the time. All the time, actually. The color palette for each level is also the same throughout the whole thing. There is no visual variety, making even looking at the game a chore. Enemies all practically act the same; rush and hit you, stay back and shoot you, throw things at you, or spawn enemies to do the first three. They don't dodge or coordinate at all. Right before each mission starts, the same unskippable poorly animated animation plays, and it lasts around thirty seconds. Or it at least feels that long.
There is a gear system which is super bizzare to me. You find gear in the levels either in chests (that function identically to Borderlands) or get them off bosses. You then have to go back to the main menu and open up the gear to see what you actually get. After this, you equip it, and have to go in game to unlock it for that mission with the in game currency that you only earn for that level. This applies to the multiplayer as well. The gear is only just stat boosts with some occasional downsides. Just stat decreases.
Optimization is poor. Even Borderlands ran badly. I have a 1070 and a 1500x, and sometimes I drop to 50 when looking somewhat far away. It's not acceptable, especially after so long. Battleborn isn't even graphically impressive. It looks like an early 7th gen game through and through.
And yet, I don't even mind it. I finished the story, even though it was terrible, the writing was laughable, and the cartoon animations are DeviantArt levels of unfinished, unpolished and just annoying. I think the gunplay is just solid. Melee characters are usually really interesting to play as, especially the lizard man previously mentioned. I can't really explain what compelled me to finish it, but I don't think it's the worst thing ever made. Not like Randy Pitchford's live performance of his original song.

Initially I refunded this game, because I personally despise turn based RTS style combat based on invisible dice rolls, but after several months I repurchased this game and decided to play it just so I could experience the story. I have removed all revealing verbs, nouns, and proper nouns to give as little away as possible about the story.

When you start the game, you will be given the option to play as one of three

affect your clothes (a very nice little intricacy) and your stats
and
leveling up. I've always been a great fan of upgradable statistics and character evolution; especially in the Star Wars universe. KotOR does levelling up rather nicely, although there is a level cap, which may be annoying to master dice roll manipulators who are experts in the art of turn based fighting. There are also Powers and Feats which can be unlocked when leveling up. Feats include passive and active abilities that are mostly not related to Force powers. Powers are soley Force powers and some force powers are classed as Dark Side and others as Light Side. Fortunately (or maybe unfortunately for some), these powers
affect your morality meter, however, a player aligned with the light will use more force points for using Dark Side powers.
A very well used party system is one of this game's best strengths. Your party can only be made up of 3 members (including yourself), although this was saddening for a different reason than you may expect of most games. In KotOR, party members will talk to each other, talk to you and certain characters will comment on their

on their

that characters you take with you change their opinions of you depending on how you act, but I can not confirm this, since I don't have time to play the entire story analysing how every single character combination reacts to me throughout the game.
The combat in this game is not my cup of tea. Leaving everything to chance and hidden dice rolls is just too unrealistic, even for a video game. However, the element of chance can make you feel like a stormtrooper from the original trilogy when using a blaster rifle and the look and sound of the blaster bolts is true to the movies.
and lightsaber combat is quite good, although the speed at which you dispatch enemies varies on your stats so if you've focused less on combat stats and more on charisma, then fights are going to be more difficult. There are a variety of different attack types for sabers and firearms which makes combat more interesting and some enemies are more susceptible to certain attack types. A variety of grenades also proves to be most useful in combat.
The lightsaber customisation is definitely very solid, with crystals being used to change blade colour (although this never affects the story, which I believe it should) and 2 slots for crystals modifying damage output and more. The hilt models are rather disappointing as they look like watered down Darth Sideous hilts, but I never paid much attention to them anyway.
My major gripe with the gameplay, which I feel was a genuine issue, as opposed to a personal displeasure of mine, was the number and difficulty of the fetch quests. I feel like even the game itself knew this was an issue as some of the dialogue options were "Why can't you go and get this yourself?" with some feeble excuse which equated to "I would if I could, which I can, but I don't want to die so I'll make you do it instead". Sometimes, the main story had what I call "obscure fetch quests", which have the same gameplay as a conventional fetch quest (go from point A to B, do something at point B, and then come back) but you wouldn't even fetch something or have the opportunity to gain many Dark side or Light side points. These appeared fairly frequently, although the story is always developing no matter what you're doing, so these quests don't feel so tedious when you actually play them. Usually, they would yield a reward of some sort when completed.
There are some rather difficult logic and maths puzzles within the game, and I'm ashamed to say that I couldn't actually work all of them out, considering this game is rated 12+. There is also one scene in the game which actually disturbed me for a couple of minutes since it was much gorier than any Star Wars game I've played in the past.
KotOR has a very nice morality system. I love the playermodel changes which come with falling to the Dark Side and I have never seen that in a Star Wars game before.
When speaking to characters, there are almost always the same set of response types: the nice, the neutral, the rude, the interrogative, the Light, and the Dark. At first, it's hard to tell whether rude is the same thing as Dark side responses, but fortunately, they are not, since I managed to become as evil as possible on the meter and I almost never said anything obnoxious. I also enjoyed the realistic remarks friendly party NPCs would make after I said something hideous or did something monstrous. I assume they would do something similar if I was on the Light Side, although since my first playthrough was Dark, I have not experienced this.
Much like in Star Wars lore, the Dark Side is corrupting and I noticed that if I said something threatening, it would often pay off. I then began to almost always risk conflict if it meant getting my own way. I always try to play RPGs as if I am myself, so being able to choose answers that are most like what I would say if it was real, but still ending up with my desired final outcome made the story extra gripping because it played out how I wanted it to. KotOR does a good job of letting you alter the story in subtle and also large ways so that you feel as though you are not being told a story, but that you are actually in it and affecting it.
A couple of inconsistencies plague the morality system, such as your party members not even commenting on the colour of your blade if it is red, and them trusting you even if you are obviously aligned with the Dark Side.
