With only little time played, it may seem difficult to take this review seriously but I think everyone can agree on the validity of these points.
- Multiplayer desperately needs a save feature - I can not stress this one enough, playing an RTS game with friends in one sitting is a major drain.
- Camera movements are clunky. There is no diagonal movement for the camera, and you can not zoom in and out whilst moving the camera. It is only zoom or move. This may seem very minor but it noticably affects the fluidity of navigating the map.
- Sending characters to an area by right clicking the desired area on the minimap needs to show a prompt of where I sent them on the minimap. Otherwise I am just clicking in the blind
-Idle animations for characters. After playing a scenario, I noticed that many characters stay in one pose when not in use, greatly reducing immersion/feeling very artificial.
- LAN play. This game does not have LAN play which is a staple to all RTS games. There's nothing like having a room full of people playing and RTS over LAN.
- Voice acting. Maybe I was not paying attention but I think I noticed that no characters have voices. Furthermore, all of the singleplayer is made up of dialogue boxes. Voice acting would further add to immersion of the game.
I dont want to sound like an entitled gamer and hopefully these are manageable and doable features that can be added in.
Feel free to criticize the list.

*The Promised Land' is a casual city building game that works great of you just want some pet game to play for a day or two. The graphics are colourful and cartoonish, and very much reminds you of the sterotypical kids-games, but in a way that didn't bother me, at least. The colonist models are fairly diverse, and only repeated 2-3 times each among 50 colonists. The gameplay is easy enough to grasp, but has a certain pace to it that kept it interesting - despite a few instances of waiting for enough resources to tick in.
The game, however, is also very liniar in the sense that your progression in the game comes from completing a number of quests. These quests do allow some level of "free" development through research, but ultimately limits the type of resources you can get, what buildings you can build and so on to the progress of the questline.
The buildings are limited to fixed, preset locations, so the freedom to make your colony as you want is more or less non-existent
The 7,3 hours of gameplay I've had is a complete run with every challenge and in-game acheivement on the highest level.
All in all I found the game enjoyable to play through, but with little to no replay value. It's probably well suited for people unfamiliar with city-building or management games as a first peak into the genre.

This is one of the best feeling games I’ve played in a while. It just really brings a unique and lovely feel in an industry filled with AAA titles and games that just don’t feel like they were really cared for and used only as a money-making tool. This game feels like the devs put in the time and decided they would rather have a wonderful game than something that would be more marketable. Now I’ll start the main part of the review.
The sounds and music in this game are some of the best I’ve seen. First the soundtrack really draws you in and makes the game 100% more enjoyable. The devs also spared nothing when it comes to "voice acting" and sound effects. They give the characters life and a kind of mystery as well as creating a magical environment. This and the music really make the feel of the game much more relaxed and interesting. Most or every creature and "person" (if you can call them that) has something to say when it/they are interacted with, creating an in-depth environment that draws you in and makes you feel like a part of the little world.
Now we move into the art style of the game. First if you don’t enjoy this art you’re not going to enjoy the game nearly as much as it can be enjoyed. With that out of the way I’ll go into my opinion (because I know how much you wana hear it). I personally love the art and the characters wouldn’t be nearly as charming without the beautiful design of the game. Every area seems like a moving and living photo that you can interact with and traverse. The creatures of the game also have a very interesting look and will usually stand out from the terrain but not to a point where they look out of place. In fact, most of the creature’s match flawlessly with the place that they dwell and have a fitting "personality" for what they look like and where they live.
really love the art and it is really a key part of the game as I see it.
The puzzle aspect of this game is somewhat lacking as most of the time they are very easy or do not have anything to do with the story or the situation. None the less they can be a lovely way to spend time and the music and art makes it so that it does not seem like your grinding. I would recommend using a guide or walkthrough to help if you’re stuck but that’s up to you and how much you want to do the game on your own. I will leave a few links to good guides and videos down below if you are looking for help.
In all this is a wonderful game and I think it brings a type of play to the table that is very refreshing and magical. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the art and music/sound effects of the game. I picked it up on sale for around $10 or maybe $7 USD and don’t regret one penny. I hoped this review helped you and gave you an idea of what this game entails.

at you and suggests you just mess with them somewhat randomly.
So you get to ride hairy asteroids, pluck moths' antennae, feed giant anteaters, climb termitary holes, and so much more. The plot is rudimentary; this is the story of a gnome-like guy who is attentive enough to hear the music hidden from mundane ears—and when he reproduces it with his small trumpet, magic happens.
Turns out the world is eager to be witnessed—you just need to know how to look.
This must have also been the philosophy that went into making the game. It's precisely due to the creators' shrewd and kind way of looking at things that the numerous creatures they've made turned out so lovely. They're not cute in an exaggerated way! But you're made to care for them due to how well their mannerisms are reproduced or lovingly exaggerated, like a dog making several circles in place before going to sleep, a chamois being tender and easily frightened like an insect, or a nuthatch being Determined Like An Arrow.
The collage-like visuals are impeccable, and the sound design is simply incredible, with many ambient actions seemingly voiced by human voices, which adds to the atmosphere of a fairy tale being told. And, on top of all that,
is also aesthetically original and does not really rely on overused tropes.
A gem, all in all.

Like the name suggests, there's headcrabs, and lots of 'em. You have 8 arenas to fight in, where you kill wave after wave of headcrabs with your crowbar. You'll find power-ups every so often that give you abilities such as faster health regeneration and temporary invincibility. There are different types of headcrabs that each have their own powers, including ones that freeze you to slow you down or burn you for extra damage. It's not an arena shooter - it's an arena melee-er!

A mindless headcrab killing simulator; I can't believe there are people in this world who would encourage such a violent act towards innocent, noble creatures like the fragile headcrabs. All you do in this game is kill headcrab after headcrab, including some of their rarer varieties, like the elusive fast headcrab (not the black variety, and much rarer one that almost looks like normal headcrabs); the mischievous fire headcrab; the calm ice headcrab; the shy poison headcrab; the powerful electric headcrab; the mysterious ethereal headcrab; and the strange hallucinogenic headcrab. Not only that, this game has several arenas for you to kill the poor, defenseless headcrabs in many ways; from using a simple crowbar, to using machine guns. It even grants you different power ups to enhance your headcrab killing; and, to make matters worse, it gives you more points the more headcrabs you kill, while an ominous voice celebrates your killing spree. Simply horrible.
However, there's an upside to all this violence. As time progresses, the headcrabs will grow stronger, until they finally overwhelm you. This is inevitable, no matter what you do. Perhaps, in my anger, I was too quick to misjudge the dev, thinking he encouraged this violence. It is clear to me now, that the dev's intention was to show us that, no matter how tough a situation might become, the weak will finally be able to overcome their foes; how nature is able to, eventually, find a way. And for that, I think, this game deserves to be played. Sure, it might be a horrible situation to go through, being forced to kill so many innocent creatures, but when the real message of the game begins to reveal itself, when the situation inverts, and all those headcrabs you juggled away begin to do that to you, you'll realize it was worth it.
All joking aside, this is an entertaining game. It's nothing more than random arenas where you can kill headcrabs, but it can be fun to play for a few minutes a day when you want to vent some frustrations. I recommend it.

It's a simple story, man loves woman, she gets kidnapped, you save her by fighting evil. Simple controls, intuitive, and very responsive. There's no confusion, everything is clear cut and you barely give off any sweat. That is for the first part of the game.
This game ramps up in difficulty as you soon get familiar with the movement, combos and controls. Does it stop ramping up in difficulty? Yes, after you beat the game. There's something in there from a range of genres. It's at time a complex puzzle game using game mechanics that you thought you were familiar with. Sometimes it's a gauntlet of enemies that you punish yourself for careless moves. Other times it's a Super Meatboy precision-esque platformer that can frustrate you, yet give you that burst of euphoria when you pass a certain stage.
It's a 2-4 hour game to just finish the story. Extra 1-5 hours of the optional bonus stages and maps.
The multiplayer portion is greatly to be desired for. It makes the game more fun. It works smoothly and allows for a shared adventure that is no different from playing by yourself, except of course, you have someone to share the memory with.
There's very little one could ask for to make this game any better.

I've checked out the other negative reviews and they're primarily relating to not running on Windows 10 (so far has run fine on mine) or technical graphical issues.  My issue is more primary.  I came to this backwards from Railroad Tycoon 3 and Railroad Tycoon 3 is so much better in my opinion I can't recommend this version.  Play 3 instead.
So why the hate ?  Hate is putting it rather high, more annoyance and frustration.
1)  Sid Meier can't resist over complicating the format.  He does this with the later Railroads by introducing junctions.  Here and in 3 the far more workable solution of the lower priority train stopping and ghosting out and having to restart when the higher priority train has passed works since acceleration is very slow early in the game and having too many trains on the same track rapidly reduces everything to a crawl.  The solution is to have double tracks (available in game) or bypasses where geographically possible so you just go directly between major cities avoiding the small towns in the middle.  In 2 (as in Railroads) the main problem is this: -  you have to preselect the carriages and thus the cargo for each leg of the journey.  Since you can rapidly get to the situation of having dozens of trains running trying to keep an eye on cargo becomes impossible so I've defaulted solely to transporting mail and passengers between towns and cities.  3 makes things FAR easier.  You set the number of carriages your train takes and your train simply picks up the most lucrative cargo at each spot - unless you give it specific instructions.
2) The economy is fritzed and you can't build industries to fix it.  So at the start of the game most cities need lumber but although there are logging camps generously scattered around the map there are only one or two lumber yards which may be on the other side of the map from your network. Without the capacity to build yourself cities don't grow.  It's also far, far more difficult to see which cargo is where on the map than it is in 3.
3)  The train animations are poor even for 1998 standards.  In 3 you have the option to fix your camera on your train and just watch it go back and forth at the start of the game when you are waiting for income to expand.
There are a few minor areas where 2 has the edge on 3.  There are far more comprehensive station additions than in 3 (and in 4 this would be a worthy area for expansion).  Trains get serviced, and topped up with water and sand in stations rather than in separate installations (which is significant because it reduces the number of times the train has to stop on a journey).  And the key issue is that trains in 2 seem signicantly more reliable than in 3 where the late stages of the game involve memorising which of your sixty engines has broken down so you can replace it after it is repaired because both games have the annoying mechanic that you cannot replace an engine at the time it is actually broken.  The mechanics of 3 makes it more difficult to expand a station than it is in 2.
My problem with Railroad Tycoon 2 is that compared to Railroad Tycoon 3 it has far worse graphics, less tactical playability, and is simply less fun.  Railriad Tycoon 3 also bookends with an awesome opening sequence with the perfect theme tune and an elegaic end scene for the campaign. The Gist:
Complexity: Not newbie friendly. It's not Dark Souls hard, it's just confusing with all the information thrown at the player. So many characters with no tutorial for them. You have to play every character or watch a video to learn what's what and who's who. That, and single player is made extremely difficult due to the low playerbase.
Playerbase: It's low... like I've felt more community in playing Duck Hunt than this game. If you don't mind playing by yourself, play Ark Survival Evolved on Single player or Minecraft.
Graphics: Meh. I've never liked the Borderlands look. It's not bad, but it doesn't feel smooth like Monday NIght Combat which has similar graphics but did so much better.
Gameplay: I think a downfall of this game is that it tries to do too much. A MOBA, a scenario-based shooter. Gear-system. It doesn't seem to do anything well.
Price: If you want the game, buy a new hardcopy on amazon or something. Unlocks the bulk of the game for less than what you pay if you upgrade  from freemium. Freemuim seems pretty lousy considering the number of characters that will be locked to you for a long time and that you are confined to multiplayer (an obvious ploy to help people with the full game find people to play with online.)
Overall: I actually feel bad for spending the 8 bucks to get this game. The time it took to install the game was longer than the amount of time I desired to play this game. It's dead, it tried, but so many other games do it better. Play Paladins or stick to Borderlands or something. It's not worth it at all.

I'm recommending this game only because it's indie, and free to play. If you're looking for a quick read with simple achievements, or if you don't mind a slightly confusing story that breaks its own mood this game is for you. If you want to know why I'm on the fence about recommending this game, read the entire review below.
For a free indie visual novel, Sepia Tears really is not too bad. I've had this game sitting in my library for the longest time, waiting to be played, and I finally gave it a chance for the holiday season, seeing how the game takes place just before Christmas Eve.
The story had me confused most of the way through the novel, up until the ending when they finally drop everything that's going on and has been going on into your lap without using the subtle pronoun game. There's little to no exposition going on until the last chapter, and even then it takes you a moment to realize what's going on. The entire way through the meat of the novel, the characters talk about "what happened" without ever saying what it is, and it leaves the reader confused. To me that just feels lackluster, even if the ending resolved most of it. For a story that tries to be heartwarming and real, it just didn't have me feeling anything until the very end. I didn't feel like I connected or understood any of the characters or what they stood for. I feel like the writing could've been much better, and stuck to what it was trying to accomplish. Most of the way through the game you're jerked between playful conversation, then right into a heartfelt conversation with no warning. People have said this seems "more real" but for a visual novel I feel like it should've either been done better, or not at all.
The art style is different than most visual novels, that like their polished typical-anime-style. If you like the art style that is typical of most anime/visual novels, you won't find it here. While the art feels rough and hand drawn at first, it still has its charms and grows on you the longer you spend reading through. The soundtrack is well made, but tends to cycle frequently enough that what's about to happen is very predictable depending on what track is playing.
I just couldn't fully get into this game. I found myself just wanting to "get through it" rather than being excited to see how things were resolved. For some people that might not be a big thing, but as an avid reader of both regular and visual novels, it just didn't do it for me.

A nice romance VN. It's mostly kinetic, there are a couple choices here and there but they won't affect the story overall, just change a few scenes. At first I found the characters obnoxious and the weeb humour annoying, but the writing and character development made up for these early-game problems. Despite Japanese influences everywhere, it doesn't take place in Japan, but rather in an unnamed Western city famed for its winters. I decided it would be set in Canada, since only bears and bear hunters live in Alaska.
+ Great writing. Towards the end it becomes excellent. The pacing is extremely slow and will probably bore many people to death, but I found it added some kind of surreal tone that contributed a lot to the atmosphere.
+ Interesting characters. They might feel annoying at first, and most of them seem like stock high school romance characters you may find in any shojo manga, but like any good shojo manga does, the side characters really make the story shine by adding relief (I ended up genuinely caring for the protagonist's sister and his best friend, both irrecoverable weebs I wanted to strangle at first), and the main characters are well-written.
- Low production values. Art is kinda hit-or-miss (although it renders the characters' emotions quite well), backgrounds are pretty generic, UI is downright awful outside the title screen. Music is good (particularly "For a Moment", which I absolutely loved), but sadly the sound quality isn't at the same level.
7/10 A good way to pass a wintery afternoon if you like VNs. Please don't breeze through this for the achievements. There's a nice story in there.

I find this novel rather enjoyable. It offers a pretty decent plot and characters. Although the story telling may be a little sloppy (IMHO) but still enough intriguing. And since the game's free, I recommend every VN fan to at least try it once.

The artwork and the general graphics, just to start with something, are awesome and feature many different styles. It's clear that the developer put lots of work in designing manga-like characters, detailed backgrounds and cute little cutscenes (you can see some of them in the screenshots!!) :)
The story is quite long and on the romantic side; the main characters are Myra and Mark and deals with emotional memories and feelings and so, I'm not surprised it touched many players.. and I've been one of them!
Although the story can be completed in little time, I definitely suggest you to read through it all and of course explore the different choices since it's not kinetic and you can change the events :)
And as I said, the story is focused on memories and on Mark's past - he's a 18 years old boy - and Myra well, it's one of the most beautiful female characters I've encountered in romantic visual novels. Even if the story revolves around the two of them (and it unfolds in a 7 days period of time) it deserves to be fully read.. as I told you before, don't rush through it 'cos it's not a short novel if you don't skip anything and with the help of great music and artwork it's really a pleasant experience.
Take your time and wait to get involved fully in the story, I read some reviewers that didn't manage to get involved and many others that needed some time and yeah, I'm definitely one of them.. it's not immediate, even if it's an indie novel and one can think it isn't deep. It's definitely deep, and Mark's monologues are very introspective and interesting. You'll probably need to give yourself some time to delve deep into the story and well, probably most of the players also can relate with the protagonists and feel something that they have experienced in their past in reading the two's memories and the diary..
Plus, the game has many hints of humour and well, whenever I thought I was on my way to discover something new the game made me re-think and put me in front of another twist in the story. I'm not writing it of course just not to spoiler it XD And because it's all free and you'll be put into it right when you click on Start Game on Steam :)
Unfortunately there aren't donation options and DLCs, the developer told us that they have been asked from lots of players to add them (or a sequel, or expansions) but I think that it's been months that they didn't add anything so well, it's still 100% free.

From the first moment I played Botanicula, I held it close to my heart as my favorite Amanita and, overall, one of my favorite games. Half of that was completely obliterated by playing Samorost 3; Botanicula is still a personal favorite, but Samorost 3 reached such a sky-high baseline in character development, design, art direction, voice acting, music, storytelling and gameplay, that my heart has no response other than to cater it even closer than it already did Botanicula.
Amanita Design outdid themselves with this gem of a game, going beyond the already superb heights they reached with their previous works of art.
With a charming flute-playing character as its lead and a universe to explore, Samorost 3 takes its players through a gorgeous and heartfelt adventure towards inner and outer recovery. What begins as a quest to build a ship escalates into an epic battle of colossi orchestrated by coincidences big and small. Like all other Amanita games, the puzzles are not tough to solve and the achievements are a delight to strive for — and do actually add to the story! The whole that Samorost 3 forms is one of charm and charisma without excluding tense moments and a touching finale.
In conclusion, I couldn't recommend Samorost 3 more. Its amazing story, its gorgeous views and its outstanding sound work make it not only one of the casual puzzle games I love the most, but also one of the best I've ever played.
PS: If you, like me, fell in love with this game, check out Floex's "Samorost3 Pre​-​Remixes EP (Free DWNLD)" at Bandcamp.

It's a fun game, it really is. I expected some solid game from Gearbox, and they delivered. The characters are cool and unique, voice acting is quite ok, gameplay is enjoyable.
BUT
There are a couple of reasons why this game just did not work, and why I can't give it a recommendation DESPITE liking it:
-The game at first glance might feel like an Overwatch clone, or a weird mixture of Overwatch and League of Legends, and if there's anything you DON'T want to do is being compared to an already existing game with better reviews, especially if you're trying to sell your own game for 30€. Hell, I got it from a bundle and I still don't think I am getting my money's worth. That's one of the major reasons this game is practically dead: It's been overshadowed by other titles that are either free (LoL) or have been getting better reviews from the get-go (Overwatch). The gameplay structure of a MOBA shooter seen in this game just didn't seem that much appealing to people, it seems.
-The game is VERY badly optimized. Compared to Borderlands games I've been having some serious issue getting this game to work properly, and I'm still not satisfied with my FPS at times while already severly crippling my experience from visual standpoint. If the game is unplayable despite setting the graphics lower than what I've got running flawlessly in Borderlands 2 then you know you have an issue.
-A major problem of the game is its lack of clarity in terms of actual gameplay. The game is FILLED with colors and objects, the problem is that it's all done in such a way it cripples one's perception. I happened to end up being attacked multiple times by melee enemies just because I did not see them coming right up my nose in such an overwhelming environment. And I didn't even get to experience the chaos of multiplayer combat, which is even worse.
-I enjoy the idea of being able to play a game like this by myself, but the game seems to have been more multiplayer-oriented, which does not excuse half-assing the single player campaign. You either dedicate yourself to making a fully-fleshed out, enjoyable single player experience, or you don't do it at all. I also wouldn't mind playing with some solid AI at this point, so I could at least have a chance to enjoy supportive characters outside of multiplayer.
-Another major issue is that there's alot of content that's locked away, yet another problem with a buy2play format of the game. Free2play games can afford locking up additional content and characters behind in-game currency, but if I've already bought the game for actual money I'd expect all the characters being available from the start. Nobody likes having to grind through the game for the sake of experiencing it fully, and every dollar spent on a game that makes you do that anyway only amplifies the distaste. AND there's microtransactions, that's basically a desperate cry for help from whoever is willing to play this game.
So, do I recommend this game? Definitely, but not in its current state. The playerbase is practically non-existant for multiplayer, and for people enjoying single-player only the game is not optimized well enough to enjoy it fully. Moreover, bad optimization overall and visually unclear environment cripple both single and mutliplayer experience. And for this amount of money one should not have to grind through the game for content or pay additional fees. I give this game a 5/10, but mostly because I like Gearbox, even if they did screw it up with this game.

Nancy Drew grew up, got an edge, and became entangled in a dark local mystery involving the supernatural. That might be enough to convince you to play Kathy Rain, but if it's not, read on.
Kathy Rain is a wonderful graduation for those of us who grew up with HerInteractive's Nancy Drew series. Many of us also had a (perhaps handed down) NES, Atari, or Game Boy, so we've a nostalgic love of pixels. We're also a bit generationally jaded, sharing Kathy's world-weariness and sarcasm. There's a darkness in both the character and the game that feels personally relevant.
Not in that demographic? No problem. Kathy Rain holds appeal for any fan of point and click mysteries. Bonus appeal if you're a fan of the supernatural and slightly macabre, and you like seeing it in pixels. The game is logical in its progression; if you get stuck, just try what you would do in real life. There's no tedious haphazard item combination. Puzzles are clean and feasible. Even with full achievements, you can complete the game in ~5-8 hours, so it's a solid adventure that won't eat all your time. (Great spoiler-free achievement guide
.)
Kathy Rain is a satisfying offering in the PnC mystery/adventure genre, comfortable to play with a nice nostalgic aesthetic. You couldn't ask for much more, but the game gives it anyway: an intriguing story and a surprising depth of themes and character. Satisfying, and highly recommended.

Kathy Rain is a story driven game done in a point-and-click style of gameplay.
Pro's:
1. Pixel styled graphics make the game extremely easy to run and a very small download size.
2. A strong female protagonist with depth, a dark history and a ton of guilt.
3. Great voice acting and immersive sound tracks.
4. Surprisingly diverse interactivity with environments that can lead to interesting responses.
5. Mostly simple puzzles and riddles so progress is easy enough for those new to point-and-click games
Con's:
1. The slow beginning gives a false sense of pacing for the rest of the game
2. Some puzzles did seem a little obscure and required a sudden burst of 'thinking outside of the box'.
3. Without spoilers; the end of the game seemed to reach out a little from what starts as a solid and down to earth detective's tale.
4. After tying up all logical ends the game seems to bait at a sequel or at the very least ends on a rather predictable note.
Pro/Con??? : There were no credits at the end... Personally I like to pay respects to those who make such an entertaining game as Kathy Rain.
Conclusion:
Kathy Rain is a promising first game for the developers and for the most part stays true to what it promises. I'd highly recommend it to anyone who wants to break into the point-and-click field or any one who is looking for a fairly good, story driven experience. For the 7-9 hours it takes to play this game I would certainly put it on my 'to play' list if you're at the very least intruiged.

BEWARE: Guacamelee should be labeled as "REQUIRES CONTROLLER" on Steam. Do not buy this game if you intend to play using mouse and keyboard unless you were born with extra fingers or like to include your toes in your gameplay.
During the area Tule Tree, right after you get the double jump move, the game becomes physically impossible to play with a mouse and keyboard.
The game does not recognize multi button mice, so I resorted to the following mapping:
LMB - attack
RMB - special
WASD - directions
Shift - grab
Alt - roll
Space - jump
Q - "change worlds"
E - "chicken mode"
Here is an example of a jumping puzzle which is plain impossible with keyboard and mouse - you have to roll through a hedge, hold the roll to avoid damage, as you are falling down a precipice double jump, then execute an uppercut and grab the wall. This translates to:
direction + roll + hold roll
jump
direction + jump
up + RMB + hold grab
all within less than 1 second. Anothe example - you are between two walls, one has spikes, the other doesn't and the distance between the walls is wide. You have to bounce between walls and "change worlds" while in the air to move the spikes from one wall to the other. This translates to (assuming starting on a left wall):
hold grab
jump + right + jump + change world + grab
If the distance between the two walls is too wide, you may have to thrown in an uppercut which transpates to:
hold grab
jump + right + jump + change world + up + RMB + grab
all in half a second.
Nope, thank you very much.

Before I start my review, here's an important tip that I had to look up:  When you're establishing a connection between two cities, you need to have a train that travels to and from the cities.  It's not enough to have the cities connected by just track.
I played this game for dozens of hours as a kid.  I loved trains, and I absolutely loved messing around with trains from different times and places.  I loved building working railroads between places I knew, especially in my own state.  (The Minneapolis to Duluth route was something I always did.)
Now, over ten years later, this game has aged wonderfully, and I can play it more seriously and understand its depth.  The UI is very handy, and after a bit of exploring you'll figure out where most things are.  For a 1998 economic simulator game, it's really easy to understand and play.  If you've played any of the Rollercoaster Tycoon games, you can learn this game especially easily.  The music is also great.  It's not the best game music, but it really adds to the mood and it fits the tone of the game perfectly, helping to suck you into the world of railroading.
There's a huge number of locomotives available depending on the map, and they all have their strengths and weaknesses.  The GG1, for example, is a fantastic locomotive when it unlocks at 1935, and it's electic fuel source is very cheap to pay every month.  However, it has a high up-front cost, and it can only operate on tracks you've built with electric wires that can power it.  (Though, if you can pay for it, do it; the GG1 is one of the best locomotives in the game considering its cost-benefit ratio.)  They need fuel, sand, and maintenance, which come from station upgrades.  A train that runs out of sand will take forever to climb the most insignificant hill, and a train without oil is at risk of breaking down.  You can counter this by building small stations to refuel your engines on the go, since trains get refitted just by passing by a station with the correct buildings, regardless of if they stop there.
There's a great variety of rolling stock, and it's fun to try and supply a city with the correct goods, which causes that city to produce more for you to ship to other cities.  Steep grades are something you'll have to deal with, and there's also corporate elements in the game like buying and selling stocks, hiring managers with unique bonuses based on railroading's most important maveriks like George Pullman, and even buying out rival companies.  However, I play just fine without messing with the corporate elements very much, so don't worry if that's not your thing.  It never gets in the way of playing with your trains.
The amount of content here is very impressive.  A bunch of campaigns of varying difficulty are available.
More entertaining, however, are the dozens of scenarios ranging from historical (railroading in Italy after World War 2, or the Americna Midwest in the mid-1800s, etc.) and fantastical (helping a royal family build a rail network and create routes connecting their capital to every other city, or being a neutral supplier to two warring countries, etc.).  There's even a full scenario editor, allowing you to create your own content.
If you're a train buff looking for a good train game or like economic simulators, buy this game right now.  It's one of the best video games in both categories, and a strong contender for the very best "Tycoon" game, right up there with Rollercoaster Tycoon 2.  If you've never played either kind of game, strongly consider picking this up.  $5 is a steal for a game this deep and fun.

From Scarlet String Studios comes Sepia Tears, a visual novel about a boy named Mark and a memory he is trying to forget.
I simply downloaded Sepia Tears because it promised to be a short visual novel with a small number of achievements that seemed to be easy enough to complete. I wasn't expecting much from it, so I wasn't really surprised when that was fulfilled.
The story is sad, and romantic, but doesn't offer much other than that. There's a lot of strange things that happen among this, and I'm still convinced Myra is some form of supernatural creature. The story actually confused me a little. Considering it's a 40,000 word visual novel, that takes some doing. I just don't think things were explained as clearly as they could have been.
I didn't really enjoy this game at all. It has its perks, like really well done character designs that are actually quite beautiful, but other than that, this was just a short visual novel to complete for achievements for me. I wish I would have enjoyed it more, but there really wasn't much to be enjoyed about it, for me, personally.

Still, later in the game the story really becomes intriguing - information you get let's you piece things together and slowly uncover the logic behind the main intrigue. Also, as the stakes gets higher, the writing starts feeling much more solid and focused. The plot itself is emotionally engaging, while art and music, even if simple, complements it rather well. The ending, although hidden behind a very nasty mechanic (
), is satifying and to some extent caught me by surprise. My eyes got teary from it, what happens rarely enough to be a recommendation in itself, if you're looking for some feels.
The the art in this game have a bit of an "amatourish" feel to it (especially the character sprites), but for the most part looks nice enough and have quite a distinct style. While there are many prettier VNs on Steam, Sepia Tears' clunkiness makes it stand out in a way, and the production values are still consistent enough to not get in the way of the story.
With very few choices, it's mostly an illustrated romance novel, but one that don't fall for cliches or cheap emotional tricks, but tells a fresh, decently-written story with moments of actual brilliance.

A really interesting look at how to create stories about trauma through horror and the supernatural. A bit Jessica Jones in the Netflicks style: Motorcycle, black hair dye job, leather coat, bad attitude but good heart, trauma gonna fix it, man who identifies with a colour. Not bad just interesting.
Some flaws: Could have used more action, faster pace. Lack of backstory/clear explanation as to the cause or history of the antagonist. Kathy's teenage trauma is really not fleshed out well enough. Suddenly at the end you're like, oh yeah I think I remember that. Was she even tramatized by that? Game didn't bring it across.
Curiosities: About that hair Kathy, I was a bit confused. It's 1995 but Kathy has a emo haircut with underdye job from 2005? Kathy is wearing a get up from 2015 too. Also, where did Kathy get the money for her custom chopper?
Score: 7.8. Speed it up next time and make the origin story and goals a bit clearer. Let's put some pressure on for a little more motivation. See you in episode 2 Clifftop.

Casual management game... assign jobs, be sure to produce food and necessary resources, expand your colony, build new buildings, sends ships out to trade for other merchandise, aquire more citizens, etc.  I finished the game is just under 20 hours, so it has a nice amount of content.

If you've played The Happy Hereafter, Virtual Villagers, or Gemini Lost, you will feel right at home directing the doings of your little burgeoning colony. There are tons of resources to gather, buildings to build and upgrade, and a good variety of areas to explore. You'll gradually manage more and more colonists with varying abilities as you explore the map and make the most of all the land has to offer, as you quest for the fabled Fountain of Happiness.
What surprised me most about the game is an the addition of "pirate battles," which really play more like rounds of Angry Birds. There are 12 of these stages, and they are satisfying and welcome diversions. I could have easily enjoyed many, many more of these battles, but really, the bulk of the game is spent building your colony through gathering and trade.
The Promised Land is a much better game that you might think it would be. Yes, it's casual fare, and it's at the top of its class.

I can understand why this is considered one of the best RPGs ever. It has an excellent plot taking up the Star Wars lore and detailling out what defines the dark and the light side of the force. More than is possible in the movies. The twist for the main character is surprising and clever. The challenges are varied, the character interaction is different depending on the chosen characters. If there is a small thing to criticize, it's how striking the choices for the good and the bad side are. Especially the dark choices are too blunt. No baddie would act so obvious in most instances.
It's reasonably easy. Without optimizing characters too much or studying the stats and their interrelations, it's possible to play through on normal difficulty. The tactical combat is manageable for players like me who aren't into action games. Early on, a combination of grenades and attacks does the trick. Once levelled up, the most battles will be a breeze. The end battle is challenging but not too difficult either with a few good shields and life resources saved up.
My favourite characters to play were Juhani and Zaalbar. I also liked Mission but she's not the best choice in most instances for my playstyle. I also played the evil android frequently. The male non-jedi characters Carth and Canderous weren't that enjoyable and I didn't use them at all in the second half of the game.

Disclosure: I know the devs.
Anyway, the thing is, this isn't, nor it's supposed to be, your regular ARPG. It's a bit old school and roguelike, quite a bit slower then your usual ARPG. It's done by two people only, with a poor budget, and judging by that, the game is good. Not that it has some monthly playing longevity but who cares about that for this price.
Pros:
-Crafting is a pretty cool roguelike element, and it's very random
-Great bosses with interesting mechanics. Too bad the models are meh-ish, but the game is cheap so whatever.
-Many abilities, which you need to find and to have them crafted, not just gained at level up
-Good atmosphere and story. The setting reminds of the original Diablo a lot, dunno why people compare it to D3 which makes zero sense. I guess they only played that one.
-Interesting approach to fighting mobs. Your usual ARPG tells you to go and destroy them by the groups, but you need to be extra careful and sometimes kite them and take them down one by one in Sunken
-Quite cheap
Cons:
-Bad start. Literally, the first hour is the worst thing about this game, which talks of the inexperience of the devs, but the gameplay gets better and better as you progress.
-The game might be a tad slower then I'd like
-Locusts. Yeah, ♥♥♥♥ those guys.

This game has all the key elements necessary to make it a fun game and keep it interesting enough to keep you playing start to finish. The graphics are great, and they never waver from the over all feel of the story.
The sound is fun and engaging, and though I'm not much into Mexican music the music they used in this game is upbeat and high quality.
The story presents itself well, and is pretty straightforward. It’s not convoluted or over blown. There’s only one major twist, but I won't tell anyone what it is. You’ll have to play it in its entirety to find out.
The puzzles are well rounded, and get progressively harder the farther into the game you get, and it can get frustrating, but that's all part of the games charm, just play through them one at a time, and enjoy the experience.
The power progression is easily spaced as far as getting abilities and using them to complete tasks.
There’s not much in the way of back tracking, but some is necessary to get everything in the game, and to accomplish all the achievements.
There are only two things I can think of, as been a slight disadvantage in the game.
First, it requires a controller (trust me on this it's almost impossible without one).
Second, there is a lot of jumping puzzles. If you want to complete everything you'll have to do them, but that's a minimal issue if you have a controller.
All in all this game is a spot on homage to old stile side scrolling adventure games. I can't stress enough that you should pick it up because you won't be disappointed.

The Promised land feels very much like a mobile port to PC - but a very good one. The Art style is pleasant to look at, and the gameplay is easy to learn, but not excessively easy. While likely not for hardcore management or Base-Building players, The Promised Land is good for a few hours of casual gameplay at least, though I wouldn't recomend it at the full seven dollar price. Pick it up on sale if you like management or base building games and need something fresh.

I reccomend this game if you're looking for something very light and can be completed within 10-12 hours.
You know the cycle: Hire workers, build infrastructure, sell excess output, hire more workers, build/upgrade infrastructure, etc.  It's a formula that is perhaps best known in association with Farmville and other "free-to-play" titles. Since The Promised Land has no microtransactions, it never deliberately inflicts you with the pain associated with the more well known fare. Your workers take time to perform their tasks but they usually finish up by the time you've checked your other spinning plates and come back. The game also throws in a poor man's Angry Birds style mini-game to handle your naval engagements. They're not bad, per se, just bland.
Pros:
- Everything, including the gameplay, is totally solid and stable.
- The game ends at that perfect moment where it's still enjoyable but it's started to go stale.
- Excellent controls and UI. It never gets in the way.
Cons:
- A hint or reminder system would be welcome. Do I train someone to be a worker or a farmer before sending them to collect silk? On that note "Worker" could be better named.
- A few more character models would've been welcome. The game's population maxes out at 50, but that 50 is composed of like 6 character models? It's like some lost Eugenics colony.
I'm picking nits though. It's a fun and breezy little game.

Blood Money barely shows its age! I still find it a beautiful game. For me, it was a vast improvement on the previous titles, and I love the introduction of the accidents mechanic. It made all the contracts more fun because there are more ways of killing your targets. I haven't played Hitman yet, so thus far this is the only installment in which I loved all of the missions.

In 2006, IO Interactive presented us Hitman fans with another chronicle-like title in the series, called Hitman: Blood Money. Though unlike the previous title, Hitman: Contracts, Blood Money doesn't recreate previous contracts from past games. And good thing I bring that up.
Now the story of Blood Money is set... before and after Hitman: Contracts. The first few missions are set before Agent 47 returned to his hotel room in Paris, wounded by a bullet, at the beginning of the 3rd game. The rest are all set after the events of that game. But aside from that, I did mention that the whole story is based on a chronicle-like plot. The story really kicks in when Rick Henderson, a reporter, drives to a house for an interview. An interview with none other than the FBI director, Alexander Leland Cayne (you'll probably remember him as the wheelchair guy but it's never explained why), who is aware of The Agency, 47's origins... everything. And he wants 47 dead. And so during this interview, he tells Rick about some of the recent assassinations that happened recently and where our bald clone was involved. As for the Agency's side of the story, they've been getting contracts for 47 and his handler, Diana, who have more than just a... professional relationship, for those of you who didn't play the previous games. No, they're not romantically involved. Diana's just more of a friend to 47, rather than just his handler. Although since the ending of Contracts and according to Diana herself, the Agency's been losing agents to a rival organization, known as The Franchise, which also has its own share of cloned assassins. And that is about it for what I can say about the story.
The gameplay is rather good, actually. Even on PC, the controls don't feel clunky and each mission's scenario doesn't feel linear nor restrictive. There are plenty of ways to carry out your assignments. You just got to explore the maps and use your head. You can also either make the death of your targets as discrete as possible or even make them look like "accidents" to simply go guns blazing and make direct approaches. Though... on higher difficulties, I recommend taking stealthy approaches, as the enemies can kill 47 in a few shots. Stealth, although optional, it's more like the approach the team from IO Interactive tries to encourage, here.
As for the graphics, they look a lot smoother, compared to Hitman: Contracts. Textures from objects and scenarios don't really look stretched nor outdated and the weapons also look fairly detailed for the time the game was released on.
I also wanna talk a little about the soundtrack of the game, which was once again composed by the great Jesper Kyd. And he did one heck of a job with Blood Money's music. Each track also plays at the adequate times of the game, in order to set the right mood to the right moment. From more calm music for when you're exploring non-restricted areas to more dramatic tunes for when you infiltrate an area where one of your targets might be or something to give a sense of danger when you're fighting or running away from enemies.
And with that said, I think it's time for the final score. Which, in my opinion, Hitman: Blood Money gets a 9/10. A near-perfect game!
If you got some spare money lying around and you're looking for a new game to buy or have a copy of Hitman: Blood Money that doesn't work and wish to play it again for example, please consider buying it on Steam. And if you wish to see more of the series, I recommend buying the other games. While I can't say much about the new, episodic Hitman game, I can only say that it looks beautiful and it seems like a really fun experience! Happy gaming!

Kathy Rain.. a woman with problems.. now which woman does have no problems, eh?  But Kathy has quite a lot of them, hiding behind an overly sarcastic style. Though when her Grandfather, the man who was more parent then her real parents, dies, she has to face all those things she buried in the subconcious, while trying to get behind the reason of his death.
All in all Kathy Rain is your typical old school pixel adventure in the style of Wadjet Eye Games or even Gabriel Knight, of which it reminded me sometimes. It´s quite impressive that the game is mostly made by one single person, since it has good (pixel) graphic, nice music and fitting actors for all characters (the game is fully voiced). Also the writing is ok, while some of the riddles ain´t quite logical ... (i was especially surprised that a scanner can scan a tape into a voice file... must be one hell of a equipment). The story also takes some turns into the unlogical and is all in all quite "serious" (so don´t expect a comical adventure, despite Kathys sarcastic commenting), despite being a mystery story.
It also has some curious achievements, which you probably won´t get all, by playing "normal".
Conclusio:
In the end Kathy left me feeling a bit strange about her.. but i don´t want to spoil too much about the ending.
It is surely a nice, little adventure, which makes you want to see the end of the story. And that´s the most important thing of an adventure game, to suck you in and make you want to see how it proceeds, like a good book. At least to me.
So i recommend Kathy all in all, despite some Minus in riddles and the ending maybe.

A beautiful and magical experience from Amanita Design. They are incapable of making a bad game, and Samarost 3 is probably their best one yet. It's a gentle, non-violent and playful game of exploration, wonder and puzzle solving, starring an inquisitive little gnome who wanders wide-eyed (or so it seems) around imaginatively-designed little planetoids that are full of eclectic life. It's cartoon realism, and all the better for it. Everything is infused with so much character, from little incidental details to the tiny animals that scurry around and make curious squeaking noises if you try and interact with them. There's such an innocent sense of humour running through the entire game, it's the perfect escape from the world.
Although the artwork is stunning - I'd describe it as photorealistically unrealistic - music infuses the entire game. Much of the time you interact with the world using a flute, prompted by a visual cue that appears as you explore or solve puzzles. The world responds both visually and musically, with Floex again supplying the tunes. His work on Machinarium was great, but here it's even more closely integrated into the game. The first time you're rewarded with music after solving a puzzle, and you see the timeless reaction from your little gnome, you're almost guarnateed a huge grin. The puzzles range from fairly easy to those requiring a bit of logical deduction, but all of them felt quite logical. There's a bit of to- and fro-ing required at one point, which could have benefited from a short-cut, but it never felt like a drag.
The game ran for 7 hours, although at least an hour of that was revisiting puzzles to hear the music once more! Once you finish the game, the world doesn't go away. Instead you're given the means to roam freely around the places you've visited, and perhaps try and figure out all the achievements (all of which involve finding ways of interacting with creatures and objects).
If you want more joy in your life, Samarost 3 is highly recommended.

The game's high-resolution textures and detailed scenery now look better than ever, while retaining the unique style that made its previous entries so splendidly inspired. The quality of its rich soundtrack is equally impressive, while fully original puzzles ensure there is nothing derivative about this title.
In this adventure, you won't just point and click; you must also pull and hold and interact more directly with the environment and its wonderfully unusual inhabitants. A few puzzles had me briefly glance at a hint guide for brevity but not because they lacked sense.
You play a charming little guy that goes out exploring floating microcosms in pajamas. His initial motivation is not entirely apparent but there's always a clear expected direction. All of this is intuitively achieved without words.
Your little guy gets enthusiastic when he wins achievements and dances when completing major objectives. It's the cutest way to celebrate progression in a cheerfully naive manner.
After the game's ending, players are free to roam the worlds in a sort of epilogue to complete missed and additional puzzles for extra achievements. Highly recommended.

I write this recommendation as someone HIGHLY skeptical of the game during its beta phase. Battleborn did not launch in an ideal state, and that must be understood because that highlights Gearbox's dedication to making Battleborn be the best game it could be. Not only has the game received extensive post-launch support for what is now very much a niche title, BUT there's a boatload of quality of life features nobody likes to talk about.
What do I mean by that? Well...
1. There's botmode, so you can play the campaign and the base game PvP modes all by yourself.
2. Almost everything has been tweaked and polished to a mirror sheen.
3. All base heroes are available from the start now. All DLC heroes can be unlocked with regular in-game credits.
4. By completing challenges, you can earn platinum, which you can then spend on Season Pass missions without spending a dime, just like in Street Fighter V with DLC characters.
5. There's multiple modes now for smaller team sizes. Campaign and Operations missions are all tuned to be far better paced as well.
6. Fair amount of PC optimization settings to fiddle around with to your heart's content.
7. They're still adding new content. In addition to the free trial for PvP modes, they've added an additional mode, and continue to improve the game.
This is a game that released over a year ago now that did NOT start off well, and it's transformed from a good idea with middling execution to a good idea with above and beyond execution. I cannot heartily recommend Battleborn enough - it's honestly usurped Overwatch for me as my go-to hero shooter these days. It's worth your time, and I'm very glad I gave it a try.

As someone who didn't encounter this game until recently, playing it for the first time made me feel as though it always should have been there along with my other favorite games through the years. KOTOR is a role-playing game in the truest sense of the term. While of course mechanically the game functions like a virtual game of D&D, the level of immersion you experience has for me yet to be matched by another RPG. This is due to a multitude of factors. The characters are complex, interesting, and lifelike. Jeremy Soule's beautiful ambient tracks further draw out the personality of each area. The writing is consistently quality and manifests in a wide range of forms from witty humor to story-altering, emotional moments. This coupled with excellent voice acting for EVERY CHARACTER IN THE GAME means your interactions with the world of the Old Republic feel real.
And speaking of your interactions feeling real, this game does a solid job on giving your decisions and actions repercussions. There exist several branches to take for each scenario you may be thrown into, and while the morality system isn't flawless and there were times I wished for more grey options, it is by no means a bother to deal with. Throughout the game you will determine the fate of many people, including that of your own followers. There is even a follower who you will not gain if you approach a situation a certain way. This willingness by the developers to let the natural consequences of the player's actions come to fruition goes a long way in allowing the player to really become their character in a way many games miss.
Let's not forget that this is the definitive "I want to be a force-sensitive, lightsaber-wielding beast" experience. It is the ultimate way to live in the Star Wars universe for a time.
Now that I've gone over everything that makes this game transcendent, let me talk about some of the issues players have had or may have.
1. Bugs and Glitches- This is an almost 15 year old game. Players frequently experience glitches that can disrupt play. For me personally these issues have never gone beyond minor inconveniences such as the game tabbing out on cutscenes. Some you will see online have experienced worse. All I can say is that there exist many resources and guides for achieving full compatibility with modern rigs, so as long as you are willing to put in the effort should an issue arise, you will be fine.
2. Gameplay/Combat- Admittedly the second to second gameplay, specifically the combat, is dated. It is turn-based, and you spend much of the time pausing to relay orders to your player character and your followers, then unpausing and watching unvaried attack animations. The animations there are, however, do look polished and realistic, and I found the combat to be satisfying.
3. Graphics- Notice a trend with these typical complaints? Once again, this is an older game, and it does take getting used to in some respects.
I personally found none of these flaws to be jarring or obtrusive to my playthrough and enjoyment of the game, but there they are in case they will bother you.
Finally, here are some first-time recommendations:
1. During the course of the main story, there is a notorious and legendary plot twist on the level of "I am your father" from the movies. Please stear clear of any online forum where you may be spoiled if you are fortunate enough to be unaware of it.
2. While many enjoy playing through on dedicated "light side" or "dark side" runs, I wholeheartedly recommend playing through for the first time as though you were really there calling the shots. React to situations and people how you would react, and see where it takes you; be it light, dark, or (likely) somewhere in between.
This game is a classic and a 10/10. If you enjoy RPGs, Star Wars, or engaging storylines in general, you will love it.

TL;DR: It's not playable yet. Go play Torchlight or something.
Long Story:
Of Audio:
The sound work is horrible, i can still hear the static tap-tap of my footsteps. Some of the in-game narratives were goodish, but in general, they were in bad quality, and the poor acting made them seem a bit silly for such a 'hardcore' game. The game has no hit sounds/effects of any sort for the player, for example the enemy arrows just dissapper into you, which makes it really hard to tell if you are hit or not (in cae of you are shot from afar).
Of Graphics:
The map looks nice, and the models are decent. Everything else? Complete utter poopoo. The splash at the start has worse quality than youtube videos from 2005. The intro video (which the game wants to show you every time you start the game) is ... hilarious? I can't honestly do nothing but laugh at it. And the game tries to sell itself as 'hardcore'. Well, you can't really be hardcore without the right atmosphere, which the horrible voice acting and poor intro video certainly do not set.
The items you equip seem to have no effecr on your appearance, which is understandable, for this is a game from small team with no time to model each item.
Of The Map:
The levels are static, which is kind of fine, though i hope they will change this later on. Static maps really hurt replayability in these sort of games. What I don't understand is, why is there no automapping? Since the levels are static, it should be easy to implement, and I see no reason why it isn't there. (Back to this later on).
Now, I must admit I only played the first level, which was somewhat dull. We got some prison cells, some zombies wandering(not) around, etc etc. The typical rpg dungeon settings. The first level seemed lacking, as because of the horrible voice acting i could not follow the story (had to consentrate not to giggle and cringe). It was just a bunch of rooms thrown together.
The boss of the first level was. well, 'lacking', so to speak. The combat was closer to point and click then actual arpg combat, for the boss only seemed to have 2 spells; one which was AoE that hit basicly the whole room, doing little damage (so easy to soak, no reason to stop hitting/move away), and some sort of curse(?) or likes, that cast a kinda nice looking effect on the player, making them unable to move (but could still hit the boss), and after a period of time, inflicted some damage. There seemed to be no way to play around these spells, so the bossfight was pure dps race.
The Combat:
I really like combat, like, really. When i play a ARPG game i expect fell-refined combat system with multiple ways to aproach the fight, that supports different playstyles, and suchs. Now, the combat in Sunken is pretty much point and click. Press 1 for damage, left-click when OOM, and Q for heal. The game decides not to explain the combat system in anyway, which could be another failed attempt to make the game feel 'hardcore'. Even the first bossfight was a dull DPS race. During my second run on the first level, i found 2 spells, so there seems to be some spellcasting system in place. However, the damage of spells is static, and spellcasting is limited by a) mana b) cooldown, and from my experience, there is no way to affect cooldown, so it's the limiting factor. With static damage and static cooldowns, going for caster type doesn't seem reasonable.
The Character:
You get experience points from killing monsters. You level up when you receive enough experience. Each time you level up, you get 5 'points' you can assign to attributes. Each attribute does something 'Each click', which seems to be a ARPG term i do not know, but I assume they meant by attribute level. Dexterity, for example, improves armor by 0.5, and crit chance by 0.1%. You start with 10 points in each attribute, so for example to max out crit chancem you have to be level 190, and by then you have 100% crit chance, meaning your attacks do 150% damage. Sounds rad, right? I haven't played long enough to actually confirm this, but this is what the game tells me when i first choose which attribute i want to level. I'll most likely write a full analyzis on how much each attribute affects gameplay later on.
The 'Hardcore':
This game aims to be 'hardcore', I like that. I like hardcore games. In fact, I'm designing a game that I'd like to call hardcore. But what makes a game hardcore? Sunkens ideology seems to be, that stripping down user experience is 'hardcore'. The lack of minimap/automapping, the lack of tutorial, or any explainations of basic game mechanics or even showing the user the keybindings (or list the buttons for the action bar thingy) seems to be their way of doing hardcore.
For me, hardcore is more about being punishing. The game should be hard to beat, not hard to play. Players should have to think about which their choice will be, and the game should support that. Sunkens total lack of transparency makes it really difficult for me to recommend it, as it is nowhere near 'the fun of a hardcore game'.
The Conclusion:
It's not ready. The developers have fallen into some pretty basic pitfalls of game design. Luckily, these can be fixed, and there is lots of material available on how to do this. here is some of my suggestions.
- Remove the intro. Seriously, it's bad.
- Add a way to skip the ingame narratives.
- Add a tutorial. The first level could act as sort of a tutorial zone that introduses the player the mechanics. The is plently of material on this avaiable on the interwebs.
- Add a hit effect to the player. It's the simplest things that make the combat so much better.
- Add floating texts to combat. I want to see how much damage i did, and how much i received. Even ascii-based roguelikes have these nowadays. Easy to implement.
- Add a way to hit while standing still, even when not aiming at any monster. Basic ARPG.
- This game does _NOT_ need more content at this point. It needs better gameplay. Look up how to 'juice' the game. Even hardcore games require some juice to make the combat more pleasing.
That's about it. Summing it up again, this game is nowhere near the 6€ pricetag it has now, but I'm still looking up to see how it develops. So, don't buy it now, come back later :)

Pros:
Early impressions of the game are very promising - I can only see the title improving upon what's there, which is already in a playable state.
Combat element isn't too hectic, like some aRPGs.
UI is simple and intuitive (which is a good thing).
Its permadeath mechanic avoids save/load spamming (also a good thing), but still allows the player to keep learned skills.

Appears to be well optimised - I've had no framerate issues or overburdened/overheating GPU/CPU like in some other games that are still in development, and I only have a mid-range PC.
Cons:
Camera is locked, so can't change the angle or zoom in and out.
Controls cannot be re-bound to any mouse buttons, like most other aRPGs.
There is no minimap or full screen map to help navigate the (pre-designed) levels. Though I guess one can eventually remember the layout if played enough.
There's no way to retract stat points if a mistake is made when assigning them.
Summary:
Of course, a lot can and likely will change in the future, so I'll update my review if and when necessary.
As it stands, I can recommend this title for fans of the genre, especially at its low price.
On a sidenote: The devs (two man team) are very active and responsive with the playerbase, so that's another plus.

I bought RCTW in the Summer Sale and have since returned it.
The main menu immediatly had a "Sims" feel too it, but lacked the polish of a AAA title. Hard to put a finger on, but it just didn't match the feel of the previous titles. Even moreso than 3. Feedback when clicking around was poor. The visuals, even on the menus, were not snappy and clicking feels bad.
Launching the game worked on my new high-end laptop, but as soon as the game loaded It became clear moving around how big a departure this effort was. Not a bad thing per-say, but at the end of the day the mechanics did not feel tight and snappy, and the enhanced interfaces that make the game so powerful (a major plus) were not executed to a polished final game level. Moving around is clunky, the tutoral screens are jumpy, full screen loading page art jumps, and the mechanics for building are not polished and are jumpy and unforgiving.
I would never return a $5 game for these reasons though. The reason I reurned it was it became clear that certain inflexibilities in the game design would prohibit the free play that made previous titles great, and bugs and odd ux designs made being creative and building great coasters painfully slow, despite the ability to technically do much more. For example, when searching in a text box, certain letters on the keyboard would not type but instead perform their hotkey functions, jumping out of the menu I was typing in and modifying the park. Hotkey rejection in a text box is basic programming. Lots of other legitimate bugs like that that robbed my short experience of any of the joy of the previous titles (even 3 which was great, despite high computer requirements for the time).

is a free visual novel with an reasonable story and a kind twist. It tells a story about Mark, who awakens from a dream of someone he could have sworn he remembers, though can’t quite remember why. He's a character whose personality is the closest one can get to resemble the cold, dead vacuum of space. Soon he meets Myra, a girl who knows more about Mark’s past than anyone should, a past Mark tries desperately to forget, and while they begin to get close, something begins to pull Myra apart.
This VN isn't short, but isn’t too long either (around 4 hours). The story is linear with the choices being few and far between, and have little impact on the actual game, the ending is confusing due to having to repeat steps.
The game have a few options on choices (6-7 options to make in game). The dialogue is stiff and unnatural. The imagery isn't nothing special, it feels too linear, despite slight changes in dialogue, and there’s only one instance where a choice makes an actual noticeable change other than dialogue.
Easy to get all achievements because the game have few options. Nice to spend some time, nothing more. Or maybe I'm not the target audience.

I was nicely surprised by Sepia Tears thinking that it wouldn’t be anything interesting. It isn’t really anything special, though it has its charm in its own right.
The story isn’t too short or too long, finishing it at only 2 hours. I won’t go too much into detail about the story due to it being one of those visual novels that lose its fun the moment it’s spoiled.
The story is slow at the beginning, yet as the story uncovered itself more and more I felt more invested. It really isn’t anything mind blowing, but it is interesting enough to get you to care what might happen next. The dialogue at times can be a bit generic, still nothing unbearable for the most part.
As for the art, I find it a bit rough or not polished enough. I really do like some of the character's design and find it a bit charming in its simplicity. The music is standard and weak at its worst. It fits most of the scenes however there are moments where the music doesn’t seem exactly fit the scene.
There isn’t any replayability despite it having choices. The story seems to be linear and only has minor dialogue changes depending on what you choose.
Gagged a bit also to some of the jokes and the small references it makes to other anime. I also really appreciate Myra’s Diary which you is rewarded to you after completing the game. It’s a summed up version of the story from Myra’s point of view which ties some loose ends in the story.
It kept me interested and didn’t really make want to stop reading which makes it okay. Just don’t expect anything high quality and simply take in the experience and you’ll have a fun time with Sepia Tears.

The Promised Land is a colony builder game sporting a huge resource management component.  Players will frequently encounter an odd-ball assortment of arcade mini-games and puzzle challenges.
The sound is good.  The game is fun to play and immersive.  The graphics are particularly cute with plenty of humour lavished in some of the animations.  There are many incidental references to stereotypes which are presented in an anecdote and comedy fashion.
The player recruits and trains villagers.  Villagers specialise in various gathering and manufacturing professions.  A few villagers need to be dedicated to research to unlock parts of the skill tree.
This all sounds simple, but the player needs to focus on each villager to ensure their need for food and socialising is met.  Fail to keep people fed with food and satisfy their need to talk or have company and they will desert their jobs and create a knock-on effect of shortages in food and materials.  Maintaining a happy balance and keeping colonists productive will keep players busy.  Success requires balancing of individual needs with the needs of growing the colony.
New buildings and professions become available as the player progresses through the game.  Upgrades to buildings and increased expertise in skills of villagers create a good sense of progression.  Villagers can learn more than one skill either via experience (Doing) or through education (Being taught).  Pay attention to the likes and dislikes of individual colonists to get the best results.
Additional areas are unlocked by reaching milestones.  The Promised land succeeds in that positive action is rewarded.  The game is moderately challenging but great fun to play and creates a sense of achievement and accomplishment.  Players also need to be cautious about expanding the colony too fast (or too slow for that matter).
Players are able to re-play many of the mini-games to try and improve performance scores.
There should be approximately 30 to 50 hours of game play to complete the game.

I took me a short while to get over the main character's annoying edgy 90's teen routine, but once the game starts going, you'll discover a real personality underneath. Other characters aren't extremely deep, but they do the job they are there to do.
It's somewhat reminiscent of the Blackwall series (another good adventure series, which you should at least try), both in visual style and themes, but tells its own interesting story.
I'm curious to see if Kathy Rain turns into a series, as I know I'll play a sequel if one ever comes out.

Knights of the Old Republic is about as close as you can get to a definitive interactive experience of the Star Wars universe. It really is the best of both worlds- it expands hugely on the Star Wars lore as well as introducing new planets and aliens and tells a great story, while gameplay-wise it's thoroughly entertaining as well. I haven't even completed the game yet but I really want to emphasise how much I'm enjoying exploring planets and the choice I'm given to join the Dark Side of the Force or continue into the Light.
However, the game isn't perfect. As much as I'm used to the combat system, that's the one part of the game that hasn't aged well and you can only wonder if KOTOR were to be remastered today whether it might be better to have real-time combat as RPGs like Fallout 3 and Skyrim have done. In several places as well I found severe graphical glitches, presumably with the grass and trees, and from time to time it either drops my framerate or crashes the game. Thankfully I've been able to resolve these glitches by turning off the 'Grass' option in the Advanced Setting menu.
For the negatives I could easily click the thumbs-down but I'm sure not everyone suffers these glitches and because of how easy the error is to fix, the graphics are forgivable. Star Wars Knights of the Old Republic stands as a classic and there's plenty of fun to be had a long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away,,,
