So I got the opportunity to play the game before it got out on steam. I played only first level back than and a lot of things changed, so here are my opinions on the game now that I did go thro all the levels almost two times before getting killed.
Ill start with some things I think should see some more work:
Music on level 2 is too repetitive, longer loop would be nice. I turned music on or off depending on the level, since some levels have pretty good music. I can understand why someone would turn it off and not hear any of the tunes later on. Since all levels have their own music that fits the theme it would be a shame if its not heard for that reason.
And the big problem, material disenchanting. Since there is no visual way to differ tiers except mouse hovering each one, disenchanting mats becomes a chore. And another question is, why do it? You will get lower level mats, but at this time you probably have all the skills learned and better gear. Only reason are potions, and that is not compelling enough to manage your mats for 15 mins only to get 5 hp and 5 mana pots. I ended up tossing all the mats some time after I get up to new tier.
And yeah there are a lot of bugs and problems that people are writing about, and kudos to devs for quick response on fixing those. Just to mention a few: exit game crash bug, no support for 32bit os, some skills are not balanced properly, bad tooltips and so on.
What I like about it is the effort invested in making an interesting death and endgame mechanics that tie into lore of the game. I would not like to spoil anything in the review, but lets just say it gives you a logical reason for continuing.
It's not just here that the game is connected to its lore. Design of levels, their size and atmosphere, monsters that you fight, music that is playing in the background, all has it's reason, that you will understand better as you read the lore books scattered thorough the levels.
Combat vise, it starts a bit slow, but as you get more mana (and you will if you didn't die and go back to lvl 1) and more skills (that persist thro death and can be improved, which makes next death just a bit more easier) you will get the opportunity to make interesting builds. If you don’t die you constantly get new skills and deciding which one to use was fun for me. Low tier skills do less dmg but cost less (and have less omph), and its the other way around for the high tier ones (although the difference in dmg is not that great and since it scales with your weapon and stats I found that all skills have use even after getting almost all the skills of the last tier). Clearing mobs around the level when you learn the best tactics for them is not a big problem, and after learning level layouts you can effectively farm them pretty quickly. Bosses are tied to the lore, and the tactics that you need to use are things that make sense. Problem I found is that its really hard to see their debuffs. Hovering over an icon to read what it does usually means my head getting smashed. But you can kill some of the bosses on muscles, which would require multiple farm runs to make possible.
Sound is ok, as I said loop on some of them is too short to enjoy, but then again some other levels have music that I really liked. If the devs have time and resources it would be nice to hear more of one sound for monster strikes, sword swings and so on. Voice acting for some characters is all right, but I didn't like the voice of the character that you hear in the loading screens. All of the books that you find have voice actors reading the text. And now that I’m mentioning it, it would be awesome if there was a journal containing all the books that we found.
Visually its all right, I would say that worst part of it is low resolution of some assets. UI needs some improvements, I like the overall style but some things should be more visible (health and mana, mouse). Spells do look powerful, and even with full screen of monsters while casting visually taxing spells the game worked fine and frame rate was really high, maybe even way more than it needs to be (maybe frame cap it).
So considering the limited manpower, time and resources I believe this is a pretty good addition to the genre. Problems do exist atm, but this is early access afterall.

DISCLOSURE: I'm friends with one of the devs. I backed this game on Indiegogo. I've also contributed some voice acting to the game.
I don't play many ARPGs. I think the last one I really put any time into was Titan Quest. I didn't really have any expectations going into playing Sunken, but I honestly quite enjoyed it.
First off, yeah, this game feels like an Early Access title. It's rough around the edges. But saying that, it also feels like it achieves a lot of what it sets out to do. You walk around a dungeon, you click on various monsters, and they die in various ways. All the while, you step further into the labyrinth, getting more powerful spells and items, as well as ingredients for crafting those two things, which I'll get to in a minute.
The combat is pretty simplistic, but compelling in that time honoured dungeon-crawling fashion. Kill things, get more powerful, kill bigger things. It doesn't re-invent the wheel but it worked well enough to keep my interest. It starts off pretty easy, but as you encounter more powerful foes, you start having to play more strategically. I found the permadeath aspect to be one of the most compelling aspects, as it made me more cautious while playing. This really came into play when fighting the bosses, and I enjoyed having to work out an effective strategy on-the-fly without a save point to run back to if I failed. That said, the game could benefit from some sort of save system. If not a quicksave or autosave, maybe a Dark Souls style bonfire system would fit the feel of Sunken better.
Talking of Dark Souls, this game barely explains anything to you. I found this both good, and bad. If you don't have patience for poor tutorial design, you probably won't enjoy this. I personally feel like it's on the verge of a good balance between explanation and experimentation, something the Dark Souls series excels at. But right now it's not really found that balance. I wasn't too put off by this, though - if you've played a game like this before, then you'll know exactly what to expect. But if you're anything like me, just be prepared to spend five minutes pointlessly clicking around to try to use the crafting system. Once I worked out I needed to find an anvil, though, it all fell into place. From what I've played so far, the system isn't particularly in-depth, but it's satisfying to use and helped add a little extra involvement to the otherwise combat-oriented gameplay.
Presentation-wise, I found Sunken quite pleasing. It aims for that grim, gothic fantasy vibe and pretty much nails it. It's a Unity game, so it looks like something from 2006, but the regular introduction of scenery changes and enemy types helps to keep it visually interesting. The music is pretty good too, or at least good enough that it didn't grate on me after playing for a couple of hours. The lore texts scattered around the levels add something for people looking for a story. It's not the main focus of the game, but I think it's compelling enough to want to seek them out. I don't feel like I'm qualified to comment on the VA quality, being involved in it myself. I heard myself a couple of times and didn't think I sounded like a complete tool - I call that a personal success.
Like all Early Access games, if you're not 100% confident in spending your money, don't buy Sunken. I personally feel, however, that Sunken really embodies some of the best qualities of an Early Access game - it's clearly made by people who have a passion for the genre and a dedication to making the game as good as they can. It comes through in the surprisingly robust combat, the decently-sized skill tree and the actually helpful ability descriptions. If you want to spend some time doing some old-school dungeon-raiding, and help a solid little ARPG come together, you could do a lot worse.

Disclaimer: I was part of Sunken beta testing.
tldr; Buy it, you'll get your moneys worth even it is in early access.
Well this is my first review ever, I'll try to keep it short and concise. I usually do not write reviews but as I was part of beta I feel I should put my thoughts on current state of game and where I see it going.
First of all this game is really hard. Not unfair hard like some rogues I played but still it wont hold punches. You need to stayed focused especially at later spins(game's term for how much times you passed all levels and restarted without dying). You progress by putting points into 4 distinct stats and you gain those points by leveling up. While 4 stats may seem not too much it opens possibilities for varied builds as every point you put into something is important. For example high level abilities cost great amounts of mana so you wont be able to spam them if you didn't put big chunk of points in intelligence.
There is really great amount of abilities, categorized into 10 tiers. With 5 abilities per tier it gives nice amount of 50 distinct abilities. In current state about 70-80% of abilities are viable imho and I hope devs will manage to bring that number up before release. Abilities are nicely done graphics wise, especially abilities of higher tiers.
That brings us to overall graphics. I would rate it as above average, most certainly passable. I do not think that more can be expected from 2 man team. Music on the other hand is really excellent and I really enjoyed it. There is certainly room to make OST purchasable. Voice acting on the other hand varies. Most of it is good but there are some parts that need improvement, mainly main character narator between levels.
Narrative is imho superbly written and while you will need to read a lot of lore books and think a little about timeline to make sense of it you will be rewarded with a tale of great depth. There is also neat secret mechanic tightly linked to the lore and whole point of those spins(hint and maybe a bit of a spoiler:
).
I would personally like for game to be a bit faster but that's personal preference and after all that's what early access is for, to gather opinions and make game suit majority of people.
I can recommend this game with certainty because after countless hours of testing it I still have desire to play it and it didn't grow boring for me. This 17h of playtime is just from latest prerelease beta which started yesterday. If you do get it, be sure to invest some time into it, lots of great stuff about this game needs to be found and game will reward you greatly if you put effort into it.

Samorost 3:
~~~~~~~~~

Music can make you feel calm, reflective, jovial and many other sensations. But can music solve a predicament for a space gnome? You see, several of his neighbouring planets have experienced fierce attacks from the three-headed space monster. Luckily, a magic flute dropped from the Galaxy right on his doorstep! Come on guys, let’s help this space gnome in Samorost 3!
Samorost 3 is an adventure / point and click /puzzle game where you control a space gnome who has a magic flute to help him resolve puzzles.
Your character will visit five planets (including the one you start the game on) throughout this adventure. Before your cute little gnome can travel from one planet to another he has to collect specific and unconventional items to create a flying thing.
As there is no dialogue in Samorost 3, your gnome will respond with a positive, negative or even a surprise “mmh” depending on what he is interacting with. Most of the animals and insects can be clicked on, as can the people.  Each different interaction will create a different reaction.  For instance, a bug can fall out of the tree if has been touched (poor little thing). Touch a parrot and it might sing. As your character explores the planets, he will come across some items, such as trees, holes and other characters, that will project sound waves (icons); make sure he uses his magic flute on them as they will give him important hints for solving puzzles via a small animation scene. You can refer to the book of hints (the book with the two closed eyes) for further help. To be honest with you, the puzzles are not too difficult to figure out and they are well-designed. But if you need a hand, click on the book (in the game menu) and align the red lights on its cover - it will show you what to do next.
The artwork and the soundtrack are just sensational, in my opinion. The game runs very well and it is easy to play for all ages. I found the menu a bit confusing at first; I kicked myself out of the game by mistake, but the auto save was there to rescue my progress.

Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Superb artworks & soundtrack
-	Nice puzzles
-	Book of hints
-	Achievement and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	A bit short
Samorost 3 is truly an amazing point and click for all ages!
8/10

***Fix for high resolution monitors****
I loved this game as a child, when bulky crts and win 98 were the cool thing. However resolutions changed and I was wondering how all these people were able to play this game when my screen was zoomed in too much. I finally got the correct resolution for the game running on a 4k monitor. The problem seems to be due to display scaling. So finally heres the secret if you are having problems with screen size. Go through your steam folder to rail road tycoon, find the exe file, RT2_Plat, right click, go to properties, click compatibility tab, and select "disable diplay scaling on high DPI settings" and wholla it should work. If you have a "failed to find steam" error make sure that your steam.exe file (can use the one on desktop) is set to "run as adminstrator." All you high resolution, large display scaling peoples, youre welcome. Please bump for people who need help. Cheers.

One very important thing I want to state is that this game is a challenge. You can pass each level with a bronze, silver, or gold medal. If you want the gold medal in the mission you really do have to understand and plan out the level in order to get it. It is not like Rollercoaster Tycoon where you can just build up a park and have it generate money. The objectives are much harder in Railroad Tycoon than in similar tycoon games. You can still complete the levels with the minimum requirements and get through the campaign, but in order to get all the achievements you must understand how the game works.
Another thing I really want to mention is that there is a narrator who interacts with you in the mission selection screen. If you end up leaving the screen idle the narrator will actually yell at you and tell you to pick a level because you are taking too long to select something. This is a really great touch, and it reminded me of Stronghold HD where if you play for hours on end the narrator will ask you if you are tired - or if you play past midnight the narrator would tell you that you need sleep because it's getting late. I really love additions like this in games.
Overall, this is probably my favorite tycoon game. Period. It's both very simple while being extremely complex.

So, between the unicorns, demon steeds, and foals, I ended up buying this game during the holiday sale.  It has ponies and magic - what else could it possibly need?  What could go wrong?
Pros:
1) Graphics.  It's a decent looking game.  Horses are well fleshed out, and the animimations for them are smooth.
2) Designs.  Each breed has its own look, naturally, and they pull them off fairly well.
Neutral:
1) Story.  The idea behind the game is...interesting.  Though for the amount of time you'd have to play to see it through, it really isn't quite deep enough.
Cons:
1) Gameplay.  It is repetitive.  Incredibly repetitive.  To breed your horses, you need to maximize ALL of their skills.  That requires playing two of the courses mulitple times per horse.  That would be fine, if not for the fact that not only can you breed each horse only once, the number you need keep going up.  To get your first LvL 2 horse, you need 2 LVL 1s.  Which is fine, until you realize that means you need four LVL 1s to create 2 LVL 2s to breed a LVL 3, and it just gets worse from there as you need more and more to get up to your LVL 5 horses.  I played for two hours and only just got my first LVL 2 horse.  Yeah.  No.
The courses are all basically the same concept - when the icon turns green, push the relevent arrow key, and your horse will do whatever its supposed to if you time it right.  The races don't use this mechanic, but even then you only use the left and right arrow, and CTLR for items.  Quests you push a button and your horse disappears for however long the quest takes.
All in all, the game looks like it had promise, but they went the mobile game route of button hitting=gameplay + waiting times to make a PC game.  There are much better horse-related games out there - nix this one, pretty as it is, for something more interesting to play rather then look at.

I recommend this game, but not at 30 dollars. Get it on sale for at least 50% off.
The TLDR: This game is diet Monster hunter. It has all the concept sthat make the game fun, but none of the concepts that make the game great.
Story: Nothing inspiring. Typical invasive alien/monster/demon/etc comign tod estory humanity, then we fight back and win. The game attempts to create a more serious in depth story with the commander or general's videos where he's slowly losing his mind. I'm sure translation is a factor here, but it jsut wasn't interesting and felt basic.
Visuals: the visuals are solid. When it come sto platformers, visuals are very important to me. For the most part, I liked the visuals. The armors all look cool, the weapons look cool, the enemies have good detail. However, the female playable character is off. Where the males look like bad♥♥♥♥♥soldiers in armor, the females look dead or souless. Like their head was attached to an android body, or they're combat dolls or something. I played through as a male, then switched to female when the game ended and it asked me to choose a new body. Armor visuals are very different for males and female, down to there 3ven being gender based armors, which was kind of disappointing. Other than the females, though, I enjoyed the visuals.
Audio: I don't know Japanese, so id idn't realyl lsiten tot he voice acting. The action sounds do their job, but nothing about them realyl stood out. The music isn't bad. Honestly, not the game's strongest point, but also one of the elast important aspects.
Gameplay/combat: This is realyl what saved the game. The game doesn't bring anything new to the table in terms of gameplay, but all of it's mechanics are implimented well. The game is fun, and if you're a monste rhunter fan waiting for the next one to come out, this can help fill that a little. lots of bonus missions for 100%ers, and plenty of reasons to need to do them (crafting). This genre likes grinding, a little, and the game does a good job of giving the player a reason to grind without creating a huge amount of grind time.
The Bosses are all fun to fight, and had different mechanics for each. Plus, there's an easy, normal, and hard version of every mission (including story missions.) with better rewards for higher difficulty. The different weapon styles all -felt- different int heir execution, and were introduced witht ime to let the player try out the weapona nd see if it fits them. The only weapon I didn't try was the bow. That said, the de3vs were lazy with basic enemies. Within the first few levels you've fought every non boss enemy in the game. fromt here on they just change their color and give them elements. A little disappointing, but the focus on this game is on the bosses, which are well done.
Veterans of this genre will not find this game to be a challenge. There are a few places I had to do a couple times, but for the most part the game was more fun than challenging.
RATING: 7/10

I came across KOTOR 1 through being an avid player of the ME trilogy and DA series, and given my ♥♥♥♥ing obsession for those gritty RPG, exploration based games and grill banging escapades it was obvious KOTOR was next. The storyboard itself is partiularlly excellent, biomes are expansive and beatuiful, a handful of companions are well fleshed out (whilst others are as abrasive as sandpaper and should either be shot to death or left on the ship). This (unfortunately) is  where my cudos end. The battle system feels particularly slow, more so than any turn based counterparts of its time and with its tediously boring item progression, you'll be looking at swing the same lightsaber config around for the next 15 hours. I'am well aware that you cant compare KOTOR's renegade/paragon system to the ME standard as the technology may not have been there, but when you're literally stomping on every poor twilek's left nut and your goody toe shoe companion's only comment is "dont do that b0ss thats a nono", it feels so UNSATISFYING dissapointing that none of my actions really even matter.

Given these statements, KOTOR stands as an archaic example of the beginnings of greatness  but falls flat on so many levels, hence unless you have a massive hard-on for Star Wars and blue alien women I definitely would not recommend this game.

I haven't played the newest Hitman or Absolution yet, but I think Blood Money is still regarded as the best Hitman game from the first four. The plot is arguably the strongest as it deals with both calculated assassinations for money and the falling apart of the ICA. It also helps put together a firm timeline following the events of Contracts, which was mostly a game of flashbacks.
If you played Contracts, then you know that Agent 47 is remembering missions as he recovers from a gunshot wound. In Blood Money, the first three missions are set before he's shot. He's shot following Curtain's Down in Blood Money, which is the opera mission (also in Contracts, confusing, right?). After that, the story really deals with Diana assigning 47 missions while also gathering information on the Franchise. They're basically a rival/elite group who want to destroy the ICA.
One of the game's greatest assets has to be its OST. From the original songs to the added orchestra, Blood Money has one of my favorite video game soundtracks, right up there with Max Payne 3.
In terms of gameplay, the game is really unique. Most stealth games usually are, but IO Interactive manages to capitalize on a game about an assassin and make it an actual stealth game. Being that the Hitman titles have existed for years, you'd think Ubisoft would have taken notes when developing Assasssin's Creed. Hiding in plain sight has always been a Hitman signature and they managed to not make it so easy to be caught with Blood Money. I know in some of the previous ones, guards were always seeing through my outfit for whatever reason. In Blood Money, you actually need to act suspicious in order to be caught. Which was a nice change.
Definitely my favorite Hitman game. 9.5/10

Sepia Tears is your average Visual-Novel game that follows the story of a high school student named Mark. He wakes up with no recall of a dream. Then a girl, Myra, appears and appears to know about Mark's past, which he on the other hand is trying to erase from his memory.
Like any VNs, there are many dialogues, interaction with other characters as well as choices that you may pick, which will determine the outcome. Though the latter, there is not very much. I can remember making 4 or 5 decisions in game, before reaching it's final ending. There is also an auto or skip option for those who are just skimming through to pick the right choices and get the achievements.
The arts are quite basic and blurred. The backgrounds were very dull on details or sharpness, which were likely intentional so we are focused on the characters. But none of them I would say, were memorable, and are all your casual boys and girls dressed in uniforms (excluding Myra).
Music is all right. Nothing much to note of that, other than that it was minimal and atmospheric.
Overall, the game isn't quite something that is replay-able. Once you've reached the good ending and have collected all the achievements there's no other reason to play it really. But regardless, Sepia Tears is a game I would recommend trying, since it is free.

The Promised Land is a ridiculously cute little time-management/city-builder that sucks you in and doesn't let go until you beat the game (which looks like it can be done in around 10-12 hrs). It's a really simple casual game but there's a lot going on and it's really enjoyable if you're looking for a relaxing experience that doesn't require a huge amount of concentration.
The basic setup is similar to a lot of other games, gather resources, build things, make stuff, sell things, get gold, upgrade buildings, get more workers, etc. There is quite a nice variety of resources and manufactured goods, and a couple dozen buildings at least, each with its own series of upgrades.  There is also a research laboratory that allows you to study half a dozen separate advancements, and those unlock buildings and upgrades in your industries and elsewhere in your colony.
The workers will specialize and become more efficient after doing a certain task for a while. I especially like that the workers themselves have preferences, and if you put them in a job they enjoy, they are more productive than if you assign them a task they dislike. I also really enjoy the way that you pick up your workers to move them to tasks, and that they totally react to you doing that.
The housing has an interesting puzzle aspect to it. You can upgrade your houses to increase the number of workers you can have, but it requires manipulating rooms in a sort of jigsaw puzzle in order to maximize the number of colonists each building can hold.
Finally, there is a mini-game simulating naval combat that basically is Angry Birds with cannons and pirates.
Nice one...good time killer. It backs me to 'Theme Hospital' times of my childhood a little. Recommended

I was about 60 seconds into playing 'Kathy Rain', just past the opening cutscene when I first got control of the titular protagonist, I  moused around and clicked on a poster: "That's from 'The Thing' one of my favourite horror movies." explained Kathy. In that moment I knew that me and Kathy were going to get along just fine, and I also knew that this was one game that I'd be seeing all the way through. 5 hours or so later (accounting for some idle time) here I am telling you to take the trip too.
'Kathy Rain' does nearly everything right. Kathy herself is a joy to work with and one of the best video game protagonists I've ever spent time with. The game is as much about her as it is about the mystery she uncovers, and while none of the supporting cast can quite match the engagement that she induces that's because she's a high-water mark. The puzzles are clever, but designed to be logically solvable, and while I'm not a braniac genius (although I do have the whole stable of Lucasarts and Sierra titles under my belt) nothing stumped me for more than 30 seconds and I was never tempted to reach for a walkthrough. I'd say the difficulty is slightly on the easy side of the genre average although good design contributes a lot to that ease; there are no moments where it feels like the game is jerking you around with 'game logic' and Kathy is always willing to offer subtle direction.
The story won't be to everyone's taste, and honestly the direction that the plot took was... interesting. I was expecting 'Veronica Mars' but this is more 'Twin Peaks' (and darker than that by the end). This is by no means a bad thing but it's definitely not the game you want to use to introduce a pre-teen to the world of adventure gaming.
You're not a pre-teen though, right? You should totally play this. It rocks.

I'm still playing this game, haven't finished it yet but I'm going through it strong. A lot of reviewers made this game out to be the return of old school games in 2016, and despite it being a fairly decent experience, there are better titles out there. For instance, I really enjoyed Primordia, Technobablyon and other Wadjet Eye Games. Don't get me wrong, Kathy Rain is going good so far, but there are inherent issues with the engine, it's not designed to accommodate things like Alt Tab, which is very annoying when I'm working and gaming at the same time. Often it would freeze the image on my screen and I'd have to restart my computer. Despite running an old engine, they need a way of accommodating modern ways of traversing applications, otherwise it becomes an annoyance.
The game itself is decent, with a fair story arc. The character is slightly unbelievable for a 90's goth girl? Seems like she has Emo streaks and then she drives a motor bike? Highly confusing. Despite that the character element and puzzles were fun and very reasonable. There was no major issues in figuring out clues or piecing things together, had to think about some but they did have a steady logical flow.
The settings are decent, but for the most part they feel a little claustrophobic. Often the emphasis of a scene is designed around the interaction of you and one character or one specific tasked object. This can be fine in Point Clicks but if over used and not given a grander context it begins to drag.
I felt like they could've used points from games like The Longest Journey, and Broken Sword, Broken Age, where they give you nice large environments instead of narrow and claustrophobic settings. This might change as the game goes on but the pattern seems rather set.
The side characters are slightly uninteresting, bordering annoying. I felt like I cared very little for my roommate, my grandmother or anyone else that I really interacted with.
Overall this title wasn't as fun as I hoped, the experience is okay however, and I would recommend this title at a discount...

I highly recommend playing this game (especially on cold rainy nights with the lights turned down), and hope there's more Kathy Rain to come! :D

TL;DR
Games great, I recommend it for $15-$30 based on what your personal taste for this kind of game is.
If you like side-scrolling beat-em ups with light RPG and easy to learn, slightly hard to master combos and enemy patterns, there's a nice variety of enemies, weapons, attacks and combos. Story is standard, if a little generic. Graphics are pretty, animations are stiff but get the job done. Gameplay is superb for beat-em up fans, lots of "Get all the S ranks" in this game.
I recommend it to fans of 2D fighters, beat-em ups, platinum games as a company, and Ska Studios titles.
IMPRESSIONS:
This game is fantastic. I'm a huge fan of sidescrolling beat'em ups. One of my all time favorite games is Dungeon Fighter Online, as well as Dragon's Crown on the Playstation 3. To give you a basic idea of what my taste is,
My top 5 games as of this review:
1.Monster Hunter
2.Dark Souls
3.Dragon's Crown
4.Dungeon Fighter Online
5.Metal Gear Franchise
With that as a base line for what I like, here's my thoughts on the game.
STORY:
Not much to say here, without any real spoilers, Aliens are a thing, they're bad, humans almost went extinct except they didn't because super tech happened based on aliens. Now mankind bounces back, with the help of YOU! Hijinks and planet eating aliens insue from this series of events.
It's a standard fare with an anime style Sci-Fi. Basic, to the point, mostly a setup for the game. No awards here.
SOUND:
Soundtrack is a standard deal here as well, mostly electric and synth, combat sounds good. Guns have decent bang and boom to their noise, blades feel nice, attacking gives you different sounds based on if you hit a CRITICAL or a back attack, or if you BREAK the opponent. Good feedback here, music is plain.
Good job on the combat noise, not so much on the soundtrack.
GRAPHICS:
What you see is what you get, nice particles, good character sprites and the enemies all look cool. Despite their messy looking details, they stand out easily. The "Trooper" tyle enemies stand out amongst all the others, and you can tell them apart from the rest in a crowd. Explosions and bodyparts go flying, honestly if you like the look of the screenshots, you won't be disappointed. The whole game looks like that.
I personally like it, so great work here.
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay to me is pretty straight-forward, you have two buttons. One for each hand, then you can jump, boost, and use the "EXCEED" ability, which is a fancy name for rage mode. The fun comes when you learn how to start juggling enemies, chaining certain attacks with bullets, knocking an enemy in the air, striking them 5 or 6 times, then stopping just before your slam dunk attack, and shooting them with your gun to keep them floating in the air, boosting under them and repeating the process with any variation you choose. The combat is what I love this game for, it's really well done. Simple buttons, grand experience.
This is the meat of the game, and my favorite part of the whole product. (Perhaps, arguably the ONLY part of the product)
HOW IT ALL COMES TOGETHER:
The way the game plays, you start in a menu of customize, craft, settins and missions. You always return to this menu after a mission, you only fight in missions. You can recieve items and rewards for your own use in crafting new gear, and since each and every enemy drops their own materials, this adds a nice level of learning "Gotta kill this creature to get his claws" in order to build new equipment. Each mission has it's own individual objective, ranging from "RACE TO THIS SPOT" to "Kill everything ever"
You can find these blue orbs in the stage similar to coins or rings in Mario or Sonic respectively, except in this game, they boost your maximum "Skill Capacity." As you kill enemies, you get Experience points to level up, which boosts your characters stats over-all. However, you also get this blue substance that boosts your "Skill Capacity" Missions can rewards you with stat boosts that you spend this maximum capacity to activate on whatever loadout you are using. These abilities range from Stat boosts, resistances to certain ailments, bonuses based on situations and equipements, and brand new attacks and movement / combat options.
The other options on the menus is customization, which is where you use the money (energy is the currency) you've earned to upgrade your gear, or make entirely new gear. There are ways to customize their stats with elements and status debuffs. You can also unlock and craft new cosmetic items, although these are fairly limited. This is a fun feature, and I enjoy it's use in the game.
Settings is standard, graphics options are limited, multi-language support, all voice acting is japanese only, resolution and effects changes are available. Nothing special here.
OVERALL:
I'm a fan of this game, and I wanted to buy it on Playstation 4 for a long while now, however the $30 price tag kept me from doing so. However, I never knew it came out on steam, and the moment I found it then saw the price at $15 on sale, I jumped on it.
I am so glad I did. This game is so worth that price to me. If you're looking for a recommended price from someone who likes this game, I'd say it's worth around:
$15 - $30
The game is priced JUST RIGHT for me to say it's worth the money.

is without a doubt the technical definition of a mixed bag. It has the charm of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ co-worker that you enjoy talking to and passing the time, but deep down you realize their soul is comprised of festering garbage and you want to set them on fire.
is fast, flashy and downright exhilarting when it works. Chaining combos/fatal moves and wrecking a screen full of enemies is satisfying. Various weapon setups are available and encouraged to be used as you progress. You will find that dual wielding works better in one situation, while a two handed or ranged weapon will succeed in another. Being able to dash omni-directionally adds to the frantic nature of fights you encounter.
On the other hand, the combat can be clunky. No matter how well you think you've mastered your style, sometimes your character just won't do what you want. Part of it can be chalked up to long cooldown frames. Other times, it's because they didn't add something as small as being able to change weapons midair.
One final, but important note worth mentioning is the
Sometimes the game will decide to be kind to your eyes, but most times it can be nauseatingly close. Earth's Dawn is definitely meant to be experienced from your couch. If you have a battle station and get motion sickness easily, you should probably avoid this game altogether.
goes a bit beyond the norm, and is another area where it excels. You unlock skills that range from making combos longer, to having a permanent HP and Defense increase. Reflecting attacks and increasing the ability to dash around like a cokehead are just a few of the other options available.
Where it gets interesting, is unlocking base skills that serve no purpose than increasing a specific attack. Say you have a TEC+3 blip to activate. By itself, it does nothing. But then you link it to the third attack in a combo. That third hit will do more armor damage. This can be really helpful, as some attacks/weapons are naturally better at breaking armor. You can end up with a
attack completely shredding their defense, or you can balance it out across an entire chain. It's left to your discretion.
If you want better armor and weapons in the game, you have to
them and eventually
their level. This is all done by getting mission rewards and specific drops from enemies, along with energy drops that act as currency. It's not as satisfying as it could be, because once you've grinded a weapon up significantly, a better one will become available to make. You can customize how your character looks with Avatar accessories and armor. It's a nice asthetic touch. Overall, the game wants you to start branching out into elements of weapons to change depending on the type of enemy you're fighting. It adds a little more depth to the gameplay, but with a major caveat: grinding.
is massive. At times, it feels like a Pay To Win title, minus the cash shop. You can't even progress the story without doing it. You need more items for a weapon? Gotta grind until they drop. Want to get those STR+3 skills to link to your attacks? You're going to grind the same mission until you've got each one unlocked. And you won't get them unless you complete the mission with an A or S Rank. A lot of times, that isn't an issue. But...only if you grind ad nauseum. It becomes clear early on that this is the name of the game. There is some variety to be had, such as speed running to a destination, kill X amount of enemies or a boss variant. But it can be a slogging endeavor.
, the game is amazing. But with the forementioned grind, you'll have to appreciate the style enough to see the same screens over and over again. Earth's Dawn is hard to put down, but also easy to hate. The current $30 dollar price tag is unrealistic, almost laughable. But at a price drop, it's worth killing eventless days with.

I have to admit my expectations for this game were pretty high prior to having played it. Also this is not a staunch "No" to the game overall as it isn't terrible, however this is a cautionary review to anyone considering paying full price for the game. I would only buy this game when/if it is significantly discounted, 29.99 is quite a hefty price tag to be asking for it, and even at 14.99 when I bought it for half off I can't help but feel I would have gotten more bang for my buck from other titles.
While the art and design of the characters and enemies are undeniably cool-looking and the story is full of sci fi tropes fans of the genre will enjoy (requisitioning alien technology for human / earthling use, an imminent alien threat...) the gameplay itself is pretty repetitive. The effects can be cool as enemies explode into colorful "firework" looking displays of sparks and particles, however defeating the same enemies with the same execution animation for the nth time begins to wear thin relatively quickly. A limited moveset for the player (you can boost/dash, double jump, slide, etc...) is expanded as you unlock other abilities, but the movement itself feels quite stilted. (If other players of the game have abilities or weapons they recommend unlocking to make your character's movements / style seem less "blocky" than what is offered at the base level, I'm open to hear them...) Some cool, large boss fights shake up the action, but the overall gameplay loop is pretty basic.
If you're a diehard fan of sci fi / anime and intrigued by the setting or look of the game I might suggest still giving it a go but I would definitely wait to snag it during a sale as what is present feels a bit thin.

You can use swords, guns, broadswords (2h great swords combined with gun), shurikens (great fast and deadly weps), crossbows, combinations of 1-h sword and gun or dual swords. Also you are not limited to 1 weapon set, later in the game, you'll get skill which allows you to manage 2 different and switch them even in missions (combat).
Skills - you can manage 5 different skill sets, each with maximum of 200 points invested. You can improve your attacks, learn new abilities such as sword shield, homing boost, max air jump increase, you can raise your imunity to several efects such as burn, paralyze, freeze etc. up to 100%, increase your HP and stats and so on.
Craft - craft is really good, sometimes you need to grind to get rare materials, but it's not that bad since combat is really enjoyable. You can craft and upgrade weapons, armor, accessories and costumes (avatar armor and head gear with no stats / effect). Once you beat the game main missions and final boss, you can start with "endless" mission where you can gain some special materials and boost your weapons even more with extra stats.
Story - story is good - i mean like background story for this kind of game. Nothing epic with movies and tons of cutscenes, story of Earth's Dawn is about few pictures displayed and narrated simply by text and Japanese voice actors (very good imo).
Music - i really like it, great tracks
Overall: original action mix with really good combat system and great and original art. Gem! :)

Earth’s Dawn is a side-scrolling action RPG fighting game developed by Oneoreight and published by Rising Star Games. In Earth’s Dawn the Earth has been invaded by a group of aliens known as the E.B.E. and due to their technological upper hand, have dominated humanity whilst facing limited resistance. This is where you the player comes in! You play as a member of an elite squad of soldiers known simply as A.N.T.I. in your quest to vanquish the alien invaders and reclaim a destroyed Earth. As a member of this elite group, scientists and military weapons engineers have equipped you with some highly sophisticated hardware specially designed to fight the alien menace through the use of their own technology. Your weapons and armor have been modified to merge both living E.B.E. cells and metal machine into cyborg-like armor that allows you to fight as a super-human.
Backstory aside, the game itself plays as a shooter-hack and slash hybrid across a 2D side-scrolling platform. In Earth’s Dawn you will have to navigate different levels with varying alien encounters and abilities and the occasional boss encounters which offer some great gameplay and challenges. In Earth’s Dawn the gameplay in terms of storyline progression works in two ways. First there are the main missions which must be completed to further unlock side missions in that same area. After you complete the main missions, you will be given a timer on the main menu which denotes the time until the next counteroffensive mission—or main mission. During this downtime between main missions it is important to complete the side missions. These side missions are a way to level up, gain skill points and collect reagents used to build, upgrade and customize weapons and armor. Completing a mission awards skill points as well as by leveling up through overall progression. These skill points are used to customize player play style through, increased damage, defensive or technological boosts to your soldier through a skill tree. In addition, you can link specific attack modifiers to certain abilities such as a down-slash or a combo move in order to boost the damage of a particular ability which drastically increased the customization of Earth’s Dawn.

I'm not someone who is intimitely familiar with platformers nor am I someone accustomed to the blissful feeling of completeing games. These were the two reasons why I felt like I had to play this after being seduced by the vivid colors and humerous writing, and I'm so glad I played Guacamelee.
Guacamelee brings me back to playing the old Metroid games on my Gameboy Advance, and the game knows it. Entire game mechanics are in-jokes which are a small part of the fantastic sense of humor of this title. The game takes place in technically an open world, where you can go to any area at any time, assuming you've unlocked the required move to reach the location. Despite being open, you will ALWAYS know exactly where to go, and the areas area small enough as to not feeling like any time is wasted traveling.
Unlike Metroid, Guacamelee features a fantastic brawling combat system which was deftly designed to grow in complexity at the perfect rate I was learning the game. Without being hindered by petty realism, you get to beat to staisfyingly beat up skeletons and throw them at their friends. Boss fights are almost always challenging but so incredibly satisfying when victorious.
The game is wrapped in a nice simple ~6 hour story where I always knew what my purpose was and what the stakes are. It's nothing very emotional but it succeded in giving the gameplay meaning.
All in all, Guacamelee was an incredibly satisfying game to complete and I'd recomend it to anyone interested in the genre of 2D platforming adventures.

I really want to like this game. It tries to be so many things: a brawler with controls like Smash Bros., a metroid-vania, an intense platformer and a collage of gaming memes. In Guacamelee's attempt be all these great things it loses its balance.
For example, I went back and forth between really enjoying myself to frustration a lot. I would be jamming out to the music, thinking that I was decent at the game and then I spend the next 15 minutes on the same bogus platforming or fighting segments. It felt like I was being cheated, after all, wasn't I good at the game just a minute ago? There are just some places where the game gets brutal and it can really catch you off guard.
Most of the bosses are just repetitive and way to random, making them less of a test then a large thorn in your side. Hence the name Guaca-Melee, this game turns out to emphasize fighting a lot and has a ton of combos. Thing is, they don't work on bosses so what's the point? In a boss battle you can get maybe 5 hits on them until they teleport away, swap dimensions or throw up another shield. Similarly, combos on regular enemies get punished as you can just get more than a few hits in before someone else takes a swing at you. In fact, avoiding longer combos and just going for random stray hits after dodging an onslaught of attacks for long time is the best way to avoid damage in the later stages of the game.
Before the real challenging bits kicked in, I was ready to buckle down and 100% this game. In order to do this I would've had to deal with Guacamelee turning into Super Meat Boy (Kid you not, saw blades and everything). Some of the collectables have insane challenges behind then while other are way too simple to obtain. It's this general sense of "Oh, you can enjoy yourself...after banging your head into the wall”, which disagrees with me. Challenge is great. Throwing yourself at a wall until you win isn’t a good challenge and certainly isn't rewarding, for me at least.
Go ahead and buy it. It can get pretty cheap. I loved the earlier stages and I might be a lot of fun with a companion, who knows? Everything is stylized and unique from the music to the characters and to the art. I’m just a tad salty that I didn’t end up loving this game. I may not like it but I would recommend it.

Cossacks 3 is fun to play but seems a bit quirky.  I do love the massive combats where I can build a large army (I was able to build well over 800 units before the game ended) and watch a fluid battle unfold agains the computer's large army. The graphics are very good running on my laptop and the game performs very well. The mechanics of the game is very fun and not too much different from most RTS games.
Every Thursday night for the past 3 weeks, I have been playing Cossacks 3 with my three friends in a coop multiplayer. During this time we have had some annoying issues with the game that almost make it unplayable. For example, tonight it seemed that I was out of sync with my fellow players. Multiple times the AI would sometimes ignore my troups as I marched through his army (as if I was a ghost). Also the AI was able to march through my closed gates. The week before, a simular thing happend to one of my friends. The week before that it was my other friend.
Another common issue is that 50% of the games we played, one of us would continually get a screen freeze that would last a minute or two while the rest of us continued to play (pausing the game for a few minutes to allow the behind player to catch up seemed to help). We all have Intel I7 CPUs and good graphic cards with excelent Internet connections. There always seems to be something weird happening to this game during multiplay, unlike other games we play.
I haven't had too much trouble playing the game as a single player, hower the campaings are not always intuitive. I found myself trying to figure out how to win the game after wiping out the enemy, only to find out that I succeeded some time ago after quiting the game (out of boredom) and then accessing the campaign menu, only to see the next game in the campaign was available. It would have been nice if there would have been a message saying I won the game instead of letting me playing on and on like that.
There was another incident where I couldn't even select my armies, which needless to say, stopped me from continuing the campaing. For now, I have stopped playing all of the campaigns out of frustration and instead playing random single player games. I must say that the few campaing games I did play were fun and challenging.
I did see a post of another patron who said that he "loves and hates" this game. From my expericence I totally agree with that statement. The game play is very fun, but the bugs and awkwardness of the campaings makes me hate the game. I have limited free time and I don't like wasting it on buggy/incomplete software.
Dispite the negative remarks in this review I do recommend this game to those who intend to play it as a single player. However, I cannot recommend it for those who plan to play it as multiplayer, for it is too buggy.
I do hope they would spend more time fixing the bugs instead of developing more DLC for this game. If they did that this would be a great game. In the mean time, I will stick with Cossacks 3 a bit longer until my friends and I find our next game for our Thursday nights.

Hitman: Blood Money was and still is quite the changeup compared to the all-time glorious Hitman: Contracts, its direct predecessor. While it really opened up the game mechanics by adding hundreds of bystanders and civilians to many of the levels, which also happen to be some of the best designed levels and environments of the entire franchise, Blood Money also butchered backstory continuity between levels and added a very annoyingly rudimentary unlock system which gave you access to many weapons and gadgets you would end up never even using once if you wanted to get a Silent Assassin rating, making most of these items entirely obsolete and therefore soiling the entire unlocking process.
Those little flaws aside, Blood Money managed to heavily build upon the best elements of the Hitman series, meaning it featured even more ridiculous accident kills, some levels with vertical gameplay (the Casino and Opera being two of my favourites) and even more different viable approaches than were already introduced in Hitman: Contracts.
And while Blood Money is currently eleven years old, it aged really well, plays even better than Absolution and can still be enjoyed to its full extent without any drawbacks. This should not be missing from any person's library with a love for stealth games and is more than worth its asking price. On sale this should be an automatic purchase.

I cannot recommend this game to the gaming population in general, or even platformer enthusiasts in general. I can only honestly recommend this game for a very specific type of player.
The game should appeal to younger gamers and those looking for a very casual gaming experience, and even more specifically, players that won't mind, or won't notice, the "cookie-cutter" level design that is repetitious and unimaginative.
However, there is an additional issue with the controls and the texture of the surfaces. That issue is that the surfaces provide absolutely no traction or resistance, meaning that the entire game is like playing an "ice" world/level in another game. This can be challenging and fun in small doses, but when a game is like that in its entirety, especially when it's obviously suited for younger and/or casual gamers, it doesn't make sense.
During my gameplay, I had extreme difficulty with this, because the character slides when you're not touching the controls, causing the cat to slip right over the edge of very short horizontal ledges and surfaces and to slide down on vertical surfaces.
Wall-jumping mechanics are also flawed here because of this slippage. It's difficult to jump from one vertical surface to another without sliding backwards or overshooting entirely.
I also noticed that the jump height and distance were inconsistent. At times, the cat jumped higher or further than it did during consecutive attempts in the same spot, and I couldn't figure out a reason for that other than design flaw. I didn't find a double jump, high jump, or sprint capability, so that didn't explain it, either.
I was also disappointed by the poor grammar and spelling, which was distracting to me and seems likely due to poor English translation.
Gamers looking for an immersive storyline in which to engage will not find that here. That aspect was also way below the average "grab the coins/gems" jumping platformers. As one who sometimes just wants to play a game without having to think too much, I can appreciate why the level design and problem solving/strategy aspects might have been purposely simplistic, but when the design itself or game mechanics, such as movement and controls, introduce illogical and inconsistent difficulty, that appreciation for a purposeful decision is replaced by disappointment for error and/or complacency. The resulting confusion and frustration completely negate any appreciation.
I actually had this game on my wishilist and was very happy to see it come up in a recent bundle offer. If I'd paid full price for this game, I'd be much more disappointed than I am, and most likely very upset.
If you can find the game for a buck or two (or included in a bundle) and the issues I've mentioned don't deter you, then this may in fact be a game for you to try. On the other hand, if you're seeking consistency, high replayability, immersive storyline, a challenging puzzle platformer, or unique level design, then you're best looking elsewhere.

**If you haven't played these games before just google 'Samorost' and you can play the first one for free - it's well worth checking out to see what you're in for - Amanita has just upped it's game in terms of production values/style since then too.**
Review:
Nice game - amazing music, animations, and art work as always from Amanita.
In terms of 'fun' I'd rate this as 'OK' to 'good'. Some puzzles can be frustrating, not because they're too hard, but because you sometimes have to go back and forth over lengthy distances which it can become tedious but this could be considered complementary to the game's unhurried vibe.
It's an artful point and click adventure with a cute story, no verbal dialogue, and some relatively satisfying puzzles that can feel a bit tedious occasionally. There's about 4-5 hours of game here (I know my playtime says different - I'd left it running in the background multiple times), so unless you're a big fan of C&P or Amanita I'd say; buy in a sale...

I'm only three hours in, but I am very happy with the game already. It's just as creative and enjoyable as the previous two games. The puzzles are cleverly designed. The artwork is richly detailed and striking. There is a charm to this game (much like the previous two) that I find soothing during some of the more obscure puzzle sections. I don't like that some of the levels can have some lengthy backtracking if you miss something or perform the puzzle steps out of order. But this is only a minor issue for me.

If you've played previous works by Amanita Design (Samorost, Botanicula, Machinarium), then you'll have a pretty good idea what to expect.  The game oozes charm and is a delight visually.  There's precious little hand-holding, so if confounding puzzle design frustrates you then you may want to seek challenge elsewhere.  Otherwise, Samorost 3 rewards patient and pensive puzzle solving - just keep trying and you'll eventually start to get a feel for what the game wants of you.  Don't do yourself the disservice of consulting a walkthrough - if you're stuck just walk away and come back to it later.  One thing that wasn't immediately apparent to me and could be helpful: the locked book on the menu is a hint system, and the lock is a rudimentary puzzle.  (Again, I'd recommend not using it if avoiding it is at all possible.  I wish I'd known so I wouldn't have accidentally spoiled one puzzle for myself early on.)  If playtime is important to your purchasing decision, Samorost 3 isn't long - I've 100%'d the game in around 5 hours of play.

This game is a must for those with any appreciation for visual arts and/or atmospheric music. With a good set of headphones, you really get immersed in the world with its incredible soundtrack. The graphics are outstanding as well, and featured some stunning bioluminescent aspects. The detail put into the environment, as well as the puzzles/achievements themselves, goes to show the care that went into the making of this game.
It was a little shorter story than I would have preferred (mostly because I would have loved to had seen more), but a number of achievements can only be found after the game is completed anyways.
However, the plot itself is actually a little weak. You're mostly just exploring and solving puzzles with no real motive for doing so. Your completion of the game has nothing to do with how you started it, so it feels more like just another completed puzzle rather than the game itself; I was surprised when the credits started rolling.
Not having played any previous Samorost game, I had a completely fresh pair of eyes on this. Overall, the imagination put into this game blew me away. There was a certain child-like wonder that really enhanced the game for me. The sound effects alone added a bunch to gameplay experience. I would definitely recommend for anyone interested in a relaxing point 'n click puzzle game w/ a stellar ambiance.

Aliens have invaded earth, and it’s up to a couple hulking dudes and limber babes decked out in space armor and pimp shades to drive those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s back into outer space (Slow motion pimp shades zoom in with gansta music).  Tossed in a purdy coat of Japanese inspired comic-book art, you can pick it up on for $24 US dollars on Steam right now.
Earth's Dawn isn’t going to win any awards for storytelling.  You are charged with reclaiming Earth from invading aliens.  You’ve hi-jacked some alien technology and now you’re a superhero laser shooting, katana swinging badass capable of going toe-to-toe with some of the galaxies scariest creatures.  Sound like a Michael Bay movie?  You betcha.
(Insert Micahel Bay)
Gameplay in Earth’s Dawn revolves around the mashup between it’s boost and juggle systems.  You can mix together melee and ranged attacks in mid-air and dance around the screen with your dashes which replenish over time.  When you’ve smashed your enemies down far enough, you can open up with finishers to execute.
A dedicated combo system would have gone a long way to make the combat more satisfying.  Where are the abundant special abilities, special melee attacks and why isn’t there a combo system to create links and cancels during combat?  With these features omitted, gameplay often feels a little disjointed as you will be at the mercy of simply smashing the attack button over and over until an enemy's lifebar is depleted.  Finisher...rinse and repeat.  Fun for a while, but then repetition sets in.
To counter that litany, the game does have a lavish loot and upgrade system.  Unfortunately, there is also shocking amount of missed opportunities in terms of this progression system.  Most unlocks are simply stat enhancers, sadly, and do little to vary up the gameplay save a few interesting movement unlockables.
On the bright side, boss battles in Earth’s Dawn are pretty epic and challenging, not to mention really enjoyable to look at.
The beautiful manga-based art style is a treat to look at while playing, and while the characters are silly and charming, the environments are far less colorful and personality-driven than games like Dragons Crown .  Animations are flashy, however, and give a nice pop to the otherwise suprisingly grey and brown dominated environments.  Yeah, there’s a lot of grey here, a lot of caves and rocks, and a lot of stone and fire.  I was craving green in Earth’s Dawn.  Trees, grass, sunshine radiating through the screen as it exists in it’s competitors games, but on the positive the game does offset this monotone environment style with effects that seem to light up those dark places.  Tons of spells and abilities burst and splash through the game space like fireworks - really fun stuff to watch.
It should be noted that the game has no english voice overs and the music is fairly uninspired.
Due to the mission structure and lack of gameplay variety, Earth Dawn will begin to feel repetitive.  Depending on your tolerance, that could be a few hours, or 15 in to the game.  Whatever the case, you’ll beg for Earth’s Dawn to mix things up, give you interesting tools and really explore deep gameplay mechanics as you progress through the game.  Sadly, that never happens.  Games like Odin Sphere present far more depth to the gameplay, more satisfying chain mechanics, and really give us more personality overall.
Also, I would like to the camera panned back a bit and some improvements made to your AI friends.  Most of the time they sit there like they are half-asleep - all they do is take up the valuable screen space that is already lacking in the first place.
I love Japanese inspired games.  And I love sidescrollers.  So for me, I enjoyed Earth’s Dawn for a few hours.  It sits in the bucket of ‘average, yet competant game.’  I can’t slam it, and I can’t praise it.
Buy this game if you already love the formula of Odin’s Sphere.  I'd say it's worth it for fans, otherwise it may be a game worth skipping.

The equipments / skills / customizations, especially the skills, are what interested me. It is unique, in a way. I haven't played that much to properly judge them, but I love what I have seen so far.
I am certain that I will be getting this again at lower price.

I recommend this game with reservations.
It has some very cool things going for it. First off, if you are a fan of board games (like me) then this definitely scratches that particular itch, most of the time. There are a handful of levels in the story mode that are distinctively puzzles - that is to say, you don't really roll the dice or draw cards but rather attempt to play the dice and cards that you are are prescribed in the correct (and only correct) order to succeed the only way possible. These levels, for me, are the weakest part of the game. Yes, there is satisfaction from figuring out the solution - and you will have to figure it out, the game isn't big enough to be able to find any walkthroughs for - but the frustration begins to set in quickly when you realize that you want to play a tabletop board game, not a puzzle.
Also, the RNG is often unfair. Now, let me clarify that I LOVE randomness in games. My favorite board games are Ameritrash style (Camp Grizzly, Fortune and Glory, Marvel Legendary, I could go on and on) and my favorite pen and paper RPGs are ones with random character generation (Heroes Unlimited, TMNT, well, anything old-school Palladium) so I am not at all one of those people who screams with rage every time he sees a game with RNG elements. However this game does sometimes take it a little far. Example: I was once tasked with killing two enemies who start out in the same room as each other on the opposite side of the map from me. After ten or so failed attempts I just happened to start the game with a Sentinel card in my hand. I placed a Sentinel in their room. Bam, two dead enemies in one round and I never had to leave my starting square. There were other times that the RNG had a similar sort of play against me. And as much as I love randomness, it is simply not fair to win or lose before you (or your opponent) even get to make a turn.
Finally, the voice acting is tolerable, but the voice casting is atrocious. And if you don't know the difference, imagine if Bobcat Goldthwait had been cast as Groot. Sure, he could have said the lines, but it would have sounded ridiculous. I have the same problem here - Sajotir in particular just sounds silly.
Now, I have bashed the game on three seperate criteria, but recognize that both the first and third issues only affect Single Player Story Mode, and frankly, board games like this are never as fun unless you're playing with friends. Also, both are small issues. I can overlook some bad voicing especially since you only hear the voices during the between-mission cutscenes. I can overlook some puzzle missions since they are not the majority. And while some will never get over the RNG issues, they were not enough to kill my entertainment completely.
So, if you are a fan of board games and tactical games that require you to rethink strategies on the fly to deal with random elements, then this game is definitely worth picking up.

This is actually a really well done board game. note i said board game.
if your not into board games you may want to pass on this as it may seem slow because each character and the dungeon go through turns.
STORY MODE most missions are more like a puzzle rather than actually playing against the dungeon but its more for teaching you how to play so i'll forgive this but there is no real replay value here once you complete it.
LOCAL CO-OP is what you'll want to play. if your not doing online. this lets X people all play on the same pc and don't worry there is nothing that needed to be hidden so no need to hide the monitor during turns.
EXIT mode if your doing single player. here you can have up to 9 human or AI. players, note the dungeon is one of these and you can have a human or ai controlling it also the other 8 players (1 character each) can all be on the same team if they wish.
GAME BASICS you start your turn rolling your dice and depending on what comes up is what you can do that turn. there are various dice that do different things based on what you pick at the start and based on your character. some of the things on the dice are sword (do 1 damage to an adjacent character), bow (do 1 damage to a line of sight character), foot (move 1 space), jump (move upto 2 spaces), dodge (switch places with a character in an adjacent space), circle (adds a reroll), card (gives you a new card) and ones that let you flip or rotate a dungeon tile. the dungeon also has its own dice that i wont get into.
most characters have 1 or 2 hp with only the darkness needing 3 hits+a reroll token to kill it but your rarely ever forced to kill one. your gives X rerolls per turn (you can set this) and there are cards that effect game play. there are also many setting for victory like get to X space, kill Y character, ect. to win any you need to be aware of your surroundings and dungeon layout.
the only complaints i can see are that its slow paced (being more board game like this is tolerable), the camera resting all the time, the spaces between the tavern boards (this is just my ocd and i'm not sure if they are this way doto the flip/rotate mechanic but it just bothers me they are not closer to each other), and game play it rather simple (characters having only 1-2hp, with no weapon, or ability upgrades though missions are over fast and there isn't much carry over from game to game).
i do like it but on that note i do admit its not for everyone and best if you can get friends to play with. watch videos and decide if its for you. this would actually be a great game if you play board games in real life and did this game instead of a real life board game as they could all gather round the pc.

A clever concept, a series of room puzzles in a clockwork dungeon setting, in which you spend your limited abilities to move, defeat monsters and bypass traps; choose poorly and you die. There is some randomness, but success mostly depends on your learning how to properly use your abilities without wasting moves.

To call this just a board game doesn't really do it justice. It's a little more sophisticated in that you play in a 3D dungeon that constantly changes. Rooms can be flipped to give a different layout or rotated which changes the exit and entry points. In story mode you take control of various characters that have found themselves in the dungeon for one reason or another and to pass each level you are given objectives like reaching an exit or killing hostile opponents. To do this you role a dice which gives you 5 actions including movement, combat or dungeon manipulation. If you end your turn on a space, next to a monster or in a deadly room, you die. You also have to contend with a mean dungeon master who will mess with the layout of the dungeon and throw new monsters in to it.
Every few levels are puzzle levels which have only one solution and you are given fixed actions to use. Some of these look impossible at first but knowing what actions you have gives you a clue as how to tackle them.
This game won't appeal to everyone, like any dice or card game, luck plays a big part and there will be instances when you simply don't have the actions required to get to safety and you will die... often! On the flip side it's also rewarding when initially it looks like there is no hope, but then you flip the board, swap places with a player, jump over a gap, kill a monster and manage to escape.
Another thing to be aware of is there is waiting, it's a turn based game and some levels have up to six computer opponents so it takes time for the computer to make all their moves. I also found it confusing at the start and it wasn't until I completed a few levels that I fully understood what I was doing and started to enjoy it.
I understand there is multiplayer against other human players which I haven't tried, or you can play against the computer. Either way you can get all of the multiplayer achievements.
This game is clearly a labour of love by the developer who is very active in the forum listening to suggestions, addressing any problems and making improvements. If you like board games or TBS and like a challenge then I recommend you give this game a go.

follows Mark, an ordinary high school sophomore, though one with a propensity for not paying attention in class. Alongside him are his caring little sister Rin, Japanophile friend Lukas, and quiet friend Lillian. Mark's life starts to change a bit when a mysterious girl, named Myra, starts to stalk him at random times and seemingly appears out of nowhere.
This game is a visual novel, a type of video game heavily story-based. Most of the game is reading the story, though there are a few decision points along the way that alters the story a little bit.
To start off with, I thought the art in the game was generally pretty good, especially considering this game is available for free. The game employs a standard anime-esque style in its artwork with chibi-style artwork for some scenes. Although it is a bit rough around the edges, I thought the art was good and an admirable effort by the game's creators.
The main purpose of a visual novel is the story. Overall, I thought the story was okay. It is mostly a romance-type plot. I thought it was creative enough that you really have to play to the end in order for the events of the game to really be put into perspective. However, I felt some of the writing could have used more work. Lukas, for example, comes off as little more than a stereotypical weeaboo and this characterization was more annoying than anything. I do not really mind the anime style in games like this, but the numerous references to Japanese pop culture (such as references to other visual novels, Rin calling her brother "onii-chan," and mention of a maid café) felt shoehorned in and unnecessary especially considering the setting is unambiguously a Western country. The side stories in the game also feel rather underdeveloped. Still, despite those criticisms, the core story was interesting enough to keep me playing to the end. This visual novel is more on the short side and it should only take around three hours to complete.
Overall, I would say that my reaction to this game is mixed, but I still give it a recommend. Though I felt the writing was a little weak, the central story is good and I can certainly appreciate the laudable effort that was put into it. If you like visual novels with a romance theme, you might like this.

Combat:
What really surprised me is how deep the combat system is. With only a handful of enemy types the game presents new and dynamic challenges by combining and recombining the enemy types, giving some of them shields which need to be taken down with specific moves, and putting some in a different plane where they can damage you but you can't damage them until you shift to their plane. The challenges in El Infierno really highlight just how deep the combat system is and are a fantastic challenge. A special mention must go out to the fantasic boss fights. They were challenging and engaging, and really tested your ability to quickly respond to varied attacks.
Story:
The story is pretty sparse, but what it does have I found very enjoyable and humorous. It's nothing that's going to change your world, but it's a cherry on top of a great experience that compliments it well.
I cannot recommend this game highly enough. If you like metroidvania games this is a must have.
