Considering the fact that Oracle was developed by a team of five, with each seemingly taking on one task all by his own, I appreciate the effort that went into it. Though sadly, I must conclude that it doesn't cut it, even from a gamer's perspective who enjoys walking simulators.
You wake up by a campfire at the shores of an abandoned island as the first piece of narration kicks in. Just as in most examples of the genre, the backstory is told through the monologues of the protaganist, who, in this case, is a solitary man that chose to escape from the society and dwell on an abandoned island on his own. Glimpses of his past life, as well as his comments on various unfortunate events that took place in the said part of his days are revealed piece by piece, whenever you reach some kind of landmark throughout your lonely exploration of the titular island.
Unfortunately, that is all there is. Oracle's overall lack of progression makes it a shallow experience at best. This being a pure walking sim at its heart, the lack of environmental or character-based interaction, as well as there being no objectives other than wandering and listening to the soliloquies on offer, are tolerable. However, it looks like dropping the clueless player into an overly vast island, which in itself does not have any clear paths to follow, was a misstep. I'm sure that many a player got frustrated and felt lost in the first few minutes. The thing is, I too, would most likely not find my way around without taking hints from the achievement descriptions. Bearing in mind the fact that one can not conclude the journey unless s/he finds all the landmarks which trigger the (decently acted) narrative pieces one by one, it's easy to assume that this may very well be a test of patience for most, rather than the calming experience it strives to be. Exploration is to be taken as reward-in-itself in this genre, unless that exploration turns to a systematical scan of the game world on offer, which clashes with the basis of it all.
The problems with the audiovisual and technical side of things do not help it either. The constant pop-ins/outs of the distant objects and environmetal props, coupled with the repetitive texturing and the pixelated skybox make it hard to suspend one's disbelief. The said pops also affect the explorative aspect of the game, since what looks like a barren plain from a certain distance may actually be housing a landmark that needs to be visited. Above all else though, the greatest deterrent is the painfully slow pace of the player character: with an island of this extent, it would be wiser to let the explorer walk a little faster, or tweak the so-called 'sprint' ability so that it actually feels like sprinting rather than a momentary thrust. Adding insult to the injury, looking around does not feel smooth either, most likely due to a forced interpolation of the mouse movement, with no remedy in sight since there aren't any options to speak of apart from the standart Unity welcome-screen with the resolution and quality modifiers. The single, soothing background track does its job pretty well though. Sadly, its impact is marred by all the factors mentioned above.
All in all, Oracle fails to impress. The protaganist's hour-long wandering does not offer any kind of catharsis for him, nor a fully-realized experience for the player. If you are new to walking simulators, this shouldn't be your starter. If you're familiar with the genre however, know that Oracle is nowhere near the quality you've come to know from the cream of the crop.

One of the first I noticed was objects in the distance show up on the edge of your screen, but they disappear when you look at them if they are far away. Archibald's Adventures is an interesting puzzle platformer - generally, it's good when it's being a puzzler and mediocre when it's being a platformer. A good deal of that has to do with the control scheme - most unusually, there's no jump button; instead, you automatically jump under certain conditions. Combined with the clearly defined grid layout, this allows for more interesting puzzles than could have been created with a 'free' jump, but it makes platforming feel pretty awkward.
There's a reasonable variety of puzzles, but most of the better ones make good use of boxes that you can move around with a magical floating bubble (?) and in some cases destroy. The bubble also can be used to 'scout out' levels and trigger some switches - it's a key mechanic of the game and it eventually feels fairly natural, though like much of the control scheme, it's weird at the start (and the fact that you can only move either your character or the bubble at any given time gets cumbersome). Additionally, you unlock a vehicle after a few areas that can grab onto magnetic surfaces, allowing for some more interesting level design.
In short, while it's not exactly intuitive, there are some neat puzzles here that might be worth checking out.

Archibald's Adventures is a great puzzle platformer, originally released for mobile devices and windows back in 2009. Seven years later, it found it's way into steam, hopefully to receive the attention that it deserves so much!
You are Archibald, or Archi in short, and with your friends, skateboard fans all of you, are showing off your skills to each other. However after a jump where your friend gets cocky, Archie wants to make the perfect jump that requires a bigger ramp. The only place where he can find such ramp is a junkyard next to professor Klumpfus mansion. Disregarding the warning of his friends, he convinces them to follow him into the junkyard where he makes the jump. To his bad luck his momentum carried him far enough to fall right into a huge pipe, leading further below ground, right into professor Klumpfus laboratory. You begin your adventure right here, as the crazy professor informs you that something has gone terribly wrong and his mansion is under lock down, lab specimens are free and there are tons of other hazards loose. But there is hope! You can lift the lock down yourself, if you manage to reach the exit of each room that is...
The controls are basic and easy to grasp as the game supports gamepad as well as keyboard. While there are no options to customize them to your fitting but I hardly doubt anyone would need such customization, as the entire game can be played with one hand by the arrow keys or the controllers D-pad. The music while somewhat repeating at first, it complements the softcore nature of the game and will not make you fed up. As mechanics go, at first you control Archie on his skateboard and a bit later you get your first real tool, a bubble, that allows you you move crates and use switches out of reach, however at this point, the game is more platformer than puzzler. After the first 2 chapters you will get the iconic maintenance pod (the wheal pod) that will give you the magnetic ability to stick onto metallic surfaces and the ability to ram or smash certain blocks, this is where the fun begins! Eventually you will control the professor himself with his jetpack! The core mechanic is that you can move blocks around, and with said blocks most of the time you will have to construct the platforms you will need, in order to reach the exit. Sounds easy? Well it isn't! For its limited controls the game utilizes its mechanics to the fullest, levels vary from easy to hard, with no difficulty tags. I cannot stress out how well designed each level is, from platform based levels, where you just need to figure out your path to the exit, to puzzle based levels, where you have to make the path! The games description notes that there are "almost 200 levels" while that is true, there are a few tutorial levels, taking them out leaves with over 180 actually unique levels! Lastly, each level visuals, further emphasize that you are, indeed, into a mad scientists laboratory!
Archibald's Adventures is definitely worth its price, as you will need to devote a considerable amount of time in order to finish the story and the extra levels! There will be time where you will feel stuck, and when the epiphany happens, where the solution will naturally appear in front of you, you will get that sense of accomplishment that sadly fewer and fewer puzzle games manage to deliver!

I got this game a long time ago from their website so I played a lot more than what says above. I love it! Such a tight well designed puzzle platformer! It uses a grid-like movement with well defined rules. For example, if you move through 3 squares you gain speed which can be used to jump through gaps. That's what I mean by grid-based. The first levels will be mostly just showing you different uses of the basic set of movement rules. Then it introduces more elements, like the bubble, then you can control a machine that sticks to metal walls etc. And with each new mechanic comes a world of levels exploring the possibilities. Seriously, the amount of levels is so large it's surprising how they kept them interesting and fun for the most part.
"For the most part". Yes, there are a few levels that shy away from clever puzzles to a more reflex oriented type of level. The majority of levels are fun and engaging though.

If you are an analytical, logistics-oriented person who can coalesce money and talent around you to achieve ambitious goals, please submit your application to Railroad Tycoon 2 platinum.
I played this game when it first came out, it's still as solid a title now as it was then, and the mechanics and controls have aged well. While some of the campaign can be quite merciless, I hardly see how that's a problem (considering today's trends towards easy instant satisfaction games).
The AI on the map can leave something to be desired. They build weird routes, and often never expand beyond their two city connections for many years. However, what they lack in physical construction prowess they make up for with their brutal manipulation of the in-game stock market. Which is a peeve, because the market can be very hard to keep up on while you're trying to build a route through rugged mountain terrain, only to find that the dickhole AI has bought out your company, repossessed all of your assets that you put up to start said company, and then locked you out of your office so they can take a big dump on your desk.
But I digress. For the price of the game on the Steam marketplace, you will get a solid return on your investment. hours of fun. Hours of mind numbing track laying, split-screening market trading, and maxing out your profit by alternatively trimming routes and tuning the makeup of the various trains that ply them.

One of the more interesting aspects of this game (that many don't like) is that it focuses on your personal wealth as manager as well as the company wealth. Again, this is more of a management sim than a transport sim, and from the management standpoint this is a very unique aspect of this game that I find enjoyable. (Yet another aspect to manage)
In depth economy (issue stocks/bonds, buy up your competitors, buy the industries, etc)
Industries are randomly generated inside map regions, makes gameplay less repetitive
Pay your competitors to use their rails
Stations have various addons to improve revenue and maintain trains
Cities grow as you supply them, and new industries appear
Old (It is 2D, the interface was designed with efficiency in mind, but it is a later 2D game)

This is one of the best sandbox and stealth-experiences out there. The graphics hold up very admirably and the gameplay is fantastically multi-layered to the point where one playthrough will not be enough for you to find out all the alternative ways in which you can complete the missions. Each mission starts as a seemingly incomprehensible maze of guard routines, restricted areas and potential witnesses, but as you walk around, listen to the people talk in the background and observe their habits you will soon understand how these different security layers interact and where there is enough space for you to enter.
Also something worthy of praise is the fact that you can do anything from mowing down everyone in your path to finishing the game without firing even a single shot. The controls had me a bit confused at first, but after a while it just clicks and all the nifty little details (like hiding weapons in trays or poisoning food) open up a ton of ways to get at your targets any way you want. Being patient yields high rewards and there is little more satisfying than having a level figured out to the extent where upon your escape your targets lie dead, seemingly by freak accidents, and nobody suspects a thing. Easily the best "Assassin-Simulator" I've ever played and a marvelous power-fantasy if you get into it enough.

Ok so...
Far From Noise is a narrative game in which you play a woman stuck in its car, balancing on the edge of a cliff.
It's about life, death, nature, purpose, creativity, dreams, stars and badgers.
The thing about Far From Noise is that it'll ask you something very special, something that we all forget to do nowadays, something that I've forgotten. This game will ask you to take your time. Don't rush things. Sit down and relax as you'll be forced to follow the slow pace of the game, but you'll enjoy it, for sure.
This game is for you if you come home after a rough day at work. This game is for you if you're searching for a meaning, a purpose in your life. This game is for you if you just want to experiment something new.
Because Far From Noise is offering you something new. It gives a vibe that is between Firewatch and Life is Strange, but without all the forced action, stress, adrenaline those game wanted to give. Don't misunderstand me, I loved those 2 games, but Far From Noise chose a direction more... pure. It's just you and the nature that evolves around you.
I've finished the game within 90 mins, but I heard they were several endings, so I might as well try to get some more (but the one I've got fully satisfied me, to be honest).
Being more pragmatic, the art and sound coincide perfectly. The visuals are gorgeous and the musics hit just right where it needs to. You'll be lifted by the compositions as you'll stare into the beautiful sunset, and the dark starry sky.
You may find it expensive, as the game costs 8$ for one hour and a half of experience, but hey, think about a cinema ticket. Far From Noise is cheaper and the experience you'll live in it is wayyyyy more unique than most of the movies you go see.
I recommend it. Play it. It'll put your mind at ease.
PS: the main character is one of the most well-written i've seen in video games.
This is very special.

"You worry about death while life ignites around you."
The aptly titled Far From Noise is a meditatory exercise in appreciating life, existence, and the universe, while two characters converse in a surreal, perilous situation. It's purely a graphical text adventure game where all you do is choose dialogue options as they pop up. A woman is interminably teetering over the edge of a cliff in her car going through a rollercoaster of emotions until a talking stag shows up and tries to calm her down. The dialogue is excellent and believable (well as believable as conversing with a talking stag would be). The stag talks like a poet finding beauty in being alone and nature, which at first annoys the main character but then she accepts that is the stag's "normal" way of talking and appreciates the contrast. It taps into the main character's quarter-life crisis after dropping out of of studying film/marine biology/architecture (you can choose either of these for a different backstory). Her fears (badgers apparently), desires, regrets, memories, and enjoyments are all explored along with commentary on the events happening currently like rain, storms, or a turtle taxi. This single-location game is able to cover enough in just under 90 minutes to give a life-affirming experience that I can easily recommend to just about anyone not quite sure about where they're going in their lives.

Far From Noise is a beautiful game. The game provides the player with thought provoking dialogue and conversation in which you are provided options to progress the story. The art is simple, unique, and amazing which is welcome in a graphics heavy gaming world. The music and sounds provide a very calming and peacful atmosphere in which to focus on the big questions presented in the game.
It is a perfect length for a single play narrative game at around 2 hours. That was me going slow and reading all options and watching the scenery.  It truly is a welcome addition to my gaming library and experience in general. I highly recommend Far From Noise.

I am a jadded gamer who buys lot of AAA releases every month and doesn't bother to finish them before jumping to a new game. But i did finish this game in just two play sessions, which speaks volumes of this game quality by this fact alone. I got this game from my Humble Monthly subscription. Being tired of Battlefield 1 multiplayer, I wanted to try something with a good narrative. So I remember about this game and install it on my gaming laptop so I can play in my bed before turning lights off. I usually never play on my laptop, despite it's a gaming laptop that features gtx 1060 gpu, as I prefer to play my big games on my gaming desktop rig connected to a big screen. So I started at 11 PM, I check the clock it's 3AM. Thanks good it was Saturday. The is a very good Pont&Click adventure that actually has very interactive puzzle that don't come down to combing stuff from your inventory until you exhaust all possible combination. The puzzles actually require careful logical thinking and answers often lie on the surface. What I loved most in this game is a lovecraftian growing mistery, which absorpts you slowly until you become obsessed with the answers.
There is no better story than that produced by your own imagination, and this game craftly uses this trick against the player. It feeds your right amount of mistery without revealing or explaining to much leaving some stuff to your own interpretation.
Well, I guess this is also constitutes the game's major flaw: despite  being a very good game with amazing story, it doesn't fully lived up to my expectations. I know that it's silly to await a small indie game to go epic and raise the stakes to the maximum, but it still it made me dream for more that it's - the game builds up the mistery to the point you start  fantasing about a big scale mistery or conspiracy, and then it's all suddenly resolved with a much smaller ooumph. It's like you exapected a 3-hour  movie, but it was just a 40-minute tv show episode.
Still it was a hell of a 40-minute tv show episode. I highly recommend this game as it's ideed  a very well done adventure. The best puzzles and dialogs I have seen in years.
And playing the game on my laptop in bed gave me such cozy feeling similar to reading a fantasy novel before going to sleep, as it only requires me to move mouse and nothing else.

My friend gave me this game as he didn't want it as part of a humble bundle, so I decided to try it.
It exceeded every expectation I could possibly have.
The pixel-graphics are implemented in such a way that makes it clear as to what is what, and there's no pixel-hunting so to speak. Holding the spacebar highlights all objects in the room that you can examine in case you think you missed something. I wasn't expecting voice acting, but every single line of dialogue and narrative is fully voiced, and spectacularly so; every voice fits the character's personality and setting. The puzzles and trials that you come across require a proper level of critical thinking; no information is explicitly hidden from you, and there is never any guessing involved if you've searched and discovered every detail available.
What started as me giving some point-and-click adventure a try ended with a wild ride of puzzle solving, investigating and getting confused at all the plot that's being thrown in my face. Even after the story, I still feel a bit confused at some story elements that will most likely be made clear on a second playthrough (in which I'll get all the hidden achievements).
In conclusion, I feel this game is severely underappreciated, and definitely qualifies as a hidden gem. I would very strongly recommend it to anyone who enjoys point-and-click adventures or a good mystery story narrative.

TL:DR
Buy this game!
Gameplay:
The gameplay mostly consists of semi turn-based combat. Mostly, you'll be picking actions for your character and letting them execute them. It's a pretty well balanced and fun combat system, and one that has aged well, but I usually prefer to play on a lower difficulty and focus on the story. You also frequently have the option to skip combat with stealth, hacking and repair skills. When you're not fighting, you'll usually be talking to NPCs. This affects the story, which I would argue is a bigger part of the gameplay than the combat is. The dialogue is well written and fully voice acted. Your dialogue options are also affected by who you have in your party, which is a nice touch. Overall, I enjoy the gameplay, but I think the story is the real draw of the game.
Story:
This game's story is amazing! In my personal opinion, this is the best Star Wars story I've ever experienced! I'm only including the movies and games, but that's still saying something. The characters and the world building are something that I think gaming as a whole could really learn from. Every planet is distinct and interesting. Every character has their own unique personality, and can even intervene if you're doing something they don't like. The followers in this are what games like fallout 4 have tried and failed to replicate. While the actual narrative of the game isn't anything ground-breaking (travel across the galaxy and save the universe etc.) that's more than made up for by the world building. Every location feels completely different, and they all feel like real places that exist outside of what you're able to see in the game.There are tons of side missions to complete, all of which are interesting in their own way. This is a game that really doesn't have filler content! The combat encounters are fun, but the rich worlds that you get to explore and the things that inhabit them are what you're really buying. I really can't say enough about how good this part of the game is!
Visuals:
This game is pretty old. If you want the newest and best graphics, you're in the wrong place. There's more to a game's visuals than the fidelity. This game has a very strong visual style that takes full advantage of the graphical power that was available at the time. As dated as this game looks, I don't feel like that takes away from the experience at all. I have much more of a reaction from the characters and situations in this game than what I've felt in almost any game I've played. Just because a game has more polygons and higher resolution textures doesn't mean it's a better game. Basically, don't let some low-res textures put you off playing an incredible game!
Sound Design:
There's not too much to say here. The sound desing is solid, but doesn't have an enormous impact on the game. Every line of dialogue in the game is well voice-acted, which really helps draw the player into the story. Mostly, though, the sound effects and music don't have a huge impact on the experience.
Summary:
This game is a must play for anyone who just wants to enjoy being a part of the Star Wars universe. This game is not for anyone looking for action packed lightsaber/blaster combat. If you just want to kill something, look elsewhere. If you want to not only experience the Star Wars universe, but actually be in it, look no further. This is what you're looking for. In case you haven't figured it out: BUY THIS GAME!

In theory cossacks 3 should be the perfect game for me as I love this type of base building, large army RTS. The formulae for a good game is there but I cant recommend this game because its just too rough round the edges and basic features are missing. I could look past the rough edges and missing features if this game had only just been released, but unfortunately its been out for ~6 months and DLC “add ons” have already been released which makes me think its unlikely the developer is going to provide the required polish this game needs to become a great game, my hope now is that the modders are able to polish this game properly although I have no knowledge in this area and don’t even know if the tools made available are adequate.
“Rough edges and missing features”
- Missing animations/bad animations (the are far too many to list, one example is cavalry that when moving will have a constant attacking animation even when no enemy is near so they look like crazy people).
- Regiments squish into each other into a ball when in combat.
- Artillery have no operators, they just move and shoot magically on their own.
- To my knowledge the is no way to set keyboard controls and not even an in-game page to tell you what the keys do.
- The naval stuff has loads of problems (for specifics, the are plenty of other reviews which highlight them).
- By default You can NOT rotate the camera and the zoom out is very limited (you can rotate and zoom out more with “cheat codes” but it does not work properly).
- personally I don’t like the scaling, the soldiers are far too big and the buildings and especially walls are too small, it looks silly (I fully understand this is very subjective and more a matter of taste but it is something that bugs me).
- generally a bit glitchy (screen flashes). This may be just me but I have a feeling its not
Positives
- With the extra work, this game could become one of the best base building RTS.
- Developers seem to read comments and take critical feedback well and are generally very polite.

I've not played for very long but I've seen enough to know this game isn't finished and shouldn't be out of early access yet. The first thing I noticed was the horrendous translation job. It's either translated with google translate or by someone who has only a basic knowledge of the language. It's dutch by the way, my native language is dutch. This translation makes for a very amateuristic looking game but even worse it makes for a very awkward reading, it's very difficult to understand the quests and such when the sentences are this unnatural.
So now I got that out of the may I'd like to say some things about the gameplay. In my short play time I haven't experienced any mayor issues like freezing or crashes but the game looks really rough around the edges. There are visual glitches everywhere and while it runs stable (for now) the loading times are too long.
When it comes to the game itself the controls bother me. They promote the game like a successor to the legendary RTC series so why doesn't it play anything like the previous games? The controls are completely different and it feels unintuitive to me. I might get used to that in time though. However, the fact that the targeting system doesn't work has nothing to do with my inability to get used to the new controls. What I mean is, when I try to remove trees, more often then not the game doesn't properly recognize where I'm pointing the cursor exactly.
Then there's the graphics. As I've set before it's really rough and doesn't look natural. The people don't look natural either as their animations look weird. All this combined makes for a game that looks fine at first sight but it never feels like a real theme park somehow.
All this is a real pity because there's actually a more then decent game underneath. None of the issues by itself are gamebreaking bugs but take them all together and you have a very broken game. Fix a few of the above mentioned issues and you get a flawed but fun game.
And that's where it bites: even though there are updates every month I wonder if the fans are ever going to get the game they want. I've tried to contact the developer/publisher to adress my issues but I can't find an official forum or anything to contact them. This worries me.
But I don't want to end on a negative note. As I've said: even though the game isn't finished I could still turn into a fun game it the developers keep updating it as they have been doing. I won't give up on RCTW yet and will be updating this review the longer I play and when the game gets updated. If I look at the previous updates it seems to me that the game does get monthly updates more or less so I expect the next one somewhere in april. I can't recommend RCTW to anyone at the moment. Hopefully that will change in the near future.

Guacamelee is an action platformer that was released in August 2013, published and developed by DrinkBox Sudios. Originally pinned as a Sony exclusive on the PS3 and Vita, it was however later ported to PC before eventually getting the "Gold Edition" releasing on all of the platform in mid 2014. Guacamelee is heavily based on Mexican culture and lore.
You play the role of Juan, a powerful luchador fighter. You will be fighting various different enemies in this platforming metroidvania style game. You start off with a very basic arsenal of attacks which you can pull off such as a basic three attack combo, but eventually you can work you way up to combos which can consist of eight plus button presses! (I never managed to pull off one of these more than once). Juan will also learn a various number of "out of combat" skills, such as wall jumping and the ability to turn into a chicken. The platforming element of Guacamelee was probably the most annoying for me, mainly because I am just terrible at the genre, but I found the jumping puzzles to be just tedious and grew very thin on my patience at times.  The fighting side of the game is done very well; the combo system and special moves you can pull off are all really well done - some fights you will end up getting swamped by enemies, but it won't matter since you can throw together a number of punches which will just knock them out with ease.
Graphically, there isn't too much to shout about, it's a 2d side scroller so generally nothing spectacular is going to be seen, however the art style on show is gorgeous. This really portrays the Mexican style of game extremely well, and is probably the game's best feature. It looks very similar to the recent release of "The Book of Life" from 2014. Whilst it has a cartoon look to it, there is still an element of maturity and darkness in some of the scenes.
The plot in Guacamelee! was nice. It is your typical adventure style story, the humble farmer who is in love with the El Presidente's daughter, the daughter then gets kidnapped, and it is your task to rescue her so you can live happily ever after.  The plot is very well thought out, offers a couple of cliffhangers and interesting twists and turn a long the way. Guacamelee also has a couple of comical moments in too to lighten the mood.
Guacamelee is another game which doesn't have voice acting in; I would really of liked to have seen (or heard) it included, because there is quite a bit of text to read through and I would of thought that having voice acting would make people get more immersed into this wonderful world on show. Having said that, the sound track is amazing. It is playing pretty much constantly throughout the game, and it never wears thin.
As I said above, the I found the platforming side of the game to be the most annoying, mainly because it is super difficult to progress in the game due to a number of jumping puzzles which had me close to rage quiting a number of times. Eventually you will get past them, it just takes perseverance and a lot of patience (something I am slowly finding out that I don't have very much of).  Most of the fight scenes are easily mastered and you probably won't find your self dying an awful lot in this game. The opportunity to raise the difficulty level may change this though, which is something more confident veteran combo fighters will want to check out.
The world in which Guacamelee is set in, is very well fleshed out. There are plenty of NPCs to interact with, loads of side quests to find and complete, most of which are of no relevance to the main story, and is just an extra way to generate funds. Touching again on the topic of special abilities, you will also find your self backtracking to a degree in the game so you can use the new abilities you have just unlocked to reach places which you couldn't before, to unlock chests, health bonuses etc. You will also find a number of shops scattered around the world where you can purchase health and stamina upgrades along with a number of other power ups.
A full playthrough of Guacamelee took me almost eleven hours to complete; this was with the inclusion of the majority of the side quests too. I would say that eleven hours is just the right amount for me. The game also has a local co-op mode which you will find adds a whole new element to the game as well and is certainly worth a second playthrough on this mode, easily touching this game up to the twenty hour mark - and then of course there are the higher difficulty modes you can play on should you desire so. There is plenty of content on offer in Guacamelee to sink your teeth into.
No technical issues here; played on 4k resolution, at a steady 60 FPS as should be expected from a 2d side scroller. You will need a controller to play this game to any degree of competency though, simple because the jumping puzzles and combos would just be ridiculously hard to counter on a keyboard. The options menu also includes a wide variety of options when it comes to selecting resolutions and frame rates too, which is always nice to see.
In conclusion, Guacamelee! is a really rounded out game, which is certainly one of the best indie titles to come out in recent years. The addition of local co-op makes this game even better, and fans of metroidvania style games really need to check this out. The price of £9,99 is an absolute bargain for the amount of content on show here too.

is a fun puzzle-platformer, developed by
studio. It was originally released as a mobile app, on iOS and Palm, in 2008-2009, and subsequently on Play Station Portable, PSP, PS3, MacOS and Windows. It wasn't released on Steam until this month.
It has an easy learning curve and very simple controls, which cannot be remapped. It is much more puzzler than platformer. You have all the time you want to look at a level and figure out what needs doing before taking any action. Each level has ample auto-save points, so you don't have to start at the beginning every time you fail. It's by no means a short game. There are a couple hundred hundred levels.
It looks, feels, and plays like a mobile app, which isn't odd, because it is one. I think I would actually prefer to play it on my tablet than on a big screen, since it seems to me like it would be more enjoyable in shorter spurts of time than in long sessions, much in the same way I prefer to play chess puzzles on my tablet. But the devs have stated on the iTunes store, where it is still available for download, that they have no intention of releasing an Android port. And I have no intention of ever buying an iAnything.
It's a bit over-priced.  I think it should be $3.99 on Steam, which is how much it costs on the App Store.  I'd watch for a sale greater than 10%, which I wouldn't be surprised to see during the Summer Sale.  Even at five bucks though, if you like puzzle games, you should enjoy this one.

Quintessential Hitman!
Following up on its predecessors, Hitman: Blood Money allows the player to take the role of Agent 47, a one-of-a-kind human clone trained to be an assassin for hire. In this installment to the series, the International Contracts Agency (ICA) is being attacked by the Franchise, another illegitimate assassination organization, and 47 is given a series of contracts to take out various clients and ensure the survival of the ICA against this competing organization who are looking to design their own clone assassins.
The level design is excellently varied, with numerous different levels ranging from suburbia to a Chilean winery, to even the White House itself as areas to assassinate targets at, each of which is an open environment with numerous opportunities to approach and eliminate your target - whether that be silently and without ever being seen or by openly engaging whoever you see.
Blood Money introduces a notoriety system to the series - if the player is caught on camera or witnessed committing a serious crime or assassinating their target, their notoriety level is raised at the end of the mission allowing guards to slowly become more and more aware of you in future levels. This can easily be countered, however, by removing the security footage from the security room if a camera detected you or by eliminating whoever was witness to your crime.
Admittedly, I'm very bad at this game despite my love for it. I try my best to be stealthy, but I inevitably end up in a killing spree in an attempt to eliminate my targets, the guards, and any civilians aware that I was in a firefight. But, that's half of the fun on its own, being able to approach the game as stealthily or as violently as you like.
Fun, game you can play multiple times.

text:
This is an excellent game, but not without it's flaws. The first half is good, with open-ended level design, creative settings, clever puzzles and superb dark humor. However, the game peters out in second half, which has less creative level design and is too unforgiving, which gives the player less options and alternate solutions. Additionally, the story drags the game down,  and the mini-bosses were not fun at all. However, the game overall has excellent level design with a large variety of different ways to eliminate your target and rewards given for silent and non-lethal playthroughs, giving the game near-infinite replay value. The core gameplay is very unique and unlike any other stealth game, and it can be a lot of fun to play if you have the patience to deal with both the game's problems and the very nature of it's design as a slow-paced, patience-testing game where trial and error plays a huge part.
The presentation overall is superb. The game looks fantastic for a game from 2006, and holds up well today, with lots of detail and smooth animations. The music is also excellent, with big, bombastic pieces for tense moments combined with subtle, ambient ones for the sneaking around. It fits the mood and is very memorable. The sound design, on the other hand, is underwhelming. The sound effects are average, but the voice acting and especially the lack of variety in voice lines became incredibly irritating the longer I played ("gonna have to search you sir!") The amount of technical polish also leaves something to be desired. I encountered several glitches, such as the floor selection on elevators being extremely finicky, as well as not being able to walk through tight areas that were clearly intended to be walked through.
Another major flaw with this game is the Inability to switch difficulty settings while maintaining past progress. Partway through this game I found myself on too high of a difficulty level, but didn’t want to lower it because it meant redoing several stages, which caused massive amounts of frustration that could have been avoided.
Overall, despite it's problems, this game is excellent, and easily one of the best stealth games of the 2000s, if not of all time. While the game was a bit too slow and patience-testing for my taste, it was still a great deal of fun and I highly reccomend it to anyone interested in the stealth genre.

I also really liked how at the end your progress is show in a newspaper form - it's really fun to read stuff about how well you did on mission. You can also upgrade your weapons and choose the stuff that will make your own play style even more unique.
If you want to start to get into the Hitman games, but you are afraid that 10+ years old game are too old for you, don't have fear. Hitman: Blood Money doesn't feel like an really old game and it's really great choice for the starters.

I don't know that I'd say that 'Antenna' is a good game but for me it is an enjoyable enough one. It's pretty short (maybe half an hour give or take depending on whether you get stuck) with only four real puzzles and the rest of the game involving following prompts and navigating the robot protagonist across the landscape. I didn't mind following the prompts, I felt that I somehow fitted with playing a robot. Unfortunately there does seem to be a bug or two and the game isn't always clear.
I was only on the second prompt when I followed it and... nothing happened. I thought perhaps I was doing something wrong so I tried different variations of pressing/holding the button and randomly pressing other buttons without any success. So I went to the community hub to see what I was doing wrong, but it turns out I wasn't doing anything wrong at all: I just needed to restart the game and it worked as it should the second time around. ^_^;
Then there are a couple of times when the game uses the '?' button as an enter key, and there I was thinking that it must have been a help button, so I was purposefully not pressing it, which didn't help things at all. Also there was a puzzle where it was somewhat tone based and there was no clear prompt on what the game wanted me to do... Actually there was something of a hint earlier in the game, but once you've started a puzzle you're not allowed to exit and go exploring.
All in all I'd say that my first playthrough was a little bit clunky, but really I'd say that the feel of the game with it's graphics, sound effects and atmosphere (and the fact that it's free!) make up for its shortcomings. Since it's a short game I went through for a second playthrough when I finished it the first time, so that I could experience it without the clunks. ^_^

Got this game when it was first relased in the late 1990s. Came back to it on Steam and remembered why I liked it so much to begin with. Lots to do and lots to learn while the same scenarios will play out differently each time thanks to radomized map resources and random events.
There is much strategy to had - certain resources require other resources to make them even more successful (bring grain to a cattle farm and then send the cattle bounty to the slaughterhouse. From there, food is generated that you can send on to a city demanding it. There's nothing like seeing the massive payday of a cross-country haul reach its destination. Or stay out of commodities and simply set up a passenger/mail route between to major hubs.
Different cities/towns require different resources. Routes will vary as you pass through mountains and over rivers as will cost to build your track network and bridges. Your opponents will do what it takes to bring you down, including set up profitable routes in your backyard, buy stock in your company, or buy local businesses that you helped to become lucrative - beat them to the punch and buy those steel mills, factories, and cattle farms before they do. Buy stock in your company or a competitor's company. Deal with economic swings, advancing train technologies, and the judgement of your Board of Directors - it's all here.
The graphics are surely dated by 2010s standards but I can look beyond that limitation to recapture the fun I had with this classic title - even now I get lost in this title for hours. Of all of the strategic railroad sims out there currently (in 2015), I still feel that RRT2 is the best of the pack.

My only dissapointment with this game is that having played the original game on my CMD64 its clear that the developer has decided to 'dumb-down' the network management aspects of the game.
In the original game the player was required to design and manage their rail network and by providing signalling solutions at every network junction.  This meant that the player had much more contol over the flow of traffic, and was not assisted by the 'ghost train' system used in RT2 and subsequent releases.
You had to plan your schedule to avoid conflicts not just rely upon trains to lass magically through each other.  As such getting it wrong resulted in actually train crashes and loss of reputation, drop in customers, and a fall in the share price.
I miss that level of immersion in the game, and it means that TTD now has the edge as far as this type of game is concerned.

Guacamelee is a 2D high-flying combo action and platforming game. The overall theme, music, and graphics are all blended together to make this game a very memorable and fun experience. Some levels or areas can be a bit frustrating as you will need to have precision control and some puzzles can be very tricky, just check out a walk-through or a video to get you passed these areas. There's a ton of content with unique achievements, challenges, hidden goodies, collectibles and costumes to unlock. The game also has a two-player option for local co-op bashing!

PRO:
* Interesting combination of fighting game mechanics and platformer.
* Nice theme
CON:
* Too much unavoidable twitch gameplay at later levels (5 hours in).
For example if you were to google "Guacamelee Tule Tree", the top non-video results are of people asking for help on how to progress through that section. That section requires 4-5 button combos executed in succession with upwards of over dozen repetitions.
Comically, one of the suggested solutions on the forum is to jam a paper under a key in your keyboard, so you don't end up getting carpal tunnel syndrome.

I think you could do the main story is 6 or 7 if you don't get sidetracked by hidden things and arenas.

A neat, prettily designed short game without much action besides walking on a strange island, discovering half-ruined landmarks and reminiscing on your relationship with a sinister woman whose influence on your life has been disastrous. The deeper nature of the narrator's feelings for and about her are gradually revealed in voiceover as he stumbles upon each key location.
Although any underlying themes are never made entirely clear, the experience in total is quite absorbing and enjoyable. That said, there are some amusingly unrealistic details, like the fact that you won't be killed even if you fall down a mountain slope - you never really fall, you just keep running along the cliff - or spend hours wandering underwater without needing to come up for air (which could simply be a device to avoid complicating the plot, but it also made me think of a certain theory that I won't divulge for fear of spoilers).
Interestingly enough, the way dry ground blends into the sea bed is poetically surreal in places, with stunning colors and blooming vegetation peeking from just below the surface of the water. The various monuments are beautifully made (if creepy sometimes) and relatively easy to find and explore - except the ancient mine which, sadly, appears to be inaccessible for some reason.
This isn't a game for action enthusiasts. It is somewhat idiosyncratic, story-driven but obscure at the same time, looking more like a demo rather than a brief but complete game. However, the lovely landscapes and dreamy atmosphere are worth at least one playthrough. The puny price and the bonus of achievements and trading cards are an additional couple of reasons to give it a try.

Character design is decent and the dialogue isn't as bad as it could be. The art is cute enough, despite not having much effort put into it. "Feelgood" aspects are present in this casual VN, so if you can relate to the protagonist, you may find this an emotionally rewarding story.
The plot meanders often and gets sidetracked. Lots of monologuing to tell the viewer how they're supposed to feel rather than just letting them feel it themselves. Major plot points misconstrued as "sweet" are honestly a little demented and creepy; it has that typical warped otaku view of romance. Backgrounds are lazy filtered photos and sometimes even defy the angle at which the characters are standing (The roof of cars are hip-level??) There's literally an unedited photo of a Zales in a mall.
It's free, and can be read through in 4-9 hours depending on your speed. It can also be skipped through if you're just looking to get achievements. If you're looking for something with major substance, this is not your game. It's a shallow afternoon killer.
There are no major gameplay flaws, and saves allow you to see all aspects of the game without trouble. It may not have tickled my fancy, but perhaps you'll find something of value within it? Either way, it's free so a peek isn't going to kill you.

Short, simple but mostly enjoyable side scrolling puzzle game, with good visuals and  a calm if somewhat lonely atmosphere,  It uses a mixture of mouse and keyboard controls, and for some parts you can use whichever you prefer, but the game will show you  if and when/where a specific one is needed
The sound slide puzzle I found to be slightly annoying though, because whether you use keyboard or mouse scroll the controls are inverted for some weird reason so down is up and up is down, and there is no option  to change it. You have to be pretty quick to move the sliders, but so careful at the same time. Yes, you learn immediately that  the controls are reversed and you need to press the opposite direction key, but when you have to move fast and  for example think "ok I need to move the slider up"  its so easy to automatically hit the key/scroll the mouse in the direction that actually corresponds to the direction you want the slider to move to , because that's a lot more intuitive and ...just generally more logical?  At least with this kind of game.
I enjoyed all the other puzzles, but that specific one, if I'm honest,  I was just kind of relieved when I finally got past it (although it's probably me being too impatient with it in all fairness)
Also for those playing on a laptop, the touchpad is very hit or miss on the sound puzzle, and because you have to be so precise on exactly where the two sliders are positioned for it to solve it makes it additionally frustrating, so if you aren't using a usb/normal mouse, just forget it and use the keyboard.
That aside, if you enjoy puzzle games, I would recommend giving this game a try, A lot of the puzzles you can have some fun with tuning into various frequencies before solving the puzzle,  and although it doesn't have much replay value once finished, its definitely worth playing through at least  once.

However, the gameplay is fun and it can be a challenge at times not to go bankrupt. What I've always liked about this game, was the ability to customize it. You can customize your in game character by typing in a new name and selecting a new portrait. You can customize your company by changing your logo, renaming it, and by renaming your trains & the cities/towns in which they serve. The game also sports a map/scenario editor for further customizations. As far as the "tycoon" aspect goes, the gameplay allows for the issuance of stocks & bonds, setting dividends, hiring and firing of managers, and instigating mergers and hostile takeovers. This game was one of the best - if not the best, in the Tycoon series back in the day. In my opinion, it still is today!

Any Gabriel Knight fans out there?
It was many years ago when I first played the first part of the Gabriel Knight series,  "Sins of the fathers", which already had a few years under its belt back then. And it was wonderful. This adventure had a great story, believable characters, a realistic setting (at least in the beginning), great (sometimes quite hard) puzzles, and a writing with some well balanced mixture of excitement, mystery and humour to it. GK1 immediately became my favourite adventure, and it stayed that way ever since.
But what does this have to do with Kathy Rain? Why would I bring this up?
Because KR almost immediately created the same feelings I had when I played GK1 back then. Almost from the title screen it felt like playing a Gabriel Knight game. But this was not only subjective - there are objective resemblances between those two games. And it was not just the visuals:
- Both KR and GK1 have a great mixture of humour and mystery, without the humour spoiling the mystery
- In both games the main character has a sidekick that does some part of the research
- Both main characters are sarcastic, somewhat messy writers riding mororcycles
- The family history plays a major role in both stories
- Both games play roughly at the same time (GK1: 1993; KR: 1995)
- Both games share a large set of common settings (like a church, a police station, a graveyard, a bar,
...)
- Both games pretty much start off with the main character visiting his/her grandmother :)
So... is KR a rip-off?
No, definitely not. While the resemblances may be uncanny, KR develops its own dark story that occasionally makes you laugh, and other times gives you the creeps, and stays strong until the
end. The puzzles can be quite challenging, but not too difficult and shouldn't get you stuck. And if you pay attention, you most probably will always know generally what your current tasks are and how you might complete them.
So basically: Kathy Rain is a great adventure. I would really love to see a second part, and it was wonderful to play something I would call a well done hommage to my favourite adventure of all time :)

A lot of people complain about "walking simulators" being too linear, but after playing this one, I gotta say...a little linearity doesn't go astray.
Unless you're someone who prefers a gaming experience with quite literally no goal or purpose, other than to wander aimlessly and hear broken shards of narrative whilst accruing the occasional Achievement, the level of satisfaction on offer here may be questionable. I tend to like games with a beginning, middle and an end, and Oracle...well, I guess it has a beginning. And some stuff which comes after.
Which is not to say the game has no redeeming features. The sound design is mostly excellent - a vivid recreation of nature in all its splendour - except that the footstep sound effects, like the painfully monotonous voice-over, don't vary much, sounding the same on wooden floorboards as they do on dirt roads. The enticingly abstract piano music which plays throughout, on the other hand, is almost enough to persuade one to forgive the game's other aural shortcomings.
The "jump" button is a true curiosity. The sound effect it creates is...er...a little immersion-breaking to say the least, and while it's sometimes necessary to use the button to access certain areas, I encountered at least two points where I was able to magically jump by increments to a preposterous height before coming back down to Earth. A glitch, I'm presuming. Nothing much to complain about, in other words, but not exactly something to praise either.
(I might also add that jump buttons are often a tad inadvisable in games which aim to be relaxing and dream-like, as the player must struggle with the constant temptation to idiotically bunny-hop through much of the game, especially if not much of anything is happening. Doesn't exactly add to the "atmosphere", I'm afraid.)
The graphics are also generally nice aside from bodies of water, which are regrettably prominent throughout and look more like a "green-screen" insert than an organic part of the game's world (you CAN walk on the bottom of the lake without dying, though; which is, er, "novel" to say the least)! The draw distance of the graphics also proved somewhat dubious, as geography in the distance can sometimes vanish or appear, depending on the angle you're approaching from (I'm assuming it wasn't just my laptop, which generally has no problems with demanding graphics; though Rise of the Tomb Raider admittedly did a good job of kicking its butt)! You'll also occasionally find yourself chasing landmarks which simply can't be reached, although there's no way of knowing that 'til you've wasted several minutes trying.
Walking speed is another frequent bone of contention in walking simulators. Here there is only one walking speed, despite the fact that holding down "shift" does try to give the illusion of slowing down by halving the amount of footsteps you hear...without the actual physical speed changing one iota. And then, of course, there's the quality of the writing, the importance of which can never be underestimated when it's the only thing resembling "narrative" in an otherwise meaningless wander. Let's just say that the writing here, while perfectly serviceable, is certainly nothing to "write home about" (pun most likely intended).
When all is said and done, the best walking simulators have a sense of focus. Even if the story only intermittently ties in with the scenery being presented, there's still a genuine sense of the player having been on a journey from which they emerge a slightly "changed" person. Sounds a tad lofty and all, but there's ultimately not much point to the narrative unless it tells an interesting story, or at the very least tells us something about "ourselves". I don't feel this game did either, but there may be some out there who feel differently.
Only recommended to those who think that "open world" design is a good thing, even when it comes at the expense of a more substantial narrative experience (and anyone willing to hunt down all twenty-four of those Achievements is a ♥♥♥♥in' SAINT, I tell ya).
Verdict: 6/10.

Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is a platforming 2D side-scrolling video game whose mechanics revolve around a continuous trial and error. Pretty hard at the first glance, it requires mastery (or a deep knowledge of the traps beforehand) that comes hand in hand with practice. I would say that it is like Dark Souls, but this game has a lot of cheap tricks that becomes a sudden death even if you're an experienced player.
Talking about the graphics, don't expect an AAA game level. Pixel art is OK and it reminds me a lot the games shown in the Angry Video Game Nerd videos, just like a 16 bits game. Music is pretty awesome and it has been created with that retro style in mind.
A lot, and I really mean it, A LOT of this game has been created having the AVGN videos puns or characters included. So you won't get that references if you didn't watch that videos. It's not that bad and it's still a good platforming game overall, but maybe a little bit too short.
If you're still thinking about buying it or not, do me a favor: watch the very first Angry Video Game Nerd video on YouTube and then check out a little bit of the game in a walkthrough video. That should help you more than anything you can read here.
Should I recommend this game? If you liked the show, and a hard and good platforming game: HELL YES! If you only want a platforming game, there are a lot of them better than AVGN Adventures, but it still worth it if you can get it at a lower price.

This game has great platforming, very good controls, and a comedic retro atmoshpere that pokes fun at NES games.
One of the first things I noticed was the controls. Running and jumping feels great in this game. Using a controller, when I missed a jump or ran into an obstacle, I completely felt like it was
fault and not the game or the controls.
I feel the challenge is good because of the variety of difficulty levels. On "normal" mode, the game auto-saves after every level, you get 30 lives and unlimited continues. There are also about 7 or 8 checkpoints on every level as well. I died 529 times going through the game on "normal" mode. Probably 100 of those deaths were on the boss of the game.
The atmosphere is what makes the game most memorable. All 10 levels (apart from the tutorial level) have a distinctive feel to them. I liked how the 2010 themed level starts with the Nerd saying: "Sure, this is what 2010 was like, puke green blocks and purple jellyfish." I also like the death blocks. They are blocks with skulls and crossbones on them that kill you instantly on contact, poking fun at how in old games
seemed to kill you.
One issue with the game is the levels getting blurred out when you beat them, making it hard or impossible to read the level name. Another thing is you can only have one saved game file and if you select the "new game" option, you will erase your old game save. That almost wouldn't be a problem since you can do the levels in any order, but the last one is only unlocked by beating all the other levels first.
Overall this is a fun, challenging, memorable game that I am very glad I spent $4.99 on.

In the realm of indie games, there are a lot to choose from. How will you know the right game when you see it? Guacamelee! is a game that catches your attention immediatly because of the name itself. It's an awesome name that gives you a pretty good idea of what the game is about: you beat up people/things in some kind of Mexican setting. And if the name alone is awesome and raises your expectations high, you're still going to be blown away by the actual game. One can use many words to describe this game, such as fun, challenging and nostalgic. The word that comes to my mind when I think about this game, is perfect. Guacamelee! is borderline godly, and perhaps the best platformer I have ever played. The game is, as described by the store page, a Metroidvania style beat 'em up. And don't be surprised when you find that there are more things in this game related to Metroid and Castlevania than just the gameplay: the game is OVERFLOWING with references to classic games, indie games and even D_A_N_K_M_E_M_E_S for those of you who like to pay reddit or ♥♥♥♥♥ or Imgur or 9gag or whatever a visit. To be honest, I don't know what websites aren't dealing with some kind of meme infection these days, not that I'm complaining. Anyways, these references are really just a huge load of fan service, and hopefully you will find them just as enjoyable as I did. But the best thing about this game is of course not the references, but the gameplay. The platforming is tighter than jeans in a vacuum, and all the punches and kicks always hit spot-on. You can also perform special attacks that also help you progress in the game, not to mention throw your enemies when they've accumulated a certain level of damage. This is really useful as you can throw the enemies at each other to knock them over, and it's just damn fun to do. The visuals are cartoon-like and really sweet to look at. The music is actually very good and always fits the mood perfectly, and even changes into something darker, more ambient and even dubstep-influenced at times when you switch from the World of the Living to the World of the Dead. You can do that btw. Unfortunately though, it's not very memorable. The story, I guess I should have brought it up earlier: you are a man by the name of Juan, who becomes a luchador so that he can save the world from a dead man named Carlos Calaca who have overthrown el diablo himself and now plans to take over both the World of the Living and the World of the Dead by sacrificing el presidente's daughter. Bad stuff, and nobody wants it to happen, so thank goodness for Juan! The characters and dialogue are sometimes funny, other times more forgettable, but very sufficient all in all. This isn't one of those games where the story is the main aspect. The ending, which I'm not going to spoil, was, however, surprisingly sad and emotional. All in all, Guacamelee! is a great experience that everybody that likes Metroidvania-style games and platformers in general owe themselves to play. One might say that the game is a little short, but if you try to find secrets and collect all the treasure, like I kind of attempted, you will definitely get your money's worth. You will also find a lot of challenge if you decide to hunt some orbs or complete the challenges in El Infierno, which, of course, is included in this edition ;) I've also heard that playing co-op is fun, not that I ever got to try it... Bottomline, this game is a masterpiece, get a firm grip on el controlador and get ready to Guacamelee!

I will start off with my personal opinion; it was interesting. Most free visual novels aren't as in-depth as this one was, in my opinion. The characters were... cute, and they were definitely eye-catching. But, were they memorable? To an extent. Their dialogues left me with a bad impression in different ways for each of them. I mean, poor Mark couldn't catch a break with how these girls treated him. Myra shows up out of nowhere, knowing everything about him, and doesn't bother to explain very much after feeling disappointed that he doesn't remember her. Then, when he actually tries asking her about herself in order to understand her better, she calls him a stalker. Wow. Now this other girl, Lillian, she's such a little intellect. Literate, smart, observant. So much so that she has to make fun of Mark for being lesser at every chance she can. And, Rin? She's self-explanatory. Mark cares about all of them and tries his best to stay on their good side. It's a little sad, but I must admit, it does build his character.
I actually found the artwork very pleasing. My only problem with it was how the background clashed with the characters. Two completely different art styles, a bit distracting, but unimportant as it at least gives us a sense of where that scene is taking place.
Overall, if you're into long visual novels, I'd say have a go at it. I played it for the achievements, of course, but was pleasently surprised by how story-rich it turned out to be.

<< that's a metric f*ck-tonne of extra maps & scenarios).  I have a thing for older games - they tended to be more demanding and more mentally stimulating than modern games - and this fully lives up to those ideals.

The right scenarios (in the zip I linked to above) will let you go for >150 years - some are even without a time limit - but you typically are presented goals - specific things to achieve by a specific time, in order to get a bronze, silver or gold medal (these goals are usually along the lines of "Connect point x to point y, move twelvety tonnes of cargo K between those two points and amass $------ personal fortune by date z").
I give you fair warning, the graphics aren't going to blow you away, not by a long shot, but the complexity, detail and the intense addictiveness of the game should tickle you if you're prone to being tickled by a game of this type.

The Buzzer speaks, and we are bound to listen
Ever wonder what it was like to listen to the tunes and programs on the old radios, before the advent of the internet and digital technology? When radio-waves were able to change to course of the history? When they reigned supreme? Wonder no longer and enjoy this short and brilliant puzzle adventure called “Antenna”, a love letter to radio waves and transmissions packed in an elegant and minimalistic style.
Visually, Antenna borrows a lot of the look and style of the Limbo game with the black and white, clean and surreal feel that will keep you glued to the screen from start till end. There are no excessive details or visual effects in the game that would distract from keeping an eye and ear out to everything that is happening at the screen. The minimalistic style of the game successfully conveys the feeling of cold, machine-like precision and mystery that surrounds the Antenna’s levels. Sound is the second equally important part of the game, with luscious and enigmatic sounds and transmissions the player will have to focus on in order to solve a few of the Antenna’s well implemented and interesting puzzles. The only gripe that I have is that it ends too soon, you will barely need more than 30 minutes to finish the game, with only a handful of well-designed sound puzzles it offers.
I definitely recommend Antenna to anyone who wants to try something different and strange, a mystery that is open to interpretation, with adept look and sound to match, and I hope the developers will one day create a full-fledged game out of this idea, telling many more stories of the monolithic effect analogue sounds and radio waves held over people in the past, and still continue to do, in the shroud of secrecy.

There's a potentially fun game in here somewhere, but there's quite a bit that doesn't make this work overall, and makes it so that I can't recommend it, even in Early Access as it grows and develops.
The biggest problem, one that absolutely needs to be pointed out, is the auto-running. It absolutely kills the game for me, and makes even simple and easy levels frustrating. This does make timing more important, but the fact that it complicates basically everything else makes the experience unenjoyable. There are several moments where you have to mash back and forth on the arrow keys to time a jump across an obstacle, or even doing it between two different obstacles, because you can't stop running. The objective of the game then goes from scaling walls and avoiding obstacles to figuring out how to get around the auto-running to successfully navigate.
The controls are also a bit frustrating. Delay in inputs means you have to make yourself jump or turn earlier than you want to, which probably isn't that bad until you play a level where optimal timing is essential. It showcases the downsides really boldly. Wall-jumping is the absolute hardest thing to do, as you'll either not jump when you want to in some cases, or not go far enough to the other side of the wall. There's even a glitch where your mummy climbs an invisible wall all the way up to the ledge. It's frustrating and hard to really replicate; it just tends to happen. It's amusing at first as well, until you run into an obstacle or fall because of it, and you may not even realize what's happening at first. When you're wall-jumping to avoid obstacles, it's a run killer. And I don't usually feel like it's my fault when I die, unlike other hard games, because the controls don't feel responsive.
There are other small glitches and bugs that aren't bad on their own, but dampen the experience overall. More than once have I wall-jumped, only to jump through the wall into my death. Some cases, I'll land inside the wall and can move around and jump out. I had to quit the game and reboot it when I beat the tutorial because no menus would pop up for me otherwise. Collision detection seems finicky, as I'll apparently have gotten into an obstacle when it seems like I've cleared this. This is most evident with the crocodile pit, but I'm willing to excuse that as just needing to be extra sure I clear it.
There are good things however! I like the vibe and aesthetic of the game, and the music wasn't annoying like most games in this genre tend to be. While you can only really jump over obstacles, the variety of traps and the methods in which they kill (or even affect) you is pleasant and refreshing. The ability to complete challenges and earn stuff at a decent enough rate is appreciated if one doesn't want to purchase any of the microtransactions, so you don't feel like you're grinding just to grind. On smaller notes, I appreciate that not only can you reduce the quality of the game, but even at the lowest settings for quality, it still looks really nice. Except for some hiccups in the period between dying and resetting, the game runs really well on my piece-of♥♥♥♥♥♥computer.
The ability to play others' levels and rate them and compete on leaderboards for each level is appreciated, but there's a major problem here; you can't preview the map before playing. The most you get is around five seconds to survey the map, no matter how huge or littered with blocks/obstacles (and this includes the time it takes to zoom out to look at the map). You have to essentially dive into these maps blindly, and for maps that are either huge, complicated, or non-linear, this is a killer. I've quit maps several times because of this. Even something small like seeing a preview of the map before I play the level would help incredibly. It would also help so I know when to avoid levels that are essentially auto-completion or not designed well, and allow me to get the most out of the game.
Normally, this isn't the kind of game I'd play, but it's free and Early Access, so I decided to check it out. There's potential, and tightened up and improved on more, I could see myself coming back to this every once in a while to enjoy. But at this stage, I simply can't recommend it.

I struggled to get into this one. I adore the Blackwell series and other recent adeventure game throwbacks like Technobabylon and Primordia, but Kathy Rain never manages to reach those dramatic heights. Uninspired puzzles, a tedious middle plot, redundant mechanics, and a Lynchian dream of an endgame all rank Kathy Rain well below titles published over two decades ago.
Ultimately, it's good enough for most genre fans, but there are far better titles out there; however, as a diehard genre fan, I truly hope we see more of Kathy because she deserves a second bout to prove her mettle. I had hoped to see a lot more from what I still believe a very clever character.
To its credit, Kathy Rain pays homage to the classics of Sierra and Lucasarts, even dropping a few references here and there (and an unmistakable Twin Peaks nod to boot). Applying the vocal direction of Wadjet Eye's own Dave Gilbert elevates the game's dialogue with a strong dramatic presence, and the background art is beyond reproach-- especially for a one-man effort.
There's a lot that point 'n click veterans will find almost all-too-familiar, though: a Gabriel Knight-style notepad for dialogue; a GK3 tape recorder puzzle; a Monkey Island 2 poem/song puzzle in which the verses correspond to a combination; and, of course, "USE"ing every item on everything just like in [insert adventure game here].  It's a game aplomb with such similarities -- similarities so frequent that you may find yourself saying "I've played this game before."  Unfortunately, the borrowing tactic harms Kathy Rain's novelty, and its untethered plot cannot rescue it.
Truthfully it would be easy to forgive Kathy Rain if the story didn't let me down. The plot's midsection drags as Kathy spends her time gathering new dialogue topics and trying them out on different characters. I admit that at one point during a particularly uninteresting dialogue, I Shift+Tab'd to Imgur and forgot I was playing the game.
The endgame leaves many questions to be answered in a LOST-Season-4 kind of way instead of a "When is Stranger Things 2 coming out?" kind of way.
If you don't mind
-an occasionally dull pace
-an ayahuasca-bender-inspired ending
-"puzzles" that rarely ask more than using the right item on the right hotspot (and the few puzzles that do ask more are as challenging as applying the only clue available to the problem)
If you've already played everything else like it, Kathy Rain could be a fine way to spend a few hours.
If you haven't already played everything else like it, there are a lot of games from two decades ago that are considerably better.

While I like walking sims, this one has a lot of the worst issues these games can have.  It looks kind of nice, which you can say about most of them. The game claims dozens of locations, but there really aren't that many places to go or things to hear.  There is no path.  You basically go anywhere on the map except the castle on the hill with the invisible wall stopping you.  I didn't get more than 45 minutes and couldn't see anything I missed.  The voice acting would be nice except there are no audio controls so the voice is set way louder than the pleasant music.   Here's the thing about pleasant music and calm narrators.  It can make a junky narrative sound completely reasonable.   If any human being said these things outside of a calm voice lulling you into thinking it's poetry, you'd think the person had mental problems.  Honestly the narrator is just gushing about a woman who is most likely a complete sociopath and the narrative literally goes nowhere.    I'd say something similar about the Drivel Path games, except that at least those are much more complete, much longer, more intricate, and are on a completely different level graphically and atmospherically.

It's a fun game, but it gets repetitive and has some crazy difficulty spikes. The game itself plays a bit like a simplified Super Smash Bros., with simple combos that you chain together. You traverse through Mexican-themed environments fighting enemies and gaining powers. Also, while this game advertises itself as a Metroidvania, it is more like a beat-em-up with some exploration. You'll never find yourself lost, and there is (with maybe an exception or two) only one way to reach your goal. There are side quests and small detours, where you collect items or solve puzzles, but they only improve your character's stats and aren't crucial to the main adventure.
My recommendation is to buy in a sale if the game seems appealing, but it is far from a masterpiece. Be sure to have a controller, too!

Guacamelee is a love letter to the Metroidvania genre, in the form of a super-powered romp through the world of Mexican folklore. You are Juan Aguacate, a destitute agave farmer who finds his village under attack by the undead army of Carlos Calaca. The love of his life, who happens to be the daughter of el presidente, has been kidnapped. What is Juan to do? Why, acquire a magic lucha mask and go on a non-linear platforming adventure, get powerups from "choozo" statues, power-slam bad guys, find secrets and navigate rather tricky jumping puzzles, of course. Guacamelee oozes style from beginning to end, with a colorful palette, excellent music and a well-used light/dark world mechanic, requiring the player to frequently switch Juan between the living world and the Mexican land of the dead via portals, often in  mid-jump.  But the game is inconsistent in difficulty. The combat is generally managable and the boss fights are quite simply awesome, but some of the jumping puzzles are incredibly frustrating. In addition, to reach the game's golden ending, it is neccessary to obtain a number of secret items, some of which are located at the end of some fiendishly difficult challenge rooms, many of which, like the trick jump room with its accursed disappearing platforms, I was unable to complete, and this left a bad taste in my mouth. The final boss is also quite difficult, requiring you to demonstrate a mastery over all the abilities you have learned over the course of the game, but when I had finished, I was very satisfied dispite not getting the best ending. I would recommend the game to any fans of Metroidvania, but with caution- it is not a forgiving experience.

This game is a solid action platformer. I love the mexican art style it actually reminds me of samurai jack crossed with mucha lucha. It's bright and colorful, and the writing is pretty funny too. The combat is simple but fun, and throwing enemies always feels satisfying.
