What the game does is alternate between light world and dark world platforms, meaning taht you have to jump, then switch worlds in time in order to land on the next platform. If you fail it usually brings you back to the beggining. So the game pushes you out of your comfort zone in order to advance and starts you back at the beginning if you fail. However this game never rushes you and encourages you to take your time to master each area.
Also this game is by no means short. There are plenty of secrets and the game encourages back tracking as you unlock special abilities that let you access previously innaccessible areas. This game also comes with 2 player drop in/ drop out co-op so you can bring a friend. Just make sure to bring a controller though.

There is plenty of things that I loved about Guacamelee. It has a very simple and to-the-point combo list. It rarely reuses puzzles and situations. Most puzzles and bosses and challenging but not too much. And most importantly, it doesn't take itself too seriously.
But, in a way, it also does take itself seriously. Its challenges are designed to be just manageable, to push you to the limits of your skill. That would have been great if you actually had that level of control. But you don't. The controls are sticky. So, for example, your "D" command becomes "arrow+D", because you were using arrows moments ago, and that changes everything. The developers recommend using a gamepad, but there's no real reason why the keyboard shouldn't work. They simply decided to neglect it.
At the same time, combat is based on dissing and receiving stuns. It is entirely possible that the enemies will chain-stun you until you die, and there's nothing you can do to recover.
I ragequit this game many times. When it works, it's awesome. But very often it doesn't work, and it often feels like losing wasn't your fault. And that is the biggest fault in a game. A player should never feel like he's being punished for things beyond his control.
I know that, technically, it's my fault for not executing the jumps perfectly. However, between the inconsistent difficulty and the imperfect controls, I don't see why I should keep replaying the same section to perfect my jumps to such a degree. The game isn't that addictive or rewarding. What stayed with me from Guacamelee wasn't the good times as much as the ragequits. And for that reason, I don't consider this game a good experience.

I recommend any game within the Hitman series, except Codename 47 because I have not played it yet. I appreciate the developers for incorporating classic weapons like the the six shooter, snub nose, and the .480 in the game. My favorite level is Curtains Down. I get to switch out a prop pistol for a real one, then I can watch the play take an unfortunate turn. I use to go in guns blazing, but that gets boring after a short while.
Taking part in the mass killing of civilians in one level turns into doing the same among other levels, then I end up cutting the system off. The exclamation points heighten the usability of the game, and as with many other levels, the points introduce different ways of completing each level. The graphics are solid to this day. I could remember the first aspect that impressed me: the ability to headbutt and punch AI's. I mean what else is there to do if I am restricted from entering  3/4's of the maps and targets need to be killed?
I love a good challenge. When assaulting a guard holding a weapon, there is a 50/50 chance that he will pull the trigger in the process of getting his head bashed in by his gun. Sure, no harm is done to Agent 47, but the gun shot alarms anyone in the area, which causes an unintentional turning point. All of the civilians start running in circles, and guards on the same side of the map run towards the area where the gun shot was heard. In addition, the civilians can pick up weapons on the ground and shoot Agent 47 for about 6 seconds, then drop the weapon and resume panic mode haha.
This is by far is the most realistic game in the series, yet it only ranks second best in my book.

I remember Samorost back when it was an old (and weird) browser point-and-click puzzle game, and I sunk hours in gameplay even then. Having followed Amanita Design since, with Samorost 2, Machinarium, and Botanicula, I was over the moon to receive a copy of Samorost 3 for my birthday.
Start-to-finish, it took me 5 hours to complete, solving all the puzzles by myself and spending time clicking various combinations for the Steam Achievements. The artwork has much improved since the Samorost 1 days, and it's a thing of wonder: each creative landscape and texture has a way to disconcert and surprise in an oddly familiar nostalgia trip, a little like "Neverending Story".
As it doesn't have any dialogue, it appeals to across generations and language barriers, focusing instead on visual and sound elements to deliver a charming experience. The puzzles presented are not always intuitive, but I have yet to find any frustrating.
While I've read some reviews saying there is little replay value, or that it costs too much for what it is, I would disagree. Samorost (and others by the devs) are a little tradition that remind me personally of those childhood days where the one game disk was all you had, so special occasions would be given to finding new, faster, more efficient ways to solve the puzzles, discover the easter eggs, or just enjoy the brainteaser once you've allowed yourself a year to forget the winning solutions.
Absolutely recommended for the artwork alone.

I really want to like this game, but the amount of bugs and the strange behaviour in general [of the game] makes it a lot harder than it really is. You can outnumber the enemy and lose, due to the factor of miscomprehention from the game. Eg. that the AI rarely cohere with the way of the player.
I've played many older RTS games (Stronghold, AoE, SC1 etc.) and those are my favourites as well - why I was intrigued by this game. But it doesn't at all live up to expectations - even compared to games of the same era or older.
Here's some examples of common bugs/AI problems that annoy me:
- Enemies suddenly running under water and becoming invincible - making units hunt them without being able to kill them.
- Your own boats are more likely to attack your friendly boats than the actual enemies. Because they miss 90% of the shots in the first place - except when one of your own boats are blocking the view for another. This renders into the problem that when you command a group of boats to attack, they'll either kill each other off or simply going around in circles in some kind of infinity pattern, while being killed by the enemy.
- If you're setting ground units to attack other ground units, they're really going for the one guy you pointed at, even if he's lagging behind or running in some other direction. This is not different from AoE for example, but that's also my main frustration with that game.
- The bots always know where you are. Planning to make a sneak attack? Forget about it, they'll have a legion waiting for you at your arrival.
Add to that uneven mixing of sound effects (some is really loud and even distorted, how that passed qc is beyond me) and the game doesn't really feel finished. Which is unfortunate, because it's really on the same level as other games, apart from being basically unplayable.
And another thing: If you're going to buy this game - stay the hell away from naval maps.

My first horse was an unsilvered gray named Rover Boy.  Upon discovering I was the owner, he wouldn't let me saddle or corral him.  He also caused enough trouble to apparently open a nearby bull pen.  My character was disabled for three game days due to a piercing incident with the bull--it didn't give a description, but perhaps I'm better off not knowing.
Fortunately, according to in-game lore, Rover Boy was really a living embodiment of one of the sacred virtues of the in-game realm; upon this discovery, I was forever left with the impression that Rover Boy was a magical unicorn.  He telepathically communicated that I was to round up the other four "Elementals of Harmony" or something like that.  This was very strange because I don't recall this happening within the game--I think I was actually hypnotized and told this in what felt like a drunken stupor, rather than the character.  Probably a bug fixed in the latest update (nobody else has reported this).
Over time, Rover Boy told me the greater scheme of things.  My destiny was to lead the horse through various training courses while he mentally played Dance Dance Revolution, earn lots of money delivering the same letter between two Alzheimer's patients to upgrade the facilities, optionally pilfer racing trophies from a nearby wagon, mate him with another ideally racially-pure horse (regardless of gender), sell them both off while accepting the new foal as my destiny, and repeat this 154 times.  Upon doing so, I would forget that any of these conversations ever happened and be forever under a hypnotic impression that I had just merely played a simplistic and repetitive kids' game about hunting blue meteoric crystals with horses for 60 hours.  Somehow, the spell didn't quite fully work on me.
I am now left with a profound sense of loss, owing to the fact that nobody else in this community seems to believe me...though they have all had the same experience as me and will simply never know.  Tugs at the old heartstrings, it does.
In the game's prologue, your professor-grandfather discovered the truth and was not believed by anyone; he was forced to entrust his grandchild with the charge of validating his discovery.  But you are not the child--the child never existed.  YOU ARE THE GRANDFATHER.  This game's hypnotic curse will not allow you to believe otherwise, but I know.  I KNOW!

It's a rare day that I find a game that gets areal combat right.  This is certainly one of them - and yet, there is so much more to Thunder Wolves than simply ( although absolutely fantastic) helicopter combat.  I genuinely love the story, despite it being  typical "AMURICA" military.  The writers really used humor to their advantage, and the characters are actually quite believable.  The voice acting really brings it all together, offering a really enjoyable story driven experience.

But I digress, let me get back to the real focus of this game: chopper combat.  The issue I generally have with air combat in games is how floaty and unresponsive it tends to be, which renders combat clunky and awkward - this game has none of those problems.  The helicopters are extremely responsive to player input via mouse and keyboard (I have not tested it with a controller, so I can't really give you any advice there), and the controls manage to be both varied and uncomplicated.  Missions last about 15-20 minutes each, and have 3 available difficulty levels - casual, normal, and hard.  As you play, you unlock new choppers and skins, offering quite a nice reward to the player.

Thunder Wolves is totally a must play for anyone itching for some decent rough and tumble air engagements.

Thunder Wolves is a fun little helicopter action game that I picked up from the Humble Store some years back. At the time, the game was not available on Steam directly, so it took me a while to get around to reviewing it. Though it has the equivalent of a third-person, over-the-shoulder perspective, its really more of a DOS-era shmup in spirit like the Strike series or Seek and Destroy, with extremely simplified controls, high health pool, unlimited ammo, a nitro boost ability, and relentlessly over-the-top explosive action.
It's 1991- so basically, still the 80s. A crack mercenary unit called the Thunder Wolves are on deployment somewhere in south-central Asia. The player takes on the role of wisecracking, foul-mouthed ace pilot Max and his equally snarky and vulgar new gunner, Blister, as they provide overwhelming aerial support for the ground pounders from their bright red-and-yellow helicopters, of which there are nine available with differing stats and special weapons. There are 13 missions across three difficulties, and an option for couch coop wherin the first player flies and controls a fixed machine gun, and the second gets an extra traversable gun and the various explosive munitions.
Games like Thunder Wolves are few and far between these days, games that place fun ahead of all other considerations. It's great fun both solo or coop and well worth the price.

Thunder Wolves is an arcade helicopter action game that attempts to capture the vibe of a cheesy '80s action movie. The action is simple and the game is fairly short, but Thunder Wolves offers up good fun while it lasts.
Don't expect a complicated flight model or realistic physics in Thunder Wolves. Expect tons of explosions, cheesy one-liners, explosions, wailing guitar riffs, and more explosions. Ammo is unlimited and you can bounce your helicopter off other aircraft and the ground with minimal penalty. There are a few helicopters to choose from, but they all handle pretty much the same.
Most of the missions in Thunder Wolves revolve around getting in a helicopter and blowing up everything you see, but the developers manage to include sniper sequences, on-rails shooting galleries, turret sequences, and even a couple of missions where you drive an APC.
Thunder Wolves doesn't have any sort of online play, but it does offer local co-op play for two players, where one player controls the helicopter and the other mans the weapons.
Thunder Wolves is low-brow entertainment that doesn't take itself too seriously. It's worth a try for action game fans.

Oracle is perhaps a great first step towards the walking simulator genre. A good game to experience what it means to play such a casual game with a peaceful environment.
The problem is that the game often feels unpolished. We explore interesting locales with our globe-trotter protagonist but some of these locations feel unfinished. You have clipping issues here and there, glitches occur randomly and some of the objects (including trees) seem to be floating just above the ground.
It's nice to have high mountains and - as the description says - a 5 square mile map but what is the purpose of this if you see a lot of "empty" areas? I saw a section of a mountainous region only to notice texture issues. You can also jump into the water but swimming is not an option - you walk on the underwater floor while looking at the plants and strange effects accompanying this experience.
The music and the voice over are great. The game reminded me of Bottle several times, however, the aforementioned game was a properly finished product. And while the story is interesting it can never reach the level the Old City Leviathan has.
I do not wish to be too critical. Oracle is a somewhat mediocre walking simulator, however, some of the greater names out there can also be purchased for the same price and offer way more insight into this genre.

Method:
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

Hitman: Blood Money is one of my favorite games of all time. It took what was good about the previous entries in the series, improved on their problems while also bringing new features to the table to set it apart from the rest. What we ended up with was a masterpiece, and a game I have had many hours of fun with. The gameplay here is simple: you start on a map with one or several targets to kill, and sometimes some documents or items to recover. It's execution is where it shines, as Blood Money allows you tons of opportunities to complete your objective. For example, there is a mission in the game called Curtains Down. In this mission, you have to kill a french actor and his producer, who are involved in a prostitution ring. You have the option of climbing into the rafters and sniping them, switching out a prop gun with a real one and killing him in front of an audience, switching out the gun and letting the other actor kill your target, blowing up a chandelier and having it drop on the producer, etc. There are so many ways to kill these targets, and I'm sure I haven't found them all. There are 12 levels in the game in total, and they all are very unique. Unlike the last game, which was very repetitive, this game has levels set in a Vegas Casino, Mardi Gras, a French Theater, a River Steam Boat, a standard house used by Witness Protection, and many more. Every level feels unique, thanks to great level design and good atmosphere. The npc's will speak with an accent or in other languages, depending on where the level is set, which really helps with immersion. The main focus of the gameplay is replayablility, and this game does it better than any other Hitman game. Every level has several opportunities for creative kills, and finding them all always kept me coming back for more. As far as the story goes, it's weak like every other Hitman game, but the story is not why you should play this game. This game does have a few flaws, but not enough to ruin my enjoyment. For instance, the ragdolls are very stiff, like the other games. After you kill someone, their body will re-straighten itself, which is a bit immersion breaking unless you push someone to their death so you no longer see the body, or use fiber wire which would normally result in a straighter body. Another issue is that you can't aim with a gun, which makes the gunplay less fun. If you want to kill someone with a gun, you have to put the crosshair on them, and the gun will automatically come up and go down when you fire. This is a shame for me since I love the blood effects in this game. A lot of detail was used in the cloud, wall stain and pooling effects but it's not as fun when you can't aim and you end up with a straight ragdoll. Other than that, this game is near perfect. $8.99 is too cheap of a price so unless a sale is right around the corner, buy it now at full price! If they charged $20 I would have gotten my money's worth, so I'm glad it's less. This game is awesome and I think everyone should play it.

Summary.
Nice little point and click game in with "retro" graphics. Interesting story that develops nicely. Perhaps a bit light on the puzzles. Did you enjoy the Blackwell games (and/or Twin Peaks), chances are you will enjoy this one. Looking forward to the next one.
The Game:
The game is simple enough to explain as it is a point and click adventure. The graphics are retro style and seldom does this feel like it hinders the telling of the story. You might have to sort to using the space bar to higlight points of interest. The pace is fast, dialog not to much and not to little. I sometimes find that endlessly convoluted dialog is just to much. Here I felt it was just right. Few items makes for litte "brute force" in combining items and points of interest. Its a logical game.
The puzzles:
Easy and logical enough apart from a few that are really painfull, and they all have to do with finding codes. That is perhaps my one gripe with the game is that some things are really hard as things needs to be sequenced just right and other things are very simple. I admit to using walkhtrouhs when I know what I need to do, but need help doing it.
The story:
Its something else, it starts out simple enough but then devlops nicely. PG guidiance is advised, not just for the strong language and some more grown up scenes. I have a little vibe of the earlier Broken Sword games, and a lot of Twin Peaks.
The main character is nicely written, perhaps a little one dimensional, but she develops ok. The rest of the characters are little more than story devices apart from perhaps grandma, Eilin and a few others.

Great game. The story is a mystery taking place in a small town with a small but eccentric cast making it feel a bit like an episode of Twin Peaks or the X Files. The game features retro graphics which may put off some folks but also features full voice overs and character portraits to give you better feeling how a character is feeling.
The game is a bit short, as it took me five hours to complete it. Also, some people had trouble enjoying the game because the main character is a punk and is irreverent towards authority figures but that really depends on what you're looking for in a character. The protagonist, Kathy, does have an interesting personality and some of the dialogue can be quite amusing especially when Kathy doesn't get her way.
I think this game has a lot in common with Gabriel Knight and worth checking out if you're a fan of the Gabriel Knight series. If you're still on the fence you can try the free demo which is available here on steam.

is the type of game that didn’t have to do much to make me want to play it. It’s a point and click game where you play as sassy Kathy Rain trying to investigate the mysterious circumstances surrounding your grandfather’s death. It’s a point and click detective game with a female lead plus retro pixel graphics; on the surface, it seemed like a no-brainer to me. However, upon delving into the game itself I found myself a bit conflicted. Everything about the game is top notch, from visuals to voice acting. The gameplay is smooth as are the controls, it’s the story that lumbers. Depending on a player’s taste, it will be either hit or miss.
I admit when I jumped into this I was eager to play a detective game, working along with Kathy to figure out clues and solve the mysteries. The first half of the game does indeed invoke this tone. You’re in control of Kathy Rain, a journalism major who has a bit of an attitude problem. Despite being a college student, Kathy doesn’t seem to ever go to class, instead opting for being lazy and partying so she has ample time to be a detective on the side. She learns from her roommate, who is the complete opposite to Kathy personality-wise, that her grandfather has passed. Kathy becomes determined to figure out what happened to her grandfather, finding clues to his past as a war veteran as well as the shady history of the town he lived in. With a quick wit and a sharp tongue, we help our hero investigate the situation, finding out that it extends even farther than just dear old granddad all while learning more about Kathy’s troubled upbringing and family issues.
And then things got weird. While I had a suspicion things would take a supernatural twist, I was hoping that they wouldn’t, but they do. Around halfway through the game it becomes clear that this isn’t just a simple detective story, there is something other-worldly happening. I won’t spoil exactly what it is, however I couldn’t even if I wanted to. The ending of the game left me very confused to the point where I have more questions than answers. Between Kathy having weird dreams and talking to ghosts, the game tries to squeeze in character development by having her overcome inner demons that had been holding her back. I commend the story wanting to do this, however I personally didn’t feel the need for the supernatural aspect to do this. The final chapter of the game unfortunately feels rushed because of it, trying to tie up the loose ends of the plot with her grandfather and the creepy town while also giving Kathy her epiphany. While the game seemed to be trying to end in a way satisfying for players, it also left itself open for sequels.
Story aside, the game itself is very simple. It’s a point and click adventure game so all you need is a mouse to play, though there are a couple of moments where you need to type something in with your keyboard but it’s not a major gameplay aspect. Using your mouse, you control where Kathy goes and what she does, clicking on objects and people to interact with them. You have an inventory system where useful and important items are collected for later use. You can inspect items in your inventory, like to read a newspaper clipping, or combine certain items to either make a new item or effect another item, like using Kathy’s lighter on a Bible in the church. The game has a few puzzles but nothing very complicated and usually Kathy will tell you enough details to figure things out. The only issue I had was that Kathy herself moves rather slowly when she walks, you also can’t double click a door to instantly go through it so you’re forced to wait for Kathy to walk everywhere.
The game is beautiful, I adored the graphic style and the choice to go with pixel artwork. It’s very simple yet done very well, lovely shading work and the character animations all seem very natural. Each character also has a portrait as well, since it might be hard to see the details of their faces on their character models due to the pixels. The backgrounds are rich, fitting well with the dreary tone of the game. There is also full voice acting and it’s done very well. Kathy has a witty line for almost everything so feel free to click away at items in the game. Every character you interact with has a voice and plenty to say making it easier to immerse yourself in the game. The music also helps with this, the soundtrack is perfectly fitting to the gritty backdrop of the small backwater town.
This is a game that packs a lot of punch in a small package, while on the surface it may seem like just another point and click game using simple pixel graphics,
proves itself to be the total package. The writing is amazing, Kathy is an engaging character full of humor and common sense and while I may not have found the story to be perfect, I enjoyed it none the less. The truth is, there could have been flying dogs from Mars that came and took over the town, Kathy herself is such a great main character I would play anyway. She carries this game on her shoulders as she rides down the highway on her pink motorcycle. While the price tag may seem a tad high, you won’t be disappointed if you add this to your library. It’s a fun experience, a well made game and also Steam trading cards and achievements. I hope that this title is only the first in many more games starring Ms. Rain.

Pros:
* Solid writing and decent if unspectacular voice acting.
* Good classic point and click adventure gameplay.
* Puzzles that generally make sense.  They make you think from time to time, but they're not deliberately obtuse like many adventure games of old.
* An enjoyable lead character.
* An intriguing mystery that you want to solve.
Cons:
* While the mystery is intriguing, the ultimate resolution is just unsatisfying.
* I didn't care for the direction the story took in the last act.
* Occasional wooden dialogue that stands out amidst the generally good writing.
* Many of the side characters are just lazy caricatures.
* Attempts at humor mostly fall flat.
I'm giving Kathy Rain a recommendation mostly because I think it's a perfectly competent adventure game with several posititve attributes.  I thought the game really fell apart at the end, and the resolution kind of leaves more questions than answers, but the series itself definitely has potential going forward.  I do wish they'd settle on a tone.  Much of the game is serious and fairly dark, as the mystery centered around why Kathy's grandpa went into a state of catatonic shock years earlier and what happened to a girl who drowned around the same time period, so the bad attempts at humor really stand out.  The further problem for me is that the game hints at a mystery that is much more intriguing than where the story actually goes.
All in all, if you like old school, point and click adventure games, this is a decent Steam sale buy.  Hopefully the developers can find a more solid footing in any potential sequels.

The presentation and music are stronger than ever, almost feeling like a childrens book at times, and though the puzzles are more challenging than they were in Botanicula or Machinarium most of them felt fair. If you enjoyed any of the previous Samorost games or Amanita's other works you won't be disappointed.

is the third, full-length game by Amanita Design. I believe it’s the longest time they’ve spent on developing a game, and it really shows with the intricately detailed artwork, beautiful soundtrack and clever world design.
Compared with their previous two games, I think Samorost 3 features some of their most beautiful art to date. Seriously, some scenes are absolutely stunning. It cannot be described with words, and has to be experienced by playing the game on a high resolution screen.
Composer and multi-instrumentalist Floex aka Tomáš Dvořák returns to score the soundtrack, and as usual, he doesn’t disappoint. It's much more abstract and lush than his previous work featuring a whole array of meticulously and beautifully arranged melodies. One of the biggest draws to it is how it is actually featured in the game, with several puzzles having some kind of musical focus.
Now, for a kind-of-negative-point. While their games have never been about super immersive storytelling, I’ll admit I was a bit lost at the beginning of the game. I knew (vaguely) to keep going, but I wasn’t quite sure where I was going. It just felt like I was chilling out, clicking stuff to see what happens next. It wasn’t really until near the end I learned about the true goal of the game. This didn’t really bother me, because again, Amanita’s games aren’t really played for the story. But it did feel weird. On the other hand, it made me appreciate their semi-open world design. It gives each section of the game it’s own chance to shine and ultimately provided a very relaxing experience.
As a final score, I’d give this a 9.1/10. This is an absolutely fantastic game. The biggest drawback for me I guess was that the spark I felt while playing their earlier games was missing from
. This may have been due to my sporadic game sessions while playing. Regardless, it’s another home-run for Amanita Design.
10 out of 10, great game
With endlessly quirky and fascinating visuals and a great soundtrack, I feel very comfortable in recommending this game to anyone who seeks a relaxing and slightly weird videogame experience.

The art design, music, and general atmosphere of this game are phenomenal, with the return of composer Floex especially helping to bring the environments and ambiences of this game to life.
The main concern that people have with this game however is the slightly lacking puzzles, which are indeed much less intelligent than those found in Machinarium, with some functioning more as a guessing game than something requiring fulfilling logical input. The puzzles can still be very interesting however, with most of them being the basis for a colourful animation or small musical scene.
The overall experience of Samorost 3 however is a very positive one indeed, and one that I feel that most would enjoy very much.
If you enjoyed any of the previous games by Amanita Design, or are just a fan of small, characterful and atmospheric indie games in general, then you should definitely consider buying this game. (Though I would probably recommend waiting for a sale.)

Hitman Blood Money, the fourth game in the Hitman series, and it brings a whole lot more to the table than Hitman Contracts did. Offering a whole new host of options, such as new tools, new outfits, HUGE groups of npcs, and even weapon customization!
It also seems like 47 has had a shower since the last game, as he can now walk past a guard without setting off an alarm, and he can even wander around common areas in his suit without being shot.
The game also offers a reputation system, wherein the police will actively build a case against you in between levels as you commit crimes and are witnessed by npcs. I think this system works pretty well, but there are irritating little things that bug me about the stealth system. for starters, animals count as witnesses to your crimes, and can raise your notoriety between levels. This carries over to NPCs with "crowd AI" who will not alert the police to your presence...but they will break your suspension meter, making it lock at code yellow until you eliminate the npc  who saw you. so that's annoying.
On the reverse side, I quite enjoyed the open freedom to kill my targets, in every way you can think of. from shoving people out the window, to poisoning their beer, to just walking in and blowing them away with a gun. I feel like Hitman Blood Money really strikes the balance between classic Hitman and Hitman Absolution, offering a much better stealth system than the originals, without sacrificing the freedom to wander around the entire map (like other games in the series i may or may be part way through right now)

3 1/2  out of 5 stars.
For most of the way, I was leaning towards 3.  But the sheer balls of the ending in which they went all out with the creepiness (for better or worse) earned them that extra bit.
I can understand why some people are ambivilant about that aforementioned ending.  No, it's not a problem that the ending is "supernatural."  (Kind of a silly complaint, as it was clear from pretty early on that this was a supernatural plot.  Not a Scooby Doo type of thing.)
However, what some people might not be prepared for is how fully the game descends (literally) into all out surreal horror.  (It's not completely out of left field.  I mean, the game had been gradually getting creepier and weirder, especially when Kathy visits that guy in the mental institution and he starts babbling about conduits to Hell.)
I'm talking specifically about the extended sequence at the end that brings to mind "Hellraiser 2" or "In the Mouth of Madness."  Gone are the familiar, comfortable touchstones of the plot, and we as the player are now stuck with our main character in a claustrophobic version of her own personal hell.  In fact, it's so well done that it might hurt the enjoyability factor of the game as it veers into genuine unpleasantness.  I mean, it gets dark, people.  (If you were hoping for a Monkey Island knockoff, this is a bad thing.  If you were hoping for a game that's unsettling, then I guess it's a good thing.)
The plot, thankfully, does resolve itself at the end.  Sort of.  Even if I wasn't entirely clear on what it all meant, I still felt some closure.  And it made me curious--if this game is successful, how would they approach a sequel?  I mean, Kathy is not a typical mystery-solver in this game.  She's not a gumshoe who goes looking for crimes to solve.  (Such a premise would easily lend itself to more adventures.)  No.  This story, rather, was entirely predicated on a very specific supernatural problem having to do with her hometown.  So how could such a scenario happen again?  Perhaps future Kathy adventures would have to be tied directly with her hometown and the "Crimson One" character introduced in this game.
Plot goes from great to plausible to wtf.  Loved the first half, hated the second half.  Was surprised the game was over when it was...felt very abrupt.

Ahh, Railroad Tycoon II. Another game resurrected from the mists of time and childhood memories of playing this game as a starry-eyed child with my train-obsessed father. Once the shine of nostalgia had worn away a little, however, I found myself able to give a more..objective review of the game. The positives? Well, the music is great, the attention to detail (particularly with the trains and historical aspects) is pretty impressive, and the gameplay, at its core, is quite addictive. As you play, you find yourself eager to expand your railway, to explore the map and find out what locomotive will be unlocked next. There's also an impressive array of scenarios/maps to play, and an amusing level editor. However, one drawback I found is that the game can be rather confusing. There are no proper tutorials, none that I could find anyway (occasional hint boxes hardly count), and it's scarily easy to run out of money, which in turn annoys your investors and nets you a game over. The interface can be rather confusing, and at the risk of sounding stupid, I don't really understand the financial side of the game (bonds and stock, etc) and how that all works. All that being said though, if you can wrap your head around the confusing mechanics, this is still a timeless classic of a game, and very enjoyable. Not the best, but definitely recommended as a cheap time-waster.

In the third Samorost game by Amanita Design Mr. Space Gnome makes a return. This time his job is not to save his little sausage dog, but rather to learn the mystery of the fallen flute. After learning a bit about the past of the flute Mr. Gnome prepares his new Onion ship (*gasp* No sausage-can ship?) and sails away quite easily to the nearest planet.
Through out his about 6 or so hour adventure he discovers many-a unique puzzles, quirky and funny characters (also baddies!), reveals the past of the magical flute and even becomes a very skilled flute-player (Oh my!).
--
Keeping the art style, gameplay and music loyal to the Samorost series, I say that this game is worth every penny even if it felt quite short (~6 hours of gameplay, almost every achievement gotten).
I bought the Cosmic Edition of this game. The soundtrack was worth the pay but I wasn't too impressed with the art book (Very simple concept art but you can't expect concept art to be always fancy, right?).
The nature-inspired environments are a sight for the eyes, there are some catchy tunes in the game along with beautiful and atmospheric background scoring and the gameplay works great. A few downrights are that sometimes you have to go to another screen multiple times (ex. the infamously hard fruit puzzle). Luckily the game won't punish you for not understanding the puzzles; The Hint Book is there to guide you with clear pictures! The story's also a good one, resembling a kind of visual sci-fi novel.
As a fan of the point'n'click genre and as a person who's been playing Amanita's games for a long while, I say that this is a wonderful game for anyone who loves point'n'clickers, creative puzzles, lovely visuals and amazing & calm soundtracks.

This is a game that I was really excited about back at it's initial release. Played through the (rather lengthy) campaign and for the most part, enjoyed myself.
Now that the game has recently gone free to play (sort of) and I only recently learned that it was available on Steam, I decided I wanted to take another look and give it another shot and here's what I can say for it as-is:
Pros:
- Good amount of characters to choose from
- Decent graphics (not mind blowing, but an edgy cartoonish style)
- Solid amount of humor and unique personalities for each character
- Campaign is surprisingly long for an FPS
- Gameplay style is rather unique considering while it is all First-person view, there are characters that use melee
- Moba-style PvP/PvE
- Good amount of customization via equipment you can earn in-game
Cons:
- While there is a slew of characters, unless you want to pay cash for them it is a very long grind (which is made even more painful if it turns out you don't like any of the characters available in the free rotation)
- Yes, the campaign is long but one might say it's actually too long and worse, it's boring. I actually couldn't be asked to finish it in the week I rented it. Not only that but even if you wanted to play the campaign you have to buy this game as it's not accessible at all on this F2P platform.
- Very limited map selection/variation
- It can be seen very much so, as a poor-man's Overwatch
- There are item/equipment boosts in game which, if someone does pay for chests to get the best equipment, it can turn into a pay-to-win game
- My experience playing the game since it went F2P has been rather painful, even in PvE due to the fact that there is at least 1 disconnect per game, making even PvE matches last far longer than I'm comfortable with.
- There is a RPG-esque mechanic in game where you level up from 1 - 10 every game and get one skill point when you level, however if you are unfamiliar with the character, you have to stop to read what the skill upgrades do in-game unless you want to take the time to learn ALL of the skill upgrades for every character before you play them which turns into a chore if you just want to get in and play or try out a new character.
- This final one is strickly personal but they turned what could have been the most B.A. character in the game into a more obnoxious Mathew McConau♥♥♥♥ (somehow). I guess, congrats on achieving what I thought was impossible? (Why is his last name censored??? Lmao!)
TL;DR
As it stands, even after going free to play, it's not an enjoyable experience. Queue times are long and there are frequent disconnects.
The creators need to change a few things imo. Primarily, adding 1 or 2 more characters to the free character rotation and rotate them frequently (at least once a week if they aren't already). Secondly is trying to figure out methods to curb d/cers (which is hard to punish if there aren't a lot of people playing the game to begin with) or trying to figure out if people are just having issues connecting to the servers/game.

Battleborn is possibly the best "FPS; hobby-grade coop campaign; genre-blended, multi-mode competitive e-sports; meta-growth, choice + epic Battleborn Heroes!" game on steam.
I will start-off by saying that I've never been a huge fan of Gear Box Software and a lot of their games never appealed to me. I was always stingy on purchasing Battleborn due to the fact the game's community was extremely tiny making it quite hard to justify paying 40$ to not be able to play with other players.
That being said, Battleborn is pretty good now that the game is free to play but still lacks a large enough player base. The game is heavily MOBA inspired, expect elements from MOBAs in it, such as unique characters to choose from, minions, leveling up your character in game, taking mercenary camps and pushing the enemy sentries in order to win, though the game has various other game modes.
Though, one of the things I dislike about the game's vast collection of characters, I found some of them don't seem quite appealing design wise (to me) and a big majority of their voice performances seem rather overacted and even full of memes, which can come off as a bit annoying to some.
It's such a shame too see Battleborn still having trouble with a player base, even after it went free to play. I guess bad launch with bad marketing can really hurt a product this much. Something I do have to state is the unwarranted comparison to Overwatch as both games are vastly different at their cores though share some similarities, they can both exist on the market alongside each other.... At least they COULD have.

Great game with a lot of potential! The character designs and toolkits are very interesting and the gameplay is much closer to a lane-based MOBA than the objective-based Overwatch.
It's really a shame that the servers are so empty, because Battleborn offers a truely unique experience. Queuing for a 5v5 match is like watching grass grow at this point, but hopefully the shift to a free to play model will bring in new blood--it got me to sign up!
If you like DOTA2, League of Legends, or especially Heroes of the Storm, but prefer being right in the action, this is the game for you!

AVGNA is a game based on the the exploits and misadventures of the Angry Video Game Nerd. You get pulled into a game via testicles and are forced to play and beat the game in order to escape. Each stage is a parody theme of existing genres and series with an excellent soundtrack that should keep your toes tapping. There are alot of easter eggs, power-ups, cameos, three unlockable characters, and multiple game modes which can provide replay value. However, now that my adventure is done, I have no desire to venture further because once the laughter dies down you begin to realise what this game has made perfectly clear since you hit start:This game sucks.
Even as a fan everything became very old, very quick. Despite growing up in the Nintendo era, this is not the nostalgic trip I was looking for. Having one stage completely devoted to poor level design, enemy placement, cheap deaths, and boring bosses is okay but devoting an entire game is just tedious and tiresome. The addition of extra characters seems like a good idea until you realise how poorly implemented they are. Besides the nerd, the only other character worth playing is the guitar guy because he's nimble and his projectile is actually useful. Mike and the meatball guy (two characters that are not part of AVGN, to my knowlege) are absolutely pointless. Mike's luigi jump and meatball's double jump are horrible and their overall attack is laughable causing you to immediately switch back to the nerd. The levels are not designed well enough to give a legitimate reason to switch or even save these characters. The nerd is so well-rounded that you don't have to save anyone but its okay that this and other aspects of the game are poorly created because its a joke, right?
I wish there was a "meh" button. If you're a fan then you won't be disappointed. Everyone else, though, you can skip this one unless you're super curious, its on sale, or you're a Kaizo-type fan. This joke isn't funny enough to overlook the glaring issues that this game has whether it was done on purpose or not. This is one of the few instances where hitting the nail on the head does nothing more than give a splitting headache.

AVGN Adventures is a very good game that brings back a lot of what made the old 8-bit classics so great. The gameplay mixes elements from various different platformers, with Mega Man perhaps the most notably source of inspiration. The game also looks great, with a cool aesthetic that emulates many different old-school games. Finally, the soundtrack is exceptional, featuring numerous callbacks to series like Castlevania and Metroid.
However, the game isn't perfect. The gameplay does take a while to get used to, as the characters' hitboxes are a bit larger than one might expect, and the platforming can feel a bit slippery at times. In addition, I think it was a mistake to include the life system in the game. Even though on normal you get 30 lives to complete a level, it's often not enough to get through it, which means you have to go through the entire level again. It may not have been such a huge issue if the game didn't have so many instant death blocks and traps, but some levels just go way overboard with them.
This wouldn't be an issue if the game over state wouldn't send you back to beginning of the level. I know that the easy mode has infinite lives, but I wish the game had a mix of these difficulty levels. The one comparison I could think of is if Super Meat Boy had a life system that would send you back to the beginning of the world if you lost them all. That would completely ruin the game.
The life system in AVGN Adventures makes the game needlessly frustrating and takes away a lot of the fun that it otherwise gives you. I ended up completing the game on easy as a result, which in turn made many bosses too easy. I wouldn't mind the countless retries in the event of death I would have to do on harder difficulties if I wouldn't have to worry about a possible game over during a boss fight forcing me to do the entire level all over again. Regardless, this is still a very good, and fun platformer where the difficulty is part of the enjoyment, it just has some issues that I wish weren't there.

I have to say, I was not expecting ALL of that.
I don't consider myself an expert on visual novels, but I do love to read and visual novels take that to the next level. Sepia Tears is confusing, slow-paced, hard to follow, and breathtakingly beautiful. I wish this got the credit it deserves. The graphics are iffy, but it's not the graphics that draw you in to this story.
Pros
+ The story: Beautiful and breathtaking once you get into it. Truly one of the better  formulated stories I've ever come across
+ Myra: She was amazing. Without giving anything away, the characterization and inflections of her personality were sometimes the only things that kept me rolling
+ Humor: There was just enough dorky stuff stuck in here and there that I actually could relate the story to myself. Entertaining and well-done
+ The Ending: No words, no spoilers. Breathtakingly beautiful
Cons:
- Story Speed: Good lord it took forever to get into the game. Sometimes I had to just force myself saying "It'll get better, it'll be better in a bit
- Mark: I tried to connect with him, I really did, but the personality and interior monologue threw me for a loop more often than not
- Repetitiveness: Oftentimes it just felt like the writer was resaying the same lines to fill another day with Myra.
Results:
Solely for the ending, get the game; it's free, it's short, and it's well-written, People will complain about the graphics being sub-par, but everyone read books without pictures long before this came out and they'll get  over it. I did have a hard time with it originally, but the closer I got to the end, the more enraptured I was with it. Truly beautiful and the ending makes life worth it.

THE FARM
-----Basic Info-----
Here you see the overview of all of your buildings. You can upgrade them

need to do is click on them...

This gives you a list of all your ponies. It tells you their level,

shows a rainbow as the current weather (the leftmost one of the three)

THE STABLE AND WELL
-----Basic Info-----
This is where you can restore a horse's condition and spirit (Condition
refills automatically, Spirit requires brushing or feeding to refill)
You can also buy new items and horses, as well as breed them.
-----Upgrading-----
Upgrading the Stable will allow you to buy new, more effective items for
the ponies (more on them in a moment) FULLY UPGRADING THE STABLE
ALLOWS YOU TO BUY LEVEL 2 HORSES!THIS CAN SAVE AN INCREDIBLE AMOUNT OF
TIME! Upgrading the well simply allows you to have more ponies at once.
-----Breeding-----
Once you have 2 fully trained ponies (see corral for training) whose
condition and spirit are full or nearly full, and you have an open room
in the stable, you can breed them.Two level one ponies breed a level 2.
Two level two's breed a level 3 and so on. But each pony can only breed
once. So to breed a levelfive pony, you'll need to raise a totalof 31
of them minus however many level 2's you bought since fully upgrading
the stable. Any two ponies can breed, even when their names imply that
they are the same gender.
-thanks to Steam user Grumblecakes for gender information.
Unfortunately, level 5 ponies cannot breed, making the whole game about
five times longer. If you want to get all of the crystals, you will need to
breed up 5 separate level 5 ponies (one of each type) I am currently looking
into breeding combinations, but nothing seems to be reliable enough to
commit to besides only buying foals of the same type to ensure their
offspring is what you need it to be.
-----The Store-----
Clicking on the store awning lets you buy items for your current pony, or
in an empty stable, allows you to buy a new pony. WARNING: ANY ITEMS YOU
BUY FOR YOUR PONY WILL DISSAPEAR WHEN YOU SELL SED HORSE!
-Stat-Based Items-
The Lamp, bucket, food and water dishes all effect the stats of your
pony. All of the starting equipment gives zero stats by default, but
I only reccommend buying these forponies that you plan on having
compete in races. Higher leves typically increase stats more, but
pay attention to the items before you can buy because the most
expensive itemisn't always the best one. I also don't reccommend
buying anything until your pony is fully trained. Doing so can make
it difficult to tell if you've finished training
-Condition/Spirit-Based Items-
The three brushes do not offer stats, but using them on your pony can
restore their condition and Spirit. Higher levels typically restore
faster, but have no other benefits.If you are the patient type, or
have other things to do while the ponies are resting, I suggest not
wasting the money. But be warned, when windoed, the game pauses if

Kathy Rain, subtitled “A Detective Is Born”, is a skillfully modernized update of the classic LucasArts/Sierra-style point-and-click adventure game genre, developed by indie studio Clifftop Games and published by Raw Fury. Aside from a couple of text entry screens, the entire game is controlled via the mouse. Your inventory lives in a handy backpack at the bottom of the screen, and naturally includes valuables like your notebook, taser, smokes, and your favorite lighter. The cursor lights up whenever you pass it over an object or character you can interact with, so you can say goodbye to the old, frustrating hunt-the-pixel puzzles of the past. The puzzles range from “braindead easy” to “somewhat frustrating,” but in the end, they mostly make sense.
There's no way to die here, either – which, while it may take away from the tension a bit, is welcome in a genre notorious for killing characters off for really, really stupid reasons. If you're a fan of the genre, this game will bring you back – while alleviating many of the frustrations that traditionally come with the package. If you're new to the genre, it's a great place to start.
Story and Flow
The year is 1995. Kathy Rain, the titular heroine, is headed back to her old hometown after finding out that her beloved grandfather has suddenly passed away. Once she arrives, of course, she finds out that some strange things have been going on. In the end, she has to face her own demons, even as she digs up those in her grandfather's past.
Is the recalcitrant town sheriff in on some dirty little secrets, or is he just lazy? Is the pushy town priest just desperate for parishioners, or is he more than he seems? Is the crabby lady who lives outside of town really five seconds away from filling you full of lead, or is she just jonesing for a sweet, sweet cancer stick between her lips? Is the mysterious, wealthy industrialist the Big Bad with his fingers in all the local intrigue, or is he just some guy? Play the game and find out.
Controls
Kathy Rain uses the mouse and the left mouse button, along with a couple of very brief text-entry sections, but that's it. Simple and straightforward. Click on a location to go there, click an item (in the world or in your bag) or NPC to interact with or examine them. Choose “Combine” to light up a smoke, drop a cassette into a tape player (remember those, boys and girls?), and the like. Your character will automatically keep track of important conversation points and phone numbers in her notebook. When traveling between areas on your custom chopper, just click the destination and Kathy will ride there on her own. The connection to Full Throttle (which is getting an HD remaster one of these days) is very much in play.
Graphics and Sound
100% all-natural pixels, love 'em or leave 'em. Highly-detailed areas that all contribute to the look and feel of the game's odd little world. You may need to play with the graphics settings a bit to make it easier on the eyes. Right-click the game's list entry in Steam (or CTRL-double click) to access the config utility. Set the graphics filter as high as it will go; if the game refuses to run, drop it down a notch, one at a time, until you get one that your card is happy with (e.g.: screenshots in this article were taken at 1080p, 4X nearest-neighbor filter setting). If you can't stand to stare at pixels, this may not be the game for you.
A free demo is available, though, so give that a shot; it's a good way to assess whether you'll like the visual and aural styles or not. And speaking of aural style, he game’s subtle, effective soundtrack works perfectly with the just-creepy-enough setting, and the voice acting is really good too.
[Eric Kei]
Summary
Kathy Rain features a well-thought out, coherent story, with some superb voice acting that complements the clever writing. Fun bonus: Most of the achievements are for silly things that are unimportant to the plot – e.g. finding a victim for your secondhand smoke, messing with a teddy bear, or even something as simple as idling too long on a screen without doing anything productive. This is a worthy title, and an excellent modernization of the classic point-and-click adventure. I'm looking forward to more from this studio in the future.

Samorost 3 is one of the most visually striking and memorable games you'll play.
What Is It? Point-and-click adventure through a surrealist blend of nature and technology in a completely alien universe.
Graphics: Incredibly beautiful hand-drawn/photography, masterful technical skill in animations, high level of polish.
Gameplay: Exploration with lateral-thinking puzzles gating progress. Despite being even less moored in reality than Botanicula, the puzzles are grounded in consistent logic. If you are stuck, you are probably missing an observation about the world or a piece of logic.
Music: The music shows up in-game as part of the puzzles, though no music knowledge is required. As usual, Floex delivers an amazing ambient soundtrack.
Length: It took me just 3 hours to reach an ending (some friends tried it out on my account which accounts for the other 2 hours), which is far shorter than most reviews purport it to be. There are really only 4 main worlds.
Difficulty: I didn't use the hints guide and never got stuck for more than 5-10 minutes on any given puzzle. They are all fair and the majority have clever solutions. No simplistic math or pattern matching puzzles that other adventure games tend to rely on. Very lateral solutions are required at times. Playing cards is a standout, as is the very first puzzle you might encounter. This has been my favorite genre for years, and your mileage may vary with the puzzles.
Value: Approx $4/hr. I would consider replaying it as well with a friend and have about 8 achievements left to find after the credits.
Recommended for: Parents with Children, People who like 'Artistic Games', People who liked previous Amanita games, People who like Creative Puzzles

Samorost 3 is a point-and-click game by Amanita Design, who also made Machinarium and Botanicula. If you have played and enjoyed their previous games, you should absolutely buy Samorost 3; it's the studio's best by far. Samorost 3 showcases beautiful artwork in the world around you, a stunning soundtrack that helps you get immersed in the game, and puzzles that are solvable through reasoning and observation, as opposed to obscure, non-intuitive mechanics. Amanita Design has also added an achievement system that both encourages you to interact with the game world and provides some extra gameplay for those who wish to complete the game 100%. With all of the work poured into this game, it's not only Amanita Design's best game so far, but is the best point-and-click I've played to date.
As is typical for this studio, Samorost 3 completely avoids use of text/reading. I like this style, but it was a bit of a pain point when I accidentally lost all progress early in the game by reloading to the last save point. That is my only criticism of the game, and I encourage you to try out the save and reload features as soon as possible in the game to avoid that issue.
For those who played Samorost and Samorost 2, one important thing has changed for this game, which I was stoked about: no more actual human faces on characters in the game. The faces are all drawn in this installment of the series. Woohoo!
LOVED this game. Original, fun, made me laugh multiple times. Must buy!

Explore a metroidvania style world riddled with hidden challenges and upgrades as well as vibrant art and off-beat humour, while building up a novel moveset that teriffically unifies twitch platforming and combo fighting. This game is a delight.

Guacamelee has a strong luchador theme, but that theme hides a mechanics-heavy Metroidvania game. Expect enemies with puzzle-platformer mechanics, bosses with puzzle-platformer mechanics, sprawling levels with puzzle-platformer mechanics, and bonus fiendishly difficult platforming puzzles with two EXTRA scoops of puzzle-platformer mechanics! The whole thing has a very tongue-in-cheek sense of humor, especially the side quests. The co-op play is a lot of fun even though half the puzzle-platforming mechanics are ill-suited to it; expect to tag-team many of the puzzle sections if you have a partner.

Guacamelee! Gold Edition which was originally put out on the PS3 Digital store and PlayStation Vita has now been made available on the Steam store with more levels and Steam Workshop functionality. What you get overall though is a great 2D Beat Em Up though with very few flaws.
The story follows Juan, a simple farmer, who while trying to rescue El Presidente’s daughter from Carlos Calaca who is the ruler of the dead world is killed. That’s right , the main character and protagonist is killed in the opening of the game. However Juan is brought back from the dead by the magic of a mask and turned into a all so powerful luchador. Juan then sets out on a adventure to find El Presidente’s daughter. That is a simple form of the story without spoiling some of the excitement. During the story however it displays it’s fantastic sense of humor. Throwing references to everything from Mario to Wreck It Ralph. You get to know a handful of fun character with the most memorable one being the old man who owns the Choozo statues that Juan finds.

As you can see the game is beautiful looking. The environments are very brightly colored and lush looking. It boats a very well done art style that looks good in zoomed out scenes as well as close up. The character and enemy types are extremely detailed as well. The music is impressive as well with the mariachi music not only fitting in well but also being quite catchy.
Off to game play we have a very well rounded beat em up / platformer at times. As you progress through the game you will get new masks which will unlock new moves and powers for you. Those moves will help destroy blocks you will come across that can only be destroyed by that move. That color scheme also later applies to enemies with shields. You will also be introduced to a light and dark world with puzzles and platformer sections playing heavily on switching between the two. It can get very difficult however thankfully the game balances it all fairly well. While it is hard the game never manages to get to the point where it is too hard to pass.
Thankfully the controls once learned are pretty tight. The game as well supports control functionality. With good controls the platforming thankfully does well. With leveled up powers you will find yourself doing moves along the lines of a double jump into a wall grab into a uppercut just to reach a platform you need. If you do mess up however and fall to your death the game graciously just warps you back up to the ledge never making you have to redo sections just to fail again.
By defeating enemies and passing areas into the game you gain coins which can be used to level up your character and buy new moves. The stations to upgrade yourself come rather often since they also serve as save points as well.
Boasting very few flaws one of my main gripes with the game is it’s length. The game is rather short lasting only a few hours. Coming in with a $15 price tag the game though is a good deal and provides a lot of fun for it’s cost. I also found at first the combat to be somewhat repetitive though once gaining new powers it freshened up.
Overall Guacamelee! is a great game. Featuring a entertaining story, fantastic graphics, and some great yet hard action and platforming you will have fun through the short journey. It’s well worth checking out.

Wow. What a treasure this game is!
From a technical perspective, I admit it's nothing impressive. The background art and character sprites are fairly simple, the music is repetitive and almost a bit plain, and the story is short and straightforward. You won't find yourself wishing you had pillow cases of this game, or wanting to pay for the soundtrack.
But that has never been what makes a game great or memorable.
No matter who you are or what your childhood was like, this game will make you feel something. It will make you remember and reminisce. The entire story is about the protagonist's struggle with having a crush, after his confession to his first love didn't go so well. And this is something that every single one of us can relate to. No matter how your first love turned out, everyone knows that feeling of how the smallest thing can take over your entire horizon until you see nothing, feel nothing, can think of nothing but the person of your affection.
And you will come to love the characters, because you've been in their shoes; you may even have been just like one of them, once upon a time. In fact, I'm certain that you were, even if you don't realize it at first. I know I was. I am a woman in her early 20's at the time of writing this review, and I've rarely self-identified so strongly with a 17/18 year old male protagonist. I adored watching the transformations and metamorphoses of all the characters. Truth be told, the steps they took as individuals were all so small--but that doesn't mean they're insignificant. Sometimes the smallest steps are the most difficult to take, because they're the most easily obscured and forgotten.
And sometimes you may feel that the characters are too self-absorbed, too caught up in themselves, and are overdramaticizing their issues in a passive-aggressive manner. But then you realize that you still do the exact same thing, even today. And for some grandoise, unknown reason, your heart will smile.
This is such a simple game. And in its simplicity it is breathtakingly beautiful. It didn't make me cry; it did much, much more.

Thunder Wolves is one of those games that every casual player should play. It's full of action, humour and of course explosions!
Thunder Wolves is developed by Most Wanted Entertainment and originally published by bitComposer Games but now published by Nordic Games, even though the game's opening starts with the original publisher's logo. What a confusing world of publishers we live in...
Thunder Wolves is a sort of top down 3D action shooter game where the game's missions are split up into 13 missions each with they're own set of difficulties which are; Casual, Normal and Hard. The Casual difficulty is the easiest mode from the whole
You control a helicopter where you can move in 360 via the WASD keys, simple enough. You shoot with the LMB and fire missiles with the RMB and you shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of enemies. The story is pretty simple, the game takes place in the Middle East in 1991 and some flashbacks to Central Asia from the 1980's
The graphics aren't the best, you won't see people in this game. The very few people you see they look like from the early days on PC gaming, the graphics in the environment aren't bad but the close ups look a bit bad, but it didn't really bother me. Some animations are pretty poor but not that bad
The voice acting at first may be bad to some people but the voice acting is deliberatly set for the 90's cheesy style of voice acting. The length of the game is ridiculously short, clocking in at around 2-3 hours just playing in normal difficulty! So overall if you played all the difficulties with the same missions it would clock in at around 8-9 hours, not the best. The game does also offer Local Co-op, but I have no friends...
Overall, Thunder Wolves is a fun game to play and it is a fun game for casual players who would like to play a short game for the reasonably pricing. Thunder Wolves is one hell of a ride!

I loved this game. I was weaned on the early Sierra and Lucasarts adventures a a kid in the 80s, and stuck with that genre until it petered out in the 90s (with some notable exceptions). The recent adventure game revival has been exciting for me in theory, but none of them have really engaged me like some of the games I cut my teeth on once did (granted, as a kid, it was easier to capture my attention than it is now). This game was a masterpiece of writing, art design and voice acting. It wasn't tough, in fact I played it through in one (six hour) sitting. But those hours passed quickly because I was so taken with the story and the characters. There are none of the absurdly difficult combine-every-item-you-have-in-every-possible-order style puzzles, and the puzzles you will face are generally easy (barring one insanely obtuse, but thematically appropriate, one toward the end), but this is a good thing. That is to say the puzzles won't make you pull your hair out and get sick of the game for a week, only to come back to it later and repeat the process.
I think this succeeds so well because it is a game for adults, and given its setting in the 90s, probably for people who lived through that period (ie. former adventure game addicts like myself). There are 'adult themes' and colorful usage of swear words, etc. Even though it's a fairly quick game (I finished it in 6  hours, as I mentioned) it's absolutely worth the $15 price point, and I hope a lot of people buy this so more games of this caliber, within this style, will continue to be made.
Enjoyed it far more than any of the other new, flashier and 'prettier' adventure games. This one provides a memorable thematic experience that will stick with you the way the Colonel's Bequest or Space Quest III (to name a couple) once did. I have intentionally not said anything about the plot, because it's better to come into this game with an open mind, not knowing what to expect next. A+.

Now, a lot of people's first experience with this game (and potentially RPGs as a whole) was with the Xbox version. I actually owned this game and it's sequel on the Xbox myself when I was a kid. I owned and played the sequel first and ADORED it, so I went back to playing this one once I got a hold of it. If there's two words that would describe how I felt playing it as a kid, they would be "disappointment" and "frustration". And to be completely honest, after playing it again as an adult, I feel the same way somewhat. I can better describe why I feel that way nowadays, of course. However, I'm going to actually ♥♥♥♥ing structure a review for once and go over the basics before I get into my reasoning for my POWERFUL DARK SIDE EMOTIONS.
KOTOR's setting is really great. It's honestly my favorite part of the game. KOTOR takes place thousands of years before the films. The galaxy is wracked with war. The Sith are absolutely wrecking the Republic, and you can actually SEE what life is like on Sith planets. There's also a neutral world full of fish people, which is amazing, Jedi enclaves, ancient ruins, the works. I'm quite fond of it.
But nevermind that. In the beginning of KOTOR, you're the best Soldier/Scout/Smuggler the Republic has to offer. Well, actually you're a Level 1 pissant, but bear with me. You were specially selected to be on this ship that's getting slaughtered when the game starts. You watch Jedi and Republic soldiers get absolutely demolished, and you and one other lucky soldier (who is conveniently a pilot) crash your escape pods right into the thick of a Sith-Occupied megalopolis world. You must search for a single Jedi who crashed on the planet as well, as they're your only hope for stopping the Sith... or whatever.
My thoughts on the inital plot is that it's kind of... meh. It's not awful, but it's not the most enthralling. Honestly, it just made me realize Bioware isn't nearly as good at writing as Black Isle/Obsidian are. To be honest though, it's just a setup, not the main plot anyways.
You escape the huge planet-city during a Sith bombardment with a party of Bastilla, a Jedi, Carth, the best pilot in the Republic, Canderous, a Mandalorian mercenary, T3-M4, an astromech droid (think R2-D2), Zaalbar, a big wookie, and Zaalbar's best friend, a Twi'lek girl of fourteen years named Mission Vao. Luckily for you, none of the Republic or Sith port authorities question why you're dragging a teenage girl around in your smuggling vessel.
You're taken to Dantooine and get trained EXTREMELY quickly in the ways of the Jedi, stumble across an ancient artifact, and then are sent all over the galaxy to find more of that artifact. Neat, eh?
In my opinion, hunting down ancient artifacts isn't as interesting as hunting down those who exiled you like in KOTORII, but it's fine. I'm not going to get into the rest of the plot here, as there'd be massive spoilers and you'd be doing yourself a disservice if you read up on it beforehand. It's kind of cliche, and the villains are all Saturday morning cartoon characters, and there's a lot of forced stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's not the WORST thing ever. It's your standard good vs. evil stuff.
Anyways, speaking of characters...
Just like the ingame map, most of your party is pretty flat. The writing typically plays up one characteristic of a personality, and your party members don't really feel like real people. Carth doesn't trust anyone, Canderous is a WARRIOR, Mission is... fourteen, yadda yadda yadda. Bastilla just wants your♥♥♥♥♥♥the entire time but tries to hide it. Every conversation with her is either her acting smug and superior, ♥♥♥♥♥ing about your conduct, or going "I'm a Jedi! We're not allowed to love! I just find you... intriguing, b-baka!" I don't know, maybe Bioware really just likes hate♥♥♥♥ing. By the way, this is the one romance options for males, if I recall.
Combat in this game runs on the Roll20 system. If you've ever played Dungeons and Dragons, it should come to you pretty easily. You have Hit Points and
Force Points, and you attack with weapons and
force powers. It's not particularly complex.
However, combat can lead to the most frustrating parts of this game. Controlling your party is a lot like being a special education teacher. It's just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ running headfirst into trouble and it's very hard to consistently wrangle them. Your party AI is laughably bad. Well, not laughably. It's really frustrating.  It's even more frustrating when Bioware insists on throwing "boss fights" at you that are just complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. If you've ever played this game and got frustrated at a boss fight, it's not your fault. You're not bad, you don't need to "git gud XDDDDDDDD". It's the fact Bioware can't design a fair fight and just makes certain enemies incredibly overpowered to pad out the game's length. It's just not fun at all. KOTORII does it sooooo much better.
The dialogue in this game is laughable for all the wrong reasons. There's not very many clever jokes, it's just "WE'RE GOOD WE'RE JEDI WOW" and "MWHAHAHAHAHA I LIKE TO KILL PEOPLE FOR NO REASON HURR". Maybe if you like cheesy writing, it's perfect for you. That isn't really my thing though. Malak is the most ♥♥♥♥ing cartoonish Sith Lord who ever lived. Nobody in this game, not even the PC, talks like a normal person. It's so mindnumbing. Your two options are generally "Wow! I love the light! I suck off Jedi because I'm so heroic!" and "I will be an edgelord for no reason! Bow to me!" You can't be "light" and heroic without slurping on Jedi balls. This word is overused, but it's cringeworthy. Just... overwhelming mediocrity.
That's not to say there aren't instances of really good dialogue though. Sometimes genuinely great writing shines through all the mediocrity. It's very pleasant when it happens.
Could you tell I actually enjoyed this game? Probably not, considering how scathing my review is. I'd say get it on sale, there's still a lot to enjoy. 7/10.

TL;DR: This is one of my favorite games for all time. It is definitely worth checking out even today.
Where to begin with Railroad Tycoon II?
I could start with both the campaigns. The Platinum edition has two campaigns: The "Original" Railroad Tycoon II campaign and the Second Century campaign.  Both cover a wide swath of history and geography, ranging from building the Trans-Siberian Railway to the introduction of railroads in the United States. While some of the scenarios in these campaigns are just simple train-routing puzzles, most of the campaign scenarios are quite meaty, taking a good half-hour to two hours to complete.
I could mention the vast number of maps that this package includes. In addition to the campaign, the Platinum edition includes 50 other maps of varying quality and a map editor if you're interested in making more. Like the campaign, these can range in playtime from a half hour to several hours per map. However, since this is an older game, I'm not sure how many other folks are making new maps for this game these days.
I could mention the replay value of all of those maps. The game has a semi-random distribution of industries at every map start, which makes each play-though subtly different.
I could mention the nearly two hours of blues music that is the game's soundtrack, or the attention to detail in the game's artwork. While it is stuck in isometric view, the game's graphics don't feel particularly dated to me. The only quibbles I've got is the lack of support for wide-screen resolutions (which didn't really exist when it was made).
But, overall, I think the core gameplay as a logistics puzzle and business game is Railroad Tycoon II's strongest element. The gameplay is truly 'easy to learn, difficult to master'. The idea of "Deliver one iron, one coal to a steel mill, then take that steel to a Tool and Die factory which produces one goods to take to a town" is simple, but actually delivering it all, at a profit, is a real challenge. The player gets all sorts of interesting decisions along the way: From where to route track to how to finance the whole operation to what locomotive to choose.
