I was not there at the start, being one of the millions of players who opted towards Overwatch instead of Battleborn, which was woefully released around the same time. There was also the fact that Overwatch was twenty dollars cheaper, so basically millions of players flocked towards the safer bet with a studio with a better track record. On one hand, we had a well marketed, Pixar-esque Team Fortress game and on the other, a cartoony MOBA that had the misfortune of being compared to Overwatch for the rest of its existence.
I’m here to tell you: It’s actually not bad.
Unfortunately the community has more or less died. I installed it about the day after it went free to play and it boasted about 1400 players. As of this writing in the early AM’s, there’s about 360 in-game. Could just be the hour and that does very likely rise in the evening but there’s no doubt that the playerbase has fallen off a bit, which is a damn shame because the game has a lot to offer. As a result of this, it may be a good idea to pick it up with a group of friends so that your queue times aren’t abysmal.
Edit: To wit, it took me all day to even get a game going so I had screenshots to share, so that may give some indication on how long it takes to play.
I’ll start with the PvE, and I have no idea when the mode was introduced but it’s a lot of fun. I randomly queued and joined another, much more experienced player in an objective-based map that took about thirty minutes to complete. Might have been faster if I knew what I was doing but they didn’t seem to mind. If there was a critique, I feel like it had a similar vibe to Titanfall 1′s laughable attempt at a campaign. In the match I played, most of the “story” was played out over a radio while we followed an NPC (which is also a playable character) around while he did some pseudoscience. After that, we’d just face against waves of enemies of variable difficulty. The map itself was creative enough with at least one death for both of us around a jump we weren’t expecting. Fair enough, kept me on my toes. The game itself was a lot of fun with a proper RPG-esque vibe as you leveled up slowly throughout the whole thing (Which is a much more rapid process in a PvP match, and speaking of)…
In the main-stay mode (is that a term?), there’s PvP. Your usual 5v5 setup but if there’s some kind of lane-based map, I have yet to find it. So far I’ve only been treated to a couple of maps which were all one lane with minions. Spread around, there’s a few mechanics of note. There’s a bunch of crystals you run around to collect which can be used to activate your three items you bring in as a “loadout” which can do all kinds of things including recoil reduction and maximum health. It’s a much more streamlined variant of the item/shop mechanic present in other MOBAs. Once you’re done with that (or you could do this intermittently) there’s a bunch of turrets around the entire map you can activate. There’s accelerators that increase your run speed to get you back in the fight quicker, supply stations that will rapidly heal you so you can avoid teleporting all the way back to base, and a few offensive turret types that will keep minions and players at bay. Everything costs crystals and the bulk is usually gained by going out of your way to collect them, and it’s a neat idea. A relative flaw is that this amount is not shared like it typically is in other MOBAs. I’ve seen huge crystal-amount disparities in the stat screen because some players just don’t know about them (I’m still in novice queues).
There’s also an Operation mode which I can’t speak on because it won’t let me play them for not owning “Operations Pack 2″ or the “Season Pass”, which is not accessibly to me despite having paid 30$ for the ‘full game’. Perhaps it’s Founder specific for those who dropped the full 75$ way back in the day. It’s a shame and a bit of an oversight and I hope they fix that, but they may not if their playerbase bleeds dry.
The command menu is fairly easy to use but the f2p-ness of the game rears its ugly head soon enough. Most games (which again, have mostly been in PvE and AI) net me around 900 ingame credits. Despite buying the 30$ full game pack, there’s about five heroes that cost ~42,500. That’s a lot of credits, and there’s the money-bought currency (because of course there is) that you can choose to do if one of those characters really appeals to you. Some PvP-based quests do give you some of those, but it would take a whole hell of a lot of gaming. How you feel about that is largely how you feel about the industry as a whole.
If I had a major complaint is that it’s a bit difficult to figure out what the hell is going on at any given point. Perhaps it’s because I chose to main a melee character, but it could also be the fact that enemy minion health bars never show up and all of them often get de/buffed with some purple haze and I can’t tell them apart from enemy to friendly. I could be slicing away at an enemy while minions are gunning my health down from behind and I can never really tell.
The field of vision is a little off compared to other games and it’s just a bit wonky to me. When I’m in the thick of battle, I can barely tell if my hits are even connecting or not, which is why I tend to take the upgrade to Galilea where, at full health, her sword will fire these ranged energy beams to give her some reach. They don’t do as much damage as her raw sword attacks do so I am just forced to wade in where the fighting is thickest, pop her AoE… thing and hope for the best because I can’t ever really tell what I’m hitting. This might get fixed with experience as I get used to it, but that won’t happen if I can’t find people to play with.
You may notice a trend here; I’m not mercilessly comparing this game to others in its genre, and that’s because I feel the game has a solid niche with many notable differences that help give this game its own soul and core. It all sadly went ignored due to its release conditions and perhaps by some less than stellar business practices, some of which are covered by Jim Sterling. I can’t speak for all of that, but in the few hours I’ve played, I have not hated the experience. Like many other things, it would probably be more fun to queue with friends. That’s really my conclusion to this; if you’re interested in picking this game I’d recommend bringing some friends along. The f2p version locks you away from the PvE side of things but there’s still plenty of AI smashing you can do together.
Ultimately I do feel like I’m reviewing what is essentially a dead game, which is why Jim Sterling called his video a “depressing post-mortem”. I just felt like giving it some attention due to its recently released free status.

But it's nonetheless one of the more fascinating/horrifying spots on the planet. And this is the Aral Sea as myth, in a sense. The quest to bring back the lost water that comes to consume the efforts of several people who are driven to try and return what is gone.
And in the sense of storyline and lore, and the immersive quality of its soundtrack and the distinctive voices of the characters, Residue is fantastic. In terms of actual gameplay though, it can be a bit rough... as a platformer some of the areas leave a bit to be desired, and the swimming is odd, but it's well checkpointed and doesn't really punish you for failure unless you miss the chance to torment some seagulls for achievements. Each of the characters moves quite uniquely (don't expect the old man to go bounding around the landscape for example) which makes for varied play. And the game isn't really long enough for any of its faults to get really grating, and it's regularly switching characters and throwing bits of lore at you which keeps things moving.
Don't expect a tight platforming experience. Do expect a good story.

Here is a suggestion. Watch a documentary about the Aral Sea distaster and donate 2 Dollars/Euros to charity instead of getting this mess. You might like the art style, but the simple fact is that the gameplay is slow, annoying and its painful limitations will kill any amount of immersion you might hope to get from this.

In Residue you mostly play as three different characters with different abilities: an athletic young boy, an old man with a flashlight and a middle-aged man with a grappling hook. All these characters interact and interweave with each other in very interesting ways, in both gameplay and story. I'm being intentionally vague about the story because I think it's good to approach this game with a clean slate - but it all revolves around a real horribly polluted lake in Asia.  The story is confusing at times but everything comes together beautifully at the end. The story is what will keep you playing because the gameplay is nothing special, and when you're stuck as the old man it can become boring - the other characters offer some nice platforming. The graphics aren't breathtaking or unique but they fit the atmosphere of the game perfectly. The voice acting is pretty solid throughout and the music is spot on. The game is short but I don't hold that against it, it tells its story concisely and effectively, without any padding or fluff.

Coming back to Hitman: Blood Money after having originally played it upon release a decade ago is bit of a mixed bag.
Hitman: Blood Money is often hailed as the best in the series and the sequel "Hitman: Absolution" was ill-received by many fans since it went away from the free-roam gameplay style of Blood Money. But this is a review of Blood Money, so let's focus on Blood Money.
Hitman: Blood Money has always been a fond game-memory of mine and now actually coming back to play it ten years later, I got to say:
The graphics are harsher than modern games, more flat and with less fancy textures at high resolutions. The game mechanics can sometimes be frustrating (trying to climb in and out of windows is always a struggle). Navigating the sometimes-maze-like levels can be both confusing and frustrating (the basement of the Opera house). The game can be very unforgiving at times and playing at higher difficulties can make it unbelievable infuriating to get detected only because of some seemingly psychic guard could spot you with his eagle senses.
But the overall gameplay is still as fun as a decade ago, despite some of it's less than polished game mechanics Hitman: Blood Money is a very fun game to play. Setting up elaborate traps, blending in crowds, crusing around the map, learning the routes of guards, waiting for the perfect moment and having it blow up in your face only to have it blow up in your face causing you to retaliate by executing every living soul on the entire map, labeling the hit as a terrorist attack is all very fun. Actually achieving the highest rank and executing the hit perfectly takes effort, planning and patience and when you succeed it is very rewarding.
Hitman: Blood Money is what you make it, there isn't very much hand-holding and it allows you to either be a total psycho or a perfect stealthy hitman, it is up to you.

Just to get it out of the way: the gameplay is not mind-blowing. While the combat is fairly unique-with a "turn-based" D&D systems determining your attacks in real time-it is not exactly engaging.  The inventory system is clunky, the gamecan be glitchy, and the RPG gameplay itself is the same as many other RPG's: Explore, get sidequests and loot, level up your party, etc.
HOWEVER, none of that matters, because that's not what this game is about.  KOTOR was the first game I played where I was willing to overlook many flaws because of how put together the story was.  As a big Star Wars nerd, the writers nailed the setting and characters to make this feel like a genuine "Star Wars" story.  You feel an important part of the Star Wars universe, amplified by the fact that you have some control over the story through your actions.  Like many Bioware games, you are given options throughout the game that decide if you are going to be "good" or "evil" (AKA jedi master or sith lord).  I think KOTOR does the best job of truly making you feel like are in that role, whether you are giving away 5 medpacks to a homeless Ithorian or force choking a former friend.  This is a game I would highly recommend to anyone who is the teensiest bit of a Star Wars fan, and maybe even to a few more people who could care less.

This is one of those times where I really wish that Steam offered something other than "yes" and "no" for recommendations. This game definitely belongs in the "meh" category.
As hidden object games go, it's not awful. The main problem is that the game doesn't know what it wants to be. Is it trying to be a hidden object game or is it trying to be a point-and-click adventure game? In many ways it feels like it's trying to be both. When compared to other HO games, it was rather lacking in HO puzzles containing maybe half of what I would get in other HO games.
Sadly, there are so many things that hurt this game, some small, some not.
The achievements are not working properly. I played the entire game without using hints at all. Yet a few of the achievements related to not using hints never got triggered.
Usage of many objects required multiple clicks - once to activate, then again to drag to the objective. Sometimes it would allow a single-click drag-and-drop, but that was in a minority. Most of the times I have to click then click again to drag-and -drop which is borderline idiotic.
But by far the biggest annoyance with this game is that so many items  were placed at the very top and very bottom of the screen so that you just barely would be able to see the items. I don't know who thought that this would be a good idea - it was probably some developer who thought "well, it will be a CHALLENGE" - but this was by far the most frustrating part of the game. There are several times where objects were almost completely obscured by the inventory bar at the bottom, which cannot be lowered, and a few times where only a part of the object could be seen at the top because the rest was out of the frame! Stupid, stupid design choice!
The story? Meh. The conclusion was more of a "you have GOT to be kidding me" due to how lame it really was. Don't misunderstand me -- HO games rarely have intriguing plots, but this was one of the weaker ones.
Again, the game isn't AWFUL. When it's not being annoying, it's standard HO fare. But unfortunately this game has a LOT of annoyances. I won't say that I don't recommend it, just be aware that you might get frustrated -- a lot. For those reasons, I have to mark this as a "not recommended". There are better HO games out there that don't have the frustrations that this one has.

Really Good Stuff:

There was actualy quite a lot of substance to the game.  Especially when you concider the price.  I've paid more for games that took less time to get through than this one.
OK Stuff:
The music and graphics and voice acting were OK and pretty standard for this type of game.
Not So Good - to frustrating:
Most of the time the Hint button would just drop you in a different screen - and then take forever to load.
We have gotten used to a Map system that let us know where the next step is. This was very lacking.
The Worst Things:
Sometimes, and far too often, objects you need for the HOG were under the center Inventory strip - and that made finding them next to impossible.
The map does NOT take you to a room - it drops you outside of a building, which you have to enter and then move to the different rooms inside. The exit/go back arrow didn't work too well and it was often eaiser to go to the map and then find the right room. Which was pity.
Conclusion:
Not at all bad. Not Artifex Mundi, but for 1/10th of the price, without being on sale, not a bad buy.

I must start of by saying only get this if you love the avgn show. That said, certain problems keep me from loving the game.
The game is a throwback to the 8-bit style of games both good and bad. The game also pokes fun of bad games and has many refrences to avgn and in those regards, this game is perfect. The problem is that if you strip those things out you are left with a game very frustrating and cheap.
Graphics 10/10- I have no problems with this game on this font...They're great and you know what everything is as soon as you see it. Some of the best 8-bit graphics i've seen.
Sound 10/10-Once again, amazing. The sound track is a real standout part of the game, with great remixes of the avgn theme and orignal work that would be at home with the nes tune greats. The audio mixing is great too, with every shot  and explosion having a perfectly timed sound effect.
Control 9/10- Any problem you have with the difficulty will not be related to this. The controls are great, the only complaint is that switching characters in boss battles can be hard on the controller since there are four characters and only two buttons to switch between them.
Gameplay 6/10-Now for my biggest issue. The game is very cheap with it's deaths. The game is going for jokes about bad design choices, but the problem is it only works if you get the joke. Because at the end of the day a bad design choice is still bad. I know this was for a reason but that doesn't make the game play better. But to be fair, it isn't awful. There are very cool moments in the game as well. I just wish they cut back on those death blocks. They're funny at first but lose me the 50th time they instant kill me.
replay 8/10-If you are a fan of the show then this game has a treasure trove of goodies. Hidden characters and cameos, secret jokes, and every frame is a refrence to the show is some way. The only thing is that all this doesn't matter unless you are a hardcore fan. There are multiple difficulties but I think the game is hard enough on normal.
overall 7/10-If you love the show totally worth it. But as a game it's slightly above average.

I never was much of a point & click fan, mostly because their convoluted, alien logic tends to leave me confused and bedazzled as to why I had to pick up a fish, slap a dog with it, and then hide as the dog removes an obstacle any sane person could've just bypassed within minutes.
That doesn't stop me from giving the genre a try every so often, a fact that I am now immensely grateful for as Samorost 3 awoke within me a sense of childlike glee and wonder I haven't felt in many, many years.
The world of Samorost 3 is about as disconnected from reality as it gets, you fly through space in a mushroom you upgraded with a bath tub and a plastic bottle, meteors are closer to sentient mangoes than the rocky visage you might imagine, and the language spoken by those actually capable of communicating is grade A gibberish. The best part of it all? Despite everything being so strange and utterly alien, the world makes sense and its easy to get a grasp on what's happening even after a single glance.
What all of this results in is a world that's so creative, and so unique, that you can't help but continue exploring it in order to find out what bizarre creatures you're going to encounter next, maybe a group of lizards singing the opera, or maybe even a bunch of goblins from 'hell' dancing around while cooking their food, or perhaps even a couple of monkeys relaxing in a hot spring that's located at the bottom side of a fruit-shaped meteor.
In short, Samorost 3 is a lovingly crafted game that's filled with vibrant, beautiful locations and events so strange that they have managed to fully capture my imagination and leave me desperately longing for more.
If you're a fan of Machinarium or other similar point & clicks, and don't mind paying a bit of a premium, you will find that Samorost 3 is a fantastic adventure that's well worth experiencing.

Hitman: Blood Money is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Sqaure Enix and is the fourth game in the Hitman series. As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness
It puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed, the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
However, the game is not without its flaws. For a game nearly 10+ years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. So, BLUE REVOLVER. I don't think anyone is going to need me to tell them about what genre this game is at this point or about any of the more superficial gameplay details - not that I'd be capable of writing a succinct, worthwhile summary of them anyway.
What I can talk about, however, is my perspective on the game as someone who has barely any experience with bullet hell shmups and had always been intimidated by their difficulty.
BLUE REVOLVER manages to teach its players a basic understanding of how to play games of this type in a pretty elegant way. It might seem somewhat gimmicky at first, but if you actually give the mission mode the time of day you will quickly find yourself adjusting to the overall speed and flow of not only this game in specific, but bullet hell shmups in general.
The survival missions give you incentive to practice the individual levels as such, the break ones teach you the bosses and the break mechanic, the invisible bullet ones show you that you shouldn't be focusing solely on your ship during gameplay, the revenge ones train your reaction times and maneuvering skills and so on and so forth.
My point is: Not only is the game fun and rewarding, it also improves your skills really quickly, allowing you to enjoy more examples of this underrated genre of gaming. Highly recommended!

Challenging platformer.
Guacamalee is a 'Metroid-styled, 2D- platformer developed by DrinkBox Studios.
The plot of the game revolves around a farmer named Juan trying to to rescue the president's daughter from the clutches Carlos (the skeleton) who is goiing to sacrafice her in order to rule the world. In order to do so, Juan chases Carlos and defeats his lackies along the way.
Soundtrack is fantastic, giving off a mexican feel and draws you into the unique world. There is no voice acting with character dialogue through text. The sound effects for attacks are also good.
The graphics suit the game well. the colours are  vibrant and  not distracting, and do a good  job at instilling the mexican atmosphere in the game. Furthermore,  the characters and stages all have a mexican styled design to them which helps invoke the mexican atmosphere in the game.
Gameplay revolves around platforming and combat. The platforming in in this game varies between simple to challenging. Some platforms only require a few moves to get to such as simply jumping on them, while more challenging ones require precisely timed executions in order to reach. For the challenging platforming areas, it is difficult to get the precise key inputs through the keyboard as it can only detect a limited number of inputs at a time. I was forced to play with a 360 controller which made the experience more fluid and less frustrating. In combat you face a wide variety of foes including skeletons, dragons and  giants which either have melee or ranged attacks. The aim is mainly to unleash as many combos on them as possible to prevent them from attacking you. You have a varity of attacks which you can used to defeat your foes or to help reach platforms from side smash, uppercut and throws. You unlock more moves as you progress through the story. Furthermore, you can upgrade you character in variety of ways including increasing health, damage and spawn delay (by spending money). Furthermore, you can play the game via local co-op with a friend.
There are alot of references to other videogames such as nintendo characters Mario and Link (with mexican vibes to them). Furthermore, there are secrets hidden withen each area which allows you to unlock new costumes for your character. The different costumes each have a unique trait, such as increasing health/damage, which you can use to change how you tackle the combat. Plenty of other secrets lie in the game including secret stage which you can unlock by collecting enough money.
I highly recommend this game to people you love unique and challenging platformers.

Samorost 3 lets you guide a gnome who dreams of exploration and space travel. Traveling from one floating island or ‘planet’ to the next, you explore otherworldly places, interact, observe and solve puzzles to find your way further into the unknown of space.
Technically, Samorost 3 is as point & click as it gets, but to describe it as a point & click adventure game is somewhat misleading. Like Amanita Designs other minimalist games, Samorost 3 dispenses with many of the trappings usually associated with the genre. There’s no boatload of items to collect and carry around. As a matter of fact, you’ll rarely be carrying more than two items with you, one of them being a trumpet you’ll use throughout the game, both as a hearing aid and a musical device. There’s (almost) no backtracking, since most puzzles can be solved within a single screen. Neither are there complicated logics puzzles that will require a pen and paper to solve. You point at a thing, click, and something interesting and/or useful will happen.
The game's landscapes are where the minimalism ends. The planets you visit are fantastic, rich and colourful places, presented to you one screen at a time. The landscapes are mostly static pictures, but they are nevertheless full of motion, sounds and life, since every space in Samorost 3 appears as a living, bustling ecosystem inhabited by a multitude of creatures.
Exploring them is a joy. You click on creatures or objects, and observe what is going to happen as a result: bushes rustle and tremble, birds fly away, strange bug-crab hybrids retreat into their shells. All of this is animated with incredible care and accompanied by some of the most astounding sound effects I’ve ever come across in either a game or an animated film. The same is true for the game’s soundtrack created by Floex, which seems less like a thing apart than an integral part of this world; less background music than emanation. Creatures sing, sigh, whisper and mumble with gusto and oh-so charming whimsy. It’s as silly as it is heart-warming and beautiful.

A little history:
This game was announced 2 years before Overwatch was even in development.  After following the trajectory and participating in both alpha and beta builds, I was instantly in love.  The tragedy is that while most people saw this game as a cash grab alternative to Overwatch, the reality was that Overwatch was the cash grab title.  Blizzard responded to Battleborn's pre-release marketing to recreate a mix of a storyless battleborn melded with team fortress 2... and then used their big money marketing to out-sell and kill the Battleborn community.
Don't listen to the hype around OW.  Blizzard still hasn't figured out how to create a proper MMR algorithm anyways.
Play battleborn.  Laugh at Attikus.  Laugh at Boldur.  Lose your breath in tears of joy and amusement as you battle with Geoff.  This game wasn't meant to be strictly competitive, it offers the entire experience of a proper campaign PLUS end game PvE options as well as a complex and well balanced PvP system.
________________________________________________________________________________
Now for the rough parts.  Yes, the UI on melee characters can make the experience somewhat dizzying until you get used to it.
Yes, new players will be thrown into matches with players who have been around since the  beta once they have leveled past 25 and are forced to queue in the standard matchmaking modes.
Yes, there is a pretty high learning curve.
____________________________________________________________________________
But try it.  This is one of the best games to come out in recent memory, and I have played a combined 500 hours across all platforms (pc, ps4, and xbox 1).  There is nothing like it on the market today, and it's a truly unique experience.  If you can deal with grinding, and learning each character, and combining PvE with PvP,  you're in the right place.  If you're looking for a simple point and shoot with little complexity, go play Overwatch with the rest of the bads.  I'll be fighting for the last star.
Hopefully will see you on the battlefields!

Spoiler free review:
I beautiful little visual novel, with a cute artstyle and a heartwarming/breaking story. It can be a bit confusing sometimes as it counts on you to catch some subtext between characters in conversation, but even if you don't, it should become clear what was meant earlier further towards the end.
My main critiscism is that there's no real choice. All the choices you make are false choices. They either immediately lead to a "bad end" screen which automatically loops back to the same choice, or the current scene has some change without any long-term impact. In the end, the story will always be the same, no matter what you choose, but your choices only make you see a few scenes instead of some others.
All in all, I really liked the story, and it''s a good way to spend ~4-5 hours of your time (I left it open for a while doing other things, but I'm a fairly quick reader). Plus, it's free. What are you still doing reading this? Go play it!
**SMALL SPOILER FOR THE END CHOICE: It doesn't spoil the actual ending, but it talks about the choices to make to get the good ending.**
The ending was also very confusing because you have to pick between two locations and then whether to give up or not, regardless of the location. If you choose to give up, it just goes to a black screen and loops back to the location choice, but the "not giving up" choice does the same. It's not very clear what you have to do since you can keep doing the same thing. In actuality, you have to go to one of the locations, choose to not give up and then go through the same sequence again and choose the other location. If you go to the second location first, it also ends and loops back around, and will keep doing that until you pick the "correct" location as a first.
It took me a lot longer than it should have to figure it out, and it's quite counter-intuitive. Something that could be improved on as well.

A love letter to the last 15 years of shmups that very closely mimics their peculiarities as well as their achievements. If you're interested in the bullet hell subgenre, this may or may not be a good introduction. In truth it's not really an introduction but a *summary* of the subgenre, a strict by-the-numbers execution of a Cave-style shooter (with faint Raizing and Shanghai Alice influences) reaching toward accessibility but never sacrificing even a sliver of its extremely specific model. First-time players are forced to play with no continues, with infinite continues as an unlock; high scores are obtained through an unpunishing but still obscure system; the game's art style is wonderfully executed but probably not for everyone.
Is it a good bullet hell shmup? Yeah, it's pretty good; the visuals are clear, the controls are responsive enough, the patterns and enemies are challenging and inventive, the learning curve is OK, and the scoring is, while not super-deep, pretty engaging. Is it a game you, personally, should give your time to? Depends on whether you think you like bullet hell shooters, pretty much.

This game relies on one mechanic to make your life living hell: insta-killing blocks, appearing and disappearing in particular intervals of time. This becomes old very fast, and the game has little to offer beyond that. Overall, it's a decent 2d-platformer with lots of jokes borrowed from the show, but there are tons of games in this genre, from Super Meat Boy to VVVVVV that would challenge, enrage and frustrate while also not forgetting to entertain.

I had a good time playing this game, but I have a soft spot in my heart for Hidden Object Games.  Oh the 12+ hours is more like 4; I left it on overnight by accident.  Others have done more complete reviews but here are some things that I noticed.
Pro : they put the effort into integrating with steam where you have achievements - and I appreciate the effort; many HOGs on steam do not bother to do that.

Suddenly your hands begin to wither as you stand at a train station. The world seems forlorn and desolate. You walk inside the train station to find an attendant who has been trapped in the same spot for….eternity? He tried to leave but never could escape, and so he now just sits around doing nothing. You begin to investigate the strange occurrences in this town…
So, this is a hidden object game first seen with Big Fish Games, but now available on Steam courtesy of 2 Monkeys and their publisher, Jetdogs Studios. Now, I had actually watched my wife play bits of this previously, and that factored into a decision I made late in my playthrough. More on that later.
The story for 1 Moment of Time: Silentville was fairly standard HOG fare, in that there is an overarching mystery you must solve. In this case, the town, Silentville, is frozen in time due to what appears to be occult activity, and you have to figure out how to reverse the curse that has enveloped the town. Nothing too extraordinary per se, but it was interesting enough
I think the story aspect of this game warrants a 6.5 out of 10. You’ve seen it before, but it is done reasonably well.
The graphics make used of washed out colors for the story board parts and lush scenery for the rest of 1 Moment of Time: Silentville to emphasize the desolation that can only come from being set apart from the wheel of time. Noting really stood out as amazing, but 1 Moment of Time: Silentville is a pretty game.
This aspect of the game I would assign a 6 out of 10. A little bit above average and fairly consistent with the genre. This was actually the part of 1 Moment of Time: Silentville I paid the least attention to, and that is in large part due to the fact that it really didnt grab my attention and hold onto it.
This is a HOG, so you can expect hidden objects obviously. What 1 Moment of Time: Silentville does very well however is blend in more traditional puzzle gameplay such as you might find in point and click games, and even has an Angry Birds-esque puzzle at one point. This does a good job of keeping the game from getting stale or boring as can often happen when simply moving from one hidden object puzzle to the next. I found that to be a particularly refreshing aspect of 1 Moment of Time: Silentville. So, that was a great element to the game, and if I was to base my rating on this alone, 1 Moment of Time: Silentville would score quite highly.
Unfortunately, gameplay is also where the 1 Moment of Time: Silentville shows its greatest failings. The first frustration I felt while playing 1 Moment of Time: Silentville was when I realized I was always going to have to battle with the item bar on the bottom of the screen. Unfortunately, a lot of the hidden objects and items you are required to click onto in 1 Moment of Time: Silentville are actually underneath that bar, so not only can you not really see those items, but since the back button is also basically right there at the top of the bar, you will find yourself constantly exiting puzzles and rooms despite your best intentions. This lead to quite a bit of frustration, and in this reviewers opinion, it was completely unnecessary. An actual back button and a collapsible item bar would have prevented these issues and should have been simple enough to implement and notable enough of an issue for 2 Monkeys to have actually done so.
Additionally, there are game breaking bugs in the game. I read about a few in the forums, and actually encountered one with maybe 10 minutes left in the game. This is where my wife having played the  1 Moment of Time: Silentville previously factored in, as I was aware of a particular puzzle in the game involving an anchor and a bird nest, and when I reached that point in the 1 Moment of Time: Silentville, the anchor vanished. I had hoped it would reappear, but it never did, and that made it impossible for me to finish the very last section of the 1 Moment of Time: Silentville. That was particularly frustrating.
So, as far as gameplay goes, if I was judging  based on the mixing of Hidden Object games with point and click puzzles, I would have rated this as an 8 out of 10. Unfortunately, the technical issues with 1 Moment of Time: Silentville rendered the game frustrating and unable to be completed, and so I must give 1 Moment of Time: Silentville a 2 out of 10 when it comes to gameplay. Highly disappointing.
Much like the graphics, the sound in 1 Moment of Time: Silentville is more of an afterthought and is mostly used to signal that you have found certain objects or triggered certain events.
Not truly noteworthy and pretty much a 5 out of 10.
While overall, I actually enjoyed my time with 1 Moment of Time: Silentville, the frustrations and inability to complete 1 Moment of Time: Silentville due to game breaking bugs and frustrating controls left a somewhat sour taste in my mouth. However, the game is also in the sub 1 USD price category, and for that price, I have no problem suggesting that you find out for yourself. It’s fairly certain that not every play through will encounter game breakers, and it’s a good enough experience as a whole to recommend playing this if you have a couple hours to spare and dont really feel like playing anything less casual. I would say get 1 Moment of Time: Silentville if you see it for 50 cents or less (such as it is right now at the time of this writing).

When I attempt to place scenery, it always seems to be defaulted backwards, or upsidedown, so 9 times out of 10 I have to move it around until it faces me. Wouldn't it be simpler just to have scenery face me first, then let me move it around where I want?
Unlocking scenery and rides now. Fine, it's the developers decision to lock everything up and force you to play through the scenarios, unless you play sandbox. But I want to build a park, and turn on research, like all the other RCT games before this one, but I don't see the research option on here at all. I enjoyed that aspect of the game, and having rides unlock as I'm playing just adds more fun to the game, in my opinion.
Placing scenery and objects. I was trying to add objects to the path, and for some reason it picked up a peep and threw him in a deep ravine, so I went down looking for him, and did not find him anywhere. Did he fall through the ground? I was getting a warning message that an "entity is under water". So I tried to remove the water, and he was nowhere to be found. The warning went away though. Personally, the message could have said, "Peep is under water", or "Help! Peep is Drowning!" Something funny like that. I still can't explain how I was able to pick him up and throw him into the ravine while I was rotating an sign object that was clipping through the path, and looked awful...
Unfortunately this appears to be an unfinished game, and for the price, I think it's too expensive right now. First: I must confess that I'm a fan of the Amanita Design. Samorost 3 is again a great point&click adventure of the small Czech team. It is really astonishing how they create worlds, stories and even a menu without a single spoken word or written text.
Samorost 3 takes you on a journey through multiple worlds full of nice details waiting to get discovered. The puzzles are always logical and not to difficult.
The only downside for me is the short playtime - I went through the whole game in 7 hours. (without looking for puzzle solutions in google and without rush)
If you ask me: Is it worth the money? Yes, absolutely.

Samorost 3 ist the loose third installment of a wonderful yet quirky series in which you're playing a small gnome who's experiencing several adventures in space. The planets impress with their organic design made out of plants and wood. The whole game gets along without any language at all. Story is told by comics or cartoons.
This point & click game differs from average games of it's genre by it's misterious but beautiful atmosphere. The scenes are rich of phantasy in which always something more can be discovered. The game has a duration of 4-5h, maybe less if you are quick. But Samorost 3 invites the player to slow down, relax and discover, not least because of the fantastic soundtrack from Floex (great artist). Expect an unusual journey with unusual graphics and sounds.
Btw: you absolutely don't have to have played the first two games. But after this you'll maybe want to ;)

Edit 24/06/2017. I have put in a considerable number of hours on Battleborn over the past week or so, mainly because I enjoy getting as many achievements as I can on the games I have played. These hours have largely been on the online games vs bots, with some story play as well. There are some good points for sure - the large variety of characters (some of which are more fun and/or interesting than others), plenty of play-style options, plenty of reactions from characters when they see others in the game, etc. The fundamentals of the game itself are strong in many respects. However, the story missions simply do not hang together well enough as a coherent whole, especially given the great stories behind Borderlands. The bots games are the only ones with a chance of getting a game. Of about 200 or so played, I have lost one, where two of five disconnected and two of the remaining three surrendered. You can win bot games 3 vs 5 with some challenge. 4 vs 5 remains easy. The queuing system itself, even ignoring the lack of players, is terrible. I wish this game every success as I am sure it would be a LOT more fun playing against other humans, but this aspect needs a major rewrite. The gaps between games (sometimes too long, often too short), the long delay before games start, the delays when someone disconnects...all incredibly painful and for no good reason. I would love to change this to a 'recommend' and for the game to take off but some things need fixing first.

Some tips that I found out rooting around in the game editor:
Spain has the best 17th century musketeers hands down.  They cost less than a standard 17th musketeer (40 food, 4 gold, 12 iron VS 45 food, 6 gold, 10 iron), and their stats are way better (+35hp, lots of armor when other musketeers have none).  They do create more slowly at 17.56 seconds, but the average 17th musketeer creation time is 12.5 seconds anyway so it's a small price to pay for such a big buff.  Give them an officer, a drummer, and a screening unit or two, and they'll mow down your enemies in the early game.
Austria also has good 17th musketeers (+5 hp, +1 firepower, and some armor), but they have the longest creation time at 18.75 seconds, and they cost more than average 17th musketeers (50 food, 14 gold, 5 iron) so their good stats are more of a tradeoff compared to Spain's.
Ukraine's only infantry unit is the serdiuk.  They're pretty unique.  They cost 70 food, 3 gold, 15 iron.  They take 18.75 seconds to create, but since they train from your basic houses they're surprisingly easy to mass up.  They do well against basic 17th musketeers without officers, but if the musketeers have an officer and drummer they will soundly defeat the serdiuks, who can't get either.  (Not that you'd play Ukraine for the infantry anyway.  Go cavalry or go home.)
Turkey and Algeria have strong and cheap 17th century pikemen (Ottoman Pikemen).  The Russians also have very good 17th pikes stat-wise, but they have a slow 5.62 second creation time compared to everyone else's 4.68.
While Poland's 17th century pikes are the weakest, they cost resources that are easier to obtain (45 food, 1 wood) and they only create in 3.12 seconds.  That's about one third faster than the average 4.68 seconds for everyone else's pikemen.
18th century Prussian musketeers are expensive, but in a mass they are murder incarnate.  400 Prussian musketeers WILL slaugter 400 of everyone else's 18th musketeers and only lose about 50-70 guys every time.  Give them an officer and drummer to boost their attack and defense to even crazier levels.  The only ways to counter them are:
A) artillery, although Prussia has plenty of tools to deal with that (cheap 18th century pikemen, decent cavalry, their own artillery), or the better option,
B) attack Prussia in the 17th century and kill them before they can build up a strong economy and send a wall of blue-clad death your way.
Algeria is a very unique civilization.  They only get a few units, including 1 cavalry unit (Mameluks, which is cool) and no musketeers.  They also CANNOT ADVANCE TO THE 18TH CENTURY.  No 18th century buildings or upgrades or anything!  Algeria wins by rushing, and thankfully they do it very well.  Use massed archers to burn down buildings, spam cheap light infantry and decent Ottoman pikemen, have Mameluks to scout and raid, and just flood the field right off the bat.  It's a race against the clock as Algeria and you'll have some intense games with them.

When I first played this game, I was unsure of myself, of what I would see within. However, the game begins with a gripping story. The game tells of a renowned Harvard zooligist, presenting his findings to his superiors. He spoke of mystical stones which would grant horses special abilities. Not believing him, he was laughed out of his position. He then gives his findings to his son/daughter and gives them the tools necessary to become the very best trainer in all of Horseland.
The gameplay is particularly gripping, and brings you all of the things you loved from Dance Dance Revolution. Once your Horse-which you may have summoned from the ice planet of Hoth, the surface of the Sun, or the depths of hell itself- masters the fine art of dancing, he can compete in competitions with other, more boring horses. This part is the most gripping, and is particularly revolutionary for an indie game. The competitions involve watching a slider move across the screen very slowly, and require no input from the player. This moves beyond anything a video game has ever done, and transcends graphics. Instead of showing the player what happened, the player is allowed to explore the depths of his imagination. As the horses gallop across the finish line, the player knows he's made an amazing purchase.
This is a game that will live on for the rest of time; the creation of this game will be the one crowning achievement in all of humanity's history. Long after the human race is extinct, this game will drift through the cosmos, telling the story of the human condition.
In conclusion: 10/10. Would play again.

I had this program on my whishlist for quite some time and i couldn't resist when it came at a reduced price during the summer sale. I tested many solutions to produce 3d models out of photographs and 3DF Zephyr is the winner. It is fast, accurate, forgiving in regard to image quality and integrates very well with all my other 3d tools, be it Blender, Lightwave or 3d-Coat. The lite version availlable on Steam provides everything you need to get your objects into 3d, whereas the aerial and pro versions offer advanced functionality used in science, medicine or geography. One feature that i like in particular is the ability to extract frames out of video files. Though the lite version is limited to 200 images it is more than enough to achieve good results. You load a video file, set the frames per second to extract and 3DF Zephir picks the best images on its own. This also allows the reconstruction of aerial footage filmed with drones, for example. Tools for image quality analysis prior to reconstruction are provided. This saves you a lot of time. Masking is also provided. It allows you to tell 3DF Zephyr what parts of an image to consider during reconstrucion and what part of the image to ignore, i.e. the background. If you create a sequence of mask images in another application (black and white, like an alpha channel) and name those with a "_mask" or "_masked" suffix, 3DF Zephir automatically loads these images as masks.
To me, 3DF Zephir provides everything i need to get my objects into 3d space. It's easy to use, versatile and provides high quality results.

This game is aimed primarily at people who enjoy really intensely challenging, lightning speed beat-em-up combat and also really challenging precision platforming at the same time. You absolutely must enjoy both of those things or this game WILL increasingly♥♥♥♥♥♥you off as it goes on.
For me, I enjoy side-scrolling beat 'em ups and also enjoy platformers, but I am not the type of person who particularly enjoys intensely punishing difficulty in either one (maybe in a challenge mode, but not in the campaign). I picked up this game mainly because I had heard it had strong metroidvania elements, and I was very interested in exploring a mexi-metroid. The game started off super enjoyable and very much mexi-metroid, which I loved. But I started getting super frustrated at the game once I got to the Tule Tree, where the game first revealed its unwavering fetish for spamming dimension shift challenges in prolongued wall jumping segments. (If you think it will be over after the Tule Tree, you're wrong.)
I stuck with it, though. It was infuriating, and I cursed a lot, but I stuck with it for a long time. I was disappointed that the metroidvania elements increasingly dwindle away and the game becomes more and more intensely focused on infuriating cage match challenges and infuriating platforming challenges where you have to execute a specific sequence of jump extenders (while dimension shifting ever other step, naturally), and the game just turns these up more, and more, and more as you advance. I kept feeling the frustration rise higher and higher as I progressed, but I kept on going.
I made it all the way to Javier Jaguar. I'm now quitting forever, because seriously: F**K THAT. Talk about a sudden and maddeningly huge difficulty spike. (Especially considering that the previous boss battle, Flame Face, is incredibly easy.) There comes a point where one experiences furious anger more than joy with a game. Javier Jaguar is the deal breaker for me and Gaucamelee. But I won't say that makes it a bad game. It is a beautiful game that I think was just not made for me. I recommend it to those of you who enjoy a game that invites you into its house with promises of cake and candy, but instead just holds you down and punches you in the balls over and over again, laughing and shouting surprise, until you cry.

The Guac! Guacamelee is a loving homage to metroidvania crammed with gaming references (you can find a dead Journey pilgrim if you're attentive), lovingly named super moves (derp) and crisp combo based combat. Framed by vengeance seeking luchadors and the Mexican land of the dead, you'll kick the crap out of skeletons through several contiguous zones, acquiring stuff every half hour or so to keep it interesting. In the end your combo suit should build from TMNT 2 three hit strikes to a ten hit juggle that suplexes everyone in the room. The art style and controls are clear and crisp, this is a technically perfect swing at this kind of game. The soundtrack is inessential and its maybe just a touch short (I would have liked another hour or so at the denoument) but it will definitely scratch the platformer itch. For bonus challenge, play with my busted Dualshock which randomly inputs L1, resulting in transformation to a harmless chicken mid-chasm or during a brawl.

There are one or two exceptions but generally I don't play platformers. Guacamelee! is one of those games that if I saw a friend play I would say "Balls to that, it looks blummin' infuriating!".
And I'd be right. It is infuriating. Jumping from wall to wall, all the while shifting dimensions to ensure that the wall you are jumping to actually exists else you'll have to start the whole darn climb all over again! It is blummin' infuriating... but IT WILL NOT BEAT ME! I will keep playing this game until I have beaten it!!!
... and that I suppose is an endorsement... It is doing my head in but by Jove I shall carry on!
(I accept that it may be infuriating me as I am a bit rubbish - so if that's what you're thinking - yes, you may be right :) )

Thunder Wolves can be best described as "Mercenaries" (the shooter series) in helicopters (and sometimes, tanks). Basically you have a bunch of wisecracking mercenaries screaming "yahoo!" "oh yeah!" while you deal out plenty of destruction via your various weapons onboard your helo, from the MG to 3 types of missiles/rockets. Pick the chopper proper for the role, and sometimes, play a bit of "rail shooter" and other sequences.
The graphcis are quite good, "fast and furious" sort of way, plenty of muzzle flashes, ping / boing and other bullet sounds, but if you play on casual just go hide behind something for a while and you're okay to continue. The catch is... since you have infinite ammo, enemy does too, and there's bazillion of them and just one of you.
The game's usually played in a 3rd person perspective, and virtually requires a gamepad or joystick, as there are plenty of things to control, as you may want to fly one way and shoot another. Missiles varies from unguided rockets to seeking missiles (require lockon) to self-seeking missiles to TV guided missions (fly it into the target). The idea of course, is to cause as much damage as possible, and sometimes, plenty of collateral damage. (You get bonus points for big explosions and "streaks")
On the other hand, the game sometimes switch to "minigames" such as "rail shooter sequence" (game flies the chopper, you just control the machine gun), "sniper sequence" (snipe guards from way back out), drone sequence (take a FireScout drone into a tunnel and blast everything), and APC/tank sequence (it's on the ground instead of in the air) for certain segments of the game.
The helos are based on real ones, but obviously they all pretty much fly alike (albeit with different armaments), and they should have different flying characteristics, but you're probably too busy shooting to notice.
It's a pretty good game for mindless shooting fun, and it's a little deeper than it appears to be. Think someone took Choplifter HD and made a full 3D game out of it, with loudmouth mercenaries, and you got Thunder Wolves. It's not a "deep" game, not does it pretend to be.

Short, atmospheric and free puzzle-based game that should take about 20-30 min on average to finish as there are only one or two serious puzzles. I liked the look of this game considering it was free there didn't seem to be anything to lose.
UnfortunatelyI can't say I enjoyed the game. There's very little direction in what you're meant to do. No story or aim to what you're doing and movement feels very slow and drawn out (although I did eventually realise you can speed up a bit by holding shift to move).
The puzzles that the game offers have incredibly unintuitive solutions. I had to look up most of them in a guide created for this game and still can't understand the reasoning for the solutions.
If you're interested in the game, go ahead and try it, as it is free afterall, but I personally would not recommend this to anyone.

I love Cinemassacre and this game pays great homage to it, and has high enough production value to get a thumbs up. It's fun for a bit, but ultimately I was not a fan of how the game artificially increases the difficulty with death blocks. They do not test your natural gaming skills, instead they exist only to turn the entire game into maddening trial and error. I like to think I did well, making it to the final stage in under 4 hours, but it was never very enjoyable because of repeated sections of levels filled to the brim with anxiety inducing death block patterns. It isn't nearly as hard as some NES games like Battletoads, but it is equally stress inducing and only makes me remember why I hated games like that on the NES.

This is one of the best bullet-hell shmups on Steam, and is a really good one to play if you're new to the genre. It's set up like most arcade games (so once you lose all of your lives it's game over), but it's pulled off so well that it's hard not to get into that "just one more try" mindset. Compared to most other shmups there's a ton of content, so if you get tired of one mode you can try another mode or weapon to mix things up. It has 3 difficulty modes which provide a good level of challenge for both new and experienced players. There 8 "special weapons" to use which range from traditional weapons like lasers and cruise missiles to some more unique ones like force fields and a short range homing attack. The weapons all play differently, so you'll have to vary your routes depending on the weapon you pick.
One of my favorite features is the mission mode. This mode has short 1-2 minute challenges that help you learn the various stages and bosses. It's a good distraction from the main game, and once you can beat all the challenges then you'll be well on your way to beating the main game. The latest patch also adds an unlockable mode where you play with 3 new experimental weapon types as well, so all in all the amount of content you get is great for the price.

This game... is fantastic. Everything about it. I really don't know how to explain it. The music and art style are so entertaining on their own, it feels like I'm looking at more of an artwork than a game. The gameplay is simple, but some of the puzzles can be very tricky to solve. I would definitely say this was worth th $20 it cost, however if you are looking for a longer game with more content, this might not be what you're looking for. It took me about 6 and a half hours total to complete this game, and that was with every single acheivment unlocked. Other than that, this game is basically perfect. My only issue was the lack of information about the controls for the menus and things like that, as there were no words, just pictures. But that's more of an issue for me than with the game. I would definitely reccomend this to anyone who is looking for something different than anything else to play, it is a great game.

I've loved every Amanita game to date and Samorost 3 is no exception.
Yay for magic mushrooms! Yay for poppy pod dream spaceships!
Beautiful, deeply crafted mini worlds with no dialog or instructions. The play and story unfold solely with images and music. It takes far more skill to do this in a universally accessible way (and to me, a far more appealing method) than forcing an ill-fitting tutorial with badly done dialog into a poorly written base story.
You must find you own path. Piecing together the play, puzzles and charming underlying story as you go. Samorost 3 is a joy to slowly explore, listening to the inhabitants and music of each exquisite world, teasing out the path to the next. Then, going back and finding all the little things you missed the first time! Tons of achievement secrets and just for for fun interactions with flora, fauna - and fungus ♥!
If you find diffucluties there is a very creative hint system... Which even if you don't want to use it to initially solve the game, is worth looking at after. Just for the little window peek into the developement.

Thunder Wolves is a great game, newest update fixes the Xbox 360 controller issue that plagued the game before (Making it hardly playable). In my opinion the developer had a rocky start but is atleast trying to fix their games (As far as i've heared)
Back to the game, this is a great Arcade shooter. It's a very linear tho, but packed full of action. The Music in the game is a bit monotonous and that can be quite easy to spot if you have an ear for music. Alot of small jokes and good personallity between the pilot and the gunner ingame.
The game plays out mainly as you being the pilot of the helicopter, you can jink left and right, go up/down and turn in any direction. Alot of invisible walls in the game forces you to move in one direction tho (as said before). Mostly you gun down everything you see but sometimes you even have to protect something or winch up some cargo just like in the good old days of Desert/Jungle Strikes games.
Then we have the parts that play out like your everyday arcade shooter, where you take control of the nose/side gun of your helicopter and gun down everything you see while the AI pilots the helicopter.
Your helicopter comes equiped with a Machine Gun, often sometype of unguided Rockets, Guided rockets and one special weapon (Controlable missile, Airstrike et.c.)
Co-op is nothing to brag about tho. First, inevitably you have to compare RollerCoaster Tycoon World to Planet Coaster.  They are the same but different.  I bought this game in Early Access and it was on a good start, however, Planet Coaster snuck up and released before this game was done which pushed this game out before it was ready.
I recommend this game because the ride physics and mechanics for coasters is pretty intricate and gives the feel that if your coaster works here the design would work in real life.  They do the coaster aspect very well, in fact I like the realism with that in this game more than Planet Coaster.  Where the game feels like it was rushed out to "live" is that there's very little outside coasters in variety, more will likely be released in the months post-release but that's what reinforces the rush to release.  It's also missing elements that they included in Planet Coaster, even if its unpolished and a little clunky like water rides (log/rapids) which are missing from this game.
While people might recommend Planet Coaster over this game, it has its own short comings as a result of releasing before it was done too and some of the features (like ride analysis) were thrown on after seeing it in this gamee.  The end result is that they both do things well that the other doesn't and in the next 6 months both will be more comparable to one another and in the mean time they are both good for the differences mentioned.
Note: I own both and I am satisfied with both purchases for the main reasons above (coaster building in RCTW and log/rapid rides in PC).

PAYDAY: The Heist is a hardcore COOP first-person shooter where players take on the role of a professional crew of heisters looking to undertake their next big score.  Guided by the off-screen A.I voiced coordinator called Bain, players must complete objectives before securing the loot and escaping.    Settings including: robbing a bank, stealing diamonds from an office to extracting toxic blood from a hospital ICU, amongst others.
Gameplay occurs across alarmed, assault and sometimes stealth phases.  Security guards, thugs, mercenaries and every manner of law enforcement stand in the way of success.  A range of actions can be performed such as: reviving team-mates, exchanging hostages for captive players, shooting cameras, breaking through doors and using explosives (and more).  Players begin with basic weapons and equipment and level-up by completing objectives and missions.  The more cash stolen the faster they level, unlocking or upgrading weapons and equipment across four in-depth skill-trees.  Skill-based challenges give additional rewards for faster levelling.
Random events keep players on their toes, forcing them to adapt their plans.  On the hardest difficulties the pace of the game is intense, where mistakes are punished, usually leading to a wipe. The game is stat heavy recording every action, every win or defeat, even accuracy.  A.I. bots take the place of crew members if not enough players are in-game.
+ Great setting if you love anything about heist films like Heat.
+ Varied, detailed and robust heists, with detailed random events provides alot of replayability.
+ Requires highly skilled coop on harder difficulties.
+ Choose loadout from an extensive extensive range of assault weapons, sidearms, deployable munitions, specialist equipment and crew bonus modifier.
+ Reach level 193 across four specialist perks to unlock the full arsenal and equipment, and their upgrades.
+ Immersive soundtrack and voice-over interaction between characters.
+ Realistic enemy assault waves with the use of a combination of dynamic entry points, smoke grenades, snipers, tazers and shields and inflitrators to change-up player tactics.
+ Robust enemy A.I. behaviour  On the hardest level they are a real challenge for most players
+ DLC maps can be played by anyone as long as the host has the DLC.
+ All manner of enemy types to deal with including: security guards, thugs, police, various SWAT, FBI hostage extractors and specials; tazers, shields, cloakers and the tanky bulldozer.
+ Hundreds of skill-based challenges; x kills with weapon y, complete map z, collect $n... and much more!
- Could do with more than the nine (total) maps it has.
- Requires very good players to beat maps on harder difficulties.
- Learning the game mechanics on these harder levels is not a trivial exercise.
- Some achievements need a dedicated team of four players with good knowledge of the mechanics.
- A number of bugs exist with the interface and mechanics.
- During the day it can be a cheaters/hackers paradise.
- Game paused for players who join in-game.  Slows down play.
- Unstable netcode.  A fair amount of dropped connections.  Maybe 1/4 of games played.  Every one counts as a failed mission.  Either host or befriend players who are reliable hosts.
- Too many 'bad' players.  Some ragequit.  Especially bad if they are the host.
- Wolfpack DLC is required to level past level 145 and to obtain access to the technician skill-tree and associated weapons, munitions and equipment.
- No controller support.
- Game is now unsupported by the developers.
* Graphics are good enough but, if you're into AAA titles they may seem dated.
* Needs more weapons only includes: four different handguns, five different primary and four secondary weapons.  Well-rendered though.  The use of a turret or tripwire mines is fun.
* The A.I. for friendly bots are flawed but can at least revive players on their own.
Payday: The Heist is one of those rare games that actually keeps you playing past the point that it should have.  Before you know it you will have wracked up hundreds of plays, perfected your strategies to a tee and spent 200+ hours obtaining all the challenges the game has to offer.  If only it were that simple!
The game is very good and captures alot of the qualities that made Heat such a great film with some excellent gameplay mechanics.  The combination of alternative objectives, law enforcement numbers and behaviour during assaults, the variety of random events, the range of weapons, deployable munitions and equipment makes each play a different experience from the last.  With the hundreds of skill-based challenges it all combines to give the game greater replayability despite the limited number of maps.
Knowing the maps, what weapons to bring and to use against which enemies is paramount to becoming a good player.  The biggest challenge for new players is to understand all the nuances of the mechanics, to learn the appropriate counters and timing of events and actions, especially firing from cover.  Otherwise they may not get the most out of this game.  Players start at the lowest difficulty and level the four skill-tree and only move on when they have the appropriate equipment and weapon unlocks.  Indeed the game is very challenging on the hardest difficulty.  Possibly the hardest of any coop PvE game I have played and therefore among the most fulfilling when everything clicks.
Those aiming to complete the game's hardest difficulty will need to find a skilled group of players.  as completing them solo is virtually impossible.  At least for some maps. Lobbies almost always have a few cheaters/hackers who kill enemies without firing shot, or clear maps with one keystroke.  Getting hold of Dorentuz' excellent DorHud mod with its tools to weed out false players is vital.  Playing with inexperienced heisters can be just as maddening, especially if youre a stickler for stats.  Hosts can ragequit or giving you one less 'win' for that map.  You can get kicked by inexperienced players too.
If you can look past those faults there is a real gem of a game here.  It very rarely goes on sale, if ever and finding a good crew of skilled legtimate players can be hard at times.  Joining the Payday 5 Years group can help with this.  Though bear in mind only 100-200 players will be playing the game at any one time.  So organizing overkill and overkill+ games may take time to setup.  The facility for players to drop into games is archaic, sometimes pausing the game for a minute or two while their client syncs with the host.  If all of that doesnt put you off, then the aging graphics just may.
Payday: The Heist is not an easy package to unwrap.  It does have great depth and requires brains and skilled finesse to for the best experience.  Dont play the game like CoD or it will punish you.  If thats not enough to dissuade you or you want to try this before Payday 2, then its hard to point to another game that is as rewarding.  Just beware of  the lack of hand-holding.  Yet with persistence win the day.  Unfortunately I doubt you get this for a steal now.... as its only likley available at full-price.

- It should be nice to switch between 3D and 2D piece depictions during a game (e.g. 2D for thinking and 3D for capturing pieces, if desired)
- As many others, I don’t like the design of some character (knights look like other pieces, the rook is quite singular but please remove that ugly beer belly)

- I can run most recent games but I have to disable features (anti-aliasing and anisotropic filtering) on this game => optimization problems that should be fixed in future.
### Conclusion:

Game looks amazing at first blush for someone like me. I love historical combat, I love the Roman era. Slam dunk right?
Not so much, once you start peeling back the actual mechanics of the game you get pretty depressed at a wasted oppurtunity by the devs. Theres so many things that needed to obviously be addressed. Here are my top annoyances off the cuff.
-This is a game where the entire beginning level terrain is mostly constrictive mountain passes. to this end, unit pathfinding is atrocious. You tell them to move through a pass wide enough for one unit and they will always attempt to deploy into some kind of battle line as if they were in an open field, which they rarely are.
-the supply system is ♥♥♥♥ing byzantine. After reading tons of forums (the in game manual is useless) I sort of kinda figured out how it works. But you cannot see what the supply flow is, or how it is working. The game tells you "make a supply line!"  with no explanation of how or why supply flows, stops, reverses ect. These sorts of things are critical to know, even in the first tutorial mission or you will find your armies melting away with no undertstanding why. It is a very large part of the micro in the game to manage stockpile rates, supply lines, ect. These are NOT things that can be hand waved in the first mission.
-The alerts are♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. Once again you have long supply lines and you will be periodically raided in your rear. The only alert you get is a little drum beat that mixes into the drum beat filled soundtrack. So suddenly your armies are melting, you dont know why. You zoom out and realise your supply lines 200 km back are being raided for quite some time. Seriously?
Again. Very cool and interesting concept. But a lot of basic interface Dos and Donts that gam designers figured out 10 years ago are missing. In a lot of ways its like playing games from an earlier era where you were just dropped in and told 'good luck'.  Every once in awhile I come back, load up the game determined to give it another try bc I like the idea so much. I always walk away after 45 minutes or so, never making it past the first tutorial bc of how frustrating the actual mechanics are. I would stay away from this title. Other Hegemonies have better reviews, start there first.

This game seemed like it would be fun.  I bought it a couple of years back and just got around to playing it now.  Seems the game has been patched a lot since I bought it, so I had high hopes.  Within the first tutorial section of the game, crashed to desktop.  I didn't have a save, so I had to start over, no big deal.  This time I made sure I saved, and I was lucky I did too, had a couple of back to back CTD's about half an hour after the first crash.  Got a cannot read memory error, but I had just saved, so no loss, then the game crashed just after loading.  I was able to play for a while, but I got stuck with huge supply problems.  I looked up how to make a supply network, deleted all the old lines, built camps, bridges, and what not, re-did my supply network, had a huge boon in extra food, but none of which was getting to my armies on the front.  Also, raiders kept popping up where I didn't have a significant force, and the defenders there had no food, so low morale, and kept getting crushed.  Then the game crashed again, for the fourth time.  I considered starting over a game from the beginning, this time employing everything I learned in hopes of not having dreaded supply issues, but the game randomly crashes with cannot read memory errors.  So I just don't care.  I won't play it again.
Pros:
The game has decent graphics and design for what it is.  A real time grand strategy game covering Caesar's conquest of Gaul.  There is some diplomacy, but most of which feels scripted or pointless, though I haven't made it far enough because the game crashes.
Cons:
Crashes.  4 crashes in just a couple of hours.  Not a good pace for enjoyment.  Supply lines seem simple, but I had huge problems supplying my army even when I fixed my lines according to the guides I copied.  Probably needed to restart doing everything correctly to not have problems.  Combat is not fun.  Units are poorly animated, and the strategy just seems to be funnel large numbers of troops through small corridors and ram into a smaller force.  The game really didn't feel so tactical as it did stressful that the only units I had nearby to defeat raiders were zero morale, no food warriors that get crushed just as soon as look at someone.
In summary, crashes were the nail in the coffin.  I didn't have fun when the game was working, and I don't want to be patient with it to discover all the little cool things I may have missed.  I have a lot of other games I can play, and this one is not worth the time investment.  Stick to EU4.

This is copied and pasted from my reivew of Hegemony III, but the same applies to Rise of Caesar:
The entire Hegemony franchise -- starting with Philip of Macedon through Rome: Rise of Caesar to Clash of the Ancients -- is sadly underappreciated, and it's hard to understand why. These are outstanding strategy games. If you enjoy Total War (I for one do; TW Rome II *eventually* turned into an excellent game with extensive patching), you absolutley should give Hegemony a try. The tactical combat is obviously less involved than Total War, but the strategic side is arguably deeper, with emphasis on things like logistics, change of seasons etc. The seamless transition between the strategic 'panned out map' view and the tactical 'zoomed in' view is lovely, and something TW doesn't offer. Makes for very fluid gameplay.
The Hegemony games seem to go on sale pretty regularly, and even at the full $30 price ($20 in case of Rise of Caesar), they are *well* worth it (half the price of a AAA title, but in my opinion, every bit as polished than the big offerings of big studios). If you're interested in ancient world warfare. whether titles like AGEOD's Alea Jacta Est or CA's Total War Rome, do yourself a favor and take a chance on Hegemony. These are hidden gems of strategy gaming.

This game is a decent enough strategy game, with very solid and well implemented mechanics. However, its gameplay very rapidly becomes repetitive, especially in the grand campaign, and somehow it manages to make an absolutely massive map encompassing the entirety of France and some parts of Italy, England, and the Lowlands feel small and congested. The campaign also disappointingly doesn't go onto Caesar's civil war after he's done with Gaul, which would've made for far more worthwhile DLCs than a couple of unit packs.
The combat itself deserves a very specific mention as one of the few mechanical areas of this game that's actually bad. Legionaries break far too easily, and you can get crippling flank penalties from like two or three enemy troops bumping into the side of your formation.
Ultimately, I don't recommend this game unless it's on sale. It's certainly worth buying and playing, but not at full price.

Alright, First review (i think)
1 Moment of Time, Is a hidden object type game where you take on the role of a helpful soul out to help silentville with thier troubles, It has all the standard features of a find game, pointer, hints, Some humor, and lots of achievements, Let me rephrase that, Quite a lot of achievements for a point and click puzzle game. A couple of things to note however, This game is a little different then most puzzle games - there are more puzzle with-in puzzles then most hidden object games - Where other games have one or inside puzzle, puzzles, this game has 11+ So if you like puzzles, You'll fit right in here.
There are a couple of things to note however about this game - Not nessarily bad, just differnent, First Most of the item examples in it are from the other side of the pond, UK, and North American players might have troubles finding certain items. The second minor issue is that there are a few items that predate the player. World war 2 era can opener's for example. If i hadn't gone camping with scout's i would never had known it was a can opener.  Granted it is a minor thing if your playing on casual, however if your trying on expert (hard) mode, and are tying to finish the game with out hints, you may have to refer to the internet to look things up, Or at least asking mom and dad.
I'd like to mention at this point, as with all hidden object games, expect to clock up some miles going here and there to solve things
Some Cons
It's short. 3-4 hours on Expert. Probably shorter if your playing causal.  Granted the many, many achievments in the game will keep you going back if your dedicated to finishing them all.
There is an issue with trying to enter the store room with out fixing the door to exit the train-station. If you enter the store room, the game will crash on and off, just for that room. Oh btw, you don't need a screwdriver for the door to the trainstation, i went looking because how labour intensive this game is. Just a heads up.
There are minor issues with finding items just out of reach at the edges of the screen. Being able to minimize the search bar and/or drag or move the screen would have helped with this.
Sound and graphics are what you would expect with this type of title,
Would i reccoment this product? yes. It's a good example of hidden object games (i own many) I only wish it was a little longer. I didn't research the producer, so i don't know if this is thier first, or one of many hidden object games. regardless, It's only a couple of bucks in the steam store, (at least when i saw it) which is peanuts for an afternoon's entertainment.
