PAYDAY: The Heist is a hardcore COOP first-person shooter where players take on the role of a professional crew of heisters looking to undertake their next big score.  Guided by the off-screen A.I voiced coordinator called Bain, players must complete objectives before securing the loot and escaping.    Settings including: robbing a bank, stealing diamonds from an office to extracting toxic blood from a hospital ICU, amongst others.
Gameplay occurs across alarmed, assault and sometimes stealth phases.  Security guards, thugs, mercenaries and every manner of law enforcement stand in the way of success.  A range of actions can be performed such as: reviving team-mates, exchanging hostages for captive players, shooting cameras, breaking through doors and using explosives (and more).  Players begin with basic weapons and equipment and level-up by completing objectives and missions.  The more cash stolen the faster they level, unlocking or upgrading weapons and equipment across four in-depth skill-trees.  Skill-based challenges give additional rewards for faster levelling.
Random events keep players on their toes, forcing them to adapt their plans.  On the hardest difficulties the pace of the game is intense, where mistakes are punished, usually leading to a wipe. The game is stat heavy recording every action, every win or defeat, even accuracy.  A.I. bots take the place of crew members if not enough players are in-game.
+ Great setting if you love anything about heist films like Heat.
+ Varied, detailed and robust heists, with detailed random events provides alot of replayability.
+ Requires highly skilled coop on harder difficulties.
+ Choose loadout from an extensive extensive range of assault weapons, sidearms, deployable munitions, specialist equipment and crew bonus modifier.
+ Reach level 193 across four specialist perks to unlock the full arsenal and equipment, and their upgrades.
+ Immersive soundtrack and voice-over interaction between characters.
+ Realistic enemy assault waves with the use of a combination of dynamic entry points, smoke grenades, snipers, tazers and shields and inflitrators to change-up player tactics.
+ Robust enemy A.I. behaviour  On the hardest level they are a real challenge for most players
+ DLC maps can be played by anyone as long as the host has the DLC.
+ All manner of enemy types to deal with including: security guards, thugs, police, various SWAT, FBI hostage extractors and specials; tazers, shields, cloakers and the tanky bulldozer.
+ Hundreds of skill-based challenges; x kills with weapon y, complete map z, collect $n... and much more!
- Could do with more than the nine (total) maps it has.
- Requires very good players to beat maps on harder difficulties.
- Learning the game mechanics on these harder levels is not a trivial exercise.
- Some achievements need a dedicated team of four players with good knowledge of the mechanics.
- A number of bugs exist with the interface and mechanics.
- During the day it can be a cheaters/hackers paradise.
- Game paused for players who join in-game.  Slows down play.
- Unstable netcode.  A fair amount of dropped connections.  Maybe 1/4 of games played.  Every one counts as a failed mission.  Either host or befriend players who are reliable hosts.
- Too many 'bad' players.  Some ragequit.  Especially bad if they are the host.
- Wolfpack DLC is required to level past level 145 and to obtain access to the technician skill-tree and associated weapons, munitions and equipment.
- No controller support.
- Game is now unsupported by the developers.
* Graphics are good enough but, if you're into AAA titles they may seem dated.
* Needs more weapons only includes: four different handguns, five different primary and four secondary weapons.  Well-rendered though.  The use of a turret or tripwire mines is fun.
* The A.I. for friendly bots are flawed but can at least revive players on their own.
Payday: The Heist is one of those rare games that actually keeps you playing past the point that it should have.  Before you know it you will have wracked up hundreds of plays, perfected your strategies to a tee and spent 200+ hours obtaining all the challenges the game has to offer.  If only it were that simple!
The game is very good and captures alot of the qualities that made Heat such a great film with some excellent gameplay mechanics.  The combination of alternative objectives, law enforcement numbers and behaviour during assaults, the variety of random events, the range of weapons, deployable munitions and equipment makes each play a different experience from the last.  With the hundreds of skill-based challenges it all combines to give the game greater replayability despite the limited number of maps.
Knowing the maps, what weapons to bring and to use against which enemies is paramount to becoming a good player.  The biggest challenge for new players is to understand all the nuances of the mechanics, to learn the appropriate counters and timing of events and actions, especially firing from cover.  Otherwise they may not get the most out of this game.  Players start at the lowest difficulty and level the four skill-tree and only move on when they have the appropriate equipment and weapon unlocks.  Indeed the game is very challenging on the hardest difficulty.  Possibly the hardest of any coop PvE game I have played and therefore among the most fulfilling when everything clicks.
Those aiming to complete the game's hardest difficulty will need to find a skilled group of players.  as completing them solo is virtually impossible.  At least for some maps. Lobbies almost always have a few cheaters/hackers who kill enemies without firing shot, or clear maps with one keystroke.  Getting hold of Dorentuz' excellent DorHud mod with its tools to weed out false players is vital.  Playing with inexperienced heisters can be just as maddening, especially if youre a stickler for stats.  Hosts can ragequit or giving you one less 'win' for that map.  You can get kicked by inexperienced players too.
If you can look past those faults there is a real gem of a game here.  It very rarely goes on sale, if ever and finding a good crew of skilled legtimate players can be hard at times.  Joining the Payday 5 Years group can help with this.  Though bear in mind only 100-200 players will be playing the game at any one time.  So organizing overkill and overkill+ games may take time to setup.  The facility for players to drop into games is archaic, sometimes pausing the game for a minute or two while their client syncs with the host.  If all of that doesnt put you off, then the aging graphics just may.
Payday: The Heist is not an easy package to unwrap.  It does have great depth and requires brains and skilled finesse to for the best experience.  Dont play the game like CoD or it will punish you.  If thats not enough to dissuade you or you want to try this before Payday 2, then its hard to point to another game that is as rewarding.  Just beware of  the lack of hand-holding.  Yet with persistence win the day.  Unfortunately I doubt you get this for a steal now.... as its only likley available at full-price.

This game has great potential and I strongly encourage you to purchase it and support the developer. You don't see actual effort put into things all that much these days. And I'm glad to witness an exception now and again.
Battle Chess, at least for now, feels like a strictly newbie-oriented chess game. The emphasis is mostly put on model/animation variety. It sure does look pretty, animations flow well enough for the most part. Fully-animated tutorial gives you some basic ideas about the rules and history, as well as an actual impression that enthusiasm is strong with these ones. If the developers aim to keep adding new piece textures, boards, clash animations etc. this may one day become the best casual chess game on steam. Not that there's all that much of competition, but you get the idea. What I'd really like to see added to the game is two things - chess-puzzles and some reenactments of history's professional arena matches. Or at least the first one - easy enough to implement, serves a clear noob-friendly purpose, all that good stuff.
Some of the minuses I've encountered so far:
1) Music volume slider doesn't seem to be affecting anything. Sound FX, on the other hand, does.
2) Bishop's voiceover work in the tutorial sucks. A lot. Coincidently, it's also the shortest one of them all. Was it really so hard to get some old dude to do the role that you had to keep it short with what you got?
All in all - you'll get about what you'd expect. Once again, I strongly encourage you to support the developer - it sure is worth the money.

I've got a love-hate relationship with AVGN because I do actually enjoy the series on youtube, but I also kind of think he tries too hard to be funny and it seems a little forced. I do feel like he has a weird and almost legitimate affection for crappy games in the same way that I have for a handful of older games and certainly a lot of older ♥♥♥♥♥♥ movies. It's relatable, and his criticisms about game design are usually pretty valid even if they're surrounded by a bunch of diarrhea buffalo dump or whatever the hell he talks about half the time.
This game somewhat mimics those old games, and I feel like that affection for them shines through here as well. That is, this takes a lot of those ♥♥♥♥♥♥ old NES tropes (a lot of them seem to be pulled directly from the mega man series) and uses them, but there's also enough polish to the game and thoughtful design so that it's weirdly well put together. It's bizarre that someone would ever bother to go out of their way to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game but at the same time make it good and fun to play, but here we are.
I'm legitimately enjoying this, and I think it's because (i don't know how much hand AVGN had in designing it actually) he actually understands what makes a good game and what makes a bad game and manages to mesh the two together into a fun little trainwreck laden with profanity and absurd amounts of gore. On top of all that, there are tons and tons of references to the series scattered around, so if you have any sort of attachment to it, that tacks on another layer of enjoyment. You don't have to be a fan or have ever seen it to really appreciate it though, I don't think.

Samorost is a beautiful synergy between artwork, animation and music. Especially music and sound effects adds familiar but unknown element to the game which make you feel almost at home -it's hard to describe it's better to understand it when you "experience" it by yourself. As for the story it fits well to the eco-friendly-spiritual world of samorost. Like I was mention before the music plays the main part of the game and its story because all creatures seems to have something like "sound souls" and it's fun to discover them by your trumpet which you have to find out where it came from by first place. So the promise at the beginning is quite simple but it gets complicated later on. The artwork was done by Adolf Lachman the same man known from his previous work -"Machinarium" which is enough recommendation. The graphics is absolutely brilliant! I love his rendering technique and his attachment to details. My favourite stage is lava like stage with little black creatures in it. I wish it could be more stages like this one! The animations are superb aswell. They are puppeteer type of animation but with a lot of complexity and variations and with all funny sound fx attached on -they are joy to watch. As for the puzzles they seems to be very "sound" focused and abstract oriented but they are fairly solvable. I had several mind blocks (especially with flower genetics) but with hint system builded on it's always helpfull to move on without being frustrated. I have finished the game and after the credits you can still collect missed achivments -great idea! All in all it's a great p'n'c game you should definitely play by yourself!

Revision 2 of review:
Ok.  So with the new considerably lower price point of this game and the fact that it has not crashed on me since the most recent update, I am now changing my recommendation yet again back to a buy.  If you have a decent machine with decent memory this game should now be playable without too many problems and it can be fun.  It's not in the same league as Planet Coaster in terms of graphics, sound design or really anything else, but if you enjoy this type of game I do think it's worth a buy at this lower price.  The tutorial can be somewhat anoying, but does help walk you through the game basics, so you're not just thrown to the wolves to figure it out or watch youtube videos to get the necessary information.  Just recognize that it's probably not likely to see much in the way of updates in the future as the development team has really been assigned to other projects, such as the mobile apps.  It is interesting to see what happens when a company like Atari decides to do a game on the cheap with a lesser experienced developer.  (they in fact went through a couple of such developers on this game).  I believe that was what essentially doomed this game.  The developers just were not as capable as those working on Planet Coaster and it is evident that they also did not have the same passion for the game either.  Communication with players was also subpar.  I do have to say that the coaster builder is actually pretty good, though.  If you play this game and enjoy it (despite it's remaining problems) and have not yet purchased Planet Coaster, do so, you'll most likely love it.  Just view the amazing things people have done with it on youtube.
Revised review:
A while back I gave this game a thumbs up, even though it had problems because I really was enjoying playing it and it had more content than the competitor, which I also have been playing since Alpha.  They had been fixing crashes and I presumed that crashes would become rare.  Unfortunately, although they have continued to add content to this game, they still have not fixed the crashes.  The last two updates had almost no crash fixes or optimization improvements - only added scenery.  Many times I have worked on a park only to have the game crash and lose all that I had done.  Today I started a new scenario in the story mode (ironcically called Crash Course) and when modifying the initial coaster the scenario starts with the game crashed several times.  Sadly, and reluctantly I can no longer recommend this game and have changed my review to a thumbs down.  The competitor's game (PlanetCoaster) never crashes on me, is better looking, offers more in terms of management now, has a much better path system and has added quite a bit more content over the past few months (plus has over 100,000 workshop items!)  PC also has another free big update coming next week and they are very responsive to player requests and concerns.
ORIGINAL REVIEW
Been playing since alpha.  It's been improved dramatically.  Hadn't played it much since the full release, but decided to play it some more to see if it really deserved all the bad reviews.  I actually had fun playing it.  It has quite a bit of content (which is something currently lacking in PanetCoaster, which I also have had since alpha.)  At the price it is currently at ($35) or less I do think it's worth a buy if you enjoy this type of game.  If you really enjoy BUILDING things in fine detail, get PC, it's beautiful to look at and better optimized.  But if you enjoy laying out a park and plopping prebuild stuff and scenery, this is a pretty decent game.  The coaster builder is actually better in this game than in PC and you're sure to get a good laugh from the animation of the peeps (some are pretty ridiculous, even though they've been improved greatly from early access).  Note: if you want to build bigger parks with many rides you will really need at least 16 gigs of ram.

PROS:
+Mission variety
+Simple and solid gameplay mechanics.
+Powerful weapons make it fun to blow things up (cool destruction effects).
+Decent visuals/graphics for a budget title!
+Cool metal soundtrack!
CONS:
-Bland and forgettable story.
-Not very challenging.
-Short campaign mode with little replayability.
OVERALL:
I'd say to get this game only if that's your sort of thing... but you might want to wait for a deal too! 15$ for a 3 hours game is steep in my book!

Guacamelee! is a platformer beat-em-up dimension-swap type game, taking place somewhere in Mexico. Your game starst out in the house of Juan, a peaceful farmer, and get called into your village by the priest, who informs you your childhood friend/love interest has arrived for a festival. You go to help her pick up chairs or something, but find out Carlos Calaca and his henchmen have taken her for whatever they need her for. You try to put up a fight but he kills you. Finding yourself in the land of the dead, you discover a lochador mask and put it on, returning to the normal world with the newfound power of the luchador, ready to save your girlfriend by fighting skeletons, swapping dimensions, and learning new tricks from a... goat... thing.
The gameplay is very fun, and although it is a platformer with lots of puzzles, it also smoothly incorporates combat within that. Dimension swapping is the main puzzle of the game, and since both worlds have different walls, blocks, and enemies, you will swap between the two frequently. I do have to say that I consider myself a veteran platformer gamer and I found some optional portions of the game incredibly aggravating, to the point where I had to quit playing and take a break. It's very rhythmic because of the dimension swap, and often takes several times to do it correctly.
The art is fantastic. The cartoon-y simple characters look very good, and the enemies are excellent as well. I also liked the art within the game. Several billlboards are in the larger towns and are full of video game references, which I thought was cool.
The music can get repetitive, especially if you are stuck on one part. It does have two different versions of the same song for different dimensions however, which I liked.
The story itself is somewhat lacking, but what they do have is pretty good. It's not really about the story, and I wasn't following the events, but they had a bit of dialogue and I understood what was going on.
Overall, I'd give the game a 9/10. It's a good challenge for anyone who wants to try, and is one of those games that is very fun to try and "complete".
If you think that pressing 10 buttons to perform a jump is funny, buy this game. Veny nice graphics, style, references to other games, but the gameplay is pretty broken.

Guacamelee is gorgeous and fun metroidvania game. Reminds me somewhat of Outland, with the switching between light and dark worlds, but Guacamelee has less of the bullet hell and more of the titular melee action. I'm not a huge fan of backtracking, but the world is laid out so smartly that even as it expands, your accumulating powers allow you to traverse the world more and more rapidly. Combat is challenging, but fair. Cetain fight setups felt cheap and unfair on first attempt, but after some careful observation and thought (and a few deaths), they were actually quite reasonable. Checkpoints are relatively generous, and placed in all the spots you'd want them. The boss fight thankfully actually uses the same skills honed during the rest of the game, rather than throwing in something out of left field. All in all, a total pleasure.

I have a ton of Steam games in my inventory. It's over 100. Yes I'm fully aware that this is actually quite small in comparison to other libraries, but I have enough that I don't want to buy any more right now. So what I've decided to do is complete every single game to the extent that I see fit, then uninstall it and shunt it into a deep, dark category in my library. This game is in said category. So far, it's the only one for which I've thought "I want to play this again."
This game is awesome. You're a luchador whose movement is heavily influenced by his special moves. The game has such a great, unique style that is very refreshing. I guarantee you that, after you devour the game, you will want to play again. It's just that good!
The atmosphere is excellent. Each area, in both spiritual planes, is portrayed so excellently. The music is intense, fits perfectly, and is composed very well. The game has an interesting take on the Mexican view of the world of the dead, and does it in a very respectful way. Like, holy crap. This game does an excellent job at making you feel like you're in the game.
The characters are good, even though there aren't that many. Each of the four bosses you fight are drawn out very well, and that one goat is quite funny. Indeed, this game is so incredibly light-hearted, with lots of references in Santa Luchita, and many instances where you will end up laughing out loud.
There's very little story to speak of, but that's not the main focus of this game.
Finally, the combat system is absolutely perfect. It is well executed, and the progression of your abilities is just right. Your fighting moves augment your movement (and hence your combat), and the developers have taken direct advantage of this fact to expand this game as far as they can. You wouldn't expect much platforming in a game primarily about fighting, but it's in here, and it's good.
Buy this game.

Well, after some thought, this game was pretty good, all things considered. What with the lack of Mexican characters that aren't a joke/generally pointless in most of the things I've seen, I was expecting the game to be dumb as all hell. It's nice to be proven wrong over these kinds of things; any of the stereotypes attributed to Mexicans present in the game are harmless and I'd be a hard sell for anyone to tell me almost anything in the game is racist or just plain stupid. (Before anyone brings it to my attention, if you're the kind of person who gets bent out of shape by dumb internet jokes instead of just ignoring them or, god forbid, laughing at them, then damn son, that's real sad.) The general feel of the first town, Pueblucho, reminds me of my mother's hometown, Zinapécuaro, while the bigger town, Santa Luchita, reminds me of the current home of a lot of my cousins, Morelia. It's all colorful and♥♥♥♥♥♥ which is excellent because that's what a lot of buildings are like when you hit the right towns.
The actual gameplay is tight and flows decently. You've got your standard 3-hit combo, your tosses (and special throws), and moves meant to keep the combo going or catch up to a distant enemy. The fact that you can dodge-cancel in this game to quickly recover and continue your attacks is good and I wish a couple more games would do this. The special moves are also good because the game's layout makes you think about how to get across the many obstacles you'll run into. You eventually learn things such as a double jump to make both combat and platforming easier, as well as possible in certain situations. The color-coded armor-breaking system was alright, but the any-hit, layered shields were a bit annoying to work against due to how fast they regenerated. I would never call the system impossible to work with as long as you actually paid some damn attention to the tutorial and practiced for more than five minutes.
The chests are all spaced out and placed in locations that will test your skills. I did enjoy that collecting enough chests filled with money would allow you to buy all the upgrades you needed, in case combos in this game were not your strong point (for whatever reason). Some of the energy and health pick-ups were the most fun I've had in a 2D platformer in a long time. The pieces of the mask (which were given to you by orbs) are the most challenging items to shoot for in this game, or at least the ones that required you to master the platforming sections. Basically, the secrets in this game are great and were placed where they needed to be without being such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to hunt for.
The music is amazing and makes me pretty damn happy while playing. The differences between the Living World tracks and the Dead World tracks match the appropriate World. The Living World tracks are, well, lively and active, they make you feel festive and want to do things. The Dead World tracks are a bit moody, but you can feel the spirit of excitement that was once there (or still is there, I guess, since you ARE there). The celebratory yells that occur during some tracks are good additions and make them feel more fitting.
The art is damn beautiful and colorful, even the Dead World sections. While I don't really care much for the flashing sections of art (I'm not at risk, they're just kind of whatever), everything else is good. Every enemy has a clear silhouette and is hard to lose track of, even when they're in the opposite world. Every attack you do gives off this energy and power that such moves would generate, like you're a super-hero (though some could argue you pretty much are). The only complaint I would give is there was one attack by a flying enemy (the name escapes me atm) that would spit fire-like projectiles at you, but you could dodge through them just fine, while another enemy with a large hammer can strike you and it's not immediately obvious that the red flow of energy around the hammer when it falls is actually fire. Other than that, it all makes sense.
In short, this game is good and if I had the cash on hand to go for the upgraded re-release, I would do so, even at full price.

(Oh boy...here come the thumbs down, but remember.  This review is based on my perspective and the "rating" system is about whether the review is HELPFUL or not)
I hesitated playing this game for a little while and I guess that feeling was right.  To be perfectly honest, I did not enjoy it for the most part.  (And thanks to people who reviewed this giving out spoilers WITHOUT SPOILER TAGS, that didn't exactly help)
You play as Mark, someone who is upset about a memory he's trying to forget.  A memory of a girl from his past.  3 years later, someone named Myra looks just like the girl from 3 years ago.  She stalks Mark throughout most of the game while Mark keeps trying to focus on a girl he actually cares about, his classmate Lillian.  There's various nonsense involving the little sister and the otaku classmate, but they're pretty unimportant save for comic relief...if you can call it that.
Personally, I found myself relating with Mark in the beginning, but halfway through the first chapter, all similarities were instantly gone.
The game's music choices are pretty nice, though I do have a complaint about the Little Sister theme that just....sounds like someone mashing his/her face on a keyboard.  There are a lot of pop culture references involving Fate Stay Night, Fire Emblem, Code Geass, 300, Touhou, Dokuro-chan, and various other sources (mostly anime I'm unfamiliar with but have heard the references to before).  There also seems to be Walfas artwork here when things aren't serious and are essentially a waste of time.  These references essentially drown you when the plot vanishes into the aether.
If you want to get into tropes (like a similar review talks about), then here are the roles (Spoilers included):
Mark:  The faceless protagonist.  Has a little sister, a nerdy best friend, and a girl he has a crush on.  He's the guy that is essentially the amnesiac who suffers glimpses of a memory that scarred him.
(SPOILER:
)
Rin:  The "Onee-chan" (Man, that irritates me) obsessed girl who....well....more or less is just a bothersome waste of time.
Lukas:  The nerdy best friend (Otacon?) who is...kinda' the definition of an Otaku.
(SPOILER:
Lillian:  The shy nerdy librarian (Maria from Harvest Moon?) ......umm....not much to really know about her.
(SPOILER:  As if people haven't spoiled it enough....
)
Myra:  The mysterious stalker who doesn't like to talk about herself and enjoys wasting your time.
(SPOILER:
)
PROS:
Most of the music is nicely chosen
The ending is great
Free
Achievements
CONS:
Useless side-story tangents
Nonsensical humor that just isn't funny
Little Sister's theme was a horrible choice for a song of any kind
Non-CG artwork of characters does feel off (It's better than what I can do, but still...)
Now I will say that I felt myself tearing up in the end.  It was a very nice ending.   But would I say it was worth it?  Would I sit through all the nonsense I had to deal with to see the ending again?   No.   In my opinion, Days 1, 6, and 7 were the only ones that did not feel like a complete waste of time.   If Days 2-5 were cut out entirely, I feel like this game would have been MUCH better than what it was.
Now, I'm not rating this down because it took me 9 hours to read it (Use that as a benchmark for your own experience).  I'm rating this down because I found myself groaning throughout more than half of this visual novel.  I know people liked Myra and I feel she did redeem herself in the end, but on Days 2-5, I wanted to strangle her so badly because of her stalker-ish behaviors and her choosing to be vague about herself.  Now if she was more like how she was on the final day, I would say I'd like her a lot more...sadly, I can't get past how creepy she was before she finally got serious.
Again, this took me 9 hours to read and for most of it, and I regretted it.  I respect this team for their efforts in this title, but there were many terrible choices with the portrait art (non-CG) and the writing.  Days 1, 6, 7, were good.  Days 2-5 were terrible.  (Days I'd choose to re-read or skip if I had to do it again)
4/10  Most of the story was a waste of time.  Read at your own risk.  (Without that ending, 2/10 easy)

The imagery and turn of phrases used is very much right up there with that of English novelists - I'm extremely surprised that this VN is totally free. A real clever sense of humour in many of the scenes from dry wit, to the less subtle slapstick and references to many games or other VNs raising many chuckles or little smiles and a cast of characters that you can't help but grow to like; being a lot longer than most free VNs (and even many that aren't!) you get a decent amount of time to bond with them too.
Oh, and as the strawberry on top of the sweet-creamy-and-delicious sundae there's a lovely original vocal track that plays over the end credits. That also happens to be un-extracted as an MP3 in the Game folder for you to listen to whenever you wish. Isn't that nice of them?

The game can't be compared to Planet Coaster.
It's lacking in so many fundamental ways, and it seems that is in it's core, which will never change.
It's a mobile game at best.
That may be satisfactory for many people though.
It has not brought much new to the table, and it even lacks quite a few things from RCT's past.
The coaster builder has it's merits, and it's flaws.
The sound design is terrible.
Coasters sound like metal carts rolling down an empty marble floored hallway, with little to no nuance in regards to to the action. They sound the same on an air-time hill, as they do at the bottom of a fast, high-G trough.
The paths....they dictate what you can do most of the time. You'll run into "no, not there" more often than not.
Many of the ride animations are incorrect, if you are a fan of authenticity.
Many of the rides are just ugly as well. Take the radioctive, glowing in the daytime "Wave Swinger" for instance. Boy is that an atrocity to behold!
The newly "re-designed" peeps are still terrible. The animations are just bizarre.
RCT 2 introduced peeps in pairs, and RCT3 introduced Groups. RCTW decided they should go back to the begining, and only have single peeps. Unsupervised children, no less.
The peeps will wander around aimlessly through your park, and ignore the very things they are looking for.
You have no clue how to satisfy them. The emoticons (REALLY?) floating over their heads are there to help, because the peeps are emotionless.

Old school top down shooter with some clever new ideas. Control ship speed to control the range of your shots/bombs, interesting level completion benchmarks, unique upgrade path system, etc.
It begins relatively simple, but I very quickly began to see the complex interactions between the different weapons on the ships, and how difficult they can make your life. My only complaint is that on a rare occasion I would be pushed to the edge of the map and pinned there, which isn't much fun in a game that is otherwise about non stop shooting action. But, each level is hand crafted in a way that forced me to approach it with a fresh strategy, and that kept me coming back for more punishment.
Overall it's a good challenge with some fresh mechanics, well worth the price of admission.

Fan of AVGN? Want to see all of the things the Nerd has ranted about brought to life in a game? This is it.

Here's what it boils down to: if you enjoy the challenge and frustration/reward ratio of classic NES titles, you will probably enjoy this game. If you don't, you absolutely, positively will not enjoy this game. And if you've never played an NES game, or at the very least never played one of the first three Mega Man games... well, "I" can't "recommend" piracy, but you should probably try playing some of that.
The reason for this is that this game borrows a lot from the original Mega Man games. And Metroid and Castlevania and there's a little Ninja Gaiden in there and... well... look; basically this game is a pastiche of the best of the NES. And I've definitely seen criticism of AVGNA because it's 'using elements from games the Nerd reviewed' or something. Let me be frank. At least I can *beat* this game. Out of the 30+ NES games I own, I've completed less than a third. This game is a CAKEWALK comparatively speaking. You want impossibly difficult? Go sit down with Monster Party for a couple hours. I guarantee you'll be looking at this game differently.
This isn't to say that the game is easy. A term I hear thrown around a lot among nostalgic and retro gamers is "NES hard". Which is to say that games from that time period, as I've said before, tended to be highly aggravating in difficulty. However, there's just no feeling of satisfaction quite like finally managing to beat an area of a classic game you've been struggling with for hours. It's honestly a bit difficult to explain what makes it different from most modern games, but I think it has to do with how cinematic current games are. Even if you struggle with a section for hours, you've primarily done it to progress a story. 'NES hard' means it's just you and the game. If there's a story, it's bare bones at best. You struggle over every obstacle just to be able to say you did. Current gaming is generally like watching a movie. Retro gaming, at least in the 80's, was more like climbing a mountain- there's nothing up there and there's no logical reason to do it, but ♥♥♥♥ it- YOU DID IT.
Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is one of the only modern games I've played that has managed to capture that feeling, albeit to a somewhat lesser degree. Like I said, the game isnt' as hard as some classic titles. And as much as I like James's work, the presence of all the reference jokes can be somewhat distracting. The soundtrack is pretty solid. I don't think it's something I'd listen to in my free time, but it works pretty well and it sounds nice.
Basically, if you're waffling, refer to my first paragraph. But for me, I recommend it.

This is a fun 2D side scroller, but I'd likely suggest picking it up only if you're a fan of the AVGN series or a fan of really hard 2D side scrollers.  There are a total of nine levels and you can play through the first eight in any order you like; completing those will unlock the final ninth level.  With multiple checkpoints throughout each level, there's a decent amount of challenge to be had in getting through the game.
One thing to note here is that if you play the game on any difficulty above easy, you're going to be subject to a life system.  So if you're playing through a level and run out of lives, you have to start back at the very beginning of that level, regardless of the latest checkpoint you got.  This almost made me give up on the game, as the very last stage got to be a bit too challenging for me on normal difficulty with a finite amount of lives to work with.  If you want to change the difficulty, you pretty much have to start over and complete each level again.
I ended up beating the first eight levels on normal difficulty, which I thought was a fair challenge, but like I said, the final level was hard enough to make me drop down to easy.  Unfortunately, that meant replaying through the previous eight levels again, although they were much easier to maneuver through on a second run.  The final level was still a challenge, but well worth getting to the end.
At the end of the day, if you're familiar with AVGN and the various characters that have appeared in the game, there's plenty of references and funny material to get you through to the end, as well as some really great music and the option to purchase the soundtrack separately.  I do think some of the frustrations in a few areas of the game take the joke of this being a hard game a bit too far, but then again, that's kind of the point - this is supposed to be a very challenging side scroller reminiscent of past generations of video games.

Let's get something out of the way real quick.  First, this game is indie as heck.  The dev team apparently isn't that large and it's pretty much an ongoing project even after release.  More on that last bit later.
Still, all of that means that there's an element of jank.  Mostly in the melee combat.  But it's nothing that the devs can't fix with a patch or two.  Second, I typically don't do reviews.  And when I do I typically am not entirely serious about the contents of them.  I'm breaking my habit because this game is that worth it if you're the sort that like modern nautical games that place you in the role of a captain.
So, Man o' War.  Think Sid Mier's Pirates open world game play meets Mount and Blade's dynamic warfare and ever changing map meets Assassin's Creed:  Black Flag's nautical combat only with more complexity to it.  Then add Warhammer's trademark bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane setting and an ever increasing number of new content drops as the devs just. keep.  churning.  out.  more. features.
Seriously.  It's insane.  Most modern devs would have made you pay an arm and a leg for what's been given post release.
We're talking wholesale expansion pack level features like being able to join nations each with their own playstyles and traits.  The ability to play in three to four new/different campaign types each with their own unique feature sets.  A constant slew of new quests and updated "infrastructure" features like a battle mode that lets you design -massive- nautical battles between the races (all of which have their own ships with armaments and feature sets you'd see literally in no other game.  The Skaven weaponized a frigging -bell-, for instance.).  And generally just all sorts of effort laden stuff that you wouldn't see anywhere else on Steam in a game that had been released.
That being said, there are downsides.  The melee combat is floaty, hard to control, slow motion trash and is essentially focused around group combat.  Except the crew sizes are so low on all but the largest ships that group combat ends up boiling down to which side can gang up on a smaller number of troops seperated from the group.  In the very late game this can change as your men have guns, but even then this is only for the default human campaign.  This is something i've seen get looked at by the devs in the past, however.  And given the current crop of complaints i'd venture that it'll probably be fixed in the future.
Ultimately however this is a minor quibble given the developer's past track record in handling this game.  So i'm giving this a thumbs up and a recommendation that you try it out if you're interested in open world pirate games.  While it's not perfect the developer's continuing efforts to update it past release instead of abandoning it with only a few perfunctory patches, coupled with the "Mount and Blade meets Sid Mier's:  Pirates" gameplay, means that this is a must have gem to pick up.   Provided they keep the updates coming, of course.

Excellent concept, huge potential, still feels like it's in beta however.
Melee combat is definitely the weakest point in the game still.  There has been improvements since it left early access, however it still feels awful.  Everyone moves as if they're underwater, combat feels sluggish and unresponsive.  Getting in good hits doesn't feel skill-based, it's all about flanking and scoring free cheap shots.  Stamina drains fast and recovers extremely slowly, making every boarding very quickly feel even slower than it already is at best.
Ship to ship combat isn't terrible, but can feel a bit unfair if the wind isn't in your favour.  Guns don't do a particularly large amount of damage, so cannon fights are mostly about attrition, whoever has the most armour and most guns wins.
Quests can be buggy, I've seen quests called "Error", and I've seen some quests that I thought finished hang around until I dismiss and abandon the quest.  You can gain favour with factions, however the process is incredibly slow and quite a grind.
Upgrading your ship over time is enjoyable, expanding this area would be good, plus seeing more visual feedback would be good.  Expanding the crew upgrading system would be good, including things such as new armours and a greater variety of crew types.  Levelling up crew is limited to "better at melee", or "better at repairs".  Nothing really interesting or anything that would make you feel even remotely attached to any crew member.  Considering how disposable crew are, upgrading their weapons individually is also a bit of a slog.
Overall a lot of parts of the game feel half-finished.  They're still updating the game, potentially in the future this game could be great, but for now it really feels like a budgetware title.

First Impressions Video: (WARNING, video contains spoilers to the intro)
Samorost 3 is awsome. It's a chill point and click adventure game about a tiny man in a white onesie as he plays with his new (and super jazztastic) horn. You travel through the vibrant and, quite frankly, gorgeous world solving puzzles and saving the world.
the first thing that hits you about this game is its art. The game is absolutely gorgeous. The fantastical aesthetic makes for a living world and each individual area builds its own personality out of the backgrounds. There's not much to say but that this game is one of the best looking games I've ever seen (especially the onesie. It's the best).
In terms of gameplay, you're going to find that the game consists mostly of environmental puzzles with a few key items that can be pickd up and used. In other words, it's no Lucas Arts game where your inventory fills up. It tends more towards the Myst style, where you alter the environment to progress.
Samorost 3 excells in letting the player discover the game. From the beginning, you know nothing about the tiny dude sporting a onesie and a horn except that he is very inquisitive (and a master jazz musician). Then, the game relys of the players own inquisitive nature to find the path forward. In other words, tiny dude's got good game design.
And this is only scratching the surface. Samorost 3 also has amazing music and some really interesting puzzles. The first puzzle that I came across (the card game) was unique and truly a breath of fresh air after so many repetitive puzzle games. The puzzles also continued to be quite fun from then on.
I cannot recommend this game enough. Between it's beautiful art, chill aestethic, and some truly novel puzzles, Samorost 3 truly deserves the onesie that it contains. Because it is just so stylin'.

"Overwhelmingly" yes

+ atmospheric, both in visuals, music and sounds
+ many things to discover, but not too many to be a hassle

+ the built-in hint system feels the integral part of the game, no need for Alt+Tabbing to lose the immersion
- some puzzles may be too "puzzling", therefore it is not a child's game
My family is a fan of Amanita Design, it is great to see that they keep up the creative spirit of Botanicula and Machinarium.
I recommend to buy this even at full price, it is a 7-8 hour long game (more if you spend your time just looking at the environment and different animals and creatures).

The game is simply enchanting. The high-definition environments are mesmerizing and I was very impressed how the creators integrated music into their puzzles. The result is an artistic harmony that somehow still manages to be a step up from its famous predecessors Machinarium and Botanicula.
The game element is very decent, too. Expect playful exploration-oriented puzzles that fit very well in the environment. The scope of the game is quite impressive with five major worlds and several other smaller locations, each original and polished with an amazing sense for detail.
Basically, this is what you get when you let a group of incredibly talented artists work for a couple of years without pressure from above, which is a dream for any game developer as much as a dream for the player. I cannot recommend this game enough.

One of the best shmups one Steam, up there with the likes of Ikaruga, Mushihimesama, and Crimzon Clover.
Great for beginners too. Most bullet hells make the mistake of making their easy mode far too easy to actually prepare players for the rest of the game(or genre for that matter). This one does not. There's also a bunch of missions that have you completing individual stages/bosses under certain requirements that help players learn the game.
The scoring mechanics are easy to learn and not punishing. With the extra lives you get from a good score, good scoring is essential to survival too. This forces some depth on a game that would otherwise just be about dodging and shooting when players aren't aiming for the highest score.

Oldschool arcade style shooter. Although I doubt these in-game graphics would've been up to the standard of the major arcade game companies of the day. The game uses an unusual abstract style where many of the enemies appear to be rather box like, although some resemble things like aircraft or tanks. Although I suppose there's nothing really wrong with them it's kinda hard to get exited about killing a box.
Aside from that, the manga style cutscene and background graphics are excellent. And there's a few backgrounds, music remixes and player skins to be unlocked, as well as "Free Play" mode, which allows you to continue after losing all your lives.  This last one is the only one that affects gameplay in any way, and the only one I felt particularly exited about unlocking.
Variable difficulty adjusts itself to the players performance, with three basic modes to keep the difficulty within a certain range. Although I find I tend to get about as far through on the medium setting as I do on the lower setting, only my score is much higher.
No weapon upgrades, although there is a choice of weapons at the start, suiting a variety of play styles. And three kinds of in game weaponry. There is a primary weapon, with unlimited power, which can be fired in rapid or concentrated mode. A secondary weapon which uses up power, each of the two characters has three to choose from with a variety of effects. I usually go for the most powerful one. The power of the secondary weapon is multiplied when you kill lots of enemies in quick succession. And finally a bomb/shield/energy drop, which will auto-activate if you get hit on the easiest setting, saving your life, but costing you all your bombs which you were saving for the boss.
Overall I'd have to say this is a fun, challenging (I've only made it to level 4/5 on normal) game.

An interesting short game with sound-based puzzles, in which you control a small robot looking for answers. That's as far as the story description for this game goes, but I must say the devs did a good job in creating an intriguing atmosphere for their game, story included. After all, this game doesn't have dialogue (unless you take into account the few garbled radio signals you encounter of someone speaking), but it does leave you wondering what's happened. Why is this robot looking for radio waves? What is it looking for? What happened to the people who built it?
Now, the gameplay is somewhat simple: it plays like a platformer, with some sound-based puzzles here and there. It is an interesting mechanic, and I can't recall many games doing something like it (there are a few, but it's nothing that you see in many games); I'd say it's good for training your hearing, if that makes sense.
Well, in short, I recommend this game.

This game is possibly the worst thing ever made by a human.  If you have received a copy of it as a gag gift (like I did), be advised that the trading cards are going for about a quarter each at the time of this writing, so it's worth running it in the background.  I took a shot at playing it just for curiosity's sake and will summarize the experience here so that you don't need to do the same.
Like most games about raising animals, it's basically a social/FB game minus the social aspect.  You have a magic horse, you level up the horse by alternating between feeding it and running it through a DDR obstacle course, then you make money with your leveled-up horse by sending it off to a race and waiting for five minutes for it to come back, you make some craftables with random drops that your horse got while you were waiting for it to come back, then you buy more horses and repeat.  I didn't get as far as the "buy more horses" part but I feel like I got the gist.
So it'd be terrible enough on the strength of being a Facebook game that you have to pay $5 for, but the implementation isn't even good.  There are loading screens when you go between single-room "buildings", and the feedback in the UI is terrible -- just as an example, the game doesn't tell you when you've done enough obstacle course grinding to max out your horse, so you might be grinding and not even actually progressing, thus defeating the entire purpose of the grinding, and this game is ALL about grinding.
I would not recommend this game to the general public.  I might recommend it to somebody with an unnatural love of horses who is soothed by repetitive tasks.

I heard this was Metroidvania, so I gave it a try, and found it SURPRISINGLY AMAZING. It has beat'em up combat that rewards you for keeping enemies in the air with super long combos, and the controls are easy to use and the combat is lots of fun. The level design is reminiscent of the levels in Mark of the Ninja, with shortcuts and extra areas added that become usable when you unlock special powers.
I found the game to be hilarious. It features liberal abuse of stereotypes and cliches of "Old Mexico", and lots references to video games (especially indie games, though obvious Mario and Metroid references feature prominently). You play as a regular dude, made into a powerful Luchadore with a mystical mask, and skeletons are invading the land of the living on Día de Muertos, and the plot basically becomes:
EL PRESIDENTE'S DAUGHTER IS KIDNAPPED! ARE YOU A BAD ENOUGH DUDE TO SAVE EL PRESIDENTE'S DAUGHTER?
There's a bit more to it than that, I guess, with chicken transformations and a goat-man and stuff... but the details are unimportant.
The game has a very generous save/respawn system, restarting boss battles instantly upon player death, which is nice. It does make the platforming sections of the game trivially easy, since if you miss a single jump, you instantly respawn back onto the last platform you were standing on (and the jumps aren't even difficult). None of the game felt frustrating or too repetitive to me (the first beat'em up I can say that about; I gave up on Shank a few levels in, for example). That said, I only got the "bad" ending at the end of the game, and I heard that the extra levels required to get the "good" ending are rather challenging.
If you like Metroidvanias, you should play this one. It's awesome.

Unfortunately, this game is nowhere near finished. The graphics are good, the coaster cam is good and it's fun to build a park.
BUT: on the managment side, everything is missing!
For example: you can't get a sortable overview of all rides you have and see how popular they are, what their profits are etc. And in the overviews that ARE available, you can't click on the name of a ride to go to it.
The data displayed in the profits-tab is completely useless to me: for example, a burger stall has an hourly profit of $2000, has been open for 2 years and has made a total profit of $2500 so far.
And if you want to create a themed part of your park, for example Sci-fi, you have to go through all options (lights, benches, etc) since there are no filters. You can filter neither on type nor on theme. We already had these options in Rollercoaster Tycoon 3, but it's all missing now.
All in all it's just not really a get at all, but more of a 3D modelling program. If that's what you're looking for, then this is for you. But if you also want a management game and make some sense of why you are or are not making any money, then you should not buy this game at all.

For those of you out there who are in search of an exciting RTS I will get straight to the point...Buy Cossacks 3. This game is loaded with hours of fun and challenging gameplay, both in the single player campaigns or random maps versus AI opponents, as well as the multiplayer battlefields. To summarize this game simply: If the Age of Empires series and the Total War series were meshed together into a complete game, this would be Cossacks 3. (If you want more in-depth information then continue reading the full game review.)
Cossacks 3 is the latest sequel to the Cossacks series published and developed by GSC Game World, a Ukranian game developer whose name may not be well-known in the gaming community. However, their work should definitely be familiar (
). This game is a "return to their roots" release based upon the game that started it all, Cossacks: European Wars. In fact, gameplay is very similar to the original with extra features and enhanced graphics to bolster it. Many RTS fans have been starving for a really solid and entertaining game to fill the void in this genre for some time and Cossacks 3 is offering to do just that.
While there have been countless RTS games released in the last decade, most have come up short in recent years, failing to captivate an audience or offer a complete gaming experience to strategic simulation fans. Probably the last notable game was Starcraft 2 (
) over 6 years ago. Gamers today desire more than just a rinse-repeat of the same old things without anything to keep them coming back for more. This is where Cossacks 3 stands out from the pack.
There are different types of RTS gamers. Some enjoy the base-building and resource management aspects. Others enjoy the strategic battlefield elements. And even more crave the bloodlust of the multiplayer arena to showcase their strategic prowess. Unlike most RTS games, Cossacks 3 doesn't just focus on one particular area. Instead, it covers all of these areas and does it exceedingly well. With streamlined research and simplified resource management, players are able to focus more on the base-building and militarization aspects.
Games can be played in the form of several unique and historical single player campaigns, completely customizable random maps, and multiplayer or multiplayer/co-op games. Each of the solo campaigns focus on specific nations during a historical point in their culture and can be played at different levels of difficulty. They offer challenging gameplay for the experienced RTS gamer even at "Normal" difficulty settings. With continued developer support for this game, its likely that more nations and campaigns will be added in the future as well. Random Maps can be played versus up to 6 AI opponents and offers various settings for map generation, starting resources, etc. Multiplayer games can be played as individual opponents fighting for total conquest versus up to 6 other opponents or in co-op battles consisting of 1,2, or 3 player teams working together to control the map. As the developers at GSC Game World promised, this game is fully supportive of the modding community and they have included a game editor in order to allow for personal modding and community developed scenarios to further expand playability and interest.
Unlike similar games, there is no true limit to army size and can easily number in the thousands as long as you provide the base support to accommodate it. This means massive battles are possible. Gameplay is based on 17th and 18th century European warfare. Currently, Cossacks 3 boasts twelve different nations with their own unique units and architectural style, along with numerous research technologies at your fingertips to gain the upper hand against your opponents. This game proudly boasts a realistic ballistics engine as well.
Another aspect that sets the Cossacks series apart is its method of combat resolution. While it still loosely employs the "rock, paper, scissors" resolution of combat, Cossacks 3 takes it much farther than other games of this type by awarding terrain and elevation bonuses, along with a true fog of war (line of sight only) to give a more realistic approach to combat. Battles are fast-paced and require quick and decisive actions so there is never a dull moment.
True to its name, Cossacks 3 is a game about military might and battlefield prowess. This throwback sequel pays homage to its roots, and while bringing RTS lovers a nostalgic feeling of days gone by, it still manages to deliver something fresh and new with modern graphics and realistic combat mechanics. The folks at GSC Game World are actively invested in this game and are already working on a ton of more content to be added such as additional nations (more unique units), another 6 complete campaigns, and historical multiplayer battles according to the
.

Red Stone Online is a game that goes back to the early days of me, when I was first finding out about PC gaming (about 2008! It's nearly been a decade.) Disclaimer: The Steam version doesn't work for some reason. Just download it off of it's main website. It's only a few GB anyway.
While it's slightly different now for me, with brand new content arising within the past 6 years during their host migrations, from map, zone, and city changes, the game at its base is still the Red Stone Online I simplistically loved back in the day. It's a translated Korean MMO that's loosely based on games such as Diablo. You'll be expecting arrowkey and point+click controls, the western side of your keyboard being used for skills and potion/buff item slots, simplistic (but well made even so) graphics, This is not a game for everyone, but if you can get past what feels initially slow (developers have made the first 100 levels easier for new players), and a bit of an aged design, you might come to appreciate the nostalgia. For a kid who never touched games like diablo back then, who was used to cool, early 3D MMOs, I still fell in love with this game. It'll always have its charm, and I'm glad I picked it up when I did. There's so many fewer players now, and many are foreign, but it still has its charms. I'll never forget some of the fun I had in this game.
10/10 would play it again when new server comes up.

TL;DR No reason to play this game except for it being free now, thus, why not?
Battleborn is a character-based (like Overwatch) MOBA-esque (like Monday Night Combat) FPS (like... Borderlands, I guess, since it's Gearbox). The characters are funny and creative, gameplay differs greatly from one to another, there is room for teamwork, RPG elements (characters have levels and skills + items) and strategy elements (towers you can buy and upgrade). It does what it should do: Battleborn brings some fun.
But is it fun
?
It is true this game was hugely overshadowed by Overwatch back then, but it was so for a reason. Blizzard made a very neat and precise shooter with incredible visuals and added a serious and in a way convoluted, yet sometimes funny, lore that is quite hidden and requires some research.
Gearbox, in turn, made a game where FUN and COOLNESS was on top of everything. Therefore combats are a bit chaotic, visuals are daunting and shooter is unsatisfying. But at least it looks and feels kinda cool.
The matches can be entertaining, character remarks are sometimes witty and funny, there is some strategic depth especially to "money" management which you use to build towers etc. and stuff.
What I didn't like... Surprisingly, a lot of things. Graphics are kinda meh, dead servers (about 1k people I think? Not sure), really slow in-game (not in-match) money accumulation (after 6 hours of play I was able to buy 1 low-price-tier character), some unfairness in terms of items* and some other things.
I kinda liked Battleborn, but the keyword here is "kinda".  I would give this game 7/10 Oskar Mike's egos.
The problem is I have a lot of different games (Overwatch included) which are actually
fun and enjoyable. Therefore, why would I bother playing this one? Why would I waste my time on this (especially since there is almost no people online and it takes 10-30 minutes to find a match)?
But don't take my word - play it! It's free*!
* sometimes you get packages, which are similar to cases in CS:GO, safes in Payday 2, treasures in DotA 2... you got the idea. There are some items in these packs which you can take with you in game, maximum 3. These items affect your character: some offer lower abilities cooldow, some give damage boost, some improve health and/or give damage resistance... DIfferent things. So, items differ in rarity, from common to Legendary. And, as you can guess, legendary items are the best, sometimes giving a biiiiiig advantage. It felt really unfair to play as a low-level character (also characters get levels outside the matches, opening new abilities and stuff) with all common items vs some high-level one with all legendaries. Not sure how big of a deal that really is, but it totally felt unfair.
** yeah, and I also dislike how the developers avoid using the term "free to play" as if it is something bad. They try to save their faces, but I think they should've been honest with us, players, and name it not "Free Trial" (it is definitely NOT a trial version nor a demo version, no-no), but what it is: Free to Play.

For a game that's been released
, Man O' War (Nothing to do with the 80's metal band) : Corsair sure is one ugly duckling. I know retrogaming is all the rage these days, what with youngsters trying to discover what exactly it was that made us of the
gaming generation tick as it were. But I didn't realise that we had got way past this and had got to recycling the
era so soon.... Well, OK so it's not
bad to look at. But it's not far off.
Before sitting down to write this one, I have had to have a bit of a semi-serious think about what it is that appeals to me about MoW:C. As I'm not at all sure if my nonsensical addiction for anything
may be blinding my judgement here. I'm enjoying it even if the graphics look like they're of a PC game from over a decade ago. The sea is about the only thing that really holds any water (pun totally intended lol). And even that looks a bit shifty when compared against the water effects used in much older titles. The likes of AC Black Flag or Far Cry 3 for example. The character animations aren't much better either, combat (on land and on deck) are laughably amateurish for this day and age, with just
options in battle (three if you count your fire arm); Hit and block. Not so different from many other games, you might think. Except the animations are about as wooden as the ships that you're supposed to be floating on (I say "supposed" as on more than a few occasions. The sea will actually clip up through the deck of the ship). And the running animations aren't that much better. Making your Cap'n look like they've had one heck of a trouser accident. Not something you should be having to deal with far from shore. Or with that said, near shore ! As you never really have any need to go way out to sea. The whole world map, although sizable and plenty huge, does string along a singular coastline. This could very well change in whatever plans the makers have for this in terms of updates and DLC. But for now there is just the one solitary and oh so very very long coastline (Which upon further investigation, turns out it's the map from the actual Table Top rulebook. Duh Me !).
Which isn't a bad thing. As further out away from the shallows of the shipping lanes, huge beasts lay in wait to gobble you, your crew and your ship. So far I have only encountered one such creature, well one
of these creatures rather and on a couple of occasions too. Probably something to do with the region I'm in, not sure. But judging by certain items that are available in the towns. There are more than a few hints that there are quite a few varieties of these Titanic sea monsters to contend with here and there.
And yes, you can go on land (to a point). There are various towns and settlements dotted along the coastline that you can stop off at to trade your wares (both gotten and ill gotten), The markets have three basic stalls with which to buy your essentials, cargo, weapons and items of vanity tat for your Cap'n. You can take on work for your ship. Doing trade runs for local merchants, or take on more nefarious works. Like assassination and piracy missions. Visit the Shipwright for all your shipping upgrades (and to buy new ships as well). Or you can just take a quick visit to the local Tavern to hear the local gossip, Hire other Captains for convoy voyages or hire fresh crew for your ship. Something which you'll be doing a lot of, if you're the kind of Cap'n that enjoys biting off more than you can chew and inviting disaster at every opportunity. Which is more than likely to happen. You will also find special units for hire in these places too. Ones that will just give you that bit of extra protection out on the high seas. Such as Wizards (of varying skill and temperament), Winged horse riding knights and Griffons. If there are anymore of these specials to be hired, I have yet to encounter them.
But if you choose not to shop at these ports, you can always choose to sack the living bilio out of them. Which works sort of similar to boarding an enemy vessel. Except you enter the settlement and you and your crew wave your badly animated arms around until everyone is dead. Then you take what you want and set sail once again. There's not that much to it. But it breaks up the constant seafaring a bit.
Either way, all towns look pretty much alike. At least the ones I have found myself at do and admittedly at the time of writing, I'm not that massively into it yet. But so far only their arrangement of features and size have differed.
The ingame menus are an absolute joke to navigate. To make your selection you have to look for the option that is the least highlighted ?? Whoever the **** thought that this was a good design idea is beyond me. But this is how it is for whatever reason. And if you're using a Gamepad for this, then
. Which is amazing considering the amount of effort they've put into configuring an official Steampad setup for this.
On the upside, MoW shines in it's representation of naval combat (which ideally is what you're looking for anyway in a game with "Naval Battles" in it's subheading, right ?). Outside of the campaign you can find the
settings. Where you can take a turn at being one of the many, many seafaring factions from the world of Warhammer. Which when devs do this without the requirment of endless payouts for DLC. Is always impressive, and this would be no exception.
The whole simulation of sailing is well implemented. You really have to watch the wind direction, as one wrong turn will leave you dead in the water and a sitting duck for enemy cannons and other various gameplay features make the game really come alive in ways you might not necessarily think possible when just judging it from it's cover. Like levelling up the crew and that. It's always a nice rare pleasure when you can get attached to NPCs in a game. As keeping your crew happy and in work, will ensure you keep various bonuses for your vessel. As well as keeping them from committing mutiny against you. Which can be a thing if you take no heed of their morale.
And this is the thing. Despite it's looks and sub par presentation. There's actually not a bad game in here, somewhere. It may look like a dogs dinner and be atrociously executed in many of its features. But the background detail that comes out during gameplay is actually not that bad. Mechanically speaking, it's a great game. Graphically however, it all just seems to barely function. And the glitches and bugs seek to crimp its positives even further. It's almost an exact mirror image of the modern AAA experience. A beautiful, slick shmup from a small, determined indie team which really shows how a passion for a genre can create great games. Challenging for both beginner and psychos alike. The powerful soundtrack and mesmerising artwork give this game a polish and sheen usually reserved for larger budget projects, and with a novel, deep scoring system there is plenty of scope for replayability.
As someone who never really played many shmups, the genre can be a daunting experiance. Blue Revolver looked daunting at first, but once you play a few minutes (and die a few times!) and you start to get a feel for the game, it grabs you.
I started playing this game with high expectations, and they were exceeded with every play. Whilst at times infurating and punishing, I never felt the game was being unfair. Every time I died, I realised my faults, picked myself up and tried again.
Learning the game, and learning from the game, is an organic experiance with Blue Revolver. You complete that first stage and you feel confident. Then you hit stage 2 and you are humbled. You say to yourself "Ok, its time to think more about positioning myself correctly so that doesn't happen again" and you start to pay attention to patterns and enemy types a lot more. You hold onto that special weapon for big guys, but soon you get confident enough to say "I can kill that sucker! I want more x64s not x2s!". With every new stage comes a deeper challenge, and the game yearns for you to polish your craft before you can truely take on the next level. It's frustrating, but exciting and enticing all the same.
Pick it up, and have a go. At this price its an absolute steal.

This game plays and looks like some sort of alpha demo of a hybrid between Mount & Blade and Sid Meier's Pirates. The 3D models are serviceable (although overused, making each race appear to be made up of a minimal handful of lifeless clones), but the world looks like a muddy, blocky mess. The animations appear to be in slow motion. Boarding combat is a boring clickfest, and NPCs tend to clip through things frequently. There are interesting systems in the background (radiant content generation, individualized crew members with small, interesting differences, special crewmember classes that can be manually controlled, weather), but they don't make up for the game's flaws or price tag. I love the background of the game (Warhammer), but a few racial-themed ship and NPC models don't fix core gameplay issues.
Man O' War: Corsair doesn't appear to be a finished product, yet it has been "released". I might repurchase it sometime in the future, if it receives some major polishing (and perhaps a fully-fledged sandbox mode, instead of "campaigns" for only three races and a custom battle mode I have almost no interest in), but it's not worth getting your hopes up or wallet out for in its current state, in my opinion.

This game has some pretty nice aspirations. It offers a grand world and many interesting factions, as well as a couple of interesting quests. But it does have some major issues lying in it's foundation.
The best parts of this game is the incredible music, the naval battles as well as the advanced trading system. But these (central) parts of the game does not fix the underlying issues with the engines, glitching and AI. The developers are adding new content and playable races which is really sick, but the game suffers from the looming presence of glitches and clunky controls.
The worst part is made apparent when you get boarded. That's when the horrible animations get apparent, and enemies start getting pushed into walls and glitch up on top of barrels that are inaccessible to you. The graphics of this game is actually pretty nice. Textures as well as character models are slightly cartoony. But the animations are just really bad.
If you walk diagonally forward you have the same animation as if you were walking straight forward giving you a strange shuffle, you walk extremely slow in combat which is really annoying when you board a grand ship that you have yet to master the layout of, and glitches will pester you. When I did my chaos playthrough I was often crippled by being unable to move when getting boarded, so i had to resort to spamming light attacks to propel me forward slightly.
The chaos progression is extremely linear and does not offer you any sense of choice, just straight up upgrades that are made available progressively. The Human campaign is where it's at. The trading is really hard to get into, but ultimately offers some nice gameplay. During the start of the game you don't know what the average price of things is, so you just have to learn by making misstakes. This could be considered a flaw in the UI, but it does follow some logic, such as iron being cheaper up in kislev than in bretonnia, and Wine being generally cheaper in bretonnia.
Another Issue I'd like to delve into is the AI. If you join into a battle between pirates and a fleet of imperials you can bet your♥♥♥♥♥that the pirate ship is going to ignore everythign else and engage you into combat. The imperial fleet will also often times not be bothered to help you. I got chased throughout Estalia by two dark elf seadragon things. There were a multitude of defensive fleets around the ahrbours I visited, but none of them so much as batted an eye. The dark elf ships followed me relentlessly even though they were surrounded by enemies, and none of my allies helped me at all!
That was just frustrating and immersion breaking. I would not recommend this game at this point in time. It is actually pretty promising, but the issues lie in it's foundations, and are not easily reversed at this point. I hope to get surprised, since the game is still getting worked on. I will revisit this game as it gets more patches to see if I'll be able to change this review into a recommendation. Do your best, Evil Twin Artworks!

Blue Revolver is a bullet hell with solid core mechanics and lots of variety. Its slick, fast, and fun to play. Its easy for players new to the genre to get a grasp on the game, while difficult enough so that adept players can also enjoy the game's 5 stages. Blue Revelover is simplifed to be sure; however, Blue Revolver still succeeds in providing excellent gameplay and thrilling moments. The art style and OST also help give personality to the game.
The game's one weakness would be it's sometimes confusing visual cues. Points earned from killing enemies sometimes blocks the screen, hiding bullets. Additionally, besides a short and ineffective tutorial, the game simply leaves newcomers into the genre clueless as to what bars and numbers represent.
But who cares?!? These are minor information problems that are solved within the first few games anyway. Blue Revolver is still an amazing and addictive game that focused on delivering excellent gameplay though the renfinement of core mechanics. It steps back from the complexities of many bullet hell games, and returns to a simpler times, while retaining the difficultly and excitement of much more complex bullet hells. Its easily of the best shmups on steam. In short:
Buy Blue Revolver. Now.

Are you the type of person who enjoys facebook games, or other gaming systems which require them to wait around while things happen mostly independent of your actions? Well, here's a game for you.
Seriously though, my friend got me this game as a joke, and to be honest, I thought it was hilarious for about ten minutes. You buy things to use on your horses and increase their stats, train them for the same reason in DDR style directional key sessions, and that's it. That's all you can really do, because what should be the best parts of this game--the parts where you take your magical horse to win horse races against all those other presumably loser horses, or take your mystic steed out to accomplish various quests like saving Timmy from the well or moving boulders for old man Henderson--are done FOR YOU. You send your horse away while a clock ticks down the time until they return. Then I guess you're all like "Hey magic horse, did you win that cool race?" or "Hey best buddy, did you fix that road block that was keeping the medicine wagon from reaching the orphanage?", to which they just whinny enthusiastically, staring at you with those big whimsical horse eyes like "DID I EVER! Man, you should've been there, it was TOTALLY cool, and look," they'll continue "I leveled up from it and everything, you really should have been there best human friend. Where were you anyways?".
Good question, game: where was I? Probably improving my stable, or buying super horse medicine, or some other equally boring waste of time so I can upgrade and care for an amazing magestic super stallion that I can't do anything remotely interesting with except look at, improve some more, then send out to do quests by itself.
That's really my overall impression of this game: a waste of time. I suppose asking this game to have an exciting story is a bit too much, but by cutting you (the player) out of the quests and racing events as it does, it really feels like a hollow and incomplete venture, and I can safely say that I'm glad I didn't spend any money on it.
