FINAL EDIT: Three years later, and Becky and the team have completely abandoned the project. It's still incredibly broken (pieces turning black/memory leaking/crashing). STAY AWAY... DO NOT give them your hard-earned money!
REVIEW EDIT: After six months, there is ONE developer remaining on this project, and an update hasn't been publically released in close to three months. The game itself is still fun as I posted below, but it's FAR from a finished product. I would advise everyone to stay away until Becky and the team release a COMPLETE version.
While still in its beta stage, Battle Chess is a great throwback to the classic 3D0/Dos classic game of medieval strategy. The 3D pieces are well-animated, with a variety of animations for each capture (my favorite being "Boogie Knight", where rather than engaging in outright combat, the knight and queen engage in a dance-off, after which the knight snaps the queen's neck), rather than the single one offered us by the original, or by recent attempts like Battle Vs. Chess. The music fits with the medieval atmosphere, and the voice acting is... okay, though I honestly miss the whiny pawn from the original.
At this moment there are stil. a significant number of bugs and crashes to deal with, but as previously mentioned, the game is still in beta, and the developers are taking input from the community as they address each. If you can look past the relatively minor bugs, $10 is a GREAT price for this early access game, especially if you are, like I, a fan of the original Battle Chess.

I'm a huge Metroidvania fan and I enjoyed the likes of Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.  Those two easily are the best of those Metroidvanias and I have played them both AND beat both of them.  Does Guacamelee! belong in the same sentence as those two?  After beating the game on the normal mode which unlocks the hard mode, I have to say that it belongs right there with Super Metroid and Castlevania SOTN.  The neat thing about Guacamelee! is that the game is certainly more challenging than those two mentioned.  And the most fun as well which should count for something.
The cool thing is that Guacamelee! pays homage to the Metroid series and doesn't shy away from the fact that it's a Metroidvania game.  This former Metroid fan who has played all the Metroid games up to Metroid Prime 3 on the Wii can tell you that Drink Box Studios certainly has met the high bar that Nintendo & Konami have set for Metroidvania games.  I could go into detail about how it is like Metroid games but I'll keep it to myself and let people buy the game and then see for themselves.

A very old and solid MMORPG that has it's great sides but also a fair share of flaws. I personally really enjoy the game and thus I will write a positive review. The game is free to play and is only 2gb, so if in doubt I would certainly try it out. A list of pros and cons:
Pros:
+ A lot of classes to choose from
+ Each class has a subclass, so even more classes
+ Each class has a ton of skills to level
+ You can choose what to spend your attribute points on. This makes it possible to build your character in any way you want (magic damage lancer, power priest and other fun stuff)
+ Can be enjoyed both solo and in groups
+ Always an event going on
+ Guild vs Guild is very competitive
(+ or -, depending on what you enjoy)
+- A tight knit community
Cons:
- Very poor translation in certain areas of the game
- Lack of game guides and in game help. You mostly have to rely on other players for your information
- It's very grindy. Especially at higher levels
- Grinding is even slower without a sphere (basically a ten dollar monthly subscription)
- The main quest is long and tedious. Fortunately, it's not a requirements to play the game
- Lack of actual quests. There are title quests that give your characters a permanent passive buff, but that's about it. They're more annoying than difficult to finish too
- Some classes have skills that are a bit buggy
That's all points I can think of in a row. The age of the game will certainly show when you play it, but in my opinion, it doesn't take away from the fun. There's also been updates recently that make grinding a lot easier, such as free buffs that can be acquired in any of the big towns.

It's a fun grinding MMO, something I'm not typically a big fan of. Unlike Ragnarok Online I feel as if it does it in a much more streamlined way with more options. Instead of killing X monsters, there's a lot of quests and different fields to level up... and the near impossibility of reaching the level cap (1000 I think) coupled with 4 optional rebirths gives a lot of character advancement. If you like growing and seeing a character continually get stronger without end, this is a good game for you. I'd recommend joining a guild early-in and reading more about the classes on the blog linked below. There's very few sources online regarding Red Stone Online, and most of them are very vague. This blog is the best source of information, and concidentally was created by the person that helped me when starting out.
I'd say the only real cons I have with the game is the idea that for the beginning, you can't really get into most of the fun stuff. The beginning grind is the most tiring, which I'm sure drives away most players. Another thing I don't like is the cash shop, while it's not P2W in my eyes it still makes a lot of things easier for the players. Unlike other MMOs however, it is relatively cheap and you can buy most of the useful stuff for only a few dollars. As a new player, I can see the biggest issues facing this game are the lack of players first and foremost -- the game's staff are very much alive though, and just within the past few days I've started there's been a couple nice events and even a new player event which is sweet.
A useful tip is to open the game through the filebrowser instead of Steam and when in-game change the resolution in settings, it looks much better this way. I see a couple reviews complaining about this, so just for future purposes you can do that.

First off: I really enjoyed Hegemony Gold: Wars of Ancient Greece. And that's part of the problem.
Hegemony Rome tries to achieve more in some aspects, for example city building. Sadly those new features are nothing compared to the loss of depth and functionality, as this game isn't the same kind of 'open world' game as its predecessor, with its ultimate freedom.
I pretty much only played the very first mission of the campaign. There were 2 parts of preparation, and I chose to go west first and not south.
My choice triggered new tasks in the west and north, so I did those too. During a march that lead me very far north, I registered a lack of supplies and sent the majority of my troops back to the nearest city.
What I didn't know: At the target I would have gained free supplies and I was expected to fight a huge battle there.
Result: I wasted the triggered free food and naturally I lost the battle with my few units, that I did not send back. It was a disaster.
Afterwards I went south beyond the Alps for more units, the second option from the tasks that I had been given at the beginning. So now I had sufficient troops, but what about food? As you might remember, food was the reason why I failed at the first place.
So I tried to prepare for another full march north, but I never managed to gain enough of supplies by a mile. And yes, I connected the frontier city with other cities and set its stock demand on high. Yet it never went above 150 food in stock, which isn't even closely enough. Or in other words, it was a deadlock.
Compared to the open world in Greece, you are now confronted with triggers all over. You have to follow a deisgned path and if your decisions differ even slightly from the idea the developers had in mind, it might mean the final end of your ambitions. If that happens already during the very first mission, I can't imagine how painful it might become later.
Add many minor control and handling issues and you have a disappointing game.

The supply mechanics are not what they are cracked up to be.
Triggers are broken.
Maps are awful corridors of bugginess -- my units got stuck multiple times in the first level.
I just don't feel like I'm running an empire. Refunded.

This really isn't a full release yet. This is still an indie Early Access title. That's something that any potential buyers should be made aware of before making the purchase.
That said, the game has a lot of heart... It oozes Warhammery goodness from every pore, and the sandboxy nature lends itself to a great many rather interesting and unexpected results; such as the pirate island of Sartosa suddenly staking a claim to mainland Remas, or a massive three-way war between Kislev, Marienburg and the high elves.
The "campaign" is very lightly structured, but this does mean you're allowed a fair amount of freedom in doing what you want to do. You'll also find that you're by no means railroaded into being a Goodbeard the Friendly Privateer... Indeed, most of the custom missions and sub-campaigns involve you performing acts ranging from "unsavor" up through "shady" and straight into "outright war crimes", and it's a pleasant change of pace.
Ship combat is combination of amazing maelstroms of furious pyrotechnics, and frustrating wonkiness. The melee combat system is *awful* for the most part, and many of the boarding mechanics are fantastically glitchy.
This is where we get into the "cons" of the game... Placeholders are everywhere. Glitches abound in the most bizarre ways and places. The naval trading aspect is, like every other naval trading system, complete♥♥♥♥♥ The RPG aspect of upgrading your character and ship is hysterically unbalanced and at times completely broken. The sea monster battles are also often quite glitchy, or just generally very poorly designed and implemented (the Black Leviathans being a rare but exciting exception to this rule).

Blue Revolver is a bullet hell with solid core mechanics and lots of variety. Its slick, fast, and fun to play. Its easy for players new to the genre to get a grasp on the game, while difficult enough so that adept players can also enjoy the game's 5 stages. Blue Revelover is simplifed to be sure; however, Blue Revolver still succeeds in providing excellent gameplay and thrilling moments. The art style and OST also help give personality to the game.
The game's one weakness would be it's sometimes confusing visual cues. Points earned from killing enemies sometimes blocks the screen, hiding bullets. Additionally, besides a short and ineffective tutorial, the game simply leaves newcomers into the genre clueless as to what bars and numbers represent.
But who cares?!? These are minor information problems that are solved within the first few games anyway. Blue Revolver is still an amazing and addictive game that focused on delivering excellent gameplay though the renfinement of core mechanics. It steps back from the complexities of many bullet hell games, and returns to a simpler times, while retaining the difficultly and excitement of much more complex bullet hells. Its easily of the best shmups on steam. In short:
Buy Blue Revolver. Now.

I really appreciate Blue Revolver's elegant scoring system. Unlike a lot of other SHMUPS, this is very easy to understand and is a blast to play; Chain to 8, and cash it in for sweet multipliers!
Other than that, it's just a damn fine game. Super slick, fast, and relentless.
Pros
- Great scoring system
- Good variety of ships; choose how you want to blast dudes!
- Amazing OST
- Entertaining amount of unlockable songs, alternate sprites, and backdrops
- Accessible difficulty settings (with an interesting scaling system if you so desire).
- FANTASTIC options. Being able to change colours and see hitboxes is A+
Cons
- Ship explosions and bullets sound a little flat.
- Some bullet patterns feel a tad too random (note: I probably just need to git gud)
- Achievements and replays are not yet implemented at time of writing.
TL:DR It's one of the BEST indie SHMUPS in recent times. Don't hesitate to purchase at full price.

Guacamelee is a 2D platformer that, in my opinion, does almost everything right. First of all the cross-platform availability, because if the game had not been available for Linux, I would most likely never have played it.
The graphics have a beautiful flat cartoon style without lines, which gives the game a stylish look without being childish. The storyline, though linear, is not strictly enforced, and you are free to roam and enjoy previously visited areas of the game. The story itself at first seems cliché, but the unique and humorous setting—a grand parody of Dia de los Muertos in Mexico, and the beautifully drawn high resolution cutscenes in the same style as the game, coupled with a great soundtrack evokes an unexpectedly strong emotional response. If you collect five out of six orbs before the final fight, you get the happy ending. This also unlocks the sad ending cutscenes in the main menu. I watched those and they made me very sad indeed.
The combat is fast paced, at times frantic, but luckily not too often. Additionally many important fights are as much a battle of wits as a battle of skill since different enemies require different approaches. It is important to find the right balance between preemptive attacks to interrupt enemy moves, dodging uninterruptible attacks, and quick moves to avoid undodgable attacks. The platforming part of the gameplay is intricately interwoven with the combat, as the various special moves you unlock have each their own movement function. Execute Rooster Uppercut at the height of your jump, and you can reach higher platforms that are unclimbable in a single jump. Execute a Dashing Derpderp to suddenly dash sideways or change direction in mid-air, or turn into a chicken to fit down a small passage! Every attack can be chained into one big combofest and it looks great too. Plus it allows you to juggle enemies helplessly while dealing continuous damage. The control is fantastic, which means that whenever I die for the umpteenth time, I still feel convinced that it is entirely my fault. Which leads me to the next part:
Practice really pays off, as does taking a break. Sometimes I gave up on an area and I would take a break—hours or days. When I returned I would suddenly find the areas far less difficult than I had initially believed. This really noticeble improvement as a result of dedicated practice—and a break to integrate the results—is one of the reasons that Guacamelee is a platformer that I really recommend. It gave me horrible challenges, but because I could really feel the practice pay off, I kept coming back for more. I even opted to complete all achievements. I think this is the first game on Steam where I got all achievements, and it is a testament to how Guacamelee is a beautiful, at times masochistic, and thoroughly enjoyable game.
EDIT: It turns out there was another platformer that would have been my first game with all achievements unlocked: Waking Mars, but one of the achievements is bugged. It's a fun game too.

Regretfully, I do have to say, I'm very disappointed about the turnout of this newest version of Battle Chess. My opinion is besides the multiple bugs rapant during Early Access which render the game frustrating to use. (On this side note, the game has only very recently been released, and so bugs are understandable; assuming that they'll be fixed in due time.)
Let me start with thegood. The graphics are great! The silly-at-heart battle sequences, as Battle Chess has been known for, are creative and hilarious, and there were a whole lot more of them than in the previous versions which played the same single ones over and over again. The design for the skin meshes is very fancy. (My personal favorite's the Bishop.)
And now, "onward" to my stark critique.
I feel as if the proud traditions of Battle Chess has been spat on and  replaced with a mocking version which claims to know BC's history but doesn't show it well in its performance. This is speaking especially in regards to the programs ability to play chess; its "artificial intelligence" ("AI"), if you will. The ability for BC to calculate moves has been severely dumbed down in GoK. Anyone who has played BC from its beginning (I myself grew up with the 1992-3 version, which I hold very dear to) will know just how damn hard the thing is to beat, even at its NOVICE level: Battle Chess's AI saw EVERY possible move and, more so, every possible opportunity to gain and save material points 5, 6, 7 and more moves down the line; it knew how to schemingly find skewers, pins, double-checks and silent evasive maneuvers that no average good player could humanly find within a few seconds (or even minutes) of thinking. BC has beaten several other excellent chess computer programs, including ChessMaster. It was freakin' frustrating as hell! Such frustrating superior "AI" has given BC its reputation. Obviously, such a hard e-opponent is designed to teach you to become a more prominent chess player, even if the defeats are diabolical.
On the other hand, it was sandbox-easy to beat the Game of King: the powerful tactics as described above simply weren't there. Rather, GoK's tactics, juxtaposed to BC's, were hind-sighted, unholistic and predictable, if not simply lunkheaded. For instance, in a game played at “Nobleman” level, the Black queen captured my pawn on g2, which is undefended by the Bishop on f1 since I moved him out to check the King, and my right-side knight on g1 hasn't previously been moved; an extremely dimwitted blunder on my part; in fact, Battle Chess 1993 was the one to harshly teach such a lesson to me over and over again. I can't even believe that, after years of experience in chess, I would make such a foolish mistake. My restricted undefended Rook on H1 was DOOMED for capture without any immediate opportunity for me to capture back!! Or, was he? The next move Game of Kings played was pawn on f7 to f5 to threaten my other knight on e4. This equally foolish move played by the computr opened up a diagonal line for my own queen on C3 to capture ITS Rook on H8!!! It's almost as if GoK deliberately DID this because it didn't WANT me to lose material points easily. Battle Chess would have never allowed itself to make such a move: unless there was an opportunity to cleverly steal more pieces from me, it would have immediately and mercilessly captured my poor Rook on H1, while leaving none of its own pieces up for danger without re-capture. I thought for a second that perhaps it was some sneaky way to expose my own queen for capture. Hey, after all, Battle Chess is known for its surprise attacks, right? Unfortunately for me, surprise attack against my queen was rarely the case. After I did indeed move her up to H8 to capture its Rook, Game of Kings didn't even seem to bother to try to capture my queen back after 4 or 5 moves. Worst of all, and this is the best part, ladies and gentleman: the black queen never took my easy defenseless Rook on H1! All of this was the "Nobleman" level, which was supposed to be Game of King's 4th level of difficulty. I simply closed GoK in dire frustration, knowing that I wasn't playing against Battle Chess; I really wasn't.
I haven't played GoK's hardest level, but I can only imagine that it's barely as good as the original BC Novice level, let alone their level 1, and BC had 10 levels excluding the novice one! I understand that there have been negative reviews in regards to BC's extreme difficulty, pointing to the fact that it's been TOO frustrating that players could never beat it. People obviously want something playable so that they’ll actually buy it. Understood.  On the other hand, I don't think that should be any reason to take out all those difficult levels altogether. Those original difficult levels 1-10 should still be there, in addition to the incorporation of easier playable levels. Again, I can't emphasized this enough: they were what defined the Battle Chess series!!
I've covered the main part of my review, but the "AI" is far from the only thing needed be mentioned.
The tutorial is a rather cheesy duplication of the one made in the 1992-3 version. It offered nothing new in explaining chess, and then the mediocre voicing of the characters were pretentious, trite, unenthusiastic and simply uninteresting. The "sumo-"sized rook, for example, spoke in a rather superficial European accent (Italian?), and one would not feel the threat of his almost-monotonic dialogue, "If you don't understand, I'll smash you." (In the original 1992-3 tutorial, the rook had a rasp, crass and intimidating voice that varied in pitches as he emphasized the different words of that same dialogue, which excellently portrayed the sense of threat that he means to.)
Speaking of which, isn't the Rook supposed to be a tower that transforms into a wretched stone beast, not a tactless obese "Sumo" guard?? Again, another proud tradition of Battle Chess which has been broken, since in all of its previous versions the rook indeed was a stone beast.
Finally, another BC tradition broken, minor though not insignificant, is the color coding: it appears that OldeSkuul has switched the colorsaround so that red is assigned the BLACK pieces and blue the WHITE pieces. I contactedtheir FB page, and BurgerBecky responded that she will create an update with the option to switch the colors around. So far, no such update was made. (I'm guessing it's on queue to be worked on after the bugs.)
In conclusion, while it's pleasantly enjoyable for a pastime, Game of Kings is as good as any decent chess program and is nowhere near as good as the Battle Chess it’s supposed to be an upgrade from. To save my pride for the chess program that has taught me so much about chess since I was7, I can't call this Game of Kings version "Battle Chess". The 1987, 1988 and 1992-3 versions are the ones I feel rightful to call Battle Chess. However, take heart, my word is only the unofficial opinion of one user in the minority, and it's not to discourage folks from buying it. As far as anyone's concerned, it does after all do the job nicely. Furthermore, most of the younger generation will probably not be able to relate to anything I'm saying, since this is probably their first exposure to the BC series. Finally, I'm aware OldeSkuul is putting much effort in making updates to the game. There's always a chance to turn an unofficial negative opinion around. ;)
p. s. I want to extend a note of gratitude to Olde Skuul and express how much I appreciate them having taken on the project to finish Game of Kings when it couldn’t be finished by Subdued Software. I was aware what financial trouble they had to go through to finally gained enough to open the option for online play. Thank you greatly for the time, effort and devotion!!

Bue Revolver has an interesting art style and is a great shmup that in my mind incorporates the best ideas of the Cave games but also provides a lot more options and features for those that are not purely captivated by getting a higher score as well as making the game more accessible overall.

The combo system is pretty cool with the combo count increasing as you kill enemies but being capped unless you use your secondary weapon to increase the multiplier. It’s a good system and one of my faves in modern shmups.
Difficulty is good and I am a particular fan of the hyper mode where the game difficulty changes to suit your ability a mechanic that seems to be cropping up more and more recently in games and is in my opinion a welcome addition. Another welcome addition is the ability to play any stage at any difficulty to practice particular sections, something I am surprised has not been in Shmups much over the years.
My personal favourite part however is the challenges that give you a specific task and set of conditions ranging from, disappearing bullets to complete the levels in 1 life. These are a fun diversion and really add to the longevity of the game.
Blue Revolver is probably the shmup I would recommend along with my personal fave Deathsmiles as a good entry point for people looking into getting into the Bullet Hell Genre.

I bought this early access over the weekend with hesitant optimism ... I spent a while playing around with it and the game definitely has promise ... some of the transitions bug out a little bit ... and some of the cuts are a bit jarring ... but the foundations are there for a faithful sequel to the original ... the humour is there (even if some of it feels a little bit forced) ... and there are now multiple combat animations for each 'combination' of pieces! ... What I would love to see is them making it a bit more adult (more blood! more brutal combat animations) even if that is an option you have to select ... and also additional character sets (medieval is already there ... but what about fantasy, futuristic, etc ... how awesome would that be!) ...
I can't comment on the AI yet as I played a game on easiest just to have a look around at how the whole thing fitted together ... but all chess games live or die by their AI so I hope that in this day and age we have a great AI ...
All in all I think they are headed in the right direction ... and hopefully they will be able to smoothen out the bumps and make this a game that I will be playing in years to come ...

I'm terrible at Shmups just in general. I cannot quite be enough ATTITUDE for sufficient GAINS, I get the concept of SHOOT THE CORE but can't quite capitalise on it. I find NO REFUGE when I need it most. Every time I play one it's like I'm being attacked by the FULLEST EXTENT OF THE JAM.
Shmup memes aside, this is an unrelentingly challenging shmup game. It has a Novice mode (and the fact I can't get further than the boss of level 3 even on that mode should tell you how bad I am at these games), called "Normal" difficulty, where the first hit you take activates a bomb instead to give you a brief period of invulnerability. Hyper mode is the game's ACTUAL Normal difficulty and plays like a standard Shmup, though by all accounts the difficulty is dynamic, and the better you do, the harder the difficulty gets. On the other hand, Parallel mode locks the game's difficulty to the max level, to give the biggest challenge. Personally, I feel both Hyper and Normal modes are challenging enough as it is.
You also get two choices of character and ship; Mae in her Mapleberry, and Val in her Urashima or ... I forget what it's called ,but something like that. They have slightly different behaviours and weapons it seems, and definately different appearances, but functionally the game plays out the same... THough the story seems quite different depending upon which character you choose.
Speaking of story, holy hell, what a cool concept! Magic that is controlled like programming code, but can build up junk data which causes anomalies in reality? Teams of "Technicians" that deal with Junk Data and make sure 'code' is clean and efficient to minimise appearance of junk data? Devices which help them do that? a supergroup of Technicians called Blue Revolver with mysteriously super powerful Devices? and a strange, super anomaly they investigate with readings eerily similar to their Devices?? All of my yes.
Couple this with an astounding, pulse pounding soundtrack, cute character designs, beautiful graphics and a Missions system which actually is meant to be a tutorial of sorts to teach you how to play STGs (good lord I can't believe I only just found that out myself), and you pretty much have yourself a winner!
It seems to lack a multiplayer mode from what I've seen, which is slightly saddening, and if you die, you gotta restart at the beginning until you amass the 4500 star points to unlock free play mode, but considering in the short time I've played it I've amassed like 2200? I'm not far off already... There's other unlocks too, like remixes of tracks, background arts, concept arts and whatnots, so that's great too :D
This game is packed solid with features and wonderfulness, and it was absolutely worth all the wait and the pricetag. Seriously, you couldn't ask for a better, more fun, more accessable STG on Steam. Do yourself a favour, and pick this game up pronto.

Every once in awhile I'll land on a game that blows me away with how much it can do with a simple concept, and today is one of those days. Games like this start out with a gameplay loop that, on its own, should be no more captivating than tiddlywinks but build up something far more worthwhile around it. And it's not a long and engrossing experience that I've just surfaced from, but working through the simple, unique puzzles for the mysterious payoff made simian.interface++ a better gaming experience than many longer or larger titles out there.
The name is actually spot-on this time, as the game is posed as a graphic user interface for monkeys. You play a test subject working through trials of the system, simply following the implied instructions for a curved and yellow reward you know too well. Puzzles come in batches of 10 or so, bookended by login screens and performance readouts. I doubt I need to worry about spoilers here but things start to happen as you work through the game that hint at a larger plot afoot.
Don't come for what little story there is, but rather the experience of seeing it told. While not much happens plot-wise the feel of how it unfolds has a definite charm, situated right between sinister cyberpunk and silly cat pictures. I found myself speeding through the puzzles just to see how ridiculous the next glitchy reveal would be, and I was not disappointed. The presentation helps sell the technicolor madness, particularly the soundtrack which is some incredibly catchy techno that takes loads of inspiration from old NES chiptunes.
I'm four paragraphs in and haven't even touched on the puzzles, which are clever permutations of an old gimmick. Each puzzle places a number of squares or lines or boxes on your screen, which you can move and/or rotate simply by moving your mouse. The goal is to snap them back into place, anything from getting a white square into a square outline to realigning a screenful of plaid. They're simple challenges made surprisingly engrossing by how much fine control you have over the figures. You'll also encounter a wide variety of shapes and patterns to make across the six tiny chapters of the game, and more still in the infinite, timed, and secret modes.
This is the total package in terms of kitschy puzzlers, but a small one at that. I saw everything the game had to offer, secret level included, in just over 30 minutes. The infinite and time attack modes could suck up some more of your time, of course, and I wouldn't be opposed to playing through it again once my memories of the two runs I just did (to unlock the secret mode) fade a bit more. With that caveat in mind, I can happily recommend simian.interface++ to anyone looking for a fresh new take on puzzlers. It's got charm, it's got challenge, and it's got the best kind of weirdness to puzzle through.

I wanted to like this game, really I did. I've been a fan of the RCT series since the 1st one, and I spent god knows HOW many hours playing RCT3. Rollercoaster Tycoon World was showing some promise when they release the first beta. It had lots of problems, but the devs were SO open to the community's feedback and input. However, I think this project just got too large for them--either that or this game became the perfect example of what happens when you try to please everyone. What's left is a game with far less options for creativity than any previous RCT game. Their coaster creator is promising but suffers from some awkward UI issues. And despite having some nice visual elements (I do like many of the coaster aesthetics), there are many laughable or groan-inducing design elements as well (let's pretend those park guests were never made). While Nvizzio no doubt did their best, this project got the best of them and fell flat on its face.
If you're a fan of the previous RCT games, this one will definitely disappoint you and send you back to the old entries in the series or, more likely, head to that "other" roller coaster/theme park sim that just came out.

In Samorost 3 you play as the titular character, Samorost, who is a gnome clad in white pyjamas who goes on space adventure among the stars. It sounds strange, and it is, but it's the sort of whimsy and wonder that has filled the game from the first (free) flash title 13 year ago. You live on a mossy, chunk of wood that floats around through space, Samorost lives with his dog in a observatory and strange creatures and people inhabit all of the worlds you explore. Early in the game you build a space ship out of a bathtub, waterbottle, stool and giant mushroom; it's wonderful. Everything in the game is amazing to look at and figuring out how things work is a joy. Every screen is a piece of art.
If you've played other Amanita Design games (Machinarium/Botanicula) you'll feel right at home here, and if you're a fan of the previous Samorost titles you'll find the same charm and game design you've come to love and more in a larger, more detailed and elaborate title.
I've waited five years for Amanita to release another full-length game. Not an ounce of disappointment.

I reccomend this game by default as it's the best golf game on steam.
With that said, this game is pretty good but lacks any kind of polishing.  Plays like EA PGA titles at heart, but it's lacking a lot.
They do too good of a job trying to capture realism that it takes away from the realism.  For example, you can't do a traditional gly over of the hole, you get two different views, an "on paper" over the top for yardage and the second is you can zoom in to the hole.  This is great as this is more realistic, but you don't have any options for checking the hole in its entirity.  So you are often hitting near blind in a way.
Putting and chipping is maddening.  The systems are pretty good as they resemble real life difficulty, but functionally they just either don't work or you have no way to judge what you are doing.  Chipping seems almost random.  You can be in a sand trap with 90% of the ball covered, but somehow launch a flop shot 30 yards past your target if your swing is at 100%.  Same goes for the rough, it seems extremely random, hit or miss, as to what your shot will do.
Putting is really good all but for the lack of literally any kind of notification for "feel" of your put.  The putter has 1 power setting of I think 145 feet, so getting the power on puts correct is 100% on looking at how far back the putter is drawn, but it's very hard to tell as the camera is straight on.  Short and long putts are much harder than they should and medium putts tend to be freakishly easy.
Overall this is a pretty good game, but it's lacking tremendously in some areas and some of the mechanics and physics of the game are grossly inconsistant.  It has one of the better realistic feels to a golf game but in some areas it's lacking to get the translation from real life to video game fair.  They tried just a little too hard if you will in terms of making the game resemble real life.
To sum it up, if you are like me and must have a golf game, go with this one, but be prepared for a few things that will drive you nuts.   If you can take or leave a golf game in your library, pass on this.
It's a good game that tried to simulate real golf and fell a little short in effort.  This is NOT a PGA game and does NOT have real courses, it's fictional.

This is definitely NOT GTAV.
What it IS, though, is awesome. This is essentially a clone of the old flip-phone game Snake, with a GTA-esque twist. The gameplay is simple, using just a couple of buttons to turn left or right and try not to run into the stuff you're not supposed to run into, and run into the stuff you're supposed to run into.
It's the kind of game that you can play for three hours and have fun the whole time, or play for five minutes and be satisfied. The art style isn't that great, basically it looks like someone drew it on a piece of notebook paper, which fits with the "Not GTAV" theme as if someone was doodling this game in class at school.
It's hard to write an in-depth review of a game that has no depth. If it looks fun, you'll probably enjoy it, but if you don't like Snake or GTAV, don't get it. It's as simple as that. I had fun with it, and if you can't afford GTAV then this is the next best thing.

BLUE REVOLVER is an excellent STG game, and easily equals (and probably supasses imho) many of the Japanese classics that inspired it. The scoring system revolves around building short chains (thankfully limited to 8 enemies) and using a special weapon to activate a multiplier. This makes scoring a bit less strict than older chain scoring STGs like DoDonPachi, and more free form. Cashing out your chain with your special weapon also makes enemy ships explode into giant pieces of gold. This is intrinsically good "gamefeel," and probably why Mars Matrix and Espgaluda 2 are classics. The other main scoring mechanic is colecting BREAK bonuses by meeting special conditions during stages (killing 90% of enemies in one section), destroying parts  of boss ships, etc. Scoring higher causes the game to increase in rank aka difficulty, by adding denser bullets and adjustments to boss patterns, and dying drops your rank. A bar at the top of the screen shows what rank you're in (green is easiest and red is the hardest). The graphics are excellent and when I die I feel like it was due to my own mistakes rather than visual clutter.
There are three difficulty modes: "Normal" where ranked is locked to the green section and gives you an autobomb, which is effectively severaly extra lives (good for shmup n00bs), "Hyper" where rank affects your credit the most, and "Parallel" where rank is locked at maximum at all times and theres also a special last boss if you're strong enough to get there. I'm not yet ;-( There's also 24 short training missions which teach  STG basics and scoring mechanics (plus some that are extra challenges like bullets that disappear), and there's a robust stage select system that lets you set the rank and starting point per stage.There's even a hitbox viewer that shows everyhit box, not just the player's but the hit box for every enemy and shot. Very cool option and idk why other STGs don't have it....
The controls are responsive, my DS4 works without a 3rd party program (and i'm assuming my PS4 stick will work as well but it weighs 15 lbs and i don't want to drag it over to my computer I haven't tried yet). The UI is thankfully designed with a computer in mind, so no doujin game quirks like keys you can't rebind or limited graphics options like you might get in a console port...
What else? The graphics look very nice, and I like the color palette! There's unlockables like backgrounds and remixed music! Two different ships with differnt special weapons offer offensive firepower or defensive options like absorbing/slowing down bullets! Great music, my favorite is the stage 4 track which sounds like a goofy middle eastern disco party! And  the all important waifu component! (Val btw)
BLUE REVOLVER is really good and a lot of fun, Stellar Circle put a lot of love into the game and it shows. You could even say its a "stellar" game ;-) ;-) ;-) ;-) My one complaint is that the announcers don't shout BOMBA every time you press the bomb button ;-( If you have any interest in STGs at all please buy this game!!!!!!!!

If you like shmups, buy this game. If you don't, this is an excellent introduction. It's not 1993 anymore so you get adjustable difficulty modes, a mess of different ships and weapons to play with, stage select right away, and a bunch of tutorial/challenge missions. It looks good and sounds good and feels good to just dodge around blowing stuff up to get points (BLUE REVOLVER respects the deep-seated gamer urge to collect gold cubes).
Veterans will recognize echoes of older games - there's a little Dodopachi, a little Garegga, a little Mars Matrix... but rather than a rehash it's the feeling of someone who is steeped in these games and came out with something new. The scoring system is more approachable and more fun than the punishing chain systems of yesteryear. The Break system combines the best parts of having weird secret stuff (like Garegga's flamingoes) with mid-level optional challenges (like getting the stage 3 1up in Dodonpachi). You get to duel a dang jet with vulcan cannons.

A modern shmup classic that's designed as a love letter to the entire genre from CAVE to Raizing to somewhat more obscure entries, yet still manages to bring its own unique flavor to the table.
The game's brimming with personality starting with just the distinctive palette, character designs and cast of announcers to a pretty thoughtful yet light and colorful framing for the action and thankfully the attention to detail goes past just the aesthetics and the OST - the general flavor of the bullet spreads is fast, with medium densities and combined with the design of the sprites makes the readability of every frame certain and pairs well with the lack of stereotypical slowdown while giving it its own sort of frantic pacing further emphasized in the methodically designed boss battles. But just like in the CAVE classics, regardless of the difficulty setting there's always a way out of every possible combination of bullets flung at you, and any configuration of attacks can be safely passed by with precise enough timing, your craft's hitbox is tiny and bullets have slightly softened edges to give you a little extra leeway, and if that somehow sounds forgiving, try pushing the rank system or outright play on 'Parallel mode'.
Survival has the game pushing back on you with its 'rank' variable that gradually raises the ferocity of enemy patterns in response to your continued success, increases it faster for elaborate scoring or lowers it with deaths. On top of making the challenge more dynamic, it provides the backbone for the three difficulty modes set apart mainly by locking it within a boundary and a couple more minor details(like the extend numbers and autobombing), which assures a smooth transition from one to the next.
But since unlike a number of games that inspired it with their focus on perfect execution, BR wants you to organically play around with all the kinds of available resources be it ammo, bombs or even the relatively plentiful lives, the impact of rank on your play never feels like an act of spite as much as a constant reminder to utilize everything at your fingertips.
Yet unlike some of the older games with rank systems like Ibara or Garegga which could start to feel almost malicious in nature if you kept doing well without actively trying to push your rank down, BR's was designed to be survivable the whole way through even when it's turned all the way up, which is also essentially what Parallel mode happens to be.
Scoring play is incredibly easy to pick up and blends with survival very well, moreso than any of the typical beginner recommendations for the genre - blow up a small chain of enemies with your primary shot and get rewarded with much bigger points through a briefly lasting point multiplier as you annihilate the reinforcements with your special weapon or even a bomb(which is frequently advantageous to do), the sound cue makes it easy to know when you can let loose, though doing that mindlessly will make you lose track of all the alternate, more efficient ways to score through keeping enemies alive to have a full chain ready for a later big enemy, extending the duration of your multiplier through bombs or just doing 'breaks' - BR's term for small challenges you get in the middle of play that involve a variety of tricks including dismantling enemy parts, not causing damage to others or ending a boss' pattern with a specific timing. Highlighted by both green sparks that pop up on break-related objects and 'shoot this/avoid hitting this' indicators, most are somewhat apparent while some will take a bit more attention to notice and a lot more to actually execute correctly.
Combine that with the aforementioned approach to resources and you have a game that'll make you change up your play run after run, the penalties for small scoring mistakes never feel overwhelming and change your pattern of special weapon use for a period every time - alternating your 'breather spots', the breaks can be learned gradually, your bombs can be used liberally for a multitude of valid reasons and you have an elegant design that's simultaneously great for beginners just trying to get a grasp on the genre and more experienced players improvising their way through.
And if all that somehow doesn't sound like enough to provide a varied run-to-run experience, you have your pick of two pilots that influence the ship's weapons in a way, three classic primary shot types and eight different special weapons, some pilot-specific, some slightly different depending on the pilot chosen, each filling its own role and bringing its own set of (dis)advantages to be considered.
In addition, the game features a challenge mode that has content that'll similarly both please experienced players with a bit of extra variety and help beginners push their limits and learn skills that'll matter on an actual full run, including using the entire screen for your dodges as you get chased by a very unhappy bullet that can only be slowed down and never, ever stops, keeping enemies alive as you wait for your sole means of attack - a one-shot shrapnel charge - to come back after every blast, learn to move in a way that lets you ignore projectiles already past your trajectory as you grapple with bullets that vanish from sight on approach or just do the standard survival and scoring challenges arranged so that they still provide a better structured practice experience than pretty much anything else typical to the genre.
If you are even slightly interested in shmups, or just arcadey games in general or even happen to be on the fence about trying your luck at a bullet hell shooter, you should definitely be picking this one up!
Disclaimer: I've done some of the beta testing and translation for the title.

To preface, I'm someone who enjoys STGs but is bad at them, so this review will take place from that perspective.
Blue Revolver is a rare STG that is both accessible to, and accommodating for newcomers, but still offers a lot of challenge and scoring depth for hardcore genre enthusiasts.
The game is mechanically similar to most bullet hells on the face of it, but has a score system I think is something that most players can find enjoyment in throughout their playtime, as opposed to say, Mushihimesama, where many new players will ignore the system after the first level, if they are even aware of it to begin with. The flow of building up a short chain on weak enemies, then cashing it in on a group of more powerful foes and watching them explode in cascades of gold is so satisfying that I find myself taking big risks, even though as a player I'm only focused on survival. There's  also  a ton of variety in shot and special weapon types, so if the default isn't your style you have a lot of experimenting to do.
For players who aren't confident pitting themselves against an unbroken run, the game offers a Mission mode, with short, punchy challenges that start off simple and ramp up, each one building on the last. Some of the more creative ones are Invisible Bullet, where bullets disappear when they approach you, and Matador, where one large bullet relentlessly hunts you throughout the level. Far from being gimmicks, these missions teach newbies good shmup habits, like looking ahead to bullets and planning proactively rather than focusing solely on your ship, and moving around the screen rather than hugging the bottom edge.
Aesthetically the game is a joy, with a lot of love clearly being put into both the protagonist and the enemies, a rarity in STGs. The character designs and VAs are adorable, and will enamour the waifuhunters in the crowd. The enemy ship designs are somewhat boxy, but this choice seems to be deliberate, as it favours clarity in gameplay, for instance when deciding what part of a boss to target first.
The music is excellent, hard pumping electronic music that isn't too harsh or overbearing, but sets a tempo for the player to blast through the level with.
Overall, I think Blue Revolver is a game that can hold its own against the big boys of the genre, and is certainly the best Western-developed STG I've ever encountered.

Great fun. I found this game to be accessible for a new player to the genre with a scoring system that's simple to learn and satisfying to master. Playing on normal mode provides you with an autobomb feature, but it uses all of your remaining bombs. While this is a very useful feature and helps new players survive long enough to scrape together some skills, it's also not very efficient and ultimately pushes them to learn how to bomb defensively when things get tough. Although normal mode has been a challenging ride for a greenhorn like myself, there's also parallel and hyper modes for those players who are familiar with the genre and strong players looking for a challenge respectively.
The music, sound and visual style are all of a very high standard with a pretty polished UI holding it all together. It’s obvious that a lot of care has gone into ensuring that readability remains very high, even when a lot is occurring on screen without sacrificing any personality for each enemy type.
Mission mode does quite a good job at teaching new players vital skills for both scoring and survival. There are also some neat challenge ideas like matador - a big bullet that follows the player around the screen and experimental weapon - restricting the player to a slow charging special weapon only while taking away bombs.
One mild piece of criticism would be the game doesn't do the best job of communicating what the breaks are for each boss/level but most can be discovered through persistent play or a keen eye. This was mainly a problem for me when trying to figure out how to beat some of the missions.
i strongly recommend this game to both those familiar with shmups looking for a new, highly polished, well-constructed challenge and anybody looking to take first step into the genre.

Some time ago, on a steam sale I bought an unknown game by the name of hegmoney: Phillip of macadonia. A basic, rough little arcade RTS with some neat ideas. But despite its rough edges I ended up putting 110 hours into it because it was fun.
So imagine my delight at seeing Hegmoney rome on a bundle star sale. Ther latest game from the same devs, but with all the rough edges smoothed out. Wow was ever I mistaken in thinking that.
In fact this game is quite the opposite. The nice clean interface is gone, now its an eyesore of icons and walls of text boxes. The epic battles are gone, now you just end up with a mess of mobs brawling all over the place.  In fact its hard to find a mechanic they have not broken. The way my army eats, I can no longer put more than a hand full of units into the field as they end up starving to death. The econmy? No idea whats going on there as one minute I have hundreds of gold, the next I'm flat broke and my armies are rebelling.
They have added the ability to requisition/build camps etc and upgrade bases, but with the broken economy I never get the chance. Oh and they added a very basic diplomacy function. Woot.
But the real deal breaker is the bugs. They are the only legions you will find in this game. Units randomly vanishing (including Ceaser himself in one game), unit hot key assignments randomly change so you end up sending in the wrong uinits. Camera locking to the terrain forcing reloads, trigger points that don't trigger....and lag spikes and crashes. And often you need to click a unit multiple times before it will finally select, and often your units will not replensish as the game will give you the recruitment blocked message, even when there is nothing blocking it.
Sure the devs can find the time to create DLC, but not time to fix this mess. They can even find the time to start making an entire new game for a kickstarter - but still can't find the time to fix this broken mess.
The only pros I can think of, is the voice acting is generally good, and the music is also very fitting. Andf the mechanic to take hostages instead of having to garrison every town was nice.
If you want to see this game done right, then grab hegemony gold. Same devs (tho hard to believe) but none of the issues, crashes or broken mechanics, and a very good game with many hours of game time. If you want Rome then get one of the excellent total war series.
Luckily it was part of a bundle so I ended up with some good games, A shame this was not one of them.

I'd like to like this game. There are lots of good features. But then there are the bad ones, and they are frustrating enough to break the game for me. The supply lines for instance. And your so called allies will do nothing at all. Not even defend their own territory from raiders. So you'll have to hunt down every raider with cavalry. Though cavalry isn't strong enough to beat the unit, so you'll have to have a melee unit to beat the raiders, and then the cavalry to hunt them down. Unless they outrun the cavalry of course, which is a very real possibility. Then they'll just run outside the part of the map you are allowed to play on, reform and return later.
You can also set an autopause when a raider is spotted. But that could be while they are standing idle outside the area you can go to, and the next notification you'll get is that they've CAPTURED a camp, not entered your area or attacked your camp. And then your supply lines are tattered, which of course is logical and a nice feature, but each time you set up the supply lines it feels like a very unneeded micromanagement. Some raiders will continuously enter your area near a city. So I built some walls and battlements and put a unit of archers in the city. Now the raiders will run to the city and then stand their while my archers pick them off one by one, then flee back to their territory, reform and repeat.
Honestly, allies are the biggest problem I have with supply lines as well as I'm losing a majority of my goods when I transport stuff through their lands. And no, there is no possibility to break the alliance and annex their lands. And the description of the supply lines are that they go one way only for some unknown reason. Each line costs some gold to maintain, and each fort (which makes supply lines easier to manage) costs some gold as well. And even though everything is connected and you have a good surplus you can still get food shortages, and I don't know why or how to fix it. Well, remove some troops of course, but then you fix the symptoms and not the cause.
Combat is too fast to become really interesting. You could flank the enemy with your cavalry, but oftenly it takes too long time and your legions will have won the day before the cavalry arrives. Even though I got the DLC, combat is fast, short, easy and boring.
This is a lot of complaints, for a game that I think is pretty fun. It's just that it has/had the potential to be great. Upgrade system, town management and the zoomable map are all wonderful, but overall, I would not recommend this game. Sadly.

It's a great game.  A lot of the complaints I've seen from others are true, but they don't bother me.  I'd describe the game as a cross between Total War and Starcraft, and that is true in that it has RTS and strategic aspects, but that really doesn't do the game justice.   It's just massive.  I'm 9 hours into a campaign, and I'm about 25% finished.
Things I love:
1. The realistic complexity:  Walking your army through a small area without many farms may very well eat all their food and cause them to revolt.  Everything in the game has a cost/benefit, and the game designers clearly went to a great deal of effort to make the game feel authentic.
2. It's addictive:  I find myself playing for 5 hours and still wanting to "just finish this one thing".
3. The single player campaign:  It basically follows Caesar's accounts of his wars in Gaul.  If you've read his memoirs, you know the entire campaign because it pretty much follows it to the letter.  I was annoyed with the final fight with Vercingetorix.  I was expecting  massive attacks from all sides, but there was just a large army sent out from the city which I locked up in a choke point and took out with my archers with zero losses.
4. The seemless transition between the strategic and tactical map.  No other game I've played has ever tried this.  They've truly pushed the genre on this one.  It took a while to get the hang of it, but it works very well.  Sometimes, it works too well.  Imagine trying to fight 4 "Total War" fights simultaneously.  This happens and it can be annoying.  On the other hand, this is only happening because I'm pushing 3 armies up through Gaul at the same time while they are also attacking my flank.  That's awesome.
Complaints about the game:
1.  It's too easy.  Granted, I've been playing these games forever, so I'm good, but after your troops get upgraded, they just roflstomp any opponents.  This is partly because the computer doesnt attack smartly and partly because the computer upgrades its units stupidly.  The computer is, however, persistant, and if you don't cover your flanks, for both your army and your cities, you will be punished.  The first hour of a map is difficult with limited resources.  After that, I've got so much gold, food, and wood that I don't even bother to optimize my cities.
2.  Balance.  This is always difficult to do, and I realize that.  Getting experience for your archers is a pain, but once fully upgraded, archers with anything in front of them to tank just annihilate any opponent in about 2 seconds.  In fact, you really don't need anything tanking for your archers.  It's only a little helpful when you're in a 2v10 fight.
3.  Crashes.  My games crash about once ever 3 hours.  However, Total War also crashes about once every 3 hours.  I just save a lot.
All in all, I've played for 60 hours and I'm not ready to quit.    It's addictive, fun, and interesting.

I picked this up in early access due to my enjoyment of the Hegemony Gold game. It wasn't optimized then so I let it sit for a while. It is now decently polished, and optimized.
The Hegemony series is in antithesis of the dominant form of RTS (Starcraft Style). It is a slow playing ballet that builds over hours where a handful of units can have a large impact and a single raid can cause problems for an unwary empire. The way supply and manpower are handled in this series is brilliant, creating a very thoughtful style of gameplay that I would love to see more often.
The bigger your empire, the more difficult it is to protect it, and manage getting the needed food and manpower to the right place.
The four story campaigns follow the career of Caesar in Gaul in exacting detail. You will invade Britain, you will cross the Rhine, and you will see your province torn apart by rebellion. By the end of it you will feel like you have conquered the place yourself, and maybe feel a little shell shocked at having to deal with pesky raiders constantly picking at your flanks.
The game is by no means perfect. If you are not a patient gamer, or a thoughtful exploiter of gaming systems you may not enjoy it. The scope of the game might have been a little too ambitious for such a small studio, and it occasionally falls apart. It is slow to start, but that humble beginning only lets you appreciate the epic scope once you get there.
Pros
-Supply lines and manpower mechanics define how the game is played. Raids can be devastating, and concentrating an entire army in one place will often cause you to lose as you run out of food or your empire is picked apart by raiders.
-New Experience System lets you specialize Legions, and even promote officers from veteran legions to lead others.
-Flanking and positioning make an enormous difference.
-You can built forts and bridges, and customize cities.
Take it or Leave it
-Siege warfare is brutal. Better plan it out.
-Naval Warfare can be finicky
-Not a lot of different varities of unit, however the differences become very meaningful as you learn how to use them,
Cons
-Slow to start
-The supply mechanic is not for every gamer
-Not as flashy as a AAA title

EDIT: I'd like to apologize for the harsh way I expressed myself in my original review. I've altered my review and made it more constructive and less emotional, for anybody who may be interested.
Before I start off, I want to make it clear that while this game does give you choices in how you interact with the other characters (a grand total of about five times,) whatever you choose makes only an immediate impact on the dialogue. The main plot is set in tracks and will not be affected by your choices.
Now. Where to begin. 15 seconds into the game, I noted that the writing seemed beautifully descriptive. In no time, that sentiment was blugeoned to death with walls and walls (AND WALLS) of text. The writing quickly became overbearing, the author taking ridiculous amounts of time to reach a single point (and frequently, no point at all.) Everything (from the inner-monologue to the dialogue between characters) is ambiguous, but in an I'm-twelve-years-old-and-this-is-deep sorta way. Seriously. A lof of the things in this game make NO SENSE, from the narration to the dialogue between characters, you're often left very confused and wondering what you just read.
The depth and personalities of all of the characters suggest that the author has not been well-acquainted with original ideas. Every. Single. Chracter. Is. A. Trope. There is not a single unique characteristic to be found in the whole lot. To add to the disappointment, despite there being *LARGE* amounts of time poured into the dialogue with all of the characters, you could take out every single one except the main hero and heroine and be left with the same exact story, only shorter and less painful to read. All of the other characters just seem like bells and whistles attempting to distract you from how dull the main storyline is.
(You're probably thinking, "If you hated it that much, then why the hell did you keep playing until you finished it????" The answer to this is because the whole way through, I was still holding out some hope for an interesting ending. Once I get into a story, as the curious sucker I am, I am compelled to see it through to its finish. Unfortunately, the ending did not justify the hours lost. The ending was actually probably the most disappointing part of this entire game. More details below, but beware of the spoilers.)
TL;DR/Conclusion: The plot isn't good, the writing isn't good, the characters aren't good, the art and music are mediocre.. it may not cost a dime, but I wouldn't recommend anyone put a second of their time into this game. I'd go as far as to say you'd probably be better off with any other visual novel out there.

This game is bite sized. I finished in just under 4 hours, with a completion rating of 80%. However, the gameplay is tight, engaging, and just the right level of difficulty based on skill.
Combat is simple but extremely malleable. The amount of damage you can mitigate/dodge/redirect is insane, and the combo system rewards everything you do, besides recieving damage.
Platforming sections are intriguing and use a combination of reflexes and crafty use of your powers. There are mild exploration elements, although most of these are dead-end puzzles with a reward at the end (think Tomb Raider reboot).
Although the game was short, I couldnt stop playing it, and spent an hour or 2 every day working through it, thoroughly intent on beating it before moving on to another game.
The final boss

Even if you're not familiar with the AVGN, this game still impresses as a throwback to the 8-bit Megaman games.  Yes, it's a lot harder, but they give you 30 lives and constant continue points on the normal difficulty, so it's not much of an issue.  It's very doable even with a keyboard.  Once you've memorized how to get past the hardest parts, and as long as you're taking your time, it's not even that bad.  Of course, the game basically taunts you into rushing head first into the various obstacles, and by the tenth time you've died to one, you end up playing so recklessly and "on tilt" that you just keep dieing, with the Nerd character giving a hilarious randomly generated complaint after each death.  The game is a bit short, like a traditional Megaman game (8 stages and an amazingly evil final stage) but for $10, it's totally worth the money.  There are a few secrets to find, like unlocking some bonus characters, and there's always the added replay value of trying to complete the game on the hard difficulty, which limits the number of lives and continues you get.

This game has a lot of potential. The mechanics are good, the pixel-graphics are wonderful, and the controls are tight. It would have been a great retro-styled platform game if it weren't so difficult.
It seems that the team who made this game decided that making an ultra-difficult game would either be funny, or a fitting homage to the older 8-bit games that many us us grew up with (many of which owe their own difficulty to the quarter-eating business plans of arcdaes).
As others have mentioned; death will occur often in this game, and it would have been nice to be placed at the last checkpoint instantly (a la Hotline Miami) instead of being forced to sit through a screen with a "funny" AVGN quote after each death. The "death block" (tiles in the environment which kill you upon touch) are pretty annoying, and do seem to stem from the developer's need to artificially increase the diffictulty.
If you enjoy ultra-difficult games, perhaps you will enjoy this. I found it to be much harder than Contra; maybe more akin to Ninja Gaiden or Battletoads. Overall, I was disappointed because I found this to be more of a test of patience than a proper game.

There is no particular story to Agent 47 however each target you assassinate has a backstory and a reason as to why Agent 47 should kill them.

For anyone into pirate adventures and/or anyone into Warhammer games and lore this is a very decent game.
I initially came across this in early access and decided to support the devs by purchasing and waiting for release. The developers have done a great job at listening to the community and adding features and fixes for this game.
The game is more of a sandbox type of adventure than a story driven one and this fits a pirate game very well. Players can choose from a number of activities including piracy, treasure hunting, trading, quests, assassinations, spying and sacking the ports of one faction on behalf of another. You can recruit a variety of crew members to man and maintain your ship including several types of ship wizards and flying creatures.
The game does have a few rough edges including relatively 'serviceable' graphics. Still, it remains as much fun as ever as your crew faces down giant sea monsters and tries to outrun chaos fleets. I expect updates and features to continue to be added after release and indeed a new playable sub-faction has already been added (The Nurgle).

Alright, so I've read most of the reviews and I can tell you guys a few thing:
Most of the "this game is great" are from players who've been playing this game for years.
Cons:
Poorly translated. (Though this can easily be worked around/ worked with. And is sometimes comical
"it is cool time" instead of this spell is on cooldown)
This game is unfriendly to new players. (Sure people will be NICE to you and you'll get power leveled some but people will ditch you randomly or stop after a few minutes of power leveling)
The game is mostly lonely until you reach the levels that most of the community is at. (The game really doesn't start being fun until this point)
Leveling to 100 is probably the most boring part but after you get 100 more options for leveling / gear / skills open up and the game becomes more fun. (At current xp rates and playing solo it'll take ~20-30 hours of actual game time to get level 100 -note- this does not include being power leveled by friends/guilds/nice players)
Xp rates are VERY VERY LOW (You can buy xp boosts with real money and you also get "berries" which are similar to rested experience in other MMOs but cost 500,000 in-game gold to aquire as well as HOURS of logged out time)
Questing is NOT the most efficient way to level...in fact it's not recommended (grinding is really the only way to level)
Requires a lot of time, THIS IS NOT A CASUAL GAME.
Pros:
Near infinite skill combinations.
Whimsical classes / skills. (I mean being a Princess who can transform into a rolling log to crush her enemies or getting really fat and squishing them under her butt is pretty whimsical)
Leveling up / gearing up makes you feel powerful. (Starting off doing 1-2 dmg then doing 200-1000 then end levels 20,000 per hit makes you feel strong / accomplished)
Stable economy for trading (prices are pretty much set in stone and fluxuate slowly)
PvP is fun and different
Guilds add a sense of community
Rewarding if you spend your time correctly. (Gaining levels actually mean something in a game with 999 levels. A level 600 and 700 are two different worlds.)
The people on this game are nice. (Not all, but most)
All in all, this game is fun. I've played it for years so I know what to do when making a new character / starting over.
It's not new player friendly, but if you are a new player read blogs people have posted and it'll help you the best it can.
-If you try this game and really bite down and do your best you won't regret it-
If you sink time into this game it will be very rewarding.

Hello i have played a few mmo's so far, so i know a few things. This game is not for the casuals let's state that right now.
PROS
There's over 600 levels with a rebirthing system. You can use it to reset yourself back to level 1, this in turn gets you more stats and skill points.
Classes they have a some pretty cool classes, there aren't many games that offer some of the classes this game does.
Tamers/summoner's, this class is my favorite so far they can have two summons out as well as two pets. This game has the best pet system that i have found. As you level up, you can put skill points into your stats which upgrades your pets stats. You also get a skill, where you can ride one of your pets to increase your movement speed.
Stat points that's right this game has them. Most games are going complete casual, where you can't build your class how you want. As you level up you get stat points which you can put point's into to increase your characters proformance. You can pick a dps class and build tank, or you can sacrfice stats to increase your luck so you can find better gear, or increase your wisdom to increase exp ammounts.
Drop rates seem good, tons of stuff drops left and right.
CONS
graphic's are a bit out dated, mind you this game came out in 2003 from what i have found. If the gameplay is good the graphic's don't mean much to me.
Genderlock classes, this game did come out 2003. When this was acceptable, but it doesn't mean they can't change it now...
pay to win cash shop, yes you can pay for buff's the costumes you can buy increase stats a bit. Sadly this i can't give them a pass on this. It's an out dated system that shouldn't exist, league of legend/dota showed, you can survive without a pay to win cash shop. So why are they doing this? If anything there elimanting more people, because of the unfair advantages.
Clunky movement, and no v-sync option. This game has some pretty bad movement, at times you will seem to get stuck on nothing. Also the graphic option's are very limited, i can't even put on v-sync so i get screen tearing. I had to use nvidia control panel to do it, i still get screen tearing tho.
CONCLUSION.
Should you play redstone? It depends on if you like old school games, where they gave you freedom of choice. If you grew up in this time of gaming, where bad movement/graphics/pay to win cash shops was a thing then you found a pretty nice game.
However if you never played very many old games, nor grew up in the time i doubt you will like it. There's a lot of turn offs to the modern gamer, but it still doesn't mean you can't try. I say try the game, who knows you may like it. After all it is a free game, what do you have to lose?

We haven't had a decent PC golf game in quite a while; at $40 The Golf Club 2 is a good buy but it's even better at $15 as it has been during Steam sales. The negative reviews are mostly from people who find the game too hard or don't like that there's no multiplayer lobby/voice chat. It's also a very unforgiving game. Most golf games you master the swing meter within 10 or 12 rounds, then the game becomes about holing the ball from the fairway and shooting 36 under par every round. Not this one. You will need to use draw and fade and maybe not swing at 100% every time. You will struggle to make par, no doubt.
Things to know:
The game is unlicensed. There are no real courses (unless someone recreated one in the frankly kick♥♥♥♥♥course creator), real players, or real equipment.
You can play it with M+KB or a controller, it's up you you. Bear in mind that THERE IS NO SWING METER IN THIS GAME and that the tempo of your swing is important. Pull back slow but swing fast and you'll feel it.
Putting is ♥♥♥♥ing hard. The greens break like crazy and it's probably the most frustrating part of the game when you miss but the most satisfying when you connect. Fast greens are really ♥♥♥♥ing hard.
The game is, in general, extremely unforgiving. Better to lay up than overshoot a green by 40 yards and blow your round. For this reason, it's not super relaxing.
You have to have an internet connection, even for singleplayer (lame).
There's local multiplayer (which is fun with the Steam link) and you can also play against up to three other "ghosts" during your round- you'll see their shots but not their golfer's model. If you've played a particular course yourself before, you'll be one of the ghosts.
The only real customization in terms of skill is the three different levels of clubs. You don't power up skills or buy a better putter or balls that bite on the green more.
The three levels of clubs add a lot more control but also introduce a lot more difficulty. You can shoot par with the standard clubs but you're going to need to use the good ones to shoot 10 under.
Live handicapping!
You can spend ingame money on a few things: buying new outfits/hats/club paints, upgrading your personal Society clubhouse, joining or donating to another Society (such as GGG), and entering tournaments.

If you havent noticed yet- There is a love - hate relationship people have with this game.
If you expect a 3 click golf swing like golf games of old-and only want to play with that, do not get this game-
TGC2 only has a mouse swing or a game pad-game stick swing.   there is not a power meter like in the tiger woods series of mouse swing golf. I believe this is an added part of simulation they wanted in their game- Just like if you were on the course yourself you would not have a digital read out in front of your face for all of those dainty 'feel' shots youll need around the greens.  (there is a practice swing option) before you take your official swing.
For those of you having trouble using a game pad I can't speak for or against this as I have never tried one- the swing mechanics I am addressing are for mouse swing.
Just like reviews you may see on amazon where people complain about an item- same item you have and have found nothing wrong with it... the difference?  You read the directions.  You took the time to see how your item works.

The course editor is really good too- It could use more objects.  The customization of your golfer and clothing and clubs is very vast.
the ball physics are realistic- the graphics, although a little washed out are very good- Blame the unity engine for that.
the online play is excellent-  it could use a little more explanation on how to play live with a friend over the internet.. but believe me.. It Does work.  (remember to check turn order box people)
TGC2 is getting a bad rap from those who say the shot outcome is not consistent.. its their swing thats not consistent.
It could also be the mouse that people are using or the area where their mouse is placed that is giving them poor shots. lets face it, some golf gamers are not todays gamer where they set the dpi of the mouse and have a clean, particle free area for the mouse to glide over--  ever see some peoples computer set up?   coffee spills and crumbs everywhere.
ok im being nice- it could also mean that they just are not that good and wont take the time or have the patience to get better.  (or maybe they think they should be shooting lights out)   So far, i havent come close to shooting par-
I can live with that.  The game does not hold your hand.  When I miss a shot I know why.
There are hundreds of thousands of courses to play- this is not always a good thing- the majority of courses are just courses someone generated using the course generator and uploaded it without so much as taking a second look or tweaking the course- For this they need to clean up the data base- there is a rating system (5 stars) I feel that any course that has been played 100 times and didnt get a 3 or better rating should be removed. The good courses have been worked by true artists and some of them are quite amazing.
I use a track ball mouse with a large track ball- I think it allows for a better feel on those subtle shots that are aggravating people.  I do wish they would institue a horizontal mouse movement though.( at this time there is only a vertical- pull back and go forward)
Over all I give TGC2 a 7.5 out of 10
