note: plenty of bugs but at the time of writing this review the devs have already fixed some of them. i've crashed/froze twice in 13hrs of gameplay but luckily the game autosaves frequently. also i've only played the singleplayer campaign and random maps against bots on normal & hard difficulties.
IF YOU'VE PLAYED COSSACKS BEFORE:
like other reviews have said, it is basically a remaster of oldschool cossacks. for $20 it's not only a great nostalgia trip, but also still a good solid RTS game, which is rare these days (and the campaign so far is much improved). the only disappointments are that there isn't much innovation at all besides the graphics upgrades, and the rough launch it has had.
IF YOU'VE NEVER PLAYED COSSACKS:
at it's core, cossacks is a unique RTS which is easy to get into but very difficult to master. you can play this casually, sitting back and building up massive armies and growing your economy, or viciously, conducting tactical strikes and capture raids. the economy and tech tree (if you can even call it that) is quirky compared to streamlined starcraft and C&C games. getting a handle on moving your units in formation and using their strengths & weaknesses can be a bit tough for new players, but very satisfying once you figure things out. this RTS is not about having an apm of 9999999 and building as many units as possible, but rather about maintaining a balanced army and economy, and using tactics and smart formations to decisively crush your enemies.

This game is to inconsistent. I believe they're working on both the mechanics, and some of the inconsistent ball play, but this game is touted as a realistic simulation experience. I'm a casual gamer, and I find it extremely frustrating that this game, at its current state, is based heavily on luck. Forget playing it with a mouse, which is fine. I use a controller, and any difficulty besides easy makes my swing so unreliable. My stick skills are above average, but even the slightest deviation sets your ball on its own path. Some gamers may feel this is realistic. I do not. Lastly, forget depth. There is no depth to this game. You have online societies, in which you can play tournaments and improve your clubhouse. That's it. If you're a golf enthusiast, who is also a gamer, and don't want a realistic experience, and don't require depth, or the ability to upgrade clubs, your golfer, or accessories, this game is for you. The course designer, I hear, is amazing. I truly don't hate this game. It's definitely not for me and I think the devs need another year or two to develop this game further. I was hoping for a cross between realistic golf, with good online play, and EA’s golf. I can’t knock them for creating a game that wasn’t what I wanted, but I can knock them for the mechanics, inconsistencies, and lack of creativity, depth, and realism. All told, I love this game. It has enough variables (swing , tempo, lie, wind, etc.) to make it feel like you're really playing golf, and that's a wonderful thing. I play with a wireless mouse, and after a lot of practice I can control it with a pretty high degree of accuracy. Two problems stick out for me at the moment:
1) This game crashes, repeatedly, and locks up my entire computer when it does. There's no way that a released title should be this unstable. (Fortunately, you never lose any gameplay data when it goes down.)
2) Sometimes, seemingly out of nowhere, iron shots just don't carry like they should. This is not just a duffer's complaint. Literally, for a few holes I'll lose a good 10+ yards on clubs I hit all the time. Of course, golf is always a guessing game as far as distance is concerned, but over 100 hours of gameplay makes me believe that something is actually wrong with the distance mechanic.
Still, I really get a kick out this game. Never played TGC 1, so I can't make any comparisons there.

Okay so this game really needs no review. Published in 2003 by Bioware. This is the game that brought the company to whole new levels. Before Mass Effect there was Star Wars: Knight of the Old Replublic. This game built off their already amazing list of CRPG's like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale series. This was their first experience doing a 3d game and so much yes.

Pros
1. The F'in writing. Back when Bioware cared more about us than their EA masters. They actually crafted wonderful stories without multiplayer shoehorned in. One of the few games where a twist works. The ending shocked me the first time as I usuallly can guess the story arch.
2. The sounds. They got alot of sounds/songs from the SW universe and they sound great for how old the game is. Hell they sound decent compared to the new SW Battlefront games.
3. The Characters. People feel like they're more alive than alot of "AAA" games craft. Hell more so than Mass Effect 3 or Andromeda.
4. The Followers. Your followers are people that have cares/desires/feelings. This isn't important in every game but in rpg's it helps you get pulled into the world. I can't tell you how many times I've just watched characters banter and was just loving their reactions to each other. Also Bioware gave you 9 companions to try out different dialogue choices.
5. Combat. This is the fun part. Playing with blasters and lightsabers with the combat is awesome. I think they could have used a few more abilities but thats just me nit picking.
6. Replayability. Since this game is where Bioware birthed/perfected its morality system you can be good, evil, an jerk, or just a normal guy not sure about his future. Since every play through has its own unique experience, there are nice subtle and not subtle differences when going back to do this.
Meh
Now as far as the graphics are concerned its rather okay considering the game is over 14 years old and Bioware really doesn't remaster games. Its still better than GTA San Andreas. But if they would update this masterpeice for newer audiences it could be amazing.
The controls are a little jankie at first but after you get used to how it works its easy to move around.
Cons
I really can't think of any besides maybe it needs a remastered version. I know theirs a mod to update the graphics a bit but c'mon Bioware this game spawned an MMO.
Summary
So this game is what solidified my love of Bioware. I played Baldures Gate, BG2 Shadows of Amn, Icewind Dale, and Icewind Dale 2, ME1-3, SW KoToR 1 and 2 and I have to say this : one of the best games they ever created. The love and hard work put into this game shines throughout multiple playthroughs makes this game run on all cylinders all the time.  If their was a rating for this game its an easy 10/10. This is what rpg games should aspire to. You don't need hundreds of fetch/kill quests in an open world to make it feel as alive and well crafted as this. Between the well written story and loveable characters(discover them yourself and watch the banter) its hard not to love this game. As far as my top rpg games it sits at number two. Tied with Legend of Dragoon for the original Playstation. For PC games it's at number one. Right above Fallout 3 and C&C Red Alert. If you haven't had a chance to play this PICK IT UP! Yes the graphics are a bit out dated but if you are fan of RPG's you have to play this. You owe yourself as a gamer to play this gem!

I really love pirate games and I'm a big fan of Warhammer so when I first saw this game on Steam months ago I was very excited for it. After watching lots of videos and others playing the game, I decided it was still a bit too raw for me to give it an honest go and waited it out. So when it finally got a full release and put early access behind it, I was excited to finally give it a chance and expected a much improved game since then.
Unfortunately, I really couldn't be more disappointed with it. Overall it's buggy as hell and very unpolished, controls and UI are clunky, the game mechanics are sloppy and poorly executed and the animations are so bad they're comical. Your characer looks like they're trying to power walk around looking for the toilet before they explode and in boarding combat the NPCs move like they're under water. In my time playing the game I boarded dozens of ships and most were spent fighting the enemy crew while I was floating far above the masts or above the water outside of the ships.
This same thing tends to happen with ships themselves as you can be sailing around outside of combat, just ferrying cargo to sell or something and your ship will suddenly start getting smashed about by invisible forces and then literally fly hundreds of feet into the air and spin about. Now, these aren't even bugs that happen every once in a while. They happen consistently, so much that the game is virtually unplayable. Custom matches against the AI are even worse and in most of the ones I tried I was spawned inside of towns or mountains and unable to move as my ship was constantly in a grounded state.
I can understand giving the game positive reviews while it was in early access, and even with all this going on I might have done the same just because it has the potential to be something great and I'd have loved to support it. But bottom line here, releasing the game in it's current state tells me that that potential isn't going to be seen if the developers think it's ready as it is. Add this game to the list of Warhammer/40k games that didn't pan out and if you're interested in pirate games try something like Tempest or Black Flag instead. According to Steam, I spent too much time playing the game trying to give it a chance to get a refund but hopefully this review steers some others away or at least let's them know what they're in for.

I hope this review fairly examines both the qualities and flaws of Hegemony: Rome in equal measure. Most other reviewers seem to be firmly entrenched as die-hard supporters, or enraged that this isn't "Rome: Total War 3."
Pros:
-Surprising historical accuracy. I alt-tabbed to check wikipedia a few times and was always pleasantly surprised. Hegemony: Rome does a great job of putting you in Caesar's sandals.
-Fantastic, seamless zoom-out world map. The world map is intuitive and looks exceptionally well. A tastefully done "seamless zoom" has been promised by strategy games for years and this one actually delivers.
Cons:
-General clumsiness in controlling units and the camera. Units also seem to alternate between odd rigidity and ending up locked in combat while seemingly doing nothing. The strange combat model ultimately makes it difficult to engage in the kind of tactical maneuvers you might expect from a game about Classical warfare.
-Supply system that's heavy on micromanagement and light on strategic decisionmaking. The dilemmas and opportunity costs which should drive major decisions just don't exist here. Basically you're always trying to feed your legions in the field, and to do so you're required to individually create "worker" units, designate mines or fields for them to use, and then manually create supply routes to-and-from cities and outbuildings. There is also little UI in this regard - a list of trade routes sortable by destination/origin or some color coding options would help.
Overall: 5/10. There appears to be no extra metagame choices offered by Hegemony: Rome's potentially interesting supply and resource systems. Instead we're left with a clumsy "Warcraft:Rome edition" that requires some mindless micromanagement on top of a stale combat system. I am looking forward to what extra patching and mods do to the game, but only the biggest strategy buffs should buy Hegemony: Rome in it's current state.

Sepia Tears is a F2P Visual Novel which has a rather romantic plot structure to it. The story is perhaps one of the best I have seen in while, at most times remaining cryptic and mysterious until the final part of the game came around. Now not giving much away about the ending but I personally found it very satisfying and the build up really made you emotionally invested in the protagonist so it made the ending that much more impacful. The game takes around 4-5 hours to complete depending on how fast you read and what choices you make. Now I have only played through this once and got the good ending, but I am assuming there are some other (worse?) ones (When I play a VN that is heavy in the feels, I tend not to even look up nor play the bad endings). Overall this game has a solid story, a solid soundtrack, and solid artwork, A must play for any visual novel fan, and hey its free (which is actually rather suprising for a game this refined).
Verdict: 7.5/10

Booted up Hitman: Blood Money two days ago, after having not played it since 2006 or 2007.
Just beat it today.
Few things I found interesting about it:
- It's a 2006 PC port. You can run it at 4k just by making an ini edit, and it's flawless (doesn't break the UI or anything).
- As far as tech issues go, there was a bit of stuttering I fixed by going into the launcher and enabling both of the SLI settings (even though I'm not on SLI), but after that, game ran like it was made for my system. Then a lot of newer games have all these compatability issues and such until they're patched... were the people who made this game just better at what they did? Or have engines become so massive and unwieldy that it's more likely that things are going to fail than work? Or a combination of both?
- I had no bugs whatsoever.
- It has a first-person and third-person view - I know games did it even sooner, but I still think it's weird how a game from 2006 had this feature, and then it was a "big deal" when the GTAV re-release introduced a first-person mode.
- obviously the textures and lighting are a bit dated, but the game still looks great. I think it's almost the perfect balance between the awkward 3D years where I couldn't believe any of it was real because it was too ugly, and nowadays where everything that goes for this style is hyper-realistic and immersion breaking because of it. This game is actually better looking to me than a lot of modern games that have that hyper-realistic plastic-surgeon-with-OCD look.
- the music is still phenomenal, of course
- the game doesn't pester you or tell you explicitly how to do everything. There are a lot of hints on the lower difficulties (on the map), but if you want to play it as a proper stealth game, you have to figure out how all the pieces fit together on their own. It has a lot of space. The game is challenging in its own way, but due to the way it's all set up, it's actually relaxing to play. I'm not being yelled at or expected to be somewhere constantly or being given game information nonstop because the people who made it were afraid that if the game stopped talking to the player for 10 seconds I would shut it off and leave. I can just enjoy it without being nagged and feeling rushed along because of the "look here, do this, look here, shoot this" mentality. It lets you play.
- the worst thing about it is some character model pop-in, like the game runs a lower-poly version of them in the distance and when you get close makes them proper (I don't think I would've noticed this during my PS2 playthrough when it was new, but on PC at high-res and everything cranked it's pretty obvious)
- To boot every level is its own theme. If any copy-paste is going on it's minimal. There's more variety in the levels in a five hour game than I even saw in DOOM. Blood Money is genuinely interesting to play and anyone who hasn't played it yet needs to get it over with and understand why most people rant about most games. Once you have the best of everything, there's just a bunch of s*** you wade through hoping to find another game like Blood Money.
- Probably the best thing about it - it doesn't overstay its welcome. I played it on Expert (hadn't played in a loooong time so why would I Pro?), and beat every level with a Ghost, Professional or Silent Assassin rating, in just over 5 hours. I did remember some of the levels, but for the most part, I was blind here. It's refreshing, because they could've gone longer, they could've recycled assets to stretch it out, but why? Why do games need to last "forever"?
I did reinstall Absolution out of curiosity.  I ran it at max settings except for FXAA (which only blurs the image).  Even though the tech Absolution uses is way better, and the textures are obviously much higher res, the game isn't as nice to look at as Blood Money.
Tech isn't everything. But when you don't know how to make a good game (something that I think needs to be a natural talent, like writing a good song or a good script - a few people have it, most people don't), you can at least learn how to push tech.  And I think those are the majority of people making games these days, which is why going back to Blood Money is... holy♥♥♥♥♥♥.. most games really *are* as bad as I think they are.
But Blood Money is a masterpiece.

I bought this game over a year ago and remained optimistic throughout the beta and early access cycle. Even while the final version was downloading, I was hoping Atari would pull the rabbit out of the hat. That optimism was immediately shattered when I was greeted with a black screen on launch. Luckily I was able to find the problematic files and delete them.
Yes my reason for this is mostly over that one bug, which apparently affects only people who installed the game while it was still in early access. But it's not the fact that the bug exists and prevented game play, but the handling of it by the Atari and Nvizzio.
When I found out I was unable to play, I immediately took to the community page and found the post saying the release was out, accompanied with instructions on deleting a file if you have problems. That didn't work. Instead it took me deleting the entire folder. Then I watched as developers and producers spent the day telling people to delete files in hidden folders and edit the registry. These are things even Microsoft advises against, especially editing the registry.
We are talking about a bug that could easily be remedied with a dozen lines or so of code and a hot fix. Instead the developers opted to have users jump through hoops, access parts of their system that shouldn't be accessed by the average user, and risk doing irreparable harm to their operating system. This is one of the biggest failures in not only public relations, but also custom service I have ever witnessed. I have been doing development for 30 years and the past 15 years has been as the owner of my own company. If I ever even dreamed of taking this approach to a failure on my part, I would expect to close the doors the next day, and rightfully so.
The latest release in the series I have loved for years has been fatally plagued by this decision from the publisher and developers. I was hopeful for improvements and expansions to RCTW, but after the lack of response over yesterday's problems, it's painfully obvious that we most likely won't see these, when they won't even fix a bug that was known at release, and causing a PR nightmare. Shame on Atari and shame on Nvizzio.

This is a functional tower defense game.
Good features:
-- Mazing.  It allows for free placement of towers, rather than be limited to a few fixed locations.
-- Uber Towers Limited.  It has a couple of uber towers, but balances them out by throttling their ammunition replenishment so that their ubers effects are not continuous.
-- Nice Graphics.
-- Upgrades.  The layered choices in tower upgrades gives the feeling of more strategic choices, instead of the common approach in other TD games where you have a simple upgrade path and you always upgrade towers to the max.
Caveat:  I only played the single player game.
Cons:
-- A couple of the towers I never found a use for.  I don't know whether they are glitched, or I simply missed the point of where they would be useful.
-- You must (of course) always have a valid path.  However, sometimes with a complicated maze, the game won't allow you to place a wall or tower in a valid location, because the changed path is too complicated.  The solution is to restart the level and change the order of placing towers so that you don't try to force a change from one complicated path to a completely different complicated path.
Eyeballing Required.  I may have missed these features, but at least as far as I know there are no options to pre-show the path the mobs will follow or to show a grid for tower placement.  This can result in misjudging the space so that you can't place a tower where you intended, or misjudging whether or not the mobs can pass thru a given narrow space.  A partial solution is that you can plan out your placement by placing walls, which are cheap and also function as the foundations for towers.

Do I recommend this game? Yep, I sure do! I did back when it came out in 2016, and I recommend it even more now that you can play the PVP aspect for free!
What is Battleborn? It's somewhere between a MOBA and a Borderlands-y FPS. If you're in it for PVP, it's an objective-based first-person action game with a plethora of characters to choose from (all of which DO handle uniquely; no two characters play quite the same). If you're in it for Story Mode, there are 8 missions (+1 tutorial and 5 DLC stories), and a treasure trove of unlockable Lore (accessed by completing character-specific challenges), all of which are indefinitely replayble for bonus XP and Loot. There's a lot to explore!
Whether you're playing PVP or Story, one thing to note is that your characters don't "level up" permanently, every character starts every mission/match at level 1 (bar one PVP mode where everyone starts at level 3) and levels up during the course of the match (up to 10). Level ups unlock bonus multipliers and mutations on your characters' abilities, giving a sense of scale to each match. Outside of missions, your characters do "rank up", unlocking additional OPTIONS for mutation during a match, or cosmetic rewards such as skins and taunts. Point is, no matter how new you are to the game, everyone starts every match at level 1, so if you get stomped, it's only because your opponent has more time/skill under their belt or a better team composition. Remember, Battleborn may be famous for not having many players, but the few who ARE here have been here for a LONG time.
If PVP against long-timers sounds scary (it sure is for me!), you can also play against bots or find some friends and play a private match together. I like story mode personally, mostly cause I just enjoy Gearbox's goofy, playful writing style, and I really enjoyed learning about each character by playing them (TIP: bring different characters to different missions, as certain characters will give bonus dialog in some key spots). The DLC operations are probably my favorite, because while the missions themselves are pretty short, replaying them again and again will give you different dialog as you learn more about the story (each mission requires 10 playthroughs to hear the whole thing, and hitting all the bonuses in each playthrough will give character-specific cosmetic rewards).
If nothing else, Battleborn fills a very specific niche that a number of other games do not. There's certainly a lot TO it, and now that you can try it for free, I recommend you ignore all the negativity you heard about the game when it came out and see if you like it!

The game is fantastic. The combat is solid with very tight and intuitive controls, enemies are challenging and boss fights are a blast. The only exception to this rule is the final boss fight, which is a obnoxious borderline cheap fight. Combat is relatively simplistic. You have basic attacks, grapple moves, and a dodge. You are also equipped with three special moves doled out at various parts of the story. Chaining melee moves, throws, and specials are seamless and fluid. Getting into a rhythm against a horde of monsters is easy and exhilarating, but missing a hit or being knocked out of a combo can be devastating.
Mastering the move set isn’t the only thing you need to do, you need to know how to take care of a group of enemies by identifying the ones that must go down first. The game has a relatively small enemy list, making it easy to remember enemy patterns and strengths. It’s this knowledge that you have to gather and remember as you make your way through the story. Do you take out the enemies lobbing projectiles at you, or do you take care of the quicker enemies first? That depends on a lot of factors you have to compute immediately when a fight starts. Not doing this may result in a very high death rate.
The one complaint I have of the combat system is that enemy attacks that have a wider area of effect tend to have hella spotty hitboxes. The animation of an arcing attack may hit your character and deal appropriate damage, while the same animation of the same arcing attack another time may hit your character in the same frames of animation and never register a hit. Or an attack that your character was well out of the animation may still be hit for no reason. It isn’t all the time, but it is enough to become noticeable.

Kaptain Brawe is a reminder that not all adventure games are equal…in fact, some really suck. No, it’s no Jolly Rover, but it’s no Maniac Mansion, either. But dammit if it doesn’t try. You can switch between characters, it has a somewhat similar look and feel to Curse of Monkey Island if it was fused with the later Space Quests…but it doesn’t entirely work.  The puzzles often don’t make much sense and as a result, you have a lot of obscure puzzles mixed with a bit of ho-hum dialogue. You could certainly do a lot worse (Jolly Rover), but it’s not entirely terrible.
Honestly, for the price, I MIGHT recommend it…but only if you really, really like point and click adventure gaming.

After putting in 13 hours as an illustrious Bretonnia privateer, I'd say this game is a buy. If you're a fan of open world, sandbox games, Sid Meier's Pirates! and Warhammer Fantasy, this is right up your alley.
The world is large and varied enough but I will say that the landmasses and towns are generic-ish and not noteworthy.
The ship designs are great, from normal human cannon ships, rammers and galleys to more inspired floating or flying ships, drakeships and lumbering Orc hulks. Overall each of these ships plays differently and is enjoyable (shout out to the Chaos Blood ship!).
Further, most of the WHFB races appear to be represented in some fashion (missing lizard men, ogres and some others) and each is unique in their design.
Ship upgrades offer two distinct paths, you can build into a speedy trader, or a more military vessel but there isn't much more beyond that. The addition of magic and flyers though adds more depth to ship expansion (also magic is very fun).
However, the combat is by far the glaring issue with the game. It feels incredibly sluggish and unresponsive. If you're coming from a Mount and Blade style background, you  will likely get frustrated with what the controls and reaction from your character.
Overall, if you're a fan of open world sandboxes and making your own fun/story, then Man O' War: Corsair is for you. Whether you enjoy sacking dirty Estallian rat holes, moving food or spices from Erengrad to Lyonesse or tackling the giant Magadon, Corsair has enough to suit most comers.

I cannot in good conscience recommend Man O'War: Corsair. It's clunky, it's ugly and it doesn't run well on my fairly powerful machine even with everything turned down or off. Maybe it gets better later on, but I can't muster the drive to push through the issues that I faced in my short time with this game. If you're interested in why that is, read on:
I haven't played the boardgame version, but I like the Warhammer world, Fantasy moreso than 40k, and I liked the sailing parts of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, so I thought I might like this too. The concept is interesting enough: Roam around the seas along the coast of the Old World and basically do whatever you like. Be a pirate, merchant or a mercenary, fight for one of the factions, look for treasure, fight huge sea monsters - whatever you want. Sail one of the many varied types of ships, not all of which rely on sails for movement. It sounds cool. The problem is the implementation.
I have a relatively powerful machine (i7@3.3 GHz, GTX 980, 16 GB RAM), but even on the lowest settings, this game won't run at a stable 60 fps. In clear weather the framerate fluctuates between 40 and just below 60. In fog and fleet-to-fleet fights it tanks to around 20. This is not acceptable in a game with graphics this dated.
It looks old. The texture quality is low, the animations are awkward, slow and stiff, the weather effects are crude. Even the menus are ugly; while the backgrounds have a nice look of parchment, buttons are just kind of plasteres on top and don't fit in at all.
Most of the sound effects didn't stand out positively or negatively, but the crew's barks are repeated annoyingly often, especially when the ship's turned into favourable winds. Yes, first mate so-and-so, I know the ship's the right way round. I did that on purpose. Please only warn me if I fail to realise I'm sailing directly into the wind. Weapon effects are decent, but I can't comment on the music with my short amount of playtime.
This is another big dealbreaker for me; It's almost nonexistent. Thinking back to Black Flag, I think the difference is that the ship in Corsair doesn't interact with the water quite as nicely. It feels like it's gliding along to smoothly even when the waves look like there should be more movement. Maybe a bit of a bigger splash when hitting a wave would've helped, or a convincing bow wave. Storms don't seem to have much impact - the waves go a bit higher, that's about it; the ship doesn't seem to go faster or have more trouble. In a blizzard, the snowflakes moved around more erratically than the wind should've allowed, seeing as the wind blew steadily in one direction. In fact, the snowflakes moved in the opposite direction of the wind most of the time.
Either the crews are too small or the ships have too many cannons. The starter ship seems to have about half a dozen cannons on either side, and with only three sailors I was able to fire at 100 % efficiency.
Another part of immersion that didn't work out for me are ports. They're basically glorified menues. The areas are very small and lifeless. Almost no one is walking around, and every interactable is either a market stall with a stoic, static merchant, or a closed door. There's no chatter, no flavour. Combined with the stiff animation of your captain running around it just does nothing to make me feel like I'm actually there. And since even running is pretty slow, I've spent more time in these ports than I'd like. Maybe it would have been better to just make them actual menus with some nice art.
Okay, ship-to-ship combat is about the same as in Black Flag, so I like it. You aim your broadsides, you fire, you try to stay in favourable winds and move so you're not too easy to hit. Every ships has several areas that take damage seperately and, if destroyed, impede the ship in some way. What's missing is a brace button. I wouldn't have thought that bracing made a difference - it's only one button, after all - but it makes combat a bit more involved and enticing. On the other hand, the sheer variety of enemy ships makes for some good encounters. Early on, I faced a fleet that included two fast ships with huge drills mounted to the prow. I barely avoided each, then fired a broadside that disabled their engine (yes, they didn't rely on the wind). The same fleet also contained ships with catapults. A Skaven ship I found later had some sort of poison wind dispenser at the prow and another type of engine which made it hard to avoid. I know that ships can have flying units accompany them, and they can be upgraded with specific defences against flyers. There are wizards of varying kinds that seem to have great utility. In short: Combat requires different tactics depending on the enemy.
Hand-to-hand combat, on the other hand... It's bad. Really, really bad. Every sailor can be equipped with a melee weapon, a shield and a ranged weapon. That's the good part. The standard ranged weapon, however, feels terribly anaemic. It has little physical impact and the target's health bar decreases by a minuscule amount. Reload times are high, and they should be, those are early gunpowder weapons we're talking about, but those factors combined make ranged combat boring and feeling as if you're not contributing much. So you swap to your melee weapon. You get three moves: attack, heavy attack and parry/block. Every move is incredibly slow, animations are very limited and you don't deal a lot of damage even with the heavy attack. There's also almost no sense of impact. Yes, enemies reel, but it's not very convincing. At least it's faster than ranged combat. Maybe there are more powerful weapons later in the game, but the lack of visual oomph is probably the bigger factor. Besides, if even a tutorial fight doesn't make you feel powerful, things aren't going well (unless it's designed to make you feel powerless, but that's also not the case here).
I've mentioned the ugly menus, but I didn't mention that some of them are also not very good at doing what they're supposed to do. Whether you want to buy or sell weapons, ship upgrades or general wares, you'll be facing a lot of wasted space. The devs went for single-row horizontal menus with not very attractive pictures and lots of wasted space to the top and bottom. The worst is the market menu where all the information is squished into the center of the screen making it hard to read. If you want to empty your hold of any cargo you have that you can sell at more than the average price, you have to scroll through the list see if you can spot the tiny line that says, for example, "Average price paid: 37 G". This is the most reliable way to spot goods you have. I'd suggest seperate buy and sell menus that show only items that are actually available or in your hold, respectively, and also colour-coding to denote whether an item is traded above or below the average price.
Speaking of scrolling: It's slow. I don't know how this happens, but from time to time you'll find a game where the scroll wheel's sensitivity is set way lower than is comfortable. This is one of those games.
So that's that. I was looking forward to this game, but found it to be disappointing on almost every front. It's a shame, really. If the devs support the game and make it a lot better, I might pick it up in a sale a year or so from now. I doubt the graphics will change, but the rest might yet be salvaged, and then it might be a good game. As it stands, this isn't the game for me.

PAYDAY: The Heist Review - Raymond KT
Summary: Players will embark on a spectacular crime spree of six heart stopping heists, including blasting their way through a downtown bank vault robbery, managing hostages in an armored car hijacking and even a midnight infiltration of a top-secret, high-security facility. Additionally, PAYDAY: The Heist challenges players with dynamic environments and adaptive enemy tactics - meaning no scenario will ever play out the same way twice. Teamwork is essential to ensure crew members provide cover under fire, guard key access points, break through various security measures and keep civilians in check. Survive wave after wave of the best that law enforcement can deploy as they shift strategies in response to player actions and gameplay style.
If you've seen Point Break or played Left 4 Dead, wrapping your head around PayDay: The Heist is easy. A cooperative first-person shooter, PayDay casts you and three bots or online friends as thieves and gives you six different jobs to go out on. Missions range from a bank heist to breaking out a prisoner to getting away from a job gone wrong, and enemy tactics change depending on how you're tackling a job.
When I first started playing, I assumed these situations would get stale as the mission objectives don't change -- you're always doing the same action in the same place -- but PayDay keeps it interesting with its dynamic leveling system. Your character evolves as you play and that tweaks the game's various heists. Each time you level up, you unlock a new weapon, item or bonus from the experience tree you have active. See, there are three trees and you can switch between them at any time. This is important to point out in the review because PayDay never explains this system in the game. I had to call the folks behind PayDay to get an explanation of how the trees work. PayDay's menus tend to just throw text at you and leave you to figure it out. I'm sure most people will do just that, but I know some folks will just walk away in frustration.
That's a shame because the skill trees are worth getting to the bottom of -- there are more than 140 levels to achieve. Once you get an established crew together, you can build teams where everyone has a specialized function. You can have a medic, an ammo man, a dude whose sole job is to handcuff hostages; it all depends on which tree a given player has been investing in. That kind of role-playing is great for people who want to nerd out and plan missions.
Playing heists over and over again is the point of PayDay. Each time I started a job, I was out to do better than the time before. I'd warn new teammates about faulty drills, coordinate taking out security cameras, and call out cops that needed to be wiped out. It was actually a bit creepy (yet thrilling) how well my friends and I transitioned into the role of criminals. We'd pull our guns, put on our clown masks, and begin working as a unit. Cue the in-office screaming and me loving the atmosphere.

Overall, the final release version of Roller Coaster Tycoon World feels like an entirely different game than the early access. Many of the game-breaking or heavily annoying bugs that are in it are gone or almost gone, and the new play modes have improved the replayability vastly.
The UI:
Let's get started at the menu, the new menu design is sleek and ergonomic, giving the game the sense of professionalism you would expect from the long time publisher Atari. The menus are easy to navigate and you don't feel yourself getting lost trying to find your way to certain features. Overall it is a massive improvement over the menu that was used in the Early Access build, which was more like something you would see from a newly budding Unity Programmer. The menu also includes a panel for what I assume are going to be News Updates, ranging from new DLC to events, etc. All of these elements give the menu a nice professional appeal.
Story Mode:
The story mode is composed of many small challenges and missions that you complete in order to progress to better parks and bigger challenges. The basic premise of the Story mode is that you're a budding entrepreneur who has been accepted into a theme park management business.(NOTE: I may be off a bit about the story, in all honesty its a bit cheesy, yet gives me a nostalgic callback to the Thrillville titles.). In these missions you are given a distinct set of main objectives to complete, be it building certain rides or increasing the parks population, and once you have completed these objectives, you can try to complete three tiers of challenges for each mission, and each one gives an increasing amount of Tycoon Points, which you can use to obtain better rides, scenery, and coaster blueprints. Overall, this mode adds a lot of replayability to the game, and offers a more realistic park running experience for those who want more challenge than Sandbox Mode offers.
Sandbox Mode:
Not going to go into much detail on this one because the premise is the same as other coaster games.
Coaster Builder:
This feature is honestly one of the main selling points of the game, due to the very personalized coaster building experience It gives you. The premise is that instead of a piece by piece coaster building method like most coaster games use, RCTW utilizes a freeform coaster building system, which means that instead of building piece by piece, you can actively shape the coaster's track shape as you build, which allows for very unique and creative coaster. Granted, if you dont like the freeform coaster building, you can use the piece by piece, which also works amazingly well. Overall, the Coaster Builder is almost enough to invest in this game on it's own.
Graphics:
Many people are going to disagree with me on this one, but I actually enjoy the graphics in RCTW more than the graphics in PC. When the devs set out to build RCTW, they seemed to have a distinct stylistic cartoony theme in mind, and they nailed it perfectly. The peeps are funny and cutesy and unorthodox, and everything has this light, low poly feel to it, which really jives with the overall mood of the game. Whereas Planet Coasters graphics are more of an attempt at a power show, to show that they have the best graphics, therefore you should buy their game. Which, keep in mind isn't bad, I just prefer the stylistic choices of RCTW more.
Conclusion:
RCTW does have noteable differences from it's predecessors, but this is what makes RCTW so unique and fun. It is a breath of fresh, exotic air in a market which was beginning to grow stagnant. That being said, if you are looking for a more traditional Roller Coaster Tycoon experience I would recommend getting Planet Coaster, which is made by the devs who made Roller Coaster Tycoon 3. The PC devs will give you more of a traditional RCT experience, but for a fresh exciting new experience, I would recommend RCTW.
EDIT:
I wanted to add an edit to talk about some other features I didn't talk about.
First off, the music in RCTW is absolutely astounding! They may have lacked in some of the other departments, but they knocked to music out of the park. The Menu music has a nice classic theme park feel, and the in game music is just as good. I would say that IMO Rollercoaster Tycoon World blows Planet Coaster out of the water in the music department.
That being said, Planet Coaster has a much better terrain editor. While RCTW's is good, Planet Coaster's is just absolutely amazing. You can shape tunnels, make more natural looking hills and mountains, and overall PC's just adds a whole to layer to theme park building.

First off 10/10 as this is a great game (and exactly what I wanted from the reincarnation of cossacks) coming from a rather small studio (with some original developers including the original artist far as I read some time ago)
AI - decent challenge, single player campaigns, interesting so far (+)
Atmospheare - Exactly the same as the original cossacks (+)
Graphics - Aren't going to knock your socks off excepting the art style which seems ageless and graceful, along with the fact the textures are better and units are in 3D now. (~)
Gameplay - Great, has some RPG elements just like the old cossacks games and can give you a decent challenge during the campaigns (+)
What they could improve - I was about to suggest more campaigns then realized I got the deluxe version for a reason, and if you played through every campaign you'd probably get around 50~ hours out of it alone. Multiplayer if you enjoy that sort of thing would mean even more. Really, I'll just complain that there aren't say, 10 missions per campaign instead of just 5 but that would just make me spoiled.
Bugs - Some have complained about bugs, only one I noticed was a minor pathfinding glitch around mines, to be expected with algorithms that complex (think dijkstra). Definitely not gamebreaking and after ordering them to go into the mine again the algorithm recalibrates and fixes its mistake.
Crashes - Fortunately I haven't encountered any, I've seen short freezes during the start of a scenario but I assume this is just the game generating all of the assets as there are quite a few troops placed at the start of every scenario. I encountered quite a few in Assassins Creed Syndicate, a triple A title, so it's rather impressive that a small studio has managed to pull this off.
Other complaints by people for example: 'unit fires at building!' seem rather petty, what, you think the developer would really go out of their way to address a players incompetancy with unit positioning rather than focus on developing/improving things that actually matter?
I'm a big fan of the old RTS genre. No 5 min battles I enjoy slugging it out with impossible ai or against other players.
Has it's bugs, but it's still a fun game

There is too much about this game that is good for me to give it a thumbs down, but it does have some fixable problems.
Much of the game is spent sailing on the water and in naval combat, and this is done spectacularly well, it is the issues "on land" however that I've found to have the lion's share of the problems.
-Blocks- I've found my character bumping into and climbing over invisible blocks while in port making getting from here to there a bit of a chalange.
-Accidental piracy- I once came across a ship in distress and was wondering if I could rescue the crew and maby gain some favour with Kinslev, but I must have pushed the wrong button because I borded them, thus gaining infamy instead.
I want to know if there is some dialogue or button to push that might prevent this in the future.
-Trade- I like the thought of trade, but I would like it to be more visible on the map somehow. Perhaps show some major trade routes and what port needs what and sells what, this could contribute to fame-infamy, perhaps make port towns grow, offer new services, different ships different quests that sort of thing.
Alternatively this could be used by someone who wants to play the part of the pirate to hunt down merchant ships.
-Graphics- The graphics of this game are not bad. They are sufficient.
They get the job done of giving you a feel of what is going on, where to go and what is where, but I feel as if they could have been beefed up or some how improved, I'm not talking World of Warcraft levels, just a little better.
-Boarding- I've found that the whole swordfighting part of the game difficult to use much less master. I just can't seem to make my charater do what I want him to do, on this im not sure if its the game or its just me. Maby this is not a bug at all and a feature, i haven't decided yet.
I allso would like to give some orders to my crew durring the fight, and I don't see any way of doing that, maby I've missed sometihng.
There is probably more that i missed but for the moment that is about the sum total of my complaints.
All things considerd I like this game and I like where it can go, I can't wait for expansion packs, new scenarios, new ships and the like.
My judgement is 9 out of 10 for a flawed but very good game that shows a lot of promise for the future!

Before reading on, remember the game is in early access and a lot may change and a lot will be fixed. With that said I am not going to go into bugs, control issues and the like as this might be improved later. I will however go into my issue with gameplay as I was experiencing the same annoyance with Hegemony: Ancient Wars of Greece.
What really annoys me is the amount of management the game requires. You need to manage food, supply lines, upkeep, expansion and battles. All in all these things are fine, but it gets so unbelievable frustrating when you have to deal with random raids from EVERYWHERE. You are trying to manage all these things and woop, you got three raids going in three seperate corners of your empire where you didn't have any forces. To make it more annoying, in the campaign you can sometimes be raided by someone who is outside of the campaign borders (the borders limit how far you can move) and you can't do anything to stop it.
What makes raids even more annoying is that they can build bridges and they build them really fast. Before you know it you have a raid group crossing over and burning farms making the management of food even MORE annoying. When I play this game, I find myself pretty much jumping back and forth micromanaging supplies, raids, and other stuff while gradually making 1 inch progress every half hour. As the gameplay stands now I find it far to frustrating to be able to enjoy it (this is only in regards to the core mechanics of the game and has nothing to do with bugs and glitches as they will surely be fixed by repair).
I wouldn't recommend anyone to play it in its current form, though the game has potential. As far as the game being frustrating, that might just not be me having patience enough for the game. I would wish for the developers to dial down the raids and random apperance of the raids across the board as currently it's just frustrating and not enjoyable.
Edit: I have to say the concept of the game is really fun however and if they dial down some on the frustration I would actually recommend the game. I read somewhere that they might ease up some on the raids and I think a change like that would even out the frustration. Therefore I think I would reommend the game as long as you have the patience and head for all the micro and macro managing.

A childhood classic of mine as well as an Apogee classic: Halloween Harry a.k.a. Alien Carnage.
Don't ask me what this has to do with Halloween. Err...zombies?
Anyway: You are Harry, a "red blooded American with balls of steel" (quoting Harry himself) who has to save other people captured by aliens so they don't have to be turned into mindless zombies and thus saves the Earth by doing this. A typical damsel-in-distress story in outer space - and with a flamethrower.
It's a 2D platformer: you run from left to right and from right to left, explore the level in order to find the kidnapped people. What makes the game a bit more challenging - and fun - is that the levels also contain doors for which you have to find levers in order to open them and you have to memorize the environment a bit so you find everything again, including the exit door. And you can't leave a level unless you've freed every single victim.
However, in this game you don't jump - you use a jetpack to fly through the air and to upper platforms. Sounds cool at first but the jetpack is powered by fuel (which also powers the standard weapon, your flame thrower). So you always have to keep an eye on the fuel meter while looking for vending machines that sell fuel. This can be a pain in the a... sometimes.
Speaking of vending machines and weapons: You have other weapons, too, like missiles and bombs. They have their own vending machines. However: whenever you enter a boss level you only have your flame thrower so these stronger weapons won't make your life easy at any time.
The enemies in the game are poor on variety: Mostly they are green-skinned zombies, a few alien-like creatures but they don't really change during the whole game. In the last few levels there may be bigger zombies but still, I wish the game had more different enemies to fight. Still, they should give you the right horror/sci-fi movie feeling a bit at least.
The bosses are a bit more challenging because they take longer to kill but they take shorter to kill you. But there are no real strategies: just fly around them and shoot them.
The graphics are very fine for the time, music and sound are quite okay.
You can choose between three different difficulty options (easy, medium, hard).
When it comes to save features: You can save and load several saving spots but they only memorize the beginning of the level. Inside the levels you have computers that you have to touch to save during the level. Whenever you die, you go back to the last computer, not to the beginning of the level. That's cool for a game of that time.
Overall, I enjoyed playing this classic platformer from my past. It's quite a short game with could have used a bit more of variety but if you love 2D platformers and can stand a bit of horror then you won't regret trying this out.

I'll be brief: I've played many a doujin novel, and Sepia Tears, while not perfect, is definitely one of the best I've read in recent memory.  I feel the writer was inspired by the works of Key, as there are not only many blatant references to them, but the story as a whole felt similar to Kanon. And that's not a bad thing. (Come on, Key! Release Kanon on Steam already!) :)
The characters are entertaining, although I felt some of the drama was a bit forced. The supporting characters like to pull the main character's leg a lot, and after a while of this it tends to diminish the impact of the honest drama. I honestly wish the choices in the game weren't purely cosmetic, since these characters are so likeable that they deserve their own endings.
But the ending we get is good enough. It takes a bit of persistence, but it's fairly rewarding. You unlock a diary entry after beating the game that fully explains the motivations behind Myra's actions, but I wish there was a little more than that. Maybe I was expecting too much, since May Sky's after story felt a lot meatier... :/
I have a few technical problems, particularly with the script. While I do like the transition to NVL to show when Mark is in deep thought, there are also times when Myra is talking instead, and the novel makes no mention of who's speaking. You may figure it out yourself if you're reading carefully, but it is a little jarring when you don't know who's talking. Aside from the rare typo, the script is pretty clean in terms of grammar and punctuation. The backlog feature is probably the best I've seen in a doujin VN, although it is a little too sensitive when I scroll up.
The graphics are a bit of a mixed bag. The character sprites look like stencil drawings, and the backgrounds look like stock photos altered to look like watercolor paintings. It's a unique style I haven't seen in a doujin VN, and for the most part, it's inoffensive. The CGs, particularly the chibi artwork, are fantastic. The normal CGs are at least consistent with the style of the character sprites, which I can't fault the artist for.
The music is mostly ambient and inoffensive, although very few of the tracks will stick in your head. The ending theme is the standout track in the novel, as the song fits the mood well and is sung pretty well, too. At first I couldn't tell if it was being sung in Japanese or English, because the lyrics were a bit unintelligible. Once I got a handle on the English lyrics, it turned out to be a pretty nice song.
For the price of nothing, Sepia Tears could have turned out a lot worse. But for what I got, it's pretty good. This is probably one of the best doujin novels you could play on Steam. There used to be three free doujin novels that I think are exceptional and totally worth playing (those titles being Brass Restoration, Moonshine, and May Sky), and with this game, a new member has been added to the family. I give my wholehearted recommendation to this VN, and I hope you enjoy it as much as I did. :)

In this 2nd version of the game you'll find a few nice improvements to gameplay slightly marred by an awkward interface. If you've played the original game, it's going to take some time to adjust. At this point, I'm 100 hours in and I'm finally feeling like I have a comfortable handle on the game.
The Pro's -
- Tempo is now a factor in most of your shots. You can no longer just pull the backswing to the precise point of power you're looking for. If you pull back too slowly, your shot could veer right or left, come up short or completely miss. The nice thing about this is it adds a further element of skill to the game, which in turn reduces the rediculous 18 round scores in the 50's. It really helps to balance out the competition.
- "Scocieties" are added to the game. Think of these as guilds or clans, meaning a group of players able to get together and enjoy the game amongst themselves.
- Club selection is added. You can now choose from many different types of clubs to fill your golf bag. 7 wood anyone?
- Career mode is nice too. In TGC 2, you have further control in easily creating a custom season of different golf courses with customizable tee boxes, pin placement, and general difficulty.
- You can choose your tee box and pin placemen! This was missing from the first version of the game and is a welcome addition in the 2nd.
- More customizations of your avatar. This is a watered down version of a Sims type customization. It's there, it's nice, but to be honest, it's not that extensive. Don't expect to be able to make a player that looks like your favorite celebrity.
Cons -
- The surface physics just aren't realistic. The best example is a shot that rolls into a bunker and then out again. Sadly, I have never seen this in real life. This also occurs in heavy rough! Imagine hitting a bad slice into heavy rough ( 12" of thick grass ) and seeing your ball bounce out of it into the safety of the fairway. Seriously. It's nice that I get some extra distance from a bad shot, but not very realistic.
- The tempo system in your swing can be overly sensitive. If your mouse is a little dirty or your mouse pad slips, your bunker shot can go nowhere or your drives can slice hard into the next fairway. It's not a huge problem, but it's annoying when you really have the tempo down pat to see your shots do this and thus ruin a round.
- Controlling power remains very difficult. A 12' chip shot should not be so hard to get the distance right but it is. You can counter this by adjusting the sensitivity of your mouse as far down as is comfortable ( I use 15 down from 40 ), Any lower and you'll need the whole desk for drives. Even with this adjusted, try pulling your mouse back to a point with 1/8th inch accuracy and still maintain the "swing" tempo. The skill required just doesn't match the skill for other shots.
- The menu has become very awkward and far less user friendly, as well as being far less attractive than in the original game. It may take several clicks to get into a society season game. I also found myself stuck at one point trying to figure out which button to press to get back to the main menu. I wish they start from scratch and re-do it.
- Jon the announcer is just plain creepy when announcing during tournaments. It really is amazing how the same voice actor can lose everything that was appealing from the first game when adding to the second. In the original game the comments were usually uplifting, positive, smooth, and sincerely friendly. For regular play, these voice bits are carried over. When announcing for a tournament, Jon takes on the soft, slightly whispering voice typical from TV, but I found it creepy if not sinister at times. His reminders that you just shot a bogey will make you cringe.
- The society system is nice, but trying to find a society that fits you is impossible. You can't pick from criteria such as difficulty, or average handicap, or size, or anything really. The list of societies is always just newest first. This has to be fixed.
- The official societies are limited. It would be nice if while I was a 9 handicap player I didn't have to compete with players with a 0 handicap or better. It's discouraging to be playing your best in an official event only to be told you wound up in 52nd place and win nothing. They really should add more official societies with narrower ranges of handicaps.
- The winnings are paltry. Yay I won 57 dollars in a tourney! The money you can use to spend on clothing options for the most part which really isn't all that exciting either for that mattter.
All and all though this is a great golf game and I applaud the designers for attempting to give your standard golf game a level of realism and skill. This tends to be lacking in many of the more commercial efforts. In spite of it's flaws, this is probably one of the best golf simulators out there.

5 Words: Very, very, very, very frustrating!!! If you want to relax after a sh±$%&* day and play a round of golf... forget it (as in real life, really)! You'll end up throwing your computer out the window! Literally. I'm not kidding!
Being able to swing your golf club at full swing is not that hard to master, but half swings or 3/4 swings is pretty damn hard. It seems that the length of the swing is not linear but logarithmic. Let say you usually reach 100yd at full swing and now you need to reach 50 yd. One will think a half swing will do. Wrong! Half swing will get you about 10% of the distance. This is valid for any kind of swing (normal, chip, punch, etc). It takes hours and hours and hours of practice just to get a feel of it. BTW, there is no Mulligan! I can understand that during a tournament or in career mode it would be a very welcome addition in a upcoming patch for casual games. That would definetly helps ease some frustration.
There is a lot of courses to play, thanks to the Course Editor. Unfortunately, most of them having a difficulty of either Hard or Hardest with some Medium and I did not find anything below Medium. Greens can be usually reached within regulation but a lot them are freaking roller coaster, adding to the frustration. So even if you reach a Par 5 in 2 strokes, consider yourself lucky if end up with Par.
There is also a carreer mode, where you create your society, select/buy your club house and create the events for the current season. Note that you cannot restart/reset a carrer. At least, I didn't find how to do it. Be careful when adding a course to your season; once it is added, you CANNOT remove it nor change it, even when the season is not started yet. "You choose that course and that name and now you don't like it? Well, too bad!". There is also Online Societies you can join/create, but I didn't try that feature I can't tell if it's good or not.
Graphically speaking, it is descent. Nice 3D but nothing to write home about. Personally I don't care much as I prefer this kind of game to have great physics, which it does. The commentator is boring, very boring, if not anoying sometimes! Monotone, no emotion; sounds like he doesn't care if you did a great shot or a total blunder. He just wants his paycheck at the end of the day. The ball physic is really good, though. One downside during the course play is that you cannot speed up to your next stroke once you hit the ball. You got to watch to the ball all the way 'till it stops. This can be very annoying on roller coaster greens.
The Course Editor is a great idea but it need some optimisation and polish. For instance, placing a tree (or any object, for that matter) takes about 1-2 seconds. If you want to build a course in a forest environment, get some coffee brewing... It's gonna be a long night. The editor's UI is a total mess in my opinion. As a former software engineer, I just can't believe this pass through the QA departement. It's usable, but not quite friendly. You select an option, the menu disappear, another sub-menu appear, and so on. Press the TAB key and main menu appear; press TAB again and you get back where you were. So it's not always easy to know where you are in the menus, i.e. from which upper-menu this sub-menu is attached to. Sometimes, you cannot pan the camera. Why? I can zoom in/out, rotate, but panning just stop working. As a side note: you cannot play your courses until you have published them. You can "play test" them, but not "play" them nor add them to your carrer's season. That's a bummer.
All in all, I have mix fellings about that game. Can I recommend that game? Hard to say. If you are an hardcore golf lover and/or a gamer who loves challenges AND you can overcome a great deal of frustration, then yes. One thing is for sure: this is probable one of the best golf game (overall) released in years. But, for me, the frustration level to overcome just makes this not quite enjoyable. Maybe with a lot, lot, lot, lot more practice I will enjoy this game as it should... Time will tell.

In short, Guacamelee is a Metroidvania beat-em-up with luchadores. It has good fighting mechanics, and a fun aesthetic, with alternate dimensions and chickens, to boot. The mechanics can get choppy, though, especially with the overly hard platforming. When you have to bash 5 buttons at once, but then switch to 5 new ones in less than second if you don't want to redo 3 minutes of platforming, it goes far beyond rage-quit material. When you do get to fight, it's a great time on of the best fighting systems in 2D game I've ever experienced. But the platforming is so TIME-CONSUMING, BORING, and DIFFICULT, that it draws focus from the well-designed parts of the game. All in all, a fine game, but the paltforming drags it down.

What to say about Guacamelee?  First, I'll just say I was surprised by it, and I mean that with the utmost flattery.  It was a game that was completely off my radar.  I saw it pop up on my Steam homepage, but it wasn't until a friend bought it as a gift for me did I really know what it was.  As described, it is a "Metroid-vania" style game.  There are a ton of video game references (and some non-video game) with in the game, if you have the patience to stop and look around you.  The game is fun, but I think the best part about it is that it is able to pay homage to classic video games without being a classic video game.  What do I mean by that?  Well, first it has it's own art style, which I really enjoy.  It's also not pixelated and not trying to be 8/16-bit retro game.  Along with it's own art style, it also has it's own unique story.  A lot of these indie games today are trying to revive the old story tropes (Knights, ninjas, etc.).  But...how many old games do you remember where the protagonist owns a tequila distillery and becomes a magical luchador?  Not many.  I mean...yes it does have classic, "save the princess" but with a different sort of mask to it.  I guess what I'm trying to get at here, and this could be argued, is that this game pays homage to classic gaming without having to look, feel, and act like a classic game, if that makes sense.  It has it's own unique voice and style.  Not saying that games like Shovel Knight, Anodyne, Oniken, and Hammerwatch are not great games and unique on their own, but they do imitate, very closely, to the old NES classics (Oniken being very much in the vein of Ninja Gaiden; Hammerwatch to Gauntlet).
What does all this amount to? It's fun.  It's unique.  It's challenging and makes me mad.  So yes, totally get this game.  You'll certainly have a good time with it, especially if you're into good ol' classic platforming.

Cossacks 3 is essentially a remake of the classic European Wars with some, but not all of the content from its expansions Art of War and Back to War.
Released a buggy and unstable mess, the game is now fully functioning except from the occasional bug and unpolishedness, because the devs did a great job patching it up after release, and are still supporting it in the future. Plus, due to the free modding tools included with the game, there is already a growing modding community.
The game is heavy on managing the six different types of ressources, building a base with a good economy, that can then supply a huge army. While not grand strategy by a long shot, I'd say it is heavier in the macro management than in the micro.
12 playable nations, with 8 to come, and a ton of different starting settings in multiplayer, from thousand to million ressources, from a few peasants to a small army, land or naval battle, 1v1, 2v2 or 3v3, or even 2v2v2, or a 7 player free for all, from no peace time to up to an hour of peace time to prepare your armies, small skirmishes or giant battles with thousands and thousands of soldiers, there is a ton of different opions how to play the game.
The AI is a bit on the dumb side, the nations are not perfectly ballanced, and the online interface is basically taken straight out of the original cossacks from 15 years ago, but these flaws can be overlooked when you crave to play a truely old school RTS again, in a time where the pressence of MOBAs has caused developers to mostly overlook what is now sadly a niche genre. And at just 20 bucks, even if you never played Cossacks before, I think it is well worth taking the risk that you might like it.

Should this game have been released in the 1999, it would be considered a "beloved old time classic with some bugs & flaws that make it feel the test of time".  Why this comparison?
- Because the game feels like a game from that era in a good, and bad way in terms of gameplay/wonkiness.
- In the year 2017 however, when the energy drink whopping ADHD "I LOVE MAH GRAPHIX" generation is steamrolling through the tunnel-runs of the Call of Duty games, this is not what the doctor ordered. I mean look at its melee combat: It's buggy! Eww.... 1/10!
Now... when you take off the old reading glasses and look at the tabletop Man'o War & Dreadfleet... You see clearly that this game has a lot in common with these two. This game is a different breed, of a time, when people were tolerant with bugs and somewhat a bit wonky format of burning down the docks.
- Variability though... this is where this game throws its punches. You can play it the way you want to.
Hunt the sea monsters. Get some odd-jobs at the pier. Track down ships, or join the Empire in a war against Bretonnia. Deliver e.x. Witch Hunters to other ports or Trade goods or hunt merchant ships, carving your life as a true-blue pirate, and as the ultimatum... Forge your fleet and raid the Legendary Free Port of Marienburg. The world is your oyster and the content keeps rolling in.
- High Elf AI in your own fleet varies, but all in all... with its flaws and bugs, and sometimes a bit wonky melee fighting(that gets more quick and intense when you level your attack speed up), this game is how a good RPG/Action indie game should be.
Offer something the mainstream does not dare to, because "it's not hip or pop". If this is what you're searching for. give this game a try. If you can't get over the sometimes clunky melee combat, don't worry, this game isn't exactly for everyone to take at a face value.
EDIT: Oh yeah, the music Rocks

I was very into all of these Apogee platformers as a child, but I never really enjoyed  Halloween Harry.  I was too young to really articulate why, but after revisiting it, I think I can put it into words.  The game sucks.  Specifically, the level design is terrible.  Each level is essentially a maze with no flow, rhyme, or reason to it.  It's a series of identical looking hallways filled with the same few enemies over and over again.  There's other stuff that isn't very well designed, but what will suck your will to live, or at least will to play this game with those few fleeting moments you have before shuffling off this mortal coil, is the lack of interesting places to explore.  For an exploration-based platformer, that's kind of sub-optimal.
It's a shame because the technical aspects of the game are pretty good, and WAIT A MINUTE ABOUT THE LEVEL DESIGN.  Since the levels are non-descript, you'll have to trudge through the same hallways a few times while you find all of the hostages so you can go to the exit and go to the next level that is gray this time instead of brown.  So naturally, the enemies aggressively respawn, and you have limited ammo that needs to be refilled.  Also, your ammo is also your fuel, without which, you can't jump.  To be clear, this isn't actually hard, but it is really annoying.  It's like playing an old RPG where you're trying to find the exit to the dungeon and every four steps an easy random encounter sucks you into a different screen where you have to kill the same four cave rats over and over and over again.
It's like that.  But if you can get past how what you're actually doing in the game not being any fun, the game is fine.  18 stars!

Super fun. Beware if you're colorblind.
I had a marathon couple of days playing this game; I enjoyed it immensely though I'm not the best platformer or combo-maker. The checkpoint locations were pretty forgiving and the gradually ratched up challenges made the game more fun than frustrating. Until the boss fight against Calaca, but for a very particular reason.
The Calaca boss fight mechanics rely entirely on twitch reactions to colored shields with zero room for error. For my particular kind of color blindness, I can only reliably detect the blue shield and the red shield. The green or yellow shields look identical; it's a 50/50 chance if I do the correct move to score a hit. Every time Calaca attacks his shield is a different color; a process of elimination cannot be used.
If you're partially colorblind, this fight will be more difficult for you. If you're completely colorblind, this fight will be nearly impossible to beat. You would have to stick with a single attack and count on your ability to avoid damage long enough for your random successes to eventually defeat Calaca's first form.
A significant portion of the population suffer from some form of color impaired vision. It's always a shame when game designers are ignorant or willfully disregard that.
