Video Review Here:
Positives
========
As golfing games go, The Golf Club 2 from HB Studios + Maximum Games has to be one of the biggest and definitely one of the most customisable.
Great effort has been placed on improving areas that were criticised in the original game.  Specific emphasise has been placed on a Career mode and the Societies feature (which comprises an interesting take on the traditional MP mode, more later..) Ultimately this dramatically adds some much needed meat to the game mechanics as a whole.
The swing mechanics have been updated and are now super authentic and even include a practise swing.  To master the new swing really does require some finesse but also provides an incredible amount of control for the player.  By adjusting your swing action even slightly, you can make significant changes to your shot and when combined with the in-game tools you really can make the most rewarding of shots happen and feel like you actually made it happen!  Of course there is the other end of that yard stick too where you know that you alone are at fault.
Negative feedback about putting from the original did not fall on deaf ears either and the putting mechanics have also received a significant layer of adjustment.  The greens break speeds might need a little tweaking or perhaps it just takes time to learn but overall the greens and putting feels smooth and natural and sinking a tricky putt is super rewarding.
The game now includes and indeed begins with an in-depth interactive tutorial, something which was lacking in the original.  It is completely optional and can be quit out and then revisited at any time.  The tutorial moves along at a reasonable pace and explains the new swing mechanics system in detail; it also does a great job of introducing new players to all of the shot types and techniques.
Button configurations are fully customisable with the Keyboard and mouse set as the default but controllers are also allowed and one of the first decisions is to select either the left or right thumb stick to swing with.  Customisation is definitely the key word when it comes to The Golf Club 2, with a new and complete character generator and a decent variety of clubs, clothing and accessories to buy and modify the possibilities are endless.
Thankfully The Golf Club 2 is a Golf Simulator and has not taken the approach where clothing and clubs give your character extra power-up perks, instead The Golf Club 2 is a Pure and Realistic Simulator and focusses on players skill, planning and recovery as the catalyst for a good round, and it doesn’t stop there;
Career mode allows you to pick or plan your seasons with great precision and once you progress enough you can start your own Society.  Societies offer very exciting possibilities; Each Society will have their own bank balance so they can choose their own clubhouse; the richer the club the grander the clubhouse can be.
You can invite friends and players to join and you can create and invite your society members to your own Major Tournaments that you have designed, set the prize money for and basically managed every little aspect of the event to your own personal liking.  Crowds will turn up for the clubs majors and the bigger the club, the bigger the crowds plus the HUD will become more TV like and the commentary will also adapt to the occasion.  As your society grows, even more options are unlocked and more can be done, this is definitely going to be the meat of this club sandwich.
With all of that in mind plus the plethora of courses available within the game and the ability to create and share your own courses using the new and improved course creator, your choice of courses to play will never run dry with The Golf Club 2.  There are literally hundreds of thousands of courses created for The Original Golf Club game and are not only compatible but cross-platform compatible, a tremendous feature!
During a round you will be accompanied, encouraged and occasionally mocked by your caddie (John McCarthy) who is really nothing more than a commentator or perhaps your inner voice.  Although upbeat and at times entertaining, the script depth is shallow and becomes repetitive pretty quickly.  There might be an option to turn this feature off but either way you will pretty quickly begin to skip and ignore this aspect of the game.
Negatives
========
The game has no PGA content or real-world known golfers to compete against.  It focus is purely on individual players progress and their associated societies.  With a price tag of £30 or more you will have to decide if this is a mitigating factor or not.
MP in the Golf Club is also a little different from the norm, rather than the traditional lobby approach TGC2 comes with three MP varients;
•	Local (which is the most like traditional MP but not online),
•	Ghost…whereby you play against previous players recorded round and choose to have ghosting on or not…
•	Finally rival mode where you play against another player online, you can see their scorecard but not their shots…options here include turn based and ball ghosting.
Despite The Golf Club 2 updating their engine to Unity 5, and some areas of the game looking significantly better there are a number of areas where the games presentation should be improved;
•	There appear to be some screen resizing issues, might be fixed in time.
•	The player created characters is great but they do look a little dated.
•	Certain aspects and area of the courses look spectacular where as other parts do not.  For example the sand mechanics are left a little wanting unfortunately;
o	It appears that sand textures, physics and animations have simply been copied over from The Original Golf Club
o	There is some significant texture popping all over the place.
o	The completely silent aircraft animations present on some courses are repetitive, flying way too close to the ground in what appears to be a holding formation and way too close to each other!  This just ends up being little more than a distraction rather than being an added realistic feature.
o	Audio across the board could do with beefing up a whole hog to really add to the ambience and boost immersion.
There are quite a few little bugs in the system, HB Studios appear to be aware of the majority of them and have a list so these should be getting fixed sooner rather than later.
Overview
========
If you’re a real golfer, and you want to play a real game of golf then this is definitely the best option on the market today.
The Handicaps, Society’s, Major tournaments, plus the unlimited options and course creations available to everyone makes The Golf Club 2 just about the best of the lot.
Graphically much could be done, but enough is done to ensure that you and your friends can join and enjoy a few rounds of golf together then enjoy reminiscing about them in your societies clubhouse, so long as you can stomach the approach employed for Mulitplayer games.
Overall, what’s not to like?  More content than any golf game in history, the best swing mechanics in history and above all the ability for you and your society to go down in history.

This game is the next installment in the Hegemony series from Longbow Games. The Hegemony series has so far shown to be deeper than most zerg-rush RTS games. It forces the player to think tactically about more than just the troops being thrown at an enemy. I have to constantly evaluate my situation on multiple levels in order to triumph. This is not brought about from complex micromanagement systems, as seen in ot6her titles. It is simply an organic result of focusing on the main aspects of building an empire such as knowing an enemies strengths and weeknesses, dealing with supply issues, and utilizing the available resources wisely. Taken all together, Longbow games have made long lasting RTS games that continue to challenge and satisfy far beyond what I have found in other titles. How well historical fact is woven into the game only adds to my enjoyment. If you are still not convinced, I strongly reccomend trying the free demo for Hegemony Gold to get a taste of the franchise.

Payday: The Heist is very similar to Left 4 Dead, in the sense that survivors are replaced by robbers and zombies by hundreds and hundreds of cops. Every mission you need to complete some tasks to make progress and good cooperative team is a must if you want to make any kind of progress. Some campaigns are absolutely great (First World Bank, Diamond Heist, Green Bridge) and some are just average, but they are unique enough to offer a different experience from each other.
Some of the drawbacks are, not so great enemy AI and level-up style gameplay. I am not really a fan of online shooters where your gameplay time puts you ahead of other players, rather than skill. At least, Payday: The Heist does not do that in a very irritating way. As long as you choose a difficulty proportionate to your "Level", you will not be lacking.
To conclude, Payday: The Heist really does make you feel like in a classic robbery movie like Heat or Killing Zoe. It is not something to keep you play for hundreds of hours without getting repetitive, but it does offer great fun for about 20-30 hours. It is not the best co-op shooter, but definitely a good alternative to Left 4 Dead or Killing Floor.

Set in the Warhammer universe, the game features a single player campaign where you sail between ports populated by Skaven, Orks, Dwarves, Elves, and the like, with lots of AI ships wandering about. Most money is made by undertaking quests, which typically involve attacking a specific ship or taking something to another port; quests become repetitive very quickly. You can also trade goods for a source of minor income; items manufactured by a specific port are clearly indicated, making it easier to buy low and sell high. Money can be spent on repairing, upgrading, or purchasing new ships, hiring crew (whom level up and unlock new skills), or equipping people with better weapons. Combat is typical for the setting: sail with the wind to go fast (helpfully indicated in green on the compass) and fire cannons off the side of the ship (the range of which is helpfully indicated with a giant red arrow). Ammunition types can be changed (grape shot for enemy crew, chain shot for sails), and other ships can be boarded for hand-to-hand and ranged combat. Combat is usually very enjoyable, and the AI provides a typically capable opponent. The Warhammer setting doesn’t offer a lot more than a traditional age of sail adventure game (Orks and crazy looking ships notwithstanding) and the title has nothing to do with its tabletop namesake, but Man O' War: Corsair is still a strangely compelling game despite the occasional bugs.

This game is pure uncut fun, it feels like a Space Quest successor - dorky character on a space adventure filled with loads of humour.
The 2D art is amazing, character animation is very fluid and pleasant to the eye, the music is enjoyable, it greatly enchances the experience. The game interface is very clean and intuitive, the puzzles involve gathering and using a lot of objects but are not overly complicated. There isn't such a thing as pixel hunting involved, but some objects can remain cleverly concealed in the environment until you take time to examine them.
The only thing to disappoint is that dialogues, no matter how funny, are not voiced over. There isn't an abundance of text to read but a point-and-click adventure game usually benefits greatly from a decent voice acting. I personally grew up playing text-only adventure games and don't find the lack of voices that much of a letdown.
Overall, Kaptain Brawe is an unforgettably pleasant experience.

In the pantheon of video games, few will stand as tall and defiant as Myst. The Miller brothers, Rand and Robyn, along with their development team Cyan Worlds (then known as just Cyan), created a truly remarkable game that has sent countless reverberations throughout the game-o-sphere (or whatever the hell you want to call it). Up their with the greats, monolithic and unsurpassable, Myst truly is out there and here to stay.
But does it hold up after all this time? Has the shine faded, the allure gone dim? Has time finally taken it's toll on a game that, in many ways, has been percieved as timeless? Well... yes and no.
Myst: Masterpiece Edition is one of the more widely-available ports of this legendary title. There are so many ports, it's quite overwhelming. But this is probably the best version of the game. I say that because it presents the classic game as it was meant to be played, with all of its point-and-click mechanics and exploration completely in tact and allowing players to use the mouse as intended. The only other port of the game that I have played would the mobile version, iOS specifically. While graphically superior, it fails with the touch controls because of how inherent clumsy a game like this, one that requires precision and careful timing to complete puzzles, becomes when a mouse cursor is replaced with sausage fingers. So, immediately, this is the best version to play.
The game is famously simple: player finds book, player falls into world inside book, arrives on Myst Island, proceeds to go on an adventure. Such a basic idea might turn players away, but it should be said that what's done within such a limited premise is quite remarkable. By completing puzzles and unravelling the mysteries of the island and the Ages (the other worlds you explore) hidden and scattered across this surprisingly limited setting, the complex story reveals itself piece by piece. Even if the end result is nothing more than a familial dispute, it's hard not to get sucked into it. Myst may not have a deep or thought-provoking plot, but it's a plot nonetheless, and it damn well works.
Now while a lot of the game's puzzles and exploration elements are still very much worth enduring, despite the frustration of its difficulty, the game files might make Myst: Masterpiece Edition a bit of a hassel. This is because the version here on Steam is not updated in anyway. It's exactly as the Masterpiece Edition was when released back in May of 2000. This
cause compatibility issues at first, but they can be easily solved if given enough time and patience. For it's current asking price, as well as constantly being on sale when Steam sales come around, coughing up the cash might be worth it.
Of course, the game still suffers from archaic graphics and cheesy FMV sequences. But if you're a gamer who loves the vibe of these old adventure games, I really can't give a reason why these factors would put you off. All in all, this is true Myst. Not realMyst, not cobbled together port, not a rehash of a classic, none of that. This is the real deal, Myst in all it's glory. It's surprisingly worth checking out, regardless of how dated it might seem.

I really looked forward to this game. While I believe that this game is currently one of the best golf games out there, there are definitely some things I don't like and wish would be changed or even removed.
Pros
- Beautiful Scenery & some of the best graphics I have seen in a Golf game
- Societies are very interesting
- Easy and depth way to hit the ball
- Customization of Character. I felt like I was in an MMO making my guy.
- Fluid creation of courses
- Ease of creating courses
- Smooth gameplay (aside from issues in the Cons section)
Cons
- REALLY not a fan of the Tempo on the swings. This is by far the MOST frustrating thing with this game. I wish it was removed entirely. There are times that I swear I use my mouse exactly the same, and I get a VERY SLOW and it is frustrating as hell. Not a fan, period. I'd much rather have an option to hit the ball for less distance, if it meant I could turn this off.
- No 3 click option for swinging. I am a disabled vet & missing some pieces in my arm I use with my mouse. A 3 click swing option would be fantastic. Heck, even take off 20% of my distance and I would be totally stoked!
- Chipping seems really weird. I try to do a 50 to 75% chip and it goes no more than a foot. EXTREMELY frustrating. I don't want to go 12 yards, I only need 7 or so. Nope, stuck with either 12 yards or less than a foot.
- Flop shots are never the right distance and always too far.
- Needs more customization in the look of clubs & balls.
- Standard Society matches. I am in the Amature Society and there are guys there who totally whoop on us. Last match, there was some guy who had a -18. There is no way any of us sub-par (nice pun) players could ever be #1 in one of those.
- Putting needs a little more forgiveness or grace. The vast majority of the time I have to putt short on purpose.
Suggestions
- Progression. One thing I miss about the Tiger Woods PGA and some other Golf games was the ability to add points to things such as Drive Distance, Drive accuracy, Putting etc... as I gained more experience or played longer these skills were a fantastic and welcome addition. The ideas for this are limitless. You stink at putting distances? Add some points in that skill to ease that and add some forgiveness. Heck you could make it take a long time to gather these points.
- Sponsors. Another huge thing I miss are the sponsors from other golf games. I understand the whole Trademark thing. However, use virtual names like "Sparrow Clubs" or "Foster's Slimeballs". Sponsors give you extra cash when you use their products in a match, and thier products slowly help your gameplay. For example, a set of used golf clubs from someone on Craigslist is going to be far inferior to a TaylorMade set. You bet I could play a much much better game with those TaylorMade's! The same thing with Golf Balls. This would be a huge welcome to the game.
- Building on Sponsors & Societies. If your custom Society was given Sponsors, it would make Custom Societies much more attractive. Your "Juan Fordaroad" Society has a Slimeball Sponsor? Everyone in that Society gets to use those balls for free.
That's all I have for now. However, even through my Cons section, this game is a great game & currently, IMO, the best Golf Game on the market. 3.5 out of 5 stars. If it also had the suggestions in it, I would easily give it 4.5 to 4.75.

This game- no, this MASTERPIECE- is perhaps one of the single most relevant and insightful games in its field. While not entirely new in concept, Secret of the Magic Crystals takes the previously overlooked horse-breeding simulation genre and introduces several new elements of gameplay that entice and immerse the player in ways I never thought possible. The introduction of the Republican Party's political platform, while unorthodox, gives the game a sort of flair and raises a lot of interesting points that pertain to real world issues. Needless to say, the game leaves the player on the edge of their seats the entire time as they embark on a quest to find the Magic Crystals. If you've ever wanted to feel alive and inspired, play this game.

This game has everything needed in a successful video game: love, drama, comedy, action...
It truly has transcended our generation's understanding of what makes a video game. This is something more; this is the quintessence of artistry in a digital medium. There are little words to express the absolute majesty of this game, from the cutting edge graphical quality to the intricate character detail with every well-purposed polygon to shape a beautiful beast on the screen.
This video game will no doubt continue on for generations to be remembered as one of the art masterpieces of the 21st century, much like the works of William Shakespeare, Vincent Van Gogh, Michelangelo, Stephanie Meyer, and J. K. Rowling.
Truly the capability to own such a game for the price of $4.99 is a steal, but if you manage to acquire it at its sale price of $0.99, you should be reported for theft for even attempting to get away with such a heinous crime.
Truly, in short, this game is no doubt underappreciated, as it is ahead of its time. Aptly said, this game is like Batman: it's the hero Gotham deserves, but not the one it needs right now. Perhaps in a world where chauvinist bigotry is not the societal norm, we can all learn to appreciate this game for its truly artistic nature.

Firstly, allow me to apologize in advance for any typos or mistakes I make. I am still crying from that beautiful, tearjerker ending. It will haunt me for the rest of my life. Her last words were poetry. But I won't spoil it for you, this game's plot is too brilliant for that.
STORY:
This game's story has everything. Comedy, tragedy, action, adventure, romance, drama... the lot. Yet somehow, it never trips over itself. You play as a young child fighting for the honour of their father. You do this by raising horses of different breeds to aid you in your quest for the titular magic crystals. Your journey will take you through seasons as you train, breed, race and sell your horses. Come rain or shine, there is no rest. You're fighting for your father's honour.
The characters are all deep and vivid, with brilliant backstories complimenting their individual quirks and mannerisms. While I won't go into depth for fear of treading into spoiler territory, I will say this: not everyone is who they say, so be careful.
GAMEPLAY:
This game may appear simple, but trust me, it's deceptively complex. It will take you hours, days even, to even scratch the surface of what this game has to offer content-wise. There are a few tricks you learn along the way, like that clicking on a rainbow nets you 100 gold pieces, or that clicking a clover brings you luck at the races, or that you actually can lead a horse to water AND make it drink by rapidly clicking on the water until the ungrateful brat takes the hint.
The racing sequences are especially intense; you can't actually see your beloved horse, you see. You can only read the nerve-wracking commentary. You may not want to play this game at night for that reason; the inevitable cries of joy that erupt from your mouth at seeing your horse return with a gold trophy will surely wake your neighbours (or "NAYbours", geddit? Yeah? Eugh, tough crowd.)
GRAPHICS
Yep, you read right; this game's recommended specs list the extremely poweful Intel Pentium 4 running at a whopping 2GHz. If you're one of the lucky few with a computer capable of running this game, you'll see that it puts all 2 of those gigahertz to good use. Crysis? BioShock Infinite? This game makes them look like someone stepped on their discs. This game is gorgeous. It supports resolutions of up to 1920x1080, and makes use of every piece of graphical technology you could think of. Antialiasing? Ambient Occlusion? PhysX? Tesselation? Anisotropy? Advanced DOF? I have no idea, but I think it might use them. This is just the excuse you needed to upgrade your rig.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
I have to say, when I was gifted this game I had my doubts. But now, I'm a changed person. This game has changed my life, allowed me to see things I couldn't before, and I couldn't be more thankful. This is a must play.

The Metroidvania-genre has become something of a niche in indie gaming, and Guacamelee is a shining example. Tight controls coupled with colorful, smooth graphics, combing exploration with a brawler combo system in fights make Guacamelee fun to play. The music relies on typical mexican instrumental, brass heavy ensemble music, fitting to the game's style and setting and giving it a certain melancholic feel, sometimes.
While the gameplay is fun, the story is rather uninspired, but that's okay. This game is more about the fighting and exploring, than the story. There is a nice little twist, however. There is nothing really new, gameplaywise, either. Also, the exploring doesn't feel quite right, as you are always guided by an arrow on the map where to go next. This is a bit sad, in my opinion, as I love metroidvanias for their laissez-faire gameplay: proceed by exploring.
Nevertheless, Guacamelee is a fun game that will give you some hours of gameplay, and some more if you plan on 100%ing it. Getting into the combo system might take a little time (it took for me, but I suck at these things, anyway), but once you got it, it just flows. By now, there's another version out, called
which you might rather buy, instead of this, as it includes an additional level. But it contains less achievements, if these mean anything to you.
Fun, colorful game. Recommended.

Guacamelee lets me fulfill my dream of becoming a burly Mexican wrestler without pandering to me or skimping on the essentials of satisfying combat.
Guacamelee is a knockout: an exception to the (perceived) rule that indie games are all about style and the resemblance of form, without the function. Drinkbox shows that they know how to honor and build-off-of the SNES-era-inspired gameplay that they reference throughout the game (new power-ups are inside of “choozoo statues”).
Read more:

Really not what I had hoped for or expected. The only game in my steam library I regret buying.
The Good: This game is unique in that it is to my knowledge the only 2D Mexican-themed metroidvania beat-em-up in existence. For the first 1/3 of the game, you'll be thinking "wow, I've never played anything quite like this". Almost everything meshes really tightly (more on that "almost" later).
Superficially, the game is great. I am usually critical of vector/Flash art in indie games (Ed McMillan's style is ugly and unappealing to me) but this game's style is beyond well done and beautifully drawn. It really captures the luchador aesthetic, and it's refreshing to see an indie game with an art style that isn't pixel art (or Ed McMillan's John K-esque gross-out shock-art style). One aspect of this game's art that really impressed me was that it uses its bold and flamboyant colour palette to its advantage: not only do the colours highlight the setting and theme, but bright and vivid contrasts make it very easy to not lose track of your character in the brawls, even in multiplayer. A++ to the art department. Colour me impressed.
The Bad: This game's music is repetitive and unmemorable. While what there is sounds very authentic and fitting, this is a game whose music will become muted very, very quickly. It feels there should be more, but there just… isn’t.
Unfortunately, beneath its shiny exterior Guacamelee! sports some very flawed game mechanics. Fighting becomes bland quickly, and about 1/3 of the way through things start to get baaad. The game tries to stave off the samey-samey-ness of the combat in ways that ultimately fall flat. Instead of increasing the (very limited) variety of enemies, the game introduces gimmicky limitations to combat that feel broken, frustratingly arbitrary, and poorly thought-out with respect to the way the characters control. They also artificially increase the difficulty to levels that border the “completely unfair / broken game design” line.
A fair challenge tests mastery of game mechanics and rewards player skill. Fair challenges are not a part of the latter 2/3 of this game. In fact, some parts of this game are so stupidly difficult (the insta-death fast-spawning exploding bomb enemies for example) that I almost stopped playing. These parts of the game do not test skill; they test patience (in the worst way) and temper. Failure during these parts is almost entirely out of player control. And I do mean literally out of player control because there is virtually no damage-invincibility or ability to recover from a mistake before your character becomes a pingpong ball. And this will happen, again and again and again…
The Ugly: Good writing can be to bad game design as is brown sugar to porridge. It can make something bland into something modestly enjoyable. Unfortunately, Guacamelee!’s writing is more like finding a hair in that bowl of porridge. Sure, it might be your own hair, so there's nothing wrong with it per se, but now you really don’t want to eat any more of that porridge because e
Outside of combat, this game’s story is overrun by a certain style of humour. Take a long sigh out of your nose. That's really the best summary. There are a few actual jokes (setup/payoff) that did make me laugh. Unfortunately they are buried in a sea of dated and cringe-worthy internet memes (???), "references" to movies, and "call-outs" to popular videogames. Yes, that last sentence did indeed say “memes", as in "injokes" with no purpose or amusing qualities beyond "hey I know what that is lololol".
Finally, the ending is an absolute joke.
And when I say the ending is an absolute joke, I mean both that it is an out-of-nowhere, context-blind, poorly-integrated reference, and also that it is abrupt, stupid, and ultimately unsatisfying.
Conclusion: I really wanted to recommend this game. After playing, I felt let-down and disappointed. Give it a pass.

Man o’ War: Corsair can be described like a mix of Assassin’s Creed: Black Flag and the Mount and Blade series. In Man o’ War: Corsair you control the character and the ship just as you could in Black Flag. The controls are simple where WASD steers your ship, right click helps you aim the cannons by showing the trajectory of the cannon and then left click to fire the cannons.
Aside from fighting enemy ships at range, you can also jump on the ships and loot and plunder to your heart’s content with the help of your crew. This crew also helps in managing the cannons, fight other pirates either they board your ship or vice versa and other stuff.
There is absolute freedom in Man o’ War: Corsair and the game completely leaves you directionless from the start. This is where the Mount and Blade inspiration kicks in Man o’ War: Corsair. You are given different quests from notice boards, rumours from pubs and trading from markets.
You can escort refugees, find treasures and loot other vessels to get you more money which in turn can be spent to upgrade your vessel. You can upgrade the mortars, the hull of the ship and various other things which lets you create your own dream vessel.
While coursing through the dangerous waters, there is nothing more exciting than spotting an Ork fleet slugging it out with an imperial fleet and you become trapped in the crossfire. The naval combat is the main meat of the game and that will be what you will be doing throughout most of the experience. It is heavily inspired by the Black Flag naval combat and if you liked that game’s ship combat, Man o’ War: Corsair’s combat is going to be right up your alley.
The third person combat is sluggish and it is mostly spamming a single melee attack until you or your enemies are all dead.  It is fun though seeing your crew and the enemy crew fight it out while you kill off wanderers like you are the star of your pirate movie. Aside from the normal enemies, you will encounter Sharks which are terrifying to come across and damage the hull terribly if you are not well prepared.
The atmosphere in Man o’ War: Corsair is brilliant and while the land exploration is non- existent, it’s the sea exploration that you should try this out for.
Quite a lot of bugs kind of take you out immersion but they are being fixed at a rapid rate. There is tons of customization for your ship and crew, solid naval combat and a game that you can make your stories from. It does not need a proper story to be fun and multiplayer is coming which will make it insanely better since nothing is better than looting and plundering with your friends.
The environment in Man o’ War: Corsair is brilliant which builds tension and the way other ships emerge out of the fog or a sudden appearance of a huge shark are absolutely thrilling. Granted, the visuals up close can be janky and the movement looks awkward. But the overview of the ships are brilliant and it gets the Warhammer world just right.
Man o’ War: Corsair features a solid soundtrack which compliments the nature of the game perfectly. The soundtrack is subtly brilliant and is one to go with the flow. The sound effects of your crew and the others are also done neatly and makes Man o’ War: Corsair’s sound design a neat little package.
Man o’ War: Corsair has a steep admission price and it does have its problems. But it is also one of the games you can make your own stories from and one of the best pirate games in recent memory aside from Black Flag. If you can cope up with a lack of story and direction and a plethora of bugs then Man o’ War: Corsair is absolutely a blast to play.

First off this isn't Black flag.  This is nothing like it.  Yes certain mechanics are similar but this is fantasy v's fiction loosely based on reality.  I'm not a Games workshop fan, but you can't ignore it these days and let's face it the back catalogue and lore is huge.
What does this game do well?  A crazy bit of escapism that has you hunting down mythical sea creatures and firing ridiculous cannons and ships with physics defying weapons of terror.  Non ship combat is charging forward with a sword that can swat enemies down and freeze them in ice.  It's a colourful world that encourages you to be as imaginitive as the ships weapons, taking on a variety of missions that could send you down to Davey Jones' locker or have you soaring as high as your mythical firebreathing pet.
This is an EA review so I will not dwell on the many bugs, but I will say that Eviltwin seem to be very proactive in fixing them.  I personally hope they don't release and leave the game as the potential for this is massive, more ships, more world, more flyers, more races, more more more.
This is not an AAA title and price reflects that well, let's see if DLC is coming and how much for before I get carried away with that though.  For a little over £20 you get a game that has a make your own story with various factions to support and campaign for, ok graphics and not as clunky as perfectionists cry combat, anda window into the world of a crazied engineer that has had 30 years worth of ideas as a GW title.

navigate a badly broken ship through a series of islets while being chased by the entire imperial fleet,
race an elven catamaran,
hire wizards and watch the enemy suffer,
try to out maneuvor an enemy flyer while whishing you had bough anti air systems but bought a big shiney axe made of a sea monster you killed,

I wanted to like this game. It has some good ideas and a good setting.
The ship and unit designs are interesting - but that's about  as far as the good goes.
It's extremely (and I mean extremely) clunky in its current state.
"On Foot Combat" - couldn't be more dull or disjointed, It is easily the worst combat I've ever played. Super repetitive, and almost comical animations.
"Ship Combat" - again, very clunky, but not quite as bad as on-foot combat. Here, you'll simply see the the AI flipping out more often than not. Most of the time I was clipping through ships and my AI ships clipping through both myself and the enemy AI ships.
This continues to be an issue when you board the enemy ship. Your AI ships will continue to try and attack, continue to flip out and clip through the ships.
This causes the ship floor to stutter and characters to bounce slightly.
This is all ignoring the FPS issues.
It's fine FPS wise - until you get a few enemy ships and a few AI friendly ships on the go.
Then now and again random freezes and severe FPS drops occur.
All in all, it's a bit of a mess sadly. God knows how it has a "Very positive" rating - but that's what Steam refunds are for.
I suspect the old "Anything Warhammer is a thumbs up" fanbase is at play here!

At first, the game was infected with bugs and high online, some were complaining about their PCs not being able to run it properly, but it lived to our day. But after the July of 2016, the sad part of this story has begun: online has gone dead. There were some remnants left out in the wasteland, and there were no place for newbies, since everybody except them knew the rules and could exploit them. We have stayed for all the pros of this game. But even then, people have started leaving the game. At the moment of the beginning of the free trial, there were about 100 people playing. Now, there are more, but this still does not give us hope of reviving the game.
Pros:
- This is NOT Overwatch. Whoever believed that the games were almost exactly the same can go out and try, because I imply that they are NOT ALIKE.
- MOBA-like mechanics in some modes. For all of those who has left DotA (and I respect you for that) - you shall feel like home, but only in FP.
- Characters. This game was made by creators of the all-loving BORDERLANDS, for god's sake. So you can expect nothing less but a lot of crazyness about the Battleborn themselves and enviroment they fight in general.
- No "Pay-to-win" mechanics. I have NO IDEA how dumb must be people that post something like "another P2W dead game, not interested in paying" on the forums. Since when cosmetics are something that makes you better? (TF2 excluded, out there it means "prestige", which is almost "skill")
- Multi-genre gameplay. Characters are completely different: some use rifles, some use chaos magic, some use their fists/jaws/melee weapons, and that is just 3-4 of them. Think about it: here you can take your vengeance upon generic "Ash Williams with the boomstick" with medieval weapons.
- Character quotes and voiceover. Completely worth it.
- Customisation. If you find it unnecessary, you might add it to cons category. Otherwise, it is a big part of the game.
- Lore and story. Sure, if you came here for something like a BioShock story (or Witcher 3 story, which I cannot understand - that is some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story), then you will not appreciate that. But for a multiplayer FPS there is much to read, discover and listen about.
Cons:
- Low online. Still. That is why WE, the old-timers, need you support in reviving this game.
- "Anti-noob" feature. Not a real thing, but made by players. If you are not a fast learner, cannot take a few defeats and are not able to quickly adapt to anything you see, you will suffer.
- Matchmaking. Same with con #2: if you cannot adapt quickly, you will die, and then die many more times, because the chance of having a veteran on your team is SLIGHTLY lower that having him against you. Trust me, I have checked.
- Too much bright lights and colors. Epileptics, beware.
- Battleborn restrictions. Unless you have paid the price, you can only play 6 Battleborn out of 30, which seems sort of crippling for me. On one side, you do not have to unlock them like we did, by completing challenges. On the other side, 6 out of 30 is.... kind of not much.
- Trolls, or "ill-minded veterans". Unlike some of us, there are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who LOVE to taunt after every kill. IF you see a person named "hup" - expect him to taunt you every goddamn time he kills you.
- OP characters. There is at least 1 OP character at the moment, with each patch/Battleplan it changes. For a long time it was Galilea, El Dragon (now grinded to dust), and each and every one of the Season Pass characters (Alani, Kid Ultra, Pendles, Beatrix and Ernest) after their own release. Now, it is almost fully balanced. You don't have to endure getting killed by Galilea and her pocket medic all the time like we used to.

As a former golfer and amateur tournament competitor (24hcp) I can honestly say that my experience of real world golf matters not a jot with regards to how much fun The Golf Club 2 is. It does genuinely scratch the itch I have had for a few years now, and I am so happy to be able to replace 'hybrid' clubs with my 1 and 2 Irons. If you have played golf 'IRL' then you will enjoy this game a lot. Here is a bit of a breakdown;
+ It looks nice. It's not 'real life' nice but yeah it's nice.
+ The swing mechanic is sensible and feels 'right'.
+ The lay of the land matters; firm fairways lead to strange bounces, fast greens lead to frustration.
+ The ability to add fade and draw to shots is really welcome, as is the real use of top and bottom spin.
- The greens are very hard to read. They could augment the moving lines with subtle shadows.
- The wind. A 3mph wind will act like a 30mph gust and a 17mph wind will do nothing. Extremely inconsistent.
- Sand. It acts more like tar. Your character is also doomed to use partial shots when in bunkers; clearly lacking a spine.
- Range estimates. You have to 'club up' several measures sometimes. Other times this will see you yelling 'fore' at the clubhouse carpark.
I can only hope the developers are working to iron out any minor issues. Nailing the wind and sand physics will be a big help, as would perhaps introducing 'types' of clubs. Any decent golfer will tell you that all clubs are not created equally, and some are more demanding than others; same goes for golf balls. They are not all the same, different brands have different properties best suited to different scenarios. Make some brands up or something.
Overall I fully recommend this game for anyone needing a golf fix, and for those curious about golf, who may go on to try it 'IRL'.
(1 Iron is love by the way, get a 1 Iron.)

I had a terrible problem with this game. The game's video playback was broken, but there is no warning or indication about this when the game runs, it simply fails to play video where it should and otherwise it seems like the game is working "normally". Because this is a game about mystery and experimentation, there is really no way to know that it is not working as intended. THIS BECAME AN EXTREMELY FRUSTRATING EXPERIENCE. A puzzle game where all the hints are broken.
Eventually I discovered that the video problem can be fixed by running the game as an administrator, but the game begins randomly crashing. At any rate I find it totally unacceptable that I had to watch a walkthrough video to realize the game wasn't working as intended.
The best solution seems to be to download ScummVM and use that to play the game (point it at "C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Myst Masterpiece"). This runs mostly fine (with a few minor audio issues) but at least I finally got to play through the game.
One additional problem, a note you find in the game with instructions (critical to completing the game) has a typo, where it says "off" instead of "on". Bizarre! I'm really astounded by how badly this version is put together.
Anyhow, Myst is an interesting game with an important place in history. I think it's worth playing, but I strongly dislike how poorly it is packaged here.

Part of the game where you grind if you have not meticulously chosen your talents and powers (the permanent and limited nature of the build can become punitive when you discover the game).By back-tracking a little too much you soon realize the relatively small number of areas to explore and very spectacular end of play but that can turn to ridicule rather quickly.

*Short Review*
This game consistantly makes lists of 'Best Star Wars games Ever' for a reason. While the graphics may be dated, The simple combat system is fun, and the story better then some of the newer movies!
*Full Review*
This game put BioWare on the map for a reason!
The graphics are dated for sure (There may be some graphics overhaul mods out there... but I personally like the graphics!), but if you can look past that, You are in for a great game!
The combat system is an interesting (and in my oppinion sucessful) mix of real-time and turn-based combat. There is a wide array of weapons, armor, upgrades, skill-builds and playstyles are possible. Each armor part and weapon with their own advantages and unique traits. Everything from pistols, to chainguns, from swords and sticks, to lightsabers
While the main character you play as starts off as being your generic nameless hero we've seen time and time again (untill THE twist... Y'all who've played it know what I mean!), your interation with the world around you are your party memebers help not only to flesh-out their stories, but your own player charcters own story.
The story of KoTOR... How to decribe the story and do it justice.... The story of KoTOR really is worthy of its own movie. The story is non-stop enjoyment from start to finish. It captivates you right from the begining and makes you want to keep going and explore. I will admit though, the first planet after the tutorial 'Taris' is the most borring part of the story... After that the story gets REALLY fun and exciting. Like most Star Wars games, KoTOR has two endings, A lightside ending and a darkside ending. While I will admit, the lightside-darkside allignment you buildup in the game has very little effect on the story (That allignment affects how you use the force), the ending you get depeneds on how you resolve a single encounter near the end of the game, and the gameplay ends the same no matter if you go the lightside or darkside. While the story for the rest of the game (and in a few cutscenes to decribe what happens after the game) totally changes, how the story plays out in terms of gameplay is the same.
Also the story of KoTOR has the biggest plot twist in Star War since Darth Vader's Iconic 'I Am Your Father' moement. Seriously, If people are still talking about a 2003 plottwist in 2017, you know its good!
All In All, I can not recomend KoTOR enough for any Star Wars fan!

Ku: Shroud of the Morrigan is a deeply flawed game. It tells a story of a young hero Ku who is on a wondrous and treacherous journey to help his village. The game is heavily inspired by motives of Irish folklore, post-apocalyptic setting and a hidden story about environmental danger we put our world at all the time. Is it good though? Well, no... but it comes close to it.
Ku SOTM has unique and captivating hand written graphics that look great and inspiring. Writing is not to shabby as well, though there isn't much of it in the game. Ku plays like a light version of Diablo hack and slasher with occasional spatial puzzles peppered throughout the game. Design of the enemies is definitely a highlight, since they can be beautiful and horrifying at the same time. It pretty much feels like a classic European folk tale: it is equally dazzling, mysterious and disturbing at the same time.
That's where the pluses end. Speaking about the darks side of things, game is too short, and you can complete it in 2-3 hours if you're completionist. It also ends on an open cliffhanger, which definitely does not help in overall experience. An important piece of game mechanic, dodge / roll action is broken since it's unresponsive and hardly useful in combat. There will be times when you'll dodge enemies’ attacks with ease, but most of the time, dodge button just won't react to your clicking or will activate with a major delay. Sound and music is unfortunately way too simple and border-line irritating with its clanking and banging.
Ku really is a tough sell. By all accounts I should give it a negative recommendation, but I did enjoy my time with it. I really hope that its developers will continue evolving their craft and deliver us the shinning sequel this game deserves. Plus, you can play it on Gaelic which makes the entire experience truly magical. So yes, I'll give it a careful recommendation, but know it is a deeply flawed game.

I think this is the only Dwarf Fortress-like game that has a multiplayer mode so far. (if you don't count Dungeon Keeper and it's modern replica War for the Overworld)
It's very hard to implement multiplayer in games like Dwarf Fortress due to time control issues. commonly you have three approaches: first approach is that any player can control time whenever they want, (like Paradox Interactive's strategy series) which gives an incoherence among players who want to fast forward certain period of their economic development while someone else is trying to micromanage an ongoing battle. Second approach is to separate each player's individual time (like Simcity 5) so that they can control their own time, which means players also need separate maps to keep the game coherent, so interactions among players will  inevitably get reduced. Third approach is that putting everything under a same time lapse and a same map (just like an RTS) but reducing complexity to make everything manageable, and that gives you the model of Colony Survival.
Problem is, that the level of complexity deduction is so high that it fundamentally changes the feeling you get in other Dwarf Fortress-like games and it sometimes renders the game a little bit primitive and boring. And also for the very reason you know that they won't add too much stuff in future under the premise of not remaking the entire game.
But after all, it's a Dwarf Fortress-like game that you can play with your friends, what more could one ask for?

The honest truth is that its painfully average. Its not great, and its not bad. This game probably would have gotten a decent foothold if it A) had a somewhat competent PR team, and B) was super cheap / F2P to begin with. As a F2P, its not bad. Its about what I expect from one. Its all there. It works, theres skins, taunts, an objective, tutorials, teams, multiplayer, gamemodes and all that.
However I would have hated to of payed full price for this. It has no where near enough content to cost as much as it did. Hoenstly I think Overwatch was much too expensive on release as well.
The gameplay isnt exciting. I didnt really feel like I was doing much of anything while I was playing. I was holding down shoot and occasionally pressing Q, E, and F. There really didnt seem to be much room for great plays, it was just kind of "you win the encounter or you dont", there didnt really seem to be an inbetween. The animation is smooth and well done, but the texture quaility, post processing, and HUD design are very lacking. In the case of the HUD it really does get in the way. The colors seem to be washed out on some maps and I can barely tell apart player from minion. It just looks like a cluster of colors and particles.
The audio is pretty well done, I didnt have any complaints for that. The dialogue is subjective, you either like the tone and humor, or you dont. Personally I think its very hit or miss. Some of the dialogue is well written and funny, and some of it is just flat out hard to listen to (just very annoying sometimes)
The characters arent original, not going to lie. Im trying to be as fair as possible but most of them are straight rips from League and other popular games. None of their abilities are really original either. Its just kind of your standard stuff.
In short, its a very average game, but it fits nicely into the F2P section. Why the dev is so against going with the flow is beyond me, it might have saved the game long ago, but its finally where it needs to be to be worth at least trying. Its a soft recommendation.

I don't get it. Am I missing something? I think I'm missing something. I mean, it really feels like I'm missing something. I've definitely gotta be missing something... right?
Antenna is a short, free, 2D game based largely around audio puzzles. Follow some on-screen button prompts to raise and activate antennae, scan the frequencies for the correct audio, traipse around as a weird, four-legged spider drone thingy, do a couple more audio puzzles, see a picture of a planet slowly become ever so slightly more distant, have the game shut itself down on you, then scratch your head and wonder what the hell you just played. There, I've saved you half an hour of having to play this yourself.
Maybe some will brand me a philistine, but I just don't get what the point of this thing is. There's no explanation given to anything in the game; no real clear objective for any of the puzzles, no set-up for who, what, why or where exactly you are, no form of context for anything at all, it's all just... stuff. Formless, meaningless stuff. I guess all just... because. I know brevity is the soul of wit an' all, but c'mon, would it have really hurt to provide even the slightest form of basic insight into anything? Maybe they hope the environment or apparent scenario will lead us to question everything and make us create our own story, but that really feels lazy if that's actually the case. That's why I almost feel like there must be some kind of inside info I'm somehow completely missing. Everyone likes a bit of mystery, but the joy of that comes from teasing us with a little information then having us chase after the rest of the answers that will eventually come. Here, there's just nothing - nothing teased, nothing to chase, just... nothing.
I guess the actual audio design itself is pretty well done, and the minimal, heavy-silhouetted visuals are as appealing as they've always been, but personally that doesn't count for very much when the gameplay itself is so lacking. I feel like someone's given me a single paragraph from a novel but then denied me the rest of the book, and by the end I was mostly just annoyed and left empty by the lack of direction or context.
If you feel like you haven't been especially catered for in the audio puzzle department and have been looking for something to fill that void, this may give you a little kick while it lasts. For everyone else, I honestly don't know what this has to offer you.

I have no nostalgia for this game, it's not something I played as a kid so I have no bias towards loving it or hating it. I played it on the recommendation of a friend and it's something I have wanted to play for a long time to appreciate a historic game and how much it defined a genre. Myst is an important part of gaming history, a point and click adventure/puzzle game that took the world by storm. It's deceivingly simple but draws you in with it's mystery and surprisingly deep puzzles all at a 640x480 resolution.
It is a game of another time when players were expected to take notes and pay close attention to the world and the small details inside of it. You are expected to think, explore and you are expected to experiment. I found very few of the puzzles  frustrating (though the design of some left a bit to be desired, the game can be forgiven for a little bad design here and there though seeming as it came out in 1993.) Even as someone who doesn't really play puzzle games all that often and isn't particularly good at them I never found myself stuck for too long and if I did get stuck it was my fault. Myst never commits the sin of many other point and click adventure games I have played in the past where you end up just clicking on random objects trying to find the way forward. I finished this game using nothing but common sense, puzzle solving skills, observation and a bit of experimentation.
The graphics of the game are extremely dated but the world is unique and interesting, I found myself admiring the places the world took me too and found an appreciation for the background that each world was given through books in the game. Little story details are left to the player to notice and many rooms in the game tell their own story simply by what you find in them. Little details strewn about which are inconsequential to the completion of the game, but help you piece together the story you find yourself a part in. I love games which leave little clues which help an observant player piece together a grander narrative than it would seem.
I'll refrain from going into too many spoilers because the plot is quite good and I'd hate to spoil it for anyone on the astronomical chance someone who hasn't played Myst before reads this review.
You are transported to a strange Island called 'Myst' and it quickly becomes evident that something has gone wrong there, you find a note from a husband telling his wife to find a secret message and you find two men seemingly trapped inside one blue and one red book in a library containing many other burned books. The men's messages to you are staticy and broken and you can't make out what they're trying to say to you. As you progress through the game an observant eye and a bit of patience will find you piecing together what happened, and the truth behind why those two men are trapped inside two books in Myst's library. Myst has an interesting and unique world which I always wanted to know more about, a fact that compelled me to play this game to it's conclusion.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys relaxing puzzle games, a good story or anyone with an interest in playing a historic game that defined a genre. A Masterpiece this most certainly is just make sure you have a notepad and a pen when you play it.

I'm convinced this game is available for the sole purpose of convincing you to purchase "realMyst: Masterpiece Edition" (updated version with better graphics).
Myst heavily relies on the hand icon to help guide you and understand various actions available.  In this version there is one static hand icon which never changes and there are no video scenes.  Some parts of the game you will never be able to figure out without the video cut-scenes enabled.
In order to get these "native" features go to:
C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Myst Masterpiece
Right click on Myst.exe --> Properties --> Check Run this program in compatibility mode for --> (Win95 or your current OS) --> Apply
Now run Myst again, should be able to see the original hand icon and video cut-scenes.  Only problem now is that the game will freeze regularly and sometimes crashes.  Have found it will even crash when not in compatibility mode sometimes.
It is essentially unplayable after a while.  If you are set on playing the "original" I would recommend getting a disk and playing it on a Win95 VM (Hope you like really slow transitions between frames).  Otherwise do yourself a favor and just purchase "realMyst."

A violent puzzler.
Hitman: Bloody Money has you returning as 47, the worlds greatest assassin. The story is told from the perspective of the CIA director, with the missions of 47 having already taken place. While you are performing hits for the agency, there are forces moving against the organization.
Each mission is a level, pitting 47 against various levels of security, scrutiny and other challenges. The player can become a 1 man army, killing everyone in sight, or use stealth and assume identities of others, setting up "accidents" and meticulously crafting the perfect kill to obtain the silent assassin ranking. Each mission ends with a newspaper detailing the event, which is a nice touch. The game truly shines by allowing multiple solutions and it's worth while to see how other players pulled off their level clears. The more professional the hit, the more money you earn which goes towards upgrading your tools.
I went for professional difficulty, silent assassin ranking for all the missions so I can't speak to much for the gun mechanics. There are a wide variety of weapons and you are able to collect more by placing a newly acquired gun into an ICA boxes. There is an option to go into fps (F1 key) if you want to go in guns a blazing. In 3rd person, the accuracy of weapons seems off at times.
Getting away clean is difficult, but rewarding. Silent assassin ranking is achieved by killing only targets (accept for accidents), having no witnesses, and not blowing your cover. On professional difficulty, you cannot leave any items such as custom weapons nor your suit as evidence. You can use undetectable items, such as poison, sedatives, piano wire, and detonators to get past security, or use the environment to sneak weapons through. You can take almost anyone's clothes to gain unrestricted access to different area as you approach your target. Avoiding detection is tricky due to keeping track of so many NPCs and trying to figure out where your new identity allows you access (or doesn't allow access is just as important). Some trial and error is needed to get the feel of the level before you can plan let alone execute your mission.
AI was solid for the most part. Sometimes I was frustrated by what seemed to be an overly suspicious NPC or a phantom witness. I watched other solutions to all the missions, and there really are multiple ways to complete them all though there will be some obvious similarities. The graphics do show their age and at times interactions with the environment or your items can be clunky (oh that panic of trying to move a body out of a door way). While some interactions may not seem obvious (like which NPCs you can talk to), there is intelligence available for every mission (for a few around $3,500 each) that will point out there existence.
Hitman: Blood Money is a challenging game, but mostly for the right reasons. The level designs with the the allowance for so many possible variations of game play make it an enjoyable experience.

Even if you have played all the other Hitman games out there, nothing beats 'Hitman - Blood Money'. This is the best stealth-action game out there !! The best thing about this game is that there are multiple ways to complete each level / your objective, and this is the beauty of it. If you like stealth games, or you are a fan of Hitman games, this is the one that you must play in your lifetime :)

Colony Survival is a survival game (duh) that deviates from the standard "solo" survival game. For early access, this game holds great potential, and even at its current state I feel that it is worth the money. There is no actual levelling system, but many items and jobs are locked until you unlock them one by one through research.
The voxel graphics may remind you of minecraft, but you will soon realise that it is not as easy. You have to build, recruit
colonists and create a town on your own. This means that you have to be a manager of sorts, ensuring that supplies are up, everyone's fed and that they can hold their own through waves of zombie that spawn at night. You yourself don't get hungry or tired, which can either be a good or bad thing depending on your preference.
Building is pretty okay, but one major gripe still not implemented is that there are no "stairs", and you have to jump to get up a block. In this game, building is important since you have to design your base in such a way that it's accessible to your colonists yet inconvenient for the zombies, while ensuring that it isn't too big since zombies spawn a set distance from your king flag, indoors or not. You can increase the distance through research, but that's only when you get deeper into the game. Assuming that you are not the kind of player to just block off the colonists at their work stations and run a place devoid of beauty, you will find that it is quite challenging to balance utility and aesthetics in base building.
You are also not a king-of-all-trades (ha) like in other games, as Colony Survival is set in such a way that 70% of crafting is only able to be done by your colonists, which places emphasis on planning and management. While it may seem manageable at first, complacency is a dangerous thing, and your town can be overrun with just a simple mistake, such as not realising that you ran out of wood planks for arrows
.
To conclude, Colony Survival is a gem being polished. The devs also pay more attention to suggestions and players' voices, which is pretty nice. There are bugs and glitches occasionally, but it's to be expected.

tl;dr Reasonably decent port of an average mobile game, just don't expect anything amazing. Around ~1.5 hours.
It's not awful, but not particularly good either. I would rather give this a neutral rating, but given the many negative ratings (which seems a bit unfair to me) I'll stick with a positive one - I didn't feel like I "lost two hours", but there are certainly many, many better games out there. Overall it feels like what you'd expect from a mobile port for a rather short adventure game.
The mouse only control scheme isn't as bad as I thought it'd be, but there are some places where you can briefly get stuck in the terrain (easy to fix, but the rate at which this occurred became annoying). There are some nice moments to the story, but as a whole it's rather bland, cliche, and unnecessarily leaves a lot of unknowns to make room for a sequel(s). The combat is boring point and click as you'd expect, with roll and stun features too. Like the movement it can feel clunky, but it's simple enough that it doesn't heavily detract from the game.
It's rather short, probably ~1.5 hours even with looking through every nook and cranny (I had some afk time). On a side note, if you expected this to be "thematically appropriate" for St. Patrick's day or other Irish festivities like I did you should look elsewhere. It has Gaelic names and one guy playing vaguely Irish music in the first act but that's about it; the rest looks more like Mad Max than Ireland.

This could have been a lovely game if more effort had been made, but it failed to live up to its vision. The best part of it was the art style and the "Celt-punk" mythology used in the game, a fresh take on things, but it's spoiled by mushy controls, tedious slogging around for overly simple quests, identikit maps, and downright bad sounds.
Pros:
+ Beautiful and often evocative and/or creepy art, with some unique ideas.
+ While there are Celtic fantasy games, this is the first technology-based idea I've seen, and that's creative.
+ Some good music was struggling to get heard in some of the areas.
+ The characters had an interesting basic design, and Ku seemed true to his namesake.
+ The fighting progression was well done.
+ Some fairly creative change-ups on the quest, with new challenges.
+ Imaginative monster/villain design that needed different approaches for different monsters.
+ Easy to figure out what to do in a particular challenge.
Cons:
- Incredibly bad sound effects. Some very common sounds such as walking and fighting are actively obnoxious.
- If you enter a cut scene while walking, you get to hear the obnoxious walking sound effect during the entire scene, because it doesn't stop the character from walking.
- Some of the cut scenes should be more tightly scripted or meaningful. They steal control from the player and can be tedious to wait through.- Tedious quest design, with overly simple puzzles, and some quests which required slogging all the way back through long and empty maps.
- Very little interactivity in most of the maps. So, interesting art but very little to touch or do. Very dull character interaction on most of the NPCs.
- Poor/weird animation in many areas.
- The map designs should be a little more distinctively landmarked; the maps hindered exploration a bit.
- A little bugginess: fighting charges you to an opponent, and it's possible to bug onto an opponent in an area that you can't get down from, like a wall. (Workaround: reload the game; you have to do the fight again but it gets you off the wall.)
- Mushy fighting which isn't very kinetic and it's not always apparent that your actions aren't taking effect.
- Inferior writing. (There are bits that were funny, but sharper writing would have made this much better.)
- Uneven pacing. (The beginning particularly is poorly paced.)
- Short. (Not as much of a con at this quality level, but if the game were improved and had more to do, this would be a con.)
All in all, while it's not outright bad, it's not outright good either -- I find myself unable to recommend it, but it's a shame because I think this could have been a good game with more attention to quality.

I first played this game when it was initially released for the original Xbox over a decade ago, and it's still just as incredible now as it was then. I would easily argue that it's the best game Bioware has ever released, and I would highly recommend it for both fans and non-fans of the Star Wars universe.
SW:KOTOR is a game that's story-rich and full of choices that greatly alter the story's course. There's several ways to complete various quests, and every time I've played through this game, I've found something new, making this a good game to replay at least once or twice. I found the companions to be interesting and complex characters that I enjoyed bringing along on the journey. Despite being over 10 years old, the game's graphics still hold up surprisingly well and aren't much of a distraction. If you're a fan of older RPGs, this is definitely a game you'll enjoy.
However, this game does have a handful of issues. Combat, for instance, can feel tedious, and battles can feel dragged out and unnecessarily long if you find yourself not properly prepared for a fight. There are some technical issues as far as glitches and bugs go, though I personally haven't run into too many of those and there's several mods and patches available to fix those and enhance your experience. Since this is such an old game and hasn't been remastered in any way, newer systems may struggle to run it properly. If your system is capable of running this, though, you should get this game because I can't thoroughly express how enjoyable it really is.

All this while still giving a number of challenges that you may need to try more than a few times. These tend to give you either a "YES, I did it!" reaction or a "Well, I'm glad I don't have to do that again" reaction. However, that is more for completion than for playing through the game itself -- you can get through most of the game without needing to do all the insane side-challenges, but doing them does help hone your skills and make the rest of the game feel easier.
There are also a variety of references to a number of pop culture and gaming references throughout the world. They don't get in the way and all seem to have been well integrated into the style of the game. The world of Mexican folklore that Drinkbox was able to portray was pretty cool overall, though it felt somewhat hammy after a while.
A very fun and challenging game. I highly recommend it, especially to those who like platformers.
Note: I have not yet tried the Co-op.

This is the first review I have ever written. I am writing this while my refund is pending. RCTW has great potential to be an amazing game. After playing for a few hours and watching streams and such for a few hours, I can not recommend this game in it's current form. I have hope that the developer will turn this around. After watching the latest stream they did, i can see why RCTW is not a success. They have forgotten what it is about. They have forgotten what makes the RCT series great. They have forgotten it is about the roller coasters! After seeing some of the pre-built roller coasters that are available, I wonder if any of them have ever rode one. There were a few things that made me consider opting for the refund, and one thing in particular that lauched me out of the station. First, i tried to build a pretty common element on looping steel rollercoasters called a cobra roll. It is impossible. Well... i cant say impossible. If i wanted to spend hours trying to get it to work i probably could have made it work, but lets get real. Who wants to spend that amount of time on one element. Since the beginning of RCT time, you were able to build  a half loop into a left or right half corkscrew, then into the opposing corkscrew piece, and finally finish of with you second half loop. Now when i tried with the current iteration in the series, i did my half loop, then into a half cor... nope... no half corkscrew piece. Instead there were multiple corkscrews, and not even in the right direction. It was going up into the air, opposite direction and behind the half loop. Now you can do alot with RCTW's spline based coaster builder, but that was just rediculous. I ended up just doing a large loop and making a few other spaced out elements before returning the track to the station. The coaster ended up being well recieved by my parks patrons, but I was about to call my doctor to schedule chemo. So a couple of days later I had an idea. Im going to try to build one of my favorite roller coasters, Kennywood's Thunderbolt. How i have built recreations in the past, especially Kennywood coasters, is to build them on flat ground then save the blueprint. Then, dig a  hole in the ground since all of their coasters are hugging ravines. So as I finished and tested Thunderbolt-ish, i was getting excited to save and put my coaster in its final resting place. Instead i think i may have found RCTW's final resting place. When i was trying to lower i found that you simply cannot do that.it would not even go down till the bottom most piece of track was touching the ground. What the $@*&?!?! I was dumbfounded. I had no solution. Since i was already frustrated from trying to make the rollercoaster in the first place and just wanted to be done, i decided to just raise the terrain and say the heck with it. Cant do that either... all of the land where there were only supports would not level out with the rest. So i had holes in the ground everywhere there were supports. The list of obsenities that proceded from my mouth were many. So that was pretty much strike two. So a couple days later, I read that they are launching the game. I also read that there would be a live stream. I missed the live part, but did watch it a few days later. Nothing new. Same crap different version. They showed off that the peeps aren't skating across the ground anymore, the new "campaign mode", and more PxP. What the heck is PxP? Oh, that is the scenery. I swear if i hear them say peice by peice one more time imma kms. Like this is ROLLERCOASTER Tycoon... not Scenery Tycoon. So much emphasis has been placed on scenery while the fuctionality of simple things like rollercoasters and paths are put on the back burner. While watching the stream, seeing that woman force Daisy out, I said to myself, "Yup... I'm done."

This game is incredible. I've been looking for a good golf game on PC for ages, and finally I've found one that delivers in spades.
Presentation 10/10
The game is very polished throughout with an easy accessible menu system and all made to look very slick. There are fully voiced tutorials to take you through all the shot types. They even have a very comprehensive in-game help.
Graphics 7/10
The game is pretty, using the latest unity engine version. Dynamic volumetric clouds move in the sky, water flows and has that nice reflection you'd expect. Lighting and shadows looks really good. There are some issues with texture pop-in at certain distances, but there are settings you can tweak to increase those distances at the cost of performance (depending on how strong your GPU is).
Sound 8/10
The ambiant noise is great, with bird sounds and atmosphere of the different courses captured beautifully. The crowd noise isn't amazing, but it's not horrible either and doesn't bother me. The commentating is quite good, although I've seen people complain about it, I quite enjoy it. I don't often hear repeated phrases, and I found his commentating to be quite accurate regarding what's happening in the game.
Gameplay 9/10
First off, the new swing system is incredible. It takes time and effort to master, but is not too difficult on easier clubs. They have really hit the sweetspot when it comes to difficulty in this game. There are 3 different club sets, ranked from Easy (Standard), Medium (Player), Hard (Tour). The harder the clubset that you choose, the more distance you'll get, but the more unforgiving the game will be on bad swings, and vice versa, the easier clubs doesn't give big distance, but is very forgiving when you make mistakes. I play on tour clubs and I find that every shot I have to concentrate in order to hit a good shot. I've had it where I'm trying to hit a green near a water hazard, and I mess up because I feel the pressure, but then I've had the elation when I've handled the pressure and hit a good shot anyway. This game is so much like real golf where you have to focus and think about every shot, and I love the challenge. I started out with a 7 handicap, but have now got it down to around a 1 handicap, and it's been awesome seeing how I've improved.
Features 8/10
Offline Single Player: There is a career mode where you play against AI scores where you can win money and upgrade your clubhouse and/or your player clothing etc. There are lots of difficulty settings and it's fun. You can create your own events and seasons playing on any courses you want. There is no AI players playing with you, but it's not really something I care too much about.
Online: There is this society feature where you basically join other people's clubs and play in their events for prize pools, and to get your name on top of leaderboards. This is good fun, and really nice to compare yourself to real people. Something I like doing is adding ghost players to my rounds with other people's previous rounds and then turning Turn Order on, which lets you watch each player taking their shots. It's like playing with real players, but without the wait, which I love. There is realtime online play with friends if that's what you prefer.
Overall 8/10
The game is fun and challenging, which is what a golf game should be. I'm addicted and play at least one round a day. It has got me swearing and cursing a lot, but I think that's the effect all good sports games have on me. Ignore the panzies who call this game too difficult and give it a try. I believe it's worth every penny!
