Before I begin, this is my first review. Now that that's out of the way let me just say in it's current state (Posted during build 0.9.2) You don't need to know anything about the warhammer universe to enjoy this game. I didn't even realize till I was 12 hours in. Now if you're looking for a story, you're not going to find one just yet save for one of your own making. Which if that's your thing, you're going to get a fair amount of enjoyment out of this game. The fights are fun and work well for me. (Though I have a bad computer and suffer horrible lag issues) But even so with the right settings the game still manages to run a decent 15 to 20 frames on the open sea.
I've only played human so far, but there is a Chaos campaign as well. Which you are pretty much stuck being the bad guy. But as human you have total freedom. There are plenty of missions to keep you busy as a human, and plenty of trading opportunities. I recomend getting the three trading based perks as soon as possible if you can't keep track of what ports are buying and selling high or low. But bare in mind your max level is 10. (Unless it's been updated since the guide was posted) Speaking of which I recomend reading that in the steam tab ingame. It's great help for beginners, but a few things are outdated.
Sea monsters are fun and challanging fights as well. And overal i'm pleased with that this game is so far, and hope the devs continue to work on it. But as for the negatives. There's a few. The missions can start to feel samey, and it's got a fair amount of bugs. But not enough to ruin the full experience. Boarding is a bit OP if costly to your crew if you're not careful, and can be done as long as you're within range of a ship's side. But just spam strong attack with a decent weapon. Sooner or later you'll win. Next Armor is all cosmetic at the moment. FOR THE CAPTAIN! Ship armor makes a difference. And hope you like hoarding weapons and shields cause currently you can only sell goods. Not weapons shields or clothes. Thankfully they do not take up cargo space. Also, you're not told this in game, but water is gotten when it rains or when you dock at a port. I was confused for a long time how to get this.
Next the auto saves can get a bit cluttered so remember to delete ones you KNOW you're not gonna go back to, or it'll eat up space. And remember to save before doing a mission, some are bugged BADLY. And finally. The journal records every action you do in regards to ports that is of importance. While this is useful when remembering how much you bought something for when trying to sell it. Finding it becomes a pain when you have to go through a hundred pages to see your most recent purchace and or sale. My recomendation to the dev for fixing this is two fold. 1 Add a seperate tab for all financhal related stuff. And 2 give us the option to erase unimportant entries. Cause seriously. This thing fills up FAST. But that's all I have to say. If you can ignore those honestly minor negatives, I think you'll enjoy the game a lot. And at the very least get a few hours of fun out of it.
If you want a simple sailing game where you fight pirates and hostile creatures including megalodons sea dragons, wyverns, and also trade and sell goods. This is a good one for ya, as it's right to the point. And mind you, the fighting IS OPTIONAL and so is the trading. You can do WHATEVER YOU PLEASE! But if you want a story, or just MORE content. Maybe wait a bit on this one, but deffinetly keep it in mind. Sorry for the long review. Hope it helped anyone who wasn't sure about buying it.

If you've read reviews that compares this game to Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you should disregard them. Ubisoft never makes good games, so unless the comparison is that this game is better in every way (I wouldn't know, I've only been let down twice by Ubisoft), it's dumb.
That out of the way, let's delve into the game. I've been playing it since it pretty much first came out on early access, and while I didn't expect much out of the game after being let down by EA one time after another (not that EA), the devs blew me away with their dedication to this game. The criticism and requests of the community are seriously taken into consideration with these guys, and the game is evolving as people play the game and understand its strong points and flaws. The UI and graphics overall got a little makeover, and it looks nice and feels mostly optomized. Combat has been changing from clunky to getting pretty okay. As far as playing a campaign goes, it's pretty much like Mount and Blade in gameplay mechanics, which is nice. With the addition of a Chaos Campaign and Custom battles, it looks like a lot of "what we want" features in the final product is actually going to make it one way or another.
$30 is a pretty solid price for this game, although if you can get in on sale I would definitely recommend that. Early Access done right.

Man o'War: Corsair (Early Access Review).
The truth of the matter is a chap could have his gaming itch well scratched playing nothing but Warhammer games these days. Dawn of War or Total War: Warhammer for the RTS itch (be that campaign, co-op or head-to-head), Mordheim: City of the Damned or Blood Bowl for turn-based boardgamery, Vermintide or Deathwing to get your Left For Dead style fix, and Battlefleet: Gothic Armada for that tactical spaceship hit. I could easily go on - but these are, to varying degrees of okay through to excellent, the Games Workshop games I currently play. So how could we possibly need yet another Warhammer title? Well, for two reasons actually: there has never been an open-world RPG set in the Warhammer Old World and there has never been a naval battle simulator set there either. I was going to go into all the usual comparisons and systems break-downs but I think perhaps the best way to convey what Man o'War is successfully doing for me is to describe my last hour of play like it was a pen-and-paper RPG game.
So my corsair was docked at the port of Hargendorf on the bitter northern coast of The Empire. My crew were paid up and I was wandering in town selling my wares and looking to see if any of my connections needed work. I have elected to do up my basic ship, having found it very much to my liking, rather than save for a larger one or invest in a fleet - neither the idea of being the leader of a flotilla or the bloated captain of a fat galleon appeal to me just yet. I want to be fast with big guns and good cannoneers, the hitman of the boat-world if you will.
So anyway I take on a job to smuggle a message from this elected official into the port of Marienberg, a fair distance down the coast. It's the furthest west I've been, and it's as good a reason to head into waters new as any. I check I've enough provisions for the trip and set sail. Once safely out of port, I retire to my cabin to watch over the map leaving the sailing to my first mate - a good man, even if his shanties sometimes make me want to jump overboard. The autopilot will work carefully with the prevailing winds, taking no chances by being near the coast. I stick it on x4 speed so I'm not here all night and I watch the map whilst I sip my tea. At the ten hour gametime mark I don't feel the need to always be on deck, trying to minimise journey time. The map shows me all the ships my look-out can see in real-time, with their heading and allegiance.
I am called on deck at some point in the dark watches of the night and we quickly dispatch a lone greenskin vessel. I take out it's wheel-house with some well-aimed shots, rendering it motionless, before dispatching their perverted souls to Davey Jone's locker. We arrive in Marienberg on the morning tide, and I quickly find the gent in question who screws up the note I was to give him before offering me a cool 20k in gold bullion to slit the throat of the woman who sent me. I like his style and that's a lot of money so I promptly agree.
The journey back up the coast is quiet but as I near Hargendorf harbour I receive word that my original employer has set sail in her battleship, intent on getting the jump on me before I dock. It's a genuinely tough battle, but I send her to her watery grave along with whatever souls were stupid enough to set sail with her. With my men mending the light damage to my hull, I retire oncemore to my cabin as we set our course back to Marienberg. I want my 20k; in my head it's already spent. There's this Amber Wizard that's been offering his services in the bar in Erengrad and that would give me enough to have a decent battlemage on board.
Halfway back again I notice a small flotilla of Undead vessels approaching on the map. I've taken on three ships before - one just has to remain sharp, to be clever and draw them out one-by-one. I head upstairs for the fight. Their pennants will sweeten this trip to the tune of 5k and who knows what dark prizes can be found in their holds? Their first ship is a little ahead of the trailing pair so I dispatch it quickly with a couple of volleys of cannonfire before rounding on it's fellows - and then this jet of green fire arcs from the deck of the larger ship and my men are suddenly clutching at weeping sores that have been torn open in their very flesh! They have a wizard on board, and he wields dark magics like nothing I've ever encountered before. I too am transfixed for long seconds, rendered inactive by the same foul affliction. One of my level three cannoneers dies from his wounds and I wonder if this will ever stop? Being a cannoneer down, that's my rate of fire ♥♥♥♥ed when I get control back. And then the cannonballs slam square into my starboard side, my usual jinking ways having been nullified by this pestilence, and my hitboxes all light up red. Another crewman dies, that's just lucky 13 of us left, and I reel at the damage caused - it's been a while since anything's got a full broadside in on me. This fight is over - it's just a matter of whether I can escape or not.
To the South lie Manaan's Teeth - a knot of islets and reefs. Maybe I can lose them in there, or maybe I'll run aground and either be boarded (which will result in a Mount and Blade style combat) or blown to smithereens. Another shot hits my prow and I run - if they hit my sails then running won't even be an option anymore. A cat and mouse game ensues where I eventually make it out of their foul clutches by hiding behind an island. I stay on deck for the rest of the journey, ready for anything - this damage is too bad for me to even begin to repair alone and I must make it to Marienberg!
Upon reaching port I discover my contact is dead, hung at dawn for a traitor. I am out of pocket, down a highly-skilled cannoneer, and a tough old marine who was damn good in a fist-fight is dead too. I got duped and I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked and it's been my best bit of gaming in Man o'War yet (and that includes the time a megalodon tried to eat me and then I got attacked by a Wyvern that dropped exploding Squiggs on the way home).
So yeah, there you go. Don't be thinking it's perfect, now - the graphics are neither brilliant nor well optimised just yet - but I am vaguely in love nonetheless. It's like the good boat bits of Assassin's Creed Black Flag but without any of those interminable assassiny bits. Also, the way all the various races have completely different crazy ways of making war means the usual circle-and-broadside naval warfare thing doesn't get repetitive. Take the Orcs, for example - they have a steamer so they aren't effected by wind and can go in reverse. They also have a blummin' great scary drill on the front for the purposes of ramming. And the Tzeentch warship just floats above the sea like a great magic castle firing out purest death (or magic, as I've heard it called).
Anyway that's where we're at at the ten hour mark. Lots of potential, they just need to make a walking animation that doesn't make everyone look like they need a crap and I'll be sold. Or maybe that's just how all sailors walk and a pasty lubber like me simply hasn't got my sea-legs yet.

This game is a life changer. Before Secret of the Magic Crystal I was just your average joe, but now after playing I'm a champion. I'm swooned with the ladies, I always get the headshot, and I have a vast array of horses to ride in to battle. Secret of the Magic Crystals is an epic horse sim RPG that sets you a 5-9 year old child loose on the cruel world of earth that had a metor crash into it to cause horse's dna to change, thus creating a new breed of mystical space horses. Your job as a 5-9 year old is to breed these space horses to make better elite space horses.
You gain money by lending your mystical non-elite or elite space horses to peasents to do their chores. Sometimes you can enter them in the king's arena for glory and money! Now of course to win in the king's arenas you have to train your mystical space horses to be the very best! Now while this task sounds easy, it is not. In order to train your horse you most slowly dance to a beat with your arrow keys. If you train too hard or long, your mystical space horse will get tired and sometimes sick. When your mystical space horses get tired you must let them sleep, but when the mystical space horses get sick you, a 5-9 year old child, must complete alchemy to cure them of their illness.
Alchemy is just 1 of 2 skills in the game you can do. The second skill is smithing. Smithing allows you to craft horseshoes, and saddles for you mystical space horses that give them bonus stats which aid in the king's arena. Alternatively you can also decorate your mystical space horse's stall with items that give them perks in the arena. Secret of the Magic Crystals also has random events, and dynamic weather. Another key feature to the game is upgrading your mystical space horse farm's buildings.
Overall Secret of the Magic Crystals is a deep complex and overall epic mysical horse breeding/training RPG sim that shouldn't be missed! 10/10 would buy and play again.

I can't get enough of this game. The aesthetics are fantastic, and the quirky theme is really consistent. Perhaps my favorite aspect though is that the game mixes difficulty with user friendliness. By that, I mean that there are some sections that are quite difficult, but the respawn points are close by and, despite sometimes dying, you don't have to repeat the same sections all that often.

Guacamelee is an action platform, of the Metroidvania variety. You play a Mexican Luchadore, fighting the forces of evil to save your love and the world. Along the way you will explore varied areas, learn new abilities, and fight a multitude of enemies.
Guacamelee is a game that is just oozing style. Everything from the artwork, to the sound, the writing, the characters and the world at large mesh so well together. You will want to spend time exploring the world and talking to its inhabitants. The towns are packed with humor and things to find.
The controls are as tight as they need to be for an action platformer. I played using a 360 pad, and would recommend using a gamepad. After learning new abilities, you will have to combine all your powers to advance in the later stages. I was really amazed at the combinations I could pull off toward the endgame.
I do have one complaint, which falls under performance and controls. Originally it felt like the game moved super fast, and I was having trouble pulling off basic combos and fighting some of the early enemies. One sequence in particular, where you must run in sidescroller fashion from a destructing environment, felt like it was moving way too fast. I was only able to pass it after about 20 attempts. Later I learned that there can be a bug with the vsync that basically doubles the speed of the game. Turning off vsynce solves the problem, however it will lead to some graphical glitches along the way. I found it a small price to pay for a playable game. After playing about the first quarter of the game at double speed, later platforming sections felt pretty easy in comparison.
Beyond my one small complaint above, I was enamored by everything else in Guacamelee. It was fun to explore, fun to see what was next, fun to fight the enemies, and just plain fun overall. I would welcome a sequel, since it feels like there are so many places for this series to go. I see that a rerelease just came out with some new levels, and while I would prefer an entirely new game, eventually I may give that a shot as well.
I completely recommend Guacamelee. While it has received heavy praise so it wasn't a complete surprise, it really exceeded my expectations. At this point you may want to purchase the newer version if you haven't played it yet, but if this game is already sitting in your backlog, move it to the front of the list.

Taking a subway late can lead to interesting places or be a meeting place for mysterious people. The three users with you seemed to come from another times and only you and your dog seem to be real, as when arriving to a cemetary, the persons became ghosts. Hina, the keeper of the place, kidnaps your dog, only for you to help these ghosts to find peace by changing the outcomes of the events tormenting them: a gone too soon journalist, a dam worker left behind and a falsely accused of witchcraft young woman...
I must say that it's probably one of the rare casual adventure games without a precise villain. Hina, the keeper, is a kind spirit, your dog is just kidnapped for making sure that you'll help her and the ghosts, lamenting themselves and feeling responsible for the death of others (though the zookeeper is the only one that wasn't driven by selfish reasons and could have save the journalist if only these keys weren't stolen). In fact, the enemies are mainly in these events and are merely humans, none being of supernatural nature. If you want to find the latter, it's in the bonus chapter, set after the main story.
I liked being sent in time and save the life of those who shouldn't have died, tormenting souls for eternity as they're regretting their choices (but again, the zookeeper felt guilty as he was a genuine man that did everything he could but it wasn't enough, I'm pretty sure that given the storyline, you'll be agreeing that he shouldn't have  be in this limbo).
The gameplay is quite the standard one for that kind of games: find items, combine them, use them, solve puzzles and clear hidden objects scenes (list of objects or find objects of the same type). I'm rarely negative for that aspect, however, here, I feel that I should perhaps warn you about some puzzles being long and kinda frustrating or that some hidden objects scenes are just annoying.
The graphics are nice and the soundtrack fits really in the game.
Yet, I was a little disappointed by this game, maybe because I was imagining something else or because I was expecting something else from ERS or because having added its profile to Neoseeker (and the whole series), I misunderstood the concept behind Redemption Cemetery (unless Salvation of the Lost was softer than the other games, as I didn't play them).
The good surprise is probably the letter let by ERS for the gamers and the puppy's room, where you can play with the puppy, if you find medals scattered in the game. It's also the only place where you'll find "achievements". The rest of the bonus are just classic: music, movies, wallpapers, minigames, concept arts, etc..
Should you buy the game? I would say that better games of the same genre are outside. However, it's still enjoyable if you don't encounter the same crash I had on Windows 7, making me switch to Windows 8.1 where it ran perfectly. However, while the price is kinda something normal for Big Fish Games, I would still advise you to buy it when there is a discount.

This version of the game adds more customization options in the course designer (additional environment themes, multiple tees and hole locations, more scenery objects). The Golf Club 2 still supports making a fully functional course in seconds, or single holes in three clicks, though multiple tee or pin positions are not automatically generated. There are also more options in course attributes (fairway width, green slope, et cetera), and the game allows for more detailed courses for those who wish to invest the time. The interface is more polished, including hole maps and a fairly extensive tutorial system, but the commentary remains hokey at best. Online leagues (called societies) are also present, and the ability to play “with” other players using ghost balls returns. The gameplay is mostly the same, although this version supports three different club types that trade distance for accuracy and it is harder to dial-in exact distances, making for more interesting golfing. There is still no power indicator, which makes shots made less than full power (namely chips, putts, and some approach shots) difficult and requires a lot of practice to execute consistently. Mouse control is improved but still not great (backswing sensitivity can be adjusted, but the downswing animation still lags behind actual mouse movement), and clicking to swing is not supported; playing with the gamepad is preferable. Still, The Golf Club 2 is definitely an improvement over its predecessor, with its addition of new course creation options and a slicker presentation, but requires a lot of practice to master its swing mechanics.

This is an overall good game with some quirks....
1) This game does not offer a causual mode. Its a hardcore golf simulator with  training, but it lacks the option to play with any digital help found on other golf games, except for a putting grid. It would be great if they gave you markers for where the ball is expected to go, and a power bar of some kind. I get that this game isn't really supposed to have this type of easy mode, but it would be nice for casual players.
2) Collision system is AWeFUL, go anywhere near a tree and the ball is coming straight down. They really need to improve the hitbox system.
3) Graphics go from very good in some areas, to absolute garbage at others. I have a 1070 and I play on ultra at 60FPS. I expect a game to look very good. This game looks great if you squint your eyes, but the textures are absolute trash, and the sand physics are dreadful.
4) The sounds are pretty boring. I find myself streaming music because the audio for this game is very low quality.
Now minus all of those issues.... This game is overall very good at being a golf SIMULATOR, not a golf GAME. It's challenging, offers a lot of ability to shape different shots, and has a lot of interesting courses to play
I find myself playing this game and then getting frustrated because the game plays out a lot like how I play golf in real life. To me, thats the strong point of this game, but as I said before, it would be great if there was a casual "Rory Mciilroy Game" type mode to make it more like a game when I want to escape on my computer.
My final opinion is that if this game becomes moddable, or if the developers release some much needed patches, then this game could seriously be an outstanding simulator. If you are a golf fan this game is still worth picking up at its current version, but I would say its value is more around $15 given all of the flaws.

I've taken my time slowly building up my captain's fame and arming my crew, and just finished a challenging quest wherein I was chased by four pirate ships. I led them into some rocky islets where two ships ran aground, then I came within cannon distance of a friendly port which began to trade shots with the pirates. This gave me time to board the main pirate ship (after first raking it with grapeshot and a few rounds of flaming cannonballs). I'm going to try to break down the game best I can.  I give it a thumbs up but with a 'buyer beware' caution due to the lack of content and long travel times.  I'm going to do my review on a 1 to 17 score assessment.
Graphics     (14)   : The reason its missing the last three points is because its great for what it needs to be, but some times you run in graphical glitches and I feel like they can still do a little touching up especially when you are in cities.
Ship Battles (13)   : I really enjoy this aspect of the game, but its hard to judge the game with the current limited number of ships you can play and things you can do with those ships.  It gets to the point where you will attack unique ships just to see what they can or can not do. Firing at an enemy ship and learning how to use the wind when you have sails to get the advantage is both pleasing and unique to me.  Another problem is the usually poor AI that you encounter.  After a while the combat will become 'business as usual' instead of exciting new battles.
Foot Combat (5)    : The combat for boarding and looting/raiding isn't something I found enjoyable after playing so many games that have been out for many, many more years and have done it better.  I didn't check thoroughly, but I don't think you can jump and that bothers me.  You can swipe at an enemy and miss them for no reason, and on top of everything the ai isn't great either.  Sometimes you will get a mission that will put you into a large battle where dodging a boarding party will be tough, and you will lose people.  Since your men level, and their skills affect your ships skills, it hurts when your more useful crew die in battle.
Sea Monsters (11)  : I'm so excited to see what other monsters they add for your ship battles, but again the poor ai really hurts this section.  They will just charge at you, get hit, submerge, try to get closer, get hit, submerge, ect ect.  If they get close, they will clamp to your ship or force you into gun combat and give your crew the scare of their lives.   When they add more depth to the monsters you fight, and a little more quantity, I think this will help make the game shine.
I will add to this later, but some of the things I should warn you about that you will probably read in other reviews is the excessive time it takes to get around from place to place.  Even with the time speed up option, it takes a VERY long time to get from place to place.  This didn't bother me, but I can see why this is a problem.  Also, some quests will throw you into a fight that might be way stronger than you can handle at the time, and you need to use guile to get past it, or use the poor AI (they will sometimes get stuck onto some land and you can just shoot them over and over again without them being able to hit you back) to get the job done.
In the end, I love the game and its direction, and I hope based on the information I gave you that you can make an informed decision on it.  If you have any questions about it, feel free to message me, and I'll answer to the best of my ability.  I just hope more people support it so we can get more games like this in the future.

Excellent for where it's at. There are still bugs and balance issues at this stage of development, but the skeleton of the game is very sound and very entertaining.
Examples of my journeys:
Early in the game, I get tired of wandering around the coast of Kislev and risk a journey through waters recently claimed by the orcs. On my way through, I encounter an orc hulk and exchange the usual pleasantries, cannonballs from ship and rocks from his catapult. Both ships are taking a jolly good beating when one of his acquaintances drops in and makes the exchange less sporting.
I fleet to Manaan's Teeth, leaving them behind and going about the salvage/treasure hunting mission I was supposed to be about anyway. The Teeth are a group of small islands jutting out from the sea, a fun navigational challenge and tricky to move through at high speeds.
While I'm searching, I'm alerted to the arrival of my new friend when rocks start splashing down around me, and occasionally into my ship. So things are kind of perilously perilous and I'm having to thread my way out of the islands and back into open sea while two orc ships play target practice with my battered craft.
I trade a couple of shots with that vessel since, but nothing conclusive as yet. Some day, though, I will sink the Mork.
And that is the fun of the game- where it works, it really works. It's very engrossing, immersive, and the tension of desperately weaving your ship about trying to get good arc on your guns while the world explodes around you is pretty addictive.
I can't wait to see what it eventually evolves into.

Ok, it's time to review this game objectively and without bias. This is a snake game where you must complete various objectives in three maps. The objectives are similar to all maps, but the difficulty changes. You can beat the game in around 20-30 minutes, but 4 difficulty modes and achievements add replay value to maybe 3-4 hours. The pure gameplay is generic snake with objectives, but it's the parody elements of this game that makes it funny and to be recommended. Without the laughts, this game would be bad to buy. Regarding copyright, this game is legal, but of course that having a known game name in it's title helps marketing it. With a generic name, this game would probably flew under the radar. At first, you would be mad at this, because now all one have to do is to create a generic game and put in the title "Not(famous game name)" to sell. But besides taxes and steam revenue, the profits of this game go to charity. So in the end, it's a good game for some laughs, and also because the gameplay works. And it's also cheap. If bad games try to sell with this kind of names, we will hopefully fall for that trick only once. That's why reviews exist. But this is not the case, so you can buy this game with confidence and if you want to support it further, buy the soundtrack DLC, whose profits also go to charity.

You could rely on the defaults completely and never touch the crafting settings if you really wanted, but you also have the tools to deal with crises.

Overall really well designed and implemented.

Ku:SOTM is a point and click action and puzzle game in which you control Ku, a 12 year old troublesome boy who is sent on a quest to retrieve a ring of power to keep your village sustained with energy. Filled with puzzles, combat and set in a unique world it's surely a winning recipe, right?
When you first emerge from the tunnels you are greeted with a colourful, friendly village full of interactive characters (make sure you speak to them all and you will be rewarded with an achievement). Speaking to them provides you with information about the main protagonist Ku who is an unruly youth constantly getting himself into trouble. Your first mission is to head out to find the leader of the village. Once you speak with him about the ring that went missing, he explains that it is the main energy source for the village and without it they are doomed. That is where your quest begins, you are ordered to head into the wilderness and hunt down a replacement ring from the North.
As you travel through the lands you are pitted against a variety of enemies and puzzles that block your path. You must hack and slash your way through your foes and chain together combos in order to do more damage and finish them off quicker.
The combat system actually turned out to be a lot of fun as it involved quickly stunning enemies, getting as many hits in as possible and then diving back out before you get hit. This can lead to some very tense albeit short battles that involve you having to be brave and tactical. The Combat Arena takes the combat to the next level pitting you against constant hordes of enemies to win score based on the number of enemies you defeat and rounds you clear. There are 4 levels to be played within the Combat Arena, each of which gets progressively more difficult. There is a leaderboard function on the game also, for you to compare your standing in the world however it was not working at the time of writing.
As I mentioned the game does not revolve entirely around the combat, there are in fact puzzles to solve in order to progress through the game. Although incredibly simple to solve they do offer a well needed variety to the game. They usually involved dragging an item with your mouse, or hitting certain posts to open a door, nothing too challenging but fun all the same.
The whole game is controlled by only the mouse which in fairness was all the game needed. You left click to move and attack, right click to roll/dodge and hit the middle button to fire your stun laser. Unfortunately the controls do feel clunky at times, especially when you are in the middle of combat and you really need to react quickly!
Musically the game felt very vacant and desolate. The music that was playing in the background was generally quiet and didn't really create much of an atmosphere. A large portion of the time I found myself concentrating more on the sounds of my own footsteps than the music itself. The only real exception to this is when you are in the village and you stand near someone playing an instrument.
Artistically is where the game really shows it's true potential. The artwork in this game is brilliant with some very interesting character designs, however the graphics really don't do them justice. Its a shame really as the game shows some true artistic potential which really hasn't been utilised.
Overall I think the game had a lot of potential but unfortunately it wasn't able to capitalise on it's strengths. The price at time of writing is £3.99 on Steam which isn't too steep but it could do with being longer. Taking only around 2 hours complete you barely feel as though the game has begun when the end credits begin to roll.
5/10 - Fun to play while it lasted but could do with polishing.

Before you read the review be warned that I will be grading this on an "Indie curve" meaning less than 5 developers
Sound 5/10
The sound is position based and is confusing as to the point of origin of the sound most of the time, not to mention the sounds   are comparitive to sound samples from a bad EDM song.
Battle system 6/10
Lacks any real depth, and most of the battle system is learning how to bug the enemies out so they can't hit you. Also your primary "slash" attack has the awesome ability to get you stuck in walls and in other places you don't belong and can't escape.
Bosses 2/10
The bosses of this game are all incredibly easy and short lived, and feel like normal enemies, except the final boss which felt more like the first real boss in the game, but still exceptionally easy. One of my major complaints is you don't heal your health after a boss though.
Artwork 9/10
The art is gorgeous and was my primary attraction to the game, however it is hindered by bad coding to fit different screen resolutions and can look a little distorted depending on the resolution you are playing in, which disappointed me greatly.
Storyline 2/10
I started out with a great concept of what needed to be done and I talked to the whole village. I was continually disappointed by how everyone didn't react to any changes in the plot at the start, or the fact you had a sword. I came for the nerd, I stayed for the gameplay.
I've been a massive fan of AVGN for years, seen every episode multiple times etc etc etc. That was the main reason I bought the game, however after playing it for several hours, I almost forgot the connection between AVGN and the game, I was really enjoying the game as a game.
2d platformers are hard to do, it's such a simplistic style, which in my opinion makes it even harder to do right. This game does it right, a lot of fun, injected with good humour and very very challenging. But the nerd should be proud of his own game, this game may be challenging, but it's challenging for the right reasons, it's well made and the challenge lies in the difficulty of the game, not flaws in the mechanics.
It is however intensely frustrating at times, my housemate who lives on the third floor was texting me asking me why I was screaming (I was all the way downstairs). You can end up losing 30 lives by dying in the same place over and over again, but the satisfaction of when you finally get that bit right is fantastic.
I've played about 9 hours and i'm currently struggling on the final boss on normal mode, but once i'm finished i'm sure I will start it all over again, I think the replayability is reasonably high.
The only 'flaw' (if you consider it a flaw) is the fact that the game is a lot of trial and error, especially on the more challenging levels. Even if you are the greatest 2d platform player in the world, you will end up having to learn a thing or two about the upcoming sections before you can complete them. But for me this is fine and it didn't stop me having fun. Plus you feel like a total badass once you can do a previously 'impossible' section with zero deaths.
All in all would give this game a solid 7 out of 10. Fans and non-fans alike can enjoy this simple, enjoyable and difficult game.

Guacamelee is an enjoyable action platformer, in which you'll play as a Wrestler on a Quest to save a girl and yeah that sounds like Mario - This game likes to reference a lot of different games, but also some real life stuff, I found it very satisfying to find eater eggs in this game.
Although this game doesn't have a perfect pacing, due to one point in the game, where the plattforming starts to get really complicating and you suddenly have to use a lot more abilities at the same time, which gets you likely stuck on a quarter of a level about an hour or two, it's annoying, but at the same time the only real negative point about the game.
Gameplay wise is the game divided into plattforming and brawler-like combat. What makes the plattforming really interesting is that you can use your wrestling moves you'll learn over the course of the game, to reach your destination. In combat you use as already mentioned wrestling moves to defeat your enemies, apart from that you can throw a damaged enemy, who can be thrown onto other enemies, which is not only efficient, but is very satisfying to do.
Even though you are very limited with the throwing when using a keyboard. Because I still don't have a controller I used a keyboard for this game and personally I found that the keyboard controls difficult to get used to, but didn't feel at a disadvantage because of the limited throwing. Apart from that the PC-Port seems fine.
Overall I didn't see any major flaws with the game, it was just challenging enough, it doesn't have a perfect pacing, but cool Easter eggs, I'll recommend to people, who are looking for a challenging platformer and like to find references/Easter eggs.

I have been a dedicated player of Roller Coaster Tycoon since it first came out and that is why I thought that Roller Coaster Tycoon World would be such a great game.  After over 200 hours of working on a park and trying out the various features of the game I found I did not like it as much as the previous version.  The game is too glitchy, for example the new path system that is supposed to allow you to have customized paths will not allow you to make some connections with other paths.  The new piece by piece building feature is a nice touch, but if you decide to rotate the building, or move it, any shops you have built inside will get thrown out of alignment.  I was very excited today to learn that the game will be fully released on 11/16, the article had mentioned it's releawse date is a day before Planet Coaster.  Being curious I decided to try out Planet Coaster and I am now regretting the money I spent on Roller Coaster Tycoon.  Planet Coaster has incredible graphics, the rides are incredibly easy to design and build, and their path system truly does allow you to design and connect the paths the way you want.  I got more enjoyment out of 2 hours of messing around with Planet Coaster than I did with 200+ hours of Roller Coaster Tycoon World.

Myst is a very story based puzzle game. The game starts off by landing you in the island of Myst, a small uninhabited island filled with puzzles to more small uninhabited islands. All that link together to find out why they are uninhabited. The game has loads of books that you can't read. The ones you can read give you an outline of what these island where like. They also give you clues to find more books with a single moving picture in them, these lead you to the island to help solve the mysteries of Myst. The story’s main beef in this game is between two brothers who are trapped in their own books with moving pictures. Each brother blames the other and they ask you to uncover there colour coded lost pages. The more you collect the pages the more they talk about the other brother and it does getting boring listing to them blab on when I could be reading all these books that either one or both of them have burnt. I would however have to say that this is a great game but I couldn’t imagine it for everyone. Especially when the puzzles in the game require you to make notes in the real world. But for a gamer who doesn’t mind that too much and like very hard and vague puzzle games then it is worth the time. Myst gets a solid 8/10 from me but if I would recommend a Myst game to a new fan I would suggest Myst 3 Exile. The only problem is that there is no current legal downloadable version so you would need to find a physical copy. It is also the same for Myst 4 but hopefully that will change in the future.

Yes, this is an early access game, and yes, there are some bugs and discrepencies. BUT IT IS EARLY ACCESS! If you want to support a game that has massive potential, and the idea that being a Pirate, accountable to no one and for hire to the highest bidder is cool, contolling your ship in battle against not just the enemy, but the wind and weather. I bought the steam version of Myst, like, a year ago and wrote a negative review because it honoured me with countless crashes and nonexistent intros. A common problem.
Now that I redownloaded it, it works nicely. The intro was there and when I quickly went to a section that used to make it crash (clocktower), it was stable. (on Win10 64bit)
Sooo... if you want to play a classic, mysterious, pathbreaking point'n'click game from the 90s, it should be a safe buy now. (note that most of the negative reviews stem from the instability of the previous, non-fixed version, not from the quality of the game itself)

It may have been a decent revamp of the game at the time, but it's terrible now.  It solves none of the vast compatibility problems you're faced with in getting the original game to work, and I was not able to discern any graphical improvements.  (I had been under the impression that the graphical update was the entire purpose of this version of the game).
If you have an XP box sitting around somewhere, you might be able to get it to run on that.  Anything newer and you'll face monumental problems in getting it to work.  (Of particular note is the need for an ancient version of QuickTime that Steam failed to package with the game (it handles DirectX and .NET and uPlay, so it seems reasonable to expect) - I've heard both 6.5 and 4 referenced; I think I was able to get the original game running with 2 point something.
is where you'll want to be going to handle this part of the compatibility issues.)
It's a pity.  The original game is quite the excellent puzzle game, and Masterpiece Edition really sounded like the most faithful remake option.  (Free-roam exploration has its place.  Uru and Myst 5 did an excellent job in demonstrating that place is NOT in Myst games.)   And yet, despite that bias, I'd have to suggest anyone wanting to play the original Myst (who isn't an old hand at wrestling with major compatibility issues or a collector of old computers) should go for realMyst.  Unlike the sequels (particularly Riven), the stuff you'll need to find isn't so much hidden as walled off by puzzle-barriers, so you won't have to worry about missing important factors in the background details because you have nothing indicating that a particular area is worth taking note of.  (There's a couple things in Riven I'd never have found in free-roam - they show up because you're forced to look at it from a fixed perspective...kinda like that sidewalk art that looks entirely 3D if you stand in just the right spot.)

The original and iconic Myst at its best: the Masterpiece Edition. I can't reccomend it enough. It's a great point and click puzzle game where you land at a mysterious island in the possession of a strange book. You find 2 brothers stuck in 2 books, each telling you to help him and not the other. So you choose. And go on a strange book trip to help him.
The puzzles aren't hard per se, but they're decontextualized. That's the hardest part of the game: trying to figure out what the hell does [insert thing here] do and to what is it related. Not that this game is hard, not at all, but you have to be good at connecting clues. Some more obvious than others (
).
Now there are some things to keep in mind as this is an old game. You may not be able to play it due to compatibility issues (Windows 10 worked fine for me but 7 did not). In that case you always have the realMyst versions. Many copies have an awful bug at a certain rotating tower where it doesn't turn North or West. It forces you to check a guide for the clues but does not prevent you from leaving that Age and finishing the game. Given how old this game is there's really no tech support from the devs, so don't bother.
There isn't a whole lot going for replay value besides the
different endings and different dialogue but it's still a wonderful experience and I definitively would love to visit the island of Myst and the remaining Ages as well.

In this game, developed by bitSmith Games out of Dublin, you will be playing the part of Ku a very undersized individual of a village that is in serious trouble. It turns out that someone has made off with the power ring that helped power the village, and now without it the village is in grave danger. You decide that you are the only one that can do the job so you are sent on an adventure to the outside world, a place that no one really knows about, and is said to be full of danger.
Graphically the game looks like it was hand drawn by a very skilled artist. Unfortunately some of the effect of the art is ruined by the fact that the background layering on the screen mixed with your character's position is a bit all over the place. What I mean by that is that there are times where your character might accidentally lose his head, graphically, because of something that is supposedly behind the character but is being rendered in a layer in front of him. Overall, though, the enemies, other characters, and environments look amazing.
The music fits the game nicely and I could definitely listen to it even with the game not on. My one issue is that the settings for sound and music levels do not save from play session to play session. So if you have that perfect balance that you want in the game, you are going to have to either take a screenshot, to make sure you get it back the way that it was, or you are in for a rude awakening if you play the game a second time.
The controls are probably the thing that doom this game the most. I do not know what happened with the controls, but I can tell you that it was not good. I started off playing with the mouse, and apparently you should be able to play the whole game with just the mouse, but it turns out that my middle mouse button, or the wheel, did not register in the game, and you need for it to work to get you out of some situations, or to solve a puzzle. Thankfully the spacebar works as a substitute. Then I got to the flying portion of the game and found that no matter what buttons I pushed, including the left mouse button, which was shown on the screen to me, there was no key registering in the game, and I crashed and burned each time. Now that caused me to have to break up my gaming sessions because I needed to then find a controller to test the game with. When I plugged in the 360 controller I found that the mouse button now worked, but as I had plugged in the controller, I wanted to play the rest of the game with the controller. Sadly this was not a permanent solution for playing the game. Several times during my second play session I had to revert back to using the mouse because I could never get the precision, or the comfort of playing with the controller during battles. It was completely hit or miss.
Alright so lets get into the actual game play. First off whomever wrote the script really should have read over it as there were some very odd choice of words used. I felt like they were trying to show how smart they could be by using seldomly used big words, instead of using language that would help the player better understand what was going on. There were also some glaring issues that drive an OCD person crazy. When entering a cutscene, if you were using the mouse chances were that you could be locked into a perpetual state of running during it, and since there were no voices to what was going on, all you could hear while you read the dialogue was the sound of your character running. Speaking of which, if you accidentally over-run the point in the level where you are about to face off against the fire bolg, it will kill you during the cutscene, literally every time. Oh and speaking of that beast, if you are stuck in a state of running when you finally have to face off against him, which you really don't get to do, you will see the cliff give way and your character will run FOREVER in the sky, and you can't advance the game. The final quick thing I have to say about this game is that it is an hour and a half game, with a to be continued slapped on the end. With that short of a playthrough, the developers should have added the to be continued on to this game.
Now there was one thing that I think the game got right and that was the use of the power glove that your character had that allowed him to lift objects in the level and position them where you would like. Speaking of the levels, I think a map could have been nice in the game, and also if the game is supposed to be linear, point a to point b, type of game, they need to make entrances to different parts of the level disappear, block it, close a door on it, something because gamers will want to backtrack if they think they might have missed something. Alright, one last thing, the random load screens that have nice drawings on them, but don't really do anything for the game, except will not disappear until you have clicked on the button, or pressed the B key if you are using the controller, it feels like the artist had some more ideas that weren't put into the game and so this is how they displayed them. It would have been nice if the game just incorporated those into cutscenes.
Alright so here's the deal folks, this could potentially be a good game, but they should have tested this game to its full extent, and also work out some of the obvious kinks in the game. I wish I could give this game a score based on potential, but that would be unfair, so I've got to say avoid this game, at least for now, and I give it a 3.7 out of 10.

To start off, this game is pretty damn fantastic, especially for a game that is over 10 years old, as of this 2016. I recieved this game, along with the rest of the Hitman games (excluding HITMAN 2016), from a friend of mine.
The graphics, though inevitably 'dated' by today's standards, still hold up really well. Not 'terrible' by any stretch of the imagination.
The gameplay is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing; so much choice is offered in how you operate and execute your assignments. Do you want to be the eponymous Hitman? The Silent Assassin who stalks his prey with poison, fiber wire and silenced Silverballers? Or do you want to be regarded as a ruthless terrorist, who mows down anyone who approaches him with a highly-modified M4 rifle or SPAS-12 shotgun? The choice is yours.
The story is pretty good too, as it includes various missions, all with highly varied level designs, opportunities and targets, which is impressive considering the baseline of this game is to 'kill the target(s)'.
The story also includes rival hitmen/hitwomen that attempt to kill Agent 47.
One of my favourite missions to date would be 'A House of Cards'.
Overall, graphics, story and gameplay all considered, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing fantastic. Don't let its 10+ year age fool you; it is well worth picking up. The methodical, tactical thinking this game employs is top-notch, and ultimately, highly satisfying once you pull off the perfect assassination without error.
If I had to critisize it, it would likely be the semi-archaic, 'dated' controls, which generally make the game feel a tad bit clunky, however, this is in no way a deal-breaker.
9/10 - Would recommend.

An extremely short, but profound game. It's somewhat simple regarding actual gameplay, but it's not mindless by any means, there are riddles; they take a bit of critical thought to understand, but they're not impossible.
One thing I have to bring up is this game's ability to raise so many questions with so little actually presented. What's going on here? Where did this come from? Is this Earth? Is this in the future? The past? Who am I trying to "tune-in" to? I can't think of another game I've played that caused me to question it so much.
This isn't necessarily a bad thing by any means; some games do this really well, some don't. Some games hide a bunch of easter eggs or something hinting at (read: forcing) a backstory... some imply a grander idea that may never be understood completely. This game does the latter - and does a darn good job at it too.
A short but very compelling game. Definitely worth playing, it only took me 25 minutes to complete, it might take someone else 10.

I started the game to have a quick look at it, next time I looked on the time was 4 hours later.

It is still an unfinished game, so expect technical and gameplay issues; most importantly, read the "Known Issues" list in the main menu. The time you are beyond these problems the game turns out to be a lot of fun. You jump into Gaul as it is conquered by Cesar (a.k.a you). Mainly you focus on conquering and dealing with the threats the local tribes are representing, but you also have to keep you economy running. Otherwise your troops will not have enough to eat and receives serious penalties. That's about it, but you can do things a few different ways already.
The tutorial is decent enough to tell you how you play, although some mechanics I did not understand up to a few hours into the game.
Overall I just can recommend this game to players of strategy games, both realtime and turn-based. To FPS gamers this might be a bit boring, but whatever suits you :)

Honestly the choices are only limited by your own roleplaying ability. The game does however have few times where you are limited to singular choices that force you to say something but they are not too immersion breaking.

This game was hard to decide considering at times it can be fun, but its extremely unrealistic to the point where it can completely end your game.
-Pros-
*Well managed economy based game
*Battles can be entertaining at times
*Fun Campaign
*Taking other villagers and using them is unique and extremely beneficial
-Cons-
*Enemy soldiers can literally walk through your lines untouched
*If outnumbered by the slightest bit, you lose by a landslide (example: they have 45 and you have 40, they will win with atleast 35-40 troops left)
*If you lose 1 defensive battle its game over
*Attacking enemy islands can be almost impossible considering the troops die almost instantly when they are dropped off from a ferry, having no chance to even attack back.
All and all its a 5/10. Game can be fun at times but extremely fustrating when you lose a 30 minute game from the enemy outnumbering you by 1 troop.
*Edit
As you gradually get use to the faster, yet desicive gameplay of Cossacks 3, compared to other real time strategies, you will find that it actually has some potential. I really enjoy this game; it has so much potential as well to make it hopefully a game that doesn't fall off your "play list" after a few weeks. I started off with a good several hours of solid game play, after that initial session I found I was just repeating things. It's good to jump in for 1 hour here and there, otherwise it can get a little repetitive. Missions are easy enough (penalties for failure aren't too harsh) and the concept of bolstering your captain and crew so that they get better as you progress is really good.
Lots of ways they can take this game to make it more immersive so that people don't get a bit bored and I hope the developers bring in some themes to allow you to build your own base of operation to add a bit more strategy and depth. There are obvious minor deficiencies, which will be ironed out I'm sure, but nothing that makes the game unplayable or too frustrating. Plus the auto-save function is a God send if you do run into issues, (dodgy first mate getting you trapped from time to time with his bizarre navigation skills).
Your ship is easy to handle, the speed-up button is your friend, especially for the long journeys to missions start points or just sailing to get from A-B, (after getting used to X4 speed, you will find that you wish there was a X8 or X16 even). Good mix of bad guys, other ships and the trade function is simple to understand and a nice little extra to bolster much needed cash reserves. The battles are good fun; both if shooting with cannons or with the boarding action to manually slay your foes. The boarding part could do with a bit more fine tuning and can get repetitive, but on the whole it's a great feature.
For an early access it has been a very good investment for me, I'm genuinely excited to see where the developers take this, they seem to be involved in the forums and listen to ideas from fellow players, much more so than many other games I have played. So big thumbs up from me so far, the avenues of potential are immense, so I hope they don't cut corners. The current game which can zap the hours, is good fun and well worth a punt.

The basic idea is good - an expansion of the naval gameplay of ACIV : Black Flag mixed with a bit of Mount & Blade, with a lot more personality. Features like recruiting, outfitting and managing individual crew members, allied NPC captains, defeating giant sea creatures etc are most welcome additions. There are also several factions, and a massive selection of ships.
However as it currently is I found it unplayable, due to unusuable production values. Visual details are in the wrong places, animations are extremely clunky, and the lighting / shaders makes everything seem dark and muddy. Given the game's third-person perspective and focus on fast paced action, the problems are compounded. Its difficult to discern ships / objects / characters during gameplay. It all becomes a muddy jumbled mess.
I understand that it is made by a small team of developers, and its probably unrealistic for them to make AAA level graphics seen in most action RPGS or third person combat games. Instead they should have been smart about it, gone for a cleaner and more optimized look, with better lighting. Or they should have designed the gameplay at tactical level and not third-person, where graphics are much less critical.
I would post this as a suggestion in the forum, but given my experience with early access communities of smaller games like this, I am pretty sure I would be insulted as a "graphics wh*re" or such, the thread derailed, and the point lost, as will soon be evident in the amount of hate this review will get. Pointing out bad graphics in a videogame has become akin to heresy thanks to the massive amount of pretense among fans. Still I would rather leave it here where it has more impact.
I will keep an eye on this as the base gameplay has the potential to be the perfect naval tactical game yet. Just a few small tweaks will make a huge difference -
1. Better lighting / shading, specifically greatly increased amount of ambient (i,e. non-directional) light during all times of the day
2. Reduce visual effects like smoke etc
3. Cleaner textures
4. Some optimizations to animation - slower, less exaggerated movements would be better
5. Needs more portraits, more distinct character models.
Will be happy to get back on deck when things improve. Cheers and best of luck (to the devs).

I feel like the best way to describe this game is by using other games. (coincidentally all games I love lol)
The sea combat is almost identical to AC:Black Flag(even the camera angle and how your captain can let go of the steering wheel whenever you want). The crew management feels very similar to Pixel Piracy, I can be quite upset when a specific crewmember that I have had for awhile dies. The faction system reminds me a lot of Mount & Blade:Warband. Factions can start wars with each other, ally, and control sections of the sea in what seems almost a capture the flag style just have a lot of ships in a section of the sea and that faction controls it (can even happen with orcs and pirates and the like taking a section of the sea from a faction). The map and supply and demand trading system remind me of Sid Meiers: Pirates, as do the graphics (although it has been years since I played that game.)
You can make a living working for a specific faction, or buying low selling high, taking sides in wars or playing both sides. The whole world is your oyster and it's set in a awesome Warhammer universe. As a fan the amount of detail put into the different factions and their ships/character models as well as the map size and locations I really feel like I am in the Warhammer universe exploring and discovering for myself. Not to mention all the things that universe brings to the table that other games could never do (because who else would make a fantasy pirate game with wizards and rat men) like having a wizard on your ship or a pegasus rider defending it (or both), magic swords and sea monsters.
Overall I strongly reccomend it to anyone who enjoys Warhammer or open world sailing games (Wind Waker, Sid Meiers: Pirates, AC: Black Flag, Pixel Pirates, etc. . .). As a person who usually goes by the rule of thumb that I want to pay less than 1$/hr spent playing a video game I consider this game to have high value. I know I will play it for a long long time well after they stop updating.

I know this review is tantamount to blasphemy, but this game is quite frankly worse than Absolution could ever hope to be, and if you've seen my review of Absolution you'll know that I'm not happy with it either.
Yes, several of the pros that people say are accurate.  Blood Money is more open-level.  Disguises actually do what disguises are supposed to do.  And of course you don't get that stupid counter at the top left corner of your screen penalizing you because you had to *GASP!* defend yourself when a guard spotted you from half a mile away because you're wearing similar clothes to what he's wearing.
But these pros don't outweight the cons by any means, at least not in my humble opinion.
For instance, while controls are customizable, the customizations don't last from one level to the next and they automatically reset to default.  This can be really frustrating if you're like me and consider, say, the right mouse button to be the button you use to zoom in with a sniper rifle.  Well, the default is X, so you go into the keymapping options and change it before starting your game.  But then, when you go into your game and use your sniper rifle, right clicking doesn't do what you mapped it to do, because the game has reverted back to the default without your consent or knowledge.  You don't even have to exit the game for this to happen.  All you have to do is start a new level, and boom, all customizations you've made are gone.
Also, the open levels are both a blessing and a curse.  If, for instance, your planned route requires you to sabotage something, sabotaging things takes quite a bit longer to accomplish in Blood Money and in an open area like, say, a suburban neighborhood, a woman mowing her lawn on the other side of the map can turn and see you, and suddenly your cover is blown and you've got twenty or thirty FBI agents zeroing in on you.
This game's controls and unpredictable nature make this game far more frustrating to me a lot of the time than a lot of other games do.  Sometimes, this makes me want to ragequit, especially if I just died.  Well, in the case of Blood Money, I can't ragequit if I've died, because dying in this game gives you a thirty second unskippable cinematic that even opening the Task Manager in Windows will not kill, let alone the main menu in the game itself.  IO seems to pride itself in making garbage and then acting like it's a Triple-A quality title while laughing at you the player the whole time for being stupid enough to buy their stuff.  At least, this has been my experience playing the two Hitman games I have in my library.
Despite all the good press this game gets, the fact of the matter is, I find Blood Money to be worse than Absolution ever could be.  Absolution is bad, but I honestly have to wonder if the people praising Blood Money while dissing Absolution are doing so more out of a sense of nostalgia than from actually remembering what this game is really like.  Like the stereotypical old geezer who falsely claims "we never cussed when I was a kid," so I think a lot of these people are looking at Blood Money through rose-colored glasses.

I am sorry to write this but this has to be done.
I was really excited about this game, hoping for another Bastion with some more of a Zelda-like twist to it, all of that in a interesting setting based on the Celtic lore.
What I've got instead is a shoddy mobile game that fails to adapt to proper, traditional controls - its interpretation of mouse clicks is laughable, still relaying on a way too large waypoint crutch, originally used for the touch input, which results in imprecise, frustrating controls and leads to really shoddy animation loops - like the one infinite run you get on all the elevators.
Gamepad input is even worse - I've tested with a wired 360 controller - menus don't navigate properly, Ku is infinitely running in place when left analog stick is in neutral position, mouse cursor disappears in the menus while controller is plugged, controls while talking to NPCs are sluggish, easily resulting in nigh-infinite conversation loops. I got too frustrated with them in the beginning to even try going back to them when combat started, so I am no able to comment on that.
I am not sure if there is a DirectInput gampead support yet - Buttons might be rebindable via *sighs* Unity launcher.
Combat. It sucks. Okay, let's elaborate:
LMB: dash to an enemy and hit it, switching enemies will chain hits, up to, I think, 4, each of the hits after the first one resulting in more and more irritatingly high pitched sound effects.
RMB: Dodge roll, uses 1 stamina, stamina bar has 3 charges [at least at the start of the game] - I didn't find it reliable in battle, as it didn't trigger all the time while in combat - though it might be related to my facing or direction of the right mouse click, so I can't truly judge that yet.
And that's it for the start - insanely boring, and really not as responsive as it should. I'd rather play Diablo 1. at least it works properly and reliably. Combat mechanics fail utterly.
And it gets worse. Not long after the beginning of the game proper you get a weapon that allows you to fire, for free, every second or so, a blue projectile that COMPLETELY PARALYSES basic enemies. Yeah, think about that for a second. Nice way to make the combat even less substantial. It's bound to MMB, or it's, supposedly, able to be fired by clicking [presumably LMB] and then SWIPING in a desired direction  - it never worked for me though, but well, we generally don't swipe on PC.
Story starts slowly, wasn't paying much attention to it due to growing irritation. No obvious typos, or grammar problems from what I've seen. Text available in English and Irish!
And after all this bitter grievances time for the stuff I actually liked: the graphic style and the music - the brass steampunk characters and structures contrast nicely with lush green environment, and soundtrack seems quite fitting, and miles above the quality of sound effects.
Game runs okay, even on my rubbish laptop, it's an Unity game, and, sadly, all options are in the launcher in the form of those idiotic profiles (e.g. Beautiful) - please devs, DON'T DO THAT, you can do proper options in Unity too!
I was forced to stop playing the game on that weird maybe flappy bird inspired thing which failed to work for me - craft dropped down no matter how I've pressed the LMB [neither one long press nor clicking like a maniac resulted in any sort of response]. I quit to main menu after that. Weirdly enough, when I tried to "Continue" later on, it failed to load my character and it's bird, or made them invisible - Level seemed to scroll okay though, so I think I was unable to reach the failure state - yet another case of poor QA in this title.
So let's recap: Basic MOBILE Zelda-like Action-rpg in brazen steampunk Irish setting. Terrible controls, Bad animations, Irritating sound effects. Interesting art direction and fitting music. Lackluster mechanics. Broken game section.
(SADLY) NOT RECOMMENDED

K:SotM is an incredibly short game. It took me under an hour & a half to complete, and I ran around searching every corner of each map.
It says it all that the length is my lasting impression of this game. It doesn't really have all that much going for it besides the visuals. The general look of the game reminded me a little of Bastion, but K:SotM does have its own unique look. The game presents itself as a top-down action game with a very distinct art style almost like each moving part of a character model is a separate cut-out drawing. This is rather pleasing on the eye, although some models have clearly had less attention than others. The screen is also too focused on the player, so you cannot see very far in any direction. I also had to use Task Manager to close the game at one point in the story, as an image that covers over almost the entire screenspace would not go away and the menu was unresponsive.
The game control scheme includes gamepad usage, however I could not get my official 360 wired control to work (and Steam forums are littered with others having issues with different controls). Instead, I had to use my mouse to play the game where left clicking moves your character & attacks, right-click performs a dodge roll, and space bar fires your projectile. The input of what I pressed on my mouse was frequently ignored by the game, causing me to stop moving at crucial moments, or for it to not use the correct weapon. The combat felt very clunky because of this. Also, there is only 1 melee weapon, and 1 projectile weapon. The lack of variety, no abilities, and only 1 melee combo attack mean that combat gets very stale regardless of the enemies. There also is not a huge range of enemies in the short campaign, although there are more variants of these enemies in the combat arena mode which adds a little extra lifespan to the game.
The audio is rather bland. There is not much of a soundtrack, none of the characters are voiced, and there are only a few sound effects in the game.
So to summarise: I do not recommend K:SotM, even if you have spare money to burn and it is on a heavy discount. There simply is not enough content here, and even if there was the gameplay is too repetitive and glitchy.
To top it all off, the game ends on a humongous cliff-hanger that cannot really be justified when the game is so short.

Standard: SO EASY i barely sliced or hooked and always hit a good chip and putting was easy - Best for a beginner
Player:  It is like a middle ground but more power focused so accuracy is still lower but it is a challange - For a Intermediate Player or those that want a nice challange
Tour: the most power out of all and accuracy is really bad here you can not play this difficulty without using a mouse and keybaord a gamepad joystick it way to sensitive to left and right for this mode. : for advanced palyers or plain just advoid all together as i could not hit streight with a X1 controller, steam controller, or PS4 controller

the game play is nice. courses react the way they do in real life.  firm fairways mean more bounce and speed and firm greens ave more bounce and are a bit faster in the putt so ease up a bit, soft reacts nice too  grabs the ball and slows it a bit so sometimes the distance is cut shorter.

so in my opinion this game is as close as you can get to real life golf in a game unless you count VR as that is totally a different aspect on the game of golf then using keyboards anf controllers.

An amazing and fun 2-D action side scroller. The game features very colorful graphics and sound that have an authentic Mexican flavor and flare to them. The control is very responsive and makes controlling your character simple. Your character controls well whether you are exploring or fighting enemies. The game also features a 'metroid-vania' inspired map layout full of bonus areas that are only accessible with certain powerups. During your quest, you will unlock additional stat increases and powerups, which allow for greater flexibility in fights and new ways to explore your environment.
The game does feature some fairly challenging sections, which require fast reflexes and good coordination in order to advance. During some of these moments I did feel like yelling at my monitor, but the satisfaction I felt after passing these sections felt oh so good.
As you might expect from this kind of game, the story is pretty bland. The dialog also feels pretty flat overall. But, if you're like me, that's really not why you wanted to play this game in the first place.
Check it ouf if you enjoy side scrolling action games with exploration elements. I certainly had a great time playing it. You will probably get about 10 hours worth of play time out of this game.

Finally got around to playing KotoR and I have to say I enjoyed it more than I thought I would. I love pre ME3 Bioware and the writing and characters in KotoR are definitely the highlights. The twist had been spoiled for me years ago, so I can't really comment on how well it is handled, but I can say the ending left me a little unsatisfied. Things just end on a whim after the final encounter, and there's nothing more said about fallen friends or the state of your companions. Would've enjoyed some plot wind down for each of them, but regardless the base game is fun enough to get a recommendation. If you can handle that you'll enjoy this game, but please don't expect a modern masterpiece, it's an enjoyable product of its time

Cossacks 3.
What can I tell you about Cossacks 3 you ask? Well if you're a PC veteran like myself then you probably played the first and maybe even second installment of the series. For those of you who did my answer is short and easy. It is basically a HD remake of the first game.
But if you are new to the Cossacks series than you are in for a treat you havn't had in years. Cossacks 3 brings back the RTS we missed for so long.
In Cossacks 3 It is your duty as a commander of the faction you choose to build up a military outpost with mines, dwellings, barracks, acadamies and much more.
After you have established your base you will need to build up an army. I am not talking about an Warcraft 3 style army with a maximum of 24 units or something like that but actually armies of many hundred man.
With officers and drummers you can turn your undisciplined horde into a well oiled warmachine. Support them with cannons and ships and victory might be yours.
If you can spend a couple of hours into one mission or  a multiplayer game and you enjoy the micromanagment of a base and army of this size I highly recommend the game. If you cannot I still recommend it because who knows when we will get a game like this again.
TL.DR
Cossacks 3 brings back the jewel of RTS from the past with a refreshing graphic while staying true to its roots when it comes to gameplay.
+Many different factions to choose from
+Multiple campaigns
+Old and glorious RTS

The Cossacks games are very similar to Age of Empires II, only with a greater scale in terms of the number of units under your command and set in the Age of Sail. - Excellent naval and land combat between units spanning from 1700-1800

- Features economies of scale, with hundreds of peasants working farms, mines, forests and quarrys to support the production and upkeep of possibly thousands of troops and ships
- Cannons are very satisfying, as are volley-firing musket formations
- Graphics are notably improved from the original
- No bugs on my end and the devs seem active in plugging any holes.
- Music isn't great

I didnt play a lot of cossacks, and I wanna make this rewiev for the new players, not those whom played it like crazy back in the day. I, myself also just played Cosssacks 3, I do not know the other games, but my big passion are RTS  Games.

Now the cons:
-BUGS everywhere. I do not know how many times the game crashed, may it be in multy player or in singleplayer vs AI. -when the host leaves, the online match is finished as well.

-Inbalaned Gameplay. What I mean by that is, there are some players which playedone of the cossacks games before, and they just ♥♥♥♥ us newbies up so bad in Online matches, and depending on the map, mercenary spam and/or Archers (Algeria/Turkey) unfortunatly ruin the game, mostly because they are overpowered and easy to spam. Anyway, there is just overall a huge balance issue in the game itself, which leads to a decline of options to play with in online multi player battles, which therefore leads to a META game style, which also is hard to graps for new players and RTS junkies who don't know the game as well as Veterans of the Cossack-Series.
-In my opinion a good RTS  should not be just "spamm to win" but most of the games I played online were just that. Microing your units is somewhat only an issue for Expirienced players, for us noobs, its just delaying the defeat. Furthermore, its is hard to grasp the concept of strategy, not only in multi player but also in Games vs AI. Most online battles are anyways decided in 5-20 mins tops. who gets first the mercenaries wins usually.
-The scenrie could/should be more. When I lock at the game, and watch the map, it feels like it isn't alive at all. Everything feels not right. There are hardly and other vegetation and/or variation in the flora and fauna. The units look very much alike, and u cant tell how many there are coming. (It looks like one unit and afterwwars your whole village got destroyed by an army of two bazillian Pikemen, it's just friggin' hard to tell, how many there are :) ) I watched a lot of footage of Cossacks 1 and two to see the diffrence betwenn those games and the new one, but I have to admit that Cossakcs 3 feels more like a graphical remake than a new game. I hardly can imagine, that the developpers tried to change their formula and implement new features in the game, while maintaining the flare fo cossacks. The game feels like a cheap try at making more money in the void and need of a new RTS game. Overall it feels rather cheaply done than like a new game.
I honestly think, that Cossacks 3 for 19.- CHF is a good pick when uwanna relive a little bit a classic RTS game, but do not expect a game that will blow you away or something like that.
