I used to love the Man o'war table top game and was really looking forward to a PC version.
THIS IS NOT IT.
Please do not be fooled by the title. Other then being set on ships and based in the Warhammer universe it has nothing to do with the table top game.
Please do not be fooled by the games OWN description:
Man O' War: Corsair.
Engage in epic naval combat and explore the oceans of the Warhammer world.
Man O' War: Corsair is a video game of high adventure, naval combat and exploration based on the Games Workshop classic Man O’ War table top game.
From reading the write up and looking at the screenshots, I didn't think it would be based the board game (I did however hope there would be at least some nod to its namesake) however this review and the reason I can't recommend it is based soley on the actually game play and prodiction quality (or rather lack of) of the game as it is.
- - - - - - - - - - - - - -
What you actually have is a VERY poor copy of the naval part from Assassins creed: Black Flag (AC:BF) with Warhammer ships.
The controls are fairly cumbersome and the graphics / textures and models are very bad for a licenced game. the less said about the UI the better!
It feels like an indy games designer played AC:BF and thought 'hey wouldn't it be cool if i ripped off that part' and then their mate suggested they could make money off it by slapping a Games Workshop logo on it. (besides it saved them the effort of coming up with some original designs -although considering the state of the graphics they clearly struggled wwith even that).
Yes I appricate the game is Early access, however this is barely ready for that and NO WAY justifies the ridiculous price tag they are asking for it.
Seeing as the game obviously had no intention of trying to replicate the board game (and yes they don't claim to) it does make you wonder why they bothered to use the Man O'War title at all... oh wait of course.. it's to con GW fans in to buying it, hoping it might have a some playability or even passing attempt at build quality.
If you liked the navel part of AC:BF - then play Black Flag - they did a much better job
If you want a computer version of Man'o War - this isn't it
If you want original game paly, design, ideas or ANYTHING original!  - this isn't it
If you want value for money - nearly any other game on steam is better value for money
IF the games developers dropped the price to £3 -£5 AND smoothed out the controls and vastly improved the models, graphics and textures etc ONLY then would I consider revising my review

i have put in almost 15 Hours into this game and as many players of the preorder hate the difficulty settings i must make a review.
Since i Play golf in real life too this will be more geared towards the developers Idea of true to life golf game.
This game as well as the developers focused on more real life golf physics and game play.  I have been with them since the release of TGC1.  this game does have a a lot of improvements from TGC1 but the focus is the same real life golf takes practice and dedication so if your not wanting to do that in a game then TGC1 and TGC2 is not for you.  Golf is a game of accuracy or power cant have one with out sacraficing the other.
There is a few bugs in the game still but over all it is well done for the way they planned the game to be "as close to real Life golf as Possible".
the difficulty lvls are very different:
Standard: SO EASY i barely sliced or hooked and always hit a good chip and putting was easy - Best for a beginner
Player:  It is like a middle ground but more power focused so accuracy is still lower but it is a challange - For a Intermediate Player or those that want a nice challange
Tour: the most power out of all and accuracy is really bad here you can not play this difficulty without using a mouse and keybaord a gamepad joystick it way to sensitive to left and right for this mode. : for advanced palyers or plain just advoid all together as i could not hit streight with a X1 controller, steam controller, or PS4 controller

the game play is nice. courses react the way they do in real life.  firm fairways mean more bounce and speed and firm greens ave more bounce and are a bit faster in the putt so ease up a bit, soft reacts nice too  grabs the ball and slows it a bit so sometimes the distance is cut shorter.
the Putting takes time as green speed and angles plus practice are required to putt most are having issues putting and that is true a golfer in the PGA practices putting more then any other aspect of the game due to it being the game maker or breaker.
so in my opinion this game is as close as you can get to real life golf in a game unless you count VR as that is totally a different aspect on the game of golf then using keyboards anf controllers.

Finally got around to playing KotoR and I have to say I enjoyed it more than I thought I would. I love pre ME3 Bioware and the writing and characters in KotoR are definitely the highlights. It's very easy to get lost in the various worlds and get wrapped up in some of your companion's backstories. The main plot is enjoyable with some decent mystery, and the way you can influence your friends' fates to a degree is satisfying. The twist had been spoiled for me years ago, so I can't really comment on how well it is handled, but I can say the ending left me a little unsatisfied. Things just end on a whim after the final encounter, and there's nothing more said about fallen friends or the state of your companions. Would've enjoyed some plot wind down for each of them, but regardless the base game is fun enough to get a recommendation. Just be prepared for some archaic gameplay conventions and lots of save scumming. If you can handle that you'll enjoy this game, but please don't expect a modern masterpiece, it's an enjoyable product of its time

I loved the first one, bugs and all.  However, TGC2 was supposed to be a step forward, alas, i feel they failed.  There are certainly some things they got right, but they just aren't enough to pull an upvote from me.
------
Wind.
Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't.  A double digit crosswind should blow the ball in the direction the wind is blowing.  I've had numerous occasions in BOTH game where the ball just ignores the wind, totally screwing up a shot.
------
Putting.
I've seeng putting in TGC2 compared to putting on a hardwood floor, and that's a pretty good analogy.  Even a slight tap can send the ball carreening accross the green.
------
Tempo.
There aren't words for how much i HATE this system.  Fast, Perfect, Slow... whatever.  Full backswing at the tee = Perfect.  Full downswing = Perfect.  Hear a "tink" ball goes 100 yards.  I don't understand why they changed the previous system that in my opinion worked just fine.
------
Elevation.
Pin is double digit uphill against a double digit wind.  I club up to compensate and the ball goes exactly the range the clubs says it will go plus rolls a bit further. So my shot is now several yards behind the pin, usually somewhere in the rough on the far side of the green.
I want to love this game.  Really i do.  However, there are just too many broken mechanics that should've been worked on more before release.

PROS
Better lighting, water looks great with new lighting.
Improvement over TGC in some areas, but then again it should be.
High detail objects.
Decent FW roll from drives.
Not in the triple A price bracket  £22 from a 3rd party seller
Career mode may hold a bit of fun ( not played it yet)
EDIT: Just played 2 rounds career  A.I. are pathetic,  the best was +20 after 2 rounds i was -12 on medium, felt too embarrassed to edit a golfer name with that kinda score...poor lambs
CONS
Feels the same as TGC in many areas.
Textures are very poor and far from realistic, and now appear more washed out.
Pitch shot is still the same as TGC and even a bit easier (get out of jail shot)
flop is a bit of a mess, i was expecting big changes here, but rather than improve it, it just feels broken and random, blading is possible but real easy to avoid.
putting is unchanged, still feels like pulling back on a sling and putts still break right off the bat ( if you know anything about golf, you will know what i mean here ) not great.
Tempo is easy to master, not really needed imo,  a more nuanced swing dispersion like JNPG would have been much better.
Some lies (edge of a bunker being one) that show 90-95% are giving weird dispersion and distance results even when hitting a clean shot, appears broken in places.
Bunkers look terrible and flat in new lighting.
Rough still too penal, like hitting out of velcro, you simply cannot work a shot to satisfaction.
Still no control over course conditions is a huge let down, not to include these choices in this day and age is very poor.
Many greens are still like ice rinks when it comes to putting, think of how a puck moves on ice for a long period at a slow speed, and you have the greens here.
Chipping still feels clunky and devoid of any feel.
no real links theme and more importantly, no pot bunkers! Golf does exist outside of north america the last time i checked.
Overall a slight step up from TGC and new comers to golf may enjoy the experience.  Those of us that actually play golf will see all the holes in this game.  TGC is a game taken seriously by its fans, but really there is not a lot here to push it into a satisfying sim bracket... A missed opportunity
Edit: Game is more enjoyable playing tour clubs, standard and player were too easy off the tee and deck, it's really the short game and penal rough that lets it down, and judging by TGC 1 they will not make the vast improvements that are required in this area.
Very hard for newbies to this type of game but a good challenge for pro's.

Three out of five stars. The short version: get blood money. The long version isn't so simple. Every Hitman game introduces itself with an impressive amount of class and enjoyment. Those first two levels are always so promising. As the game progresses, however, those shining promises diminish onto bitter lies.
The variety of weapons and tactics you learn would lead you to believe that every level will be thick with choices as to how you'll progress. There should be a variety of ways to kill your targets. There should be thought provoking scenarios that will make you feel like you've accomplished something upon completing them. Instead you're given two, maybe three ways to get within attack range of your target. From there you can do a "silent assasssin attack" that will rarely be something you'll figure out without immersion breaking trial and error. Instead you'll end up throwing a hammer at his/her head or just shooting them and running away with a terrified Zoidberg "whoop whoop whoop whoop!". I've never seen a sandbox game that so actively discourages exploration and experimentation. Enemies pop in and out of rooms with the predictability of pokemon in tall grass, the game intentionally thows you for a loop as to what disguise you'll need CONSTANTLY, and awkward fight controls make shooting your way out of anything a joke.
In the end it is fun though. After pointlessly dying a thousand times each map becomes less chaotic and more predictable. The massive levels are very fun to run around in once you know where you're going. Killing your targets is usually satisfying which does give the game some replayability. The repetitive soundtrack is at least nice to listen to as well. All in all I just barely give this game three stars. The cool concept works well and the mechanics work often enough that you usually feel somewhat in control of what's happening. This game wouldn't be so infuriating if the immersion wasn't so good before it was ripped away by a bad design choice.

After finally completing The Angry Video Game Adventures for the first time i can only say...WOW.
STORY: The plot of AVGN Adventures goes like this: One day the Nerd and his friends were playing a ***** game, when suddenly the TV sucks them in, the nerd tries to escape, but he gets grabbed by the sack and he enters Game Land to complete 9 levels and find out who the **** is responsible for this.
PRESENTATION: AVGN Adventures, like many other games, looks like an old retro-NES-SNES-game and by that i mean that the game has a mixture between 8 and 16 bits type graphics and sound (all tho you could argue with 32 bits for the sound, but that's besides the point). The sprites and backgrounds are well done and detailed, the framerate is consistent (at around 60fps) and the music ¡is kick-***!, everything in this game looks colorful, eye catching and different from one and other.
GAMEPLAY: AVGN Adventures plays like a 2D platforming shooter from the NES era with a very high difficulty. You platform around and shoot the enemies with the NES Zapper to progress and you can get upgrades or sub-weapons to add to your arsenal.
The game has 4 Characters to play with and each of them has some especial attribute, tho you do have to find the other characters. First there's "The Nerd", which is my personal favorite, he's the most balanced character of them all with a decent run speed, a decent jump high and he does decent damage, BUT! he is the only character who can use the upgrades and sub-weapons + he can stand in place and shoot in 8 directions, he is personally my character of choice most of the time. Then there's the "The Guitar Guy", he might seem like an awful character at first since he cannot use any sub-weapon or upgrade, he can only fire straight forward and he's jump is very...meh, BUT! he is the fastest of the bunch and his proyectiles can go through walls, proyectiles and barriers and believe me that doesn't sound like much, but he is very useful later on, especially on the final boss. Next there's "************ Mike", he has decent run speed and his weapon has a little range, BUT! he can use that weapon to destroy certain walls and he can jump the highest. And then theres "********-Man", he is the slowest of the bunch and he's jump is TERRIBLE, BUT he's the strongest and he can do a "not-so-helpful-double-jump", personally i never used him, and i feel he's the worst of all the characters. You find these hidden characters (excluding the Nerd) by using the abilities that each of them have.
Now while the game does have all of those characters, they are actually not required to beat the game. YEAH every level was designed in a way so you can complete all of them with just the Nerd, but while this is true, certain parts of the levels will be a **** ton easier if you have a buddy along with you, so keep that in mind. Speaking of the levels, the level design, for the most part, is pretty good...that's all i can say about it. This is certainly good level design, but i feel like sometimes got lazy when designing some parts of the levels. Each level has some sort of gimmick in them, but aside from that each level plays pretty much the same way. One of the things that this game loves to throw you is death blocks (pretty self-explanatory), there's like a bizillion of them throughout the game and the placement can be very brutal at times. The levels have some very fun set pieces and creative enemies (tho some of them are just re-skins of other enemies).
Overall the level design for the most part is really good, but there are some parts that are designed to anger you AND OMG they succeed. The game is hard, in a Castlevania, Ninja Gaiden, Zelda II, Megaman type of way. Now don't worry it's not as hard as any of those, but some of them can make say the phrases that the nerd says every time you die. But quite frankly only 2 of the 9 levels legitimately angered me and by the 2-3-4-6-8 playthrough of the level...it wasn't that bad and i felt like most of my deaths were fair and even if you feel like you are having a hard time, the game has different difficulty levels. I recommend normal mode for your first playthrough, it gives you 30 lives and 3 beers (which are this game life bar) and even in the highest difficulty, there are a lot of checkpoints throughout each stage.
At the end of every level there's a Boss which will require a different strategy to defeat and you will have to memorize the patterns in order to beat them, tho some of them are very easy.
The game has a lot of references to the Angry Video Game Videos and any AVGN fan (like me) will feel right at home with the over abundance of references, jokes and even cameos from other youtubers and enemies of the Nerd.
So overall with great graphics, music, bosses, characters, controls, decent level design, references and much more, Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures gets and 8/10. Definitely worth your money...and i can't wait for the sequel!!!.

If all you are looking for is a game that's full of AVGN fan service, then this one is it (assuming you can make it through more than one level without throwing your controller at your TV).   There are some hilarious nods to just about all of the memorable AVGN characters and events.   From a 'sh!t pickle' hidden in each level to unlockable playable characters, each will delight the avid AVGN fan.
Unfortunately that's where it ends.
If you want a game that's fun to play and offers rewards for exploration (the way any good platformer should), then I would probably steer clear of this one.    This game goes out of it's way to parody every single BAD platformer the AVGN has ever reviewed, and the end result is an excercise in furious frustration.   But it's worse than that, because there are actual design choices that were made that just make the game unbearable.
Example #1:   The 'death blocks' - a completely obvious crutch used by the game designer to add artificial difficulty to the game.   You'll find these in EVERY. SINGLE. LEVEL. and in the worse possible places.   Like floating up the screen a boss battle...   they don't even bother to really theme these death blocks for each level either.   Just cheap.
Example #2:   The 'enemies' pretty much fall into the same few categories and are themed for each level.    The generic 'fireball' enemy for instance.   In one level it's an actual fireball, in another it's a ghost, in another it's a green plasma ball with a big grinning smiley face plastered on it.   It's so obvious it's painful.
The list of re-used and re-skinned enemy types goes on and on...
There are other annoyances with the game as well, like the 'YOU DIED STUPID' screens with the randomized one liner generator.   That gets old after the first few times you see it and can't be skipped quickly.   And the actual 'GAME OVER' screen doesn't even go so far as to do the random one liner thing - it's just 'YOU SUCK, YOUR WHOLE FAMILY SUCKS' etc.
Thing is, I almost gave it a thumbs up based on the AVGN fan service alone...   but when you strip that away you're left with a game that tries and fails to be a good platformer - on purpose.

Man O' War: Corsair is one of a number of games come to PC based on old Games Workshop miniature games - the specialized games. These weren't the big titles like Warhammer and Warhammer 40k, where players might buy hundrets of miniatures, but even just a handful would be enough to have a fun evening with friends.
Some of these games have been translated with 100% accuracy to the PC: Blood Bowl, Talisman, Chainsaw Warrior, Warhammer Quest, Space Hulk. Others like Battle Fleet Gothic and Mordheim have ben addapted more freely.
Man O' War: Corsair is going a bit further with this freedom - and it is a good thing.
The old board game was about players taking turns moving their fleet in naval battles. But le'ts be honest, while the Sea of Claws is interesting, naval battles never were something that Warhammer Fantasy fans truly cared about. Not in the way that 40k fans cared about the big space battles fought during the Horus Heresy.
So it makes sense to use Man O' War: Corsair to explore intriguing parts of the Warhammer world in a new way:
In Man O' War: Corsair you play as the captain of a ship. In the single player campaign this will be either a human captain or a chaos captain. The human captain can be part of one of seveal factions(Empire, Bretonnia) or independent. The Chaos captain will follow a god and have their goals and starting fleet reflect this choice. You can freely sail your ship from Kislev and the Sea of claws, down to Tilea and Sartosa. On your journeys you can fight pirates or become one yourself, fight orcs, chaos marauders, dwarves and elves. You can pillage towns or defend them against enemy fleets. You can trade or search for lost treasure.
You can do all that with a variety of ships - the majority of the miniature range are being digitized (sadly the team being small, they had to draw the line somewhere and Chaos Dwarves and Norse will have to be left for a hopeful expansion). You can upgrade your ship. You can hire loyal, or not so loyal crew for your ship, and train them as they gain experience and equip them. You can hire wizards, and air support (grifon riders, pegasus nights etc.). And you can hire allied captains with their own ship, to slowly build up your fleet. You can gain reputation with factions and even join them.
In skirmish mode you create a fleet of any faction in the traditional way of buying with a point system. That means Empire, Bretonia, Orks, Dwarves, High Elves, Dark Elves, Skaven, Khorne, Tzeentch, Nurgle and Slaanesh.
Sea Monsters. They deserve a special mention, because there is nothing like sailing the high seas and have a huge shark surface next to your ship, ready to take a bite out of your hull. OK, maybe there is, but it involves a large narwhal like monster surfacing next to your ship, in the fog and ramming your ship with its horn. Or a Leviathan's maw opening up, ready to swallow your ship whole.
Man O' War: Corsair is the one game that allows you to travel around the Warhammer world where you want and at the pace you want. The only thing that stops you is unfavourable wind.
Good hunting, sailor!

I've been very pleasantly surprised by this game, given Games Workshop's rather hit or miss history with vidya games.
Pros:
-The game's accessible to people who don't know much or anything about Warhammer Fantasy. You can just hop right in.
-Sailing controls and mechanics are super simple to master
-Being able to arm, name, and level up your crew so they're not just a bunch of faceless mooks is nice. Even them getting injured permanently is a good touch for depth and immersion
-New crew members aren't absolutely useless if you lose a veteran
-You don't lose the weapons of crew members who die
-You don't have to stick to any one method to make money
-Your starting ship is good enough to stick with for a long time and can be tricked out to be really good
-Ship combat can be get pretty tense and fun, satisfying to watch a pain in the butt enemy sink to the bottom
-Wizards
-Getting unique magic weapons
-Boarding actions are pretty fun in spite of clunkiness
-Plenty of factions, easy to take advantage of the conflicts between them, making for some fun manipulation of backstabbing
-The servants of the four Chaos gods are all distinct from each other (damn you, Tzeentchian floating magic tower!)
-They fixed the friendly fire problems, I think you can still shoot your crew but your melee weapon passes through them.
-Now you can board enemy vessels during boarding actions, which is a good addition.
Cons:
-There's no hard numbers on anything. You sort of have to assume weapons that are more expensive do more damage (I'm guessing this is something that will be fixed before full release)
-Armor seems to be purely cosmetic (goes along with the no hard numbers thing)
-Hand to hand combat during boarding actions is pretty clunky.
-Even with Reik's Fashion DLC, not a lot of player character customization
-No visual customization for your ships
-Only 5 or so models for human crew members on your ship
-The Champion of Khorne campaign is fairly lackluster at the moment. It's fun initially, but with no way to really use trade goods beyond getting tiny amounts of favor for them and no way to get new weapons for your captain, you're left with a slogging grind to build up enough force to take each port without a real means to improve yourself or your ship's armament in a meaningful way.
In the end, as it is, I'd give this game an 8.5/10. I think it's a great idea and well done so far. It could use a bit of refinement in some areas, but all in all I'd highly recommend this game, especially for anyone who enjoyed the ship combat of Assassin's Creed 4. Depending how they improve it before full release, it could bump up to 9/10.

Word Tactical is recently thrown around a lot and it usually refers to games like Operation Flashpoint, Armed Assault, Ghost Recon, Swat etc. Despite their history, many tactical shooters have being changed over the years and they are going further and further from their origins with each new entry.
Among the good old games there was a small first person shooter developed by Innerloop studios called Project IGI.
IGI series was not very popular and was killed after the release of a second game, IGI 2 Covert Strike. Despite that the series is unfairly underrated, both games are very enjoyable to play even today.
As a huge fan of IGI series I got quite excited when I first discovered Beyond Enemy Lines, because like every other fan, I was waiting for IGI 3, even though I knew it won't happen. Now 14 years later we get a spiritual successor to IGI, developed by a single developer.
After playing alpha version for several weeks and finally getting hands on the finished game I can proudly say Polygon Arts you did it!
Project IGI is a first person shooter set during Cold war. You play as an IGI agent David Jones, who is tasked to track down stolen nuclear warhead by infiltrating various locations to get the right information and blowing up a few things along a way. If the lack of creative narrative is pushing you from buying Project IGI, gameplay certainly won't.
Beyond Enemy Lines shares the same formula and throws you into mud from the start. Levels are large and each offers multiple routes and a long list of hidden items.
Unlike most games of today, health doesn't regenerate when you're injured. In order to recover, you need to search for medic kits. So exploration is highly recommended.
One thing you can really count on is that this game will kick your a55 and if you're not purely focused on a mission from start to finish, you're gonna take a serious beating. Enemies, although not very smart, have very powerful weapons and they rarely miss and if they catch you by surprise you'll end up six feet under. It can get very frustrating at times, but it becomes very satisfying when you return them a favor and beat a level.
As I've said, enemies can be problematic. Once they lose sight of you, they'll come back to their regular patrols or even get easily distracted once they see a dead body or hear you whistle. As silly as that sounds their dumbness is the only way you're gonna beat the game. If enemies would chase you mercilessly, as in Far Cry 2 for example, game would be nearly impossible to complete.
Once they take damage, some enemies will return fire, while others will run and hide.
Animations are not done very well. Once enemies see you, they all react in a same way before they open fire. You no longer see arms when climbing a ladder, nor when using a map computer and also barrel of your rifle can go through walls and objects.
It's important to know that none of these things break the game, nor ruin the experience.
If going in alone into a fortress full of well trained enemies sounds like a mission impossible to you, then what I'm about to say will break you completely. There is no mid-mission saving. No quick saves. No checkpoints.
When just one mistake could wipe up your entire progress and push you back to start of a mission, you'll play the way it's meant to be played by carefully planning your each move and checking every corner. This kind of gameplay creates a huge amount of tension from start to finish and gives you a feel as if you are in a real life situation.
Like every game, it has it's faults, but if you are failing, it's simply because you're not playing well. This is a game about critical planning and surveillance. It forces you to think before you act, search for elevated positions, tall grass and bushes and attack enemies when they least expect. Enemies in this game are like obstacles, like switches you need to turn off in order to progress, but the real challenge is to figure the order you need to turn them off that best fits your playstyle and unlike Project IGI, some enemies change patrol patterns or spawn on different locations every time you start a mission, so you have to think on a fly.
Game doesn't have a huge list of weapons, as you might expect, but weapons are varied. Weapons like your pistol and MP5 are equipped with silencer for stealthier approach. Assault rifles like M4 and AK47 are very powerful, but not very accurate.
This totally makes sense because most enemies carry a Kalashnikov and if it wasn't nerfed, it'd be overpowered and because it's very common, you'd never round out of ammunition. M4 in the other hand fires 3 rounds burst and is very useful at medium and short range.
Shotgun is useful to devastate enemies at short range, just as a Dragunov for a long range.
Overall, weapons are far easier to handle than in alpha version. When using a medical syringe, you can see the percent of health points left in a syringe, just as you see an ammo on a screen when holding a weapon. You can choose to heal yourself as little or as much as you won't, until you run out of points of course.
Heads Up Display is very small and simple and controls are easy to remember.
There are no grenades, machine guns, nor grenade launchers. However, there are plenty other useful tools, like a map computer, night vision and binoculars. Map computer gives you a satelite view of a whole mission and highlights enemies and the objectives. Binoculars is very useful for seeing enemies in the distance. You're not forced to use of these and I personally prefer listening to enemy footsteps and run and hide when things go wrong, rather than searching for them on a map computer.
Beyond Enemy Lines sadly doesn't have a multiplayer, but considering I'm a developer as well and I understand how big trouble it is to set the server running, I can't blame him. After all everything from gameplay, to story and level design, website, trailers, articles and so much more was done by just one man.
At the end of a day, Beyond Enemy Lines is a great game that lives on it's promises. No one ever said that this game will be easy, nor feature scripted sequences with a groundbreaking narrative. It's what it's meant to be, but if you don't like IGI games, chances are they you'll not like this one either.
While many may say that Beyond Enemy Lines is a modern game with an old school gameplay, unlike most so called tactical shooters, Beyond Enemy Lines stayed true to it's original formula that made IGI games great in a first place and improved upon it.
It's a game that takes time to master, but once get the hang of it, it will become very enjoyable and addictive.
Rating: 8.5/10

This is a game worth supporting, and it's a great throwback to Igi. But at the moment the game's unfinished so I decided to refund it, but I got full intentions of buying it back later when it's more complete and hopefully there is a full demo of it instead of the kcikstarter early alpha (which is how I found out about the game and thought the game would be finished by now but apparently the pre alpha demo more or less felt like the latest version of the game I just played).
I know this game's a one man job and I applaud the developer for it.
I'd like to list a couple of complaints that I have with the game that I hope he gets to fix it.
1. The most annoying thing with it is the animations, especially when you're climbing up a ladder and you keep climbing into the air even after you've reached the top of the ladder onto the platform. Also some animations between gun switches, aiming down sights would be nice.
2. Your hand / gun disappears or clips into walls. Not just some random wall, but EVERY wall. There is no collision against a wall feeling because you sort of pass through it a little. Once when I had my hand/gun near a table, it looked like my hand was cut away and was kept on the table. Don't know to explain this properly, but collision physics was lacking in short.
3. The menus and the way you bind keys. This is no deal breaker, but sometimes I had to press Esc to go back, and sometimes it does nothing, and I have to click on the Back button. Problem here is the Back button looks kind of invisible so I was stuck there doing nothing for a while until I found it.
4. The lady who briefs the missions is waaaaaay too loud in every mission. (Well I just reached the second mission but then, it was just too loud on both the missions so I doubt it would change in the later missions), anyways it's something that needs fixing for sure.
5. This maybe a game design choice, but the first mission was awfully dark in some places thanks to some dark shadows, and the lens flare totally blinded me too. I know game's meant to be realistic, but that kind of realism needn't be there when it hampers gameplay. But it's not a deal breaker, just a minor annoyance which would be better if fixed.
As for what's done right:
1. Game runs smooth on my somewhat high end rig . i7 and gtx 970, no performance issues of any kind, and I'm very happy with the 21:9 ultrawide support.
2. The entire Igi game design is just so addictive and  challenging and fun. This is what games like Far Cry, Sniper Gw3 etc are trying to do, but that open world mechanic kind of sometimes results in more quantity than quality sometimes. But I'm happy the first two missions that I played had good quality in level design and enemy spawns.
3. Ai was pretty decent. Sometimes I felt they didn't react when you shot them, but I wasn't completely sure I hit them as i was using my silenced smg so I could be wrong here. Would need more playtime to know but I had to get the refund going sadly before I cross the 2 hr limit.
4. All in all game's great. If you can look past the Ok graphics and some bugs, it's a definite buy. I'm ok with the graphics, I just find the bugginess a little jarring for the experience. In short, it's a great but incomplete game. If you're a fan of IGI, you will get EXACtly what you wished for. Pretty much everything from IGI exists here, including how u can see enemies thorugh your satellite map thingy, the way that you approach your missions etc etc. I want this game to succeed and I want to support the developer, and I feel bad for applying for a refund right now. I'll be back for sure with an updated review in the future sometime. Cheers Polygon Art.

The Golf Club 2 is an incredible Golf game and improves on the original game in every single aspect imaginabl. The customization options just simply go beyond anything you would expect from a Golf game. The graphics are sharper, cleaner, higher quality and higher resolution textures in just about everything. The rocks look good, the grass you can EASILY tell are just on another level of detail compared to TGC1 and the detail on the golfers that you can customize to your hears content is just amazing! The PostFX lighting is MASSIVELY different then TGC1, and makes everything pop out and look amazing! I was shocked how badly the PostFX worked in the original game and it was nice to see just how much they've improved it this time around.
It almost feels like MMO level of customizations here when it comes to customizing your golfer, from male or female, to facial and hair designs, skin colour, hats, clothes, oh, you can litterately colour EVERYTHING except the balls (but those are apparently coming in an update after launch) so I may update this review if that ever happens?  You unlock clothes by earning the in-game currency and this can be achieved by participating in rounds, playing against friends, winning tournaments, going online etc. and fortunately the game is REALLY forgiving when it comes to how much you earn per round of golf (depending on finish) and it's nice, it's not like you are going to unlock everything really fast because there is just so! much to unlock, but it's nice to know its not really grind fest like most MMO's can be. I think 700 credits for finishing a round by yourself and not in a tournament is very forgiving in my opinion and feels just about right.
You constantly feel you are progressing towards something! which is something in most golf games you just never really feel you are doing! now the game has added a full career mode! not only can you enjoy a very good singleplayer experience but it also has progression to make TGC2 feel a LOT more of a complete golfing experience. There is the course creator which is just CRAZY amazing, being able to full design your own course in a completely free sandbox editor which is the very tools the devs use to create the courses iis just incredible! this adds an INFINATE replayability value that NO OTHER golf game can provide... It's the level of detail and what you can do inside the course editor will blow your mind. They've done a lot of improvements to it like adding multi-level water so creating amazing waterfalls, and a lot of other things and quality of life changes to make it easier and better to create courses. If you don't like spending all that time creating, you can create a proceedually generated course instead in seconds! and just edit that if you wish.
Societies I'm still learning but the ability to upgrade your clubhouse, to actually OWN a clubhouse in the first place, level it up, buy new ones, bigger ones, and set clubhouse events is just amazing and something the multiplayer community desbrately needed to be fair. This adds a WHOLE new specticle on multiplayer in TGC2 over it's predecessor. You can customize a lot, but the one gribe I would have about it is you can't walk around inside the clubhouses, I think that would have been absolutely stunning! instead of a panable picture! so you could really REVEL in your greatness of your clubhouse and could have acted as a social lobby perhaps.
The Swing Mechanic is vastly different and it DOES take time to get used to. There are 3 types of clubs (Standard / Player and Tour) which the varing difficulties which really impacts the new swing mechanic in a couple ways. I would definitely suggest just sticking with Standard until you  get used to the tempo mechanic. The main difference here is that Standard club set plays more like the original Golf Club game and is a lot more forgiving in the swing direction, the other two levels are not and you have to be VERY good to use those but its a really nice feature for those that thought TGC1 just simply wasn't challenging enough. I cannot explain properly how the new swing mechanic works, its just hard to describe but timing is everything, you just have to be patient with it.
The bad.
The menu system in clunky AF! and wish they had reduced the sheer amount of menus especially when trying to add friends into a round. Which leads me to the next bad point, how the heck after all the complaints you did not add a full lobby system for friends or players to join into? It was my biggest gripe from the original game that you had to go through menu after menu just to send an invite and this was only once you had started a round, and then having to wait for everyone to join the same course at the same time and be at the starting tee before we can even turn on "Turn Order." This should have been a lobby setting that you should enable/disable before you even start the round.
Having invites that are sent to your in-game email is EXTREMELY ANNOYING and cumbersome. The third issue was the sheer lack of ball customization, considering in the E3 trailer we saw HB Games own logo on the balls, it would have been absolutely awesome to have been able to customimze our balls a bit, with logo's or just being able to colour them! I wouldn't have minded to having unlockable balls you pay with in-game currency! just to add something different to the games.
There is so much to say but I just wanted to give a general run down on some of the features as this review could turn into a book more then it is already. I highly reccomend it, the sheer amount of game you get for the price is just WELL worth it in my opinion, there is just so much here if you love Golf games. This is by far the much Superior Golf Game out there right now by a looooooooooooong shot. There isn't a single golf game out there that comes close to matching what this game has to offer. Any potential golfers just would not regret your purchase!

Cons

This game. Oh. My Dog. Yes.
I first played this game when I was 5 on my dad's computer, so admittedly there's some nostalgia bias here. But I've played it many times since then, and it really is fantastic. It's old as balls in computer game years, but it holds up.
This is the type of puzzle game that takes some commitment from the player - you'd better have a notebook handy to write down all the clues and hints along the way, because the game does not make things easy for you. Full disclosure, I still haven't beaten the game because I always get stuck on one particular puzzle. Every year or so I make another attempt, hopefully this will be the year. That said, the challenge is what makes the game worth it; many puzzle games nowadays are way too easy, and it gets boring. If Myst gets boring, it's because you're stuck and you may need to take a break, think about it, and have another crack at it later.
Biggest complaint is that it's a little awkward running on modern OS's; I was able to get this running on Windows 8.1 with (so far) no issues, but it can be a little clunky on some people's systems. Make sure you have Quicktime installed, and check the Steam forums for good compatibility settings.

Where's my ability to make custom peeps? Or design scenarios? What happened to the hundreds of different ride types? For Fans of the 1st TGC, you will enjoy the 2nd TGC.
If you've never played TGC and if you're wondering this vs. Rory it's almost uncomperable. Yes they're both golf games, and yes i enjoy them both, but it's like comparing arma to call of duty. They're two very different beasts indeed. While TGC is not so sim that you need to be a pro golfer in real life to understand the game, it is just sim enough to be extremly rewarding in a way that shooting -22 on tiger never will be. I've played rounds where i've been well over par that were exilarting, and that is not an exaggeration. Watch youtube gameplay or buy the original on sale. It won't be for everyone, but for a certain few like myself it's exactly the golf series i spent half a life time waiting for.
Pros
- The swing has that distinct TGC feel but with more polish than the first go round.
-fairway roll seems improved in a way i can't put my finger on, but has seemed 100% organic in my first 5 or 6 rounds.
-There's already heaps of courses
-Seems alot easier to get in the "swing of things" -pun- ui, controls, many many things seem cleaned up.
-not perfect, but heaps of graphics sliders(see cons)
-sorry, that most of these are kind of the same, but alot of fat has been cut everywhere.Most everything from a user standpoint seems slighty tweaked in ways we all asked for. Feels more like the game HB set out to make than ever before.
cons
-graphic sliders are things that WILL be course dependant and could use a little recommended help window. the tree quality and distance sliders cranked all the way up will have night and day effects depending on the direction your facing alone. on one green it was the difference of 70 fps from my 1st putt to my second. 98fps to 26fps.seriously. then on a links style course with few to no tree i was averaging about 118fps.
-water textures for me appear to be fairly low res from most angles and have had an awful shimmering motion blur effect behind some greens. don't know what's causing this. or if it's course specific.
-The loading is pretty awful  off the course and needs to be addressed.navigating the socities menus are a dial-up modem crawl. even opening the leadboards is a brutal trial of patience.the option to download favorite courses to my hard drive to speed that section up atleast would be a great feature, but that's only one part of the problem.
-The launch has been pretty crap from a consumer prospective. noon release time, during the summer sale, with/without preload (never did find out if it had it),with regional release dates and pre-order bonuses not being given away to people who bought on the first day. This is just not how game releases work anymore. It just felt so 2012. Even gamestop and ubisoft still give you pre-order bonuses if you buy a title within 24 hours of launch. and midnight.for the love of god always midnight.
- FFW button for shots. My 100% most desired feature. please ad this. it makes rounds go by so much faster.watching a ball roll down the middle of the fairway 9-12 times a round just eats into more time i could be playing and practicing.
Love HB. They seem like great guys, and i know they read these, and i know they care. This game is proof they care about finding solutions. So far i'm really enjoying this game, and i hope they keep squashing bugs and making it better and better, So my cons weren't meant to bash the game. just wanted to draw attention to the few things i hope they'll tweak and learn from. Great game guys. i'm going to go put another 50 hours into it real quick.

"Completely unimaginative and drains the colour out of what I'd imagine game design is all about."
Currently should be repackaged as an unstable early access game that's just come on steam by a new developer. That's what it feels like.
You know... one of those games that has just launched it's early access with a limited number of features. And hasn't yet released it's 30 - 90 regular updates.
There are early access games with more content and attention to detail than this has. I appreciate that the old Cossacks games may not have had the simplest of features such as building rotation. What about even just an outline for farms? So you know where the crop will grow?
Sure these things I just mentioned don't make or break the game. But I would have liked to see the most possitive thing said about this game to not just be, "it looks pretty". There are no original features in this game. I really lack to find any real insentive as to why i bought this. I can remember in one of their games a rank fire option, which back then blew my tiny mind.
Why do away with fun things like that? No real tech tree at all. Just a bunch of buttons that heal troops or make harvesting faster. It's completely unimaginative and drains the colour out of what I'd imagine game design is all about.
It is so lacking in features I don't feel the game has any identifiers, and it almost feels pointless picking a faction to play. Their that similar. They really need to be fleshed out and more interesting to play. Instead no matter whether you play musketeers or melee infintary, you have the exact same limited options available. And in the end I suppose... why not? It all looks like millions of bees attacking the same flower, when in combat.
It just feels like "Cossacks HD", except they haven't made any attempt to make it the least bit better, more interesting or up-to-date/standard for the player.
None of this really covers the fact that the game constantly crashes, full of bugs. You don't know if the game will crash on the next thing you build or the next formation you command. How can you play a game like that? Not to mention it's had one of the worst game launches I've ever seen on Steam.
The AI is taken straight from the older games also. From what I remember playing of them and this one, the AI basically railroads forward with little intelligence. The first wave I ever encountered from the AI which was on "impossible" mode, was something like ten priests and a single cannon.
At the moment, and I doubt this is an area GSC are thinking about fixing, the AI builds up just hundreds of spearmen and I've seen them use two different cavalry. They don't use formations or tactics of any kind. And when you are attacking, you can sit on the edge of their base. While looking at the fact they have a MASSIVE square of spearmen and they won't register it. Obviously this means theres an aggro range. And then it becomes as I mentioned before, a fullscale bee attack. Blobs of troops that attack the first thing closest to it.
Which makes me wonder why they've had so much trouble releasing this game. Clearly it's been released too soon, but I don't see how that could happen when theres so little content, basically a prettier version of their previous. And it kinda sucks when the best thing (only thing) you have to say about the game is either, "this brings back such nostalgia" or that it has pretty graphics.
At the moment I wouldn't recommend this game. It's current state of crashing, for me makes it not worth having purchased it. Sometimes theres a bit of smooth gameplay and I've enjoyed that, but even if the game gets fixed to a stable standard. Unless they add what I feel are missing features and much needed details, I'm not sure I feel good about this purchase at all. The aspects about this game that I do enjoy will become old and boring very soon.

Super Space Meltdown is a top- down 2D rogue-like dungeon crawler set on an alien infested space station.
The game has a nice soundtrack which sets the tone of the environment very well. The sound effects have a retro feel which complement the pixel-art style very well.
The pixel art is well defined and colorful. All the sprites on screen are distinct in style and shape. However, there are no options to adjust graphical settings, such as windowed support, adjusting resolutions, adjusting refresh rate, or any more advanced settings.
The gameplay premise is simple. Complete each level within 60 seconds. If the timer runs out or you die, you restart from the beginning and play a random series of levels maintaining the equipment from the previous run. This is where the rouge-like elements come into play. However, it does become repetitive after a time. Perhaps farther in could yield more exciting level design or a boss fight, which would add some much needed variety.
The controls are difficult to get used to. Your character can play equipment, such as mines or turrets, and shoot with your rifle. Your character can only shoot in a straight line. However, nowhere in the game is there listed a tutorial for any of this information. The game needs a tutorial for the controls, or at least a list of key bindings, which you also cannot currently rebind. Also, this game would benefit hugely from controller support, or at least the ability to rebind keys.
Overall, I would not recommend this game yet, despite its price, which is $3.99 at the time of writing. It is a simple game that provides enjoyment, if repetitive, at the most basic level. If you enjoy rogue-like games, this is up your alley. However, this game fails in any kind of customization. Hopefully an update comes soon which could allow four things which would benefit it heavily; Controller support, an in-game tutorial or at least a list of controls, graphical options, and key bindings. After those changes, this game would be vastly superior to its current form and would be worth an extended play.

Super Space Meltdown is a game.  Yep.  It's a game, you can just spam the fire button for great justice, the special weapons all feel relatively useless and your gun auto locks on to anything that is in your "lane" North, South, East, or West of you, you can also only move in those directions, no diagonals here. You have 60 seconds to beat each floor, and each floor is also randomized.  The enemies rarely attack, and when they do attack their shots are somewhat easy to dodge, also enemies take a ton of shots to kill, your hand will hurt.  Some stages seem to feature laser traps that near instant kill you if you're caught in one.  The game offers no instructions on how play the game, and feels clunky with keyboard controls and no way to remap them ingame.  Though using Xpadder to map the buttons to my gamepad certainly helped a ton.  The game is also locked into Fullscreen only mode, and for one reason or another kept crashing on me when I launched it.  I was finally able to get a good launch and record some of the game play (I played poorly).  All in all, you get what you pay for.
Some thoughts that could improve this game.  First and Foremost, being able to attack diagonally.  Many times I lost a few seconds of time because an enemy would just move to one of my diagonals making me have to fully reposition just to hit them, even though the enemy was still adjacent to me.   Second, maybe progressive levels?  What I mean is, I like the random aspect, but maybe make enemies on lower floors easier/take less shots to kill, but they get harder the more floors you go down, this could encourage the use of proper tactics and not just mash spacebar.  I feel as though that you need more health/ammo pick ups (Unless I just somehow missed them), as well as maybe tweak the special weapons some, as I felt they were a bit on the useless side of things.  The Turret was nice, but you can't retrieve it, or replace it once you've used it, and it doesn't last long before it explodes.  The grenade is really clunky, its explosion range only seems to damage the imidiate square that it blew up in, same with the time bomb and proximity mine.  The Proximity mine could definitely use a buff, make it to where it blows up the square its in, and the squares adjacent to it in a 3x3 grid.  I didn't like the fact that the enemy needed to be directly on top of it to register "Hey I need to blow up now!"
All in all, for the pricepoint of the game, its relatively decent, but it didn't hold my attention all that long.  I'd give it somewhere in the ballpark of 4/10, decent, but not great

Colony Survival! It's a great game to play slowly getting more and more improvments but seriously can't the colonists just learn to fight for themselves :)

Colony survival is one of those games that I always wished I could play - a colony management/building game but that actually lets you be a person in the game and not just a disembodied overlord. That niche is something I always wanted to get a chance to play - where I could help my colonists fight and wander the streets of my town myself.
So that is essentially what this game is. You not only get to build your colony (however you wish in style) but also get to wander around, fight/defend, mine, give orders, organise defences, and be a part of what you create. It looks very similar to other voxel games, of course much like Minecraft, but if you are like me and loved Minecraft and the Kingdom mod for that game then CS is heading in a somewhat similar direction.
The game is (at time of writing) in EA so you of course have to be aware that nothing is fixed, there will be more features and content coming down the line, and some features are not there yet. For instance, currently the colonists lack personality or dialogue and mechanically move from bed to their jobs and back again, even lacking AI to run from a zombie if it is attacking (rather they go on as if the zombie isn't there until they die). Similarly there is no means of managing your colony from a central location - such as a monarch's desk - but rather you have to go to each person's desk to change their orders. Other nice features such as ordering troops (other than where they guard), melee attack, and such are yet to be implemented.
BUT none of this detracts from the game!! It is EA and the devs are always updating the game, very much engaged with listening to players' feedback and desires for the game, and the game itself still has a lot of good content, is fun, and for me is definitely worth the price!
For instance, you can build however you want (like in Minecraft). So want a castle? A moat? A lake city? A floating city? A small village? Walls? No walls? Where do you want your farms? Want houses/buildings for each profession or have them all together? All are possible. You can upgrade your guards through four levels, mine several different resources (all of which are useful), buy things with gold (a bit basic at the moment, but like I said it is coming!), have numerous different professions for your colonists, research through different things to build more, open up new professions, and even expand the size of your kingdom! There are zombies to fight (about three different kinds) - which, while limited at the moment is something I believe the devs will keep adding to so as to add variety - and you can choose difficulty and whether they constantly attack or just during the night. And so much more.
I paid the full EA price for this game, and as I currently have 19 hours in the game and still have not opened all research - let alone that more is coming - I definitely found it to be worth the price and more! It has been fun, made me want to play it more, given me ideas for this playthrough and others, made me think not just how tough I need to be as a character but also that I have to build defences, keep an eye on my kingdom's resources (i.e. can I build more guards? Will they have enough ammo?), and think how best to defend agains the next attack. All while trying to make my kingdom look cool! So is it worth it? Yes. Fun? Absolutely. Does it have potential? You are damn right it does!
Just keep in mind it is EA and how the devs DO regularly update the game and listen to/engage with players and you won't go far wrong. Like Minecraft and wished you could also have colony running mechanics? You will like it. Yes there is not as much for you to do to update your character yet and no there are no dungeons (that I am aware of), it is very much (at the moment) focused on running the colony - but there is a whole world of things this game could (and hopefully will) implement and the devs certainly are on the right track with how they work in taking the game there.
As with all games, check an LP on Youtube to see if you like them (and keep in mind that some LPs are the older versions of the game) but for me, I love it and really look forward to seeing more!

The problem with this is that it is clearly made for console and not for PC. Naggie the tutorial fairy tells you jump is A (when it isn't for PC) and so unless you looked at the controls before playing the game you have to guess what the controls are. Also, the fact that you can't use the mouse is the real deal breaker for me, I have to use the keyboard fully, which doesn't sound that bad but is an issue when "up" and "Jump" use different keys and you can't use the mouse it means that it is really hard to find the keys that feels right.
So be prepared to have to spend about 30 minutes changing the controls to feel good.
It really annoyes me that they made this port to PC with the very low effort. But the game is good and if you like the AVGN then you will be able to get over the controls, to improve it i would say to go into the controls and make I,O and P as the attack.

As the many other reviews indicate, Besiege is a great and interesting game that allows you be as imaginative as you wish and use it to bring destruction to the medieval-style enemy sites with your creation. Starting up Besige, you are presented with a map of the world that allows you to select a location and level to attemt. Once in the selected level, you will see the enemy structure that you will attempt to destory in order to complete the level and move on to a new, and slightly more challenging one.
In the editing phase of the level, on screen you will see a number of options and menus that enable to build your creation, fine tune the details, customise it, remove or place parts, view it from various angles and so forth. After that you are able to try out what you have build and see how it interacts with the various objects in the map.
What you see in your mind and believe will work will not always do so in the game, sometimes even breaking apart before you even have the chance to move it about. The amout of control and the capabilites of your machine lies entirely with you, so if you decide to place metal armour or heavy artilery on it, then it will act accordingly. Sometimes even the smallest things that you didn't oversee during the construction phase will send you back to be fixed. The amout of tools in the game allows you to be able to expreiment with various combinations of defensive or offensive building materials. It can be as simple as building a medieval-style cannon or a fully fledged machine.
When attempting a new level sometimes you will be able visualise it and solve it first try or at other times it will require a bit more experimenting.

As of beta 5.2,
TL;DR - Has issues, is buggy, and a ton of fun to play. Buy if you want to sail the seas and get rammed by orcs/chaos/megalodons.
The game already feels like your typical AAA release, missing content, incredibly buggy, and rather poorly optimized.
But given this game is half the price of a AAA release, and is in early access, that just makes me more excited to see what this becomes. The game is definitely playable (although I've had it slow to sub 10 FPS in large naval battles, damn Chaos), and a hell of a lot of fun.
Pros:
- The core gameplay loop is very satisfying, as is watching your enemies slowly grow from the horizon. There's trading, combat, boarding, raiding and razing ports, etc.
- The game steadily allows you to gather wealth, with missions paying well without feeling like they're required to make profits, which is important since all the coolest things in this game are pretty damn expensive.
- The naval combat is very well done and a lot of fun, making it worth it to fight even if you are a trader. Very cathartic and enjoyable.
- The game world feels fairly fleshed out and alive, with dark forces constantly conducting invasions into human land, and with relations, alliances, and wars between the humans, dwarves, and elves.
- Epic battles, watching things approach from the horizon is amazing, and to get into huge battles with navies or with monsters is just awesome.
- Communicative dev team, immediately makes it better than most other Early Access titles.
Cons:
- Pretty sure this game has a memory leak with loading and rendering ships, after playing a while my FPS steadily declines, even when I'm alone at sea. This fixes when reloading from a save (or restarting).
- On the last point, the game isn't well optimized, with my point in the intro of how low my FPS can get in large battles.
- Had instances of extreme crashes that forced me to hard reset my computer (power button).
- There are some bugs that are incredibly annoying (getting stuck in your ship during boarding, flying beasts breaking and teleporting on top of you)
- Flying beasts as a whole are seriously a nuisance, and in my opinion should take less hits. I'm not at threat of dying to them ever, but it takes a lot of time in order to kill.
For thought:
- This game would definitely benefit from a multiplayer campaign.
- Like seriously.
All in all, I heavily recommend this game.

There simply is not enough content to justify the price.  Even for Early Access this is minimal at best. No animations, weapon models, or varied enemies. The game lacks basic features like being able to assign your workers to a specific task. The world generation provides no reason to explore, as there are no spawning enemies, biomes, wildlife, points of interest, etc.
The interface is pretty clunky. The command mode as 1 and 2, then 3-9 being your inventory is an odd choice that you never quite get used to. Having Left click as cancel, and right click as confirm feels backwards, especially when there are no UX considerations like tooltips, the ability hold to drag in the inventory, placehelpers (for objects), etc. A lot of the interface feels like guess work for the player.
I also ran into multiple bugs during my 6.5 hours, some causing me to lose random workers for no reason. Many times the worker count would erroneously be displayed in the negatives which caused red text to run all over the screen.
Maybe at $10, but at this price I am disappointed in where this stands and can't recommend as a purchase.

Myst was one of those games that really took the world by surprise.  It's an adventure game in a first person perspective where you click on your screen to turn or move forward.  Unfortunately, the resolution is stuck at a 640x480 detail level, so full screen does not look that pretty by today's standards.  What changed in Myst compared to other games is that you were told absolutely nothing and given no direction whatsoever.  This is all about exploration and figuring out what the world expects of you.  Now, this can make it extremely difficult if you are not able to catch the little clues hidden throughout the world of Myst, or this can make it really feel like an adventure as you search every nook and cranny for the clues needed to pass each puzzle throughout the world of Myst.  There are different islands to go to which offer different environments and a variety of puzzles.  The world itself can feel very lonely at times since the only characters you will see are typically embedded in books where finding pages throughout the world will help reveal more of the story.  However, the story is very short and succinct compared the long list of puzzles that you will go through.  A classic in its time.

Hitman: Blood Money
I remember playing this game a long time ago and having a blast. Revisting it on Steam was very much worth it.
+ Agent 47 now has more choices than ever when taking out a target. This game is awesome, and leaps ahead of its predecessors. Each assassination has many, many different ways to be pursued, a lot more than Contracts, Silent Assassin or Codename 47. Feel like staging an accident at an opera? Head backstage and swap the prop gun for a real one, then blow the chandelier foundations up with explosives, so they drop on your 2nd target. How about taking out a target in FBI witness protection? The target is having a birthday party for his child, so you can incapacitate a clown and walk right through the front doors. Then slip into the sauna where a spare FBI suit is and strangle your target to death with fiber wire. This is just the tip of the iceberg. So much variety it's amazing - which also means HUGE replayability.
+ Graphics are pretty damn good for 2006, they hold up really well for a decade old game.
+ Story is cleverly interwovern between the assassination missions, revealing more of the plot as you progress. I found it to be quite interesting.
+ Stealth is superb in this game. You're going to need disguises, be it a waiter, garbage man, chef, policeman or whatever is applicable for your plan. Certain areas are restriced to those with access, so you're going to need the right disguises or move silently to avoid guard patrols. Hiding bodies is crucial to success, and for the first time in the series these can be concealed in freezers boxes or long, wooden crates.
+ How professionally you perform your hits impacts on your notoriety and how much money you earn. Cash can be spent on body armour and health upgrades or modifications for weapons like silencers, scopes and sights.
~ A lot of Hitman: Blood Money's gameplay revolves around understanding guard patrol patterns, timing and then perfect execution (this is of course if you're trying to achieve the perfect assassination). On the higher difficulties like expert, only 3 saves are permitted each mission and it can actually be quite difficult, until you work out the patterns. This is both good and bad. On one hand, there's too much focus on the previously mentioned mechanics which are time consuming. It can take hours to get the hit just right, with minimal civilian and bodyguard casualties. You'll be reloading endlessly, trying new combinations or methods to find what works best. On the other hand, this is part of the reason the game shines - to be the best assassin you have to perform like the best assassin. You need to think ahead and be on top of your game. It's a double-edged sword.
- Controls are a bit awkward, takes time to get used to. Could have been more polished for sure, but it's just a matter of adaptation.
Overall Score: 9/10
Conclusion: Best Hitman game of the series. It has style, great visuals, smart level design and solid storytelling. Don't miss out on this game, it's only a few dollars on sale.

TL;DR: the game is super fun despite its age. It has a few small issues, but overall I would wholeheartedly recommend it, even to people who are just sort of interested in Star Wars and its lore.
Full version:
Likes:
The game is really fun and pretty, despite its age. The structure of the game also makes for pretty decent replay-value. Customization is a little lacking in my opinion, but it's still more than most other games of this type from its age. Everything is taught to you clearly, but rarely does it feel like your hands are being held.
Dislikes:
The boss fights are honestly stupid. I play somewhat casually, so I usually skip out on super good gear if it looks stupid, but make up for it by turning the difficulty to easy. This isn't a problem for 99% of the game. During boss fights, it's a HUGE problem. Every bossfight is the following: get all of my team to turn on shields, place all my mines, then spam stasis and critical hits, then use 5 healthpacks over the course of the fight (in addition to all members using Heal). Even then, boss fights last anywhere from a minute to five, just to kill 1-3 people. Like I said though, the rest of the game doesn't have this problem, so this is a small complaint.
Hates (huge spoilers):
SERIOUSLY ♥♥♥♥ EVERYTHING ABOUT THE STAR FORGE. Every room is designed to take up as much time as physically possible, as they're all just big long rooms with disorganized waves. You can expect 10-30 people in any given room on the Star Forge. This makes it so you have to kill tons of people before your party can regen any force. Even if all your party has heal, stock up on healthpacks because you will run out of force halfway through a room, even with three Jedi. To top off this trainwreck of a level is the Malak fight. I considered going to my local church to ask forgiveness of whatever diety I angered to deserve such Hell. The Malak fight took me easily 20-30 minutes on the easiest difficulty, and required perhaps 100 or so healthpacks of varrying stregths. You CANNOT have enough adhesive grenades and healthpacks for this fight. Even still, you will get some form of cancer every time he sucks health back from a Jedi captive, despite the fact that it takes 3 minutes of spamming attack and healthpacks and nothing else just to get him there, and he does it maybe 10ish times. In addition to the cluster♥♥♥♥ level design and cancerous Malak fight is the fact that my favorite companion, Bastilla, dies. I don't know if there's a way to save her, but I'm not replaying the game to find out. It still hurts, though.

So... I just played this game for 25 hours in 2 days. It has to be one of the most fun, addicting, and if you get the settings right difficult... (and therefore more addicting) games I have ever played. Must put zombies on day and night at double spawn rates to truly experience this game. Finding the balance between gathering food teching up and building inumerable amounts of arrows for your guards is amazingly satisfying. Finally a game where you build walls in a functional way not just to look cool but because you can actually utilize the functions. Ramparts can let you double up archers if placed right, murder holes can give your guards a way to help defend your doorways, you need stairs to get your guards up on your walls. you have to balance out between your day and night shift guards, you need to be thinking things like who will guard where and at what times? how many guards will I need?
Maximizing efficient use of space is a MUST on the walls, for your farming, for your housing. Managing resources properly will make or break you, with literally thousands of zombies attacking you at all times later on in the game if you accidently run out of firewood or bronze you will be overrun within minutes as your ammunition reserves slowly deplete, almost as if your living that scene in aliens where the auto turrets are counting down rounds, 200 rounds left, 180, 120, 100 ,50 rounds remaining, 30, 20... oh♥♥♥♥♥♥.. Of course  you could always go into siege mode to wait for help from friends or try to wait the hordes out as you gather more ammo... but as a wise man once said "Hey man, I don't wanna rain on your parade, but we're not gonna last seventeen hours! Those things are gonna come in here just like they did before... and they're gonna come in here... and they're gonna come in here AND THEY'RE GONNA GET US!" This game takes the best aspects of minecraft and combines them with the best aspects of city managment games, tower defense games, and even in some ways rts games... Finally the game I have been dreaming about for years has arrived, if we get any kind of pvp or even just some better coop features this game will be among my all time favorites.
There is a constant sense of dread as you watch hundreds of zombies get closer and closer to overwhelming that base you worked for hours to build . Better yet... when you realize they are going to push through, and you scramble to bolster your defenses only to watch them come pouring through the gates and eating everything you worked so hard for which would be depressing you would think... but no it just makes you want to play more. Until you end up like me... playing for 15 hours straight, waking up and playing for 10 more hours before spending another hour writing a review and then most likely 4 more hours thinking up your next base design and strategy.  10/10 my social life is ruined again.

It's a very good game despite the high difficulty and if you love a challange, this is a definate buy.

Mostly I wanted to write this review to support the developers and tell them i'm loving it so far. But this is a review so I suppose i should tell you why.
At the current time of the review the game is in version 0.4.1 and should have a fair bit of content in it to keep you entertained as long as you are good setting your own goals and enjoy either the Warhammer Fantasy setting or a old school navel setting. I mentioned setting your own goals because at the moment the game is like a sandbox, you get slapped into a ship that you get to name and are thrust into a tutorial (which i beleive you can disable in you want to get stuck strait in), but after that there is no main quest line nothing that stands out as something obvious you should do.
Here is what you can do, there are a variety of ports you can go to on the map, at these ports you can repair your ship, hire crew, buy stuff (weapons or trade goods), upgrade your ship or buy a whole new one. You can also talk to a drunk who might tell you intresting things perhaps about ports where you can sell goods for more dosh or maybe where wizards that you might wanna stick on your boat will be. Finally you can get missions, there are generic missions which have no real special name which pop up randomly in ports but also some of them have proper quests there will be some dialoge where you find out whats up, and i have really enjoyed thr 4-5 of these i have come across so far.
Aside from missions you can also so seek out hostile fleets (or make friendly ones hostile) as you can see fleets on your map, you can also find sea monsters to fight and they can be interesting and terrifying.
Currently i feel the game is quite stable i have had one error crash thing and once when i boarded an enemy ship the boarding action didn't end (but dont worry only happened once to me and the developers are working on it/ may have fixed it if i never update this).
The Boarding is solid you can shoot them with your gun or draw a sword and there is basic block, attack and targeting controls its nothing amazing but for me it works really well (don't board/allow Skaven ships to board you or you will suffer the vermintide).\
The grapics aren't amazing but they work well and get the point across, it is early access so i guess they could be improved but i wouldn't be that dissapointed if these where the final graphics of the game.
All in all I don't have anything really negative to say about the game, well not anything that i think will last such as those 1 off bug things i encountered. Currently i'm saving for a new ship (which takes a fair bit of cash) but i'm enjoying earning money weather it be hunting monsters or enemy fleets or even boarding friendly ships to steal there cargo if i'm not that concerned about angering that faction. I heavily encourge you to buy and play this game and if you like it recommend it to more people so that the devs can make the game even more amazing then theya re currently planning.

Basically, there is a reason that this game is among the top 10 best selling PC games of all time.  Myst is a classic, although you probably already knew that.

The older generation had the original Star Wars films, but for me, this game and its sequel are what helped define Star Wars growing up.  Memorable characters, thoughtful dialogues, epic journeys between worlds, and a triumphant ending — this was, at the time, the epitome of role-playing games.  The writing is so good and the environments so diverse that I have memories of a great adventure for every major character and location.
Now, I am under no illusions that KotoR has aged well.  It is pretty rough around the edges.  The interface is clunky, and the graphics are, well, old.  Taris is a somewhat bland starting area.  But once you make it into space, the plot escalates into epic space-opera proportions.  Everyone can be talked to, and there are tons of unique side missions.  Each of your companions reacts differently to the same sitaution, and has a well-developed backstory.  Sometimes their past catches up with them.  Maybe yours will too.
In this era of gaming, does KotoR hold up?  Yes; despite its roughness, it is still a very solid RPG and has it where it counts.
