It's basically
for comics.  The kind you want when you are experienced enough to know what you want to put down, and have redrawn enough references that for your project you don't need many.  Even the ball and line person representation for a human reference is beautifully minimalistic.
, I used to compare this to Clip Studio or MangaLabo.  But honestly, it's not a fair comparison.  The software includes the essentials for that comic that has all the characters you already know because you've sketched them several times.  The  perspective tools and custom panel tools are there too.  If you're working on something you're not familiar with, ArtRage has great reference options after the developer fixed what I told them I couldn't do.  MangaLabo has an amazingly quick geometry 3D planning for rooms.  Clip Studio has many tools to help out anyone who doesn't know what they want to draw and a lot of tools for painting.
At the end of the day, if you know what tools you need and you don't overburden yourself with all the tools you don't, you're making the best decision for your comic.  So be honest with yourself, with your level and your degree of knowledge of scenes and characters.  If you're clueless on the scenes, but know your characters, Mangalabo might be the right tool. If you're a bit clueless on everything or plan to paint a lot, Clip Studio might be the right tool.  If you know your characters and your scenes... you go back and forth between sketching and writing your idea to clearly develop it, simply sketch through, then Comicado might be the right tool.

This is a great, light weight all-around art software ^^
IMPORTANT: IF YOU'VE BEEN ON THE FENCE ABOUT THIS SOFTWARE, PLEASE BY ALL MEANS BUY IT NOW. It's going to dissapear from the steam store as well as the developers website so unless you own it now, you'll never be able to purchase this program again once it's gone. And it's better to buy something even if you only kind-of want it when it could go bye-bye any day now. Even if you never use it, you might as well get it just to own it and not have any regrets.
I've used it for just about everything art and photo related though it's specifically tailored for making comics and webcomics - which is the main reason I wanted to get this program. And kindly enough a dear friend of mine bought it for me as a birthday gift and i've been using it ever since. I use it for just about everything - editing sprites for mods, making finalized character sheets for my webcomic after scanning my artwork into the computer (yes, i'm one of the weirdoes who mainly draws on paper), editing photos i take with my camera, ect. In addition I'm actively working on a webcomic and this software has helped me transfer my art from paper to digital page and because of the pannels and text systems, I don't have to worry about hopping from program to program to get all of that other stuff done.
It's lightweight and runs on practically nothing which is good if you have very little space left on your computer for high-tech softwares that risk making your computer combust into flame.
It's also a cheap art software compared to a lot of art softwares out there. You have your free paint tools and photo editors, but those may not come with a lot of options or may just be 'lite' versions of full softwares. Photoshop can cost up to 600 bucks, OpenCanvas on Steam is normally 50 dollars and Comicado is 30 dollars and has the bonus specialty of being geared toward making comics - so if you're making a webcomic anytime soon then by all means buy this software.
The only downside i can really think of is that it may not have as many brush types those other programs may have. In addition there's a weird issue I've had where I cna't stretch the windows horizontally, only vertically... There's also no option to change how the windows are displayed. The window with all of the available colors for example I can't utilize completely because it's a long bar full of colors by default and there's no way to stretch the window or change how the colors are displayed to take advantage of all my options... but for me that's become very minor, just something I'm used to and that isn't a big hassle anymore. This also applies to importing images you may want to edit. I often find myself having to shrink down my own photos otherwise they won't appear in Comicado... But as i said before, it's just something i've come to deal with... Unless you're dealing with really HUGE images, you don't have anything to worry about.
Some other issues I discovered is that the maximum picture size you can have is 6400x6400 HOWEVER, if you type that into the board set up, the software crashes... I think the biggest image I've gotten away with is 6310x6310. So if you wanna edit super large images, you may be out of luck (hopefully this and the importing issue will be resolved in the dev's successor to Comicado, which you can read about in the forums)
Conclusion: If you need an art software or if you need to get your webcomic off the ground and don't want any trouble then this software is a must-buy. Buy it before it goes away forever.
I give Comicado 5 'plz stay on Steam'(s) out of 5.

First Impression:
Lack of tutorials which many have mentioned. I am not sure why the developer did not promote his tutorial on the front page which gets you started with most of the stuff.

Why you would not buy this software?
1- If you are not good at drawing this will not improve on any of that. Develop your drawing skills first. Even with the pose options you will not be able to draw good if you are not familiar with the anatomy of the drawing.
So if you are buying this software thinking your comics are going to look any better most likely they wont.
2-If you don't like to explore the software yourself stay away from it most of the help you will be scavenging through the discussions. If you are the type of person who posts a thread the minute you get stuck with something - this software is not for you.
3- Everything has its own layer - text , poses, everything - its not photoshop - once you get past the whole everything in its own layer you should be able to move through the whole drawing process relatively faster.
Though this software seems complete I hope the developer listens to the users and fixes several misplaced menu options. Pose creation does not have pose delete or rename - you have to go through the preset manager.
Also the smoothing option is wonky you will have to play around till you find the sweet spot - which might not exactly be what you need.
All said and done - for the discounted price I can recommend it. Its not Manga studio but than for the discounted price its worth it - which I recommend the developer to reduce to that permanently.
I highly recommend checking out the guides posted by the developer - they will answer most of your questions.
The lack of proper pictorial manual is simply unacceptable - seems like the dev is highly dependent on having the user already used and being familiar with other photo / illustrative tools.
Also if you plan to draw with a mouse - please don't buy this software.

Man O' War: Corsair is an Early Access naval sandbox game set in the Warhammer Fantasy universe. The game's campaign mode (currently all there is) sees you take the helm of a Corsair ship as a human captain (there'll be an alternate Chaos campaign somewhere down the line as well as a batlle game-mode) with a human crew. As you sail around the game world, visiting the numerous ports found across the sea, you'll find trade opportunities as well as odd jobs to complete for gold, fame and faction relations.
If you're familiar with Assassin's Creed: Black Flag, you'll feel right at home with Evil Twin's game. Corsair is focused around naval combat and exploration with the odd bit of monster hunting and melee combat thrown into the mix. Right now, naval combat is where the game really shines. The Corsair you begin with is a fairly strong ship, good enough to deal with a large group of smaller ships or a small group/individual larger ships. You'll be firing from either side of the ship, aiming using a large red arrow which displays the arc and distance of your shot and between barrages it shows you progress on reloading the cannons. Different ships have different setups mind you. Some ships have enormous cannons or trebuchets on the front while others are focused on regular cannons on either side of the ship.
When you're in combat, you have a overview display of the ship you're targeting as well as your own ship (the display for your ship is also visible outside of combat). These show what weapons a ship has and where as well as how many crew members and how much cargo is onboard. As you attack each other, the overviews will change to reflect how damaged a section of the ship is. A white X will appear on a section that's been destroyed and sections appear orange if they're on fire.
Depending on how your ship is equipped and how many crew you have compared to your opponent, chances are you'll want to stay at a distance and use your cannons to gradually destroy your opponent's ship. However, if you get close enough to a ship you can board them and take part in the game's recently implement melee combat. When you board the ship, enemy crew members will board the ship and attack you and your crew members. You can use melee weapons, shields and guns bought from the game's ports against the enemies you'll face off against, ranging from Humans to Orks and even Khorne. Melee combat can be quite fun but its clunky, too basic and very buggy in its current state, though it has only recently been implemented. Currently you can do a light or heavy attack as well as block. The animations and controls for mechanics are very rough around the edges as it stands, definitely the weakest part of the game. And as I mentioned this is also the buggiest part of the game. I've had a couple of instances of enemies that were supposed to be there simply not exist, enemies getting stuck on their own ship and the most frequent bug is enemies jumping over and getting stuck between the two ships. With no way to end a boarding event other than defeating the opponents (sometimes this requires killing them all, other times they'll given up and surrender) these bugs can be very frustrating.
Combat isn't just restricted to humanoids though! There are several behemoth creatures scattered across the map, including megalodons and giant narwhal creatures. Combat with these creatures is a lot of fun but fairly basic at the moment. They'll appear a little ways a way from your ship so you can shoot at them before they go under again, this repeats a couple of times until they're close enough to your ship to get out of the water and attack the ship. Defeating them nets you some nice resources to sell at the next port you visit.
Speaking of ports, there are around fifty ports owned by friendly factions (The Empire, Bretonnia etc.) as well as a few hostile ports owned by Orks or Pirates. Every port has a market where you can trade goods, a notice board where you can pick up jobs and a dock where you can repair and refit your ship, hire crew members and buy hand weapons. You can also buy new ships at the docks (though they're very expensive so you'll be focusing on upgrading the Corsair early on rather than saving for a ship). Larger docks have a wider variety of ships to purchase and some upgrades to the ship require that you're at a larger port too. Ports also have a tavern which seem to be for story missions but these haven't been fully implemented yet.
The missions you'll be picking up from the notice board are usually just general quests like an assassination mission to kill a particularly pesky pirate or an escort mission to protect a cargo ship on a run to a nearby port. Some ports also have mini-story missions, usually these are also single objective missions but you have some interaction with the character offering them and they all have a story behind them, often related to the faction controlling the port. Apart from the ship races which I didn't particularly like, I found all of the missions enjoyable and a good way of steering the player through the world, there's also a decent variety of mission types as is but it'd be nice to see more later in development.
It may be rough around the edges and need a lot more work but even in its early stages Corsair is a lot of fun, particularly during the naval combat the game is focused on. For what it offers I would argue that the price is a tad high and I think it may be off-putting to a lot of players so I'd recommend picking this one up at a discount of somewhere in the region of 25% off.

My Opinion - Game is worth 10-15 bucks as is. Has all the pre alpha flaws - mainly lack of polish due to still being in construction; but i haven't been this excited for a game in a while. So much potential. I was convinced to buy it cause of the good reviews and i'm here to add another.
Gameplay -
Phase 1 your an aspiring king looking to start a villiage. You get to explore the map to pick the place where you are quite literaly planting the flag of your future kingdom.
Phase 2 build, protect, research, explore the minerals under your claim, manage the  FVP ratio - Food - Villiager - Protection ratio that is. The more villigers in your town the more appetising it becomes to the zombies so you'll need more protection, which increases your villiagers which increased the amount of food you'll need.  The difficultly of FVP is dependent on how cleaverly you build your castle. Its pretty dope.
Phase 3 Growing your tribe into a village, that into a town, city. Researching different techs. This is were i'm curretly at in the game.
Favorite aspect of the game? The 'evolving' crafting system is why i'm so excited about this game. When your a nobody you have to do all the things yourself and might even have to help plant food, chop trees. As the game pregresses and your villiage gets bigger you can hand the annoying 'craft more nails' to the artesian whom you just unlocked. Long story short your the king. You can micro manage if you want, help the peasants out with there work, cut trees, stand guard with your faithful pals at night. But you can also go back to being a king and do kingly things - like add another defensive tower on the North wing, manage FVP, hire more scientists, eat bread.
Cons?
If the art style of minecraft bothers you, you wont like this
Lack of good resource icons - some you have to simply read to understand what they are (They will probably clean this up later though)
But if you like designing, building and defending the things you just built this game is for you. Its looking to be one of my favorites. a few more addons and tweeks and it could be better than minecraft. Like minecraft it also has coop so thats cool.
I'm hoping they add reasons to leave your fortress in the late game - trade, cure zombieism, explore for unavailabe resources idk

I've played a lot of stealth games, and I've loved a lot of stealth games. Whether it was cleaning up the streets of Hell's Kitchen in Deus Ex, sneaking past Hammerites in Thief, or assassinating tall boys in Dishonored, I'm no stranger to how a stealth game works. Stick to the shadows. Avoid lines of sight. Analyze a room. Clear the sector of all guards and move onto the next.
Imagine my surprise when I played Hitman: Blood Money.
H:BM features a completely fresh and unique look on stealth games in something I just haven't quite seen before. The name of the game is hiding in plain sight--mixing yourself in crowds and seeking out your targets without attention. Player emergence runs wild in a game with absolutely no objective markers, yet an insurmountable amount of options and paths.
Each level is sprawling and huge, with tons of people littering the landscapes. Seriously, this engine is capable of putting a
of people in a room. Each level has dozens of ways to complete it, whether it's you slipping by with a few guards hot on your tail, or you absolutely slaughtering an entire area, or just you walking amongst others while causing "accidents."
Not only is it such a fun romp to go through, but levels offer so much replayability, that you're probably going to come back for seconds, or perhaps even thirds.
Buy it.

So... You want to draw pictures, or more specifically, a comic.
Well, this software is built around this particular use case. It can also do illistrations, but it's not built around that use case quite as much as it is comics.
You have the vitual 'paper' of the page to be drawn. You don't draw directly on this, like in MS paint. You have panels. For an illistration, a panel can be the entire page. When you're making a comic, you'll have more then one, and you can easily resize and move them around  a bit after drawing them. It also allows you to distort the whole panel if you want. There's lots of options there. Inside these panels, you have your standard layers, like in everything that's not MS paint.
It will take mouse input, so you don't need to buy a $100 tablet (or $250 tablet-equipped laptop) but if you have one, that also works. It has drawing guides, like French Curves for us Drafting people, that let you draw smoothly with either method.
Pros:
It's cheap, Buy it once and you're done
Has some tools very useful for it's inteded application.

Guacamelee is a sidescrolling fast-paced-mexican-themed-action-fest where you play as a luchador who must battle to reunite the world of the living and the dead in harmony. The influence of Super Nintendo all-time classics such as Zelda: A Link to the Past and Super Metroid are very obvious in Guacamelee.
The GOOD:
- The graphics are exquisitely beautiful. The bright colors and fun-to-look-at landscapes create a very rich and visually appealing world.
- The action is fast and smooth. You can create some crazy insane combos if you learn how to chain them correctly. It reminded me a lot of Street Fighter where, if you can execute, then you can pull off some very satisfying hurt-filled awesomeness.
- The music is pretty sweet. It is Mexican themed and a lot of fun to listen to. I would find myself humming these tunes randomly without thinking about it. That's when you know it's done well.
The BAD:
- Some of the platforming areas can get really difficult and will require you to have patience and good reaction times. Some people may not enjoy this part as it can get a bit frustrating.
- It is not required, but a controller is recommended for this game. I personally completed the entire thing with a keyboard, so it's definitely not necessary to have a controller if you are comfortabe with a keyboard. Whatever you prefer.
- I can't really think of anything bad about Guacamelee, maybe just a few things to add/improve on. Like maybe making the dojo always open so you can practice combos, little things like that.
As a side note, the boss fights can get pretty difficult. They are are all 100% patterns though and you just need to learn their visual/audio cues and how to react to them. You cannot just try to zerg the bosses, you will die. Have some patience and learn their patterns, react accordingly, and you will take them down in no time!
Overall, Guacamelee is a lot of fun, very pretty, and is definitely a current era title with some influences from classic Nintento. Guacamelee takes about 8-10 hours to complete.

Hey all,
I played all Cossacks games and all Cossacks-like games (like American Conquest). So this is my background.
Cossacks 3 is an iteration on Cossacks 1 more than it is an iteration of Cossacks 2. A true back-to-the roots game that takes what was good, gives it an uplift, and maybe makes some modifications here and there.
This is a PvP or PvAI game. The campaigns aren't all that interesting, or at least, don't interest me all that much. It's in PvP where this game shines and I'll tell you now why.
The factions:
Each nation is unique. Now while some may be only slightly different than others ( almost all nations have pikemen and musketmen) there are some that stand out (ukraine for instance doesn't have pikemen or any melee units in barracks, algeria uses bow-and-arrow instead of gunpowder and a lot more unique stuff). There are varying quirks in the building tree for each nations... for some, the 2nd barracks costs more or less... for instance, as Prussia, you can very easily get a 2nd barracks while for most other nations, you need quite a bit of time to get the resources for a 2nd barracks.
Does this make the game unbalanced? Yes. But so far, I've not detected an unbalance you can't fix by playstyle. There are some nations that clearly have the long-term advantage over others, but htere are other nations whose cheap tech and units make them very good early aggressors.
Not all units are the same either. Upgrades differe. Some nations can upgrade attack and defense to a certain level for, say, pikemen, while others can tkae them up to way higher levels.
These and more are differences that give spice and uniqueness to each nation. Some differences can play a huge role in how you play, others will just be minor specs to take into consideration.
Techs also vary with some nations having been barred from certain techs while others having more.
There are a few types of maps, Land, mediterranian, mountaneous or plains, but at the end of the day you have 2 types of warfare areas
-Land warfare (infantry, cavalry, cannons)
-Sea (ships)
Terrain plays a role. Hills are better for increased range and a well placed defense tower can force the enemy to take the long way around if they want to get at you.
This is a mass-production game. If you played the old Cossacks or played Supreme Commander, you know what i mean. You build massive economy, massive armies, and duke it out. Either in big battles or small skirmishes. You have a way to put infinite numbers of production from your production buildings and I suggest you use it... but be careful, some eat up more gold than others and you may end up no gold when you need it.
Tips:
In MP and SP against very hard and impossible AI -> build WALLS to prevent people from sendings Cossacks to raid your farms and mines.
Make sure you always look at the income of mineral resources. Unlike for food, wood and stone, which shows you the number of people working there, for minerals, you have the total gain per second. So if it shows 8 in gold, that means you get that much gold, rather than how many ppl are working in gold mines.
Keep up in tech. Library techs are the key to having a good robust economy.
Don't prioritize getting to XVIIIth century... most games are over before than.
If you meet a bug, don't get angry, it'll probably be fixed soon. I lost a game because my artillery bugged out and got destroyed after they fired a shot. It got fixed the next day and haven't seen this bug since.
Overall, buy and enjoy this unique game. There really are few like it.

To sum up, if you're into the lightgun genre or you already have the peripheral, then go for it. The shooting feels great, the weapons are diverse (pistol, shotgun, some assault rifles, etc.) and the game itself looks sharp and decent with a variety of levels and situations. Few QTEs sprinkled here and there which are mostly an annoyance. The challenge is there though and the arcade mode is loads of fun when you unlock it. Otherwise, if you're here just for the story mode, you can safely skip without feeling like you've lost anything that special.

Speaking of which, the 8-bit designs used for the various sprites and buildings makes the game seem so simple despite having a good amount of detail. The gameplay istelf is very addicting and I find that the more I fail, the more I want to keep playing to see how far I can get. The random events that occur add to the flow of the game and make sure there aren't many dull moments. The goal of the game is to protect your village from different enemies every winter (cool that concept itself) and the fact that you can research things and improve your buildings and population makes it more complex than a normal survival game.
All in all, "VilleTown" is an unique, old-school looking tower defense game that keeps you playing constantly with real-time changing seasons. Thumbs up, very addicting.

It has a lot of interesting tools, and it has enough going for it to satisfy any comic or manga artist. And worse case scenario if it doesn't suit your needs, there's no reason you can't start each page on this program then add finishing touches with a more advanced one if you have it.

I was a bit unsure if I should buy it or not when I first saw this program. I couldn't find a single review or opinion on the internet or user review in here, but after reading the Community Hub I decided to give it a try, and here what I think about it:
Pros:
- Weight: It's quite a lightweight program, so older computers can run it.
- Perspective tool: It helps a LOT when working on sceneries. You can use up to 3 vanishing points, and it's easy to adjust the angle.
- Pose Tool: I was really curious about it, specially since it's something I always missed in other drawing programs and how it would work with angles and perspective, and it work quite nicely.
- Panels: They may feel a bit odd at first, but they really help a lot. You draw inside them, and then you can position and adjust them in your comic.
- The Developers: Not only they've been helping newbies to the program, giving tips and instructions and making guides on how to use it, they also been listening to the users.
- Price: A good program for a fair price, what not like about it?
Contras:
- The UI: It can be a bit hard to understand on how to use for begginers, but it's not hard once you learn on how to use it (which for me didn't take long, around three to five minutes poking around the program).
- Lack of Guides and Tutorials: It's a fairly new program so, which means it's hard to find tutorials and guides on the internet, but as I said earlier, the developers have been of great help with guides and answering users questions.
- Tablet - It's highly recommended to have a graphic tablet to use the program, and sadly not everyone have or can afford one.
So yeah, I do recommend this program.

Hitman: Blood Money is easily the best game in the series. And can easily be considered one of the greatest stealth games ever devised.
The reasons are numerous. Hitman Blood Money is a radical improvement over all of the previous games in the series. Taking elements that worked well from each of the previous games, and putting them in a single package. Coupled with numerous additions. Hits can now be completed by making the act resemble an accident, which typically is required to achieve a Silent Assassin rating. Additionally, after each hit you can view a newspaper which documents in detail what you did during the mission and even includes an artists rendering if you were seen by a witness.
But that wasn't all. Hitman Blood Money was ahead of it's time in a lot of regards. Much like the previous games you could practice your weapons in 47's hideout. Along with collecting weapons in missions that you could use in other ones. But you could also upgrade your weapons with things like different stocks, magazines and silencers. Normal today but relatively unheard of at the time outside of uber tactical games.
One flaw the previous Hitman games would occasionally have is missions would get a little samey after a while. They'd occasionally blend in together with a similar theme. Almost every mission in Hitman Blood Money is distinct, from an opera house hit to a mission taking place on a mississipi river boat. I remembered every single one, and their uniqueness adds a huge amount to how superior this game feels over the previous entries in the series. It really feels special and like the developers worked extremely hard on every single mission.

Hitman has always been about two basic things; stealth and killing. Truly the series has become iconic since its original release 16 years ago. This game is, in my opinion, the apex of the series, tying the finest of all the games in the series together brilliantly. A swan song perhaps as this was last in the series before IO had been bought, along with this franchise, by SquareEnix.
In this game Agent 47 returns in a series of missions as recounted during an interview and flashbacks between a reporter and the former director for the FBI. The story is actually interesting and builds to a pretty unique conclusion. The missions and settings are well diverse if not seemingly nonsensically strung together. As agent 47 it is up to the player to decide how ton carry out these missions.
If the player chooses to go in guns blazing, there will be witnesses which will more than affect the mission and the score, it will also affect future missions via 'Notoriety'. The more notorious Agent 47 becomes the harder missions may also become as guards and civilians will be more suspicious, making the stealth aspect all the more difficult.
If the player chooses to be stealthy the game really shines. Watching guard patterns and memorizing hiding places is only part of the challenge. Often there are alternative ways into and out of areas, or little secrets to ferret out that might make performing the mission more interesting. Intel may be bought with cash earned on missions that will offer tips or clues as to where items may be stashed for use, or a secret about the target or people in the area that might prove handy. Ultimately these are not necessary as the player has many options to take advantage of. The truly masterful player can earn higher ratings and less notoriety if hits are performed as covertly as possible, or better yet, made to appear as 'accidents'. Disguises are also fun, and a bit silly, but then what could possibly be out of place when a six foot tall, frowning bald man with a bar-code on his head dresses like
?
At the end of each mission the player's performance is evaluated in the form of a newspaper page, which is also loaded with Easter eggs regarding the story and game. Fire a lot of bullets and the story about the assassination will describe the killer as unprofessional, amateurish, even sloppy. Little touches like this really help set the experience apart from other games, lending humor and finesse to the scoring system that, even ten years after the initial release, remains very unique.
There are issues, however. The game is, as mentioned, over ten years old, having been first released in spring 2006. The graphics are very dated, though this does nothing to really hurt the game itself. Other problems are bigger, but still not really too bad. The AI can behave a little oddly, at times I'd seen a civilian simply standing in place like a mannequin with their arms out, then suddenly come to life and begin freaking out. Other times the guards might inexplicably repeat a task and throw off their routine, making the mission a bit harder as the game does not play out as it was intended. It was a curve-ball, but I didn't mind the added challenge of trying to work around something totally unexpected. Some of the animations are aggravatingly overdone, making Agent 47 kind of take his time doing certain things rather needlessly.
This is the kind of thing that can get the player discovered and feels aggravating. Again, not a game breaking issue, but in a game where timing is important I’d like for things to move a little more simply and less like a lengthy ballet. Again, not a game breaker, but still very annoying.
Overall this is a fantastic game with a lot to offer stealth fans, and everything Hitman fans love about the series. Recommended!

Hitman:Blood Money is one of my favourite games in my entire steam library. It's just so damned good. I've personally never played a hitman game before this one, but because of it I'm probably going to buy more Hitman games.
I'm not good at this review thing, but I'll try.
H:BM Is a game where you play a bald clone who's job description is "kills people for money." It doesn't matter the requirements, Agent 47 will do them.
In other words, you are kind of a badass.
Every mission is a new, different experience with new, different people. From sneaking into a wine tasting event to pushing a woman dressed like a devil into a pit of sharks, every level feels different and awesome. The targets you have to kill are all varied, all actual PEOPLE. That being said, that illusion is broken a bit when it comes to the AI, as well as the general look of some of the NPCs. The game has an odd shade to it; the lighting in the game giving a slightly eerie feel to it some times. It also tends to make some NPCs look a bit on the ugly side.  However, that is excusable. It's a game from 2006, and it looks pretty good for that area. That however, is irrelivent. Sometimes, the AI pisses you off because it is all the same, slightly stupid AI. NPCs tend to do dumb things, oft times yelling at you for no reason or just staring at you gormlessly. Everyone stares at you, even while in disguise. The actual annoying part is when NPCs see a dead thing. Like a normal person, they ask: "U k m80?" and then they see the actual death, and go "o snap he ded wat do panic" and run off to get an officer. The problem is, when someone dies, it's buisness as usual a few minutes afterword. But, I suppose common sense vs gameplay mechanics.
Everything else about the game is fantastic. The controls are nice, having three different buttons to  perfom actions and select what you wish to do. Some quirks such as Hitman's inability to strangle or knock people out from the front, his apparent love of jumping over all the things, the fact that some rails do not seem to have the ability to have bodies thrown over them, and the magic that is invisible walls that never seem to stop you except when it makes the least sense. I'm looking at you, one weird fence that I can't throw thing's over. However, these are nitpicks, and the actual game is fantastic. You constantly feel ♥♥♥♥ing awesome when you take down the target, and even when you do play the game like Ground Hog Day and abuse saves, you still feel like you've accomplished something. Every level is an intricate clockwork of amazing level design, and there is always one weakness in the security. and finding those weaknesses or seeing opportunities or even devising your own crazy plan that works in the end (With a couple hitches) is a fantastic feeling.
Plus, Diana is pretty cool.

is an addictive physics based building game, which at its core challenges you to build a machine to overcome a specific goal (level). Contraptions are engineered by putting together preexisting blocks, just like Lego. Using items such as wooden beams, wheels, cannons, spikes and many more, you can create simple but functional designs to lay waste on a battlefield or steer clear of a minefield or even fly to destroy airships. And if your patience, creativity and ingenuity know no bounds, Besiege will still allow you to construct some extremely complicated creations which will amaze all (free build mode) through the steam workshop (google search "Besiege Creations" and get ready to be awed).
+ Very high quality title for an Early Access game
+ Fairly priced for the amount of content in the game currently (with more to come)
+ The build editor is powerful and encourages creativity
+ A level editor was recently added; hopefully it will mature into a complex scenario builder
+ Support for steam workshop with 10's of thousands of user contraptions & skins
+ Multiplayer is great fun, especially when competing against friends
- Campaign levels are on the simplistic side, with just a single objective (task) to clear each
- Allows the usage of steam workshop within the default campaign (stifling your own creativity)
- A handful of workshop contraptions are so powerful that can easily clear any level
- No steam achievements or trade cards (yet?)
TL;DR:
is one of these rare gems of a game that keeps getting better with time. Grab it while it is still so cheap and you will not regret it! Highly recommended (for anyone creative or otherwise)!

- The (controller) controls are perfect, not just with its bindings, but they're responsiveness. They play a massive part in making every brawl not just enjoyable, but satisfying.
The game, although challenging in some parts, never feels unfair, even when you're choking on spinning death blades of doom for the 40th time.  To put it concisely, the game is really bloody fun. If this is all that matters to you stop right here, click buy, and fall into the Mexican wrestling dreamland that is Guacamelee.
- The graphics are not only undoubtedly pretty, but have a truly unique feel about them. The Mexican/Piñata aesthetic really helps the game feel like more than just another indie brawler. Dimension swapping in particular is fantastic. Changes in not just surroundings, but colour palette when swapping really makes the game feel special.

- Just perfect. The way that the same musical themes are used to convey completely different tones in different areas is just superb. The slight musical sharp/flat change between dimensions is an especially nice touch.
- It's fair to say that the majority of brawlers don't rely on writing and plot to get their player through the game. Guacamelee is no exception. The plot itself is forgettable archetypical nonsense and the characters aren't all that memorable. Ordinarily, in a game that concentrates its efforts on game play above everything else, this can be forgiven. What is less forgiveable is the completely unmissable LE MEME HUMOUR plastered all over the world.
There's nothing really wrong with subtle meme humour accompanied with a wink and a nod to understanding players. Guacamelee however had less winking, more hitting you in the head with a meme frying pan whilst screaming TROLOLOLOLOLOLOL. The 'humour' went from quite funny, to groan worthy to honestly, downright embarrassing.
Between the many MANY meme posters, unimaginative move names ('Derp Derp', I mean really) and self referential, pandering 'humour', the game suffered in an area where it's genre would usually have had an easy pass.

I was expecting a fun beat’em all, and that’s exactly what I got.
The gameplay is top notch. As you keep unlocking new powers your possibilities grow and beating enemies comes more naturally.
Combat sequences are fun, even though I found the fights a bit too easy at first. But they get tougher as you approach the end of the game. Then, you unlock the Hard mode. It does get way more tougher.
I wasn’t expecting the platform sequences (bought this on a hunch), but they were pretty fun too. These get more complex and original as you gather new powers, mostly putting your timing to the test.
The power-up system is maybe the down-low of this game. It is not bad per say, just very basic. You unlock new powers when progressing through levels. These give you new movements for combat and platform sequences. You can also buy health and stamina enhancements, but there are no major powers to get there, except maybe one that makes ennemies weaker more quickly. That is it.
There are also a bunch of collectables to gather so can get more health / stamina / cash (that buys health / stamina). This may extend the durability of the game somewhat.
The nice touches are the humour, references, lightheartedness of it all, and what’s best is that you can play with a friend just by plugging in a second controller (only locally though).
If you like platformy beat’em alls, or beat'em-all-y platformers, I definitely recommend this game.

A couple seconds might not sound like much, but it adds up overtime.
Included is a YouTube clip I recorded of this. A note: I was trying to get past this part where you need to jump into an Uppercut into a portal and then walljump a couple more times for almost 15 minutes before I begun recording. Yes. That's an entire hour of me jumping up and down trying to perform a combo move that was as simple as pushing two buttons.
And before all the potential angry comments come flooding in, I KNOW ABOUT MICROSOFT GHOSTING. I HAVE DONE THE TEST AND IT SAYS THAT I AM INDEED PRESSING BOTH KEYS. THAT IS NOT THE PROBLEM HERE

I really like this game.
I'll start out with what I like:
the building mechanics are pretty nice and crisp, and the game plays properly like a sandbox in the sense that you can do as you please. Me and my friend have had loads of fun building mazes to elongate the zombies travel paths and kill chutes so that we can make short work of the ones that make it through.
The colony managment system is pretty fun, and you are forced to use your colonists to do certain tasks that you just aren't capable of doing. It's a nice way to make them relevant. It's also great to see them going about their tasks, and gives you a sense of a lively town as your workers bustle about doing their tasks.
Here's what I think could be improved:
the pathing for the A.I. is very, very limited. They can only travel in a linear direction, and currently don't have the ability to strafe. There's to animation for your guards to draw and shoot their bows. The number of aesthetic blocks is pretty limited also.
The zombies have no variation yet either. They all look the same (except for the tougher guy with the green eyes) and can only go linear directions. This leads to some funny moments where you can force them to chase you even though your on the tile verticle to them. Since none of them have any special abilities, there comes a point where the game becomes very easy when you create a maze for the zombies to move through to get into your base. Where I'm at, hundreds of zombies are forced to funnel through my maze and two guards make short work of them as they get confused on where to go.
TL;DR:
despite its current limitations, This game is still extremely fun in its current state. Ive had a lot of fun getting my colony up and running and defeating the hordes of zombies marching on my doorstep. This is a game that I can wait for future updates on. I would definitely recommend this game.

i would like to say that i came into this game expecting nothing. but as i continued playing i soon realised that this game is hardcore. it has a whole lot of depth to it. the goal of the game is to make baby horses. you level up your horses' stats (yes, this is an rpg) then get them to breed with a horse of the same level to spawn a horse with an increased level. here is a detailed look at the game.
story - 10/10 grandpa found out that some magic crystals affect horses but nobody believed him. journal guys ridiculed him. so he gave some two kids a crystal each.
graphics - 10/10 even the greatest of gaming machines will struggle to run this beast of a game at the "Fantastic" graphics setting. however older computers can still run it, as proved by my limited edition windows 97.
gameplay - 10/10 you make your horse run over some sticks and maybe even a log by pressing the arrow keys at specific times to help increase the horses' stats. sometimes your horse can get infected from jumping over too many sticks, so you have to give it a shot to heal it. you can also send your champion horse on quests such as delivering a letter to a guy in some town, or maybe even pull a cart of sticks. as you go on your quest, you can find ingredients to craft things. the game has a very complex drug crafting system. your horse can find herbs and spices as it completes quests, which you can mix together to create drugs. the drugs have no none effects at the moment, but this is an early beta, so it will be implemented soon. there is also a horseshoe crafting system. your horse can find bars of various metals lying on the ground, which he or she will pick up and store for later use. you can craft differing horseshoes from different metals. i currently have a titanium horseshoe on my front left leg, a silver on my front right, and steel horseshoes on my muscular hind legs.
overall - 11/10 this game is beyond perfect, though not for casuls. i highly recommend this game as a gift for kwanza or veterans day or maybe even easter.

I bought this game on sale back when I played PAYDAY 2 on a friends account with family share. I saw quite a lot of hate for PAYDAY 2 and quite a bit of love for PAYDAY: the Heist, so i thought I would give it a shot. So here's what going to get some people anger... PAYDAY 2 really feels better then the original to me.
PAYDAY: The Heist
Pros
-Cool consept and rather well done. (For the time, this game was a masterpiece back in the day, not so much now.)
-Friendly A.I. is helpful. (A bit to much at some point, it's almost impossible to take police hostage in this game.)
-Would be ok if you have freinds to play with. (Soloing on this game is a choir.)
-Large Maps
Meh
-Difficult. (If feels like "being difficult for the sake of being difficult". At some point the game gets way harder and you have to earn upgrade to make things feel less frustrating.)
-Upgrade "tree" (You have four classes and each one gets upgraded as you "earn money". So you get one upgrade per class per player level. Rather a branch more than a tree.)
-Most of the steam store pictures are developer stagged.(The games animation isn't as complex as shown: third, fourth, and fifth pictures.)
-a couple missions that are not in PAYDAY 2.(like 2)
-No story (Put on your mask, grab your guns and lets go, not bad, but the characters don't really have personallity.)
- High damage weapons.(A couple shots will take down a cop, but thats not much help when you're being swamped)
Cons
-Bad hit boxes. (this really struck me as a problem, you can't make leg shots and sometimes it feels like some shot don't connect.)
-Hostage system. (In this game you have to really hurt cops to get them to surrender to you, if you don't kill them by the third shot or your A.I. team mates don't kill them.)
-Only a few heists. (PAYDAY 2 has way more variety.)
-All heists are loud. (All but half of one, this is odd as some guns have suppresors. PAYDAY 2 has stealth missions, while they may be a bit unrealistic they add a new challange.)
-Community is sparse.(Highly recommend playing with friends, if you have them to play with.)
Personal thoughts
The amount of DLC for PAYDAY 2 seems like the main complaint; which is odd, because you don't have to buy. The DLC for this game is ok, you get some guns two heists and some upgrades you can unlock. PAYDAY 2's DLC does seem small compared to this one, but the devs are trying to keep that game alive and they have to earn money some way or another. There really seems to be a lot of people who think that they should just be given things.
I really do believe that PAYDAY 2 is better, it has its problems sure, but they really improved on the first game. I'm not saying this game is bad, three out of five or so, but other the that there is a better option. Unless you really want to know what this game is like,  just get wait for PAYDAY 2 to go on sale and buy the Game of the Year edition.
TL;DR
Meh, 3/5. PAYDAY 2 is an improvement, wait for GOTY edition to go on sale.

Payday: The Heist is a 2011 FPS developed by Overkill Software, and puts you in the shoes of one of four criminals who, by working together, seek to take down the next 'big score' by robbing banks, extracting prisoners, stealing diamonds and a fair amount of other stuff in between.
The game plays mainly as an FPS with a couple of strategy/defense elements mixed in to the recipe: upon the start of a heist (not all, but most of them) you are given the chance to walk around the map and pick out surveillance cameras, guards, and the like, and to get into the best possible position before everything kicks off.
Once the masks are on, the weapons are drawn and the yells/swear words start flying, the players are guided by their mission organiser, Bain, whom warns them of objective notifications, incoming police assaults, etc.
Naturally, the cops aren't gonna shrug their shoulders and say 'eh, we'll let the interior security deal with it' are they?
So they send in special units in with the waves, that are very hard for one player on their own to take out, Left 4 Dead style: The Taser can stun players, the Cloaker can incapicitate players instantly if they get within melee range, Shields carry riot shields, and (MOTHERF*****G) Bulldozers are walking tanks, deadly at short range and a pain to take down.
While the game shines at its most in multiplayer, solo play is also an option, but at times the AI can be too incompetent: They always defer objectives to the player and can sometimes be a little dumb, running into firefights to try and get you back up if you go down without taking out the immediate threat first.
The graphics are a little bit of a mixed bag as well. When looking around the environments, it's quite stunning, but when viewing models up close... Not so much.
Despite these minor setbacks, Payday is still an awesome co-op game to play with a pal, or two, or three for an afternoon of robbery and assault. While it's sequel may have now beaten it by more than a big margin, the first game is still a great place to start, or if your rig is sadly not powerful enough.
8.5/10.

For full disclousure: I am a friend of the devs.
I've been waiting to see what these guys were making for a long time and I fnd myself pleasantly surprised by this awesome little gem.
Basically, the game is a mix between a resource management and tower defense game.  You go three cycles building up your town, assigning citizens to various roles, and researching new abilities and structures.  During the fourth cycle, enemies will zerg rush your town, attacking every building in their path.  Your warriors and hunters will fight them and your builders will repair any damaged structures.  You can also help out by casting abilities that assist in battle.  After the cycle ends, life resumes for the next cycles until the next winter.
Gameplay is simple, yet engaging.  You must constantly pay attention to what resources you need, who needs jobs, what to research, and deal with occasional events that require the player to make a choice.  This occasionally got a little overwhelming, but once I got into the rythem of the game, I had no problem keeping up.  You just need to remeber to never let anyone be idle.
All in all, this is a neat little game and I'm glad I get to see the hardwork of my friends pay off.

First I'd like to say I don't have the nostalgia for this game since i've only played the older ones within the last few years.
I think the problem I have with this game is the fact the developers said they didn't plan on changing much from the original because they felt the original was near perfect. I honestly wish there was a "sort of" button for recommending becuase its not bad and its not amazing.
Pros:
-Battles can look cool: Massive battles and units falling at the sound of gun fire (don't expect it to look like the screanshots/gameplay videos posted on the store page though)
-Easy to learn: I just jumped in and learned how to play after 1-2 matches.
-Good veriety of factions: England, Sweden, Turkey, Russia, Alergia. good mix.
-Building designs are a beautiful nod to older RTS games: every faction has gorgeous custom buildings
-Massive armies: you can have thousands of units on screen (even with more difficult AI you don't really get to even a thousand.
-Classic RTS replay value with multipler and random maps vs AI
Cons:
-Simple and archaic AI: All AI plays the same, builds pikemen, sends same size armies around the same time, won't help allies, It is pretty much a stalemate when they fight each other. I've played this game for a few hours and was able to easily play against very hard AI without difficulty. On normal, I found that every nation will spam merceneries from other factions.
-Very slow gameplay: It doesn't feel paced like AoE, C&C, and other classics in the genre. Getting to the next age (only available to european factions) takes forever.
-No unit type grouping: You can't just select musketeers and pikemen and expect them to position themselves with melee in the front, so even with small armies you'll have to have multiple groups created by unit type.
-No different game modes really: other games like AoE AoM etc had king of the kill, and other gamemodes that added a lot of replay value. This game won't even position allies beside each other. you might find yourself restarting multiple times to spawn by your ally.
-Outdated mechanics: as mentioned before, I find the biggest fault of this game the developers unwillingness to update and change the game (they said in interviews they just wanted to keep it close to the original because it was perfect). AoE 3 did a much better job at this if your enemy was building tons of calvery, build spearmen etc. this game just feels like you could go with a standard pikemen, musketeers, and cannons to take care of any army. Different nations don't handle that differently. This is what AoE 2 did, in following games they fixed it, each type of culture played very differently. The only real difference here is a few units and the middle eastern factions inability to advance in age.
-Range won't melee even if their sprits have swords or bayonets on their guns UNLESS they're the 18th centry endgame units for europeans. Again i found AoE 3 doin't a much better job of this.
-Some bad sound design; if you play as turkey and click on the town center the noise it makes is like playing a harp with an angry cat, it hurts your ears.
-Advancing in age just unlocks a new barracks, a few new units and some new tech. Why am I building 17th century troops over 18th at this point?
-Attaching drummers to groups won't auto keep them at the back of the army. Attach a drummer to a pikegroup, send them to attack move another army and watch your drummer drum is way into hell as he runs through the enemy line.
I made a lot of AoE 3 references because it is the most similar game in style and setting. As said before, developing a game that doesn't surpass a decade old game in graphics, gameplay, and balance sort of secures this game as being mediocre. Also "Cossacks 3 is a rare combination of war, economy, army developing, building and upgrading that couldn’t be found in any game for the last 15 years." AoE 3 was 11 years ago guys.

The only reservation I have about this game is the $20 price tag they stamped on a game that lacks almost all content, and disagree strongly with the Dev's thinking about bumping that up to $25 mostly because there's very little content, at this point its mostly just proof of concept.
Now to the actual game, I very much enjoy the idea of this game, making a colony in a first person type of "Minecraft" feel and automating all of the jobs in said colony, although at the moment there's only a handful of jobs you can assign your colonists, but they're talking about adding many more. Your colonists themselves have basically no AI with no selfawareness, running into the zombies without a care to do their assigned tasks, although the devs have started adding job priorities so thats a start.
Also at the moment the animations are basically non-existant and there's very little variety to the blocks which makes intricate building a thing of the past. So all in all, you've basically bought a Minecraft with a colony mod. But I have hope for the future of this game.

Cossacks 3 is a solid remaster of the 1st edition in the series, in the sense that it graphically excels and revisits a title that did a lot right with RTS. This is a beautiful remake with a few minor additions thrown in.
What was done right:
- Graphics. Goes without saying, a great looking title.
- Tech trees are massive and interesting.
- Units play nicely, battles are interesting.
- Simplistic and laid-back style of play.
- Battles can be huge - depending on your processing power.
- Follows a great foundation of a game that many liked.
What needs tweaking:
- Walls are not seamless on corners when spawned, a small edit making walls seamless would be nice.
- You can't rotate buildings? Why?
- Buildings can't really be built closely together, each one requires too much space. With walls nearby it would be ideal to have the building mesh with the wall.
- Not many buildings, not many units? Should be more.
- No unit or technology progression in campaign.
- The AI moves erratically and doesn't seem well programmed (at this stage).
- You can't always see spawn selection colours on units due to them sometimes being hidden under models i.e. wheat fields.
- When referring selected units to buildings, sometimes they don't go at the first click, this becomes frustrating after a while. The clickbox needs to be expanded on buildings.
- Gates should be built rather than just spawned in.
- The red cross spawn location markers are sometimes hard to see against some ground textures which blend with the colour of the marker. A simple outline would fix this.
- Performance issues in large engagements for average PCs.
This is a respectable addition to the series, is it worth its current price tag? Not in its current state, it is in dire need of edits and fixes. Give it some time for devs to deliver fixes (they seem responsive to feedback), then consider a RRP purchase.
Still has a ways to go, but the glory is still here

Well, I have Hardly played the game, (on a friend's Reccomendation.) and I See A Great deal of potential in this game. It's an interesting game, if not particularly good at this point, but worth a look nevertheless. there are a couple issues I have with the game, but we will cover those later. first, I want to say that this is a game which, though lacking in polish, seems to be on the road to minor success, perhaps ending up as a "Cult Classic" of sorts, which tends to be a good sign. thankfully, this is not a full release, for if it was, this would be considered an unacceptable and worthless thing, however, being in it's early days as it were, I hold out hope that it will improve. Among my issues is that the controls are terrible, somehow managing to be slippery and stiff at the same time, and the frame of view is way off where it should be, seeming too zoomed in for easy gameplay. the concept is fairly fun, and the execution is decent, but another glaring issue presents itself very quickly. the in-game instructions, and even the PDF, Don't tell you how to do ANYTHING. you almost have to look up a guide online to get anything done, most annoyingly, the things that it doesn't cover are things like HOW to not have seige mode happen every 5 minutes because it doesn't tell you how to connect the banner to the world after telling you that the banner isn't connected to the world. I thoroughly enjoyed Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag, especially combatting against large groups of enemy ships. Man O’ War: Corsair is basically that, minus the assassins, plus the naval action. I will avoid comparing the two from now on, or the whole review would be just that. It is based on the world and story of Warhammer and the Man O’ War tabletop game by Games Workshop.
Your goal is to become the richest and most powerful man sailing on the seven seas by attacking and plundering enemy ships and selling what you gain from them, buying items cheap and selling them where they are more expensive, doing dangerous favours for gold and saving and escorting ally ships. The only thing that is more important than getting rich, is not getting blown to pieces or eaten by a shark.
When you first load up the game, you are brought to what could be a great character creation screen. I say “could be” because the game is currently in Early Access and at this moment in time only allows you to change your character’s gender and name. After deciding whose story you want to create, choosing the difficulty of the game - easy of course, unless you’re hardcore - and picking the name and emblem of your vessel, you are entered into a tutorial phase of sorts. It consists of blowing a few ships up whilst having the controls displayed on your screen, assisting you on the beginning of your journey.
After passing the tutorial, you are forced to sail to a town called Norden and buy some fish. Sounds exciting, right? The game features a nice and functional trading system, where certain villages produce certain goods and allow the purchasing of those goods for a cheap price. The items bought can then be taken to other villages that don’t produce said goods, to be sold for a larger amount of gold, making you profit.
Moving between the ports can be risky, as you can find yourself fighting Orcs that want you dead, especially when there are several ships coming toward you. Some of the frog men's ships are equipped with drills, allowing them to charge at you, reducing your ship’s armour by a hefty chunk, leaving you, like me, a blazing fireball in the middle of the ocean. Taking one or two of the enemy ships out is relatively easy when using the side cannons on your vessel, three or four quite a lot harder, but when there is a group of five or more, you want to get out of there immediately. I made the mistake of attempting to take down five ships, and let’s just say I am glad you can load saves.
You can also choose to board opposing ships, shooting the holy hell out of your enemies and raiding them of their cargo, or you can let them sink and drown horribly, living the rest of their short lives without air. If you choose the latter of the two options, you are a monster. In fact, you are a monster anyway. There is no way of escaping it, you’re attacking Orcs.
Although enemy ships are dangerous, sea monsters are just as bad, if not worse. They can tear your ship apart if you’re not careful and if you don’t fire at them enough, leaving you in a terrible situation if your ship is almost succumbing to the attacks of the angry, ugly ocean-dwellers. They, too, can be deterred or killed, using the power of the side cannons on your ship. Basically, firing aimlessly at them until you feel safe. Oh, and they are absolutely huge and immensely terrifying.
You are also given the ability to change the speed of the game, whether you would like to slow it down to get some epic cinematic shots or speed it up to get to your destination faster. This is a great feature that has been executed very well and comes in handy a lot, so you don’t have to wait twenty minutes to get to a port.
A game featuring ships and wide open spaces requires a large map, which Man O’ War: Corsair has. There are over fifty ports to visit, which is saying something. It doesn’t seem massive when you change the speed of the game to four times as fast (the fastest it allows you to go to,) but when you are fighting and evading enemy ships and sea beasts, it easily takes a while to navigate. While I couldn’t give you an educated guess as to just how big the map actually is due to the fact that I have a short attention span when it comes to measuring and maths, you can trust me when I say it would take a very long time to explore the whole area.
I
have some framerate issues every now and then, which is strange because I can run GTA V on my computer on ultra settings without any problem. My drivers are updated and I have better than the recommended requirements to run the game but it still drops to about 5 FPS occasionally. This compromises my gameplay sometimes and takes from the overall experience, especially when it gives the enemy AI an advantage over me. It could just be my rig, but I am 98% sure it isn’t.
The graphics are great, being a fun sort of realistic and the ships are very detailed, you can tell it would have taken a long time to make them. The music is a mixture of epic and epic and the sound effects are that you would expect from a game of the genre, as well as the captain frequently barking orders and shouting at people to clean the deck, ignoring the fact that you are being shot at by several different ships at the same time.
Despite the game currently being in Early Access and supposedly that for another few months, it is great fun and I believe it has a lot of further potential. Of course there are a few small issues and bugs here and there, as with all Early Access titles, but I can guarantee in a couple of months it will be a game to call complete.

This is an open world naval combat game that takes place in the Old World of the Warhammer Fantasy setting.Players will be able to take command of various ships as they battle,plunder, and trade their way from the ports of the Empire to Araby.
It is based on the Games Workshop tabletop wargame Man O'War.
Pros:
+Good use of the Warhammer Fantasy License.
+Great concept for a naval wargame, it's as unique as the original board game was when it came out.
+The artstyle definitely comes from the best Warhammer Fantasy tradition and it makes the game much more immersive.
+Naval combat is exciting and fun and the tutorial-as-mission is a great way of introducing game concepts without bogging the player down in overly-simplistic step-by-step instructions.
+The ship-to-ship combat operates on similar "fields of fire " as other games in the genre. Broadsides are the most effective method of destruction unless you have a ship with a massive front-mounted weapon.
+Generous with the types of ships, with more to be added.
+Not only will there be high seas combat but also the ability to attack, loot, and raze ports.
Cons
-Lack of melee in the boarding actions, although this is likely to be changed
-The only race you can play in the main campaign is Human and while a Chaos campaign is promised, it does not seem likely that the other races of Warhammer will be added.This is unfortunate because of the sheer breadth of the Warhammer Fantasy Races. Unlike other settings, the non-humans in WHF are very iconic and unique to the genre.
-No word yet on modability for the game, but I think this would be an amazing Steam Workshop-supported title.

Man O’ War: Corsair:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Captain. . . Captain. . .  Starboard! We have a ship coming towards us. Do you recognize the emblem on the Sail? No Captain! How many sailors on the deck? At least thirty, Captain. . . But…  But what sailor? They are all looking green Captain. Green! Give me the spyglass before you tell me frogs are sailing a vessel right at us! ARRG, they are green alright, it’s an Orc ship! Everyone to their battle post, this is going to be a fierce battle!
Man O’War: Corsair is an exploring / adventure/ action combat naval game which takes place on the coastline of the Warhammer world. At the start of the game, you will have to give a name to your Captain and slightly customize your new ship. Then you will be lead into a couple of missions which will teach you the combat phase and what to do when you reach a port. Actually, quite a good tutorial. Then it will be all up to you!
You will be able to visit up to 50 ports in the world. There, you will be able to visit locations. At the tavern, you might find some very interesting information - about treasures, what type of stocks other ports are running low of, and more. At the Market, you can buy and sell stocks for a profit. At the dock, you can purchase weapons for your Captain and your sharpshooter, refit or repair your ship, purchase a new ship and recruit crew members. Don’t forget to check the noticeboard; this is where you select your mission!
At sea, well you might have a nice, peaceful journey from one port to another, or you might engage in fierce battles with pirates. You will have close encounters with mighty and frightening sea creatures, too. You can see on your map where those confrontations are most likely to happen. Naval battles are really fun and I find the mechanism really easy to use. Shooting cannonballs to your foe is simple - all you have to do is move the camera to the left or right of your ship, and by holding the right button on your mouse a red curve arrow will appear. Then move your mouse forwards or backwards to choose the distance, “FIRE” and hopefully you will hit your target. Oh, by the way, they will fire back at you, too! It can become hectic when you are facing more than a couple of ships at once. Try to get as close as you can to a ship if you want to board it. If you decide to do so, your Captain will draw his weapon and you will start to fight on the ship. You will be able to swap characters between the captain and the sharpshooter but make sure to protect the Captain (yourself) very well if you are playing the sharpshooter. If he dies, it is game over!  Eliminate the crew of the opposite ship and you will win the battle. It’s really fun to play! Oh, I nearly forgot; it is most likely that you will acquire the ship’s cargo upon your triumph.
In terms of graphics, they are good. However, I would like to see more detail on the coastline and ports. It is a bit bland. The control works fine and I personally have not encountered any crashes so far.
Man O’ War: Corsair is a very impressive early access game and it shows massive potential. I can’t wait to see more!

Blue Estate is a pretty fun rail shooter game that has a weird storyline being told by a
.
The story does end quite quickly but I still enjoyed it.
You get 2 different weapons each level in the story mode, your stock weapon which is a pistol, and another weapon that is relevant to the level you're playing in one way or another, like a shotgun or an SMG.
I personally only used the pistol as,
, I have better-than-average aim, and with good aim the pistols are much easier to use when you want to consecutively hit headshots while not tanking your bullet hit-rate percentage.
The Story-mode is quite short, about 2 or 3 hours, but the meat of the game,
, is where the real gameplay lies; that's where you will be spending most of your time playing this game, as is with most rail shooters.
Seeing as it is a rail shooter it naturally requires you to have some form or level of
aim to not constantly die, or to get some self-satisfying stats at the end of each level.
Getting close to 100% headshots at the end of a level while also keeping a high bullet hit-rate is quite satisfying.
All-in-all it's a great game for what it is.
It's a rail shooter that is meant to be played most in the Arcade-mode, but even if you get tired quickly of
arcade-modes I think it's still worth it if you just want to complete the 2-3 hour long story mode.

Now let's begin by listing of the good points in this game
- it is pretty straightforward

My negative points on the other hand....
- The character design is a massive joke. Gearbox really outdid themselves
- Your gunplay and abilities have no real impact. Many other have the same copy-paste ability across the board (circular damage AoE, frontal cleaves, backdrops, etc.)

- The character voice lines makes me question who the target audience for this game is.

This palette is for some reason rapidly changing when certain shields are activated or debuffs are in place. Expact Violet, Green and Black unity on the screen that will give you no indication if this is a friendly or an enemy creep.
- The netcode of this game is bad. Melee attacks need ~.5 seconds to register. Multiple people reported this problem as well. I am not an isolated case.
- By the time you download the 44gb(!) of the free version, this game is probably dead again.
The rumours are true. It's not some "right wing website" trying to tell you that this is a masterpiece getting bashed by an evil internet agenda. "This is just another typical Minecraft ripoff."
Well, not really. This game actually has depth to it beyond the creative freedom it offers to those who like to build. As opposed to wandering and finding a place to build a house, this game encourages sticking to your first chosen location and producing a large colony, which then undergoes survival at the arrival of monsters every night.
Cons thus far:
- Fairly stagnant, especially if you're playing alone.
- Not enough variety in blocks to build with.
- Landscape is somewhat boring.
Pros:
- Strangely fun even with limited content.
- Great modding community.
- Devs appear eager to please. They listen and implement new content, creating a better game with every update.
- Though it appears fairly complex, the gameplay mechanics are easy to jump into and understand.
- Overall very enjoyable.
Weird in-between pros and cons:
- Price is $20 right now, and if you like the game and intend to play it, this is a fair price in my opinion.
- Some graphics requirements.
Things I really would like to see in the future:
- Some sort of dye process, allowing players to colour blocks of almost all types, so they can build with a chosen material AND colour, as opposed to being limited to just one.
- Landscape improvements. I would love to see some ruins of former colonies, possibly with colonists that can be recruited for a fraction of the food cost. Also things like rivers, deep forests, maybe some deserts or snow biomes, and maybe even something of a hostile biome, with fog and scarce resources.
- Weather! Minecraft itself has sun and rain, that's it. Boring! I would be amazed to see varying intensities of rain and snow, and maybe even fog! It gets me into the game so much more. These weather effects might change gameplay slightly, with rain causing crops to grow faster, and snow causing them to grow slower. On top of this, maybe seasons in the far future, with seasonal crops.
- More food options. Last I've played there have been berries and wheat, which is fine as far as gameplay goes, but I would like to see more recipes, such as soup or cookies. Maybe livestock too. This to me is like the coloured blocks thing, it gives more chance for a player to assume a personality, as opposed to pumping out the same thing like a factory.
- More monsters. In harder versions of the game it would be great to have a mob that can climb blocks, or something similar.
- More animations. Miners standing still at ores kind of puts a damper on my immersion.
Overall, I would reccomend this game to anyone who enjoys building stuff in games, and relaxing while gaming. I may have only about 8 hours on this game currently (all in one world), but I know I will come back again and again as time goes on, because of the type of content the devs are adding. It's fun, relaxing, and honestly satisfying. I usually stand at my tall tower to watch the sun go down over my happy kingdom.
Final comment: Early access but fully playable. Enjoy!

Man O’ War: Corsair it's a video game adaptation of the now discontinued Warhammer theme tabletop game also named Manowar. The objective of the game is to build up a ship and a crew so that you can sail the seas in the search of treasures, pirate other ships and build alliances with factions.
The main gameplay has you sale your ship using the wind to determine your speed and mobility. Combat is done through the use of cannons by simply adjusting your range indicator to match where you want your shot to go. In addition to long rage combat, you can also bord enemy ships and engage combat between the cruises. The crews will fight until one ships surrenders. While you can't take over someone else's ship, you can take whatever cargo they are carrying. If at any time you are killed or your ship is destroyed, it's game over and you must either restart or load the last save to continue.
Man O' War: Corsair does a really good job at balancing realism with fantasy in a way that makes the combat feel realistic but not at the expense of fun.
One of the biggest problems I've had getting into naval combat games in the past is that a lot of them were to focused on creating a realistic ship experience instead of a fun one. Man O’ War: Corsair accomplishes this by making every ship have a unique set of weaponry instead of just having more advanced ships be simply bigger ships of the smaller ships, more advanced ships will be outfitted with crazy weapons such as catapults, drills, rams and absurdly huge four cannons; increasing the depth of gameplay immensely.
The gameplay is more simplistic than any other naval combat games, having to adapt and deal with an unprecedented variety of ships keeps the gameplay from getting stale. A tactic that worked on a standard human Corsair ship may completely backfire on an orc ship. For instance, the first time I've encountered an orc ship, it was much smaller than mine but it was outfitted with a drill and a paddle propulsion system. Naturally I would try to gain distance on the ship but the power propulsion hit faster than I was moving and it ended up doing massive damage just by ramming into me.
The main progression in the game is done through collecting gold by doing quests, trading goods between towns and plundering goods from other ships. After you get enough gold, you'll be able to buy a new ship. And the starting ship is actually one of the most well-rounded ships in the game. You can use this opportunity to buy specialized ships that will allow you to do certain quests more effectively. You may not be able to take out bigger orcs ships using your starter ship and that's where a slower ship with a large cannon in the front may become useful.
Warning: Don't try to hunt the Black Leviathan fish, you will regret it!
- Support for Trading Cards and Steam Cloud.
- The chance to be a pirate and fight orcs at the same time!
- Giant sharks and other monsters of the sea waiting to attack you at any moment.
- Nice tutorial to help you understand the naval genre experience. If you’ve never played a naval game before, it can prove to be a great opportunity to learn.
- Unique concept that will keep you playing for hundreds of hours after the game gets out of early access.
- A lot of fun moments, like when you try to hunt an Black Leviathan and you lure other pirate ships with you near him, then Black Leviathan eats them all, you must try it, it's a fun experience.
- A variety of ships and ways in which you can play.
- More simplistic gameplay than any other naval combat games for those who don't like the realistic genre.
- No support for Achievements.
- The rewards quest system is incredibly unbalanced. There are some quests that can take you a very significant amound of time that often reward you with much lower gold than simple quests.
- Low framerates. It still needs a bit of general optimization to get the framerate more consistent.
- The graphics, while suitable, need quite a bit of work.
- No fast travel option between the ports.
Man O’ War: Corsair it's a delight for those who have spent in the past over a dozens of hours in Assassin's Creed: Pirates on their phones/tablets or Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag on the PC. I'm one of those persons who separated from social life only to play Pirates on his tablet all day long. And this game is no different, even though it's in early access at this time, it has a lot of potential to be an addictive game.
If you're a fan of the Warhammer universe or any naval games, I recommend you to try it. The high price is reasonable for all the content that the developers promised and if that bothers you, wait till it gets out of the early access and watch a few youtube videos to check if the game changed. If you like it, buy it.
I'm giving it an 4 out of 5.
