It does bring a lot of extra heat though so make sure your ship is fully upgraded before converting to piracy. (it's easy to gain faction standing with the pirates by sacking a couple of empire ports)
The weather systems are fairly well done but there seems to be a lot more stormy weather than calm and sometimes that can feel a little oppressive. I'm sure some weather options could be added to compensate for this later so it's a minor really. A battle against an empire fleet in the dead of night with booms of thunder and lightning crackling across the sky certainly add to the atmosphere, although the rolling mist can get in the way of targeting enemy ships.
There are creatures to hunt down too and I've had a couple of jump out my skin moments when surprised by them (looking out for them and not realising they are bearing down to chomp on my ship).
There is a good variety of ships to have to deal with as the game stands and I've found that slightly different tactics work best when dealing with an individual ship type. There is not really a one size fits all.
One thing that the game really needs to implement as soon as possible is different shot types (Chain, grape). It will make immobilising ships a useful tactic when being pursused by an empire fleet. You can still take the sails out as the game stands but alternative shot types that do that job more efficiently would be an excellent addition.
All in all a very enjoyable sea romp with enough there to keep you busy as you wait for the game to be updated. On that note the devs seems quite receptive and have implemented changes based on user feedback. They seem to be quite busy with patching and getting the foundations right before moving on to implement wider ideas. I see that as a positive in development terms.
As it stands in early access I would have no hesitation in recommending the game to others.

Man O' War: Corsair is a 3D Naval Combat game set in the Warhammer Universe. For the most part, you choose the kind of Captain you want to be. You are not forced into joining certain factions or doing preset story missions that are the same every time you play. Visually stunning with fantastic ambient sounds, this game has the huge potential to be one of the best Indie Ages of Piracy style games to hit Steam in quite some time.
Against all odds and with a stroke of luck, you manage to get your small sailing ship to dock for much needed repairs and to take on new crew. From here on out, you live by your own terms. This is a feature I really appreciate in these kinds of games. Each time you replay the game, you can choose to play it differently. Do you want to be an honest merchant trying to earn your keep via buying and selling of trade goods? Sure, you can do that but just watch out for Pirates! Perhaps you dislike the notion of having to spend your hard-earned gold on trade goods that you will earn you only a meager profit. Have you noticed how low in the water some of those Merchant ships are sailing….ripe for the plunder. Maybe you are sick and tired of seeing those Pirates prey on the Merchants and want to clear the seas of as many of those scurvy varmints as you can. You can pretty much be any kind of Captain you want to be… and more! Well those are the standard Age of Piracy tropes out of the way; it’s time to show how this game sets itself apart from the other Age of Piracy naval combat games!
Orcs, wizards and mythological beasts. That’s right, not only do you have to fear pirates (or pirate hunters you scallywag), you have to fear the bloodthirsty Orcs and the devilish beasts which want nothing more than to send your ship to the briny deep. Orc ships look considerably different from those of humans. You will shiver in dread when you see the ships themselves have huge, barbaric and menacing looking claws ready to grab and drag your ship into their firing maw. If you are lucky enough not to encounter Pirates or Orcs as you make your travels between the ports, you might very well find yourself being attacked by a massive shark or sea serpent! In fact, the first time you encounter the shark is during the tutorial, and it is very fearsome. Despite being just a game, it actually instills a bit of trepidation in you as you fight it. It is highly detailed with deadly looking teeth. The last thing to mention in this section is the Wizards, just added recently; they can be a member of your crew or the enemy. Unlike your normal crew armed with mere firearms and melee weapons, wizards can cast spells to aid their colleagues in battle. I have not had much experience with the wizards yet, but they definitely will add a fun new element to the game.
Sailing the high seas is the best part of this game which is a good thing, because the ports are just clickable buttons and text. When sailing, everything, from the ships to the sea and the monsters it hides, look beautiful and highly detailed. The diurnal cycle, changing weather, and ambient fog all make for a realistic and pleasurable sailing experience. The ambient music changes to a much more dynamic track when you are in danger or combat. It really helps pull you into the experience. All in all, despite being a very Early Access title, it almost feels like it is a complete game as it is despite the fact the Developer is currently actively supporting it and adding new content.
A telltale sign that it is Early Access though is the fact that right now there is very little in the way of character customization options. You can choose the name and gender of your Captain and that is about it. There are only two character models in the game currently. You can also name your ship and select the sails it will fly. Lastly there are currently three difficulty settings which affect how much gold you start with and how much of your damage is repaired for free upon docking at a friendly port.
Ports, despite not being entirely that interesting to dock at, can be quite appealing in their own way. There are towers stationed near each of the ports. If you have been hunting too many of their ships, or they just don’t like you for not having green skin, you will come under fire if you attempt to dock. You can then battle it out with the fortifications if you choose to, or you can turn tail and try to sail away before any of their ships engage you.
Despite just being buttons, the ports still feel lively. While at ports you can repair and upgrade your ship, take on new crew and buy them new weapons, trade supplies, listen to gossip, buy clues to the location of hidden treasure or take on mostly randomly generated missions. There are several kinds of missions that can be available. There are the special missions related to just that particular port (such as a zombie outbreak!), and then there are the common ones. The common ones can entail racing another ship to another port, bounty hunting, escorting another ship, or moving cargo around. The common missions can get a bit repetitive, but they are really just there to get you to move between ports and get you a little gold in the process. You are far better off just living free and going where you want when you want and selling what booty you plunder on the way. Chasing treasure maps can be quite fun too. You get a map which is basically just a picture of a landmark and a name. You find the place in the world and search for the treasure, it might be there, it might not be. You might find a completely unrelated wreck to salvage in the process too.
One thing that is lacking from this game that keeps me from saying it is the best Age of Piracy game ever is the fact that despite being able to board enemy ships, all you can do is loot their cargo if you win. You can’t capture their ship and take it as your own. This is quite disappointing. I’d love to be able to make up a fleet of ships that I have captured, or in the very least, just be able to take control of their ship, abandoning my old one. Currently the only way to get a better ship in this game is to earn enough gold to purchase it. This can take quite some time depending on your luck.
One other observation to make before closing is the controls of the game and the AI. When sailing the ship, the controls are very simple and fluid. I have no complaints at all about the controls or the responsiveness of the ship. The ability to switch between and control the special crew members of your ship also works quite well, in fact that is a feature I rather like. The only real complaint I have is the AI itself and I am just being nitpicky here due to the fact the game is so early in the development cycle that this kind of issue is easily forgiven. The AI in the game is quite buggy still. Often during boarding missions, enemy crew or my crew get stuck together or to objects and just run in place rather than entering combat properly. A good example of this took place when I was battling an Orc ship that heavily out gunned and out crewed me due to all the battle damage I had already sustained. I knew I was about to sink so I quickly initiated boarding action in the hopes that I might get extremely lucky. It started and the orcs swarmed over. They slaughtered my crew for the most part… but I didn’t die. There were no orcs left on my deck… puzzled I switched to my sharpshooter in the crow’s nest and quickly spotted the problem. Three orcs were stuck together, another two were glued together with one of my crew floating just above them. The rest were just kind of running in place. I used the sharp shooter to pick of the orcs, killing my floating crewman in the process and won the battle. I gained reputation and got a discount when I repaired my near death ship. Thanks to that bug, I lived to tell the tale!

is an open world naval combat game that takes place in the Old World of the Warhammer universe. Apparently it is inspired by a tabletop game from Games Workshop and I had no idea. Therefore, I’ll retain myself from comparing the two.
Before starting the game, you get to name your captain and choose what kind of background he comes from. You also get to name your ship and choose your own flag. Right after you’re done customizing your ship and your captain, you’ll be thrown into the high seas and right into the middle of the action. From the start you’ll be accompanied with a very competent and welcoming tutorial that will teach you pretty much everything you need to know. Still, I think it is worth mentioning that the tutorial itself is incorporated with story missions, thus creating some kind of cohesion between the teaching of game mechanics and the storytelling of the game itself.
As with most open world naval games, there are plenty of things you can do in ports, you can take on missions in the tavern or learn if there is a shortage of a type of resource in another port so you can sell it there and profit more. You can also buy and sell cargo, which you can also acquire during encounters. The encounters not only reward you with resources such as gold, but they also increase or decrease your fame with the several factions. Gold can be used to purchases new ships or upgrade your current one, as well as hire more crew and crew members like a sharpshooter which you can directly control.
If you’ve played Black Flag you’ll feel right at home in terms of ship combat. Just turn your camera in the direction where you want to shoot and adjust the range at which you want to fire, then just sit back and watch as a glorious barrage of cannonballs is unleashed upon the enemies. Still, there is a lot more to the combat, you have to keep an eye on the way the wind is blowing and watch out for HUGE sea creatures that won’t stop until they can get a hold of your ship. There are also various different ships which use different types of weaponry placements like your standard Man O’ War and a ship with a big mortar cannon in the middle.
If that isn’t enough to convince you, then I should also tell you that you can switch between playable characters on the fly. This plays a huge role during boarding action. If you fancy a more close quarters experience this is the way to go. Still, melee combat is not available in the game which is a big bummer. On the other hand, after having a look at the forums, the developers seem to be taking into account player suggestions so, hopefully, melee will come in the future.
If there is one thing I really love about Man O’ War: Corsair is the voice acting and the music, they are just spot on! Both one and the other convey and provide that feeling and atmosphere that is reminiscent of a Warhammer game.
As for the visuals, the characters, the ships and the ports also have that Warhammer feel to them but I do admit that the world is not really that much detailed. Some textures are somewhat bland, especially rocks, land and structures of the ports. I wouldn’t really mind this but the only thing that bothers me at the moment is that the game runs kind of bad. Even with every graphics option turned down to the minimum in the menu, I rarely get over 40fps with an i5 4460 and a 970. Still, from what I gather, the developers are waiting until everything is in place so they can start working on the optimization, which I really hope they do.
My only complaints about the game at the moment, as I’ve mentioned, are the lack optimization and that faint feeling that the world feels somewhat empty at times.
The naval combat is great and tons of fun and the same goes for the boarding combat. The wind and the variety of different ships provide for some really interesting and challenging engagements but the wind is somewhat of a bummer when you want to go to somewhere that is a bit far off because there is no fast travel, only the option to make time go faster.
In terms of content, the world does sometimes feel somewhat empty but with the latest update this became a lot less evident, so it seems the developers are taking player feedback at heart. This update added over 32 ports which include a whole new region that expanded the world, a new fleet, port attacks and more types of ports. Overall, all I can say is that, most of the main game mechanics are already in place and the core gameplay is a lot of fun.

is a tremedous suprise from the very first moment. We're talking about intensive action shooting with great sense of humor, that I just haven't seen around in video games that much.
A fast paced action On-Rail Shooter, with a huge replayability factor, that will make you focus on targets and laughs at random jokes and twists that no one really expects!
Play as two different characters for twice the fun, while involved in the world of deadly mob wars. Tony Luciano, the son of the Italian mafia boss, who just wants to rescue his girlfriend, and Clarence, who's trying to make an extra buck. All of this narrated by a detective who's just a little over himself from the presence of the glamours stripper Cherry Popz!
Two modes are available; Arcade mode adds extra level challenges where you have to kill the maximum amount of enemies with a specific gun, to unlock a superior gun afterwards, till the top of the chain, the golden AK-47. Being shot adds more enemies to kill, so this mode is perfect to train anyone who's not used to this type of games. Being fast and precise is the most important.
Story mode rates you by points, combos, collectibles, nutshots or headshots, and several other skills. Doing at least 6 of them, grants a 4 star rate.
Unlocking new levels in Story mode, grants news ones in Arcade. You can't unlock weapons and use them, but you pick up some heavy armour along the way, making that some of the best moments in the game. Nothing will make you happier than hitting 15 or 20 headshots in a row with an assault rifle, it's just that good. In fact, headshots in this game are incredibly satisfying. Shooting sprays of bullets into the enemies' bodies will most likely result in a complete fail!
Interactions within the levels by picking items, swift doors or objects, melee enemies, grant you extra scores, and adds a lot of fun. Mini games such as killing enemies by a certain order, or head hunting is a great way to practice and change styles.
Levels are fantastic from a design point and to anyone who appreciates authenticity and good visuals.

I don't like rail shooters. I don't like not being able to control my character. But I still ended up liking this game. It still suffers from the quirks of the genre, like when you're lining up a headshot and the camera moves making you miss, I can't stand that stuff. But the game is generally easy enough that it's not too bad of a problem here. The nice thing this game gives you is even though the screen is full of guys shooting at you, you don't appear to take hits. Instead a yellow circle will appear on one to tell you which enemy is going to hit you next, and when it fills up they shoot and you take damage. As long as you pay attention to the circles and keep on top of it you can get by pretty much unharmed. There are also lots of ammo and health refills throughout the levels.
The game has personality, though I don't really get it. There's always someone talking, either your character or the narrator, and they say bizarre things so it's always interesting. It might try a little too hard to be funny, but it's not obnoxious. You play as two different characters, some Italian mob guy who's a bit dumb and a more methodical assassin. I liked playing as the second a lot more, even though he mostly uses the same set of guns, but for some reason it just felt a lot more satisfying to play as him, maybe because his pistol is silenced. His dialogue with his support team was also a lot better. The main annoyance is each one has some quirk to disrupt gameplay. There's this running joke of the Italian's hair falling in his face obstructing your view, or chihuahuas grabbing on the assassin's legs that force you to look down when you're getting shot at. In the latter I think you're briefly immune, but with the hair you can still take damage. You can flick it back up just by pressing up so it's not so bad, but while I think they were trying to be funny with it it's more irritating than humorous.
There's only 7 levels so it's a pretty short game, even though each one can take 20-30 minutes. I beat the story in 3 hours. You get 4 lives per stage, continuing right where you left off when you die, and I assume when you lose them all you have to restart the entire level. After you beat the story mode you can play the levels again in arcade mode and try for better scores.

Blue Estate is an on-rails shooter a la House of the Dead with a lot of interesting mechanics and fun levels. It's a throwback to arcade games of old and is extremely responsive and satisfying. That said, it's got a bevy of problems that hindered my enjoyment. First of all, the story and humor were pretty bad. While there were a couple jokes that made me smirk, the majority of the jokes were extremely out-of-place and pathetic (the Death Star joke in the final level for instance and the constant intercutting of text during story sections). The story, which is very present in this game, is full of holes and the experience ends with you feeling like you only bought half a game. The final level doesn't even have anything to do with the main plot and is more a side story than anything else, or a bridge to the next portion of a story, leaving you wondering what the point was.
So the story mode is a huge problem despite the fun gameplay. And another problem is that there's not a lot of replayability in my eyes. While the game is fun, I don't know that it's fun enough to warrant multiple playthroughs, especially given the poor humor that interrupts the flow. I think if you want to play an on rails shooter and don't mind there being a lot of bad writing, you'd be fine with this. But as a complete experience it's too short, too stupid, and seemingly incomplete.

I remember seeing my classmates playing this game back when I was in middle-school and promising myself that one day I would have a nice enough computer to play it. And ~15 years later I finally made good on that promise.
Star Wars - KotOR is the closest I've felt to actually being a Jedi (or Sith, depending on how edgy I felt that day). Every time I watch the Episodes I, IV, V, VI, I tend to have some alcohol in me and find myself wishing that I could cast off these chains of reality and live as a Jedi, traversing the Universe with my green lightsaber, interacting with aliens and searching for mysteries to unravel. But until that day comes, KotOR will remain as my Jedi playground.
When I first started a character, everything seemed okay (camera, sounds, difficulty, story-immersion), except for the combat. The combat is turn-based, meaning the game pauses and you queue abilities for your character to carry out, unpause, and watch your character go at it. Initially, I felt this combat system would turn me off too much. However, I pushed through the first hour and came to realize that as more members joined my renegade squad, this type of pause and queue abilities combat system was the only way to sufficiently control multiple characters at once.
Never playing KotOR when it first came out, but playing Mass Effect when it was released, KotOR definitley feels like the spiritual predecessor to ME. You're the captain of a tiny spaceship out to save the galaxy with your ragtag team of misfits. However instead of biotics in ME you have the Force in KotOR (much cooler) and instead of no lightsabers in ME, you have lightsabers in KotOR (again, much cooler).
If you like Star Wars, this is a must-play.

A lot of people say Knights of the Old Republic gets better after Taris. I agree, though from what I've seen people act as though the game becomes amazing after Taris. To that, I disagree. I haven't beaten Knights of the Old Republic, but I have gotten three of the four McGuffins you require to beat the game. This game is only barely a roleplaying game. Sure, it has the trappings of a RPG, with levels, stats, modifiers, and dice rolls, but these things do not a RPG make. Choice and consequence are the two things any good RPG should provide ample amounts of. Knights of the Old Republic does provide them, but they're so binary and limited that it really leaves the game in a worse state than it could and should be.
You are an agent(or a Knight, you could say) of the Republic(the Old one, not the one from the Star Wars films) who is quickly flung onto the Sith-occupied planet, Taris. These Sith aren't like the ones you may be familiar with from the films, at least not most of them. These Sith are a military force, who mostly can't use the Force. There are a few who can, not referred to as Sith but as Dark Jedi. The Sith are led by a Dark Jedi, Darth Malak, comrade of the fallen Dark Lord of the Sith Revan. It's your job to retrace Revan and Malak's steps with your companions(or Knights), uncovering the mysterious circumstances that led to the rise of the Sith and the corruption of Revan and Malak.
Sounds cool, right? Well... It could have been. You're given lots of choices in the game, but the problem with them is that they're either as evil as kicking a puppy because you have feet or as good as only being nice to people because you are a perfect human. The game even encourages this in its mechanics, with some choices(read: most choices) giving you Force points, which push you towards the dark side or light side of the Force. Any Force abilities you might obtain through the game are tied to these points, with it being harder to use abilities that contradict what side you're closer to. And, unless you plan on not doing any of the side content, you will be forced to move towards one boring, nuanceless side. All of your companions have an aligment as well, save one who's pretty much dead neutral and is basically equivalent to R2-D2. Their alignment means nothing for them, but for you it means that they'll annoyingly swat down choices you could have made if those choices don't play to their aligment. Usually, this happens with dark side choices, as only two companions having a dark side alignment. Most choices have no consequences for those they don't immediately effect, which also is a fault.
But, on companions, most of them are uninteresting. They each(save one) have a special quest related to their backstory, which you can embark on once you exhaust their dialogue trees enough and are greeted by a messenger. These quests are usually a little more interesting than normal quests you'd encounter, but ultimately still aren't amazing.
Gameplay is fairly boring. You generally run through empty areas, and maybe run into a purposeless bunch of enemies to fight every now and again. Oh, and remember those Sith from earlier? Most of the planets you go to won't even have a single Sith soldier on them, so take a good look at those shiny suits they wear while you're on Taris. Also, as you attempt to jump to hyperspace to get from one end of the galaxy to the other, you'll be intercepted by Sith ships and forced to play an awkward shooting minigame. It's not particularly difficult, but it's very annoying and out of place. The combat in the rest of the game is fairly uninteresting, you click an action and whoever you're controlling does it, or fails to. There's basically no strategy involved, as using light side Force techniques will make you and your companions nigh untouchable, while dark side ones fry enemies before they really have a chance to attack you.
The graphics are fine. Uninteresting most of the time, but ultimately there's nothing wrong with them aside from that.
The music is unnoticeable at best, and annoying at worst. The soundtrack is nothing like the Star Wars films, so your quest through the galaxy is best accompanied by a playlist opened in the browser and the ingame music turned all the way down.
Ultimately, I would say pass on Knights of the Old Republic unless you really like Star Wars and are unwilling to look up what happened, or to buy the sequel and ask one of your companions in that game.

Cossacks 3 is a return to the origins of the franchise.
I write this, but it really means they copied Cossacks: Back to War pretty much one by one,
which in my opinion isn't a bad thing.
Some graphical and technical improvements here and there and done.
That's Cossacks 3.
From a technical point of view the game is working fine on my machine except for
a small issue with my anti-virus program identifying the game as potential threat.
The game's running smooth and while the old 2D look certainly can't compare to
today's AAA bombast works it also has a somewhat carefree feeling to it.
Cossacks 3 is by no means a realistic game, be it aesthetically or gameplay-wise.
As such I actually like the graphical quality, especially since there's a lot of detail on each unit.
The "pixely" look just fits the image in this case.
In terms of gameplay the game is a mix of Total War's and Age of Empire's combat styles.
You can have units run around freely or put into tight formations, meanwhile the controls
are much more like your regular rts than the slow and more realistic way Total War handles unit movement.
Combat itself is decently paced, certainly more tuned for a faster pace than musket warfare actually played
out in real life.
An particularly interesting part of the game is the abiltiy to capture peasants and some buildings, which enables
the player to build the according units/buildings of that nation.
On the economical side of things there's plenty of ressources to gather from different sources, from fishing to
mining the principles are pretty standart outside of peasants having to enter mines and stay there to gather
exotic minerals with mines being upgradable several times to increase the number of miners possible.
One part I find particularly nice about Cossacks 3 is the large number of research available with pretty much
every research having a useful benefit to the average player.
It goes from simple +10% more damage for gun powder units to ridiculous +90% building construction speed.
From increasing artillery range by 5% to sending out a balloon that reveals the entire map permanently.
Additionally the game is differentiated into two ages.
At the beginning you have access to 17th century technology (Old age musketeers, swordsmen, etc.) and after researching into the 18th century (Requiring buildings and heaps of ressources) you get technologies like the before mentioned balloon or grenadiers.
In the end there's the question whether I would recommend buying Cossacks 3 or not.
Personally I think if you like the rts genre you'll be enjoying your time greatly.
Several fairly long singleplayer campaigns with secondary objectives, including small events that change depending on your decisions, will keep your attention for hours.
After that playing skirmishes with AI/players will bring more hours on the clock.
If there was one major issue I had to pick out it would be the lack of evolving.
Gameplay-wise the game is pretty much Cossacks: Back to War 2.0 without any mentionable changes.
Cossacks 2 was an okay game, lacking a lot of polish while suffering from several weird game mechanic issues.
However it atleast tried to be a new game.
Cossacks 3 doesn't, perhaps in the future it'll have addons that mix things up, but right now it feels like the developers
were too afraid to change the formula up at all.
That said, Cossacks is one of those timeless games that one can play every now and then even in a few years.
It's not large and it's not expensive, but it's fun to play and the AI at higher difficulties will deliver a decent challenge.
Hence I'd give anyone who likes the rts genre the recommendation to buy this game.
Though I'd suggest waiting for a sale should you run on a tight wallet.

"Wouldn't Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag be great if it didn't have anything to do with Assassin's Creed?" I'd oft ponder, sailing away from another shattered, smoking ruin in the oceans of said game. It wasn't until I'd come across Man O' War: Corsair that the question was answered: both of them are welcome additions to the naval combat genre. Although I enjoy AC4: Black Flag more for its refinement (this review is based on Early Access build 0.1.2) and my dislike of the so-called 'Assassin' side of the game makes me appreciate the Jackdaw segments far greater, Man O' War: Corsair matches AC in its execution of being on the high seas; all it needs right now is more of it.
Originally a tabletop game by Games Workshop, Man O' War has been turned into a turn-based tactics title into a real time naval simulator. Still based in the Old World (none of your Age of Sigmar tripe) with familiar factions, Corsair allows you to travel Manaan's realm without the worry of timelines or story, thrusting you into an open world brimming with adventure and possibilities. Or in most cases, have you sail gently in the open world. Upon starting the game one can create their Captain, currently only Empire and Independant captains are available. Naming them, assigning their gender and a name to their ship is all that can really be done in terms of character creation, but the game will allow for customisation later on... if you're willing to get your boots wet.
There isn't much of a goal to Man O' War: Corsair - you can choose to be the Saint of Sartosa, ruining your reputation with friendly ports by indiscriminately attacking any nearby ships, or you can build up strong friendships to get better prices when trading with the Empire, and have them at your side when fighting the Orc and Pirate blight. There
quests you can do in the port towns along the coastlines, such as races, escorts, courier service and assassinations of captains and their vessels, each intending to fill your pockets with coin on a job well done. However the freebooter in you might just wanna have fun, entering the seas aimlessly or heading to mega-map blips indicating gargantuan sea monster locations (currently there's only 2 sea monsters: gigantic narwhals and sharks) or to take out some ships and plunder their booty.
When dealing with ships the combat is divine, even better than my favourite pirate game (the one mentioned so frequently above), as it allows you to damage individual parts of the ship. Want to immobilise an enemy? Burn the sails! Are their bombardments too much? Take out the mortars! Are the enemy getting too close? Destroy the ram.... or drill, in the case of the Orcs! Damaging individual parts makes the game feel more strategic, even if in this build of the game it's not immediately noticeable. Not to mention the cosmetic damage including torn/burning sails, fires bursting out, ships being chipped away at and blown to smithereens makes it all the more engaging! However the boarding could be better; the captain can't aim to save their life, with poor mouse and movement controls making player characters feel like they've got two peglegs and two hooks for hands. Considering how poor their aim is, I wouldn't be at all surprised if they had two eyepatches on. This is a stark contrast to the ship weapons though, with sensitive and precise controls that respond immediately, allowing for fair and fun combat.
Unfortunately the game doesn't look or run too well. It's not terrible which is a pleasant surprise given how the game takes place almost entirely on water. The textures are incredibly poor, as are some of the particle effects, making me often repeat myself saying "this is too early for early access". And that phrase applies to the content too - although many have gotten 40+ hours into the game, I struggled to get much more than four before being fatigued. If you're going into this game, you have to have the mindset of a goal or a desire, be it to plunder or to parade your mighty ship across the ocean.
The way I recommend early access games is thus: if the development of the game were to cease right now, due to any reasons (tragegy in the developers' lives, taking the money but not updating, etc.), could I recommend this game? Currently, it's a hard yes. It's a great game for naval enthusiasts and those who love piracy in video games, and because it's a niche genre it's a safe purchase.
, the Warhammer license alone will not be enough if you're not into sailing games. If you've never played one but want to experiment with the genre, this is a good one to try.... but also try others like Sid Meier's Pirates! and AC4: Black Flag.

Evil Twin Artworks have returned with their long awaited second title in Man O’ War: Corsair. Given how good their debut title, Victory At Sea has proven to be with an ardent fan base who still play the game as avidly as they did when it was first released it is unsurprising that they were determined to remain with a naval themed game. However, instead of having a focus on World War II they have instead paid for a license to launch a game themed on the Warhammer 40k universe and based upon the original now out-of-print table top war game by Games Workshop. At its peak its popularity was among the very highest of all of the table top games with who played it clamoring for a return of the title ever since the franchise made its debut in the video gaming medium.
It was only a matter of time until a developer decided to take the sailing features from Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag and add features from other games that inspired them. In the case of this game I can clearly see the inspiration from the classic Sid Meier’s Pirates! as well as old school adventure and RPG games with the way in which the ports are established. To be perfectly honest, however, what I am seeing a lack of at the moment, beyond the humans and the orcs races, is the Warhammer universe. However, it is early access and there is clearly a lot of work that is needing to be done before the devs can claim that their game is feature complete. It is also very apparent that the developers have placed a heavy focus on getting the game play right before they refocus on the secondary components of the game. Therefore I can say with great confidence that the game play itself is going to be of a very high standard as it is already mostly fluid and enjoyable. Things such as races and
Something that I am fond of is the way in which the game introduces itself to beginners. If you’ve never played a naval game before it can prove to be a very daunting experience. That the developers have introduced a very good tutorial without being too hands on thus allowing for the players to make mistakes and to learn from them is very good. This increases the game’s accessibility to the entire Warhammer 40k fan base who may never have considered playing an at sea game before. It proves to be intelligent game design.
From a technical perspective the graphics, while suitable, need quite a bit of work if they’re going to reach their potential. I like what they devs have done in using the graphics to build a dark and foreboding atmosphere within the game but the combat graphics could do with being made a little sharper. The sound is more than adequate.
A number of early purchasers have already spent tens of hours in the game already. So although some players have reported that there isn’t a sufficient amount of playable content within the game, and there is a lot more to be added, there is clearly more than enough to keep those who find themselves addicted entertained.  Therefore even at the relatively steep asking price the value proposition has already been met for many. I hope that when the game leaves early access that Evil Twin Artworks provide as much support for this game as what they have with Victory at Sea. If they do so then purchasers can look forward to a game that is not only popular at release but one that has sustainability built into it as well.
Man O’ War: Corsair has the potential to be one of the more addictive games to emerge from Steam’s Early Access Program.

Hauntingly lovely coastlines serve as the backdrop for picturesque battles with barbaric and mysterious races of men and beasts. At times grotesque and gory from the bloodshed, and others eerie and silent; the ship’s deck is the scene of all the action in the game. The sea literally rolls with fog. Fans of Warhammer’s Old-World adventures will find it home.
Evil Twin Artworks has created a trail of missions across the Great Western Ocean. Your map shows your progress and helps keep up with open missions, which are logged at the top of your screen. The game is built around a minimalistic concept of sea battles and Warhammer lore. And, it does a good job of staying within that focus. It is definitely a niche product for long-time fans of the tabletop games and collectors.
The sea battle’s mechanics were straightforward and simple to learn. But, boarding was by far the most fun part of the battles. There seemed to be more action there. The ship itself was easy to pilot, and was able to be turned around almost on a dime. There was a fluidity of movement on the waters that was ascetically pleasing. There was night and day progression, and changing weather. The weather didn’t seem to have an effect on the physics of the ship. But, it added to the ambience. The game definitely has atmosphere.
I was most pleased with the art of the game, and collecting the backgrounds. They are artistically done and suitable for profile use. I have never played the Warhammer games myself; neither the tabletop games, nor the video game series. But, it’s hard to miss the popularity of the lore.
The graphics did not run well for me. The game was sluggish and laggy, occasionally freezing. While playing I experienced low framerates. And, many visual glitches and errors presented. It’s clear the game is not quite ready to come out of early access very soon. For example, characters would merge, like when the first mate took the wheel and the captain never moved. Her hat was visible protruding through the front and back of his chest. They were combined on the wheel.

The content will surely be more fleshed out in the final release, but for now, it seems a little overpriced if you are looking at only what the game offers at the moment. The devblogs suggest that much more is in the works. I would love to see what is in the works for the ‘custom battle’ option that is still locked in the menu.
The AI performed randomly, walking back and forth around the ship. You could hear the characters repeating stock phrases when in various menu screens, repeating the same phrases about manning the ship. The sound effects were great. But, the music was limited. And, for now, the game is limited to single player, which just doesn’t seem to fit with the Warhammer concepts.
There were some personalization options. I was able to choose a female captain, which was quite unique I thought. But, the dev plan offers the potential for playing other races. That would be great. I battled a shark. I find myself more into the mythological creatures of the sea than into mythological beasts, like orcs and skaven. Leviathan, the Megalodon, and sea monsters are enough to make the game enjoyable. Rather than a pirate game, this is more a story about adventure and the bravery of exploration of uncharted waters. “Here there be monsters.” The game does that well. I think the sound of the clanging bell in the opening screen lends so much to creating the feel of the medieval world; so gloomy and atmospheric.

Blue Estate is an on-rails shooter that uses Saints Row-esque humor to try and keep the gameplay fresh in a genre with little that can be done in terms of innovation. The game focuses more on gameplay, using story as nothing more than a means to an end, so most of it's rather generic or just straight up boring. You play as a gangster, Tony Luciano, who's relationship with a stripper named Cherry Pops sees him mow through dozens of rival gangsters in his attempts to retrieve her after she's taken. Blue Estate is a rather short game, clocking in at just under three and a half hours on my first playthrough, and I think this works in the games favor since if it had dragged on for much longer the experience would have started to get progressively worse and more repetitive than it already is. There's only six or seven levels and each one seems to have its own story that only loosely connects to everything else, you even switch characters a few levels in, which is an incredibly odd choice for a game that's this short. There isn't much that Blue Estate does to freshen up the on-rails shooter genre, but to its credit it isn't like there really is much to work with.
As aforementioned, Blue Estate isn't particularly focused on story and also makes an odd change in your player character not but two missions into the game. Blue Estate's story is already on the lower quality side and do make such a switch with so little time left in the game is both pointless and also cheapens any building story that was already started. Similar to if you were given eight hours to write a school paper, and with four hours left you decide to throw everything away and start again, it just doesn't make any sense, especially in an already poor story. But the story being of poor quality doesn't really get in the way of gameplay too much since Blue Estate was developed to focus on gameplay without really needing a story. The story is definitely functional and serves its purpose but there's a noticeable difference between something that's good and something that just barely works.
I'm not really going much in depth about Blue Estate's gameplay here because there really isn't a single thing that Blue Estate does any differently than just about every other rail shooter that's out there on the market. Blue Estate seems to attempt to differentiate itself from the rest by using dark humor in the most obnoxious way possible. Some games, like Portal for example, weave humor into gameplay and use it so that the moments where you aren't doing something are still enjoyable. Other games, like Blue Estate for example, wield humor like a great hammer and swing it about with the intent to beat you upside the head until you start laughing. I found myself getting progressively more frustrated as the game went on and they re-used the same jokes and tricks over and over again until they had beaten the humor right out of them, the ones that were actually funny in the first place. The game uses the joke of a chihuahua humping your leg six or seven times throughout, on top of other reused jokes like the first protagonist's hair constantly flopping into his eyes. There's nothing wrong with using humor as the driving force of a game, and there's nothing wrong with dark humor either, but Blue Estate does both horribly and instead of making you laugh, you just end up wanting to go play something else.

This is a really great on rail-shooter, just know it is short (about 2-3 hours / 7 levels). still its really fun if you/re into these.
if your not sure what a on-rail shooter is think of a FPS but you have no control over where you movement.
you start with a pistol and will get either a shotgun or machinegun (not both) during a level. your pistol has infinite ammo but your secondary weapon will not but you can grab ammo during the level. the game is mainly set up like an arcade game so points from headshots, nutshots, fast swip inputs, breaking items, and some head shot mini games are your main goal. the only real power up is a slowmo that will come on automatically, or can come up as a shootable item in story mode but in arcade mode it can be activated as a power up.

So outside of an arcade, rail shooters are extremely hard to find nowadays, on any platform. It seems that fast paced multiplayer shooters (think Counter Strike and Call of Duty) or open world pseudo shooter/tactical games (think Day-Z, Far Cry, etc.) are the way to go for most developers nowadays. So it's sadly pretty rare to find anything that breaks the mold, and when you do, the end result is not always that great.
With that being said, however, Blue Estate The Game was a welcome addition to my steam library and breath of fresh air after playing an endless stream of fast-twitch, zombie horde, open-world shoot 'em ups. It's actually based on a graphic novel of the same name, which I've read and definitely reccomend.
The game is silly and over the top, and buyer beware, it has plenty of dirty adult humor, if that's not your thing. But if it is your thing, my goodness have you come to the right place. Half-naked mermaids floating in glass tanks, corrupt businessmen, drug dealers, rampant crime of every kind imaginable - these are some of the things that are commonplace in this game. Please ignore all of the terrible reviews it recieved on sites like IGN, it seems with their typical PC mindset they missed the purpose of the game entirely, and instead of focusing on the fact that this is at its core a simply
game to play they decided to focus on the games "degrading" humor and its misguided social ideas.
Anyways, enough about that. Back to the game itself. While not overly long, Blue Estate is enough to satisfy anyone looking for a fun, retro feeling arcade on-rails shooter. In a world where most gamers are given massive open worlds to explore with dozens and even hundreds of trivial tasks, I found it fun to sit back and only really have to worry about pointing and aiming in a game for a change. The story in Blue Estate is nonsensical and simple, and I couldn't really tell you all the little details if I tried - but hey, if you're looking for a deep story in a black-humored crime-themed rail shooter, you've definitely come to the wrong place. Suffice it to say, the story is funny enough and entertaining, alternating between two protagonists, a crooked down on his luck hitman and an ex-Navy SEAL.
It's by no means a perfect game, and there could have been more of an effort on the developers part to create better boss battles, among other things. But overall, I found the environments and levels in the game refreshingly fun, and most of all, the gunplay kept me satisfied all the way through.
If you're looking for some kind of epic shooter or extreme realism, then of course look elsewhere, but if you're looking for some old-fashioned arcade rail shooter action on Steam, it's tough to beat this one. It was worth every penny in my book, and if you get it on sale, it's a steal for sure.

It is an on-rails shooter, so bear that in mind that there is only so much you can do within such a limited framework. Still, I must congratulate the developers as I believe they managed to make the most of what this style of game can deliver.
A fairly short game with some replay value but it does manage to give a good 3-5 hours of solid entertainment. That is, if you like the style of the good ol' action movies of the 80s, because Blue Estate has spades of that (most notably the cheesy humour that's so bad it's good).
I think the most genuine endorsement I can give is that I wished it lasted longer.
So the game itself is more than enjoyable if you don't mind the style. Price/value is always subjective but personally I think for 13€ it's alright. If you find it too much for such a short gametime, just wait for a sale as it definitely worths a purchase at a discount.

Lets get to it:
Gameplay 4/5:
As I'm sure you know, its a four player coop fps where you and your teammates perform different heists. Similar to the Left 4 Dead series, when you run out of health you fall down and your teammates have to come help you up before a timer runs out, but unlike L4D theres no rescue closets in this game, instead there are civilians.
Players can shout at civilians to force them to the ground and then tie them up, and after a while the police will trade your teammate for a civilian, the time before the police will trade your buddy depends on how many civilians hes killed, the more killed, the longer of a wait.
Assaults: Assault waves are when waves of police come and assault your team (simple enough, right?), almost every heist will begin with an assault wave. The police won't trade for civilians during an assault waves
Specials: Just like L4D, there are four special units in the game, each one acts uniquely and is best taken care of differently
Heists: Unfortunately there are only nine heists (six without dlc) in the game, so you can finish the game pretty quickly; fortunately each heist plays semi-uniquely. Each heist will probably take somewhere from half an hour to an hour. Theres not even a level editor.
Online: Surprisingly the online community is still very active, enough so that theres still at least five people online at one am
Music 3/5:
Very actiony music, suits the game well
Graphics 3/5:
There graphics you would expect from a fps
Overall 3.5/5:

This is why i loved Supreme commander, it has a little bit for everyone. Are you a more strategic and die hard rts' of ye olde past and love prolonged heavy engages? Supreme Commander and Forged Alliance are for you. If you're looking for more of a arcade faster paced rts? Supreme commander 2 is for you.
Honestly, Supreme Commander 2 on it's own is a great rts, it's just not a very good successor to the forged alliance. Campaign also is meh. Even with that, the game is still fun. The only big gripe i have with it is the technology progression system. In the older games the tech 1 units were still as important as tech 3 units as they made up the backbone of your army. All the SupCom 2 system does is unlocks some new units via Research points and improves upon base units.
It really makes you think by making you think what troop are you going to make if they have planes or rockheads.

Ok, this review is like 7 years to late, but whatever I've been thinking about this game and this series lately so here we go.
This game is not Supreme Commander Forged Alliance.
And That's not a problem. SC:FA is one of the best rts ever created imo. The pure strategical depth and options and paths to victory puts most rts games to shame.
And I would never have gotten into SC:FA if it wasn't for Supreme Commander 2. This game takes the scale and the majesty and epicness of the first two games and makes it an easily accesible game for casuals like me.
It doesn't have the same depth as the prior two, but compared to most modern rts it still trumps or equals them. Each faction has at least a few paths to victory that feel unique and each faction does play differently, especially lategame.
Graphically, it got a little simplified, but it still looks great and you spend most of the game extremely zoomed out anyway so the tanks looking like toys doesn't bothter me.
In conclusion, I recommend this game to anybody who hasn't played Supreme Commander before, because it will change the way you see rts games and challenge the idea of scale of them and make you desire more similiar games, and then you will find SC:FA and because you're already in love with the system you will be able to stomach learning the more demanding technicalities of that game.
I still play this game over the others when I'm looking for a fun relaxed rts session.

Let me start this with three /really/ important points.
-If this game weren't misconstrued as the same kind of game as Overwatch, It would not be as dead as it is, right now.
-If Overwatch did not have the Blizzard brand name on it, this game would not be as dead as it is right now.
-What I'm saying is, that this game is friggen fantastic, but it's been killed off by Brand name bullcrap and Bandwagoners.
Battleborn is a seperate experience from Overwatch and in all honesty, simply /more/ of an experience than Overwatch will be until Blizzard actually does something with the game.
Things you have un this game that are awesome:
-CHARACTERS THAT AREN'T GENERIC STEREOTYPES. LOOKING AT YOU GENJI, AND YOU HANZO, AND ESPECIALLY YOU TWO, REAPER AND McCREE. Each character in Battleborn is wacky and chock full of good old, OG personality and jokes. Some of them are relatable, some of them are fed up with people's bull and some of them just want to watch the world burn. You've got space vampires, psychopathic witches, a penguin in a mech suit etc, etc.
-An actual story mode. It's episodic, so I can't call it a campaign, but there are Bosses, mini bosses, Loot-splosions, witty and sometimes crude exposition, the occasional player-character interaction and good old multiplayer co-op shenanigans like leaving your friend behind to deal with a boss that they're totally unprepared for.
-The Helix Rig, aka A PROGRESSION SYSTEM. Each match you join sets you at level one (level 3 if you're playing capture in PVP) and as you level you can pick one of up to three talents/perks/skillthings that we call 'Mutations'. For those of you unfamiliar with MOBA precepts, this means that the grenade you shot at level 1 can suddenly burst in to napalm or explode and drop smaller grenades that explode again and it's youre choice! Is a skill not to your liking? Do you wish that that boring old leap you have did somerthing else? Say no more! level up and adapt that s**t to fit your needs or personal peference because level system!
-Different Kinds of PVP*. Meltdown is a fairly standard MOBA (Two to three lanes full of minions that you need to do stuff with to beat the enemy) experience but with the Battleborn fun twists. Capture is, well, Capture. Dunno what you expect there. Incursion is one lane, kill the enemies, destroy their crap, build your own crap and kill them some more until you take their base for your own. There are two other  game modes that I myself have not been able to play because of the lack of people online in this game.
What I'm getting at here is that this game is fantastic. It's fun. It's innovative. It's funny! It's cute. Most importantly it's dead as hell and it doesn't deserve to be. So let's fix that. Bring Battleborn back to life. Come enjoy the insanity of the game that should be slamming the market.
In a sense, I'm asking you to help me prove that there is still hope for the gaming community as a whole. This game, all of  the great things it has, all of it's flaws, are gone to waste because of a fascination with big name company and the bandwagon hype they produced.
To risk being seen as an idiot, Let's make gaming great again. Stop settling for less just because everyone else does.

Early Access Watcher Reviews
Game: Man O' War: Corsair
Version: Full Release
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Game Footage:
Original Review is available in discussions page at our group.
The game has come a long way from the meager offerings presented when it entered early access. Numerous factions managed to get added with their own ships types, melee combat was introduced to make boarding attempts easier and Khorne was represented with its' own playable "campaign." It has brought an interesting spin to the original 1993 board game and offered a look into the rarely visited naval skirmishes of the Warhammer universe. Unfortunately, there are still several technical issues and plenty of gameplay features in need of work before this sailing simulation can break away from the label of mediocre.
Currently the game features two game modes: a sandbox (campaign) and the custom battle that allows players to set at most four factions against each other. This custom battle mode is the only means to play any of the factions outside of the humans. Back to the sandbox mode, the player is dropped into the overworld as either a Khorne follower (kill everything that breaths to gain favor for the Chaos god) or the Independent captain. As the Independent, you can maneuver from port to port accepting quests (in turn building reputation points for shop discounts) and participating in trade or pillage cities/ships as a pirate. Both options are entirely player decided as the game lacks any real established campaign and relies more on the motivation of the player similar to something like Mount and Blade. There are some quests (usually one per port) that include a solo story, but this is about as far as the plot of the game goes outside of the game's factions battling each other for hopes of conquest.
As the Independent, it is possible to stay completely neutral with most of the factions, but there are a couple that will always want your skull mounted on their broadside (Skaven, Chaos, Dark Elves). This is where the naval and melee combat come into play. Naval combat functions similarly to the Assassin's Creed 4 system of aiming and firing a barrage of cannonballs until a ship either boards or sinks. If a ship decides to board or the player engages in pillaging towns, the melee combat is activated. The melee system is by far the game's weakest property due to floaty attack animations that boil down to hammering the left mouse button and hoping that moving your character to the left won't make them spin 180 degrees. The use of firearms are permitted during these fights and provide a more accurate method of dealing with enemies. There use to be a lock on function that made it easier to focus on individual units, but it was scrapped along with friendly fire. The naval combat is bland at best, but it is certainly the prefered method over the frustrating melee combat that can be avoided most of the time unless you play Khorne, which requires a lot of it due to the razing function for favor.
Along with giving captains a leveling system, the ship management system saw the addition of crew member positions on the ship, individual leveling, recruitment of mages for additional firepower and ship upgrades. Crew positions grant bonuses to the speed of repairs, reducing provision usage, fighting proficiency during boarding and providing a small chance for crew members to just become injured instead of dying. Most of these bonuses are tied to the type of traits crew members have and can either be unique (identifying treasure in lookout) or learned from leveling (rigging proficiency, cannon proficiency).  Allied ships can also be hired to tag along, making it possible to create a fleet to act as your backup in times of heightened tension. It is one of Man O' War: Corsair's better additions and makes combat easier to overcome, especially when fighting against a Skaven Doombringer or the infuriating Tzeentch Great Winged Terrors.
The open seas are met with plenty of factions vying for control, but not every captain seems to have their AI in check. It is common to see certain ships running around in circles, ramming into a surface or just acting unresponsive even when you decide to pump their hull full of cannonballs. Allies and enemies also have a fixation with the water, falling into the ocean during boarding attacks for random reasons. Some also decide to sit fights out by standing in corners or jumping into walls. Most of these issues are beneficial for the player by reducing difficulty, but what is the fun of shooting fish in a barrel?
On the technical front, the major issue continues to be the frame rate inconsistency. I can understand the fluctuation when the game speed is set to x8 or even x4, but when sailing from one port to another on x1, the rates can plummet from 45 to 10 without warning. Stuttering is also common place when peering out of the spyglass and just looking around in general. The worst offending issue, however, comes with an annoying mouse hitch that causes the camera to get stuck for a couple of seconds before it can be un-jammed with furious mouse wiggling. One final warning comes with the loading screen deciding to quit and forcing a restart of the application. None of these issues are game breaking, but they do make for a frustrating time during confrontations.
I have played Man O' War: Corsair off and on during the development and despite all of my issues I respect the developer for making the most out of their time in early access. The game has come a long way and the added features (whether they work or not) were implemented in a  timely fashions. Unfortunately, I think they would have benefited from another year in the program to construct their planned campaigns, fix the continued optimization problems and add rework textures. They could really use more music as well, which only seems to start playing when the player engages an enemy. Regardless, this final look did not turn out as well as I hoped and I have to issue a warning to anyone interested in purchasing: prepare for issues and don't go in expecting a full campaign. I wish the developers great fortune in their future endeavors and hope one day I might come back to a more complete game.
Pros
- Many factions to fight with their own unique ships
- Naval combat can be enjoyable, if ultimately shallow
- Out of combat time increase up to x8 for quicker sailing
Neutral
- Plot is very thin, relying on motivation of player to carve own story
- Music mainly missing outside of combat
- Difficulty is hit or miss due to AI
Cons
- Frame rate fluctuations and stuttering
- Mouse cursor hookups
- AI problems
- Melee combat
- Loading screen issues
Note: If you decide to purchase, I recommend turning off Water Reflections under video options to help with the frame rate. It doesn't fix the issue, but it helped me in terms of overall numbers.

Very solid game even on first landing onto Early Access.
The sheer size of the game world is staggering and follows in a similar vein to the likes of Mount & Blade except that you traverse the entire world (or oceans in this case), interact with other vessels and visit ports all in a persistent realtime and open world manner.
The atmopshere of the game really puts forward the dark undertidings one would expect from something taking place within the Warhammer fantasy universe, and the various races are already depicted true to their source material.
One personal gripe I have is the impact of fog during combat can make identifying and tracking your targets extremely difficult when you're knees deep in 'pea soup' fog conditions, however this is clearly a intentional design decision to make environmental factors matter and impact combat significantly and whilst it's a slight annoyance personally for some I suspect it will only add more enjoyment to the entire experience of a game that holds no punches.
There's still a lot to be added in terms of additional features which the developers have documented clearly in their published roadmap and the developers come across as very eager to take part in discussing new ideas and features with the community, but already what is present makes for a game that offers the oppurtunity to lose hours to.
Early Access done right.

---What is Man O' War: Corsair and is it worth buying?---
This review is based on the earlierst version of the game and thus some features will be missing from the game. Do not expect a full game!
Man O' War: Corsair is a high seas adventure set in the warhammer universe absed of the man o war tabletop.  A very unique setting wich hasn't been used before. This game isn't a replica of the tabletop at all instead they made a real time adventure game out of it. They are making many of the tabletop ships in nice detail in this game. At first you will think how this will ever work with how weird some ship models look. But it actually works suprisingly good. It looks realistic and you can totally immerse yourself in this game.
As of now, you can only select 1 captain male/female(wich is nice) but many more options will be added through early acces such as starting off as a Bretonnian, Empire or even a Chaos captain. There are different ships you can buy but you will be spending most of your time on the corsair ship. However you can upgrade this ship that is somewhat cheaper than buying a new ship. You can also hire a sharpshooter for your ship that you can control yourself wich is really cool. And for the ones who like it, you can walk around your ship inspecting your crew whenever you want and your 1st mate will take over the helm.
This game also offers a now still small trading system and will be expanded the more ports will come through development. You can make some sirieus money if you make it safely to a port with the gargo. You can also offcourse steal gargo from mechant ships however you will have few save havens left afterwards.
The quests in this game can be devided into 2: 1 being the kind of bigger and more scripted quests wich can quite suprise you sometimes. They are also pretty fun to do. 2 are more optional and less rewarding such as ship races and assassinations and can be found in almost every other port.
Again if you buy this game now expect to recieve just a bit of what to come, for the road map go here:
This game has HUGE potential probarly the most potentional then any other early acces game out now. But the question is: Do you want to support the developers and help them developing the game?
The developers are very kind and have love for their game and listen to everyones suggestions. You will see them replying often to threads in the forums. They want this game to be community based so when you buy the game, you can suggest things yourself and you might see it come in the game!
I recommend this game to people that are warhammer fans and who are just interested in naval games and early acces.
Please do not buy if you expect it to run perfect or be completed the next week. You might have some frame drops but I haven't expierenced a single crash in my playthrough
This is just a buy suggestion, I have no control over your money but if you decide to buy the game I would very much welcome you to the community :). I hope the review was clear enough for you to help your decision.

Soul Reaver + Castle Crashers + Castlevania: SOTN = Guacamelee!
Did I mention this game is amazing?  Well it is.  It's vibrant, detailed, fluid, challenging, everything desireable in a platformer or a brawler.
The thing that really amazed me the most, was that every time I thought, "ok.  Neat trick.  I guess I'll spend the rest of the game doing this.  I can dig that," it turned out there was an even cooler set of moves, and puzzles that required them, right around the corner.  I thought I had seen it all from these kind of games, and boy was I wrong.  Specials affect combat and exploration at the same time in a way that ought to make most competitors jealous, and it keeps throwing them in at a steady pace all the way to the end of the game.   Each move is color coded, which enhances the evolving visual motifs of the game as it progresses, but also emphasises the unique role of every move and the way they chain fluidly together.
I can't think of a single game that continued to impress me so much by redefining the core gameplay, again and again, all the way to the end.  The only real complaint I have about this game is that it's over, and I've seen it all.  Other than that, it's one of the best games I've ever played.

In the realm of tactical RPGs, RE:I is in a unique place. Aesthetically this is not your typical high fantasy game, but instead you pick a team of 3 individuals to 'explore' various locations, meeting various people and creatures you have to defeat. Second, a full game will last around 3 hours depending on difficulty, and there isn't an emphasis on story like you might see in a game like Banner Saga or Jeanne d'Arc. But it does have its own charm; you can choose between 20 different character with their own personalities and back stories, however superfiscial. There are at times even interactions between different combination of characters.
Battles themselves are also unique. Every character has 3 different attacks: Physical, Demoralizing, or 'Convincing' for lack of a better term. Either beat them into submission, talk them into submission, or convince them you are agents of good. It doesn't matter in the end; each of these 'attacks' will drain a standard health bar on a given creature, your goal of which is to reduce to zero. How hitting someone on the head with a shovel, and then telling them how awesome they are 'defeats' them is anyone's guess. But it doesn't really matter. The important part is
there are big consequences to choosing one attack over another, even if they all work on the same health (the game calls it 'spirit') bar. In addition to 3 primary attacks, each character will gain 2 special attacks that run the gammut of your typical RPG abilities: Stun, AoE spells, group heals, debuffs, etc. While there is a rock paper scissors mechanic to battles, it can get deeper when you are offered a greater reward for demoralizing them instead of befriending them. Or maybe the enemy is weak against demoralizing, but none of your characters have strong demoralizing attacks.
While most of your gameplay will be ensuring you survive battles, there are 2 other gameplay areas: The Adventure Map, and the Global Map that exists between adventures. On the Adventure Map, your crew moves from point to point trying to gain as much treasure, knowledge, or status as possible. Each time you move to a node you use up food, and as you are limited in the amount of foood you have, it's impossible to cover everything. Each Adventure Map ends in a boss battle before you are sent to the Global Map to reap your rewards.
The Global Map is where you choose how to spend your spoils. Money buys equipment, knowledge unlocks various buffs, and status recruits 'helpers' that buff your party in various ways. While there are 3 different resources, there doesn't feel like there's enough difference between them.
Renowned Explorers: International Society is good enough. It's probably worth it on sale. It has a lot of charm and interesting enough gameplay for at least a few runs through. With multiple difficulties, Iron Man mode, achievements, and 20 different characters to choose there's a lot of game time to be had; don't let the 3 hour play time mislead you.
It's like X-Com, FTL, and a choose-your-own-adventure book had a baby :3

Secret of the Magic Crystals is a horse breeding simulation game which is based around the gripping tale of a meteor which has crashed into the earth. You, the player, are the grandson/daughter of the man who discovered the magical properties of the crystal inside this meteor; it has a profound effect on horses, eventually turning them from lowly ponies and small colts to majestic unicorns and Pegasus’.
But hold your horses! We’re getting way ahead of ourselves. Before fusing these magical crystals with your horses and quickly creating a nobler beast with which to race and compete, you must first train your horse and force it to compete in various menial events to raise money. With the money raised, you will be allowed to improve your farm, house more horses and fix up the gate (an excellent addition). Whilst this creates variation in the game, it is hard to see where it fits in with the “crashed meteor” plot line, a flaw which many enthusiasts have concerns with.
To level up, you must breed your horse with horses which complement its level and type, and in consequence, the horse will rise in level. However, it is rather tedious training your horse to be certain levels and making sure to consistently breed properly to ensure the correct leveling pattern whilst also concentrating on the economic circumstances of your farm and your social status as a horse racer and breeder among the general horse-enthusiast community. This consistent multitasking sounds extremely demanding, but in reality is reduced to a set of mini-games, most of which are the same rhythm game with a different animation in the background.
The graphics and art style for Secret of the Magic Crystals are of a higher quality than what you would expect from a game like this. Although the training animations and movements of your horses appear to be of the quality of glorified QuickTime events, the lens flare of lanterns and the decent anti-aliasing on the horses tail show a quality of graphical value which I was pleasantly surprised by as a player. However, the art style is where the true beauty lies; with warm, sharp colours and flowing environments, Secret of the Magic Crystals showcases an art style which utilizes a colour palette similar to Team Fortress 2 in a brand new context. I was extremely pleased with this.
The soundtrack of the game is also surprisingly entrancing. With menu music that brings memories of ABBA’s famous Dancing Queen combined with other tracks which feature solo acoustic guitar and ambient percussion, I found myself bobbing my head with the rhythms on various occasions. Furthermore, the sounds of chirping birds, waterfalls and pleasant gusts of wind create variation which is definitely appreciated.
To conclude on Secret of the Magic Crystals, it is a game which will take a little getting used to at first, but for any unicorn breeding enthusiast/horse trainer; it is a game that will perfectly suit your needs. The main issue with Secret of the Magic Crystals is that more time needed to be spent on magic crystals. However, for the price of $4.99USD, the game is extremely impressive.
FINAL SCORE: 8 UNICORNS OUT OF 10.

One of the greatest games I have ever played.
Released in 2003, Knights of the Old Republic set a new standard in narrative storytelling and gameplay. To this day, KOTOR has inspired many great role-playing games such as Mass Effect, The Elder Scrolls, and others to create a story so rich and engaging it could feel authentic, and Bioware and LucasArts have done so.
KOTOR plays out like an actual Star Wars movie, except the fact that you and your companions control most of the action. The story immerses you into the world and provides many awesome moments, whether funny or surprising. Along with that, the music is fantastic, as it blends classic Star Wars music by John Williams and new music from Skyrim composer Jeremy Soule is a unique, nostalgic way. Combine that with new and exciting worlds to explore, and you got yourself a great combination.
The characters are very well developed, with each having their own distinct personality, especially the nonchalantly murderous assassin droid companion HK-47 (who affectionally refers to humans as "meatbags"). What's great about KOTOR is that you can make your own unique character. Whether male or female, good or evil, or brash or cautious, the choices you make and the relationships you have with each character can impact your in-game destiny greatly.
The game, however, has many bugs, which can impact quests to a degree. Some can be fixed, while some can't, but none  can break your game to a severe extent. This game is nearly fourteen years old, so if you encounter some technical issues it may not be your computer, just the game.
I had an absolute blast with this game, and I can guarantee you will have one too. If you love Star Wars, great storytelling, awesome characters, great levels, and overall an awesome game, then this is the game for you.

So I only JUST played this for the first time. It's the one Bioware franchise I just never got around to, mostly because I hated the turn-based gameplay. But lo and behold, I finally played it and....
I'll start with the negative here: this game hasn't aged well and badly needs a remaster. The controls aren't particularly good (in fact, I highly recommend the tablet version if you're gonna play this) and the combat is pure♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't care how hardcore of a tactician or stats-based fan you are, the combat simply isn't enjoyable to sit through. The animations get stale so fast, and unlike, say, Dragon Age Origins or the classic Infinity Engine games, it doesn't feel like there's a lot of input involved here aside from the occasional powercasting. I didn't feel like the ultimate jedi badass when I got to the end of the game in terms of pure gameplay (see Jedi Academy for that).
What's worse is that the game doesn't natively run at 1080p and above. You absolutely need a Widescreen mod for this to be enjoyable. Why they chose to only update KOTOR 2 and not this is beyond me.
Anyway, the real reason you would buy this is because you want to witness, believe it or not, one of the best Star Wars stories you'll ever experience. This is the kind of story that adds some much needed depth to the lore and universe of Star Wars. The characters are almost universally great. Your choices actually *do* matter in the sense that you can mold your character to either a Jedi or Sith alignment, and the variable outcomes for each of your companions is impressive. The best part is that it captures the spirit of Star Wars, with the occasional fan service and references, without feeling like it's rehashing or ripping off previous Star Wars stories (yes, The Force Awakens, I'm looking at you).
I'll admit that the opening levels are painstakingly slow, and it takes a while for the game to get going, but once it does, damn is it good. A lot of awe and adventure in there. Whether you actually buy this or not completely depends on how much you value story. You're not buying it for the gameplay, just don't even think about it. Even if you're not a Star Wars fan, I would still recommend it for the story.
