If you are looking for an up to date pre 1900s period RTS game, great news, THIS IS IT/THE BEST.
I have played the game for 26.4 hours (Both single player campaign and multiplayer 1v1 vs a buddy) since it was released (three days ago, I got it two days ago), and I have 425 hours playtime in Age of Mythology Extended edition and 45 in AOE 2 HD edition. I have never played/heard of a Cossacks game before, I just was lucky enough to bump into a you tube video on it when I was looking for a more recent RTS game set in the medieval period-pre 1900s.
This game is an absolute dream come true. It takes everything that irritated and annoyed me about Age of Empires and similar type games and fixes it/does it better.
1) Ability to auto que all units including villagers (AOM has this too)
2) The pace of the game and troops movements, everything, means there is less focus on how fast someone can click a mouse, leaving you with more brainpower to use actual strategy. Stratagy such as troop formations, baiting and use of decoys to trick enemies while flanking with other troops, stealing villagers, capturing/destroying buildings, etc. etc.
3) Eliminates many of the cheap CHEESE tactics so common place in AOE type games, for example you cant go around spamming military buildings or towers or castles.  My friend tried to beat me with his usual b.s. tower/tc spamming b.s. strat and he LOST ha ha ha ha. Instead, legitimate and crafty tactics and back and forth wars are fought in large scale, and its awesome!
4) Less fighting with your units clicking a thousand times. There is micro, and it is important, but its pleasant and not a click fest.
5) Numerous other cool touches such as troops running and battling through forests (you can even hide in forests and your opponent might not see you!), really awesome looking cannon fire with smoke (best Ive ever seen in any rts tbh), ability for troops/peasants to die of starvation without food, or other maladies to occur if short in other resources, ability to capture enemy buildings/artillery/peasants/mines, officers and marching drummers, and numerous other little touches that make it obvious its in a class above others.
6) More civilizations choices, more unique things about each civilization, more upgrades
7) Even though it sounds complicated, its actually easy to jump into and it has an excellent tutorial to get you up and playing quickly- so even RTS noobs can jump in easliy.
I can't think of anything else I would want added, its basically the perfect game that I would have tried to make myself.
OK, now you're probably worried about the bugs, which tragically has given this game 'mixed' reviews instead of 'very positive'. There was a really worrisome bug in which my mouse would not work at all unless I disabled 'display scaling' (google it if you dont know what that is), fortunately by reading the 'bug thread' I was able to  reduce my display scaling to 100% and I can now play in 4k and mouse works. They are fixing this issue and most others at lightning speed- shockingly they actually are reading the bug thread and are actually fixing the bugs quickly- the other two bugs I had and commented on in the bug thread are already fixed!
The game has never crashed on me, and is totally worth buying right now, as it is. Steam has a refund policy if you are worried about 'bugs'.
Playing against my friends is awesome, I bought extra copies to play on my home LAN (it doesnt have official LAN play, you still have to go through their multiplayer servers, but it works for a local LAN party). As far as playing versus 'the amazing internet dudes who have way too much free time on their hands', the only way that will be enjoyable is if they add some kind of accurate skill rating or ranking system, so people of equal skill levels can play each other. There might already be something like that in place, I did see some number in the multiplayer but I'm not sure if its related to player skill or not.
The single player campaign is HARD even on the easiest difficulty. But its amusing- carefully read the tips that come up during the campaign, such as when they advise you to build up forces but not too long (because the opponents will get too strong). Brute force isn't always the answer, try to think of a tactic to accomplish your aim using the correct unit/s for the task.
In summation, there isn't any other pre 1900s RTS game anywhere near as good as this game is, and I've tried most all of em and described why this one is superior. Reading the sky is falling reviews about bugs..... the play experience is really great, doubt you'll even notice any and if you do, get the steam refund.

AVGN Adventures, as you probably figured looking at the screenshots, is a sidescrolling retro style platformer. What makes this one different from all the other retro style platformers is that it is based entirely around the concept and exploits of the Angry Video Game Nerd.
AVGN decides to play a pretty bad game, as he usually does. However, this game decides to pull him through the TV, sucking him into the world of terrible videogames and bad videogame tropes. The plot is very simple, and only really serves the purpose of giving you the setup to actually play through the adventure.
If you're not really a fan of the AVGN series of videos, then this isn't for you; the whole game is designed to be a playable homage to the Nerd and everything that the fans love about him and what he does. The whole game is jam-packed full of references that most people familiar with the series will get and appreciate, as well as a number of deliberately bad game design choices that make their way in as a result of his frequent complaining of said issues in many of his reviews. It all adds up to a game with themes that are very faithful to the titular hero.
The levels are deliberately very tricky, and oftentimes you'll find you die a lot in each one. Most of the levels often have instances of trial and error. You will most likely die not knowing how to navigate certain obstacles the very first time, or not react quickly enough not knowing what's about to come. To offset this style of difficulty, the player is given a total of 30 lives to work with. This is usually enough to make it from beginning to end of a level. But it's in this feature that lies my main criticism with the game.
The system of 30 lives to make it through any given level is fine, however my main issue with this is that upon completing a level, your remaining number of lives will carry over to the level you play next. This means that unavoidably you will always start subsequent levels with significantly fewer lives to work with, and you might find that you won't even have anywhere close enough to beat a level the first time. Get a Game Over, and you lose your checkpoint progress.
There is no way to reset your lives count except by getting a Game Over, either. I've tried to save, quit and come back into the existing save to see if that would work. Sadly the save does save your current lives count, meaning it was intentionally designed that way. So if you begin with a meager 5 lives, you will either want to just kill them off at the start or use them for practice in the early part of the level, because you're probably not going to get too far with them.
That issue aside, AVGN Adventures is a really fun game for fans with great graphics and awesome 8-bit music. Highly recommened if you love AVGN!

Edit as of 5/1/2016
Those weird lighting issues are gone. This game looks waaaay better now that everything isn't bathed in shadows. Great progress so far.
TL:DR
I'm not going to lie. I've kinda fanboyed out for this game. The sheer potential and the broad focus the game has taken makes it this weird Pirates!/Black Flag/Warhammer hybrid. And yes it's actually as awesome as that sounds. However, being  an early access product, the game is clearly rough around a few edges (most notably lighting and shading) and the animations could use a bit more work.
Gameplay Footage:
How does it play?
Think AC's Black Flag combat system (with more depth) , a quest system, special crew members, boats of downright crazy designs that you can use (one boat is basically just a giant cannon in the front which takes up half the boat in size), and a boatload (ha) of other features like Monster attacks. Did you say monster attacks? Yup. Within the first 15 minutes of playing the game you fight Orkz, and a giant ♥♥♥♥ing shark (megalodon) with more spectacular factions and monsters on the way (griffons/wyverns are planned next). You will sail around the coasts and seas of the Old World from the Warhammer fantasy universe while playing through an entire story. The core mechanics are solid and this seems like an amazing start but there is definitely some work to go before this is a full fledged product.
What is planned in the future?
-A (seriously) ridiculous amount of content.
-Fully customizable character (think MnB: Warband type customization)
-Full story Mode
-More monsters
-20 or so factions (seems to include all races from WFB)
What is wrong now?
-Because of lighting and shading, it's kind of hard to see anything in the game at night. It doesn't help that there is an  unsual amount of fog in the northern areas that you're in. This makes night battles an absolutely painful challenge.
-Animations are a bit wonky in areas and movement can feel jerky or floaty (depends on if you're walking around on the ship or just sailing the ship). Because of this, it's hard to hit targets in boarding actions or in monster attacks. For example, when you fight a Megalodon, you're supposed to shoot it in the eye... I'm not saying it's impossible, but I am saying that after about 6 megalodon attacks, I've only shot one in the eye with my hand cannon once.
What can be improved?
-I'd definitely start with the previously mentioned lighting and shading. Visibility is a major part of the game and not being able to see through fog and the deck of your ship being coated in pure black despite nearby lighting sources makes it hard to truly enjoy the beautifully crafted ships or to be able to combat effectively against enemy ships.
-Animations that seem fluid or have a realistic weight to them could really push this game up to where it needs to be.
-Couple of graphical errors like blackboxes appearing out of nowhere, standard Early Access stuff.
-Boarding actions could be a bit more forgiving, it's a bit difficult to shoot the right enemies when the ship is bucking and crewmen clip through each other... I'm about 60/40 on shooting my teammates and enemies. I'd also like to see a bit better boarding combat system be implemented if at all possible. Maybe some melee fighting from the main character or something.
-Would love to see the voice acting fully implemented. What's currently in the game is not too shabby but there are moments when voices cut out or it seems lines just haven't been fully voiced yet. Can't wait to see that finished.
In summation
This game is well on it's way to being a damn good title. It's already got a very solid foundation and in it's current format, it's a lot of fun to play with enough surprises and challenge to keep you playing for a few dozen hours. Definitely recommend it to Warhammer FB fans or people who are looking for a Fantasy take on the Black Flag/Pirates! formula.

The game plays similarly to a fantasy version of Wing Commander Privateer or Elite.  The controls can be tricky to get at first and the content is still clearly being implemented, but even at these early stages the game is entertaining.  I think as development continues and as player feedback is received, the game will likely continue to be a solid addition to the Warhammer Fantasy universe.  Thus far, highly recommended.
Edit - This is an early access game - unless you're ok with being a part of the development (i.e., if you're ok with not having a finished product right off), you may want to wait a bit before purchase.

Despite being a big fan of turn-based strategy, I resisted buying this game for a while. Little did I know that I was depriving myself of one of the more fun, clever, and unique titles in the genre. The two misconceptions I had initially were...
1) That the game boiled down to rock, paper, scissors. While this mechanic is present (it works similar to how the Fire Emblem weapon triangle does), it's just one of a whole slew of things going on during the game's many encounters.  There are resistances, weaknesses, buffs and debuffs, character and enemy statuses, various rewards for handling encounters in different ways, and on and on. Once you get your footing and start understanding the game's many systems, combat becomes a real delight: a strategic (and sometimes literal) dance that requires balancing a dozen or more factors to reach a desired outcome.
2) That everything seemed a bit simplistic. Don't let the cartoonish look fool you, Renowned Explorers features great depth on both the strategic and tactical layers. I've played for over 30 hours and only just feel like I'm getting a real strong grasp on advanced gameplay and how to maximize my score. While the fact that a single game only lasts maybe 3-4 hours was initially a disappointment, so much of the joy from the game is playing around with different crew combinations and taking on different challenges that I've come to appreciate that games can be completed briskly. This also makes it palatable to play 'Adventure Mode', which features auto-saving and permadeath.
Generally, I'd recommend ignoring the "Discovery Mode" that allows for save-scumming and lower difficulties and just diving in to Adventure Mode on Classic difficulty, the game's recommended setting. While you'll take your lumps early on, the failures will be quick and you'll get to experiment with a variety of teams. Plus, the first time you succeed will really feel like an accomplishment. And I say this as someone who is generally too much of a wimp to play Ironman in games like XCOM and the like.
Overall, I heartily recommend this for anyone who enjoys turn-based strategy!

When was the last time you insulted a sheep into submission? Or complimented a mummy on his wrappings? Or engaged in a battle of charms with a vampire? Unless you’re leading a way more interesting life than the rest of us, or have already played Renowned Explorers, the answer should be never. And that should also be the big reason you ought to play Renowned Explorers, because the battles are nothing like you’ve ever experienced. They’re far more than battles of wits, far more than rock-paper-scissors strategy, and support a game far more charming and entertaining than most adventure jaunts you’ll find.
The Renowned Explorers are a club of intrepid adventurers brought together by a common love of antiquities, danger, and glory. They hold annual competitions to see who can amass the most prestige for themselves, and you just happen to want a piece of that. Assembling a crew with two other like-minded explorers, you embark on a series of five expeditions around the globe to uncover treasures and secrets for the world. If you play your cards right and use every tool at your disposal, you can claim the title of Most Renowned. Otherwise, you’ll leave behind little more than rumors of your last great journey.
At the heart of this title is something of a text adventure. Each of your expeditions sees you leading your crew around to points of interest in whatever region you’ve jaunted off to. At each point you’re given a description of what’s happening, and a load of choices in response. Depending on your decisions you might end up finding a hidden treasure, scoring some gold or research, battling bandits or natives, or pulling yourself out of some other dire predicament. These story snippets are the gears that power everything else in the game, and considering how many systems that covers it can be daunting to figure out how best to approach a simple text prompt.
Your options at each stop are usually presented with a percentage of how likely you are to succeed, which is heavily dependent on your crew, their skills, and other decisions up to that point. Characters are loaded with six different stats, a list of skills across multiple disciplines to learn, and slots for different pieces of equipment. Challenges may call for specific skills, completion of previous encounters, or sometimes just the luck of the draw. Success means scoring tokens which are converted to currencies used to gear up between expeditions, while failure can cost you stat penalties, supplies which are used to traverse the map, or resolve which works as your extra lives in combat. While the text portion of the game generally won’t end a run on its own, it can tee up a defeat in combat with mounting penalties.
Combat isn’t the main focus of the game, but it’s perhaps the most unique element. Encounters play out on familiar hex(ish) maps where you and your foes take turns moving around and using skills. The difference here is that instead of different weapons or attacks, you have three schools of abilities with wildly different effects. Aggressive actions are attacks, devious actions have negative emotional impacts, and friendly actions have positive ones. All of these when used on enemies deplete their spirit, and reducing it to zero defeats the unit. But everyone also has an emotion meter that tracks whether they’re happy or sad, and what specific emotion that puts them in. Furthermore, there’s an overall mood determined by the predominant actions on both sides which can incur huge (like 50% huge) bonuses and penalties depending on how the two teams are feeling.
The interplay between these different approaches affords a wealth of tactical options. Each mood affects attack and speech stats, so a clever player will make their enemy enraged before hitting them to lower their armor, or sadden an enemy that’s about to attack to lower their speech. Items can play a part in this as well, boosting key stats or even giving bonuses when attacking enemies with certain emotions. Really you have enormous control over the approaches your team can take, but to succeed in more difficult areas you have to focus on one or two and stack up your bonuses for it.
The same is true for the resource game, as winning the game requires you to accrue enough renown to beat out the other explorers. Renown is earned from most things you do but there’s a ton of ways to boost your earnings, and ways to focus on a few resources to really pump your results. Gold is used to buy items, status lets you recruit an entourage that provides further bonuses from tokens earned, and research lets you unlock studies that produce all kinds of powerful effects. Choosing how to spend these currencies to build your renown machine is the real meat of the game, and mathematically-minded players may find plenty to chew on here.
With a design this tight there’s not much to critique, aside from seeing the same encounters over and over as you sink more and more time into the game. The variety comes from the different crews you can assemble, and the different choices you make in building them up, but you’ll still end up reading the same passages again and again. It’s an issue the developers seem keenly aware of if the different expansion DLCs are any indication, and there are so many treasures to find and unlock anyway that it shouldn’t be too much of an issue. Wrapped up in such a charming presentation, it’s doubtful you’ll have any bones to pick until at least a dozen or two hours in. The unique strategy and combat may take some getting used to, but once it clicks you’ll have a hard time stopping yourself from launching just one more expedition.

Not saying it's bad, it's actually good but it's certainly not better than PAYDAY 2 nor does it deserve the amount of praising it gets from the fans. Online is still quite playable and I get people joining my games frequently even though there is only like 200 people playing it. Blue Estate is the story of a mafia Don . . .'s good for nothing son who crosses the non-specific Asian mafia trying to rescue his girlfriend/favorite stripper. After killing a Kim Jong Ill expie and being sold out by his father he then flees to Jamaica. How he does that is a little baffling given that last we saw he was knocked out by two Russian gangsters who implied they were going to bury him alive. Meanwhile a former soldier becomes a hitman to save his mothers home and begins killing off the leaders of the Russian mafia, who incidentally own a chain of fried chicken restaurants. And then there's something about a stolen race horse and a plant that makes drugs and a trip to Cuba and then it just kinda ends without any resolution. Adding to the confusion is the fact that the whole adventure is being related to us by way of a private investigator, who's narration is constantly being interrupted by government fact checkers. Maybe if I had read the comic book this was based on it might make something approaching sense but as it stands, I'm completely lost.
The game is a rail shooter, something of a holdover from the heyday of arcades, meaning it puts you on a predetermined path, and while there are occasions where it's possible to jump in and out of cover at will, the game does all the moving for you. If you're worried that a lack of movement controls will make the game feel too static, don't be. The game still manages to be very dynamic, in fact the camera movement can be so sudden that it interferes with your aim. There's a variety of weapons available; In addition to a standard pistol that never runs out of ammo there are shotguns, rifles, and magnums picked up over the course of certain levels that you'll need to find additional ammo for. Pretty much anything that isn't shooting or reloading is done by QTE's, but they are fast, simple, and more or less inoffensive; even if they are pretty repetitive. For all the nonstop craziness going on beating the levels isn't too much of a problem, in fact the whole game can be beaten in less than three hours. There are Boss fights and while they turn the difficulty up a notch, they mostly seem to exist to inject a little more personality into the game. The real challenge in Blue Estate comes from trying to rack up high scores. There's a points system for skill shots and completing mini-challenges such as killing enemies in a certain sequence or scoring a number of quick head shots. While I enjoyed mowing down thugs, I can't say that I really liked it enough to replay it in the hopes of getting higher scores and achievements.
I played on a mouse and keyboard, and while that worked well enough I feel like this suffered from the same problem that most rail shooters do, without the light gun and the overall arcade experience to back it up this comes across as a little lacking given what typical shooters can do these days. The right peripherals probably add a lot to the experience, though. While the irreverent zany humor is funny, it's also one note and overplayed. After about an hour the gangster cliches; the often recycled one liners start to lose their punch. Nonetheless Blue Estate makes for an fun off-the-rails kind of on-rail shooter. It might not be worth full price, but on sale I think it's definately worth picking up.

Secret of the Magic Crystal(s)
Review by Protoss
What is Secret of the Magic Crystal(s)? It is a collection of four minigames with a bit of nonsensical storyline about you having to breed five magical horses. You get magical horses in the fifth generation and for each generation beyond the first you need to raise two horses of the previous generation. Luckily after your stable is fully upgraded, you can buy second generation horses.
This means that, unless I made a mistake, in total you need to fully train 1+2+4+8+16 = 31 horses for your first fifth-generation horse and then 1+2+4+8 = 15 horses for each fifth-generation horse (provided you fully upgraded your stables), for a total of 91 horses.
How do you train horses? Well, you do the same four minigames over and over. Luckily once you got the catch, which is after a few minutes, the minigames are not at all difficult, and you also have to do each one only once per horse. The game just remains repetitive until the end. that you can see after a total of around 17-20 hours of playtime if you force yourself through the repetitive minigames again and again. The whole money management aspect really does not matter much, it seems only tacked on to hide there is no substantial gameplay. Which it fails to do.
Because of its fantasy horse setting the game is seen as a troll game by a certain number of people and therefor often at sales gifted to other people. This trend has taken a somewhat recession after the introduction of the Steam Trade system allowing you to store games in your backpack. Yes, for those newcomers, there was a time where you could only activate a game or reject it, and that was the high time of this game as a troll gift, together with Bad Rats! This also will be the most likely reason why negative reviews will be rated down, unfortunately countering the whole intent of the review system.
- The graphics are nicely done, although not top-notch. They very much fit into the fantasy setting, and I really don't see where to complain other than them looking a bit old (but still good enough).
- The sound also fits nicely, it is not disturbing but also fits into the setting.
- Atmosphere and Story are for all real intents and purposes nonexistant.
My sincere apologies, at the end of this review, go to the developers who after almost three years still do a good job of at least community info and free patching. For example, when achievements stopped working this year (2013), they fixed it. Not liking the game mechanics doesn't mean I don't appreciate that bit of work! In fact, I was surprised to see it fixed when I recently checked the forums, since I simply stopped expecting developers to give anything about their game after a certain period of time which lies between one and two years.
Recommended: No, unless you want the achievements, as they are easily obtainable by grinding

Okay, so first off I loved this game back when it first came out. Still love it in terms of story, depth and all the characters.
But the game hasn't aged well and that showes Why? Because it has no default widescreen options that don't make everything look squashed and add the most annoying borders to the game, plus you can't even use outside applications to force it to widescreen since Steams EXE for the game is encrypted. To get around you you have to manually edit the game's INI file to allow it to use windowed mode, which is just all kinds of kinds of stupid IMO.
So, it it worth playing? IMO, yes. The game is very much a classic for a reason. It's got a compelling narrative, lots of quests to get lost in, a cast of well fleshed out characters and NPCs that you'll grow to love or hate depending on personal tastes and overall it's a testament to why LucasArts was considered the King of Kings back in their day.
So, it it worth $10? If you can get past the fact that you can't do native widescreen resolutions and have to basically play in windowed mode, then very much yes.

As you may be able to tell by my profile picture, i love this game very much. Note that this is coming from someone who played alot of overwatch and to me it's no exaggeration to call battleborn superious over overwatch. True, overwatch had better marketting, more lively voice acting and a bigger team working on it but looking past that, battleborn has much more to offer. First, battleborn has a story mode wich overwatch lacks and has many PVE features for those that either want to avoid pvp gameplay or like me arent very good gamers. The characters dont feel cliche and werent designed to appeal desperately to specific crowds, instead they feel more organic and much more real. The dialogue itself too is very funny and even references to current internet memes correctly wich is a rare thing.
But personally, what makes this game great to me is the leveling for specific characters. Cutting back to a more personal trait (the fact im not a very good player). In other games i oftenly ended up using items ment for defense on attack, and vice versa. But this game allows a player to pick a character designed for defense and upgrade them to become easier to use on attack. Take Galilea for example, obviously with her ability to block out damage and close quarter attack range she is ment for defense and ambushing, but her shield throw that lets one stun enemies can easily be upgraded to aid in an assault, making her offensive when upgraded correctly. While im certainly not denouncing overwatch or denying that battleborn has flaws (the deadly neurotoxin taunt for Attikus is specifically unfunny and immature, even by my standards.) i just find that this game is much more entertaining and friendly than overwatch wich leans heavily to competitive gameplay, wich is something blizzard tends to do.
While it is still up for debate wich one is the 'best' to me this game easily beats overwatch due to a wider variety of characters and gamemodes, cartoon graphics and more casual gameplay.

A very charming rogue-like that melds the push-your-luck gameplay with an original turn based combat system that uses "emotions" as abilities, where moods dictate the flow of the battle. All encompassed under the umbrella of a fantastic exploration theme.
Different party configurations lead to different "story" moments within the expedition and the colorful cast of characters, their personalities and abilities, add to the replay value of the game. No two expeditions are the same. And while they are indeed perilous, the difficulty can be tweaked to your liking:
The Adventure Mode is the recommended way to play the game. Fail an expedition and you are done! The game saves at specific points and when you quit.
There is also a Discovery Mode that pretty much removes the rogue-like aspects. You are able to save whenever you want and are free to retry any failed expeditions and battles lost. This is useful if you just want to learn the stories behind the characters and wish to avoid wasted time if something goes bust. Do note that luck and percentages play a part in the outcomes so be wary! If randomness irks you in videogames, this mode might ease the pain.
In addition, both modes include four difficulty settings that affect turn-based battles and the skill checks of the challenges/trials that you face. They range from Easy to Impossible.
With or without the DLCs (though I recommend both of them), the game encourages multiple runs. Kudos to Abbey Games for constantly adding content patches that enrich this little gem. Highly recommended!

Okay, so first off I loved this game back when it first came out. Still love it in terms of story, depth and all the characters.
But the game hasn't aged well and that showes Why? Because it has no default widescreen options that don't make everything look squashed and add the most annoying borders to the game, plus you can't even use outside applications to force it to widescreen since Steams EXE for the game is encrypted. To get around you you have to manually edit the game's INI file to allow it to use windowed mode, which is just all kinds of kinds of stupid IMO.
So, it it worth playing? IMO, yes. The game is very much a classic for a reason. It's got a compelling narrative, lots of quests to get lost in, a cast of well fleshed out characters and NPCs that you'll grow to love or hate depending on personal tastes and overall it's a testament to why LucasArts was considered the King of Kings back in their day.
So, it it worth $10? If you can get past the fact that you can't do native widescreen resolutions and have to basically play in windowed mode, then very much yes.

I will begin this review with an important note: I knew the twist before playing the game.
Nevertheless, Knights of the Old Republic 1 was a very good game with a solid, albeit cliche and formulaic story, good characters, satisfactory gameplay, and an environment that captures that "Star Wars-y" feeling. The soundtrack is solid, and the game is not too buggy (although I encountered some quicksaving problems here and there that were a minor nuisance.
If you like Star Wars and you have not played this game yet, I implore you to do so, because the hype for this game is well deserved. I would give this game a 7.5 or 8 out of 10. It has its flaws, but it is a solid Star Wars game that deserves to be in the conversation for best Star Wars game of all time.

When working on this game, Bioware had a bunch of ideas that Lucasarts wouldn't allow for to eb put in. Bioware would take those ideas to make Mass Effect. A classic that created another classic.
The similarities are very apparent: voice actors, story tropes and themes, even the interaction-highlighter are used in both games. What KOTOR does differently is make the 3D action use turn based startegy. Consider it Bioware's missing link from cRPGs to action RPGs. For me its the best of both worlds; it's complicated and requires thought, but is simplified so that it's never overwhelming.
People hail this game for its story, and I agree. The best part of the story, as usual for Bioware, is their character arcs. You'll be recruiting Wookies, droids, Mandalorians, and others. The writing is also top notch, and provide some actually nuanced interactions and puzzzles to solve. You have probably heard about how good the story is, so I'll point to the biggest criticism I have: The dialouge choices are way too binary. While the situations are grey, the coptions to act on them are black and white. You're either evil or good, and no inbetween options are given. Good luck trying to be Han Solo, you'll just turn into Boba Fett or Luke Skywalker.
Is this as great as people say? As a fan of Star Wars and Bioware, I'd have to say, "pretty damn close." If you can look past the limitations that are because of the technology at the time, you'll expereiecne one of the best Star Wars adventures ever created.

MOAI 3: Trade Mission Collector's Edition is a time and resource management game that doesn't offer much new over the previous two titles. That said, the previous two games are pretty good for the genre, as is Moai 3.
There are a few additions that don't add much to the gameplay, abilities (which are visually represented and passive .... and may not do anything at all!) and items, which you can equip from the main menu and these give you in-game bonuses.
The game felt as long as the previous titles, but there are an additional 20 levels under an easy to miss icon at the bottom of the main game once you have completed the main game.
Overall, if you like time and resource management games, you'll be happy with this one. Graphics and sound suit the theme, it doesn't take the genre in a new direction, and is a casual time-sink that takes few risks, but you'll find yourself wanting to gold all the levels anyhow!

MOAI 3: Trade Mission Collector’s Edition is a Casual / strategy / resources and time management game. You will start the game on the Island of Tikku-ana. If you are familiar with the first 2 games, well you probably know the drill. You will control a minimum of 2 workers and give them orders - to collect food (pond or plate of fruits), remove road obstacles such as trees, rocks, fill big holes or open treasure chests. You will have to build farming fields (food resources), quarries (stone resources), sawmills (wood resources), gold mines (coin resources) and more. Each time you built, upgrade a structure or remove an obstacle it will cost you specific resource (s).  The aim is to achieve all tasks in each level before the time runs out. It can be tricky at times.
When you open a treasure chest, you might get some well needed resources or artefacts, but you could also pick up some special abilities to help you finish the level on time. Something like the “Sandals of Speed” which will move your worker from one point another faster. However, it will be for a limited time.
If you finish the level on time, you will score points and add whatever artefacts you found to your Backpack. Your hero can wear up to six artefacts and can gain an increasing percentage on the production of goods, speed and much more.
The game has 100 levels and each time you beat a level, you can retry the same level on a higher difficulty.  If you are stuck on a level, don’t worry as the game as a strategy guide available for you if need be.

Time management (city-builder+puzzle type) casual game, with plot tied into previous series. Mechanics are mostly standard for the genre: workers, upgrades, artefacts (spells), equipment and superficial primary stats; though there is a enemy-clicker element on later levels, with superficial tower defence. Visuals are calm and pleasant; sound design is fitting, with a lot of audio cues for states of progression. Level design is nice — despite repetitive nature of the genre, tasks and maps feel distinct and diverse. Later ones are also somewhat frantic and challenging.
Game can be played in 4:3 but feels too much zoomed in. Native resolution in window is weird, but native aspect ratio seems to be nowadays common 16:9. So if you have 4:3 screen and can tolerate borders — i suggest you to play in windowed mode.
Story somewhat relies on player being already invested in the characters (this is my first game in the series) and overall is toothless and plain, reminiscent of old RTS games, though with interesting moai theme. Which, on the other hand, means that it was really easy to avoid mistakes in the narrative. Names and descriptions of difficulty levels did caught me off-guard and cracked me up rather hard. Also i like that they did choose to use statues with hats and eyes.
Bonus campaign takes place after trade mission returned home and adds 13+12 of new levels to the main campaign comprised of 40+38 levels, about pacifying the volcano and dealing with damage.
There are in-game achievements, which for some reason are not tied to steam. Mostly progression-based, resource accumulation and optional mission-based. But "coconut thrower" is misleading and actually means the bandits from end-game levels, rather than the usual bandits.
Trading cards feature characters from the game and have nice artwork; emoticons are utilitarian, some looks nice and fitting, while others are too small; profile backgrounds, on the other hand, are not very good, they are really blurry and it seems like they are pretty low-res.
Overall it's really solid game in the genre, more focused on mechanics, rather than on the heroes and some thorough story.

I've only played a few turn-based strategy games, but after finishing the Age of Fear trilogy I intend to play a lot more – including any future Age of Fear games that should emerge. The tabletop-style maps are not fundamentally all that different from the grid-based battlefields of Fire Emblem and XCOM, but I personally got a warm fuzzy sensation from painstakingly positioning my troops where I thought they would be most effective – plus, the lack of a clearly-defined grid makes human error a more distinct possibility, as there were times when an enemy was able to charge through a gap in my formation that I'd thought I'd sealed up. The fact that most movement can only be conducted in a straight line also forces the player to plan ahead, lest reinforcements end up trapped behind the allies they are trying to save – something which gives added value to units with the segmented move skill, who can dodge around front-ranks troops to engage the mages and archers who usually hide near the rear.
Although most battles will eventually devolve into a massed melee at some point or other, the band of beer-swilling dwarves plays quite differently from the army uniting the disparate forces of nature. The Dwarves have tough infantry and ale that heals them at the expense of dulling their skills for a few turns, whilst the Forces of Nature have diverse options including cannon-fodder plants that can regrow if they are slain in battle, sturdy ents, mushroom-people archers, a drider whose quick attacks can be devastating if he is properly equipped, and a huge spiky bear. In the aftermath, the player is taken to a menu where they can recruit new troops, teach veterans new skills, equip or sell items that have been found or stolen in battle, and purchase other pieces of equipment. The capacity to customise your main heroes is quite extensive, and even your lowlier soldiers can carry a couple of potions, allowing for a wider range of tactical possibilities than even the previous two games provided.
The visuals are simple but effective; different units are easily recognisable, and although the animations are pretty basic they get the job done. The tabletop-gaming aesthetic serves a useful function, too: in, say, a Dwarf-versus-Dwarf battle, your troops will have different coloured bases from your enemies, so you can distinguish between them at a glance. Age of Fear might not be a treat for the eyes, but it's no eyesore either – I'd much rather have functional graphics that work reliably than a glitch-ridden mess, and I'm glad AoF has the former.
The two campaigns each took me around sixteen hours to complete, approximately twice as long as the average campaign in AoF1 or AoF2; the occasional plot-based decision, varying difficulties, hidden secrets and achievements all offer a player excuses for replaying them, if you're that way inclined. The Dwarf campaign wasn't much to write home about, consisting mostly of short angry people being rude to other people and then fighting them (the story of my life…), but the tale of the Dryad and the Drider had more of a narrative arc to it, plus a trio of heroes whose bantering made up for the fact that many of their troops were literally vegetables.
OVERALL
If pressed, I would confess that this was my least favourite of the Age of Fear games. Maybe this is the result of me playing all three games back-to-back in the span of a few months, giving me a case of Turn-Based Tactical Fatigue; maybe it was because AoF3 was undergoing a transitional period in the weeks I played it, as the developers grafted open-world elements onto the campaign in a fashion that gave the game a work-in-progress feel to it – but there was a certain je ne sais quoi about playing the two campaigns in this game that left me a little less enamoured than my experience of the previous games. Nevertheless, I did play them, and I did like them. The core gameplay remains the same, so it's unlikely to win over anyone who disliked the previous games, but the ambition and dedication on display by the developers – introducing new characters and factions with each game, and releasing free patches and upgrades at what seems to be a rate of more than once a week – should be applauded, especially in these times when the monetization of video-games is a much-debated issue. All in all, the AoF blend of turn-based tactics and role-play gaming mechanics has produced another good game, and I look forwards to seeing where the series goes next.

Absoloot is jam-packed with action and bullet hell, where you can choose to play in either Offline or Online mode. Currently, offline mode includes: Death Match, Looting, Runaway King, Teams and Treasure Hunt. This seems to be frowned upon, because of how it strong encourages the participation of more than one player. Heck, it doesn’t even provide a Single-player option.
You can only play 2 or 4 player-mode, and Multiplayer is a definite 1+ player requirement. Multiplayer is Empty, and that’s a confirmation from both my time of searching and as stated in other reviews.
The music isn’t quite what you see on the trailer, but the one shown in the video does demonstrate the action quite well. The art and graphics are also good, if you’re into pixel graphics. The effects and motion camera are likely one of the biggest highlights of the game. You see bullets fly, splash damage, impact explosions and all else that you would expect in an Action game. There’s also a good variety of maps, all with a different theme, style and colour-design to it, so kudos for that.
The Credits and options are also available on the main menu, but I found that the latter was quite limited. You could only choose between Blood effects and FPS. Including a wider range of control for features such as Music Volume, Graphics quality and other effects would be preferable.
In conclusion, I thought the Absoloot was okay. The only real issue here is the lack of a Single-Player mode, and one that should be available for newly published games such as this one. Without this option, it can really cut off a huge part of the players that genuinely enjoy the game, but are unable to find others to play with. Or they simply want to play Solo-instead. Other than that drawback, everything else is fine. I give it a thumbs up.

Secret of the Magic Crystal(s)
Review by Protoss
What is Secret of the Magic Crystal(s)? It is a collection of four minigames with a bit of nonsensical storyline about you having to breed five magical horses. You get magical horses in the fifth generation and for each generation beyond the first you need to raise two horses of the previous generation. Luckily after your stable is fully upgraded, you can buy second generation horses.
This means that, unless I made a mistake, in total you need to fully train 1+2+4+8+16 = 31 horses for your first fifth-generation horse and then 1+2+4+8 = 15 horses for each fifth-generation horse (provided you fully upgraded your stables), for a total of 91 horses.
How do you train horses? Well, you do the same four minigames over and over. Luckily once you got the catch, which is after a few minutes, the minigames are not at all difficult, and you also have to do each one only once per horse. The game just remains repetitive until the end. that you can see after a total of around 17-20 hours of playtime if you force yourself through the repetitive minigames again and again. The whole money management aspect really does not matter much, it seems only tacked on to hide there is no substantial gameplay. Which it fails to do.
Because of its fantasy horse setting the game is seen as a troll game by a certain number of people and therefor often at sales gifted to other people. This trend has taken a somewhat recession after the introduction of the Steam Trade system allowing you to store games in your backpack. Yes, for those newcomers, there was a time where you could only activate a game or reject it, and that was the high time of this game as a troll gift, together with Bad Rats! This also will be the most likely reason why negative reviews will be rated down, unfortunately countering the whole intent of the review system.
- The graphics are nicely done, although not top-notch. They very much fit into the fantasy setting, and I really don't see where to complain other than them looking a bit old (but still good enough).
- The sound also fits nicely, it is not disturbing but also fits into the setting.
- Atmosphere and Story are for all real intents and purposes nonexistant.
My sincere apologies, at the end of this review, go to the developers who after almost three years still do a good job of at least community info and free patching. For example, when achievements stopped working this year (2013), they fixed it. Not liking the game mechanics doesn't mean I don't appreciate that bit of work! In fact, I was surprised to see it fixed when I recently checked the forums, since I simply stopped expecting developers to give anything about their game after a certain period of time which lies between one and two years.
Recommended: No, unless you want the achievements, as they are easily obtainable by grinding

If you like On-rails Shooters don't hesitate, this is the best on steam!

+ Good humor
+ Smooth, fast-paced & action packed gameplay.
+ Long levels
+ totally playable with a keyboard and mouse
- A bit short (but rail shooters are about replayability and getting the high scores)
- Okay graphics, nothing special
TL;DR: Definitely worth spending $12.99.

Let's get the negatives out of the way first. The story is garbage. Story in a rail shooter? Who cares, right? But even by basic storytelling 101 standards, it's a mess. Plot threads are introduced and instantly forgotten. There's no throughline at all - the plot just drunkenly veers back and forth from subject to subject without any real overarching point, and the story doesn't "end" so much as "stop". The game's ostensibly a violent, dark comedy, but the jokes are all absolutely tepid. The humor falls flat at every conceivable turn. The references are forced and not especially clever, the running jokes are just tiresome - honestly, the toilet humor is probably the closest it ever gets to being funny. It's not entertaining, or amusing, or interesting. But you'll notice I still give this a "Recommend". Why?
The game's a blast to play. Blue Estate is a rail shooter that does a swell job of embracing its genre. Every level is a brilliantly dynamic, fast-paced, hectic environment that still provides you with plenty of room to react even while keeping up its frantic pace. Enemies all fire continuously, to avoid the usual rail shooter pitfall of them standing there staring slackjawed for no reason to give you time to shoot. Instead, yellow indicators give you a way to measure how long you have until they'll actually hit, so you can prioritize your targets. Stages generally give you one or two optional secondary weapons, and they do a very good job of pacing out the ammo drops so that, if you're fighting efficiently, you can keep using them throughout the level. (The final stage is a weird exception, where the extra weapon's ammo capacity is so steeply limited it's often useless.) The game's a bit on the easy side. I played on "Abnormal" (which I infer is the game's "normal" difficulty), and I noticed a fair amount of auto-lock in the aiming. I don't know if this is mitigated on higher difficulty levels, but it does make things very easy. The main challenge, instead, is in racking up the highest possible point totals, which this makes surprisingly fun. So, while it's a flat-on-its-face failure in many departments, this is some of the most satisfying and fun rail shooter gameplay I've encountered in the genre. For what it's worth, it is VERY short, and not especially deep, so I'm not sure that Steam's current $13 price tag is necessarily worth it. But if you can nab this on sale, and you like rail shooters, I'd encourage going for it.

Although Blue Estate is a solid cinematic rail shooter on its own accord, its main selling point is its tongue-in-cheek, goofy narration style (which, ironically, is a spoof of the original source material).
Blue Estate is an interesting specimen. It is obvious from the start that it follows the veins of old-school parodies, full of cheesy one-liners and two different narrators that either involuntarily or consciously make fun of everything. To put the humour in perspective: one of the bosses is a bra-wearing Kim Jong Il impersonator who knows matrix style kung fu.
Those who read the comic this game was based on may look surprised though, as the series was actually a dark, gritty thriller about the shady underside of the entertainment industry. They should know that this game only reuses the likeness and names of some characters, but they are cast in different roles and personalities.
As a game, Blue Estate is an old-school story-oriented rail-shooter; meaning, that no matter how many times you play it, each enemy and item will always be in the exact same spot at the exact same time. Also, the levels are full of cut-scenes (which can be sped up once you played through them).
Aiming is very… console-friendly. By default, the reticule snaps to enemies, including critical hit spots, from afar. Luckily, this can be turned off, but even then, the game is only mildly challenging (so much so, that a patch actually moved the default setting from the first to the middle difficulty). The challenge lies more in scoring a perfect run and getting all achievements, which can also act as a good replay incentive for this otherwise short little thing.

First, my knee jerk reactions to this game.
Pros:
Better UI and unit control.
Better graphics and destruction.
Cooler map flavors and terrain feature.
Some really awesome unit types.
The ability to upgrade units and buildings.
Very streamline experience.
The tech upgrades are cool.
Cons:
Dumbed down from previous titles in terms of strategy.
Unit types knocked down considerably.
Game depth has grown shallow compared to previous titles.
Not many maps compared to previous titles.
There is a clear way to play, not many choices in how you build an army.
End game is boring.
I completely understand why they made this game the way they did: to appeal to more people. They made it easier to get into, lessened the learning curve, and added a few gizmos here and there. But for me, a veteran of Supreme Commander, I find it... lacking. It seems empty and hollow, shiny and new on the surface with the new soundtrack, commander designs, and tech system but I keep wanting to go back and play Forged Alliance. I do not like this game.
But this is a fair review.
The basic elements are still there. Massive battles, large maps, and plenty of explosions to stare at. In terms of graphics the game is much bigger and badder. But that's where the improvements end for me. Combat is stale, tactics are simple a simple race to upgrade your units faster than your opponent and spam them fast as you can. There are no more tech tiers, just a few tech trees. It feels restrictive and expects you to play conservatively in the beginning until you can overwhelm your enemies with numbers or higher-tech units.
Now if all of this is just sounding like a lot of fun, go ahead and buy this game. It's only $13 and will honestly give you a lot of fun and enjoyment. For me personally I prefer Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance, which is a much more advanced and difficult game, providing more challenge. And I like that. Anyway, this is a great entry to the Supreme Commander franchise but not a great representation. It also doesn't stand out from most strategy games unlike Supreme Commander 2 which is much more standard.
Once you get the hang of this game I strongly reccomend you play Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance and read the review I left there.

(NOTE: I do enjoy AVGN on youtube. I respect and enjoy his content, but his game just didn't work out for me.)
I wish there was a Mixed opinion for reviews, but since there isn't, I have to make it a negative.
When I was 12, I was very curious about this game when I saw it was rated M on the 3DS/Wii U. I was like, "what the heck? How can a pixelated game like this get a M rating? That's stupid." That was the time I never heard about the Angry Video Game Nerd. So when I found out the game is on steam, I bought it on sale to see what it's like. Well... since I was 12 I wasn't use to language, I stopped playing after 5 minutes, and never touched the game ever again.
Now after 2 years... I came back to this game since now I'm use to language, and it has been a while.
Now to the actual review:
Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures (AVGNA) is an action-platformer. Nerd and his friends were playing a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game, which caused Nerd's friends to be sucked into the TV. Nerd almost escapes, but then an arm comes out the TV, and grabs him by his... balls... and gets pulled inside the TV. There isn't much of a story, but it's an alright and appropriate opening for this game.
The gameplay at parts can be fun, but most of the game is filled with cheap deaths. The first level isn't all that bad, and the easiest out of the whole entire game. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥vania is more difficult, but yet still passable. Happy Fun Candy Time is even more difficult, to the point it can make you get quite frustrated. Future ****balls 2010 feels easier than Happy Fun Candy Time, but it's still quite hard. Blizzard of Balls is like Future ****balls 2010: It's easier than HFCT but it's still quite hard. Thy Farts Consumed has the coolest moment in the game, but the level is quite difficult, and needs some thinking.
Dungeons and ****holes has a part that is quite unexpected for a cheap death, but the level is quite hard. Beat It and Eat It is a... low graphic porno stage... that actually made me rage quit. It's mostly the second hardest stage in the game.
That's how far I got, but you know where I'm going: The game is hard as hell. The game does make fun of bad level design, but that doesn't make it any better.
The gameplay does go overboard with the death blocks. They're everywhere... and in every level. If you touch one, it's an automatic death. Since these are in every level, and everywhere, you will die a lot. To make things worse: there is different type of death blocks. There is a type that just stays in place, a type that disappears for 3 seconds and reappears for 3 seconds, a type that you need to be close to see where that death block is at, etc. etc.
When you die, you get AVGN references to the show. They're suppost to be funny, but for me, they just appear just childish and cringeworthy. If Nerd said it in the show, it's funny, but if you read it, it's not that funny and you just want to get back into the game (the death screen lasts for like 5 seconds each. No joke.).
The game does have positives, though.
The 8-bit graphics are the best I've seen in any game. Everything is very detailed, and you know what you are looking at.
The soundtrack kicks♥♥♥♥♥ They did a good job on making the soundtrack sound amazing, and fit appropriately into levels.
You can use a controller. That makes the game much more easier to control since using a keyboard doesn't really work well for platformers.
TL;DR: But even with its positives, Angry Video Game Nerd Adventures is just a game that is only made to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. I know it's suppose to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, but making a game way to overwhelmingly difficult just ruins the fun of the game, and it won't make you want to come back to the game.
I will try my best to finish the game, but I can't recommend it (really wish there was a Mixed option for reviews). 5/10.

Fireburst is a fantastic looking car combat game that lives and dies on its fire attack nitro boosts that can also kill you. When your car overheats you explode and respawn. Ramming through a red barrel will make your vehicle heat up considerably. To keep your vehicle cool there are plenty of puddles, water falls and blue barrels to drive through. Its an interesting mechanic that has you watching the flames on your windshield rather than the action on the course.
Its a game that puts forth a lot of style, attitude, presence and ascetic. Almost every locale is a beautiful vista whether its driving along side a dam or on an oil rig the game looks superb and even the most mundane areas look incredible thanks to light, shadow and style. This shadow can be your downfall, because there are no headlights even in a darkened train yard. Its easy to get stuck in a dark corner. You can always adjust the brightness in the options to see better.
The game plays good and runs smooth. Its like a lot of other arcade racers where you control with forward and backward rather than a real brake. There is a boost button that doubles as a weapon and you have the ability to see behind your car and change between a chase cam or a hood view.
The vehicles look great as well. There's a diverse array of cars, trucks, racers, muscle cars, dune buggies, jeeps and even vans. There's something to your liking each with its own stats for speed, acceleration, handling and heat resistance. They all have their own heat attacks such as leaving flaming tire tracks for opponents to drive over and heat up. A fire burst, a fire shield and a fire wall. The longer you hold the boost, the greater your range.
Of course the issue is using these attacks heats up your vehicle, so why even use them unless there's plenty of water around and even if there's a pool or waterfall, that means your opponents can benefit from them as well making it useless. I think of the combat as a gamble. Who will die faster? You or the foe next to you? That's my real problem with the game. So I relegate myself to using it only as boost when my engine is cool.
The game starts with eight racers to chose from each of which is a caricature of a stereotype that gives Fireburst its flavor, flair and style. You have the seasoned stock racer, the juggy goth, a big money businessman with a mohawk, an old hippy ladies man, a slim blonde nerd with glasses, an Asian schoolgirl that might be too young to drive and so on. They all have their own stats and they all say things as they race. Its part of the game's attitude for the old hippy to say "I could be your father," or someone else that says "yes they're real."
The voice work is good and believable and sometimes what I think is glitched. The old hippy keeps sputtering the same random comments over and over with no break in between. Perhaps it was just him or that circumstance. I've come across another visual glitch that had the game stuck in black and white until I quit the race and went to a new one.
As for the game itself there are three major modes, a challenge campaign that lets you participate in different challenges for each driver. I consider this to be the main mode because its the one that lets you unlock new vehicles and new drivers. I'll be honest and say while I'm not into drivers as characters, this game does  a good job of making me want to unlock them. The real problem is the challenges themselves are difficult and convoluted due to the fire mechanic.
Some events are simple like make it through a warm-up lap and then a qualifying lap. Others force you to win or win without wrecking more than three times. Then there are some which force you to hold your boost twenty seconds without wrecking. On paper this might sound easy, because let's just put a bunch of hoses, puddles and blue barrels around, but that's what makes it challenging. Doing all of it for twenty seconds. Even doing it for five is a challenge, but you need to start somewhere. These challenges turn me off, but for anyone that's into them, they are different for each character with each one putting you behind the wheel of a different vehicle.
With the other two modes, they're more mundane, a race and a destruction derby. The derbies are built in figure eights and they're really a testament to game design. This ensures that someone will always zoom by you giving you enough time to destroy them and that way the maps stay short and sweet. The races are what I care about and there are twelve in all at least from the start. After one race, the same race starts again and that's a let down. These are closed circuit courses with two or so laps taking place in real world environments. Airfields, an oil refinery at night, a fright port, a gorgeous giant bridge similar to the Golden Gate with a different bridge below it and so on.
I stress even if these locales seem ordinary, the game and its aesthetic makes them incredible. You'll find ramps, jumps and branching paths in each of the courses. There are places to drive through parked cargo planes. Other areas have shipwrecks or driving by moonlight. The look awesome and they play awesome. A lot of work was put into each one to make it feel special with a twist. The refinery lets you drive through moonlit water. The oil rig has ramped walls and even the fright depot has jumps and tunnels beneath towering cranes.
For people that like to hand tweak settings there's a program launcher that lets you update controls before you get into the game, along with advanced settings to let you update the ini files yourself. It would have been nice to have all of this in game rather than having guess work, but something is still better than nothing. You can tweak your graphical settings the same way. The texture pop in is noticeable when outside of a race. The character and vehicle textures both take a split second to load and its a problem larger developers still struggle with, so I can see past it.
When you respawn, you're already driving and you just fade into reality again. Its a good way to keep the action going, but make sure not to respawn in any other vehicles. I've also managed to hang up on some questionable places and explode even when trying to get unstuck. It feels like that issue could have been better. The whole exploding for ramming something too rough in an arcade racer seems to take away from the fun factor. I found myself exploding far too frequent. What's odd is the fact you can explode on the simplest things, yet try as I might, i could never roll a vehicle. Sure I'd drive on the side of a wall, but never roll or explode.
There is local multiplayer splitscreen and online multiplayer, but a budget title a year after its release always has a struggle keeping players playing online.
Fireburst is a tough game to enjoy its main challenge mode. There's a higher than necessary skill level for what is essentially an arcade racer. You can always slide the skill slider to your preferred level, but even then it feels like there's no happy medium where racers can be competitive. Take out what makes the game unique and it would make for a better experience while crushing the soul of what makes it unique. Its a tough toss up, but it should stand on its gimmick even if sucks the joy out of an otherwise fun experience.

When working on this game, Bioware had a bunch of ideas that Lucasarts wouldn't allow for to eb put in. Bioware would take those ideas to make Mass Effect. A classic that created another classic.
The similarities are very apparent: voice actors, story tropes and themes, even the interaction-highlighter are used in both games. What KOTOR does differently is make the 3D action use turn based startegy. Consider it Bioware's missing link from cRPGs to action RPGs. For me its the best of both worlds; it's complicated and requires thought, but is simplified so that it's never overwhelming.
People hail this game for its story, and I agree. The best part of the story, as usual for Bioware, is their character arcs. You'll be recruiting Wookies, droids, Mandalorians, and others. The writing is also top notch, and provide some actually nuanced interactions and puzzzles to solve. You have probably heard about how good the story is, so I'll point to the biggest criticism I have: The dialouge choices are way too binary. While the situations are grey, the coptions to act on them are black and white. You're either evil or good, and no inbetween options are given. Good luck trying to be Han Solo, you'll just turn into Boba Fett or Luke Skywalker.
Is this as great as people say? As a fan of Star Wars and Bioware, I'd have to say, "pretty damn close." If you can look past the limitations that are because of the technology at the time, you'll expereiecne one of the best Star Wars adventures ever created.
Do you wanna be a Jedi or Sith lord? Fantastic story, fun and strategic gameplay, and long term consequences depending on your actions. Oh and lightsaber crafting.

This game is the reason I couldn't really like Hitman: Absolution. I propose my thesis: this game is really fricking awesome.
Exhibit A: there is a level that is just you in your hideout. You are not some kind of traveling salesman hitman, peddling your stabby-shooty wares door to door in a car you probably stole from a developmentally disabled man. You have your own little underground hideaway where you can try out your sniper rifle on pop bottles, tell your pet canary he is a pretty bird, murder rats, and sing Ave Maria without the menu screen music reminding you of your tin ear.
Exhibit B: Diana! I mentioned in my Absolution review that Diana failed to live up to my expectations in that game, so here's why she's better in this. First, she's her own character. She's busy doing her own thing, scheming, organizing, conspiring with the powers that be to create the bizarreness and awesomeness of that final level. She isn't just stealing some girl and then waiting to be horribly murdered on the toilet. Second, she's mysterious. She's always in shadow, you never see her face, you never know what she's planning. I think maybe we were supposed to instantly feel wrong in Absolution where you see her face on her file, but it's just thrown down in a picture on a file in a cutscene while another character is talking, so it doesn't really have much weight. Also, the only time we see her in Absolution she is naked. So there's that. Finally, she's a really good handler. She's calm and detailed and you can tell she and 47 work well together.
Exhibit C: the levels are fun and colorful. Absolution was kind of grey and dreary at times with lots of industrial levels in factories or labs, and even when it was somewhere fun like a barber shop or a tiki hotel everything is sun-faded or blown the heck up. In Blood Money the levels are set in abandoned amusement parks, over-the-top stereotypical suburbia, a steamboat paddling down the river. Everything is very distinct and self-contained.
Exhibit D: In this game the cutscenes tell one story, a kind of serious one, but because the cutscene world of the two plot-framing doofuses and the level world of the doofus who got murdered by a scantily clad woman at a Christmas part are so very distinct it doesn't feel like the tone is just very confused.
I can't really think of any more exhibits at the moment, so here's a list of fun things to do in Blood Money.
1) Drop a piano on a bird-lady.
2) Throw a cake on the floor, then pick it up again and use it to blend in the kitchen.
3) Run around in a bath robe blowing up cook stoves.
4) Snipe a dude off a Ferris Wheel.
5) Break into the goddamn White House and upset the First Lady's tiny obnoxious dog.
6) Show up to a private wedding dressed as a drunken hillbilly, shove the bride's father into the swamp, and drive off into the everglades on the priest's air boat.
7) Shove people off a boat because that's what they get for going on a boat.
8) Dress like a sexy pool boy, murder absolutely everyone at a birthday party, almost get away with it, forget about the family dog, and get your squishy bits bitten off as you go to escape.
9) Befriend the neighborhood garbage man.
10) Leave a bunch of corpses to ride up and down in the casino elevators.
11) Strangle people in the bathroom of a playhouse because that's what they get for not supporting Allegiance at the Tony's.
12) Run around a parking garage getting shot to death by a jillion cops and dudes in dorky masks.
13) AVE MAREEEEEEEEEIIIIIA

MOAI 3: Trade Mission is the third game in the successful time management series by Alawar Entertainment.  Although this installment does not have quite as many changes and improvements as the previous, it remains an enjoyable take on the genre that provides plenty of challenge for those who seek it, along with relaxing gameplay for the more casual-minded gamer.
This time around, we follow Tapa-tui’s leader and Bright Light as they venture off island to neighboring Tikku-ana where they begin a new adventure together.  Gameplay is relatively the same, consisting of multi-tasking activities as efficiently as possible while managing resources to complete specific tasks (build, gather, trade, etc.) in an effort to beat the clock.  The only real change is the addition of gold mines which offer coins as a resource.  All of the other series improvements are present including the ability to equip items that offer specific perks and the secondary bonus objectives for each level with additional challenges to overcome.  Granted, the game plays the same as MOAI 2, but that didn’t bother me much as I felt they got the formula just about right with the previous installment.
As the first Collector’s Edition in the series, we get a few neat extras including a Strategy Guide which gives helpful tips for each level if you find yourself struggling.  There’s also downloadable wallpapers and music tracks (something I’ve been awaiting for a while now), and additional levels available once you’ve completed the main story scenario. Unfortunately, there is no Steam integration for the achievements, which is a pretty big bummer.  But I hope this is remedied in the future as they really added value to the previous 2 titles.
Honestly, I wish I could say more than I have, but MOAI 3 is essentially a continuation of MOAI 2’s story with the same great gameplay, but little more.  If you enjoyed the first two games, you will definitely enjoy MOAI 3.  However, if you were hoping the series continued to progress in gameplay improvements, you’ll likely be disappointed.  Still, I'd recommend it to fans of the series as well as newcomers who are looking to dip their toes into the time management genre.
Bottom Line: Recommended for fans of the series as well as newcomers to the genre.

I'd like to start off by saying that I've actually beaten this game.
Second, I should note that I'm a horse person. I've been riding hunt-seat for quite a few years now, and consider myself fairly well-versed in equine knowledge. But you don't need a lick of knowledge to play this game.
You got this game from a friend, didn't you? Probably during the Winter or Summer sale. Because no one in their right mind would buy this game for themself, unless it was to occupy a seven year-old for a while.
But whatever. It's in your library now. And if you want to 100% it, you have to beat it. And to beat it you need five level 5 horses of each different breed.
The objective of the game is straightforward. Get the magic crystals. It took me about 20 hours to accomplish this, but I bet it could be done faster.
The game is simple. Buy a horse, wait for it to be an adult, train it to max, breed it, sell it, rinse and repeat. It just takes a very, very long time since you can't breed a level 5 horse with another horse.
Each level 5 horse requires sixteen level 2 horses, eight level 3s, and four level 4s. All of which need to be trained fully. Each training segment is a simple DDR-ish sequence that takes maybe a minute and a half each time. You have to train a horse six times for it to be fully trained.
And you have to do this with every. Single. Horse.
Obviously, this is a good game to play while watching Netflix or YouTube on a second monitor or something. There's quite a bit of waiting involved, so if you want to catch up on a series while you play, this is the best game to do so in.
Some things you should know about the game:
- save files don't transfer from computer to computer
- there's a crap ton of Engrish in this game
- the game will pause if you click out of the window
But, I suppose it all comes down to this: Did I have fun playing it?
And to that I say: Yeah, I guess. Give this to your young siblings and let them have fun with it.

Basically, I reccomend this game. It is not by definition a "good game". It is absolutely a running joke to many buyers. Gameplay: Look, people are gonna tell you it's boring or uninspired. It is. But, seriously, watch the trailer: it kinda advertises itself as a generic, no gimmicks rail-shooter. What is an issue, is the portrayal of EVERY character in the place. There are good ways to incorporate race in a game, there are bad ways, and somewhere, deep down in the depths of depravity, there is the way this game depicts race.
You're a white guy, shooting tonnes of Asian guys, to start with. And those Asian guys are caricatures of long outdated stereotypes of Asian-Americans. The voices are exaggerated beyond offensive, the first boss is a pudgy martial-artist with a shrill voice and heavy accent, and the main character constantly makes 'jokes' about the setting which do nothing but degrade all involved.
The place is full of strippers and sex-workers, which make up the only female characters (as far as I've seen) and which are treated with exactly no respect, with both the narrator and the main character hurling a near-constant barrage of derogatory slurs and sexist 'jokes' at them, including the main character's supposed girlfriend.
Every effort has been made, it seems, to pose the women in this game as senseless bimbos, existing only as sex-objects for the characters and grotesque exhibits for the player's benefit.
VERY NEGATIVE: Racist, sexist, ableist, fatshaming... I doubt this is even tolerable to many 'Meninists' out there.
So is this game worth $13? No. The gameplay is not substantially better than a unity-powered flash-game (though it is admittedly longer).
Is this game worth $2? Uhh, maybe. Personally, I wouldn't buy it in hindsight, because I find the plot and structure of the game disgusting, but the mechnics are sound and there are few hiccups, so if you can stomach it, then sure.

Absoloot is jam-packed with action and bullet hell, where you can choose to play in either Offline or Online mode. Currently, offline mode includes: Death Match, Looting, Runaway King, Teams and Treasure Hunt. This seems to be frowned upon, because of how it strong encourages the participation of more than one player. Heck, it doesn’t even provide a Single-player option.
You can only play 2 or 4 player-mode, and Multiplayer is a definite 1+ player requirement. Multiplayer is Empty, and that’s a confirmation from both my time of searching and as stated in other reviews.
The music isn’t quite what you see on the trailer, but the one shown in the video does demonstrate the action quite well. The art and graphics are also good, if you’re into pixel graphics. The effects and motion camera are likely one of the biggest highlights of the game. You see bullets fly, splash damage, impact explosions and all else that you would expect in an Action game. There’s also a good variety of maps, all with a different theme, style and colour-design to it, so kudos for that.
The Credits and options are also available on the main menu, but I found that the latter was quite limited. You could only choose between Blood effects and FPS. Including a wider range of control for features such as Music Volume, Graphics quality and other effects would be preferable.
In conclusion, I thought the Absoloot was okay. The only real issue here is the lack of a Single-Player mode, and one that should be available for newly published games such as this one. Without this option, it can really cut off a huge part of the players that genuinely enjoy the game, but are unable to find others to play with. Or they simply want to play Solo-instead. Other than that drawback, everything else is fine. I give it a thumbs up.
