[
===
Age Of Fear 3 is a top-down 2D tactical RPG / Strategy game with management elements. In this title you will be in command of an army composed of many different units of your choosing, ranging from walking trees, to orcs, to undeads, to mercenaries: a lot of different fantasy characters and species are present and almost all are recruitable for your army. The game consists mainly of two separate modules, one is the map and story where you decide what to do and where to go, while the other is the battlefield where the numerous battles take place. This title is pretty much old school in many ways and that nowadays is a really good thing.
===
The first half of the game, so map and storytelling section, works as any normal map you can think of, there will be one or more locations to choose from, and each one will be a different branching of the story, if there is a branching available, not always the case. Dialogues will be prompted and you will be able to make choices such as which party support during a multi-faction fight, which way to go in some dungeon, and things like these.
Such choices will impact what enemies you encounter and whwere the story goes pretty importantly. There is a management screen before each battle where you will be able to equip both Heroes and normal units in detail, each with customizable skills, inventory and progression, and also buy and sell units, dismiss existing ones, and evolving surviving ones who got experience.
The second part of the game is the battlefield, which is depicted as a standard, old-school 2D top-down field with all the units on it. Each unit can be analyzed to gather information, this applies to everything from doors to environmental hazards etc. so yes there is a lot to read and learn in each battle about enemies and environment alike.
Combat in AoF 3 is turn-based. Each character will be able to either move or use a skill (unless a special ability allows both), have its own movement range and attack radius. Equipment on heroes often grants passive and active unique skills usable during battles instead of regular attacks. All of this applies also the the enemy, the only difference being that if one of your Heroes dies, the battle is immediately lost, so you should move them wisely because enemies will make them priority targets.
Sounds simple? It is not. Each enemy has its own equipment, statiastics, resistances and whatnot, you WILL have to learn all of them in each battle and act accordingly, and this game has a rather complex system of stats so defininitrly not something for beginners. Killed units are lost forever unless a special ability allows them to resurrect after battle, those who survive a fight will often be able to level up and gain new abilities and traits, becoming better.
Also, certain abilities will allow you to convert enemy units to allies and retain them after battle, this is a feature not often seen in this type of game and helps varying the gameplay in a good way. Battles can also have victory or defeat conditions of their own, so each battle is different in some way.
There is a HUGE amount of units and equipment in this game, many battles to fight, and two different campaigns. Content-wise, there is plenty to do and see.
Standard difficulty is fair enough, pretty tough i have to say, even for a hardened RPG veteran like i am i found it tough to get through certain fights, but never anything unbalanced or broken. Higher difficulties sure will be a kick in that place tho.
Overall, the rating of High challenge is to be given, since the game system is rather complex, higher difficulties are really, really hard as far as i've seen and managing a balanced army for each situation without waste is something that will challenge even veterans of the genre.
===
Graphics are pretty simple, 2D sprites. Backgrounds, maps, portraits are of decent quality, characters have enough detail to be on-par, but overall the game is set on sufficent to decent levels in this field. For a game that clearly throws everything on gameplay and content and not graphics, it is acceptable.
Soundtrack is actually pretty good, sound effects and unit chatter are remarkable for the simple fact that the developers gave unique lines to each unit, and there are a whole lot of them.
Issues were fixed from the developer temporarily, until a more permanent fix for the previous issues. No problems to report here as of now. Use the RESET button in the game options if performance is still bad, as the developers fixed it.
Nothing to report.
Enemy AI is good, they will target Heroes and other sensitive units if they can to bring a rapid loss to the player, generally will mantain a decent formation sending melee units first and ranged behind to support, as far as i could tell, AI at Standard rank can be a good challenge already.
UI is pretty old school and not very immediate in many things, which can be a good or bad thing depending on who plays. In my case, a good thing.
Nothing to report.

Another fine entry in the Age Of Fear series.
I won't go into detail about the mechanics, as you can find that in numerous reviews for this and the last two titles. Safe to say, if you liked the last titles, you will like this one.
In fact, if you like turn-based tactics with a touch of RPG, and you don't need fancy graphics, this is a safe bet.
Instead, I'd like to point out the additions to the series:
There is now an overland map in which you can pick multiple optional missions as well as the branching within missions sometimes.
With the two new armies there are many new units to choose - and you will meet a lot of units known from the last games.
A bunch of new items and spells.
The graphics themselves have improved, even if just a bit.
My gripes with the series are still mostly the same:
Enter or space do not end the turn. This is a standard in the genre and should be in this one, too.
EDIT: This has been improved, enter now ends the turn.
Units can not walk around a corner, which is annoying. Instead of just the initial walking circle, the actual distance walked should be counted. At the very least, units should be able to walk as often as they want until their range is "used up" or they did some action.
Sometimes, after a while of playing, the performance when doing any action tanks and I need to restart the game.

A quality, quirky,  old school tactical combat game.    Seems to have a bit more polish than AoF 1 & 2,  and a  good bit more content , though otherwise very similar.  The big challenge with the grid free combat system is positioning your army so that you balance protecting  vulnerable ranged units, while not keeping such a tight formation that you cripple maneuverability. It can take a few hours to learn well before it starts becomming fun. If you're not sure you'd enjoy the combat,  you could buy the much cheaper AoF1 or 2 first -  the combat system is exactly the same.
This game shares the same flaws as AoF 1 & 2 - much of the writing reads like it needs a copy edit. The UI is a little clunky and takes some getting used to.
Other than that,  decent army building & level up system,  good and varied music & art, with a charming story. While all elements of the game are only budget quality,  everying coheres together well. A fun and most enjoyable experience if you like the old school.
Easy to learn, hard to master, with a good story. I would like to see more of these games.

A game based off of a youtuber sounds risky, even more so when the game is $15, but surprisingly, AVGN Adventures is pretty good despite some issues. The games control is silky smooth (although I reccomend a controller), and the graphics are colorful and full of charecter, and the music is fitting and memorable. The games difficulty is high, but MOSTLY fair. I say mostly because there are points where the game doesn't quite live up to the name, and on higher difficulty modes where lives are few and far between, It's a real hastle when an unexpected instant death block comes on screen, leaving you less than a second to react. Another issue I had with the game is that alot of the games variety of enemies are just clones. I noticed on several occations that I would find an enemy in a stage based off of horror designed like a ghost, and then go to the hell level and find that exact same enemy with a new sprite and same sound effects. Yet another issue I had was that the highly mature and rauchy humor throughout the game is really not very funny. Even when the game quotes the youtube sensation himself, without any context, the jokes just come off as immature and childlike. But even with all of these issues, the game is still really fun, warrenting another playthrough from me. Just be careful with the unlockable difficulties unless you're a masichist.

As an AVGN fan for years, I really wish I could recommend this game. I really do. The game was clearly created with AVGN fans in mind, and is so filled with references to episodes that you'll really like how many cool touches they are to the game. From The Nerd's death trap from Super Pitfall, to the three spirits of Christmas from the Home Alone episode, you really wouldn't believe the amount of in jokes have been added to the game.
But I have to look at this from a gamer perspective, and honestly? It's one of my least favourite 2D Platformers to date. The developers fell into the Mega Man 9 pittrap of flanderizing Nintendo Difficulty by thinking "throwing down as much♥♥♥♥♥♥as possible" is all fair game. Unfortunately, it isn't. It isn't good level design, it isn't good difficulty balancing, it's simply fustrating, simple as.
And I know the joke of the game is meant to parody the silly things in bad games, but that's the problem right there. The game can lampshade the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ design, and cheap layouts as much as they want, but it doesn't change the fact they're present in the game, and they're unbelievably annoying to deal with. From rooms filled with Death Blocks, that are in unbelivably idiotic layouts and locations, to the point where it feels like flat out luck to get past them.
And if you have to play this game on a keyboard, get ready for even more pain, because the keyboard controls are even more of a pain to deal with, and unusally glitchy. For example, I tried to switch the layout to use W,A,S,D as the arrow controls, but as soon as I started the level Future F**kballs, The A button wasn't letting me walk left, instead just turning the character in that direction.
There are also four playable characters in the game, these including AVGN himself, Couch Guy, Mike, and Bullsh*t Man. Unfortunately, I only found myself playing as Mike, and Couch Guy for most of the game.
AVGN isn't a bad character, and he's useful for situations where you need balanced jumping, but Mike has a very powerful ranged attack, and an extremely high jump, which makes platforming slightly easier, while Couch Guy has a very good long range weapon that arcs, and goes through walls, and he has the fastest speed of the characters in the game.
The worst character by far however is Bullsh*t Man. He has a double jump, but his speed is so terrible, his weapon is so useless because it isn't long range or very powerful, and his normal jump is terrible, with his double jump just giving him a very slight boost to make him have the normal jump of maybe Couch Guy (The third worst jumper in the game).
The cameos in this game are also kind of cool as well. Seeing Angry Joe, The Completionist, and Jim Sterling in the game was certainly a cool little surprise. That said however, there was some really glaring obmissions, and I'll give you AVGN fans one guess as to who it is.
THE NOSTALIGA CRITIC THATS WHO.
I mean seriously, even if Nostalgia Critic hasn't done many game reviews, he's still done Blues Brothers, and Babe's Kids, and he's done a ton of video game movies/tv shows, and that doesn't even talk about the fact that NC is Angry Video Game Nerd's rival. They had a battle that the internet still remembers to this day.
James Rolfe himself has cameoed in NC's movies, as well as Doug Walker (The person behind The NC) cameoing in the AVGN Movie, so I was incredibly disappointed that he didn't even get a mention in the game, when other Youtubers like Egoraptor did get a cameo (Personally, I'm not a fan of Game Grumps, but that's more personal opinion more than anything.
On top of that, the extremely fustrating level design of the game also ends up ruining some of the jokes. For example, it seems very clear they created the game with a death toll in mind, like Super Meat Boy did, but where Super Meat Boy was a fast paced platformer with extremely short levels, AVGN Adventures takes more of a Mega Man style, which really doesn't suit the style. Mega Man levels are generally very long for a death toll kind of idea, and when the player is getting killed over and over by cheap layouts, rather than their own fault, then it only ends up fustrating them.
It doesn't help that when the player dies, they get a random quote from the AVGN talking about how the game is a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ The problem is there's only about 10 to 20 of these in the game, and so, by the time you hit maybe the end of the first level, depending on which level you start on, you'll be so sick of these quotes. What makes it even worse is you can't skip past them until you've seen the text written out, meaning you have to wait about 5 to 10 seconds each time before you respawn.
If there's any positives to the game, the graphics are pretty good, and inspired by SNES games, and the music is surprisingly really awesome, and as I said, the injokes, references, and cameos are pretty cool to see, but in general, AVGN Adventures is a completely disappointing mess of a 2D platformer that falls into almost every pitfall that the Nerd has pointed out in bad games over the last  9 years.

I typically don't write reviews, but since I've been very dedicated to this game for a while, I'll give it a try.
*Gulps* Here goes...
I'll start off with this: Battleborn is a truly underrated game. With Overwatch being released around the same time, Battleborn became overshadowed and never had a chance to reach it's full potential. Many believe it's dead.
However, I think there's still a chance for this game. A very, very small chance, but it's still one regardless.
Ever since release, the devs have continuously updated the game. More characters, maps, modes, operations...The game has definitely improved from it's base form.
With that being said, I'll try to stop mentioning Overwatch in this review because I firmly believe the two are great games with more individuality than similarity (I also play Overwatch, so this is coming from someone who plays both).
Anyway, on to the positives and negatives of Battleborn. It truly doesn't get the credit it deserves even though most of the positives outweigh the negatives.
POSTIVES:
The Genre- Battleborn is truly unique because of what type of game it is. At first glance it looks like a first person shooter, but playing the game quickly made me realize that there is MOBA elements as well. It's a combination of both: there's quick paced moments and long term strategy involved. I think it's a refreshing change and makes it stand out from other first person shooters and Mobas, as it takes elements from both.
The Characters- This game has a variety of characters. From an unconventional clone soldier, to a gentleman sniper, to a vampire samurai, Battleborn has a character and playstyle for /almost/ everyone. Not only is the cast unique game play wise with their abilities, passives, ultimates, and helix, but also stand out for their personalities and lore. The character writing is quite humorous and enjoyable.
The Game Modes- Battleborn has many game modes that can suit everyone. There's first the pvp aspect of the game, where there are four modes: Incursion, Meltdown, Capture, and Face-Off. Then there's the pve aspect of the game, which contains Story Mode and Operations. You can also set private matches. There's versatility with the modes in this game, as you can either play by yourself, or with others.
NEGATIVES:
The Genre (What, again? Yes)- Even though I consider the genre a postive, it can also be seen as a negative. Due to the mixture of genres, it can cause quite a bit of conflict with players. People that play first person shooters for example, might not enjoy the MOBA aspects of it, and the MOBA gamers might not dig the fps additions. This shrinks the amount of players that would truly enjoy the game.
Small Playerbase- Unfortunately, cause of you-know-why, this game has had a smaller playerbase since launch and has been shrinking every month... Because of this, the queue times to play with other players tend to be horrendous, thus driving off more people. It's best to play this game with some friends, but this problem still remains.
Repetitive- This is very dependent on the player (this doesn't affect me, but I can see this to be the case with others). Battleborn can possibly get very repetitive for some people once you've beaten the story, finished lore and ops, etc, thus becoming a boring experience and not putting that much into time into it. Fortunately, the devs have been adding more features since launch, so hopefully this won't be a problem anymore.
In conclusion, Battleborn is an underrated gem and is quite worth it in my opinion considering the amount of content in the game. I truly hope this game doesn't die and continues to live on.
P.S. Happy 1st Annivarsary Battleborn :)
Edit: Since the game is free trial, you have nothing to lose by trying it. Granted, you won't have access to the full game, but you can at least try it out and form your own opinion whether the game is for you or not. Playing the game hands-on is much better than simply reading reviews and basing your decision on just that.

This could've been the Co-op shooter of the year if it wasn't for Gearbox's obsession with ESPORTS and "HUHH WE BETTER DAN OVERWATCH".
Seriously, this game's -only- similarity with Overwatch is that you pick from a roster of heroes, and yet it seems half of their marketing budget went into trying to hype up how much better of a competitive game BB is compared to OW.
Big surprise, the competitive is total garbage and now the game is sitting on life support with maybe 100 concurrent players per day. Who'd have thought that the company whose only real accomplishment was a co-op FPS/ARPG would have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue how to develop and market a competetive Moba?
And it's a damn shame, because the co-operative side of this game, short though it may be without the season pass, really shines with the potential of what could have been. No two characters feel samey to one-another, there's plenty of enemy variety (Three main enemy factions with 12+ enemy types each, plus some non-factioned enemies), and the missions themselves offer a good chunk of variety in objectives and bosses. The gameplay itself is also pretty nice, blending the moba-style leveling/abilities with the class-based shooter gameplay way better than I was expecting it to.(Disclaimer: The above statement only applies to the co-op. Somehow, the exact same gameplay manages to be complete and utter♥♥♥♥♥when you play in comp.)
At the end of the day, my time with the co-op only makes me wish they would've focused entirely on it, giving us some sort of 25+ mission campaign stocked with replayability instead of the just-barely-able-to-call-itself-a-campaign package that we got. Conversely, the competetive made me want to vomit.
If you want a co-op game that you can play in ~1 hour intervals to burn time with some buds, then definitely give this game (and season pass) some consideration, but if you're looking for some hip new competetive Class Shooter and/or Moba, stay away from this like you'd stay away from a dumpster filled with burning anthrax.
PS: The humor's pretty hit-or-miss I guess? A good chunk of the main campaign delves into that whole "haha guys wasn't that joke funny haha" crap that modern Gearbox has become known for, but the season pass missions actually have some funny stuff, as well as the character one-liners. Just don't expect anything on the level of Tim & Eric or MDE, it wouldn't be Gearbox writing if it didn't appeal to the lowest common denominator.
8/10 Co-op
0/10 Competetive (I normally calculate these final scores with an overly-complex multi-score method whose math I leave out of the review. I completely skipped doing so for this game's competetive, it's just that not-worth-your-time.)

Alright. I'm basing this review off of the game itself, not the other factors like the playerbase, matchmaking, etc etc. That is a problem created by players, and fixed by players. So, for any prospective buyers, here's my pros/cons list of what I believe to be an extremely enjoyable game.
Pros:
-Wide variety of characters, each one feeling highly unique from the last
-Singleplayer/co-op story mode, complete with voice acting and all the Gearbox comedy you'd expect from one of their games
-Unique leveling system, which can make each playthrough of a character different from the last.
-Lots of cosmetics, if that's your thing (I love them, myself)
Cons:
-Story mode can feel a tad short and shallow, though the gameplay is still quite enjoyable
-Voice acting only slows when in the level up screen, which can make it somewhat annoying to read through perks, if there is dialogue going on
-The leveling system of each character can feel a little bit grindy, coupled with the loudout system
Overall, I love this game. I wouldn't recommend paying full price for it, but if you notice a sale, I recommend picking it up. At a sale price, even the story mode on its own is worth it, in my opinion.

Certainly a must-have for fans of the Hitman franchise. Grab it for cheap during a sale.

Someone's gonna want to shoot me for saying this, but I don't care: I think Payday 2 is better than Payday 1.
BANG
With that said, here's my comparison for the two, staying as factual as an opinion can be, so you can decide for yourself what you want.
Payday 1:
Pros:
-Large, complex heists
-RNG is much less significant, you'll never be screwed before you start.
Neutral:
-Very difficult. This could be a pro or con depending on your perspective, but Payday 1 will destroy you if you go in without preparing, and will probably destroy you even if you do prepare for it.
Cons:
-Low weapon variety
-Upgrade system: The upgrades are given to you in a specific order within 1 of 4 "trees" (really, they're sticks, a straight line). This means that, even if you never use the Crosskill, you may still have to upgrade it before you can upgrade the Brenner.
-Loot system- You're paid for completeing objectives, meaning that you could make potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars without ever seeing the vault (in fact, there's a farming method involving playing First World Bank on the highest difficulty, completing the first few objectives, then suiciding on the first assault wave).
-Only 9 heists- it may sound like plenty, but you'll get tired of them fast as you try to max out your upgrades
-Enemy AI is incompetant
-Allied bots are useless
Payday 2:
Pros:
-Much larger variety in heists, even without DLC
-More characters
-Many more weapons
-Upgrade system-You buy a weapon, then you modify it. No trees involved.
-Stealth heists
-Loot system: You're paid for securing loot. In many cases, you have to bag loot and carry it to a secure area.
-Greater enemy variety
-More contacts (you aren't just listening to Bain the whole time)
-More variety in difficulty. Death Wish and One Down are just as hard, if not harder than, Overkill was in Payday 1, but the lower difficulties ease you into the game, allowing you to get equipment and experience to prepare you for the harder difficulties.
Neutral
-Enemy AI is smarter. Not by much, but it's there.
-Allied bots are more useful. Again not by much (unless you want to install this:
), but at least they can soak up tons of damage while you accomplish things.
Cons:
-Alot of DLC (however, sales are frequent and significant)
-More simplistic heists
-Weapon mods are almost entirely controlled by RNG.
-RNG can screw you over easily (it's possible for a stealth run to be made near impossible by a door to the camera control room not spawning-it's not even a glitch)
They're both good games, really. But if you're a newcomer, I see no point in buying Payday 1 when Payday 2 exists

Guacamelee! is
a beat'em-up/metroidvania hybrid. Whilst this may sound like a mouthful and a muddled game, what we get is a fun, cool and decently long adventure romp, that is sure to please many people around.
Juan is a farmer who, when his love is kidnapped, takes on the mask and becomes a Luchador! Thus he begins his quest to save his love, smash Chozo statues and kick as many skeletons, cacti and bosses to faces Cacala, a mysterious soul who has the form of a skeleton. Along the way Juan unlocks powers from the Chozo statues and some bosses. What is very cool about this game is that many of the powers translate to combat (which, as mentioned, is in a beat'em-up style), such as the [Rooster] Uppercut not only sending the enemies into the air but also giving up a lift mid-jump. Or the Dashing [Derp Derp] helping you kick multiple enemies whilst going a little bit further horizontally.
You can also change dimensions to reveal platforms or passages, or turn into a chicken to go into smaller passages. These are used for some challenging, but fun, platforming and puzzle sections.
The soundtrack is also great, mixing Latin music with some techno. And almost all songs have alternate versions, for the Light and Dark dimensions. These transition well, and the soundtrack feels relative the the setting and tone of the game, Mexican, Upbeat and overall fun.
I finished the game at around 65%-70% completion, so I still had a lot to collect, and I played the game for a good 6 hours (it says 12 as my file deleted... grumble grumble...). This percentage is made up of Health Containers, Stamina Blocks and Orbs (hard-to-find objects for the dedicated). I finished Cacala's final form with difficulty, but not to a extent where it felt cheap or annoying.
Guacamelee! is a fun game, with a good soundtrack and an easy 6 hours of gameplay. Looking for a good game to spend some time with over the weekend? Grab Guacamelee! (and the soundtrack) and you won't regret it.

I've played this game about 3 hours, give or take. I don't want to pretend to be an expert already, especially how voxel based games tend to lend themselves to extensive hours of creative building. But, at the moment, I've managed to touch all of the content the game has to offer, outside of cosmetic differences (biomes, etc.)
The base premise reminds me of Dwarf Fortress, in a way. You can, and should, set your colonists up to automate all aspects of resource gathering. The only direct intervention you -need- to do after a certain point is to bring in more colonists and build structures.
Combat is simple and straightforward at this point. You shoot zombies. Your colonists can be assigned to shoot zombies. Zombies want to kill you, your colonists, and your banner. Your colonists don't have the best aim, but they can take down anything moving in a straight line towards or away from them reasonably well.
It looks beautiful. Even the colonists have a certain charm to them.
At the moment, there isn't much true depth to the game. But there is a lot of juicy potential. I have a few suggestions.
This game can, and should, turn out to be great. I have faith. I'm content with the price at this point if it means the possibility of something deeper.

In their zeal to make a game that features all the things the AVGN has complained about, they managed to make a game that is only slightly below average. One would expect that the novelty would make up for it--having useless power-ups, cheap deaths, and all that were intentional design choices, after all, so you know that you're buying into that when you buy the game. In addition to this, though, AVGN Adventures has clear problems that should have been fixed.
Serious Problems:
Movement. The characters move with all the precision of Meat Boy. This makes playing the level "Beat Em and Eat Em", which features a ton of slippery surfaces, even more frustating. The imprecise controls are one thing, but there is something else that combines with them that, honestly, threaten to make AVGN Adventures unplayable. And that "something" is:
The camera. Rather than centering the AVGN, AVGN Adventures has him just slightly to the left of the center when you're moving to the right, and just slightly to the right of the camera when you're moving left. Changing directions on the fly becomes borderline impossible, because the camera shifts, too, which can and will totally screw up whatever difficult platforming section you were trying to get through. And that's a problem because of:
Knockback. The knockback in this game is weird. I'd tentatively say that the knockback consists primarily of you getting hit UP, not backward or forward. In good games, knockback is predictable, and can even be taken advantage of. There's none of that here, and the unusual knockback will be a source of many deaths, simply because it's non-standard and very difficult to get used to. And, naturally, there aren't very many platforming sections that don't feature enemies coming at you, because:
The level design in AVGN Adventures is horrendous. It's dull, uninspired, and boring. As ProJared rightly pointed out, there are actually only a few enemy types in the game, and what they look like simply varies based on what stage you're in.
And, as ProJared also points out, the developers substituted instant death blocks instead of creative level design. Predictable disappearing/reappearing Deathblocks appear in almost every stage, and they're not really difficult to get past; it just requires you to wait. There's a lot of waiting in this game. Something ♥♥♥♥balls is the most obvious offender: half of the stage is filled with instant death beams that are ridiculously easy to avoid and accomplish little more than making you wait for 3 seconds every 15 steps. This will almost certainly be the first level that you beat without dying at all.
And you'll be glad to not die often, because dying is tedious. Even though there's an obscene number of checkpoints, even on Normal mode, death is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because the developers thought it would be funny to have a random AVGN statement about what he'd rather do than continue playing--every. single. time. you. die.
And you die a lot. That's kinda the point of the game, supposedly being Nintendo Hard. But it's not. This is AVGN Adventure's main flaw: it PRETENDS to be Nintendo Hard by throwing a lot of cheap deaths at the player, but it's actually a very easy game. This is no I Wanna Be the Guy, which throws up a lot of cheap deaths AND is Nintendo Hard. I can't quantify what the difference is.
It's a short game. It can be beaten in just a few hours, which makes that $9.99 price tag WAY too high. For $2.99 or $3.99, I could recommend this. But at $9.99? You're paying more than $1 per hour for an experience that... just isn't that good.
People often say that the music in AVGN Adventures is awesome. But that's not true. The only level in the game that has good music is Something ♥♥♥♥balls, and I'll give it that--that level's music is incredibly awesome. But that's only one-ninth of the game; what about the other 8 levels? They're nothing special, and a few are actually annoying. One stage has really awesome music, but 8/9 of the stages have boring, uninteresting music, yet the game is still cited as having awesome music. It doesn't. It has one stage that has awesome music. The rest of the music kinda sucks.
Almost all of the bosses are the same, too, including the final boss. There are one or two exceptions, but most of the bosses just move around in a figure 8 while shooting things.
So here you have a game that would have quickly faded into obscurity if it didn't have the AVGN's name attached to it. There's a sequel coming out relatively soon, and my sincerest hope is that the developers took a few lessons in creative level design before then, because I don't consider filling a stage with death blocks, using only 5 or 6 enemies, and making players wait constantly to be "creative". Even the final boss is just a rehash of several other bosses in the game, with nothing unique or new going on anywhere at all. Take that $9.99 and buy the Mega Man Legacy Collection instead. You'll get way more entertainment out of Mega Man than AVGN Adventures.
To that, you're probably saying, "Well, duh!"
And that's my point EXACTLY. They're both $9.99.

It's a simple premise: shoot and jump your way through each stage, all while collecting power ups and dodging an insane amount of obstacles. That's it. And it works. Aside from the great gameplay, this is also a fantastic low-brow homage to the games of yesteryear. The incessant profanity made me laugh, too.
Buy this game. Expect a torrent of swear words and colorful metaphors to explode from your mouth, but it's a gratifying experience when you finally beat it.

Cossacks 3 "RE"review (October 2016)
It appears most of the game debilitating bugs and crashes have been worked out after release although it was very aggravating having to deal with such nonsense for a paid for product. I think the price did reflect properly but regardless if it had been $60, I may have just asked for a refund instead of waiting out the patches. That being said, I am happy to see the devs reach out to the community directly (see comments below) in an effort to work with and through the software issues in an attempt to address them as quickly as possible. I have never seen a dev studio do this and it speaks volumes of magnitude for GSC Game World.
The game plays well now, the audio score is fantastic and the effects of the muskets and cannon are tremendous. It certainly has the old school base building elements and micro managing of the economy in check.
Unit upgradability can get tiresome and in my opinion detracts from the combat elements but overall this can be overlooked as this is the "tiering" element of the game.
Formations are cool and do play a vital part into overall strategy. Hint for the noobies, adding an officer and drummer to a formation requires at least 36 of the same unit type. 36 is your magic number so don't forget it. These little types of requirements are not immediately apparent but do come in time as you and gain more experience with the gameplay.
Is it the most epic RTS of all time, no but it does bring back the old school to the new generations of operating systems. If you are in the market for an Age of Empires type of game on an epic combat scale, then this title might be for you!

I bought this game in...December 2014, Jesus. Anyway, now I've finally finished it, and here are my thoughts.
Gameplay-wise, KotOR is just the Star Wars tabletop RPG system transplanted into a game. Now, I've spent a lot of time playing the Star Wars tabletop RPG, so as soon as I figured out what was going on I got the hang of it fairly quickly. It works pretty well overall, with plenty of space for different playstyles and gameplay options. However, being a tabletop system, it's dice-based, which means lots of random variation in combat. This occasionally can be ♥♥♥♥ing frustrating, especially when you're close to killing an enemy and then you get 5 misses in a row instead of a critical hit through no fault of your own.
The game looks fairly dated, although the prerendered cinematics are generally alright. The skyboxes are pretty, too.
The writing on the characters is nice, and the voice acting executes it well. The plot is similarly well-done, and has a few fun surprises and quirky interactions.
Occasionally it suffers from an issue where the engine and memory limitations severely reduce the scale of environments. Several times you find yourself in an impossibly large city, which the game can only represent with about 8 locations and a small crowd of NPCs.
For some reason, the first world was the most boring one for me, leading to my long gaps between trying to play the game. It does get better later (although that's not a very good excuse).
The game stretches the limits of its own mechanics to bring you as many new and interesting experiences as possible. Every mechanic seems to have been carefully analyzed to see if it could in some way yield a new gameplay element. For example, at one point, you use the ability to place items in containers to place a grenade in a pile of bones to kill a rancor. It's fun, and it leads to several gameplay situations you wouldn't think of.
The difficulty curve is all over the place. Some boss fights are astonishingly easy, while some random, everyday fights can get really goddamn hard, leading to levels of save-scumming not seen since the original Fallout games. Some of this may be due to quirks in my character and party builds, but it really seems like they didn't quality-test the combat enough.
The Steam port is...not great. It's actually pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥. Graphical glitches abound, sometimes leaving giant lattices of gray and brown blocking out the screen. Crashes are somewhat common, especially near the end. During the already annoying turret sections, control is near-impossible because the mouse sensitivity skyrockets for no reason. None of this is a deal-breaker, but do be warned.
Overall, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is good. It's well-written, it's interesting, and it has core gameplay that's satisfying and varied. The randomness and jankiness of the combat sometimes gets in the way, it's a bit boring at the start, and the whole thing is kinda unstable, but these issues don't overcome the best parts of the game. I recommend it.

The soundtrack matches the game's atmosphere very well, and is paced to amplify the current mood the player is being presented.
It is worth it for anyone interested in good gaming stories, stealth games, or action games to play this game once, as it is an excellent example of all three of those aspects.

This game is challenging. Not only are you and your crew severely outnumbered and outgunned (naturally; this is an FPS), your counterparts in law enforcement quickly take your heist efforts quite seriously. In practical, game-playing terms this means they will, among other things: mousehole (read: use explosives to give themselves additional, alternate points of entry and attack), insert SWAT teams via helicopter, conduct aggressive assaults, and deploy special units who can ruin your crime spree before it gains steam.
Luckily, this game is also a lot of fun. You can unlock a lot weapons, gadgets, and accessories--all of which are highly upgradeable--to make your livelihood as a professional criminal at least a little easier. For me, Payday's biggest hook is its replayability. Besides all the stuff to earn and upgrades you can get, there are: multiple difficulty settings, the option to team up with AI partners or other players, achievements and challenges, and variability within the heists themselves--you could play a given heist ten times and each time it could unfold differently.

Blue Estate is an excellent rail shooter that brings me back to the days of arcades playing House of the Dead and Virtua Cop. This game has basic shooting mechanics while you mosey along a predetermined path, like a theme park ride, or every US president election for the past hundred years.
What Blue Estate brings to the table is its own weird sense of humor full of pop-culture references,♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes, and a nerdy narrator telling the story as if he were some noir detective. There are also some cool visual effects scattered throughout levels that give the visuals a bit of a comic book feel, without going full-blown cell shaded graphics or anything headache inducing.
The scoring system is fun and encourages replaying levels, with scoring more headshots (and nut shots), shooting collectible items like balloons, and taking less damage. There are also contextual sorta-Quick-Time-Event things that take advantage of the arrow keys, but they rarely interfere with the action, and only spice up the gameplay so it isn't just a mouse affair.
TL;DR: Fun rail shooter, funny jokes, arrow key QTEs, doesn't overstay its welcome. GG

This is actually a surprisingly good game. The track design is very nice. There's an array of cars and drivers, which you select separately. Each car and driver has their own stats, and they add together for some customization. Each car has a different paint-job depending on the driver as well.
The game's main gimmick is heat. There's a strong risk-vs-reward element, and it's all about managing heat. When your car overheats, it blows up. When you use boost, your heat gauge rises. As you boost you also cause one of a few flame effects, depending on your car. Some cars leave a trail of flame when boosting, some have a ring of fire, etc. These are your weapons, since any opponents caught in your flames take on more heat themselves.
Any water on the track will cool you down if you drive through it, be it blue water barrels, puddles, waterfalls, or skimming the surf.
No idea how well multiplayer works, haven't seen anyone online to try it with.
I can see this becoming a sleeper hit.

Al Emmo and the Lost Dutchman's Mine is not my favourite Adventure Game. The story lacks the weight that would drive a more serious plot; there's no underlying urgency or driving force. As a result, I felt like I could stop at any time.
With that said, I enjoyed the humor and the story quite a bit, more than enough to see the game through to the end. I also enjoyed the growth of the protagonist from a shallow and pitiable (but likable) character into a much stronger and more complex individual.
There are also other things I liked about the game. The puzzles are solid, challenging and enjoyable. The artwork is simply stunning. The supporting characters are fun and interesting. The music, while not particularly memorable, complemented the settings perfectly.
Overall, the only element I felt that had weakness was the story. Al Emmo would have benefited from having a darker undertone clearly woven into the story right from the beginning. This element would have contrasted the humor and ultimately strengthened it. In addition, the urgency that a darker element could provide would have given the story a drive that it lacked.
However, if you can get past this point, you'll find Al Emmo and the Lost Dutchman's Mine to be a fun, humorous adventure, and an overall decent game.

I played the original version of Al Emmo back in the days when it was first released in 2007, I beleive. It's nice to see that things have been continually improved upon in this new Steam edition with enhancements to both the visuals and voices. I think this is a rather under-rated adventure game, tbh. Game has many throwbacks to retro Sierra adventures. The game world has unique narration vocals for everything you can possibly look, interact and talk with! And every inventory item in the game has NPCs saying unique lines when showing them your items. In an era where most new adventure games trim the fat, so to speak, by limiting interactions and forcing players to use a single 'smart' cursor to cover all interactions, it's refreshing to see this adventure has a very descriptive world where the level of interactive modes and descriptions invites you to explore further instead of just guiding you along a binary path where they can either interact or not interact with a hotspot. The characters were all interesting enough to hold my attention and the story is just 'there', I suppose, but it never left me feeling bored or made my thoughts wander off. This game's sense of humor will probably resonate more with some people than others, as much of the humor is slapstick innuendo. Personally, I liked it and felt the quality of the writing was quite high. Your mileage may vary with the jokes though. Puzzles were well placed and seemed to be set to just the right difficulty. I was never stumped for too long, but also never really felt that anything was unfairly illogical. Overall, I enjoyed my time with Al Emmo and it's a recommend from me.

It’s an on rails shooter (similar to arcades) but it’s pretty good using a mouse. The emphasis here is on accurate shooting rather than holding down the trigger. A bunch of enemies show up and they can’t damage you until a circle above their heads fills up so you have time to take out the whole squad one at a time. Headshots are pretty much the only way to do this so a basic pistol can get you pretty far.
The disappointment comes in the lack of weapons or upgrades. You get a pistol and either a machine gun, shotgun, or a revolver and unless you’re using the machine gun, it doesn’t make sense to use it because reload time and clip size are more important than damage spread. So most of the time, I played the game clicking one head at a time. It’s challenging once you turn off aim assist but the game never evolves away from that. Since there are no upgrades and you can’t choose your characters or guns, the gameplay never evolves and becomes kinda samey.

My opinions on Blue Estate The Game are a bit mixed. On the one hand, it's a competent rail shooter with a pretty decent sense of humor. On the other hand, it's short and doesn't offer a whole lot of replay value, making it's $13 non-sale asking price rather high, considering the many better alternatives you can buy at that price.
Blue Estate plays a bit like Virtua Cop or House of the Dead, but instead of a lightgun, you use either your mouse or a controller. I'll admit that I've not tried playing with a controller, but I honestly can't imagine it'd be very good. On the other hand, a mouse makes the game pretty easy, in theory, and it is rather easy, usually. Every once in a while, you'll get prompted to move in a direction, which can be accomplished either by pushing the arrow keys on the keyboard or moving the mouse in that direction. There are also a small variety of "mini-game" parts to the levels, which generally task you with shooting enemies in a certain order. There's also a more powerful alternative to the pistol in every level, with different degrees of power and ammo capacity (and limited ammo), which usually become your go-to weapons once you pick it up. (The last level would be an exception, in my opinion—a five-shot revolver that, while powerful, leaves you reloading more often than it's worth.) These mechanics help to keep the gameplay from ever really getting stale.
The story/writing also helps a bit. You play as two characters: Tony Luciano, the semi-incompetent son of the local don who starts out to rescue his favorite "dancer" from an Asian gang that kidnapped her, which leads to the don's favorite horse Blue Estate being kidnapped; and Clarence, an ex-Navy SEAL mercenary hired to clean up Tony's mess—and to get Blue Estate back, because the Don loves that horse much more than his son. Admittedly, the story's nothing to write home about, but the game's always throwing some form of dumb joke or absurdity at you, either from the characters, the incompetent geeky detective narrator, or via the "FPS Authority", who kindly interrupts the game every once in a while to bring the narrator's hyperbole crashing to the ground, point out the unlikelihood/impossibility of a situation, or compare a situation to a John Woo or Michael Bay film.
The game only takes three hours or less to complete, which is fine—it ends right about when it's about to outstay its welcome. That said, there's really no reason to dive back into the game once you complete it.
Like many games, this is a console port, and like many console ports, this game has a rather severe lack of options. You can adjust the gamma, adjust the sound levels, and adjust the controls to some extent. That's it. For most people, this is a non-problem, actually. The game should run fine on any reasonably modern PC, with full support for high refresh rates and natively rendering at the resolution you play at, unlike certain other rail shooters. (I'm looking at you, The Typing of the Dead: Overkill.)
Now while I did actually enjoy my time playing Blue Estate, due to the fact that Steam doesn't offer a mixed recommendation option, I'm going to have to recommend against this game. It's short, has poor replayability, doesn't do much to innovate, has a sense of humor that not everyone will enjoy, and its asking price is much too high when not on sale.
: If you're really hankering for a good rail shooter, pick this up on sale for cheap; otherwise, you're not missing out on anything major by skipping this game.

A visually pleasing game. A few funny references here and there, but not over-the-top too many.
You can unlock different costumes in-game that best suit your favorite style of play. My favorite is the chicken suit; in the middle of a tough fight I can hide away and regenerate some health.  The Skeleton suit lets you do endless supermoves. Another suit makes your slams really strong. And so on.  When you get into some of the really hairy fights you'll almost wish the slamjam song were playing.
The gameplay is fun, beat-em-up with strategy involved, but also platforming.  In fact once you get about halfway through the game some of the jumps and platforming tricks you have to do are a little frustratingly difficult.  With a little practice and patience (you get as many fall-off-the-screen deaths as you want), you can make it through.  Except maybe a couple of the secret items... getting them (tula tree and sierra, I'm looking at you!) are fairly insane no matter how much you've practiced.
Don't speed-run, at least not the first time. Take your time and enjoy the game.  The boss fights each have their own flavor and they each seem fairly impossible at first, but then you clue in on the boss's strategy after a couple tries... almost reminds me (not really) of the old NES game Punch-Out... the bosses are HARD at first but they telegraph most of their moves and once you learn to read the tells and react... presto.
And oh. Make sure you have a controller for this one.  You *can* play with the keyboard... but don't do it.
The only con I can think of, is that if you're a completionist, you might throw your laptop across the room (then kick it a few times for good measure) at the Tula Tree...  that and you can't decide to marry X'tabay.  Caliente!

I did'nt think this game would be fun but it actually was. First impressions; yes, it looks exactly like Minecraft with a texture pack, yes the people look like weird stick figures, kinda like south park canadians, it looks childish honestly.
This game is FAR from childish im my opinion. It does give you creative freedom, and most of us lack that.
Cons:
-Lack of Content
This game has so many unique abilities for the player(s) It does have biomes, different ores, blocks, woods, trees, stone, wool, you name it. But it still lacks more. There's science to research, but not many. There's blocks to create, but not many, There's jobs for villagers, not many. There's specific farmable plots of land you can put down, but not many. This game needs, flags / banners, character customization, AI customization, dyes, glass, carts, posts, fences, etc... There will probobly never be enough honestly.
-Greifing
Currently in servers, there's no way to prevent greifing, punish it, nor fix it.
-Servers / Server Commands
Servers get very buggy and laggy. They are hosted off the admins computer, which even if their comp is decent, the servers still tend to lagg. Also, there's little server commands available to admins. You can set ones group and permissions. Meaning their ability to teleport or cheat. Once they have this you can't revoke that power from said people.
-Textures
The textures are really nice looking and beautiful. But with some of that 3D modeling, it takes a toll on your comp. Also, where ever you go, as long as it's the same biome, the grass is the same. No random dirt blocks, gravel, no change in texture. Same with stone underground. Characters also look bland and unanimated. There should be a way to chage a character.
Even though there are many cons, no game is perfect, but this is close. Even with all these cons, the game is still in early access. Everything we have right now is subject to change. The devs are working hard to raise this game. There's a modding community already modding this game. This game has so much potential!

ジャンルはステルス性重視のサードパーソンシューティング。ゲームの目的は組織から標的の暗殺を請け負い、様々な方法でターゲットを殺害できる（絞殺・毒殺・溺殺・崖から突き落とす・銃殺・事故死を装うなど）。暗殺がどれだけスマートに行われたかによって支払われる報酬が変わり、受け取った報酬で武器や装備をアップグレードできる。また、報酬は任務にかかわる情報（ヒント）を購入したり市民からの悪評度を下げるためにも使えるため、いかに高額な報酬を得られるかが次回以降のステージ攻略へと直接影響する。

This is a depressing situation, much as I loathe to admit it.
As someone who has played Battleborn, Overwatch, and Paladins, I have to say that I thought this game was probably the best. It just had more going for it: it had a story mode (even if it wasn't much), it had more unique game modes, more like an actual FPS/MOBA hybrid than a recycling of TF2's game modes. The characters were interesting and varied, and I immediately set goals of who I would try to unlock first (I basically started maining Ambra as soon as I got her). I didn't regret paying for this game when it came out. I still don't: even though I suck at FPS games and my computer strained to run this game, I enjoyed it.
Unfortunately, the game is simply dead. Virtually no one is playing it; the last time I loaded it up, it took ages just to get a less-than-full party playing one of the story missions (I didn't try the PVP modes, mainly because with my computer, the performance level hinders my ability to play competitively. There might be more players there, but I've heard there aren't). So unfortunately, I can't recommend the game on that basis: it's a really fun game, but there are so few people to play it with that it probably is not worth your money. And I hate that.
If the game ever goes free to play (as some have speculated it will), then I say give it a shot; I certainly will be back. Until then, RIP Battleborn.

I've got a few gripes about this game;
- Most of the humor is corny and imo just plain annoying
- The story isn't too interesting and relatively short
- Using the mouse to shoot while your character is moving is infuriating, this makes combos so hard to maintain and makes it necessary for you to turn on aim assist
- Gameplay doesn't offer much variety other than the environments
- Even though the bosses are unique, their fights don't offer much of a challenge and ends up being incredibly tedious, especially the Bloodshot boss

Overall; if you can get past all these negatives ,which pretty much sums up the whole game, and have nothing else to play, get it, but ONLY if it's on sale

I am a child of the 80's and love these adventure games.  AGD interactive and Infamous adventures have done a great job in preserving these games and giving them a little twist.  Al Emmo keeps with the spirit of these old games. Adventure, Puzzles with a quirky sense of humor. It is an original game that will keep you entertained.  Adventure games from this era keep you really engaged.  Talk to everyone, click on everthing and think outside the box. This game is exactly what it says on the tin. A retro styled point & click adventure game that takes inspiration from the golden era of Sierra and Lucasarts. While the game is quite old now, I still remember first buying it almost ten years ago when Telltale Games were selling it on their store. I enjoyed it back then and I like the improvements to this new enhanced edition. The game is a very niche title made for adventure game fans from a specific era. The newer generation of gamers who are unaccustomed to this style of old school adventure games may be left scratching their heads and they may not understand what the appeal is. But as a gamer of the golden era I absolutely revel in a game where every single item has a unique description and there's a large, dangerous and very descriptive open land to explore with interesting characters and quests to solve. Yes, this game has all that and more. It's classic Sierra adventure, through and through.
It's a bold risk on the developer's part to use such a non-heroic character for their protagonist, but I don't think the game suffers for it. In fact I found that I actually got attached to the little guy! A few little quirks here and there can't override a solid adventure gaming experience. It's a thumbs up from me.

Al Emmo and the Lost Dutchman’s Mine is a reminder that while games come in many forms nowadays, there’s nothing quite as satisfying as a classic adventure.

Himalaya Studios (formerly Tierra/AGD Interactive) has a long history of making quality adventure games and they don't disappoint with their first paid outting. While not quite up to the standards that I had expected from their King's Quest remakes, Al Emmo is still a hilarious and fun romp through a Western town. It's full of in-jokes and bad puns, which is a plus to anyone who wants a good laugh. The puzzles are pretty intuitive and with some thought can be easily solved with time. There were a couple minor things that I found mildly offensive, but not enough to diminish my overall experience. For anyone who wants a good comedy adventure set in the Wild West, I highly recommend this one.

Well, here goes my review to one of the best RTS ever made.
If you never played or owned any Cossacks game, i wouldn't even bother thinking about if you should or shouldn't get this game, because it simply is a
. If you love RTS with building aspect then there is no way around this game. Absolutely flawless core game for singleplayer experience.
As of this point i really cannot recommend the multiplayer of this game. 5 out of 5 times i've tried to get into a multiplayer match there seemed to be some kind of issue with the connection or the game not working. I'm sure they will fix this and make the mutliplayer actually work. I would highly recommend holding off on buying this for the multiplayer.
Well, what is there to say, it's basically the same original Cossacks you probably loved back then and will probably love again. If you want to get more fun into an old game then i sure would get this. It's a classic game with new art style and up to date graphics and sounds. Some elements have been taken out, and some new elements have been implemented.
They seemed to have taken out the 18th century ship of the line, which was an absolute beast in the original game. And further the option to repair you ships of the line has been removed. I assume for balancing purpose.
But one element that has been added is the option to "re-fill" your soldier formations with "loose" untis who are close by. This gets rid of the issue of having to break up your formations if they are missing units and then having to re-form them to get them back up to full strength.
The most amount of units i have had so far was around 1.500 units including peasants in a 1v1 match against hard NPC.
With GTX 980 ti sc i was still having 60FPS even with more than 800 units on the screen at the same time. Occationally it dipped down to just below 60, but never had any major FPS problems. So far the game seems to be surprisingly good optimized, because i was initially expecting worse. But of course there is always room for improvements.
The game seems to run perfectly fine, not a single crash yet after 8 hours. And i have not encountered any bugs or glitches.
+ Great looking game with up to date visuals
+ Good performance on high end systems
+ Nostalgia and revival of an old beloved game for a decent price
+ Perfect experience for singleplayer game
~ New music which might not be everyone's taste. I personally enjoyed the original music more.
~ Peasants "answer" for selecting them is more quiet now. I liked to get more of a response from selecting them as in the original game.
~ Some gun sounds and explotions sound less cool in my opinion. Better quality audio but less crackin' and boomin'. But it depends on personal preference.
- Multiplayer doesn't seem to work yet. I'm sure they will fix it though.
- Drummers don't drum anymore. (no marching drum sound) (i always found this to be very atmospheric)
- Some old features as mentioned above have been taken out.
- Decent selection of Nations, but less than i expected of would have wished for.
Overall i would still recommend this game, especially for singleplayer. For me it has been a solid experience so far and i enjoyed every bit of it. To all multiplayer folks and low-end/med-end systems i would probably wait until it is more polished. But eventually definitely get it!

When I play Renowned Explorers, I tend to get into obsessive sessions with it, especially when attempting the weekly challenges (another great way to enjoy the game if you go on the discussions page). You can play just to enjoy the exploration, the feeling of going on a new expedition and the wonder and surprise when you see something new, or you can go the competitive route and try going for a high score, testing out all of the different strategies to do so. I've enjoyed the game in both respects, and the devs have done great work at patching the game to better both types of players' experience. There are two DLCs that add a lot to the game for a great price, but aren't at all required, and if you're like me, you can milk the game for a lot of hours at a fairly low price, and I'm still not done.

You would be hard pressed to find a game that has more love put into it than this. Renowned Explorers is a Rogue-Like placed in the 19 century where you explore distant lands to explore and gather treasures from. Not only does it manage to be a fantastic Rogue-Like, but it also has great character personalitys and humor within it.
You will start out wondering what to do and how everything works, but it won't ward you off with anything that's too hard to gain a grasp of. No matter your skill level, everyone can enjoy this game in equal measure. You'll gain a sense of pride as you see your end-game score getting higher and higher as you continue to improve, learn, and make your own strategies.
As I said earlier, the characters within the game are the delicious side to this savory steak. All character have unique personalitys (including backstorys on the title screen) that you will grow fond. No 2 characters are alike here in this wacky but lovable group of Renowned Explorers. They are even given unique voices and animations for their attacks that just adds even more likeability. Even the side-characters and areas you explore are easy to adore.
This is one of the greatest games of all time in my opinion, and to top it all off, the community is incredibly welcoming and kind. If you are atall interested in this game, I implore you to take a chance on it and fall in love with the craft and detail of it all.

Al Emmo and the Lost Dutchman's Mine (AEatLDM) was a point & click adventure game that I honestly didn't think I would bother playing, but I had it from buying bundles it featured in, so I gave it a go while keeping my expectations cautiously low.
So the narrative revolves around a middle-aged balding virgin named Al Emmo who ventures to a small town to meet his bride.... who he paid for. However, when she meets him and it turns out that he has no cash to his name, she quickly leaves. Emmo is then awestruck by another lady and sets out upon his mission to win her heart through a series of ideas to impress her and also make himself a little cash over the course of 9 chapters of varying length. The entire game hinges on the way this story plays out and Emmo's comedic interactions with everyone around him (and also how the narrator berates Emmo for being a useless human being). The game has many short-comings, but comedy is definitely not one of them. I found the game was able to make me laugh a lot, cringe often, chuckle every few minutes, and it even managed to develop a sort of bond (through pity) for the hapless Emmo. Unfortunately this game suffers almost everywhere outside of the writing though. One of these areas is the way the game is broken down in to chapters, with each chapter being a new day. Some chapters are quite long, but there are a couple where you literally have to find a couple of items and they only take 5 minutes. The pacing of the game never quite feels right because of this.
As a computer game, AEatLDM plays incredibly slowly... even for a point & click game this plays slowly (which is really saying something). Every animation feels clunky, and Emmo himself moves so painfully slowly that you could die of boredom when transitioning screens. Some items are quite obvious that you can interact with them, but some are part of the pre-rendered background and are not obvious at all which leads to the game feeling padded as you often have to re-visit areas to find items you did not pick up earlier. There is a quick travel system that allows you to go to quickly visit about 5 landmark areas which probably saved me from just quitting this game completely, but even with the fast-travel it still felt like a chore re-visiting old areas. Aside from the slow gameplay, the puzzles are often not very logical. While this is to be expected in a comedic game, it can seriously hamper players trying to progress as answers often do not make sense. While the gameplay itself is tedious, for the most part this does not stop me enjoying point & click adventure games, however the final boss requires some quite precise movement (and timing) which this game simply was not designed for. The final boss ends up being an incredibly messy affair where even if you are doing the right thing you will still end up dying over & over again due to the frustrating movement of Emmo.
Now if you have actually loaded up AEatLDM, you may have noticed something straight away... the game is ugly. The cartoon cut-scenes are actually quite well done, but the game uses low resolution and during gameplay you will be staring at some very pixelated scenes that are usually saturated with yellow sand. The graphics are just about good enough to get by, but there is nothing good to actually say about them (so I wont). You can mostly tell what item is what, and what is actually happening on the screen, but due to the low resolution there are no small details that you can admire. What you see is what you get, and nothing more.
The sound is at odds to the graphics in that they are actually quite good (mostly). The voice-acting is clear, and every character has a distinct voice. The soundtrack is not particularly inspiring though, which is a little annoying considering there is often a lot of "adventuring" between your conversations. Also, there is one character who has TERRIBLE voice-acting and scripting. The barman, who Emmo meets at least once every day, has some of the worst voice-acting I have ever heard. His scripting does not come across as realistic and his voice sounds like it was recorded in a garage on a 20 year-old microphone. It is a real shame as that one characters brings down the rest of the game when everyone else is actually quite well written and voiced.
This may sound odd after mostly pointing out the game's various flaws, but I actually enjoyed what time I spent with Emmo. This is not a good
at all, but it is a
. If you like laughing, and also point & click games, then give this a go. It certainly has a very unique charm.
a final note of warning to those of you that are achievement hunters: avoid this game.
The achievements are mostly very well hidden and rather cryptic. I completed the game and only managed 5 of 20. I dont mind this, but I know some people might find that off-putting.

I really enjoy my time with this game!
While I am not a fan of games that try too hard to 'bring back the past' by featuring 8-bit graphics and old-school mechanics borrowed from NES games, I do enjoy hard 2D platforming games that require patience and memorization.
AVGN Adventures is definitely it's own thing and does not rely on you having any sort of nostalgia for the genre. It has a distinct visual style, very well implemented mechanics that are both old-school and new, and is just generally one of the few examples of a modern 2D platformer done right. Sure, there is a little bit of trial and error, but I would say that patient players will not find themselves frustrated with the level design and the death traps. The level design is devilish, but not unfair! Really, all of your skill depends on whether or not you can remain calm and on how fast you pick up on shortcuts through levels and boss fights. Secrets are hard to find (I would say impossible) and I would suggest looking at a guide to find all the cameos and characters to help you on your way through any of the higher difficulties.
If you are a AVGN fan, you'll definitely get more of a kick out of the game as there's lots of references. I can imagine the 'dialogue' in the game being grating to non-fans as you can't turn it off. That quickly becomes a problem for anyone that wants to replay the game multiple times, as the dialogue still remains there.
The game can be beaten in an hour on lower difficulties, but the game banks on you replaying it on higher unlockable difficulties. If you like earning achievements, this game makes it really satisfying to get them (for the most part). I played it for 8 hours according to my timer, and I have only beaten the game on 2 difficulties so far (Normal and Old-School). All that changes is that you have more limited amounts of lives and harder to beat enemies to face (as well as other small things).
All in all, AVGN Adventures is definitely a memorable 2D Platformer and definitely an instant-classic for AVGN fans. For everyone else, though, this will just be a fun experience for a few hours. I recommend it to anyone who likes a simple game with challenging level design and a lust for earning achievements.
This game is only going to appeal to those that like a great challenge and can be persistent. All in all, for me, it was a great experience.

I would like to recommend this game, but in its current state, I can't quite do that. Colony Survival is a neat idea on what visually looks like Minecraft with shaders. You build, farm, mine, and harvest wood to build up a colony of villagers. You can create jobs for villagers to do such as farm, mine, grind wheat, bake bread, run a store, chop down trees, smelt ores, etc. However, the game doesn't give you the tools to make managing these villages easy, or quite frankly at all.
Colony Survival also lacks where it counts. The game has zero animation for anything. Shooting arrows, mining blocks, placing blocks, etc. The game has almost no content. There are no doors, windows, ladders, stairs, etc. You have a few rudimentary stone/wood blocks and tools. No room for outside the box creativity.
I would place this game in the "Wait and See" category because the concept is fun and intriguing. However, the severe lack of basic game function just doesn't make it worth the $20 price tag.

Wasn't completely sure if this game would be something for me, so I bought it on sale. Have to say, never thought it being so addictive. Easy to understand, not as easy to master. And although there are generally only 15 different expeditions (of which you have to finish 5 to win the game) the developers added so many features to allow for a great replayability. E.g.:
- 24 explorer characters with different pros and cons allows for a huge amount of different possible explorer teams of 3 characters; even more considering the different captain perks of each character
- all expeditions are shuffled with every playthrough, i.e. map design is random; also some events/actions as well as trophies could be exchanged
- literally hundreds of different possibilities for character trainings, power-ups and entourage/helpers
- with DLC "Emperor's Challenge" the game offers additional daily and weekly challenges
- campfire stories introduce evolving character relationships and additional character buffs
This was well invested money and I can only recommend this game.

If you can read, watch movies, or listen to music, you've probably experienced something where not everything was laid out explicitly for you. At this point you become an active participant - if you want, you try to make your own meaning from what you are given. Alternatively, you can walk away and go back to something that doesn't challenge you. The Steam community have alerted me to a third option - get really angry and leave a negative review. But the choice is yours - which is not something the DOTA2s and Team Fortresses of the world can offer.
In Antenna, the mechanics match the narrative impeccably, insofar as it's an experience of discovery and creation. It certainly does have a 'story' - you just have look for it. You don't have to like this game, but if you try, you actually might.
Pros:
- Step in the right direction for storytelling in games
Cons:
- Doesn't have trading cards, cross platform multiplayer, real-time weapon change, collectables, microtransactions or explosions
Note: the tone deaf might struggle with a couple of the puzzles - many solutions are based on tones.

This is the gaming equivalent of a film short. This mystery game is a study in creepy, dark atmosphere and odd (but fairly simple and intuitive) sound-based puzzles. The biggest downside to playing this game is that it has little to no explanation as to what is going on, what happened in the past, when this is, where this is, what you are doing, what your purpose is or what anything is supposed to mean. This is really kind of tragic and extremely frustrating because playing this game will make you want to know. BADLY. The atmospherics and sounds of this game are truly haunting.
In my interpretation of this game You play as an automated robot, a sort of mobile backup system, left over on a planet after an apocalyptic war/other global catastrophe with the sole purpose of activating machinery to raise ancient antennas in order to boost a repeating, automated short-wave homing signal so it will then be strong enough to get into space to attract...something...to the now destroyed planet. But that's just my interpretation. I don't really know what this means and in the total absence of any explanation I'm just imagining things. But hey, that's life.
Good things:
+This game is FREE.
+The controls are good (if you can figure them out and figuring the controls out is part of the game)
+The sound is truly excellent. It is atmospheric and haunting and creepy. The shortwave radio frequency sounds are particularly amazing and creepy.
Mediocre Things:
+/-There are not very many puzzles.
+/-The graphics are highly unique. Everything is portrayed as shadows and silhouettes. The graphics add to it but at once tell you frustratingly little about what is happening.
Bad things:
-Very short game and some puzzles can be a little obtuse, especially if you are not used to the kind of puzzles which commonly occur in mystery games. By very short I mean that this game lasted about 50 minutes for me and I got every single steam achievement this game has.
-This game lacks any replayability whatsoever. This game is an experimental experience more than an actual game.
-Not knowing what this game is about is very frustrating.
