I greatly enjoy BattleBorn. I'd go as far as to say I enjoy it more than Overwatch. Rather than focusing mainly on the positives and negatives of BattleBorn, I shall compare it with Overwatch quite a bit, as well as my dissapointment in the community for abandoning this game. Of course, this review is completely capable of changing in the future, likely to include either more positives or negatives or whatever, but the basic premise I believe will stay the same.
Now, I will admit that the game has its problems. However, the community is to blame for them. Instead of giving proper feedback about the problems, or suggestions on how to make the game better, the community simply left a negative review and left to play Overwatch.
Honestly, Battleborn has so much more potential, or had more potential, than Overwatch.
Some people see BattleBorn's stylized graphics as lazy or less-polished than Overwatch. And while I do like Overwatch's style of graphical design much more than BattleBorn's, I can tell you this is not the case. It is not laziness that resulted in these graphics. They're somewhat like the Borderlands graphics. But for some reason, people seemed to like Borderlands graphics, while crapping on BattleBorn's. Probably because Overwatch offered much greater graphics.
I greatly prefer Battleborn's gameplay over Overwatch. The games may be very similar, but there are great differences. Battleborn playstyle consists of adapting a loadout according to your surroundings, the gamemode and your enemies, as well as your playstyle. Using Helix upgrades mid battle to configure your playstyle, as well as gear loadouts. This offers so much more brain stimulation and sense of actually doing something, than Overwatch. I can compare Overwatch, while being a good game in and of itself, as being a bit of a mindless shooter. There's not too much strategy to it. In fact, I'd go as far as to say it has a bit less strategy than TF2. While this may prove well for people who want to mindlessly play and praise the game for its graphics, in the end, I personally don't feel like I have accomplished anything. Sure, I'll still play Overwatch, but it is not near as brain stimulating and exciting as Battleborn. I'll play Overwatch when I feel like gunning down enemies and testing my reaction times, rather than decision making and all of what I previously mentioned combined. And admittedly, there are times where I feel lazy like this, so Overwatch comes to the rescue in those scenarios.
Now, the gamemodes between the two vary. Overwatch has payload and all that. Battleborn has gamemodes that mainly consist of escorting bots, and a mode that captures points. But a great part of Battleborn is the story missions and operations, as well as vs bots gamemode. Overwatch really could have used these types of modes. With so many heroes, I find it enjoyable to hone your skills against bots whenever you feel like you want to, and level up your character without fear of wasting time with an incredibly incapable team. Now, I do believe Battleborn could have used a more, PVP battle type for an optional choice. Like Overwatch escort, assault, and so forth, to give an option to players who want to just fight each other, and not focus at all on bots and escorting them. That would have been a nice option. BattleBorn's gamemodes in ADDITION to the Overwatch gamemode types.
Also, BattleBorn is on steam. Something that Blizzard didn't do due to greed. They already have all the money from WoW. It's not so much providing for players as much as it is making themselves money at this point, just looking at the price of Overwatch itself, and the crate system. Not putting their games on platforms like Steam is just stingy, and it really shows the greed of the company. Battleborn seems to really have the interest of the community in mind and at heart, as they have not completely abandoned the game. They are still updating it! And the way that is gives out skins and crates, it just so much superior to Overwatch.
Originally, when Overwatch and Battleborn were released, I thought this was going to be great. There was going to be a healthy competition between the two companies. Better, more frequent sales of in-game items and the game itself. Faster, better content updates to both games, each company putting their absolute best into each game, to create two overall similar, but at the same time, different, great games. And I believe if BattleBorn was even able to put up enough of a fight, Overwatch at this point in time, would be even better. Not to mention BattleBorn as well, being so much greater than it already is. Both companies would have to work on updating their games frequently, and pleasing their fanbase as they have the fear of them switching over to the other game. I would have been playing both Overwatch AND BattleBorn at this point, I imagine. Unfortunately... People seemed to completely overlook not only the base game BattleBorn itself, but the incredible potential that it posessed. They just all abandoned Battleborn, giving Overwatch the complete monopoly over everything. Now Overwatch is putting out updates whenever it feels like doing so, casually and lazily. Very little competition at all. And while Paladins has proven to provide some aspects greater than Overwatch's, (Better customization system, weekly quests, PVE, etc) too many people are hooked on Overwatch, and Overwatch has recieved so much praise without any competition, that it is too late. Paladins is more focused on appealing to its audience than battling Overwatch at this point, since it knows it has no chance. Too much time has passed without any competition facing Overwatch, and unless they introduce something or pull off something exceptionally great that gains a great deal of attention from gamers all around the globe, Overwatch will likely remain the dominant game, over both Paladins and Battleborn.
And sadly, as a result, the servers of Battleborn, while somewhat inhabited, are mostly empty. And this makes me sad.
People failed to see the differences between the games, and simply saw Overwatch as the superior version of BattleBorn. And now, people are taking BattleBorn for granted, simply assuming it is the same game as Overwatch, just worse. Overwatch is still taking inspiration from Battleborn. Just look at Uprising. Sure, I will admit there are differences, but there is no question that there was some inspiration taken from Battleborn. I never imagined Battleborn would fail this badly. I dreamed of competition, what makes great games greater. But, the people are to blame for what they have now. What is lesser than what they could have gotten.

Again, this review is capable of changing in the future, likely to include more positive and negatives between the two, or include more information in general, whatever I may think of in the future, but probably not changing my mind about the overall conclusion. Just putting this out there, that my review hasn't reviewed EVERYTHING each game has to offer, and times in the future may or may not come where I will add on to this review.

I very much enjoy battleborn, its just a shame about its minimal playerbase.
When it first came out, battleborn was often confused as an overwatch clone as they were released at about the same time, this is absolutely not the case.
Battleborn is in fact quite unique, and I would consider it one of the best first person (kind of MOBA) out there.
The characters all have different, well designed abilities and personalilites, and games take a comfortable half an hour each time. What is fantastic about battleborn is its simplicity, allowing the few abilities available to be used tactically.
There are times in other games where the player can feel buried in items, abilities and synergies, but battleborn puts emphasis on gaining mastery over a few abilities and using them well, which is a refreshing change.
There are some issues with the game, as there are undoubtedly some unblalanced characters. There was also a lack of maps, and as I mentioned before, the playerbase is sadly very low, so it can be EXTREMELY tricky to find a game at this stage. The PvE is also quite poor, as it can be pretty boring. Due to the low amount of players, buying the game at this stage might require a lot of waiting for PvP, so look at the PvE too.

This game is very extraordinary and therefore I'm writing a review about it because why not.
Battleborn is a game that takes humour and FPS and combines them. It's not meant to be serious like the Call of Duty franchise, or completely goofy. Many of the voice lines have made me laugh over the 70 odd hours I've been playing. Not just PvP, but PvE is also included in the package, and I love it for that, it's just a shame that the popularity went the way it did.
I will now go over the many pro's and con's of the game.
Pro's:
-Humourous jokes and lines made for all characters and even some for specific maps.
-PvE is always nice to have if you do not feel confident with player vs player content yet.
-Considering the community is small it is also very friendly and even have a discord where you can find people to play with and such.
-Skin and taunt customization, like Team Fortress 2.
-Lore achievements are implemented, and even challenges for you to unlock them, along with Titles you can earn from just playing the game.
-Different classes varying from Offense, to Defense, and Support.
-Wide variety of maps and detail put into them is astonishing. Different flank routes for PvP, and very open areas for PvE. They've thought about every possible situation that could happen when playing, and took advantage of it in ways, such as the flankers.
-Different game modes like Capture Point, and a few ones that are similar to MOBA's and then ones that are just unique.
-Devs still continue to make progress on the game even when it is at its lowest point in time.
Con's:
-The game does not feel as polished as it could be, various bugs here and there. Most likely due to low funding.
-Low population, often feels like the game is dying if you play at rare times.
-Poor advertising and marketting, people can easily buy the game for cheaper on third party websites rather than Steam, which charge £25.00 when people are getting it for about £2-4. If this were to change, popularity and sales would easily increase and they could work on flaws in their game.
-Tried to compete with Overwatch and lost dramatically, the game released at the wrong time and place.
-Game gets bland after time, the PvE is often repetitive, such as defend the objective or take out all of the Thrall/Varelsi.
-
Overall, Battleborn is
a bad game. But I do fear that in the next upcoming years, the game will die. It's a sad thought to see a game this good get treated badly because of its reputation. Although if the devs were to make some changes, like making it Free to Play, then I could see it working. The game on console is currently doing better with popularity than PC and steam, but my point still stands that the game is too expensive and puts people off of getting it.
But seriously, in all honesty I recommend this game, all old players are always willing to help new players when they start the game, because of the friendly community. Thanks for reading and speech over xd.

Gameplay is overall great but buggy, controls feel natural, mechanics are good. I didn't have any hard time trying to follow the campaign. Creating paths is horrible. When I can't make a straight road through an empty piece of flat land it's just bulls
t. I cannot connect two existing roads, the snapping points are horribly located, going from one size to another size road is buggy as hell or just doesn't work, etc. It just sucks.
Sometimes it feels like you can just farm peeps, build a nice park, put the game on full speed, and wait a few months. The peeps will get bored, but it doesn't really affect your revenue. Maybe it would be nice to implement a gamemode where you have to keep building to satisfy the peeps.
About peeps, they're less complex than RCT3 it looks. They don't stick to groups, visually at least. In RCT3 you would have families walking together, I miss that.
Staff is a bit weird, you get no info on how far the mechanic or janitor spots need to be away from each other, but you do get a 'heatmap' when placing the building. What use does it have?
I realize this is an early access stage, but the game lacks content. Coasters, rides are fine, not too much, not too many. Would like to see swimming pool expansion packs though ;). But the game lacks decoration. The only props are some rocks, spotlights, candy canes, and dutch-looking facades. The rest are all general trees, benches, trashcans, lights (which don't light up very well, my park is full of them and I still get complaints about it being too dark), etc.
But, this is forgivable, as this is in an early access stage.
Performance just sucks. This game uses an excessive amount of ram after a while, do you not know what memory managment is? I have 8GB, would like more, but it should be enough, when this game uses 7 gb of ram, it's a bit absurd.
In the start it ran fine, but overtime it would use more memory, and almost crash my OS. What I also do not get, even when memory usage is at 50%, and my GPU and CPU are not being utilized to the max, it still lags!
About savegames? I can't load the first game I started after closing my game once. The game just "stopped working". No excessive GPU/CPU/Memory usage while loading, it just crashes. Haven't tried sandboxing yet.
I suck at writing reviews, but I hope I got my point across. I really want a new rollercoaster tycoon. And this one is aiming in the right direction. Start by fixing performance, then fix common gameplay bugs like pathing, building etc. then go on to fixing exploits like money farming etc. THEN start adding content.

I enjoyed playing the game, but like others, found myself with not much left to do after only 7.5 hrs. Hardly worth the current $20 price. HOWEVER, this game has great potential. Here are my ideas:
1) More monster variety
2) Have the ore deplete after awhile, so that players have a reason to extend their mine shafts. As it is right now, once a handful of each ore is uncovered, I have no reason to keep digging other than for stone.
3) More building materials: glass, fences, doors, ect.
4) Animals! Introduce shepards to the game, that will tend to farm animals for leather, milk, meat and wool.
5) Allow the villagers to breed as long as there are enough beds, it would give the game a more natural feel by allowing the colony to expand on its own.
Yes, these ideas sound a lot like Minecraft but most of the reason I loved playing this game was because it had a Minecraft feel, but with reasons to build a city. In Minecraft, it was pointless to build beautiful cities that had only defenseless villagers wandering around.
Keep up the good work and keep improving, I'll be anxiously awaiting updates for sure.

Colony Survival is a colony management game that's actually quite fun. Basically the objective of the game is to expand your village. You can recruit people, and you can set them proffesions such as a miner or wheat farmer. Ultimately, the game boils down to pure automation so there is quite a lack of interactivity.
This game is enjoyable to play when you have a nice village set up with defenses and farms and managing food and beds for people. Pretty soon though, it gets to a point where it just gets boring. There's barely anything you can do, if you've erected efficient defenses against attack monsters, then at night time there's nothing really for you to do. I would just go AFK and wait until it's day time again.
The visual side is very well done in my opinion. The game bears sleek voxel graphics and beautiful shaders, and it's quite visually appealing. Unfortunately, the lack of interactivity and variety does mean this game turns into monotony. I can easily see this game improving, if only they added more content, which I'm sure they will. In it's current state, it feels very barebones.
For a few hours, it is quite a fun experience. But when the asking price is $20, I don't think that is very good value for a game with so little content. Buy it if you enjoy developing sophisticated structures and bases, otherwise there's not much else to it.
This game isn't bad, but it's currently lacking content to justify the $20 pricetag.
I also must note it is currently very early in development.
I will definitely update my review as this game progesses, because it does have very good potential

As a veteran of the franchise for over a decade now, I am finally giving people my feedback on my second favorite title in the franchise. Supreme Commander 2 or Sup Com 2 as some people call it, is a Massive RTS game featuring units such as tanks, plasma equiped robots, fighter/bombers, submersible aircraft carriers and even mobile flying factorys! That kind of line-up is standard for the franchise at this point, where it will use basic looking or functioning traditional units and special hybrid or versatile units in massive scale battles.
The core of Supreme Commander has always been in large armies battling on even larger maps on land, sea or air, with technological upgrades being made to your army in game to help turn the tide of battle and eliminate the enemy commander unit. For new players into the series, I would say the learning curve as well as the gameplay is generally very easy to learn like any other RTS out there. You learn what units are effective against another, how to effectively build up a base and defenses as well as utilize various strategies to ensure victory. Although, that last doesn't happen very often. One thing that both separates and comapres Sup Com 2 to other games is that there is a lack of strategy at some points. One thing that annoys me is how easy it is to get high tier units and the research tree in general.
That's right, if you're a veteran like me, or have played the previous Sup Com games, then you know what I'm talking about here. Unlike the original Sup Com where you simply built individual land, air and naval factories and upgraded those factories to tech levels 2 and 3; in Sup Com 2, that system is gone and replaced by the tech tree, which acts as your research guide and planner throughout a match. Everything that the respective faction you play as will be able to 'learn' and unlock in game is laid before, ranging from unit unlocks to simple stat boosts. This honestly improves the system from the original games, becase before, you had to tech up each individual factory in match, but with the tech tree system, you can upgrade any structure or unit for continuously produced researched points. Research is a new resource in Sup Com 2 that can be produced by simply standing still, but it will take a VERY long time for you to earn points that way, building actual research stations that 'speed up' research or through combat, but you'll always want to build a few research statoins regardless of your playstyle.
-A side note: Resources in Sup Com 2 haven't changed much, you still build mass extractors over mass deposits for mass and build energy generators anywhere you can build them. But, now instead of managaing your economy to priortize maximum efficiency to build units and structures in the previous games where you had bars and the lower the bar gauge meant you couldn't build something as effeciently as you could were it filled up, you now simply spend mass and energy like currency to build units and structures. Personally I like both systems because of how they make each game feel unique in a sense. The same goes for research though, like I explained above, you earn indiviual research points over a period of time and spend a speciffic number of those points to unlock units and upgrade your army on the fly. Very important to note: if you purchase an upgrade, then every unit affected gets that upgrade immediately; none of that building new units over old ones to get the upgrade.-
In regard to the units themselves, they are very unique in the new art design for the game, going from a 'realistic' look to a cartoonish look, which I personally enjoy, because it looks less depressing with more colors. As with all Sup Com games, you need to wait it out and see the differences between similar acting units in order to understnad them, though that has been severely downgraded by the new system in place. Tanks are slow, but tough and have medium-esque fire power, Assualt Bots are glass cannons, anti air is much weaker than their emplacement counter parts, but still effective early on, while mobile missle launchers are absolute beasts against stationary and big targets. Mobile shield units always run out very quickly and always stay at the back of large force, so you can never properly cover your advance, mobile anit missle units are kind of a hit or a miss sometimes, while the high tier experimental units feel underpowered and lacking. In the old games, just one experimental could turn the tide of battle, usually because they took so long and so much to build that they were worth it, but in Sup Com 2, you can spam them in like ten minutes and ruin that tenseness from the previous games. There are very few experimentals that actually pose a threat on their own, but they don't actually feel like they were worth getting in the first place at times.
Regardless, the gameplay is fine and while there is no 'right way' to play it, I would suggest trying to embody the sprirt of the original games and duke it out in massive large scale conflicts with hundreds of units on your side. The story takes place twenty five years after the expansion to the original game, but I really wouldn't pay to much attention, for you will not care anything about those characters.
So, in short Supreme COmmander 2 is grand RTS game with a simplified resource management, research system and base building system that literally anyone can figure out, but I would still reccomend doing the short tutorials to either introduce yourself to some of the franchise's core mechanics, refresh your understanding of something you forgot or learn about some of the new features in place.
Enjoy.

Cossacks 3 = Cossacks 1 HD
Is this bad?
No, not at all. For a Pricetag of 20€ you get a solid Cossacks 1 HD.

As of its current state, I cannot recommend Cossacks 3, as a customer who played Cossacks 1 (Art of War specifically) I really enjoyed the first game and was excited when they announced Cossacks 3.
Cossacks 3 is essentially an HD remark of Cossacks 1 and although I am alright with that there are several issues and missing content in its current state which made me unable to recommend the game.
1.There are missing animations and some animations do not cycle properly making the unit move in a very strange manner.
2.There are some issues with the units, for instance sometimes the peasants would suddenly stop working or will not repair/build the building I ordered them to.
3.Unit pathing seems odd.
4.Sometimes the main menu or in game, the music would either not play or have two soundtracks play at the same time.
5.When creating a custom game, you cannot seem to preview the map before playing, since there was a small box on the bottom right hand side, I assume that box was meant to preview the map you will play in. Additionally, unlike Cossacks 1 there does not seem to be a choice to adjust the map size right now.
6.In skirmish mode, it seems like the editor mode is not deactivated because in skirmish mode you can actually use ctrl c + ctrl v to copy units and buildings. Which in my opinion, is a massive overlook from the developers.
7.I did not play multiplayer mode yet, but from what I have seen in the discussion, it appears that disconnecting is a very prevalent issue.
8. Minor complaint, the drummer does not make any sounds when they are on the move. Just is quip that bugged me quite a bit.
Despite these flaw, I still did enjoy the game, The graphics update was fine IMO, (after playing a bit of 3, I played a quick game of Art of War and the difference was massive, at least the HD remake was better than AOE 2's). The soundtrack and sound effects is quite good, although I did enjoy one's a lot more, tje sound effects of the muskets and cannons sound more realistic.
I do like how resources do much more than just create units and buildings like in other RTS games. For example, food will continuously be consumed by your population and if you run out of food your units may gradually starve from famine. Long range units need iron and coal for ammunition and firing, so if you run out or mismanage these two resources those unit cannot fire at all.
Another twist which I do enjoy in the Cossacks series, units can actually be killed if they are near an exploding building or if they get hit by flying debris.  Essentially, I enjoy the game because it still does retain the elements Cossacks had which separated it from its competitors.
Overall though, due to the mentioned issues, I cannot recommend getting the game full price in its current state. It’s best to wait until those issues get patched or wait for a sale.

Short version: Highly recommend this as a fun, tactical/strategic RPG. Cartoony artstyle, quirky humour and some really interesting and unique mechanics for the turn-based combat. High replay value.
Long version: At first glance Renowned Explorers seems a decent, light-hearted, strategic rogue-like game involving turn-based tactical fights. The more you play however, the more you notice and appreciate all the different layers of the game design and mechanics there are, that when put all together make for a much deeper game than it may first appear.
You select a  team of 3 explorers, from a large roster of characters from 4 different classes. Each character has different perks/abilities and they each have a different bonus when selected as captain, which gives them all a different playstyle and they all have different synergies with other team members.
You take your selected team to 5 different expedition locations, which you pick from a growing list of options and move across randomly generated maps, resolving encounters with skill checks from party members or in tactical, turn-based fights.
The combat involves a unique "mood" mechanic, where abilities/attacks used affect whether your team is Aggressive, Friendly or Devious and the same applies to the enemy. This creates a shifting rock-paper-scissors game, where one mood will be advantageous giving a buff or a debuff, but use of another ability may shift the mood to a different buff/status. Additionally individual units have emotions such as Excited, Enraged, Saddened, etc that add extra buffs/debuffs.
Enemies have different weaknesses and resistances to various emotions and some react differently to changing moods as well. The amount of interplay between skills, emotions, moods and positioning/attacks all adds up to interesting gameplay with a lot more depth than the cheery cartoon artstyle may hint at.
Once you get used to the gameplay, a full run only takes a few hours, but the RNG nature of the map layouts and loot placement, as well as the large roster and combinations of team members, perks, items, skill bonuses, etc gives a huge amount of replayability. The developer support is great as well, with new daily and weekly challenges rotated in, which gives incentive to try out new team compositions/strategies than you may be used to.
A note on the RNG for skill checks throughout the game - the breakdown of whether or not a roll will succeed in the game is excellent. It shows you what your chance is, what the skill check is based on, as well as the contributing factors from character skills, items, buffs, etc are, so if you want to boost your chances/eliminate RNG you are given the information to do so.
Overall, an excellent game with some great and innovative design choices and mechanics. Great replayabilty and definitely recommended.

This game is very extraordinary and therefore I'm writing a review about it because why not.
Battleborn is a game that takes humour and FPS and combines them. It's not meant to be serious like the Call of Duty franchise, or completely goofy. Many of the voice lines have made me laugh over the 70 odd hours I've been playing. Not just PvP, but PvE is also included in the package, and I love it for that, it's just a shame that the popularity went the way it did.
I will now go over the many pro's and con's of the game.
Pro's:
-Humourous jokes and lines made for all characters and even some for specific maps.
-PvE is always nice to have if you do not feel confident with player vs player content yet.
-Considering the community is small it is also very friendly and even have a discord where you can find people to play with and such.
-Skin and taunt customization, like Team Fortress 2.
-Lore achievements are implemented, and even challenges for you to unlock them, along with Titles you can earn from just playing the game.
-Different classes varying from Offense, to Defense, and Support.
-Wide variety of maps and detail put into them is astonishing. Different flank routes for PvP, and very open areas for PvE. They've thought about every possible situation that could happen when playing, and took advantage of it in ways, such as the flankers.
-Different game modes like Capture Point, and a few ones that are similar to MOBA's and then ones that are just unique.
-Devs still continue to make progress on the game even when it is at its lowest point in time.
Con's:
-The game does not feel as polished as it could be, various bugs here and there. Most likely due to low funding.
-Low population, often feels like the game is dying if you play at rare times.
-Poor advertising and marketting, people can easily buy the game for cheaper on third party websites rather than Steam, which charge £25.00 when people are getting it for about £2-4. If this were to change, popularity and sales would easily increase and they could work on flaws in their game.
-Tried to compete with Overwatch and lost dramatically, the game released at the wrong time and place.
-Game gets bland after time, the PvE is often repetitive, such as defend the objective or take out all of the Thrall/Varelsi.
-
Overall, Battleborn is
a bad game. But I do fear that in the next upcoming years, the game will die. It's a sad thought to see a game this good get treated badly because of its reputation. Although if the devs were to make some changes, like making it Free to Play, then I could see it working. The game on console is currently doing better with popularity than PC and steam, but my point still stands that the game is too expensive and puts people off of getting it.
But seriously, in all honesty I recommend this game, all old players are always willing to help new players when they start the game, because of the friendly community. Thanks for reading and speech over xd.

What do a bizarre mafia triad, a missing horse, and two protagonists with a penchant for wanton violence all have in common? They’re all featured in Blue Estate, a rail shooter based on a novel by Viktor Kalvachev. This is one of those games where you know from the very beginning what the rest of the game is going to be like. Blue Estate features loads of shooting, a story that doesn’t take itself too seriously, more shooting, some quick time events, mini games, and a bunch of crazy boss fights.
Gameplay is pretty smooth for an on-rails shooter and getting headshots (or nut shots) consistently with the mouse isn’t particularly difficult, especially with the warning circle system giving you an idea of which targets should have the highest priority. Occasionally you have to tap an arrow key to match on-screen gestures for actions such as picking up items, knocking back projectiles, or various other actions. Hitting the key immediately as it comes up will give you a “speed freak” bonus which is essential to getting higher scores and rankings. Getting hit isn’t too big of an issue unless you really screw up and determined players will be able to keep alive long enough until the next health pickup.
There’s not much to complain about with this game unless you’re not a fan of the humor or have really bad reflexes. I did find myself fighting the double right click weapons switch in the final level because there were so many things going on at once but it was an easy beast to tame. I also felt this would have been a game better experienced on a big screen TV with a light gun setup but for what it’s worth I still had fun using the mouse  (it just didn’t feel “natural”).
An important point to note about Blue Estate is that it’s geared more towards completionists and doesn’t have a very long story. If you’re not that kind of player, you may want to wait until the game goes on sale so you can really get your money’s worth, as the average playthrough from start to finish is around 3-4 hours tops. For all you achievement hunters though, this is a game you definitely shouldn’t pass up.

Guacamelee is definitely a fun and enjoyable game, but I still have a hard time recommending it to others. Yes, the artwork is unique, yes, the controls start tight, and yes, there is much to do in the game, but as you progress the game's flaws start to bare themselves openly. For instance, any hit from an enemy knocks you down. ANY hit. That means you see the same falling down animation from either a minion or a boss. That's fine, until you take into consideration that this game is also a platformer, i.e. being attacked while jumping to a floating platform can and will happen. In addition to this, the game likes to throw multiple enemies at you at once, which makes any attempt at advancing in the level frustrating due to a multitude of enemies, floating platforms, and a hero that takes any hit like a basketball player
. Another frustrating element in this game is hit detection. It seems the game will arbitrarily decide if you've hit someone hard enough (even if it's with a special attack) to stop their attack or not. Many times I've blue punched someone straight in their chupicabra face and they still just float there firing flame balls at me. Plus, the game is dodgy when it comes to dodging! Once again, it will arbitrarily decide if you've successfully dodged something, or if it's dodgeable at all. For whatever reason, some attacks you can dodge, then others you can't, then the ones you couldn't now all of a sudden you can... Clearly it annoys me. Combine all of this together and what do you get? An extremely frustrating game. Not necessarily impossible, but not necessarily worth any amount of effort required to put into it, especially when you take into consideration the challenge rooms found later in the game.
My gripes aside (there are others, but if you read other reviews I'm sure you'll spot them), if you're not in any way, shape, or form attempting to be a completionist, grab the game. It's fun, unique, and lighthearted. But if you're wanting to master this game, good luck. Many sections will become the bane of your existence as you attempt to collect all the pieces of your mask. Play at your own risk, but most importantly, enjoy the show.

With almost 500 hours, I now feel I can give an honest review of this game. This IS my first review, hence why I see so much potential in this game because i normally don't do reviews. Also, 1/3 of these hours are from me being afk in game while working on additional content for the game and my server, so keep that in mind. (This will be updated in the future if nessecary)
Here are some of the conerns I've seen from potential players of this game:
1. It's expensive
- Keep in mind, this is an early access game. To continue development on a game, you need funding, funding that will overall improve the quality of this game and allow the developers to potentially get better gear for developing the game, hiring more staff to work on it, and allow them to live off of funds so they can put more time on the game.
2. Servers
- Yes, there are issues with servers. You'll be playing on one that you've put 20 hours in, only to never see it again after it goes offline. Yes you can play in single player, but lets face it. Multiplay Is what keeps these kind of games alive, and some of us server owners know this. Currently there ARE several dedicated, 24/7 servers that are out right now that have wonderful communities and helpful staff, and server owners ARE communicating with each other so they can provide entertaining playing experience for everyone. This way, you won't have to play alone or just pray that the server your on goes down. So don't think every server is the same on this game as far as reliability. This game came out a few months ago, it's only now that you will start seeing more dedicated servers pop up. We hear your cries, and we are responding with answers.
Also, it's relatively EASY to set up a server for this game, so if you want to set up a dedicated server, you can easily, and if you'd like help, there are plenty of helpful people on the forums.
3. Content
-Yes, there is a lack of content in this game. Right now all you can pretty much do (base game wise) is craft a few jobs, recruit some workers to farm food, craft nessecaries, and protect your NPCs. If you've still got your hopes pinned on Silent Hill Homecoming being a return to form for Konami's seminal, if increasingly derivative, survival horror franchise, all you need know is that, about an hour before the final credits, it turns into Hostel: the Videogame. Things start off pretty well for Homecoming though – if you can forgive an opening which doesn't so much slyly tip its hat to Jacob's Ladder as lob its helmet at it – as eminently likeable protagonist Alex Shepherd returns home from war. His brother is missing and the town of Shepherd's Glen – a lake's throw away from you know where – is in eerie disarray. It's an intriguing – if familiar – premise and Homecoming does a reasonable job at pacing its reveals, maintaining an air of mystery that carries much of the game.
It might seem strange to jump straight onto a game's story but survival horror – with its contrived game mechanics – has always been a genre where narrative counts. Despite its best efforts though, Homecoming can't deliver, and what starts off well ultimately descends into confusion and predictability –eventually, the only real reason left to follow the story is the nagging hope that it can't possibly be as stupid as it thinks you are. It's disappointing for a series that set the precedent for narrative delivery across the medium, albeit one that's failed to live up to its own standards over the years. Charged, presumably, with the impossible task of juggling the franchise's persistently impenetrable cult mythology alongside the more intimate psychological horrors of series darling Silent Hill 2, it's hard not to feel sorry for developer Double Helix.Unfortunately, Homecoming misses the mark on other occasions too and, while Double Helix has does a respectable job of bringing the aging franchise roughly in line with modern day expectations, the end result is a competent, if hollow, facsimile of its predecessors that fails to capture the series' melancholy soul. Homecoming's successes lie in the careful aping of Silent Hill's conventions and, in terms of sheer iconography, there's little to match the series with its fog-shrouded streets, industrial Otherworld and the constant oppressive drone of Akira Yamaoka's unmistakable score. Certainly, Homecoming ticks its checklist with gusto but it's nostalgia rather than innovation that is likely to keep long-time fans engaged.
Admittedly, tweaks to combat, control and camera make for a far less torturous affair compared to previous Silent Hill offerings – and there's no arguing that a kick up the♥♥♥♥♥♥for the series was long-overdue. Combat-wise, Homecoming eschews Silent Hill: Origins' fussy obsession with melee combat, focussing on a limited number of – upgradable - melee weapons and firearms, all with unique attributes that come into play when certain obstacles or particular enemies appear. In truth, Homecoming's implementation of hand-to-hand combat, first-person shooting and dodging is still awkward and unrefined though, made all the more apparent by the game's incredibly aggressive enemy AI. Too often Shepherd's abilities simply can't contend with the feral attacks of your opponents and the best course of action is to leg it away. Six franchise entries where a well-timed pout is as good as any amount of prescribed ineffectual flailing and you start to wonder if combat is really necessary at all…

So this game is getting my reccommendation because its quite obviously a work in progress. The developers seem genuinely interested in what the community has to say, and for that they get my recommendation.
The issues I've noted with the game so far are for the most part already described, but for the uninformed, I'll go into them briefly.
-Pathing and structure layout needs work
-Peep and employee control needs work
-Game starts to lag after large amounts of items are placed
-The coaster design panel could use some smoothing over, I just have some issues with the way the controls are layed out
And those are the most major issues seen in most reviews. Now for the fun part, what I truly like!
-The game is absolutely gorgeous graphically, it was high time for an updated RCT and this game captures that spirit wonderfully. You can tell that although its a work in progress this is truly going to be a wonderfule heir to the series.
-The theming, while in true RCT style can get slightly excessive, allows for a wonderful array of customibality (probably spelled that wrong, ah well). Everything from the music to the cues can be colored and placed, and they've added things like fake walls and beautiful plazas and centerpieces that allow you to create whole sections of thematically designed park. You can get lost for hours just placing correct pieces *just so*. I'd love to see more themed items soon.
-The notification panel is handy. With smart phone like features it allows you to view park info and see both the good and bad fairly quickly. Not exactly a new thing, but definitely well updated, although it needs some work.
-And overall the HUD layout seems fairly streamlined and definitely more modernized. It could use a bit of tweaking here and there, but its fairly easy to use which I suppose is a priority.
Anyways, so that's a few of my opinions. Hopes this helps both the new and the old Tycoons in their buying/desicion making.

: While there is a lot of good points to this game, I cannot recommend it as the photos do not scale well (if at all) on smaller monitors with low resolution. (see last paragraph for details)
The game starts with a single image explaining that someone has a very busy life and was always running and doing things, then s/he gets into a serious bicycle accident and is laying wounded on the ground, reflecting on the life they had lived ... you have 630 heart beats to restore their memories.
The first time I played this game, I literally had no idea what I was doing ... it seemed like there was just a bunch of photos and you were clicking randomly. I didn't get it - honestly, I was feeling frustrated trying to figure out what I was "supposed to do".
After I finished it the first time, I realized you were telling the person's life story through their memories. That's when the game became really enjoyable for me.
The second play through I tried to imagine what it would be like to be laying injured on the ground alone, and going through the memories of your life - so when I played through, every picture represented a memory of something important, something they treasured the memory of. What kind of person is this? What did they hold dear to them? What are the 85 memories that matter the MOST in their life? In answering those questions you create a story in your own mind about who this person is and what they value.
The game play through is very short - for me it was about 10 minutes or so for a lifetime of memories. I didn't consider this a big problem as it fits the whole theme of your "life flashing before your eyes" in the moment of death (so I found that thematically appropriate), and the price was reasonable for the game length.
I also liked the music, it was really nice. I was happy to find the soundtrack included in the game files.
This isn't your typical game, and many people may not enjoy this. Perhaps because I play a lot of visual novels, I am used to taking small bits onscreen and turning them into a larger, more in depth story in my own mind. For me, I felt the main part of the game was using your imagination to create a story through the images you chose, and the bigger story of putting the images together into a lifetime of memorable moments.
The one HUGE drawback to the game is there is no way to change the window size or photo size. I have a older windows PC that exceeds the listed requirements. However, the windows PC monitor is quite small (as it needs to fit in the corner of the bedroom). Playing this game at all available resolutions and following tips in the discussions forum still did not resolve the issue where I didn't get to see the text boxes at the bottom of the photos or the captions at the bottom at the ending. The lack of ability to see the full game images and the inability to see the text boxes did limit how much I was able to enjoy the game.

7.I did not play multiplayer mode yet, but from what I have seen in the discussion, it appears that disconnecting is a very prevalent issue.
8. Minor complaint, the drummer does not make any sounds when they are on the move. Just is quip that bugged me quite a bit.
Despite these flaw, I still did enjoy the game, The graphics update was fine IMO, (after playing a bit of 3, I played a quick game of Art of War and the difference was massive, at least the HD remake was better than AOE 2's). The soundtrack and sound effects is quite good, although I did enjoy one's a lot more, tje sound effects of the muskets and cannons sound more realistic.
I do like how resources do much more than just create units and buildings like in other RTS games. For example, food will continuously be consumed by your population and if you run out of food your units may gradually starve from famine. Long range units need iron and coal for ammunition and firing, so if you run out or mismanage these two resources those unit cannot fire at all.
Another twist which I do enjoy in the Cossacks series, units can actually be killed if they are near an exploding building or if they get hit by flying debris.  Essentially, I enjoy the game because it still does retain the elements Cossacks had which separated it from its competitors.
Overall though, due to the mentioned issues, I cannot recommend getting the game full price in its current state. It’s best to wait until those issues get patched or wait for a sale.

Looked pretty fun when it first came out, and when a DLC and steam sale came around I decided to buy it. I enjoy this game very much. The rock-paper-scissors mood system works with this game. To some people, it may not have replayability because there are set interactions on each map. It feels to me that the game is a lot easier when you have a scientist in your crew and no soldier, even when you are solving encounters aggresively.

This game has a pretty fun and rather unique approach to combat stages: you can fight your way out of them, sure... But you can also resolve matters in a friendly way, or break the spirit of those opposing you with mockery and intimidating words. Each style – peaceful, agressive, and mocking – work like a "weapon triangle", meaning one of them is weak against another one and strong against the other. By resolving more and more conflicts in a certian manner you get more "inclined" to this style which starts giving you bonuses for resolving conflicts "your way".
On adventurer mode, you can generally afford to "lose" your teammates twice per expedition until it's game over, so you have to be careful and cunning with your tactics and decisions. It's a good thing you don't actually need to reset because the game prompts you to do so anyway, which is might be a minor thing, but is still a very nice minor thing. Classic mode is absolutely brutal: once your part loses all of its resolve, it's over for you – forever. Resources you have to carry out expeditions are also limited, and you get penalties when you run out of them, so you have to plan where you go around the mission level in a careful manner. Boss fights could prove to be quite challenging, especially when you have debuffs and AOE-casting mobs keep swarming your party. While the stage design is nothing to write home about, some of the stages have classic choking points and "healing tiles" that can end up being your downfall.
The places you explore, aka expeditions – as they're called in the game – are all very varied, with their unique setting, opposing forces you confront, and local mini-plots. I especially liked the expedition to this Peruan-looking place where my explorers ended up finding an ancient treasure, banishing a necromant girl and overthrowing the government, all in one fell swoop.
There are also RNG challenges that utilize your team's traits: diplomatic, athletic, archeologist, etc. Those traits aren't only used to pass skill checks, but also offer some combat bonuses. Some of those skill checks are simple events, some of them are a series of skill checks. It's important to know your team's traits and keep an eye on opportunities to enhance them, as leveling characters doesn't have an effect on that area, but on their skills in skirmishes only.
There's plenty of characters to chose from and teams to form; some of the character combos even unlock some sort of short story snippets and give those characters some kind of bonus. All characters have a preference for two ways of resolving combat situations, so it's important to make a team with the same dynamic, as well a teammate who's efficient at "healing" in critical situations. Interestingly enough, you can also neglect "healing" completely and go for an all-out agressive playstyle – there are plenty of variety to the character roster to be able to pull that off.
There's a simple overarching story about how you're supposed to beat this Disney's Lady and the Beast Gaston-lookalike for... Uh... Fame, I guess, and you sometimes confront his goons on some of the expeditions as well. I'm pretty sure the story part might as well not exist because it's just so meaningless, and it's definitely not the game's strong point.
Overall, gameplay is top-notch and is surprisingly challenging. Exploring different places the world has to offer that all look so varied and unique is also a blast. Trying out different playstyles and party combinations helps a lot with the game's replayability. The fact that the soundtrack sounds very boring and uninspired and the overall plot feels kind of random don't really do much damage to my impression of how good this game is.

Oh where to begin... This game is such a hidden gem in the sea of indie games. You form a party of 3 characters with different backgrounds and specialties from all over the world. Your goal is to surpass Rivaleux and become the most Famous Explorer in the world which you do by gaining Renown. The game consists of three segments: exploration, combat and the world map.
On the World Map you can set the location of your expedition, spend Insight(which you earn through expeditions) to get resources, hire helpers or specialists to help you on your journey, do research to benefit your party and buy trinkets to boost your power. All the tokens you get and the treasures you find also give you Renown. After you are done managing, you are off to find secrets and treasures on your adventure.
When you start your expedition, you start to explore the island, each tile using supplies. Exploration is fun and intriguing; forcing you to make decisions depending on your overall goal, the side goal and your supplies. On most tiles you will get events. The stories and the writing is engaging and the decisions you make will reward you with tokens -which you can use on the world map- and treasures -which give you Insight and other rewards of your choice-. Another positive is that although the game is still random, the randomness is reduced by how you build your party. Such as a "Diplomat" having the chance to persuade your enemies. But during most cases you won't be able to escape from the encounter and that brings us to combat.
The combat is very unique in which you can not only win aggressively but also by talking things out or mocking your enemies. Your approach, combined with your enemies' approach will determine the mood of the battle such as Tense, Friendly or Brutal. These moods give your party buffs or debuffs depending on the rock, paper, scissors-like combat triangle. You will also get different tokens depending on the way you solve the situation, some events even play out differently if you get through them in a specific way.
All in all a fascinating game that hooked me like no other did recently.

Renowned Explorers is a turn-based strategy game set in the 19th century. You take control of 3 explorers, 1 captain and 2 crewmates to go on a handful of explorations to earn prestige and treasures.
You are a group of 3 persons, Each character have their Stats and Alignment that will help you in getting all kind of treasures and out of battles and net you more bonuses. Different team captains have different super powers, and so, each game with a different captain usually require different strategy and even different playstyle. Sometimes you will fight for the treasure, other treasures you need a certain ability to gain it and/or improve your chances of obtaining said treasures.
On the World Map you may choose a handful of expeditions that open up each time you venture forth and from there you may take any number of paths you choose to get to the treasure and boss. Paths are the same but each tile you land on may have different discoveries, positive/negative effects, and/or currency.
Combat in this game is done by a simple Rock/Paper/Scissors style. You will have either Aggressive/Friendly/Devious, each having a weakness and a effective counter.
The game keeps a fairly lighthearted and humorous theme throughout, which is aided by its bright and colorful art style. Don't let this fool you however - there is a surprising amount of depth to be found in the games combat and exploration systems.
Pros:
+ Turn based combat
+ Large variety of enemies and encounterable NPCs
+ Loads of characters to choose from, each with unique abilities and captain perks. Makes for a huge diversity of playstyle variations
+ Large amount of replayability, though the gameplay doesn't vary so much after about 100+ hours
+ You need to replay many games to unlock all treasures and Abilities for all characters
+ You can save your progress, so if you ruin in some point you can Load it. Unless you prefer to go hardcore (Adventure Mode) where progress is saved automatically and you can't revert to previous save states
+ 4 difficulty settings for the game
+ Great for all ages
Cons:
- Only around 8 maps and locations you can go
- Eventually the replayability slows unless you have a leaderboard mission to top the charts
- Can be frustrating
TL;DR:
8/10
Turn-based Rock/Paper/Scissor treasure finding strategy/adventure game with a large variety of unique, lighthearted humorous characters and simple animations.

Overall I've spent +400 hours playing this game and it's still one of my favorites. But like Brink, and the arena shooter Shadowrun game, this too is a basically dead in the water. I honestly don't understand how people could compare this to Overwatch - imo both games couldn't be any more different. Battleborn plays more like Monday Night Combat competitive, with minions and PvP, while Overwatch is more like TF2. Sure there's the unique heroes, but that's the only similarity I can see.
Graphically, it's a personal preference. A form a cell shading, similar to Borderlands but a little more tooney. But the difference between high and medium graphics settings are minimal, so lower end systems shouldn't have a problem running the game. The game definitely runs a little better than at launch, which it was suffering some memory issues and unoptimizations.
Gameplay, it's fun. The different heroes take a while to get used to, but become easy to master after a couple games. My favorite part of the game is the leveling system. Similar to something like Heroes of the Storm, you level per game from experience you gain from CPU kills, player kills, or objectives. As you level, you can choose between two skill enhancements, basically either going more defensive, offensive, support, or tactical. Each character is different, each with their own Special skill also midway through a match to help sway the match. After each match, your hero also gains experience which will unlock mutations, which give you a third skill to choose from in-game. These can add completely new characteristics to your heroes skills.
Overall this game should have succeeded. If you loved Borderlands, you should have loved this game. Similar comedy, similar gameplay, fun combat, tons of replay value. Also, a note on the 400 hours of play: it's split between sp, and waiting for games in the lobby for mp.

In short: Play it, don't buy it. The campaign is very limited, the pvp is great but queues are deserted.
There is a fairly trivial fix to save the game from oblivion: adding a very large pvp map with lots of optional goals. Think of WoW's Classic Alterac Valley: the queues are permanent and you can join the battle any time, a match could last for several days and you get great loot at the end.  But this dev team seems focussed on bringing short, e-Sports type modes that nobody takes seriously because EVERY OTHER PART OF THE GAME works to RUIN THAT IDEA. Having skill levels and gear rarity means pvp requires very clever balancing. And when I try to describe Gearbox. "clever" never comes to mind.
Let's compare it to WoW a little more: BB is a lot like a MMORPG, but it doesn't have a game world. It only has raids and pvp maps. Your avatar has levels, equipment and skills. So it's very much as if Gearbox was aiming to make a MMORPG without the technical means to make a permanent game world. So the play breaks down into either going on raids, which are simply the main campaign story with progressively harder maps and random loot, letting you be better at raiding, but there's no shared world here so... There's no real point in raiding.
You won't even use the great gear you got from raids in the PVP modes, which is the fun part of the game, imho.  If you've been a long-time World of Warcraft player, you'll remember that long ago people didn't have pvp sets and raiding sets, you just wore your best gear all the time.  But Blizz couldn't figure out how to balance things so they split them up into sets.  Battleborn devs won't admit that they're no better than Blizz, so they haven't even bothered thinking of gear balance.  All the cool gear you get as a reward from raiding is actually a HANDICAP in pvp because it's so expensive to activate.  Interesting gear gets routinely nerfed, and there's basically no synergy between character skills and the special gear (for example an assassin that should get a bonus on weakened character doesn't benefit from gear that applies weaken on foes).
So basically this all comes down to the devs not willing to admit that the game they made is not the game they were told to do. They keep choking the player base because management is telling them to make eSports/competitive but players just enjoy beating the crap out of each other when they actually get a match and telling stories about it later. The focus on competition means you can't join short-lived maps, and the player base is becoming hostile.
But if they went instead for a LONG-LIVED melee royale with rewarding goals (like Alterac Valley used to be, summoning Ivus ftw!  Solo capture mines and win by attrition & turtles!),  then it would be more of a RPG like they were meant to do, not seen as an Overwatch clone without all the spit and polish Blizz is capable of.
Fun game, very underrated, but it's definitely missing its mark.

This is, apparently, my first "rail shooter" so I'm not going to judge the genre by this game.

The lack of controller support is also a negative.  The game's setting appear to let you use the controller, but once I was actually playing the game, the only way to do anything was mouse/keyboard.
Perhaps rewriting the game's interface for a PC port was a bridge too far - I don't know enough technical stuff to be able to say.
The Story
The story is light-hearted noir (similar to Pulp Fiction, LA Confidential, etc).
Unfortunately, in the few minutes I played, there was very little story, just a constant stream of Asian badguys, muttering in Classic Cliched Asian-speak.  If we're going to play with ethnic stereotypes, why not be at least a little clever about it?
I think there is some real potential here with this material, but I'd much prefer the game to be structured in a more traditional manner.  Because, apparently, I'm no real fan of "rail shooters."  I wanna be able to move around, duck, dodge, dive and duck.  And shoot.
If you're a rail shooter fan, this game is for you.  If, like me, you are not, I'd avoid this one.

As one of the other reviews mentioned, this is a Minecraft clone with a different focus.
Rather than exploring and crafting things, you'll spend most of your time managing your resources(food, arrows, wood, iron, etc) and recruiting colonists. You'll give them jobs and grow your city.
For each colonist you recruit, the zombies attack in greater numbers, so you'll need to hire more guards. But your guards need arrows, so you'll need to recruit crafters. But crafters need supplies, so you'll need to hire miners and foresters. Everyone needs food, so you'll need to hire farmers. And food needs to be cooked, so you'll need bakers.
It truly is a great concept and a very fun game. But let's not get ahead of ourselves--it IS early access, which means there's currently only one type of monster (zombie), one type of guard (archer), and certain functionality isn't present at the moment (why can't I smelt my own ore?!? Why can't I assign and reassign colonist jobs?!!) , so the game does get a bit repetative faster than it really should.
But assuming that the developers continue to add variety and functionality to the base of their game, this will definitely be a must-have for any fan of the Minecraft genre (not sure what else to call it).
My only issue with the game is that once I have enough workers to make my colony self sufficient(took about 2-3 hours), there's very little incentive to keep building.
Still, I'm happy so far with the $20 I spent, and I'm anxious to see what the final product looks like.

First and foremost, if you are not a fan of the Nerd, blue humor, NES hard gameplay, and parody, turn around. This is not the game for you.
AVGN Adventures is a love letter to everything that is the Angry Video Game Nerd. You've got the Rolling Rock health display. You've got familiar Cinemassacre characters. You've got Super Mecha Death Christ. You've got Glitch Gremlin. You've got the NES Zapper as your main weapon. You've got hilariously vulgar lines coming from the Nerd at every new element in the game. And you've got homages to some of the Nerd's best moments.
As for gameplay, it's kind of like Mega Man in that you run and shoot similar to the Blue Bomber. You also have stage selects before each level and, after defeating the previous bosses, you fight in one final stage that throws everything at you. It also throws in a little bit of Super Mario 2 in having different playable characters with different mechanics.
The music is the absolute best part of the game. Each level has a driving theme that's also an homage to a certain game. While my personal favorite is the theme to Future ****balls 2010, the Laughin' Jokin' Numbnuts theme is just crazy.
It's not a perfect game at all, but it is more competent and has had more care given to it than most of the games James has played on the show. If you're a fan of the Nerd, you should've already gotten the game by now.

Honestly, compared to the first games (F.E.A.R. and it's non-canon expansions, Extraction Point and Perceus Mandate), this sequel kinda felt...flat. The weapons, the scares, and even the enemy AI just doesn't feel as appealing as in the first game. While yes, the gunplay is MUCH better compared to the first game, where you felt like you were fighting the game itself just to be accurate, the guns just feel...too easy in this game. They control more like Call of Duty or Battlefield (With the exception of the Assault Rifle on Full Auto past close-mid range) which just makes them feel more generic and less unique like they did in the first games. Secondly the scares are so...weak. Where as the first games continue to leave me chilled and freaked out even today, F.E.A.R. 2 failed to scare me even once. Not once did I feel in supreme danger from the super natural or Alma herself, and honestly that might be attributed to the fact scares are in short supply. Whenever there IS a scary segment, it fails to drag on long enough to instill any fear in me like F.E.A.R. 1 did. The timing and length is all wrong and leaves me disappointed for scares. I feel they were trying to mix scary segements into normal battle, but while Extraction Point got this down RIGHT when you were attempting (and failed) to rescue Jin, Project Origin just falls flat on it's face during every attempt to give you a scary feeling. Third, the A.I./the enemies, dear god. It's...it's so attrociously bad it hurts. In F.E.A.R. and the expansions, I felt as though enemies would try to keep you at a distance when first engaging, and set up in good firing positions to try and pin you down while others flanked, only rushing you if you drew too close or they were desperate. But in F.E.A.R. 2, all I felt was that (aside from the starting levels), most enemy encounters would have them all rushing you and moving into the closest avalible spot just to gun you down. I would be swarmed and feel unable to even do a thing because I was low on Slow-Mo, or I needed to reload. The grenades in this game did not help too much either. If you remember in F.E.A.R. and the expansions, grenades had unchangable 5 second fuses that were only overridden when they hit an enemy, where they detonated immediately. In Project Origin this is dropped for the ability to cook and time your grenades so they detonate when you want. While this works wonderfully in such games as Call of Duty, Battlefield, and many modern shooters, it completely fails in Project Origin. I'm often rushed by enemies so quickly I do not have the time to properly cook and time a grenade to thin them out because by the time I've got the pin pulled, I'm already being preforated by multiple Assault Rifles and Shotguns. Forth off I HAVE to mention the difficulty levels. There are a total of 3 difficulty levels in the game. Easy, Normal, and Hard. Each changes the amount of damage enemies do, what their accuracy is like (whether the game decides if they miss or hit you), and how much damage you do in return. Easy is...well easy. Enemies hardly ever hit you and their weapons do minimal damage, and you absolutely destroy them with your own. It also has a unique feature that if you ever take a lethal hit (a hit that would kill you out of easy mode), the game will automatically apply a medkit to you to save your life if you have one in supply. Normal...honestly feels far too easy as well. When I have armor on, I hardly, if ever, lose it to start taking health points. Oh yes, they changed the armor and health function as well from F.E.A.R. 1. Now it works on a Doom sort of function, whereas you lose Armor before you lose Health, (With the exception of some enemies which only attack health directly like Alma herself, and two weapons). And because of this and the fact Armor is in decent supply, I rarely, if EVER, use Medkits for any reason and I just decimate everyone in response. It feels so...foolish. So I naturally went to hard difficulty, and dear god Monolith got this SO WRONG. The jump from Normal to Hard is SO INTENSE it feels messed up. Like there was supposed to be 4 difficulties but they forgot to title "Impossible" as one and just decided to make "Impossible" "Hard mode" and put that in the game. Armor is the ONLY THING that saves you on Hard because a single enemy can literally almost 1 shot you instantly with a burst of fire without it. When you combine this with swarming enemies, this makes things so difficult it's not fun. I found myself just SWEATING and BEGGING for armor when I had none because I KNEW a single guy could kill me instantly, it was frustrating. FIFTH: It's bugged. I had multiple moments where the game just didn't load properly and I was in a black void with blue lines for outlines of ONLY the basic walls, or the floors, walls, and ceilings failed to load and I couldn't progress without restarting. On one ocassion a threshold near the end of the game was fully bugged and I fell straight through the map and died (I lost no progress. thankfully the checkpoint had been close by), and ONE TIME (just once though), as I had to reload a checkpoint, the load screen blanked out and the bar and flavor text vanished, along with any triggers so I had to Alt+Tab and close the game manually just to continue. Sixth, the game's "saving" system is so...bad. Instead of the fun and adaptible "Save whenever you want" system that Monolith used for the first installments, they opted for a full on "Call of Duty" style Checkpoint system where your only way of progressing is to go from checkpoint to checkpoint. And you get no free will here. Your options are "Load From Last Checkpoint" and that's it. No manual saving, no option to reload a save, no multi save feature. Just a checkpoint and that's IT. That's so awful it just...it hurts honestly. And finally the ending. I'm not going to spoil it here since you can do that yourself but...it's so confusing and short it's just...it's terrible. I can't understand it and I don't think I ever will. Do I recommend this game? Yes, because it's still at the very least entertaining if you like to shoot things. Do I like this game? Not really no. It's not horrifying enough to satisfy me, the guns are the only good things and even then they're mediocre, and the ending is...just atrocious. Final rating: 4/10 Please learn how to horror.

BUT this does not make this a bad game and it does not deserve the negative reviews (nobody plays it don't buy it), since that is NOT the games fault, it is to blame on bad release timing, being released at the same time as Overwatch and often being compared to it...
Battleborn is a really good game, with a good Story Mode and very fun Gamemodes against both bots and other player (if you find some).
The characters are very creative and give a great variety to it, no character is like another, they all feel different and play different, the Level-Up-System and Item-load-out in Battleborn adds to that.
You can play every character in hundreds of different ways and allways find something new and enjoyable with them. Any character can easily be a support, a "pusher", a damage-dealer, etc.
The game is influenced by both shooter and Moba games, having modes and elements of both genres.
The game keeps true to the Borderlands humor we know from well Borderlands and has a enjoyable storymode, that might proove chalenging if you are on your own.
In short: If you like Borderlands and want something while waiting for Borderlands 3, try this; if you like heroe shooter and want something different to the others, try this game; if you like mobas, but also the FP-perspective, try this game.
Really try to give this game a chance, watch gameplay videos or Let's Plays, try to see for yourself how you like it and don't handle it as "a failure", because it isn't.

I really liked the game, it's a non-violent turn based strategy/exploration game.  You use a combination of compliments, insults, and other dynamics (or just kill them).  I would definitely recommend playing it.  You explore maps, and then have movement based combat where you try to deal with enemies, or just locals who you have to use diplomacy with.  It was really a cool game to play.  The art is nice too, good animation and coloring, etc.
However, I just wanted to give a heads up to the developers about two things that made me quit playing early that hopefully they could remedy for the sequel (because I would buy a sequel if these two were smoothed out):
1)  You are discouraged from exploring each part of the map because you run out of supplies much too easily.  As a title with exploration in the name, I like exploring, but I missed out on little bits and felt I had to rush to the end.  At least give some option to customize your explorers easily so that playstyle is a viable option (not just an option, but viable).  Hand of Fate the game had a mechanic where you could explore every tile and be rewarded for it (exploring).
2)  The campaign (I believe) was just a hard race to the end and if you got behind too much, you would still be playing to the end but you would have really lost about halfway through (I'm not sure if I'm explaining that correctly).  Especially when you are learning, it feels tedious to be exploring mechanics (because you are learning the game) and then know that you're going to have to start over just because you weren't playing the "right way," for instance, exploring a lot.  For instance, instead of a hard fail, perhaps do gradations.  For instance, in some games, instead of a hard countdown to failure (it's effectively a countdown in this game), SteamWorld Heist has security levels, where the longer you spend in the level (and not every level, only some), more and more turrets show up to make it harder to escape the level alive.  This way, people can explore, and even give themselves a challenge, without a hard fail.
Hopefully there's a sequel, it was a very cool mechanically funny and interesting game!  I know I wrote a lot about my two biggest pet peaves, and didn't write enough about the good parts, but it's only because I want to buy the sequel and have the sequel be even better than the first!  Great job!

Despite the many tweaks and bugs that need to be fixed, this is a good game.
I instantly was thrown back to the old RCT 1 and 2 days. This is nowhere near as good as though, but this game is well on the way to be that great.
The grid system needs to be overhauled. The center of the grid should line up with the entrance of the park. This way one person could create a perfect symmetrical park with the entrance. It always looks off center the way it is not. The grid should perfectly be centered to the park entrance and the edges of the map boundaries.
The water and land modifier needs to be overhauled. Water is awful. They need to return to the old system from RCT 1 or 2. The water should just fill a pool instead of acting like a hose. Same with modifying land heights. It should be a click and hold feature. And the brush sizes should be larger and snap to the grid perfectly. Mine were all of square because the grid off square.
These are a couple issues I have with the game that others haven't really mentioned. Most people just complain about bugs and optimization so I stayed away from that.

Part character brawler, part puzzle platformer with optional precision platformer sections, Guacamelee! is thoroughly enjoyable as a whole.

Beyond the numerous references to video games and Internet memes, Guacamelee!'s clean and vibrant portral of Mexican culture and folklore stands on its own. Combined with the delightful soundtrack, my senses were pleasantly engaged throughout my playthrough.
It's a nice touch to view both endings without actually requiring to complete the optional objectives. At 6-8hrs, Guacamelee! didn't outstay its welcome and I'll probably return at some point to chip away at more of its side-content.
