The BEST $7.99 you will EVER spend!!! I don't know how this game doesn't cost $40.00! It is amazing.
The world is simplistic but beautiful. And whatever you can think of to build is probably possible. A walking robot with cannon for arms , a flamethrower mouth, and a helicopter head...no problem. A gigantic wheeled seige machine with boring drills in the front and a swinging flail that ejects different types of bombs...just make it. It's freaking hilarious to try to construct something like a Steampunk flying machine and watch it flip over and explode because you had a poor design. It's even cooler when you tweak the design and it really does fly...and shoots stuff!!

I started the campaign after looking at the settings to see how the controls worked.  In the first campaign portion of the game, you have like a house or castle in front of you. The object  was to destroy the house. I built a simple four wheeled machine with a cannon and succeeded. This machine did not work on the second campaign screen which had like a lighthouse on a hill (just gorgeous!!). I tried to build a flying machine but being a beginner, I had the weight all wrong and it kept flipping over because the cannons wee too heavy in the front. Then when it finally flew, it fell apart because I did not use steel braces. I kept tweaking it,  but couldn't get the weight right or make it stable as it tried to lift off,  however I did manage to make my machine pop a wheelie. So I popped a wheelie just high enough to shoot the cannon into the lighthouse....mission accomplished despite the fact that I'm a horrible builder.

The next mission was a castle. I noticed a bomb by the front wall and tried to use my cannon to blow it up. It didn't work. And there were archers shooting my machine so after about a 30 second arrow onslaught, it fell apart. So I built another wheeled machine with rockets on top. (took me about 3 minutes) But when I placed the machine on the ground the rockets fell off because I did not secure them, I reset and launched the rockets as soon as I hit the ground. The front castle wall exploded and dead archers fell out of the tower. I tried to go through the rubble but couldn't get traction so I went around. Another house on a hill inside the castle walls was still standing. But I had already launched my rockets. I reset again (takes seconds) and added some blocks to make the rear of my machine higher and installed two cannons high up. (took less than a minute). I restarted, blew the wall up with my rockets, looped around the wall and blew the house up with my cannons...mission accomplished.

The next mission had a beautiful tiny village filled with sheep and bombs. I had to steer through it carefully because the sheep kept detonating the bombs by stepping on them. It was a gory mess. I made it through unscathed. Most of the sheep died.

The last mission I tried had me placed in a quaint little woodsy area and surrounded by little soldiers that looked like knights. I still had the wheeled vehicle. They swarmed me! I started running them over. They made a squishing sound. My tires would lose traction in the blood. (I'm not kidding.) The bodies piled up in a big bloody mess, and it created a wall of gore I could not get through so then  I simply  backed up and and mowed down the ones behind me until both the dead and the living blocked me. There were so many that I just began to drive like a madman, swerving to areas where I felt I could get through without getting too many bodies wrapped around my tires. After killing like a hundred or two of them, I ran over a bomb I didn't see in all the carnage and I exploded. I quit so I could write this review.

Update: I loggd back on and joined a server where a guy said you could do anything you liked. All I had to do was click on his profile and join his game. The server he was on had a floating island and I just sat there in amazement as I saw about 6 guys creating stuff, running around, some of them fighting with the creations they had made. There was a military helicopter and it looked real and actually flew, unlike my own creation in the beginning. There was a giant steel snake that was probably one of the coolest things I've ever seen in a video game. It slithered like a real snake and even though it was mechanical it looked alive!!!! It was fighting another dude's massive armored vehicle filled with gadgets that did God knows what. There was another small vehicle with a long mechanical arm that would seek the enemy and try to pick them up and throw them off the island....he succeeded once before the snake used a drill that was mounted on it's tail like a rattlesnake to knock him into the abyss. And one guy had a flying dragon....yes...a flying dragon that dropped bombs. I can't make this stuff up...it really happened!!

There were so many fascinating machines that I didn't even build anything. I just watched in awe and laughed until I cried (It's the truth!) at the machines buzzing around attacking each other.

You would see someone building another weird machine in a corner and when he finished it, he would enter the fight. Sometimes his creation just flipped over and exploded like my amateur designs. Sometiimes the contraptions drove crazily or flew around like a confused bird until they fell off the island. But many of them actually worked and it was
as entertaining as anything I've ever seen. You just COULD NOT BELIEVE what you were seeing. I could not believe how much genius went into some of these creations and this was just 6 random guys on one server!!! It's simply amazing. You could have a blast just building stuff and never even play the campaign or do pvp!!!

So there's a campaign mode that's a blast and supposedly gets harder as you go on. There's a Pvp mode with noobs like me and dudes who make stuff that looks like they studied engineering for 26 years. There are private servers where people just build stuff and clown around like the one I visited. Supposedly a map editor will be available soon and you can make your own beautiful scenarios!

Buy this game NOW before the developer comes to his senses and charges $40.00 for it. It's worth every penny!!! Heck...I laughed more in 15 minutes of watching the antics of these bizzare creations than I did in two hours of watching comedians on TV!  This game is brilliant !!! Pro's: too many to list Con's: It's less than 8 bucks and its more fun than most of my $40 AAA titles...there are no cons.

Campaign: Tollerable
Game mechanics: Over simplified compaired to series before
Difficulty: Beginner C&C
An unfortunate end to great gaming series: SC/Forge then... this...

This game is horrible. Of course, that should be no surprise, because of how low I saw the ratings for this game, but... holy crap, this game is absolutely awful!
I've never been a big fan of Kick-A**. The comics sucked, but the movies were pretty decent. They never did anything particularly for me, but I can get why people love that particular character and his universe. But where the hell did this game come from? Someone, please, tell me! This game came out an entire year after Kick-A** 2. Who approved of this? Who agreed to this project, and released it in this state?
Okay, the game isn't ALL awful. Whenever I think of some of the worst games I've played like Manhunter or Kane and Lynch 2, they had awful controls and graphic design. Kick-A** 2 can boast graphics ripped off of Borderlands (but they still look good) and a game that actually functions. Walking Kick-A** doesn't feel like controlling a rubber chicken. Take notes, Manhunter! Take f***ing notes!
EVERYTHING else in this game is rubbish though, so stop your notes on controls and graphics, Manhunter. The game, in summary is, walk through straightforward poorly designed levels with arrows telling you where you need to go, fight 5 enemies or so, wash, rinse, and repeat.
Of course, you could learn the cool trick I learned. If you walk about ten feet from the fight, the enemies will completely forget you exist, causing you to blast through levels with ease.
This doesn't work with the boss, unfortunately. And it's here that a lot of the problems dispersed evenly throughout the game culminate into a big, moist hairy pile of filth on the shower drain. The combat is basically Batman: Arkham Asylum but watered down to punching and dodging. And even dodging is a little flakey, since you can only sometimes dodge enemy attacks. Only sometimes. And forget about enemies with guns. At that point, you're screwed. And if you die during a boss fight, it doesn't load like the other levels where it remembers all the enemies you kill. No, you do it all over again. And the frustrating combat system can be massively frustrating.
The icing on top of this sh** cake is the horrible, horrible, HORRIBLE voice acting. The actors sound like foreign vacationers stopping by America and getting tricked into doing the voices for this game. Hit Girl pronounces the word "nihilistic" like "Nih-HI-lis-tic". The opening line in the actual game that Kick-A** delivers about the Punisher is just as fantastic, too.
This game is awful. But it looks a little pretty. So judge it for yourself. I'm sure if you're masochistic enough, you'll learn to love this game. But I'm giving it a 3/10.

The opposite of Excitement.
You know you've been too long in the rpgmaker ghetto when you start using phrases like "well, the game balance is actually not terrible." It's not, and Incitement 3 could have a worse story. Its polish is not strictly awful so long as you don't think about words like "art assets" or "custom tilesets", and for fifty cents or so it's got a pretty okay gameplay to money spent ratio.
But it is a cartoonishly stock rpgmaker title with cludgy attempts at custom portraits and too-bright colors for the somewhat confused utopia/dystopia that it's trying to portray. Its plot follows a continuity that you're probably not invested in, and its combat system is the precursor to the surprisingly good one in City of Chains.
All in all, it's pretty safe to give this game a miss. You won't be kicking yourself for buying it like you would with Data Hacker, because the team involved with Incitement 3 seems like they a) care about improving, and b) care about making a non-awful product, but you could put the fifty cents you'd spend here towards City of Chains and be happier for it.

I held off buying RCTW because of the mostly negative reviews on here. Since buying and playing though, I have enjoyed the game but can see why it has attracted some negativity.
I think a lot more work is needed to bring this game up to an acceptable standard but as it is Early Access I am hoping the devs will deliver on their promised improvements, and soon. I have found the game becomes quite quickly boring due mainly to the lack of content, especially park transportation (Devs: please add URGENTLY!!). The lack of flat, water and other non-coaster rides also limits the game severely; I mean, you can only have so many teacup rides and observation towers in a park.
The lack of supplied scenery is bad and I have found it difficult to use the workshop items, mainly because a lot of contributors dont proivde any sort of description for their work.  This comment does not lessen my gratitude to the creators of such content for their hard work and generosity in sharing!!
The scenarios are somewhat irritating. In RCT3, if you fail a scenario you get another chance in a month or so but in RCTW, if you fail after 12 months, you lose the whole lot and have to start again from scratch. I can usually reach Bronze Level easily in these but then lose everything after the 12 month period has expired when trying for Silver and Gold.
I think the animations need some tweaking. For example peeps floating along paths, doors and gates do not open and close with peeps floating through them etc. Small items but important for the overall feel of thepark. Control of park staff is a major issue especially the janitors. In earlier games, I likes being able to assign work areas for staff.
I found one "bug" that has been annoying i.e. when placing most of the "upmarket" restaurants, I cannot connect paths to them. Even on a completely flat sandbox park I get the red error indicator when trying to join paths to, for example, the Ice Cream Parlor and Salad Restaurants (and others). I am fairly sure this is a game issue and not my lack of understanding on placement.
Rollercoaster Tycoon and Transport Tycoon were the first games I played on PC and I love the tycoon genre. This latest version of the RCT franchise has quite a way to go but overall, I would happily recommend it.

Antenna is a short and simple puzzle game with a very unique art style that seems to derive from games like LIMBO and Closure. If you enjoyed either of those two games, or the many other games like it, it's likely you'll enjoy this game too. The story is pretty simple, you play as a lonely robot in a world unknown, and your objective is to contact someone out there, using the radio towers and other equipment the robot hopes to find someone out there, anyone out there. The puzzles are pretty simple once you realize how to solve them, and the atmosphere and sound in the game is quite pleasing to go along with the simple game play. I do really wish there was a bit more to this game, because it's fantastic, unfortunately it's very short and doesn't have a lot to offer. I recommend playing this game when you've got nothing better to do, as it's not a game you'll have to spend a lot of time in and it's an easy game to complete in it's entirety.
Average Play Time - 20 to 30 Minutes.
Average Re-Playability - N/A.

Right from the get-go, you're placed in a situation where you don't know your♥♥♥♥♥from a hole in the ground, and that's basically the way it stays right up 'til the end.
TL;DR: This game is your Freshman college experience, with less booze.
Pros:
+ Pretty stunning atmosphere (in fact, it's really all there is to the game).
+ Visuals were dark, but crisp (think Limbo).
+ Sounds were actually interesting. Take some time to give them all a listen.
+ Cool twist on a puzzle game. Very few games I've played have had puzzles based solely on sound.
Cons:
- Lack of any real overarching story.
- Expensive.
Overall, I give it an 8/10. I'm probably not going to play it again, but it was a good experience for the ~30 mins.

This game is good, very good.
To start of this game is about exploration. Each game consists of 5 expeditions. After each expedition you can buy, research, expand entourage and a handful of other things to boost your expedition.
Its also a RPG, you must select 3 predefined characters to go out and explore with 1 being the captain who has his own set of cpt attributes. Your characters gain skill, interact among themselves and the world they explore.
The gameworld is cartoon style with a good sense of humor in it. Expect to be laughed at by hyenas, spitted by Lamas or teased by  monkies to name a few.
Combat is not all about physical. You can play agressive friendly or devious. Then there is the overall mood of the battle and charachter moods to keep an eye on. This mood system gives bonuses or weaknes and has a big impact on the outcome. It does take time to get familiar with.
The reason why this game is good: its so deep and rich of stategy features its a real challenge to play. Constantly the game challenges you to make decisions and without proper planning you will fail, a lot.  But, This is one of the few games where failing is not a bad experience. It motivates to try again and apply a different strategy.
A few cons. The learning curve is a bit steep, and you will probably buy all DLCs.
Overall, recommended for strategy and RPG gamers.

So I picked this game up for £9.99 and I'm not a die hard FEAR fan by any means, I haven't played the third installment and I never finished the first game because the repitition and complete failure to scare me even once made it too boring come the 4-5 hour mark.
Now, I understand that the first game has gone down as a classic thanks to the satisfying shooting and combat AI which I can appreciate, but the 'squad' based system it's famous for quickly became indistinguishable from every other above average shooter after 4 hours, and considering I bought it for a horror experience I was rather disappointed - speaking of course as someone who doesn't really hold FPS games on a pedestal (having never really put time into classic FPS games such as the original doom, turok, wolfenstein etc.)
FEAR 2 isn't its predecessor however, I only mention these problems I had with the first one to argue why I do not have these problems with FEAR 2. It was the first one I played in the series and after playing both the first and second games now - as someone who focuses more on the horror and story-telling side of the game - I can say that FEAR 2 is far superior to the first. Maybe not in its shooting mechanics (which are still remarkably fun regardless of any downgrades the weapons have recieved), but in immersive horror with incredible psychological horror sequences that do not necessarily rely on jump scares (although many will use them), but instead create a tense atmosphere within which you have no idea what, or where your enemy is.
The story of this game is told much better, with characters in much more common contact with you, and more squad members to be picked off by Alma as the game progresses. With your closest allies being K. Stokes (voiced by Cortana from the Halo series I think, though admittedly this would not be her best performance), who goes through the confusing journey at the same time as you so as to get a voiced reaction to the revelations and psychological horror of the game (as you yourself are again a silent protagonist), and Snake Fist, a mostly faceless companion who serves as the context giver in regards to Alma and her connection to Becket (your character), also offering mild comic relief at times.
The story itself feels a lot more connected to your actions in this game than in its predecessor; it was common in the first game for you to go through dozens and dozens of enemies shooting through a corridor without any development in the story. Although this is also kind of true for FEAR 2, it mostly suffers from this at the beginning in the lengthy hospital sequence, but after this the characters are in much more common contact with you, and thanks to a new enemy type in the form of the 'specimins', the game varies in combat enough that in sequences without story development it won't feel like a drag. However, that doesn't mean players will be kept strapped to a chair to watch the story develop either, as most of your communication is over the comms system, meaning it doesn't lose appeal for people who want to be left alone to run and gun.
Your encounters with Alma are dramatically increased from the first game, and with the inclusion of 'ghost' sections, specimins, some new mutants found in the destroyed city, the horror elements of the game are much more effective than in the original FEAR - this is something that I found very irritating about FEAR; the fact that its called FEAR and yet could not be more lazy about the horror aspects of the game. Alma is present but doesn't do much, and theres only so many times her walking down a corridor can scare you. It doesn't even use that many jump scares, which could be argued makes what few jumpscares there are more effective, but to me just leads me to forget that I'm playing a horror game at all. FEAR 2 is definitely more deserving of a horror stamp; the game actually scares me. The sequences of the game where soldiers stop shooting at you are genuinely intense, with Alma and other ghostly beings manipulating the environment and often jumping right at you (doing damage I might add, adding the fear of dying and having to go through it again). The specimins get annoying after a while, but a section at the end where it throws a dozen of them at a time at you can really make you sweat.
I've ranted on, which I tend to do, and if you don't want to read any monologues then I'll sum it up like this:
Shooting - 7/10
Story - 7/10
Horror elements - 6/10
Voice acting 6/10
Worth the asking price? Absolutely
An Improvement on the first game? If you agree with me that the shooting got tedious, it lacked in actual scares, and didn't give enough story to keep you going till the end - then absolutely.
I love this game, I think it's miles better than the first, and this is my opinion. What you loved about the first game is not done as well in the second game, but what you thought needed improving in the first game is absolutely improved upon in the second. And if you disagree, you've only lost out on £10, and at a 4.5 hour run time if played on medium difficulty, you'll probably know if you love or hate it while you can still get a refund.
Overall: 7/10

I have spent more hours than I care to think about playing darned near every decent FPS game in the past 25 years, beginning with the original Doom, Quake and Wolfenstein classics, when games were on floppy discs.  I am a F.E.A.R. fanboy; played the original game through several times when it was released, and loved both the expansions, Perseus Mandate and Extraction Point.   For some reason I never got around to playing this one at the time of its original release, so when F.E.A.R. 3 came out I decided to complete the collection, and to play this one before installing and playing F.E.A.R. 3.
I am tremendously disappointed in this game.  It is mediocre at best.  While there is some fun running and gunning, I have to echo the negative comments I've seen from other reviewers who gave this game a "thumb down."  The best weapons from the previous installments in the series, such as the ASP rifle, dual-wield pistols and (I believe) the HV Penetrator, have been removed, and replaced with unremarkable crap.  Quicksaves have been eliminated in favor of scripted save points...hello, console gamers.  You can now only carry three med kits instead of ten, which seems to have been offset by most enemies (but not all) dealing less damage than before, and by not losing any health in most instances until your armor has reached zero.  (WTF??) The use of slo-mo is no longer key to successful combat.  The 'scare' scenes seem contrived and out of place most of the time.  Instead of the really well-done uber-enemies like the assassins and spirits of the earlier games, we get silly-looking creatures that scuttle and run and jump around impossibly fast and trigger "mash your RMB as fast as you can" cutscenes, or big, hulking, nearly immortal zombies that stagger around with red wires seemingly attaching them to the sky.  The replicas and other humanoid enemies no longer have sneaky smart AI, but simply come at you shooting.  Much of the combat has become boring and/or irritating instead of challenging and fun.
What once was a really creative, unique and fun PC game has been killed off and replaced with a mass-market console shooter. More's the pity.
UPDATE:
I tried to post this update a few minutes ago and it seems to have disappeared.  So if somehow my first attempt survives and this becomes redundant, my apologies in advance.
A few additional comments based on having completed the game now.
First, I was wrong about two things.  The old "HV Penetrator" weapon, my favorite from the previous F.E.A.R. games, is still there, although you don't get it until very late in the game.  It seems to be not quite as effective as before, and the graphics are different, of course, but yes, it still exists, under a new name.  Also, the old nearly-invisible and fearsomely quick Assassins are still here, too, but again not until quite late in the game.  The other paranormal enemies remain more irritating than effective, IMO.
Second, I do owe some compliments to a few aspects of this game despite my overall negative review.  There are two really fine new weapons, the sniper rifle and the plasma energy weapon.  The sniper rifle is just great to use, and while there are only isolated sequences in which it's useful, in those sequences it is VERY helpful.  You're basically dead without it, in fact.  You also have the ability to grab some extra ammo and then keep the weapon in your four-weapon inventory until it comes in handy again, and it will.  In the brief instances in which you actually have to battle enemies who are using the same weapon, they will be telegraphed by visible laser beams, as in some other games, but this is fair, as the alternative would be for you to get shot and take a LOT of damage before having any idea where the bad guys are.  Once you do see them, they may be a bit too easy to kill, but the battles are still fun.  The other new weapon worthy of mention, the plasma energy weapon, is very similar in operation to the BFG from the old (and new!) DOOM games.  And it's great fun to use, as well as being devastatingly effective.
Last, I owe a shout out to the devs for the relatively brief, but fun sequences in which you're able to pilot a mech--called "power armor" in this game--as they are a blast even though they're not particularly difficult, as compared with, say, the tank-driving sequences in games like COD or Medal of Honor.  Both the sniper and power-armor battles here are welcome diversions, although brief, from the regular grind.
That leads me to my last major complaint about this game.  I mentioned in my first review above that I found the combat irritating, and it became even more so as I progressed through the "intervals."  I couldn't quite put my finger on why this game irritated me so in comparison with the original and the two expansions, but having finished now, I think it comes down to the way in which the enemies appear.  In the original and expansions, you got clued in that a battle was about to start by hearing the replica soldiers talking to each other, which was basically your cue to hit "slo-mo" before opening a door or going around a corner.  If you handled it well, you could often get in a couple or several kills without taking too much damage, and by saving often and using cover and slo-mo well, you could even complete an entire firefight with minimal loss of armor and health.  Sometimes that wasn't possible, but you still had a reasonably good chance of completing most of the combat sequences  without dying.  The exceptions were the occasional battles with the "nightcrawler" troops, who were very nearly too powerful, but could still be beaten with care and lots of quicksaves.  They were challenging even on "normal" difficulty, but I never found those battles as irritating as even the "standard" battles generally proved to be in F.E.A.R. 2.  In this game, while you still normally get a pre-firefight warning from replica radio transmissions, the similarity ends there.  Now, rather than coming into an area where all or most of the enemy are already present, you get a long, tedious parade of one, two or three enemies at a time, each spawning out of nowhere as you dispatch their predecessors, but making their presence known chiefly by shooting you with impossible accuracy and often from improbable distances or angles. They even seem to be able to shoot through brick walls and solid cover at times.  I found myself exclaiming in frustration many times over as I progressed through the battles, something I rarely do.  I mean, you expect  bad guys in any FPS  to be numerous and more or less deadly if not killed fairly quickly, but the parade of enemies here seemed to drag on too long most of the time, especially given the three-medkit limit and the relative paucity (it seemed to me, anyway) of armor and medkit pickups.  The battles with the "elite power armor" (i.e., giant mech WITH ENERGY SHIELDS) were also frustrating, in that the mechs are armed with dual miniguns with infinite ammo, they apparently can see you even when you're behind walls or other cover, their bullets seem to deal out significant splash damage, they can keep hitting you even when you sprint, and the ONLY way to drop their shields is by tossing EMP grenades, which you can't do effectively without standing in line of sight and thus getting hammered by the miniguns, or shooting overhead power transformers, of which there aren't very many, and which only exist outdoors in any case.  When you get their shields to drop, you have maybe three seconds to do damage before they come back up, and you get to do the whole grenade/slo-mo dance over again. After getting waxed about a dozen times by the first one of these,  I ended up taking the easy way out and adjusting the difficulty to a lower setting to finish them off.  I hate doing that, but..
And then there's the ending.  WTF???  Subject to varying interpretations, none of which is very satisfying.  Overall, I found it lame.

When people talk about which Hitman game is the best, Blood Money is the game I see most often. And over a decade later this game still holds up as a fantastic stealth-puzzle game. There's no story baggage from previous games here, which combined with the tight controls and refined gameplay, make this (or the new 2016 game) the perfect Hitman game for newcomers.
Hitman is a very unique kind of stealth game. There's really no other game quite like it. If there's one word that describes Hitman's gameplay, it's
. This game does not hold your hand at all and the first time you complete a mission it most likely... won't quite go as planned. You may have a huge pile of additional corpses on top of the ones you were meant to kill or had a police officer walk in on you dragging around a half naked body while dressed as a chicken. But that's fine because you're not really meant to ace a mission on the first go. Hitman is about observing, learning and experimentation. You'll watch guards go about their patrols, picking up on certain areas and items they interact with so you can exploit them to get one step closer the offing your target(s).
With every run you learn more and more about the map and it's inhabitants. You will execute different plans with all the information you've gathered in your head and the amount of freedom this game gives you to play how you want and experiment is amazing. Attempting to put two of the map's puzzle pieces together and succeeding feels great because you did it all by yourself. By the time you pull off that glorious-feeling Silent Assassin run (or if you want to take it up another notch: Silent Assassin + Suit Only), you'll know the map like the back of your hand. Hitman is definitely not a game for the impatient.
One of the most distinct and recognizable aspects of Hitman is it's disguise system. Once you knock out/kill an NPC you can take their clothes (bar civilians) and use their status to access areas of the map that are otherwise restricted. Slipping in as a staff member or police officer feels awesome. However in Blood Money the disguise system is too forgiving imo. In all my time playing this game I have never once been found out with a disguise on. The only way you'll ever be caught is if you're trying to. Don't worry, this doesn't make the game a cake walk (I still haven't managed to pull off a Silent Assassin run on two of the end game missions) but it certainly feels odd that guards never seem to question this guy who was apparently hired to be a bodyguard, waiter, clown and lifeguard all at once at this party.
But all in all, Blood Money has aged brilliantly and is a fantastic entry in the franchise for both veterans and newcomers. It's an absolute steal at it's standard price, let alone the 80% off deal right now in the Summer Sale.

This game is pretty good being in early access, i got dragged into this game from a youtuber playing it and i thought it was really cool concept, i eventually got it and it lived up to what i thought it would be like.
Note: you will get into this game thinking "Oh, its just another minecraft clone you mine, craft, build, whatever" but those are just about all the similarities that minecraft and colony survival have together, and what is so cool about this game is that you have to use all the features or it gets boring really quick.
You have to hire colonist with your starting 300 food and beds maybe a bowman and 2 berry farmers then you can do whatever you want next, build a mineshaft, hire a crafter, get to work on wheat farms, and more. the bowman protects you and your colonists from the angry monsters that look like miners. however they only spawn when you get some colonists so your not being rushed in time. after a few nights you can hire more and more colonists till you get a village/kingdom and with the limited number of blocks you have, you can actually do a lot in terms of houses and structures, not much with other things but you still can do stuff.
Now to the pros and cons
PROS:
~Biomes (I have only seen about 5, Forest, Plains, Taiga, Mountain, and Snow, but there is probably more)
~Colonists (You finally don't have to do everything yourself!)
~Graphics (Gets a bit repetitive and a bit grid like if you pay attention to certain blocks but amazing eitherway)
~Ambiance (Its really descriptive on when its night or day)
~Detail (Looking at a block from the side actually shows some 3D look to blocks. Thats cool)
Cons:
~Not enough gameplay unless you restart multiple times (Seeing some sort of conflict that only happens on certain days would be pretty cool)
~No Weather (No Rain, Snow, Storms, etc.)
~Not enough blocks (Seeing some different blocks/items would be cool to work with)
~Not enough variety (Seeing some different variety in blocks in how you place them would make the game more realistic)
~Sounds (Some sounds were a bit too loud, like when jumping into water, it sounds like a cannon ball and it freaked me out when i first heard it)

~Weather: I think it would be better if you could get rain and lightning storms, just immersion into the world not really needed
~Animals: Wheat is a pretty good source of food but what about animals? Animals could be in farms and stuff and you could get meat, milk, wool, and more from these animals
~Disasters: Floods, Storms, other disasters that would happen naturally,
~Stronger Monsters: Some Monsters are bigger, take more arrows. (I think I'm trying to add more ways to fail...)
~Biomes: maybe something like a desert surrounded by mountains
~More Blocks: Things like Wool, Carpet, more Flowers, Plants, etc.

I tried KotOR because it was a Star Wars game, and fell in love with because it was one of the most amazing games I've ever played.
The graphics and combat may be outdated, and the AI a little frustrating when one of your squad mates falls behind and you have to wait for them to catch up before leaving an area, but I think the flaws are easily overlooked when compared to the engaging, branching story that offers multiple endings depending on the choices you make.  Over the course of the game you will visit several unique planets, expand your crew of playable squad mates, and obtain multiple side quests that are varied and interesting, and never feel repetitive.  You will also gain new abilities and force powers as you level up and complete your Jedi training, and it's up to you whether you embrace the Light Side or fall to the Dark Side.
I am on my third playthrough (though Steam will show you fewer hours than I've actually put into this game, as I own it on disc as well) and it still feels like a new experience.  I have no doubts that I will replay this game multiple times in the future.

A tactical RPG/adventure/strategy game with roguelite elements where you don't have to kill anyone - and they can actually kill you with kindness too. It's a real thing.
Renowned Explorers is in the same vein as FTL for general structure. You go on adventures, choose what course of action to take based on each situation, and get urged toward the ever present end of the game by a timer (in this case, supplies) counting down a punishing you severely for milling around in search of goodies too much - and these adventures are periodically broken up with combat. And if you lose, you start over from scratch in rogue-lite fashion (unless you're playing on the easier adventure mode). That's about where the similarities end.
Renowned Explorers combat is tile-based tactics-RPG style battles that feature a roshambo style "mood" system. Characters can use either weapons or words to do battle, and depending on how they use either, the general attitude of the combat can shift to be friendly, deceptive, or aggressive (read: actual fighting.) So, yes, you can actually befriend every enemy you come across instead of shooting them in the face. Or call them mean names until they're too depressed to continue fighting. You monster. But you might not want to stick explicitly to one strategy, because your approach also changes the prizes that come with a successful battle. There's a lot more complexity to it that I really can't touch on in a brief review, but the whole battle system works strangely well.
If you're someone who enjoys adventure roguelites like FTL and Convoy, I implore you to give Renowned Explorers a try - it might just be your new favourite. Or if you want a somewhat chill RPG experience, it's good for that too.

This is an awesome game--an platformer for anyone with love for the likes of The Legend of Zelda, Metroid, Mega Man, and perhaps even new platformers like VVVVVV.
The game plainly wears early-Nintendo influences, but it doesn't feel derivative. Luchadore-style combat is quick, combo-heavy, and gets steadily more complicated (and tougher) as the player progresses through the game. Story progress is pretty straight-forward (no getting lost in that sense) but there's nothing stopping the player from exploring as much as they can of the world--assuming they have the powers to do so. As the player progresses, more pathways open up as new abilities are unlocked, and the end goal is closer. The classic way of doing things--the player and the character's skills grow, and that is damn satisfying.
There's a lot to go out and find, and a good deal of it is really challenging to get--but not infuriatingly so. A few really tough parts might take a little extra work, but it's satisfying when it pays off.
Guacamelee has amazing art and music, too, all heavily influenced by Mexican culture. The story is simple (another man saving a woman love interest from evil, sadly), but the ending (both of them) manage to be touching. There's also local co-op, too, which I imagine is really fun (which, uh, would make the story: man AND badass lady luchadore spirit save woman from evil, which is a bit better)!
Basically, play this game. Its music and art make it a gem already, but the great gameplay makes it pretty essential for anyone who appreciates the other aforementioned games.
Oh, also, you can turn into a chicken. 10/10

I generally don't like On-rails Shooters too much when played on anything but an arcade machine with light guns, but this game was a total blast. I'd never even heard of it until I got a key for it from a bundle and decided to check it out. And I'm so glad I did.
Blue Estate is based on a comic book series of the same name which I'm not familiar with, but that didn't matter for the story as it was self-contained and easy to follow. It's not a great or deep plot by any means, but the writing and many moments were genuinely funny. It really doesn't happen often that a game makes me chuckle a lot for the RIGHT reasons, and is good and fun to play on top of that.
The gameplay is just fantastic; unadulterated non-stop action with very satisfying gunplay, ragdoll physics on defeated enemies, moments where you jump sideways through the air and take out a group of enemies in slow-motion and scoring for pretty much everything you do. I also like the way they handled the enemies and the threat they pose for you. Since you can't move of your own accord or always have the option to cover, the enemies will miss most of their attacks. When an enemy is actually about to take a shot which is going to hit you, it will be indicated by a circle which is filling up, allowing you to take out the enemies which pose a threat to you first. It's a short story mode, my first playthrough taking under three hours. To make up for this, it has an arcade mode which you just have to play because it's a lot more different from the story mode than I expected and non-stop action to an even higher extent, and there is also quite some replayability and reasons to challenge yourself if you go for the achievements or a leaderboard position.
Controls-wise it worked out really well with a mouse and keyboard. Well, I only used the mouse for aiming, shooting and motion quick time events, but I think those directional quick time events can be mapped to WASD or the arrows keys instead. There is an option for auto-aim, which in normal circumstances is only negative to mouse aiming, but in this case it was very convenient because you don't control your character's movements and it makes up for the times where he's strafing slowly. My only issue with the controls is that reloading your weapon is done by right-clicking once and switching to your other weapon is done by right-clicking twice. I didn't know this was even a thing at the start and thought my mouse was broken or that it was some unexplained boss mechanic. There doesn't seem to be a way to change the buttons for that, and it's just too easy to accidentally double click with how fast-paced the game is.
I'd strongly suggest picking up this game for a good price if you're looking for some mindless, satisfying and awesome fun and some (in my opinion) great humour. To make a comparison to some other games, I'd say this is a mix between a general feeling of The Darkness II without the supernatural aspect and the slow-motion sequences of Max Payne while the sexual and racial themes of the humour reminded me of Shadow Warrior. If anything I hope this review introduces this game to anyone who might be interested in it, because if it wasn't for a bundle this would have gone completely under my radar but I ended up really liking it.

Loved it! It's a bit dated for sure, but I totally love the concept/story, and the horror and psychological parts were so cool.
The Good:
-Graphics and lighting still hold up pretty well
-Performance is significantly better than the original. I'm running on a GTX 1080TI, so that obviously shouldn't be an issue, but the first game literally didn't go above 30fps and regularly dropped into the 20s (yes in compatibility mode)

-The main game, though pretty short, felt a lot more put together than the first.
-The different types of guns are really cool. Lasers, machine guns, shotguns, hammerheads. And piloting a mech is SO much fun.
The Bad:
-Gun mechanics are mega clunky.. Not too bad if you're only fighting a few dudes, but it gets infuriating when you die because your aim goes flailing due to distant explosions. And the ADS is entirely useless as I can shoot a guy directly in front of me and nothing with happen, so just stick to hip fire.
-Clipping into objects is a big headache when I'm trying to jump over something, or take cover when under fire. I just get stuck on what seems like everything
-The main game is GREAT, but Reborn is TRASH and can be avoided if you're not super dedicated to learning the storyline. Random difficulty spikes, it's only 40 minutes long, and the only fun/horror/conceptual part is the very end, so not really worth the time.
It's overall super fun though, this is the first time I'm playing through the series ever and I'm totally hooked!

Buckle up, buttercup, and over the next few glorious paragraphs, I'mma learn you a thing I only myself just learned yesterday about this little thing we call Cossacks 3.  Tl;dr at the end.  I think we'll start smartifying you by explaining what kind of game this is.
Cossacks 3 is several things.  Not the least of which is a reboot and 3D evolution of a classic real-time strategy game called Cossacks: European Wars.  Yes, European Wars.  That one.  Not Back to War.  Also known as the standalone expansion for European Wars.  There are only 12 nations (not 20) and the the nations involved have maybe one or two unique units instead of...well, two or three unique units.  The year 2000 wasn't really known for its asymmetrical strategy titles.  Sure, that had been all the rage since Star Craft was released a couple years before, but we all know what a flash-in-the-pan fad that garbage was.  It certainly didn't have the staying power of Cossacks: I Forgot Which One I Played Now That You Mention It Wars.
No, it was definitely European Wars.  I remember fondly getting off the triceratops I rode to and from school, in a blizzard, uphill both ways, and eagerly going to the computer in the family room. I would get out the Compact Disc (that's what we called downloaded content in those days) and popping that sucker into my computer.  Which was basically an electric shaver powered by a hamster wheel and stapled to a Wheaties box.  I would play for hours as I raised hundreds and hundreds of colorfully animated sprite soldiers to do battle against my friends or the AI.  Most of these soldiers would die needlessly in frontal assaults so ill-advised that the ghost of General Robert E. Lee himself would slap me in the face and tell me I wasted the lives of that division charging up that hill "Like I did that one time."
Cossacks takes the winning formula of proto-Napoleonic tactics: standing shoulder to shoulder and firing at the enemy point blank and...well, it just takes it.  It faithfully reproduces the tactics of the period.  Watch in fiendish glee like the Antedeluvian god that you are inside and recruit hundreds if not thousands of now 3D rendered men.  Put them in a rank and file, column, or square formation, and tell them to advance ever forward, firing and stabbing everything in their way.  The battles are less bloody than I remember.  Come to think of it, this version has no blood.  That's kind of disappointing.  But oh well, it's been a long time since a game of this age has come close to reproducing the feeling from European Wars.
Speaking of games of this era: A lot of people say this game is like an Early Access version!  Well, that's probably because it is.  Unless they are selling the Cossacks 3-Just In The Nick of Time Edition, it's pretty clear what you are getting, numb nuts.  I can hear you now: "Hey handsome, why is the game not in Early Access officially then?"  Well, Short Round, that's probably because it doesn't qualify as Early Access.  For example, most games in Early Access aren't 99.9% of the way done, with all promised features in a basically functional state. Emphasis on basically functional for this one.
Sure there are bugs.  But it wouldn't be a release from our favorite Eastern European developers, GSC Game World if there weren't any.  And if you spot a localization error, that's not an error.  That's just an inside joke.  There's nothing funnier than an inside joke 16 years later.  Sure, hundreds of people could have corrected that sentence.  But gosh darn it, it brings a smile to my face seeing my Musketers try their hand at Musketeering.
Since getting the game just one day ago, there have been three updates, one of which enabled multiplayer.  Total time without multiplayer: 16 hours.  Most of that time I was kickin' it with the AI and sleeping.  Or was I working?  Oh my.
Speaking of bugs, some people seem to be under the impression that this game just don't plain work.  Well, let me ameliorate and co-mulgrify that situation for ye right now.  The game runs fine.  Assuming you aren't using the same electric razor powered by a hamster wheel stapled to a Wheaties box that you used back in the day.  A toaster should do just fine.  Just make sure you installed the latest drivers, and popped open the side panel to clean out the blackened crums of a thousand departed Pop-Tarts before you play.  I have played for just about three hours (which in fairness is only 2 complete matches the way I play) and I haven't had one CTD, crash, graphical glitch, or super-volcano eruption resulting in the extinction of mankind yet.
The game experience is much like the original.  It even retains many of the same balancing values for units and costs for tech upgrades.  So that's right, McGillicutti: you can advance to the 18th century in under 15 minutes and immediately purchase a tech that reveales the entire map, thus robbing yourself of the surprise and wonder you are supposed to feel when 50 Janissaries show up in your camp, kill everything and capture all your crap.  I only do that rush to see the look on your face, and that darn balloon tech spoils it each time.  Too bad there's nothing that can be done about those Janissaries though.  Probably should have bought some Pikemen or something.  But oh well.
Aaaaanyway, what else is there to say about this game?  Lack of blood...recaptures the original in full 3D...nails the classic formula for warfare of the period...massive gratuitous battles...cheap teching strategies meeting up with cheap rush strategies that will keep the forums lively with debate about what exactly is OP for decades to come...yep I think that just about covers it.  What's that?  You want to know if it's worth getting?  IS that what I was supposed to be flapping my gums...er...clattering my keyboard about?  Well, shucks, son.  Maybe it's best to explain it this way:
Tl;dr
Pros: It's basically everything that the original, vanilla Cossacks 1 experience was.
Cons: It's basically everything that the original, vanilla Cossacks 1 experience was.
And quite frankly, I can only recommend that experience.

Without much storytelling and lore, the game throw you into a series of everyday scenes where you enter into it casually like a pedestrian, try to pass some forbidden areas, kill often the most protected people here and then walk away. There is actually a strong statement here: 47 killed so many people yet he can wander in front of any policemen. This fact tells so many information about how this man and his job is supposed to be. You are going to kill people but you have to keep yourself in the sea of people as much as possible.
The highlight of the game is that the chance is based on people’s activity rather than physics. You are not looking for some seconds when the guards turned around or light is off so that you can move from one cover to another. Despite the scale of the map, most of the time you act in places like small offices for 1-2 people, corridors of dorms or a dinning room of a public place which are either small or crowded with people. This means the traditional cliche of stealth gameplay is effectively forbidden, you have to go with Hitman’s way. People do not view you as an enemy to start with, and they have their own things to take care of. Chief, cleaners, maintenance workers and doctors, they will be able to enter this or that forbidden areas by doing their normal work. Connecting different people’s routine will give you a chain that lead you to your target. Then the job is to kill each ring of the chain as quietly as possible and get their clothe as disguise. The chance of the final kill is usually interestingly hidden inside the target’s personality, you have to observe him not as a moving object, but as a human in order to find the best way. The negative of this is that sometimes you can get lost when you lack some real life knowledge to understand what is going on. Can I enter this room with that guy’s clothe? What is the proper things to do in this place?
This is excellent. However, the game sticks to this model of gameplay till the end and did not do any mind blowing things in later levels. You will easily figured out some patterns that prevails each level. Also, some disguise, usually the guards’, are over powerful, making you able to travel straight up from the entrance to the target.
This game deprives many of gamers’ privilege they are custom to in modern day’s games. As a game where being discovered is a half game over, there is not any parallel to the witcher’s sense or iDroid and you are in the danger of getting caught from people emergent from places you cannot keep an eye on. The only surreal assistance is a big map you have to jump out of game screen to check (time does not stop) which tells you the position of guards and targets. Its strength is greatly weakened by the numerous doors, stairs and channels of any forms. All these add immersion and push the players to think in the same way as their characters instead of a semi god outside the game.
This game has a very rigid stealth system. There is a very clear boundary between do’s and don’ts. The guards, especially in later levels, are too intolerant for a modern society. Entering the wrong place, holding a gun, climbing, dragging a body, shortconnect the wire... will draw attacks immediately. Considering the lack of covering system and the intensity of enemies in higher difficulty, gun blazing does not seem to be a way at least for me. The weapons you collect in levels serves more like trophies.
However, it does not prepare a smart control to match that kind of rigidness. E is associated with infinite amount of actions. Opening doors, taking elevators, dragging a body, looting, hiding weapons in a container... the system helps you determine which action applies. In many situation where several actions applies you might get unwanted result in the most urgent time. For example, when you are in front of the door but want to drag a body. When you pick up a gun from ground, you by default hold it in your hands instead of hiding it, and might forgot that and walk with it... Using wire to suffocate people, which is one of the corner stone of the gameplay, is annoying, sometimes you crawl to the back of the target but cannot trigger the action, move a little, you might just be discovered.
I also had a feeling in some levels that the stealth system is not self-consistent and is interfered by some “higher orders”. That is, you are supposed to perform certain actions in certain places, and you will be punished if you get one of them (action and place) wrong even if that deed is not that different from the right one. For example, in one level, you can find a special chemicals in the kitchen and put it in your target’s cup, which is in a bar crowded with people, to cause him to do certain things and open the opportunity to kill him. On the other hand, if you want to be straight and use your own poison, you immediately get caught by guards.
Many of the factors mentioned above made me to believe that this is a game that need to encourage save/load. You have to get familiar with the places and people in a new level in order to find opportunities, which is in no way transparent. You might also want to try some new ideas of killing. Or you just want to test some of the game’s mechanics out of curiosity. However, this game is saying “save/load is a stupid thing” by restricting your chances of saves and forbid you to save in-level progress when exiting the game. Therefore I often need to sacrifice a few runs to explore the game. Sometimes my careful plan fails when it is near the end by some stupid mistakes caused by control problems and I have to go back to a much earlier load.
The last mission is disappointing. The game throws away everything you gained since you started playing, both the in game items and player’s expertise in this game, and drop you into a straightforward shoot them up battle. I understand that the last mission need some intensity, but this is a very rude way to create it. It is also a narrative failure. Whether you stand still and head shot every one surrounding you or flee to a safe place to shoot and gradually take enemies out, it is at odds with the game’s depiction of 47 as a quiet, precise and elegant killer.
This is a game that is elegantly designed but does not show off it loudly. Whether you will get joy highly depends on your ability to deal with unfriendly designs.

I intially went into this game with low expectations I have been dissapointed with licensed product before (having played a myriad of movie tie-in shovelware titles in my youth.) However I was very impressed with AVGN Adventures, a game that will appeal to both long-time fans of The Nerd and fans of hardcore retro platformers.
This title was released in 2013, developed by FreakZone Games and published by ScrewAttack. As shown by The Nerd in his episode "AVGN Games", games about The Nerd and his angry world have existed long before this game came out. Many of those titles were homebrew titles often created by one person and released on the Internet for free. AVGN Adventures is the first commercial AVGN game and certainly the title with the highest production value. Visually, the game features rich and colorful pixel art in additional to some smoothly animated effects (The Nerd exploding into several bits and pieces a la Fallout 3 is a highlight.) The soundtrack hearkens back to the video game days of yore, featuring an engrossing score that fits right at home with the games overall difficulty as well as sound effects that further  draw you in.
The gameplay is almost perfect for a game of this genre, it's hard but not unfair, and it's levels are fun and all vastly different from eachother. My only true gripe with the game is the finicky keyboard controls which unfortunately makes jumping and landing with precision challenging. This problem is of course erased when you plug in an Xbox 360 PC controller, however it does not erase the games overall difficulty. This game is not recommended for anyone who's not familiar with NES titles like Mega Man, Ninja Gaiden, and Castlevania as the difficulty of this game mimicks that of those classic titles. Also, the game doesn't have much replay value after you complete it for the first time which is acceptable for a $10 game but it would have been a nice feature to unlock additional levels or harder difficulty levels after you complete the game.
It's definitely worth your money if you like hard-as-nails, old-school platformers!

Payday is an amazingly fun game. I like how simple, independent games like these always manage to get me to sink many more hours into it than any of the higher budget titles that are out.
Unlike most shooters out, Payday forces you to play realistically. Your goal is not to rack up a body count, but to perform a heist. When a Rambo tries to run into the open, and play the bad♥♥♥♥♥ they end up getting horribly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arrested, and then left behind as his teammates progress through the stage. The game just has a really intense feel as you yell at civilians to drop to the floor and shoot out surveillance cameras in preparation for police arrival.
I have seen quite a few complaints about the AI being 'too sentry,' but imo, it is very realistic. The task force units feel professional and trained as I would expect any officer charging into a bank heist, or general hostage situation, would be. However, they are quite careless about shooting around civilians and you will often find yourself feeling like you are trying to save innocents from a reckless police riot.
Overall, this game is soo good I bought it twice. Once for PS3, and once for PC. The only reason I do not give this game a perfect score is because, regardless of how good it is, it could have been better. I would like to have seen more content in the game, and could come up with a huge list of easily implemented ideas that would have heavily deepened the game-play. Also, this game does not hold your hand. It took me too long to figure out how to access and change my progression tree. Many game features you may only discover through playing with others, such as hostage negotiations.

I have been a die hard RCT fan my whole life. I still play RCT3 all the time, 12 years after its release.
I have been following RCTW since it was first roumered, and I was extremely excited for it. I had waited over a decade for a new RCT installment, so you can imagine my anticipation for this game.
I am sad to say that this game is not good. I was okay with it being released in early access rather than a finished game, but it isn't even close to ready.
I was expecting all of the features of RCT3, plus a plethera of new features, rides, scenery, interface, and better graphics.
This game has none of that.
It is basically a stripped down version of RCT3. There are hardly any rides, there are less themes than there were in previous games, the graphics are bad, and it is poorly optimized (it freezed and lags on my PC that can play virtually any game on ultra settings). On top of all that, the path system and the terrain system are totally broken. They claim to fix it them in every update, but it still doesnt work.
The best part about the RCT series was that you were able to imagine a dream park, and then build that exact park. RCTW doesn't let you do that, and most final products come out uglier and more awkward looking than you imagined.
As of right now, I cannot recommend this game. I don't know what Atari was thinking charging $50 for a game that is years away from being complete.
If I were you, I would pre-order Planet Coaster. It looks like they will be releasing a complete game with all the features we want.

Don't let the cartoony graphics fool you, this is one of the most compelling adventure/strategy games I've ever played, and I've been at for 35 years now!
I got a good fifty hours of joy just out of playing through the game, without too much mix/maxing or stressing about the finer points of the systems. Then another 50 hours working out those systems and starting to actually game the game.
Now I'm getting more value out of the thing by actually planning, in detail, my expeditions before I run them. This approach reveals the sheer genius behind the game design and exquisite balancing.
For each expedition, you're trying to work out a sweet spot between (a) your choice of three characters (from a menagerie of 24 total), (b) your expedition pathway - five expeditions per game, selected from 14 expedition locations, (c) your character upgrade pathways; (d) your campfire chats; (e) your approach to encounters - aggressive? devious? friendly"; (f) the items you are intending to prioritise getting, and what bonuses to pull off them; (g) your town-building options (research pathway and entourage).
Sorting out the interactions among all of these interrelated systems is loads of fun. You always have to make some compromises, you can never quite cover all the skill bases you'd like. Basically you're trying to set up a snowball of resources that continues to build throughout the game... sometimes the snowball grows way faster than you imagined it, other times it seems to just run flat.
The joy of discovering an unusual approach to all of the above - it's just immensely rewarding. I only just managed to finally get a score of over 10,000 - which is sort of the ultimate accomplishment in the game. Now I find out reading on the forums that scores of over 17,000 are possible - so clearly I still have a long way to go building a better snowball!
Aside from the strategising, the game is wonderfully atmospheric. The cartoon graphics have grown on me a lot, they are full of personality and I can only congratulate the character designers (text and graphics) for creating 24 highly evocative mini-characters with just a few strokes of the pen, and a few sentences of text.
Any cons? Not many... I have encountered some glitches, and the game crashes on me about one session out of 20. Some of the encounters are a bit too vague and could use some more imaginative drafting. That's all I can think of!
I can only recommend this game in the highest of terms for anybody who enjoys strategy, puzzles, and adventure games, and who appreciates a game that can be played quickly, but can also be meticulously planned for a deeper experience.
Oh, and you have to be happy with randomness! If RNG makes you aggro, seek elsewhere. A "wheel of fortune" is an essential part of this game's mechanics!

This is a really charming game with a surprisingly deep level of strategy.  Giving the player the option of resolving conflicts peacefully, cunningly, or through open hostility feels less like RPS than in most games that use this mechanic.  These choices are presented in a much more thematic context that can have an impact on overall gameplay beyond choosing what's most convenient in the moment.  The game is short, but there's plently of content to provide replayability.  I find myself going back often in an attempt to top old scores.  There are also online challenges on a regular basis.  It should appeal to players of squad tactics games, roguelikes, and anyone who enjoys themes of exploration without taking their games too seriously.

This game is nonstop charm. It's like if FTL, XCOM, and a mid-90s PBS edutainment cartoon had a baby. The visuals are cohesive, bright, and fun. The characters and writing are all cheeky and well done. The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward to pick up, yet has a suprising amount of depth. There are a dizzying amount of branching paths that the game can take every time you replay it, while managing to mostly avoid the feeling of RNG unfairness that procedurally generated roguelikes can--especially since most variation is based on choices you made.
Can't recommend highly enough. Goofy fun on the easier difficulty levels (especially as you see each area and the zillions of unique challenges/encounters for the first time), complex and interesting later on as you use what you know to craft specific strategies tailored to following a particular path. The Emperor's Challenge adds a whole new dimension, as you can get thrown repeated curveballs that can shake up your strategy and keep the game from falling into the rut of "find winning strategy, put it together to win every time."

Long ago, there was the age of rail shooters. Your arcade would always have at least one, either a big name like Time Crisis, or one of the cash-ins. now with a PC in nearly every home, the poor rail-shooter has fallen by the wayside, a forgotten relic of an age that doesn't really cater to their 'unique' platform. Also Rambo *shudders*
One of the better rail-shooters I've touched in quite a while, Blue Estate brings a fresh and on-point experience and hangs around as long as it needs to. The controls are tight, with just that little touch of aim-assist where you need it without ripping the controls from under you. The screen is never overloaded with icons or indicators. It implements modern elements such as a cover system and destructible environments. It just does everything perfectly.
With the base game down pat, does it deliver a decent plot? Mostly. It has plenty of tongue-in-cheek humour and its bizarre moments. It also knows when to tone it down with a character change four levels in to a more sensible character. By the eighth and final level, you do feel a bit over it, and the tone reflects that, I think. I believe it could have ended better, but it was satisfying none-the-less.

I beat this game in less than two hours, and 20 minutes of that was on the first level.
It's a slow, dull beat-em-up where you walk up to a group of thugs, beat them up, regenerate your health, clear an obstacle (door, electric wire) and then rinse and repeat. There seems to be less than half a dozen finisher moves and each one takes a good 15 seconds or so to execute, so you might as well strike the enemy a couple of extra times instead to save yourself some time. Combat is as follows: X, Y, X, Y, X, Y. Oncoming attack? Hit B to dodge. X, Y, X, Y, X, Y. If you want to vary things up, you can try different permutations of X and Y, but it doesn't do much. There are combos you can do by hitting three attacks one after another, which momentarily stuns the enemy, but there's very little difference between them and dodging an attack breaks your combo anyway.
There's no variety in the combat at all. You're constantly fighting the same two kind of enemies, normal and big enemies. They do occasionally have weapons or a shield. You'll be fighting a big thug with a shield in one level, then in the next level a big police officer with a shield. Your moves remain the same throughout the whole game. How about letting me use that baseball bat I disarmed from an enemy? Isn't that beat'em up 101?
Around the second level I got tired of beating up countless groups of enemies, so I tried just walking past them... it worked. In fact, you can walk past about 80% of the enemies in this game. Occasionally there will be a gate you can't climb over until you clear out a group of nearby enemies, but any other type of object (electric box, ladder) you can interact with while in combat.
For some reason Kick♥♥♥♥♥has a Spanish accent. The voice acting is atrocious. Besides having little to no emotion, almost all of the voice actors mispronounce words (parkour = parker, goth = ghoth). Every other time you climb a ladder, for some reason Kick♥♥♥♥♥spouts "Damn. Why the hell am I doing this?". You'll be hearing the same taunts over and over throughout the game.
Besides the issues with clipping, invisible walls galore, the camera obstructing your view in combat, and the lack of mouth movement when characters speak, I actually like the graphic style of the game. If they had put a bit of effort into making the combat fun and varied, maybe put some things to do in the levels besides beating up on groups of thugs every 30 seconds, they might have had a decent game.
The game also screws up your system font every time you launch it. Many thanks to the German reviewer here for finding out what the game does:
The game disables ClearType in Windows. To re-enable it, go to the Control Panel and search for "Adjust ClearType text". Check "Turn on ClearType" and hit next a few times to make your fonts normal again.

Well, looks like DrinkBox has done it again! The Toronto-based developer delivers the laughs en masse in this Metroid-vania style beat-'em up - like a nice piledriver to the face!
Not since Ubisoft's great title Outland have we witnessed a game that aspires so mastefully to Super Metroid and SotN (down to the "Chooze" statues!). The fighting is sublime and satisfying, albeit perhaps lacking some depth. Also, don't expect epic boss battles like you would in Metroid or Castlevania - they are pretty uninspiring here. Still, you'll be too busy laughing your faces off at the wonderfully humorous dialogues, characters, and subtles jokes injected in the world of Guacamelee (okay, maybe sometimes not so subtle). The platforming is tight, and the level design is smart, challenging, yet never infuriating. A clever map-tool system removes the frustration of not remembering where that blocked path you saw at the beginning of the game was - something every Metroid-vania game should rightfully embrace.
Aside from the aforementioned humor, Guacamelee's presentation is excellent. The plot, while predictable and cliché, is light-hearted enough and never takes itself too seriously. The art design is some of the coolest I've ever seen, and the vibrant color palette matches with the ambiance of the game's Mexican vibe. And the soundtrack? Well! If you like Mexican folklore-techno, then you might as well buy this game just for the soundtrack! But seriously, the designers successfully blended the classic Mariachi sound with a modern electronica twist. It shouldn't work, yet it does... very, very well! Those upbeat tunes will stick in your head long after the game is done.
So all-in-all, this is a great game from a amazing indie developer! Can't wait to see what's next from them!

Do I recommend it? Absolutely, at a bargain price it's a great game to have and to play in coop with a friend. WIll I be playing it ever again on Steam? Absolutely not.

The goal of the game is to take care of a unicorn and raise its stats by playing a lot of repetitive race games. The games are kind of like Summer Games for the C-64 or Apple II in the 1980s, where you can do the equestrian event (horse racing), except Summer games was more fun and had a better framerate and sound/music.
There's a magic cauldron that you can use, where you mix magic ingredients into it and try to come up with items that your unicorn can wear (like better magic horseshoes to increase speed). You can get more ingredients by doing "quests" that show up in a mailbox that you need to click on at the gate area.
I haven't actually done any quests because I was so discouraged by the slow pace of the horse races that I couldn't bear the idea of another minigame.  The races go at an extremely slow pace, and last several minutes. On the bright side, I think my unicorn's stats increased substancially after the race, so the monotony of the experience did at least reward me with something.
Grooming the unicorn is the most entertaining part of the game - you can brush your unicorn's hair and clean its hooves and polish its horn. The unicorn will sparkle quite a bit after being cleaned, and grooming my unicorn did make me feel some sense of accomplishment when it was done. This was ultimately the highlight of the entire game for me.
It's also worth nothing that the framerate for this game seems stuck at around 20 fps, even though a modern machine should tear these graphics apart at a million FPS.
In conclusion, I feel Secret of the Magic Crystals is far too complex with its ingredient mixing and unintuitive UI for a kid to play, yet the mini-games themselves are far too simple and slow for an adult to play. This leaves the game with no real target playerbase, making it a game that I can't really recommend to anyone, even if it was free.

I love the first game. Unfortunately FEAR 2 has very obviously been made with consoles in mind. For starters, the PC settings are less customisable than the first game. I couldn't map actions to the side-buttons on my mouse, for instance. This game also features moveable cover that has no practical purpose; tragically, this has replaced the actually useful left/right lean from the first game. Basically, some static objects can be moved (once) by the player into a different predetermined location. You're probably not going to want to do that in the middle of a gunfight since the animation wastes several seconds. But the best reason against not flipping these desks and tables is that the cover they provide is useless. Enemies can still shoot your head off, so it's usually much better to hide behind a wall, or hide behind the unmoved object because they typically provide just as good a cover in that state as they do in their moved state.
Another console gripe I have is the new checkpoint system. You cannot manually save in FEAR 2. Some of the checkpoints are poorly placed —requiring a silly amount of walking to return the spot you died at. But they're generally okay albeit less convenient than manual saves.
FEAR 2 also has that AAA game rubbish action movie feel to it. The game even boasts a toggable film grain option in the settings menu because... why? There are gratutitous setpieces involving falling objects and explosions which don't add anything; they're just cheap ways to make the game feel more epic. One of the worst levels has the camera shake constantly while you sprint across a high platform as the facility you're in collapses and explosions undermine its structure... except that there's no real danger because the world doesn't react until you cross invisible lines which trigger a pretty spectacle to keep your dopamine levels high.
This game's abundance of invisible lines also dictates when enemies appear. It feels like no enemies were naturally placed in this game. They just wait for you to pass an invisible line before they're conjured into thin-air. This means that if you have to reload a checkpoint you'll notice the same enemies coming at you from the same angles and becoming visible at the exact same locations.
Then there are the two instances where you go inside a robot. You can control them, blast people with your infinite-ammo machine gun, and blow them into a million pieces with your multi-rocket launcher! And there's no chance of you losing these sections either because nobody can really harm you. And if your robot does become damaged then you just have to hold still for a little while so that it can recharge its batteries. These sections, sadly, aren't exciting. They're just low-effort ways of keeping up the game's novelty.

I love this game's art style.
It's an on-rails light gun game, so the controls (with keyboard and mouse) are a bit weird at first, but you get used to them.

This is an on rails shooter. These types of games were super popular in the 90/early 2000's in arcades playing with a friend with light guns. The change to solo mouse and keyboard on pc makes it lose a lot of lustor. The mouse can be over sensitive but with some fiddling it works well enough. The biggest problem is repetition. Every single level you fight the exact same enemies, maybe with a fresh coat of paint. Theres basically regular guys and then armored guys. Theres 3 boss fights. Thats the game. The levels are decent length but rather uninteresting. Theres a graveyard, a chinese den, and then a bunch of corridors, hallways, and complexes. The environments aren't interesting and you can't explore them anyways. Theres no stealth or anything to really change it up. The other problem is theres 3 weapons all game. You get reskinned versions of machine guns, pistols, and shotgun. Even though its a different machine gun you may pick up it plays the exact same. The levels start to drag on, and feel repetitive as you just do the same thing against the same guys with the same guns in the same corridors.
More variety, weapons, environments, and mechanics could have kept it much more fresh. The story also doesn't make any sense and seems to be on speed drugs, as the conversation is super fast and nonsensical. The game isn't terrible and is close to a recommendation, but not quite up to par.
