After buying this game on a whim a number of years ago, I finally got round to finishing it. A large portion of what took me this long was I got stuck on the penultimate level and was too stubborn to look up a guide for it. Luckily I have shed such stubbornness (to a degree) and checked out a few bits online.
This is the sort of game I love; as evidenced by my surprising playtime on it. Given that the skilled or the chaotic could easily speedrun this whole thing in a couple of hours, it's testament to the game's credit that you can just as well explore, play about and cause general havoc for scores of hours and be just as happy.
It is, first and foremost, a stealth game where you get additional rewards for completing objectives in complete secrecy. Note that I say 'additional' rewards, because there is no real penalty for blasting your way out of a bad situation or picking off the odd innocent along the way. As long as you complete the objective, you're golden. And that's how this sort of thing SHOULD be. Yeah, there are some consequences on higher difficulties, but if you go for the expert modes you're probably the type to get it done with no collateral.
The sheer variety and genius of the levels is staggering; from a vineyard to a casino to a steamboat, no two levels are similar, each requiring their own unique approaches. By use of disguises (most obtained off the corpses or unconscious bodies of their former owners), you slip into an environment undetected and proceed to get the job done. Whether you set up little accidents or prefer to look them in the eye as you headshot them, there is scope for it all.
Where it gets tricky is some areas require very specific tasks performed before you can proceed; the penultimate level is one such situation. I was unable to work out the specific task and eventually gave up trying. Admittedly almost every single secret in the game can be learned by strategic waiting and watching, but sometimes I just don't have the patience for that; especially as on higher difficulties, death means start from scratch.
While I'm complaining, something that repeatedly bugged me on my latest playthrough was how twitchy the NPCs are. When in disguise, you can logically do anything the similarly-dressed NPCs can... This is not the case. I've been turned away by my fellow bouncers, shot at for being a secret serviceman with a gun and executed then fled from because I took one step too far in a public space. I've heard some things about bugs, but I don't know how many of these were bugs and how many were just the mechanics.
Equally the NPCs can be brainless when it comes to hard evidence. I once walked out of a lift, leaving behind a naked dead body (after donning his clothes as a disguise), and the police outside the door ignored me to check on the dead man. If I'd been in my suit, they'd have shot me on sight. I'm not complaining too much about that sort of thing because, in truth, I'll take any break I can get from the bloodhound AI.
My final niggle is with the control scheme. It seems to have been designed for a controller because you have movement controls and then three basic buttons for almost all interaction. This gets infuriating when you're trying to drag a body away from a closed door and one command flits between DRAG and OPEN DOOR. That was certainly awkward for the guard on the other side... A less minimalist control system would have been nice, allowing for more precise actions.
Blood Money is frequently called the best Hitman game in the series and, after finally completing it, I see why. It's fun, gripping, decently well-told and carries many hours of messing about. I remember once I went through each level killing literally everyone; I failed at this in one level because I ran out of bullets for all the civilians. Tragic.
I highly recommend this stealth game with shooter elements as it's one of the best in the genre. Plus the 1st/3rd person toggle is brilliant for precision shooting. Give it a go.

As an example, I played a random 21 questions game, and in order to finish the game with a score above ZERO, the winning player would have to be intimately familiar with:
Our Man Flint
Reality Bites
Song of the South
She Wore a Yellow Ribbon
Myra Breckenridge
all of the seven dwarf's names
most titles of Jerry Lewis' filmography

You'll hear the comparison to Minecraft with this game of course, but that is nothing new. However where Minecraft felt like you being the ruler of a lonely little kingdom, Colony Survival feels more like being a king/queen with some actual subjects. Granted they don't have much personality. but they do make things run more on their own when it comes to things like resource gathering and crafting. That in itself can be a bit of an issue simply because removing the need for you to gather resources can make it less challenging. Of course you have to balance that with protecting your colonists from the undead hordes, so that is somewhat offset.
The big downside with this game that you hear from people is that it reaches the "endgame" period pretty quickly. It can be pretty tense in the beginning when you are stretched for resources and your colonists keep dying, but it doesn't take long before you can start to reach the point that you can leave things to run by themselves. Which is great, but it leaves you with not much to do once you've crafted everything. This is something that I encountered in Minecraft as well, and the solution is the same here. Find yourself a project. That's it. For me I decided that the modest villa that I was using as my main base would make a great town hall and set about making a city wall and filling it in with actual houses for my colonists to live in. I do hope that more gets added before too long, but as long as you have a good imagination this is a great game to play.
For my closing words I would just recommend two things:
1.) Go into this game with a plan/endgame strategy in mind. If you know what your long term plans are it makes it much more fun.
2.) Do yourself a favor and play with "double monster numbers" on. You could put the option that makes zombies spawn during the day as well, but you will draw out the tension much longer with the greater monster spawns.

It's not my cup of tea, but I'm giving the thumbs-down for objective reasons.
It's an on-rails 1st person shooter, where the player is not in control of their avatar, which is ok since a story is being told and dialog is spoken in certain locations / orchestrated situations, the events are planned out. What you have to do: Shoot. Point the mouse at people (and sometimes things) and click. Right click to reload and/or to cover if you're in a respective spot.
For what it is (Which I personally do not like.), it's very well done. Mostly. And here is why it does deserve a thumbs-down:
The one thing that a game like this
fail is the mouse cursor movement, but that's precisely what they did fail.
The cursor uses some weird acceleration instead of the one you know from your operating system or, probably even better, no acceleration at all like you know it from
first person shooters. Granted, you move the cursor, not your view like in FPS, but still I feel that no acceleration would have been better than this crappy acceleration. Getting the mouse to target was cringe-y work every time. That was the main challenge (in the first level), to get the pointer where I wanted it.
(Someone pointed out that they don't experience mouse acceleration in this game. Well, I do, and it's not the system's mouse acceleration, because that has completely different character, so it must be the game's own implementation of mouse acceleration. Because of this, and because I have a lot of experience with other games on my current system - and no such problems - I stand by my opinion. I just don't have good reason not to.)
The options allow to change the mouse speed, and you can also switch to "raw mouse", but I believe the developers misunderstood what this means. The correct meaning is that the mouse input is read on a low system level before any alterations have been made to it. Raw mouse is useful if you want your hand's position on the table to correspond directly with a position on screen (or with the direction you look), no matter how fast or slow you move the mouse. But in this game's raw mode, there still seems to be acceleration. What very obviously changes when you switch to "raw mode" is that the built-in mouse speed slider stops working and the mouse becomes quite slow. Mind that a speed slider is not at odds with the concept of raw mouse input: While you don't want acceleration, you still want to be able to adjust the scale of the required motion; this would still be direct position-position translation. Well, you can't adjust it in this game when you switch raw mode on, and that might even be all the switch does.
So, you constantly fight against the crappy input. Really, all you have in this game is mouse motion and left/right click, and they
the mouse motion. Unbelievable. Just think about what this means. What kind of people are at work here. What they thought when they decided "Yep, sell this now". They must be mentally damaged in some way. It's like when your product is a football, except it's not really spherical.
I played through one full level, which took like 10-20 minutes. I would have aborted earlier, but I wanted to make sure that I have some persistent progress, and I wasn't sure if I'd have to play the whole level again if I'd abort in the middle. With this in mind, it was somewhat annoying to fight through the same places several times, but someone who likes this kind of gameplay might even like that.

Blue Estate is a fun rail shooter that is probably the closest we’ll ever get to a House of the Dead: Overkill 2.  While not as funny as Overkill (I freaking love Overkill’s ending), Blue Estate still shares an over-the-top, gritty, and tongue in cheek tone. You play as Tony Luciano, the son of a LA crime lord that the game disclaims from the beginning as an awful human being, and Clarence, a soldier turned hired gun dragged into cleaning up Tony’s mess so he can get the money to save his mom’s house. The voice-acting is actually quite solid, I especially liked Clarence, who just exudes fatigue over all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t he has to put up with. The game is also mostly funny, though it may not always hit, and contrary to official reviews isn’t really hateful or edgy at all, Tony slings like one slur but he’s explicitly a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥and a boss even calls him out on it.
Gameplaywise Blue Estate really modernizes the rail gun shooter genre and adds some really neat mechanics. One major mechanic  is that enemies that are about to shoot you have a yellow circle around them that eventually turns jagged right as they’re about to shoot. This gives you a very clear indication on who’s going to hit you and gives you enough time to react so if you do get shot, it’s probably going to be on you. You also use the mouse to “swipe” which usually act as QTEs but are also how you pick up health and ammo, which gets rid of the frustration of old rail gun shooters where you can miss a pickup because you have to shoot it. The swiping mostly works well, but I ran into a few hiccups on the final boss. Blue Estate also looks and runs fine, I ran into zero bugs.
Blue Estate is a little bit on the short side, but there is arcade mode, co-op, and two harder modes that apparently don’t ♥♥♥♥ around, so that extends the game a bit and its only thirteen bucks which is totally worth it. Overall Blue Estate is a modern rail gun shooter done right.

Critics seem to hate this game, quoting "lack of morals, offensive dialogue and so on.". If this doesn't bother you and want some mindless fun, you should get this game.
Here's what I got from this game:
- Mindless fun at its best. It combines the thrill of mouse aiming/shooting in an FPS without other mechanics that may need more engagement.
- Game in normal mode is over in 3-4 hours. After finishing it, I still have two modes: Arcade mode (plays differently than the story with a different mechanic) and two other difficulty modes "Abnormal" and "Crazy Train". Abnormal ups the difficulty considerably.

Blue Estate (based on the comic series) is an on-rails shooter of the variety of a cop/crime satire. You play as either Tony or Clarence who have distinctly different weapons and personalities. Narrated by Roy Devine, a private eye detective, commonly elaborating in places he would have no true knowledge of is often interrupted by quips from the FBI stating how inaccurate his findings were in an often (attempted) humorous fashion.
I'm told that the PC version does indeed support “lightgun” peripherals as the console counterparts of this game were designed for move controllers. I did not test things these personally but I've heard no issues with any major brand. I used the mouse controls for this. You can play entirely with the mouse but there are some gestures to be had with the arrow keys and well as perform the swipe actions required in some sections. Either opening a door or attacking a melee character about to affront your senses.
As an on-rail shooter you can expect an arcade mode and score attack stuff. That's all present. It's pretty strait forward. There are pick-ups that require swipe actions from health/ammo to slow-mo and secret collectible things to shoot each episode/level. There is a yellow “next damage indicator” that can be extremely helpful in mitigating restarts as there are limited amounts each level and this can prevent guessing as to which enemy has it in for you next.
Tony has this mechanic in which his hair falls into his face rather often and Clarence has this thing about a Chihuahua humping his leg that tends to get in the way more than is an interesting task or challenge to be had. I feel like they rely too much on the same jokes and definitely try too hard to be funny. For something based in satire I think I chuckled once, maybe twice. For instance, when the Kim Jong-un representative was in play he attempts to shoot a rocket at you and fails. His dialogue is simply “Why do you shame me weapon?” Which was one of the few moments I felt some respite.

Musketmen who stand  ground will not fire as the enemy is too close and will not melee either wiping out the formation usually. especially with musketmen, the officer seems to run in when your shooting meaning he dies and there is no way of adding a new officer without reforming the squad, meaning they lose any amount of kills that squad has accumulated.Formation seems to have little or no effect on the units ability to function, in cossacks 2 there were roads and column would mean faster travel and less fatigue, while line formation would make the unit ready for battle and square formation would help when attacked by cavalry. Units do not seem to gain xp like they did in cossacks 2 and do not flee and break formation when they are being destroyed which almost renders tactial advantage useless. Its not all bad i do like that graphically it is very well done and that the resource and training is as it was. As a package i feel like this game is not finished but in summary it has the potential to be a fantastic game that provides hours of playtime.

This game should be labeled EARLY ALPHA at best. It is obviously needing a lot of patches to even be considered playable. Basic gameplay is fine, it looks pretty good, but there are so many things that are buggy and so many crashes that it could hardly be considered a 'stable release'.

My recommendation comes with a major caveat. I personally had to request a refund because the game is frankly unplayable in its current state. I am not referring to the multiplayer not yet being functional. I am not referring to the bad grammar in some bits of dialogue, I am referring to an obnoxious crash that keeps occurring. I never get more than 15 minutes of playtime in before the game inevitably freezes up, a "ding" sounds out and an error message pops up with some nonsense I don't understand. In the one hour I played, I encountered this crash 4 times.
I hate to say it, because I absolutely adored Cossacks: European Wars as a kid, and I hyped this game up to no end. But it is tragically the first game I have ever had to refund on Steam.
I don't even know if it is the company's fault but frankly it is happening, and with the unreliability of PC gaming due to gamers having tons of different hardware combinations, I can't say whether or not the issue will ever be fixed, or indeed if any others are even having this issue. Therefore, I felt that it was probably safer that I got my money back rather than wait for a game to be fixed that may never be fixed.
With my own technical difficulties out the way... Cossacks is one of the best strategy games out there in my opinion, and Cossacks 3 plays effectively the same- which is both to its credit, but perhaps its biggest flaw. The upgrade to fully 3D graphics is more than welcome, and somehow the series' aesthetic and atmosphere carries its charm across to the third dimension. However is a shame that camera rotation was not introduced, and it is also very disappointing that somehow in spite of the game being a reimagining and new direction for the series, it looks, feels and plays almost identically to prior Cossacks games. But I cannot emphasise enough, if you have not played prior games, then this is not going to be an issue in the slightest. In fact, if you have played Cossacks but not recently, it is still not a problem.
I am still excited for a modern Cossacks, and I'm more than ready to join the fray online. But I guess the game is not ready for me yet. I will keep an eye on message boards to see if others have encountered the issue, and hopefully I will hear the news that the problem has been fixed. And then I can say with certainty that I will be buying the game again.
In spite of my technical difficulties, I would recommend all strategy fans to pick this up, because I have not seen many other people with the issue I encountered, and in the worst case scenario you could always get a refund too. And for the price this game is going at, it's probably worth the risk anyway.

First of all: This game will definitely make sense only to fans of the Angry Video Game Nerd alias James Rolfe (duh...).
All in all it is a sweet, hard platformer that spoofs not only a lot of old, bad games of the Atari and NES era but also the Angry Video Game Nerd "culture" (like him collecting beer bottles for health and his constant cursing).
It is challenging and funny (already if you play in easy mode), colourful and full of detail.
The graphics are fine, the music is okay but also a little bit forgettable (with the exception of the AVGN theme song in 8-bit). The sound effects fit but can be annoying sometimes (but I guess that was even on purpose, like: Annoying sh*tty game reference = annoying sound effect).
A handful of different levels, a lots of secrets to find and a couple of Steam achievements additionally keep the player going.
As I said: A good game and tribute to this angry internet reviewer but mostly recommended to players who at least know who that is and what he does. To others...I don't know, it could appear extremely random and needlessly hard ;)

I really wanted to like this game, old school graphics, difficult platformer...these are my favourite tags.
However, the awful:
-level design
-controls
-hit boxes
-cheap attempts at difficulty (and also lack of difficulty, as the first boss took me two attemps)
-glitch screens that freeze your game when switching between any two menus screens
would all have a chance at being forgiven, if it wasn't for the respawns.
For a game that boasts about being difficult and killing you a lot, 19 second respawns are unforgivable.  And I'm not even going to mention the rng messages in the respawn screen, though I do give them credit for slowly becoming true as the game slowly drags away at the minutes of fresh air around you.
In short, if you get this game as a gift, you're still not getting your moneys worth, the only remotely okay thing about this game is the soundtrack.
